working_summary: An unsatisfiable formula has no assignment that makes every clause true. The question asks whether one fixed efficient verifier can always check a polynomial-length certificate of that impossibility. The certificate format is unrestricted as long as it is sound for every formula. This is equivalent to asking whether NP equals coNP. The project concerns the possibility of universally concise explanations for the failure of all candidate solutions, rather than lower bounds for any one particular set of proof rules.

title: Superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds
importance_reason: A fundamental lower-bound milestone for unrestricted computation, with connections to matrix complexity, proof techniques and the limitations of nonuniform algorithms.
formal: Does there exist a total function \(F:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)*, computable by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and satisfying |\(F(x)|=|x|\), such that its unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not \(O(n)\)? Explicitly, for every \(C>0\) and \(N\ge 1\), must some \(n\ge N\) satisfy \(CC(F_{n})>Cn\)?
definitions: \(F_{n}\) is the restriction of F to n-bit inputs, with n output bits. \(CC(F_{n})\) is the least number of gates in a directed acyclic Boolean circuit computing all these outputs exactly on every input. Each gate may compute any Boolean function of at most two input bits: the full \(B_{2}\) basis, including AND, OR, XOR and negation. Input nodes, constants 0 and 1, and designated output wires are free; gates have unrestricted fan-out and there is no depth bound. Gates may be shared among outputs. The family of competing circuits is nonuniform: the circuit at one input length need have no effective relationship to circuits at other lengths. In contrast, explicitness of F means a single deterministic Turing machine outputs \(F(x)\) in at most p(|x|) steps for one fixed polynomial p, with no advice. The empty input has empty output. This card fixes a polynomial-time interpretation of the source’s broader word “explicit” and preserves its allowance of n output bits. Changing between \(B_{2}\) and the usual bounded-fan-in \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis changes size by at most a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Exhibit one such polynomial-time function and prove that \(CC(F_{n})/n\) is unbounded along arbitrarily large input lengths, or prove that every polynomial-time length-preserving function has \(O(n)\)-size nonuniform circuits, with the hidden constant allowed to depend on the function. A fixed bound such as 10n is insufficient. The precise target is not \(O(n)\); it does not additionally require the ratio to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. A superlinear single-output example would also settle the question after padding the output with zeros.
context:
A circuit is a finite computation with a separate design for each input length. Intermediate results can be used many times, and different output bits can share the same work. This sharing is a central source of power: a lower bound for formulas, which cannot freely reuse intermediate results, need not hold for circuits. The target here leaves depth, fan-out and Boolean operations unrestricted apart from the two-input gate bound.

The explicitness requirement prevents a counting argument from solving the problem. There are vastly more Boolean functions than small circuits, so most functions require exponentially many gates. But describing one by its entire truth table takes exponential space, and selecting the first hard truth table by exhaustive search need not yield a polynomial-time function. We need an efficiently specified computation and a proof that every circuit for it exceeds every fixed linear bound.

Multi-output functions make the question especially concrete. A fixed, efficiently constructible binary matrix \(A_{n}\) defines \(F_{n}(x)=A_{n}x\) over the two-element field. Its n outputs are parity sums of selected inputs. Computing every output separately can cost \(\Theta (n^{2})\), yet a clever circuit may share partial sums across rows. Counting proves that some matrices need \(\Omega (n^{2}/\log  n)\) gates, but an explicit superlinear lower bound remains unknown even for this linear-algebra setting. A lower bound against XOR-only circuits would not automatically rule out smaller circuits that use nonlinear Boolean gates.

The polynomial-time convention also separates this question from NP versus P/poly. The desired F already has polynomial-size circuits because its algorithm can be simulated by circuits. Showing that it lacks linear-size circuits would separate two size scales within efficient nonuniform computation; it would not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Conversely, proving superpolynomial circuit lower bounds for an NP language would address a stronger resource barrier but would not by itself make that language a polynomial-time example for this card.

For one output bit, Li and Yang obtain a \(3.1n- o(n)\) lower bound over the full two-input basis. Their functions are affine dispersers, meaning that they remain nonconstant on every sufficiently large affine subspace of the Boolean cube, and suitable examples are polynomial-time computable. The proof refines gate elimination: restrict inputs so that gates disappear while retaining enough difficulty in the restricted function. Raising the constant was a substantial advance, but any fixed constant still falls short of the present target.

Cavalar and Oliveira’s 2025 work develops another route through the fusion method and combinatorial covering problems. It translates circuit lower-bound questions into suitably defined two-dimensional covers and proves strong bounds for random graphs. The remaining challenge is obtaining the necessary explicit cover lower bounds. A reformulation that can express the desired hardness is valuable, but does not yet provide the hard polynomial-time function.

Two 2026 developments clarify proof techniques. Carmosino, Dang and Jackman formalize convergent gate simplification in selected bases and construct efficient refuters for a classical parity lower bound. Their constructive proof notion concerns finding errors in proposed small circuits; it is additional structure on a lower-bound proof, rather than a superlinear size bound.

Raz’s July 2026 revision studies natural proofs specifically for linear maps represented by matrices. Under the stated cryptographic assumptions, pseudorandom matrices with unusually small circuits obstruct large, efficiently recognizable classes of hard matrices. Different constructions yield barriers above near-linear or linear size. These are conditional restrictions on a defined proof strategy, not an impossibility theorem for proving the desired lower bound by other means.
why: This asks for the first unbounded improvement over linear size for an efficiently computable unrestricted circuit task. It isolates a basic gap between knowing that hard functions abound and proving hardness for one explicitly computable function.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No superlinear unrestricted Boolean circuit lower bound for a polynomial-time length-preserving function was located. The question fixes the source’s explicitness convention; recent gate-simplification, covering and conditional natural-proofs results do not furnish such an example.
progress: 2018: Wigderson’s Open Problem 5.8 asks for an explicit n-input, n-output function with circuit complexity not \(O(n)\). | 2021–2022: Li–Yang improve the general \(B_{2}\) single-output lower bound to \(3.1n- o(n)\). | 2025-03-21: Cavalar–Oliveira publish a fusion and graph-cover framework for Boolean circuit lower bounds. | 2026-02-20: Carmosino–Dang–Jackman give constructive gate-elimination proofs for a classical linear lower bound in selected bases. | 2026-07-23: Raz’s revision adds a conditional natural-proofs barrier for superlinear lower bounds on explicit linear maps.
working_summary: A multi-output Boolean function can share intermediate computations among all its output bits. The question asks for one polynomial-time computable family whose unrestricted Boolean circuits exceed every fixed linear size bound. The saved formulation uses as many output bits as input bits. An arbitrary hard truth table does not satisfy the explicitness requirement. The project seeks a modest but fundamental lower bound demonstrating that some efficiently specified transformations intrinsically need more than a constant amount of circuit work per input bit.

title: Exponential circuit lower bounds for 3-SAT
importance_reason: A sweeping quantitative lower-bound target for the canonical efficiently verifiable problem, directly connected to nonuniform complexity and the foundations of exponential-time algorithms.
formal: For the explicitly encoded n-variable 3-SAT function \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}\) defined below, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that \(CC(\mathrm{SAT}_{n})\ge 2^{cn}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\)?
definitions: For each \(n\ge 1\), enumerate all clauses on variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) containing zero, one, two or three distinct variables, each with either sign. A zero-literal clause is false. There are \(M(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{3}2\)ʲ·\(\operatorname{binom}(n,j)\) such clauses, with \(\operatorname{binom}(n,j)=0\) when \(j>n\). Order them first by length, then by the increasing tuple of variable indices, then by their sign bits, with 0 meaning positive and 1 negated. The input is \(b\in \{0,1\}^{M(n)}\); its jth bit says whether clause j is included. Let \(\Phi _{b}\) be the conjunction of included clauses, with an empty conjunction true, and define \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}(b)=1\) iff some assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfies \(\Phi _{b}\). Thus every input is valid. CC counts gates in a directed acyclic circuit with one output, arbitrary Boolean gates of at most two inputs, constants 0 and 1, unrestricted depth and fan-out, and exact correctness on every b. Inputs, constants and output wires are not gates. Circuits may be chosen nonuniformly for each n. The exponential parameter is the number n of variables, while the circuit has \(M(n)=\Theta (n^{3})\) input bits. This fixed encoding and the restriction to 3-CNF are an editorial variable-parameter formulation of the source’s exponential SAT circuit question.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed eventual exponential lower bound for unrestricted circuits, or prove its negation: for every \(c>0\) and \(N\ge 1\) there exists \(n\ge N\) with \(CC(\mathrm{SAT}_{n})<2^{cn}\). A circuit family of size \(2^{o(n)}\) at all lengths would suffice for the negative direction, but that is stronger than the exact negation. A lower bound only against bounded-depth, monotone, formula, uniform or proof-system models does not settle the question. A circuit upper bound \(2^{\alpha n}\) for one fixed \(\alpha >0\) remains compatible with a smaller positive lower-bound exponent.
context:
SAT asks whether a collection of local constraints admits a simultaneous Boolean assignment. Here each selected clause prohibits one pattern on at most three variables. An assignment can be checked efficiently, but the conjecture says that deciding whether any assignment works requires exponentially many gates even when a different circuit may be designed separately for every n. It is a quantitative strengthening of the question whether NP has polynomial-size circuits.

Fixing the representation is essential. An n-variable 3-CNF can have \(\Theta (n^{3})\) distinct clauses; writing a list of literals instead introduces binary variable names and a different bit length. These encodings are polynomially interconvertible, but a claim exponential in the literal number of input bits is not invariant under polynomial changes of encoding. This card therefore fixes both the representation and the variable parameter. The target is \(2^{\Omega (n)}\), which is \(2^{\Omega (M^{1/3})}\) in the number M of circuit inputs.

There is a simple matching exponential scale for an upper bound. For each of the \(2^{n}\) assignments, form an AND requiring \(b_{j}=0\) for every clause that assignment would falsify. OR these tests over all assignments. The resulting circuit decides \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}\) and has \(O(M(n)2^{n})\) gates. This is an explicit construction showing what exhaustive search means in the chosen nonuniform model. The conjecture allows substantial improvements in the exponential constant, while ruling out the absence of every positive eventual exponential lower bound.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis concerns uniform algorithms and the number of variables. Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane’s sparsification lemma relates general fixed-width CNFs to disjunctions of sparse CNFs, with at most \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) branches for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). This explains why variable and clause parameters are closely connected in exponential-time reductions. It does not automatically turn a uniform hypothesis into a lower bound against arbitrary circuits, and the precise almost-everywhere quantifiers on this card are part of its target.

Even much weaker general-circuit lower bounds remain elusive. Li and Yang prove \(3.1N- o(N)\) gates for particular explicit single-output functions of N input bits. That is a theorem about carefully chosen affine dispersers, not an exponential lower bound for SAT. A counting argument can prove that most truth tables are exponentially hard, but it cannot identify SAT among those hard functions.

There has been important progress by linking faster satisfiability algorithms to lower bounds for other circuit classes. Williams proves that nondeterministic exponential time has languages without polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC restricts depth while allowing unbounded-fan-in Boolean and modular gates. The distinction matters in two places: the hard language need not be in NP, and the competing circuits are not unrestricted. This theorem demonstrates a powerful strategy without resolving this card.

Algorithmic progress continues within the exponential regime. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint refines the analysis of the existing PPSZ algorithm, reporting a randomized general-3-SAT running-time base of 1.307031578 and a slightly smaller base under uniqueness. The authors retain the same algorithm and unique-to-general lifting theorem; their improvement comes from a sharper combination of inequalities with rational certificates. These are upper bounds, with randomness and success guarantees, rather than lower bounds for exact circuits. A constant base above one remains compatible with the target.

A positive answer would rule out polynomial-size circuits for this NP decision problem and therefore imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). A negative answer would not imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\): circuits of size \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\), for example, would refute an eventual exponential bound while still being superpolynomial in the input size, and a nonuniform circuit family need not be constructible by one efficient algorithm.
why: A precise worst-case formulation of the belief that satisfiability retains exponential complexity even with arbitrary nonuniform preprocessing by input size. It separates exponential hardness from polynomial hardness and from bounds tied to a restricted computational model.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unconditional exponential lower bound for unrestricted circuits deciding variable-parameterized 3-SAT was located. The card specifies an almost-everywhere bound, an explicit total clause-incidence encoding, and n as the variable count; it does not assert exponential hardness in the \(\Theta (n^{3})\) encoding length.
progress: 1998–2001: Impagliazzo–Paturi–Zane develop sparsification and reductions preserving subexponential complexity in variable parameters. | 2011–2014: Williams establishes NEXP lower bounds for constant-depth ACC circuits using satisfiability algorithms. | 2018: Wigderson states the exponential SAT circuit conjecture; this card makes its parameter and encoding explicit. | 2021–2022: Li–Yang prove a \(3.1N- o(N)\) general-circuit bound for explicit functions; it is neither exponential nor a SAT bound. | 2026-07-12: Jiang–Cai report a small improvement in the randomized PPSZ upper exponent for general 3-SAT.
working_summary: The saved 3-SAT family uses a fixed encoding of which clauses on n variables are present. The conjecture asks for circuit size exponential in n, even when every input length gets its own arbitrary circuit. Its scale is stronger than merely excluding polynomial-size circuits. The variable count differs from the total number of encoded clause bits, so the parameter must remain explicit. The project aims to prove that searching for a satisfying assignment retains essentially exponential difficulty even under nonuniform computation.

title: PH versus PSPACE
importance_reason: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? Equivalently, is there a fixed integer \(k\ge 0\) such that the truth problem for fully quantified Boolean formulas belongs to \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\)?
definitions: Languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*. PSPACE contains the languages decided by deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input of length n while using at most \(C(n+1)^{a}\) work-tape cells, for constants C,a depending on the machine. The read-only input tape is not charged, and there is no polynomial time limit. Set \(\Sigma ^{p}_{0}=\mathrm{P}\), the deterministic polynomial-time languages. For \(k\ge 1, a\) language L lies in \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R and a polynomial p such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) exactly when \(\exists y_{1}\forall y_{2}\exists y_{3}\cdots Q_{k} y_{k} R(x,y_{1},\ldots ,y_{k})=1\), where each \(y_{i}\) ranges over \(\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) and \(Q_{k}\) is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Set \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup _{k\ge 0}\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\). The integer k is fixed for an entire language; it cannot grow with an input. Machines and predicates are uniform and have no advice or oracle. A fully quantified Boolean formula is an explicit Boolean formula using AND, OR and NOT, preceded by quantifiers binding every variable exactly once; variable names and the entire formula are binary encoded. Its truth uses the ordinary successive quantifier semantics over \(\{0,1\}\). The language TQBF consists of its true well-formed encodings; malformed strings are rejected. The number of quantifier blocks in TQBF inputs is unrestricted.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq \mathrm{PH}\); the reverse inclusion is already known. Equivalently it places TQBF in one fixed \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\), which would put every PSPACE language in that same level by polynomial-time reductions. A negative resolution proves that some PSPACE language, equivalently TQBF, is outside every fixed level. A separation at one fixed level or an oracle-relative result alone does not answer the question.
context:
Polynomial space lets a computation reuse a bounded amount of memory for a potentially very long time. The polynomial hierarchy instead organizes efficiently checked conditions by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal choices. For example, an existential block asks for a witness, a following universal block checks every challenge to it, and another existential block can give a response depending on that challenge. The question asks whether any polynomial-space computation can be expressed with a fixed number of such blocks.

The formula \(\forall x\exists y (x=y)\) is true: after the value of x is fixed, y can take the same value. The formula \(\exists y\forall x (x=y)\) is false because one bit cannot equal both possible values of x. Thus replacing a sequence of dependent choices by one initial guess changes the problem. A formula with arbitrarily many alternating choices describes a potentially long strategy, even though testing its final Boolean condition is straightforward.

A quantified formula can be evaluated by recursively trying the two values of each variable and combining the answers according to its quantifier. The procedure reuses memory after finishing each branch; it need not store the exponentially large game tree. TQBF is PSPACE-complete. The standard alternation theorem also identifies polynomial-time alternating computation, with no fixed bound on its number of alternations, with PSPACE. Neither characterization shows that an arbitrary number of rounds compresses to a constant.

The definition of PH initially lets different languages use different fixed numbers of blocks. Nevertheless, equality with PSPACE would imply one common finite level containing all of PSPACE: TQBF would belong to some \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\) and every PSPACE language reduces to it. Therefore \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) would collapse the hierarchy. Conversely, proving that the hierarchy has infinitely many distinct levels would separate it from PSPACE. A separation \(\mathrm{PH}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) alone does not establish that every hierarchy level is distinct; this is why the card differs from the non-collapse question.

Grüne, Johannes, Orlin and Wulf’s February 2026 results make many multilevel optimization problems complete for individual hierarchy levels or for PSPACE. Completeness locates the problems within the classes; it does not prove the classes different. Egidy’s 2026 oracle construction illustrates another distinction: relative to that oracle, PH collapses while remaining strictly below PSPACE. This is a statement in a model with an additional oracle, rather than a resolution for ordinary machines. Historical preprints claim equality or non-collapse, but the sources checked here do not establish either as a settled theorem. The review did not independently audit those claimed proofs.
why: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.
status_note: No established resolution found in the primary-source search through 11 September 2026. The checked 2026 results concern completeness and relativized class relationships. Historical preprint claims of equality or non-collapse are not counted as settled theorems; their proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2007: The cited textbook draft states TQBF completeness, \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\) and the collapse consequence of equality. | 2026-02: New multilevel optimization completeness theorems preserve the bounded-level versus PSPACE classification without separating the classes. | 2026-02: A sparse-oracle construction separates PH from PSPACE while allowing PH to collapse; the result is explicitly relativized.
working_summary: Does every polynomial-space decision problem lie in the polynomial hierarchy? PH allows a fixed number of alternating quantifier blocks for each language. PSPACE also describes polynomial-time alternation with no fixed bound on the number of alternations. Equality would put TQBF in one finite level and hence collapse PH to that level. Completeness and oracle results illuminate the distinction without settling the ordinary class equality.

title: NEXP versus nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\)
importance_reason: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.
formal: Is there a language \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NEXP}\) such that, for every fixed circuit depth \(d\ge 1\), every fixed exponent \(k\ge 1\), every constant \(C\ge 1\) and every \(N\ge 1\), some \(n\ge N\) has no depth-at-most-d Boolean circuit of size at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) with AND, OR, NOT and majority gates that computes L correctly on every n-bit input? Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subset \mathrm{TC}^{0}\) for nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\)?
definitions: \(\mathrm{NEXP}=\bigcup _{a\ge 1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{n^{a}}): a\) language is accepted by one nondeterministic Turing machine whose every computation branch halts within exponential time \(2^{n^{a}}\), up to a constant factor, for some fixed a. An input is in the language exactly when at least one branch accepts. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, constants 0 and 1 and one output. AND and OR may have any positive fan-in; NOT has one input. A majority gate on m inputs outputs 1 when at least \(\lceil m/2\rceil\) of them are 1, including a tie when m is even. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size is the number of operation gates plus wires. Repeated connections count individually, so their multiplicities cannot encode uncharged weights. Depth is the maximum number of operation gates on an input-to-output path. All circuits compute exactly on every input; no average-case correctness or randomness is allowed. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of languages having one fixed depth bound and one polynomial size bound across all input lengths. The family may be nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct its nth circuit. NEXP machines are uniform and have no oracle or advice. The formal quantifiers permit the lower bound to be witnessed at infinitely many input lengths, rather than requiring failure at every sufficiently large length.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves that one language in NEXP has no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family, with depth and polynomial exponent both unrestricted constants. A negative resolution proves \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq \mathrm{TC}^{0}\). A bound ruling out only \(n^{k}\) gates for one fixed k, or only one fixed circuit depth, does not by itself establish the displayed separation.
context:
A constant-depth circuit applies only a bounded number of layers, but a majority gate can inspect many inputs at once. For three bits it returns 1 on 110 and 111, while returning 0 on 100. Thus majority is not a bounded-fan-in local operation. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) permits many such gates in parallel and lets their outputs feed later layers. The depth bound stays fixed as input length grows, while the number of gates and wires may be any fixed polynomial.

Parity is difficult for constant-depth circuits using only AND, OR and NOT, but it is easy for majority circuits. A threshold test for whether an n-bit input has at least t ones is implementable with a majority gate and suitable constants. Two adjacent threshold tests identify an exact number of ones, and taking an OR over odd counts gives parity with a polynomial number of gates in constant depth. This example shows why a lower bound for the weaker gate set cannot simply be reused after majority is added.

The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\), exponential time with an NP oracle. Their \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\).
why: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.
status_note: No \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subset \mathrm{TC}^{0}\) resolution found through 11 September 2026. The checked March, July and September results retain different hard-language models or fixed depth and polynomial quantitative bounds. The September preprint has a source comment raising concerns and is recorded as an unverified claim.
progress: 2011: Williams separates nondeterministic exponential time from polynomial-size ACC circuits, a subclass of \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). | 2026-03: Chen–Tal–Wang prove \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) gate lower bounds for depth-two threshold circuits and a hard function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\). | 2026-07: Ren–Williams prove near-maximum unrestricted bounds for a class with a promise-MA oracle and advice. | 2026-09: Near-cubic depth-two wire bounds are claimed in a preprint with a critical source comment; this is not a \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) separation.
working_summary: Does some NEXP language escape all polynomial-size constant-depth majority circuits? Majority gates make this circuit class substantially more powerful than constant-depth \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) circuits. Williams established the corresponding separation for ACC circuits with fixed-modulus gates. Recent threshold-circuit bounds still restrict depth or polynomial size and use different hard-language classes. The target requires one ordinary NEXP language outside the entire nonuniform class \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\).

title: NL versus UL
importance_reason: A basic class equality tying directed reachability, isolation, pseudorandomness and the structure of low-memory witnesses.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\)? Equivalently, is there a single nondeterministic Turing machine that decides directed s–t reachability using \(O(\log  N)\) work space and polynomial time, has exactly one accepting computation on every reachable instance, and has no accepting computation on every unreachable instance, where N is the explicit input length?
definitions: An input consists of a finite directed graph with labelled vertices and explicitly listed edges, together with vertices s,t. Reachability asks whether a directed path from s to t exists; the length-zero path is allowed when \(s=t\). A machine has a read-only two-way input tape, \(O(\log (N+2))\) read/write work-tape cells over a fixed finite alphabet, and a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation. Every computation branch must halt within a polynomial in N. NL permits any positive number of accepting branches on yes inputs; UL permits exactly one. On no inputs both classes require zero accepting branches. A branch is a sequence of transition choices, not merely its endpoint or output. Rejecting branches need not be unique. Machines are uniform finite programs without advice, randomness, oracle access or additional catalytic storage. The equality asks whether every NL language has some equivalent UL machine; it does not require a computable compiler converting descriptions of arbitrary machines. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logspace reductions, so its UL membership suffices.
answer_criterion: Prove a uniform \(O(\log  N)\)-space unambiguous algorithm for all directed reachability inputs, or prove that some NL language is not in UL. Any positive construction must remain unambiguous on every input without assuming that the supplied graph itself has a unique path. A polynomial-time algorithm using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, or an unproved hardness hypothesis is progress rather than a solution.
context:
A nondeterministic reachability algorithm can guess the next vertex of a path, checking each edge as it goes. It needs only a current vertex and a step counter, so logarithmic memory suffices. The difficulty is that a graph can offer many successful sequences of guesses. An unambiguous algorithm must retain the ability to recognize a path while allowing only one successful computation.

This restriction is weaker than determinism. The machine may still branch many times and have many rejecting computations. On a reachable graph, only one complete branch may accept. Consequently, \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) would explain something about the source of nondeterministic power without establishing \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\). A proof that \(\mathrm{NL}\ne UL\) would, however, also separate deterministic and nondeterministic logspace, since \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq UL\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\).

One approach is to assign positive integer weights to edges so that every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. Reinhardt and Allender show how such min-isolating weights support an unambiguous reachability algorithm. If the weights are polynomially bounded and can be generated in deterministic logspace from the graph, the resulting memory use remains logarithmic. Randomly choosing suitable weights can give isolation, but does not provide a uniform deterministic construction.

Reinhardt and Allender also prove NL/poly=UL/poly. Here a polynomial-length advice string may depend on the input length and be shared by every input of that length, without any requirement that the string be generated efficiently. This is evidence that isolation is possible in a broad nonuniform sense. Removing the advice is essential to the ordinary \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) question.

The strongest checked unconditional general simulation uses more than logarithmic memory. Van Melkebeek and Prakriya give an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation of NL using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space. Their work reduces the randomness and weight-description costs of isolation. The remaining square-root-of-logarithm factor is small numerically, but it is an unbounded factor in the resource defining the target class.

The inherited 2025 paper by Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams develops new hardness-versus-randomness tools for isolation. Its main conditional unambiguity theorem concerns the linear-space analogue \(\mathrm{NSPACE}[n]\subseteq\)USPACE\([O(n)]\), under uniform circuit lower bounds with specified oracle access. The March 2026 Pyne–Tell survey gives a refined version. These assumptions are unproved, and the linear-space conclusion should not be reported as an unconditional logspace equality.

A February 2026 revision by Arvind, Chakraborty and Datta gives reachability algorithms in a catalytic model with UL oracle access. Catalytic computation permits extra memory initially containing arbitrary data, provided that the data are restored at the end. This is an interesting way to use storage, but it supplies resources absent from a plain UL machine. The headline about derandomizing isolation therefore does not resolve this card.

Hoza proves a new limitation in July 2026. Suppose one weight assignment must work for every layered graph of given width w and length \(\ell\), without examining which edges are actually present. Such an oblivious min-isolating assignment requires weights of magnitude \(2^{\Omega (\log  w\cdot \log  \ell )}\), so polynomially bounded universal weights cannot solve the general problem by this route. This restriction does not cover assignments that depend on the actual graph or other unambiguous algorithms.

A solution would determine whether many successful paths are ever intrinsically necessary when computation has only logarithmic memory. It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. The challenge is not to name a canonical path mathematically, but to recognize one with the required uniqueness guarantee and very little working storage.
why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.
status_note: The checked general unconditional simulation still uses \(O(\log ^{3/2} N)\) space. The 2025–2026 hardness-based results remain conditional, catalytic results use additional resources, and Hoza’s July 2026 lower bound excludes only oblivious isolation. No settlement of uniform \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1997–2000: Reinhardt–Allender show that min-isolation supports unambiguous reachability and prove the nonuniform equality NL/poly=UL/poly. | 2017–2019: Van Melkebeek–Prakriya obtain a polynomial-time unambiguous simulation using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space; CCC 2017 and SICOMP 2019. | 2025-06-18: Doron–Pyne–Tell–Williams derive linear-space unambiguity from substantially weakened but still unproved uniform circuit lower bounds. | 2026-02-06: Arvind–Chakraborty–Datta’s revised catalytic isolation result uses extra restorable memory and UL oracle access. | 2026-03-30: Pyne–Tell survey recent isolation results, distinguishing the classical conditional \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) theorem from newer conditional linear-space simulations. | 2026-07-23: Hoza proves that deterministic oblivious min-isolation for all layered digraphs requires quasipolynomial-size weights in the general parameter regime.
working_summary: An ordinary nondeterministic reachability algorithm can have many accepting paths of computation. UL requires at most one accepting computation for each input while retaining logarithmic workspace. The question asks whether this unambiguity restriction changes the class NL. The machine may still have many rejecting branches, so this is weaker than demanding determinism. The project seeks to isolate a unique successful witness efficiently, clarifying whether ambiguity itself is a source of computational power in small-space graph problems.

title: L versus NL
importance_reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).
definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so \(s=t\) is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic \(O(\log  N)\) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has \(N=Theta(n^{2})\) bits, \(O(\log  N)=O(\log  n)\). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
context:
A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within \(n- 1\) edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses \(O(\log ^{2} n)\) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.
why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly retains the directed logspace question, and the February 2026 hardness result concerns restricted graph classes without resolving it. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of L versus NL.
progress: 1970: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in \(O(s^{2})\) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm. | 1987–1988: Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\), so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms. | 2005–2008: Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem. | 2025: Doron, Pyne, Tell, and Williams give two algorithms such that, on each directed graph, at least one succeeds: deterministic polynomial-time, polylogarithmic-space transitive closure, or nondeterministic logarithmic-space random-walk estimation. This per-graph alternative does not give the first algorithm on every graph or reduce its space to \(O(\log  n)\). | 2026: Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

title: Existence of TFNP-complete problems
importance_reason: A central longstanding completeness question for all of TFNP, with consequences for the organization of total search and established links to bounded arithmetic and proof complexity.
formal:
Does the class of total polynomially bounded search problems with polynomial-time verifiable answers contain a complete problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions?

Writing this class as \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) and the reduction as \(\le_m^p\), the target is
\[\exists Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \forall R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\le_m^p Q.\]
The same fixed relation \(Q\) must work for every \(R\). For each \(R\), a reduction computes one \(Q\)-instance from the input and converts every valid answer to that instance into a valid \(R\)-answer. The question is unrelativized and concerns the whole class, including problems whose totality follows from different mathematical principles.
question_excerpt: The search for a complete problem in TFNP is of primary concern to certain fields such as cryptography, but it remains open whether such a […]
definitions:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), let \(\Sigma^*\) include the empty string, and let \(|x|\) be bit length. A search relation is a subset \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\). An answer to input \(x\) is any string \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); no uniqueness or ordering of valid answers is required.

The relation belongs to \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) if all three conditions hold. First, there are positive integers \(a,b\), fixed for \(R\), such that every valid pair satisfies \(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^b\). Second, a deterministic algorithm decides \(R(x,y)\) in time at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\), for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Third,
\[\forall x\in\Sigma^*\ \exists y\in\Sigma^*,\qquad R(x,y).\]
Thus totality applies to every binary input. A relation based on a structured encoding must also prescribe a valid answer for malformed instances; restricting the domain to inputs promised to have a solution is insufficient. The output bound is part of the relation: an overlong string is not a valid answer.

Algorithms use uniform finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machines over fixed finite alphabets, with binary input and output. Time counts bit operations, input handling and writing the output, in the worst case over all inputs. A pair can be encoded as \(\langle x,z\rangle=1^{|x|}0xz\), whose length is linear in \(|x|+|z|+1\); malformed encodings may be assigned an arbitrary fixed output. All functions used below are total and polynomial-time computable on their full encoded domains. There is no randomness, advice, nonuniform circuit family or external oracle available to these functions.

For \(R,Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\), the reduction \(R\le_m^p Q\) means that there are functions \(f:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) and \(g:\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) computed in deterministic polynomial time such that
\[\forall x,z\in\Sigma^*,\qquad Q(f(x),z)\ \Longrightarrow\ R(x,g(x,z)).\]
The bound for \(f\) is polynomial in \(|x|\), and that for \(g\) is polynomial in \(|x|+|z|\). The decoder may use the original input \(x\). This is a single transformed instance with a single returned answer; correctness must hold for every possible valid answer, without controlling which answer is returned. The reduction does not itself compute an answer to \(Q\), and the quantification over valid answers is not an oracle supplied to \(f\) or \(g\). Multiple adaptive instance queries are not the reduction in this question.

The complete problem \(Q\), its verifier and its balance bound are fixed before \(R\) is chosen. The reduction functions and their polynomial constants may depend on \(R\) and \(Q\), but not on the particular input. No single effective procedure that recognizes TFNP membership or produces reductions from arbitrary verifier descriptions is required.

A negative answer is the exact opposite quantifier statement:
\[\forall Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \exists R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\not\le_m^p Q.\]
The target is completeness for a search class under the specified search reduction. Completeness of a decision language, completeness for a proper TFNP subclass, or an NP search problem that lacks answers on some inputs does not by itself satisfy it.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify one relation \(Q\), prove its polynomial balance, deterministic polynomial-time verifiability and totality on all binary inputs, and establish the stated reductions from every \(R\in\mathrm{TFNP}\). A negative answer must prove that every candidate \(Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\) fails to receive such a reduction from some relation in the class. No effective enumeration of all TFNP problems is additionally required. A subclass-completeness result, a separation relative to an oracle or a conditional consequence alone is insufficient.
context:
The source states nonexistence of a many-one complete TFNP problem among the central conjectures connecting computational complexity and proof systems. This card asks the equivalent yes-or-no existence question, so the commonly stated conjecture predicts a negative answer.

Polynomial verifiability and a polynomial answer bound can be given by machine descriptions, but totality asserts a condition over all inputs. This semantic requirement prevents simply treating every polynomial-time verifier as a total search problem. Pudlák relates the general completeness question to the ability of fixed arithmetical theories to capture total search, and proves a universal-problem result for suitable classes whose totality is provable in a fixed theory.

Many important subclasses have complete problems tied to particular existence principles. The December 2025 manuscript studies further oracle hierarchies and collapses within TFNP; these subclass results do not supply a complete problem for the entire class.

The MFCS 2024 oracle permits a TFNP-complete problem while SAT has no polynomial-time optimal proof system. This separates two conjectures in that relativized setting; it neither constructs an ordinary TFNP-complete problem nor rules one out. Worst-case completeness alone also does not specify an average-case cryptographic hardness guarantee.
why: A complete problem would give one universal task against which the difficulty of every efficiently verifiable total search problem could be compared. Its nonexistence would establish a structural limitation on extending the completeness framework from decision problems to all total search. This is a central question connecting complexity classes defined by semantic conditions, mathematical existence principles and the strength of formal proof systems.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: MFCS 2024 introduction, Pudlák’s 21 November 2017 manuscript Section 4, and the 26 December 2025 hierarchy revision introduction and Section 2.1. The June 2026 abstracts of Provable Reductions in TFNP and Randomized separations in black-box TFNP address different, restricted reduction settings; their proofs were not audited. The checked sources do not resolve existence of an unrelativized many-one complete problem for all TFNP. This is a bounded source-open review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2017-11-21: The checked survey manuscript gives the full search-reduction definition and places the no-complete-problem conjecture in a program relating total search to finite incompleteness. | 2024-08-23: MFCS publishes the oracle separation while explicitly retaining the ordinary many-one completeness question as open. | 2025-12-26: Revision 1 studies hierarchies and collapses among TFNP subclasses and continues to distinguish their complete problems from the general completeness question.
working_summary: TFNP contains search problems with polynomially bounded, efficiently verifiable answers guaranteed to exist for every binary input. The question asks whether one problem in this class is complete for all the others under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions. Each reduction makes one transformed instance and must decode every valid returned answer correctly. The complete relation is fixed universally, while the reduction and its polynomial bounds may vary with the source problem. Known subclass completeness and oracle results clarify the structure without settling this general existence question.

title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
importance_reason: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
formal: Do constants \(a,b,c>0\) and \(q\ge 1\) exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a \(\log _{2}(N+2)\) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most \((N+2)^{b}\) symbols over an alphabet of size at most \((N+2)^{b}\), with perfect completeness and soundness at most \((N+2)^{- c}\)?
definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with \(O(\log  N)\) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most \((N+2)^{- c}\). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.
why: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.

title: \(\mathrm{P}_{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{R}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model
importance_reason: The defining complexity-class question for exact computation over the reals, connecting TCS to algebraic geometry and numerical computation.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb{R}}\) for the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered field of real numbers?
definitions: Inputs are finite tuples \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), with input size n. A machine has a finite program and finitely many fixed real constants. It can store and copy real numbers, perform +, −, ×, and division by a nonzero number, and branch on the sign or equality to zero of a stored real, at unit cost per operation; the ordinary BSS input, output and register-shift operations are included. \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb{R}}\) consists of subsets of the disjoint union of the spaces \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\) decidable by one such deterministic machine in polynomially many steps as a function of n. \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb{R}}\) consists of sets for which membership of x is equivalent to existence of a real witness y of length bounded by a polynomial in n that is accepted by one deterministic BSS verifier in polynomially many steps. Machine constants are finite and independent of input length; witnesses may contain arbitrary reals. The target is equality of these classes, not equality in a finite-precision or bit-cost model.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The BSS model treats exact field operations and order tests as elementary computation. Its version of nondeterminism allows real witnesses and captures basic real algebraic feasibility problems.

This separation is a foundational question about algebraic computation over a continuum. Classical P versus NP does not by itself answer it: the input representation, cost model and certificates differ.

The recommended paper studies Boolean inputs to real computation. Proposition 1.1 identifies \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\), where the superscript 0 permits only machine constants 0 and 1. PosSLP asks whether an arithmetic straight-line program using 0, 1, addition, subtraction and multiplication outputs a positive integer. Theorem 1.4 places PosSLP in the counting hierarchy.

With arbitrary fixed real constants, \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}/\mathrm{poly}=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R})\) is Conjecture 1.2 in that paper. These Boolean-input results do not settle equality of deterministic and nondeterministic BSS classes on arbitrary real inputs.
why: The defining complexity-class question for exact computation over the reals, connecting TCS to algebraic geometry and numerical computation.
