title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
importance_reason: The answer would determine whether many geometric existence problems admit the same kind of efficiently checkable discrete certificates as classical NP problems.
formal: Is \(\exists\mathbb{R}=\mathrm{NP}\) under polynomial-time many-one reductions between finitely encoded decision problems?
definitions: Let ETR be the following language of finite binary strings. An instance is an existential sentence \(\exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R:\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), where \(\Phi\) is an explicitly represented Boolean formula with atoms \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Each \(p\) is an integer-coefficient polynomial, supplied as a list of monomials with coefficients and nonnegative exponents in binary. Parentheses, connectives, variable indices and all lengths are explicitly encoded; invalid encodings are rejected. Truth uses exact real arithmetic as mathematical semantics, not unit-cost computation. \(\exists\mathbb R\) is the class of languages reducible to ETR by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in input bit length. \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length binary witnesses checked by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. Equivalent fixed finite-tape machine conventions may be used. The question is unrelativized.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:
Real solutions describe geometric positions, distances and continuous parameters, but need not have short rational coordinate descriptions.

The complexity class organizes a large family of geometric recognition and realization problems. Its known containments are \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\).

Relativized structural results do not decide whether ordinary finite binary certificates suffice for the unrelativized class.
why: The answer would determine whether many geometric existence problems admit the same kind of efficiently checkable discrete certificates as classical NP problems.
status_note: Primary sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the precise target was located; this is a bounded literature review, not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2024: The compendium presents the class, its containments and unresolved comparisons. | 2025: Structural and oracle results leave the unrelativized equality unanswered.
working_summary: Existential real formulas ask whether polynomial constraints have a real solution. The input is a finite binary description of the constraints. The class contains NP and is contained in PSPACE. The question asks whether it is exactly NP. An oracle separation or a rational-coordinate obstruction alone does not answer that class comparison.

title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
importance_reason: Determines the representation-size cost of determinism when compiling knowledge into a form supporting exact model counting.
formal: Is the following nonuniform size separation true? For every \(C\geq1\), integer \(k\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), there is a DNF formula \(F\) of size \(s\geq N\) such that every d-DNNF circuit computing exactly the same Boolean function on the same input variables has size greater than \(C(s+1)^{k}\). Equivalently, is there no single polynomial bound on the size of a d-DNNF representation of an arbitrary DNF? No efficient construction or conversion algorithm is required on either side of this size comparison.
definitions: Inputs are Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). A DNF is a finite disjunction of terms, each a conjunction of distinct literals with no contradictory pair; the empty conjunction is true and the empty disjunction false. Its size is one plus its number of terms and literal occurrences. An NNF circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output, leaves labeled by literals or the constants zero and one, and internal AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in. It may share subcircuits and have unrestricted depth. Its size is its total number of vertices and edges. The variable set of a gate comprises variables labeling leaves that reach it. Decomposability means that the variable sets of different children of every AND gate are pairwise disjoint. Determinism means that, for every OR gate and every assignment to the union of its children’s variable sets, at most one child evaluates to one. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions. Equivalent circuits agree for every input assignment, with no error or auxiliary existentially quantified variables. There is no common variable order, tree-structured decomposition, restriction to decision gates, or uniformity requirement. Polynomial comparisons use the DNF representation size, including all literal occurrences; ordinary explicit gate/edge encodings give the same polynomial-versus-superpolynomial distinction. The family formulation using polynomial-size DNFs in the number of inputs is equivalent after permitting unused input variables as padding.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified superpolynomial size separation, or refute it by proving that one polynomial bounds the minimum equivalent d-DNNF size for every DNF. A negative answer need not give an efficient converter. A lower bound for decision-DNNF, structured d-DNNF, or a broader DNNF input family does not meet the stated unrestricted-output, DNF-input criterion.
context:
Decomposability separates the variable sets of conjunctions, while determinism makes the alternatives at each disjunction disjoint. These restrictions support exact model counting in time polynomial in the representation size. A DNF already satisfies decomposability after inconsistent terms are removed, but its terms need not be disjoint.

Capelli’s June 2026 habilitation explicitly asks for a superpolynomial d-DNNF lower bound for DNF formulas. The known separation of unrestricted DNNF from d-DNNF uses a broader source representation and therefore does not settle this DNF restriction.

Even if every DNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representation, finding one in polynomial time would have additional counting consequences. The source distinguishes this algorithmic conversion issue from the existence of small representations; conditional conversion hardness supplies no unconditional size separation.
why: The question measures an inherent space cost of making overlapping explanations disjoint while retaining decomposable structure. It determines whether the simplest compact disjunctive representation can always remain compact in a form suited to exact counting, independently of how difficult that form is to find.
status_note: The source is a June 2026 habilitation, not an undated historical manuscript. Its Open question 1 and a targeted subsequent-work search were checked on 13 September 2026; no full DNF versus unrestricted d-DNNF size separation was identified. This is a bounded status check and remains source_open.
progress: 2026-06-15: The habilitation distinguishes the known DNNF versus d-DNNF size separation from Open question 1 for DNF inputs, and separately explains the obstacle to an efficient generic conversion.
working_summary: A DNF formula describes satisfying assignments as a union of conjunctions, whose cases may overlap. The proposal asks whether some polynomial-size DNFs require superpolynomial-size deterministic decomposable circuits for the same Boolean function. Determinism requires disjoint alternatives, while decomposability requires conjunctions to separate their variables. A separation would show that imposing these useful structural restrictions can force an inherent representation-size increase. The question is about the existence of compact equivalent circuits, so hardness of efficiently finding a conversion or a separation for unrestricted DNNFs does not by itself answer this more specific size comparison.

title: CLS versus FP
importance_reason: Determine the tractability of the common core of fixed-point search and potential-based local optimization.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
definitions:
Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{NOT}\), constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of \(S,\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}, n\ge 1\), satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(0^{n})=0^{n}\) and \(S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\). An accepted output is a bit string \(v\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(\mathrm{P}(S(v))
e v\), or with both \(v
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(\mathrm{P}(v))
e v\). In particular \(v=0^{n}\) is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of \(T:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{r}\), with \(m,r\ge 1\). Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with \(V(T(w))\ge V(w)\). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. PPAD and PLS are the classes reducing to End-of-Line and Localopt respectively. The source proves that the either-solution problem is complete for their intersection and that CLS=PPAD∩PLS. These equalities give the stated equivalent discrete formulation of \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\); no new smoothness or numerical promise is introduced.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform deterministic algorithm always returns a permitted answer within a fixed polynomial in the combined input bit length, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Solving both component instances is not required. A restricted-circuit algorithm, a randomized algorithm alone, or a conditional hardness implication does not establish either unconditional answer to \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\).
context:
CLS captures total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani proved that it equals PPAD∩PLS, connecting this optimization class to two discrete existence principles.

The equivalent task presented here gives two independent succinct problems and asks for a solution to either one. The known completeness theorem means that an efficient algorithm for this task would solve every problem in CLS. The theorem identifies the class; it does not supply a polynomial-time solution algorithm.
why: Determine the tractability of the common core of fixed-point search and potential-based local optimization.
status_note: The source establishes the class equality but does not decide polynomial-time solvability. The individual discrete specification was rechecked on 13 September 2026 against the locally saved full paper. The prior 11 September status search and a small follow-up search supplied no verified resolution; the latter was inconclusive, so status remains source_open rather than a claim of exhaustive current verification.
progress: 2021: The source establishes CLS=PPAD∩PLS, leaving polynomial-time solvability as a separate question.
working_summary: CLS describes total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. The source proves that it is exactly the intersection of PPAD and PLS, two classes based on different existence principles. The equivalent discrete question gives one succinct path problem and one succinct local-search problem and asks for a solution to either. The requested algorithm must be deterministic and polynomial in the length of both circuit descriptions. A resolution would determine whether the common part of these two search classes is computationally tractable.

title: Polynomial-size circuits for EXP
importance_reason: Tests the power of polynomial-size nonuniform computation against exponential-time computation, a central circuit lower-bound question.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), decidable by one deterministic exponential-time algorithm, whose circuit complexity \(s_L(n)\) satisfies \[\forall C\geq1\;\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\forall N\geq1\;\exists n\geq N:\quad s_L(n)>C(n+1)^{k}?\]
definitions: \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\geq1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{a}})\), with the usual multiplicative constants and polynomially equivalent deterministic multitape Turing-machine encodings. The input is an arbitrary binary string and the machine decides membership without a promise, advice or oracle. A Boolean circuit on \(n\) inputs is an acyclic graph using fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, constants, and one output. Its size is the number of noninput gates; replacing this by its explicit gate-and-wire encoding length preserves polynomial size. The quantity \(s_L(n)\) is the minimum such size for exact agreement with membership in \(L\) on all \(n\)-bit strings. Circuit choices for different lengths are arbitrary and need not be computable. The class \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) comprises languages with \(s_L(n)\leq C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\) depending on the language. The quantifiers in the question require one language defeating every polynomial size bound; they do not require a lower bound at every sufficiently large length. The source uses exponential-time notation in a truth-table generation discussion; the card uses the standard union defining EXP. Using \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\) instead gives the equivalent class-containment question by polynomial padding.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\), including an EXP language and the quantified superpolynomial lower bound, or prove its negation \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Different hard languages for different fixed exponents, a lower bound for a restricted gate basis, or a consistency theorem alone do not settle the question.
context:
The deterministic time hierarchy separates polynomial from exponential uniform running time. It does not rule out small circuits chosen independently at each input length, which is the nonuniform issue in this conjecture.

Wigderson states the separation as Conjecture 8.6 in a discussion of explicit hard Boolean functions and pseudorandomness. Counting shows that many truth tables need large circuits, but the conjecture additionally places a hard language in a fixed uniform exponential-time class.

A 2026 preprint by Atserias and Müller proves a consistency result relating bounded arithmetic to \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Consistency of the separation with a formal theory is distinct from a proof of the separation itself.

The public note proposes a weaker upper-bound question: whether every EXP language has subexponential-size circuits. For example, one precise convention is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{EXP}\;\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N:\ s_L(n)\le 2^{\varepsilon n}\). Polynomial-size circuits would imply this upper bound. It is consequently weaker than the containment \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\), which is the negative answer to the present separation question, rather than a weaker form of the conjectured lower bound. The displayed convention specifies this contextual variant; it is not substituted for the card’s original target.
why: This is a central test of whether explicit computation can be proved to require large unrestricted Boolean circuits. Resolving it would cross the gap between uniform time hierarchy theorems and lower bounds that defeat arbitrary nonuniform circuit families.
status_note: Conjecture 8.6 is open in the saved 2019 source. On 13 September 2026 the targeted later-work check found a 2026 consistency result, whose abstract does not claim the separation. No full resolution was verified; the later proof was not independently checked. Status remains source_open.
progress: 2019-08-06: The saved book draft states EXP outside P/poly as Conjecture 8.6 and explains its relationship to generating hard truth tables. | 2026-04-28: The preprint reports that the bounded-arithmetic theory \(S^1_2\) is consistent with the circuit separation. This is a result about formal provability and consistency, not a resolution of the class comparison.
working_summary: EXP contains problems solvable in deterministic exponential time. The question asks whether every such problem could nevertheless have polynomial-size Boolean circuits chosen separately for each input length. The circuits need not be efficiently constructible, making this different from a polynomial-time simulation. Time hierarchy theorems alone do not eliminate that nonuniform possibility. The project seeks a lower bound strong enough to defeat arbitrary length-specific circuit designs for some language with an explicit exponential-time decision procedure.

title: Exponential depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) lower bounds for E
importance_reason: A strong explicit-circuit lower-bound frontier for a basic shallow gate model, tied to circuit minimization and far beyond the known unrestricted square-root exponent.
formal:
Does there exist a language \(L\in\mathrm E\) whose characteristic functions require exponential-size depth-at-most-three Boolean AND/OR circuits, with arbitrary fan-in and input negations, at infinitely many input lengths?

Let \(f_{L,n}(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), and let \(S_3(f)\) be the minimum number of AND/OR gates in such a circuit computing \(f\) exactly. The question is
\[\exists L\in\mathrm E\ \exists\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad S_3(f_{L,n})>2^{\delta n}.\]
Here \(N,n\) are integers. This makes the source’s class lower-bound target precise as failure of subexponential-size depth-three computation for one language in E. No almost-every-length strengthening is imposed.
question_excerpt: It is still unknown if E requires depth-3 AC0 circuits of size \(2\Omega (n)\) , and using the Kabanets-Cai connection, natural approaches to an NP-hardness result […]
definitions:
The class \(\mathrm E\) consists of languages \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) for which there are one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and a fixed positive integer \(c\) such that, on every binary string \(x\) of length \(n\), the machine halts within \(2^{c(n+1)}\) steps and outputs the membership bit of \(L\). The machine uses fixed finite alphabets, and time counts tape operations, input handling and output. There is no advice, oracle, randomness or promise restricting inputs. No separate space bound is imposed. The same \(M,c\) work at every length. This distinguishes E from unrestricted exponential time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\) and from exponential-time computation with an NP oracle.

A circuit for an \(n\)-input function is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Its sources are constants \(0,1\) and literals \(x_i,\neg x_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\). Each internal gate is AND or OR of a nonempty finite list of predecessor values. Fan-in and fan-out have no fixed bound; computed values may be shared. A gate may also have a single predecessor. An output may be a literal or constant. The circuit must agree with the function on every assignment to all \(n\) variables.

Depth is the largest number of internal AND/OR gates on a source-to-output path and is at most three. Input negations do not contribute to depth; there are no internal NOT, parity, modular-counting, threshold or arbitrary truth-table gates. The size is the number of internal AND/OR gates, counting a shared gate once. Constants, literal sources and wires are not separately charged. The minimum over this class is \(S_3(f)\), which is defined for every Boolean function because a disjunctive normal form is available. Constant and literal outputs have size zero. Both possible top-gate orientations, including OR–AND–OR and AND–OR–AND, are allowed; the lower bound must cover the entire stated class.

All bottom gates have unrestricted fan-in. Neither the function nor the circuit is required to be monotone: a circuit can use both polarities of every variable. Although the notation refers to the depth-three AC-zero gate model, candidate circuits here are allowed exponential size; a polynomial-size restriction is not built into the minimization.

The circuits compared at different input lengths are completely nonuniform. They need not have computable descriptions or be produced by the machine deciding \(L\). The E condition applies to the single language whose membership functions are being computed. There is no extra algorithmic requirement to find a smallest circuit or compute its size.

The same language and the same positive exponent \(\delta\) must work for arbitrarily large lengths. A different hard function chosen independently at each length qualifies only if the resulting family has a single E decider. The displayed claim is equivalent to the existence of such an \(L\) with
\[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2(S_3(f_{L,n})+2)}{n}>0.\]
Its negation says that every \(L\in\mathrm E\) has \(\log_2(S_3(f_{L,n})+2)/n\to0\). Thus a refutation permits the sublinear exponent and its rate to depend on \(L\), and does not require an effective procedure for constructing the circuits. The phrase exponential lower bound is interpreted at the class-noncontainment level; the source does not spell out an almost-every-length quantifier.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence statement. A proof must establish one E language, its uniform deterministic exponential-time bound and a positive constant exponent for a lower bound against every allowed circuit at infinitely many lengths. A refutation must prove sublinear logarithmic circuit size, as specified in the definitions, for every E language. Counting hard functions without an E evaluator, restricting bottom fan-in or monotonicity, allowing an oracle in the evaluator, or proving only a square-root-exponent lower bound is insufficient.
context:
The source proves hardness for minimizing OR–AND–MOD circuits and discusses the resulting lower-bound consequences for that gate model. It explicitly separates those consequences from the open question for ordinary depth-three AND/OR circuits. Changing a modular-counting bottom layer to an unrestricted OR layer changes the relevant lower-bound problem.

The February 2026 manuscript describes the longstanding unrestricted depth-three lower-bound frontier at a square-root exponent. Its new matching result is for monotone circuits with bottom fan-in at most three, and its exponential dependence on the input length is in that restricted model. It does not cover all circuits minimized by this card.

The target language is allowed an E computation, whereas the related depth-three cards use NP explicitness and different exponent thresholds. Their statements therefore retain distinct evaluator and quantitative requirements; an implication should not be inferred solely from the word explicit.

The gate-count convention is used consistently in the target. Polynomial changes between ordinary gate, wire and description-size measures do not change existence of an exponential lower bound when its positive constant exponent is unspecified.
why: Exponential lower bounds against very shallow Boolean circuits remain a substantial explicitness problem, even when the target language may use deterministic exponential time. Resolving this question would sharply advance the distinction between an arbitrary hard truth table and one generated by a uniform computation. The source also identifies this lower bound as an obstacle to extending certain circuit-minimization hardness arguments to ordinary depth-three AND/OR circuits.

working_summary: The question asks for one language decidable in deterministic time exponential in input length but requiring exponential-size depth-three Boolean circuits. The circuits use arbitrary-fan-in AND and OR gates with input negations, sharing and either top-gate orientation. A fixed positive lower-bound exponent must hold at infinitely many lengths for the same E language. There is no uniformity requirement on the competing circuits and no restriction on bottom fan-in or literal polarity. Recent exponential results for monotone circuits with bounded bottom fan-in do not establish this unrestricted lower bound.

title: Randomized evasiveness conjecture
importance_reason: A major longstanding structural conjecture in query complexity, asserting a universal quadratic barrier for randomized recognition across all nontrivial monotone graph properties.
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge 2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and every nonconstant monotone graph property \(P\) on n vertices, its randomized adjacency-query complexity with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) satisfies \(R_{1/3}(P)\ge c n^2\)? Both c and \(n_0\) must be independent of P. This card asks for the bounded-error randomized evasiveness conjecture.
definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(E_n\) be the set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \([n]\). An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E_n}\) describes a finite simple undirected graph: \(x_e=1\) means e is an edge. Every one of the \(2^{\binom n2}\) assignments is a valid input. A graph property is a function \(P:\{0,1\}^{E_n}\to\{0,1\}\) invariant under every permutation of the vertices, with the permutation acting on each edge’s two endpoints. Monotone means \(x_e\le y_e\) for every e implies \(P(x)\le P(y)\). Nonconstant means some input has value 0 and another has value 1; for monotone P the empty graph has value 0 and the complete graph value 1. No monotonicity across different vertex counts is imposed. A deterministic query tree is a finite binary tree whose internal nodes name edges, whose outgoing branches carry the possible queried bits, and whose leaves carry output bits. On input x it follows the branch specified by each queried \(x_e\). Its cost on x is the number of queries along that path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution \(\mu\), independent of x, on such trees. It has cost at most q if every tree with positive probability has depth at most q. It computes P with error at most \(1/3\) when \(\Pr_{T\sim\mu}[T(x)=P(x)]\ge 2/3\) for every input x. Define \(R_{1/3}(P)\) as the smallest such integer q. The distribution and trees may depend on P and n. Sampling, storage and all computation on previously obtained answers are uncharged; only queries revealing one adjacency bit are counted. There is no uniformity or efficient-construction requirement on the trees, and no description of P is part of the queried graph. Queries may be adaptive. Input distributions, promises that a no-instance is far from P, quantum access, certificates and other graph oracles are absent. Cost is worst-case over both the graph and trees in the support, not expected over those choices. The only approximation allowed is the stated probability of an incorrect membership bit. In particular, a graph missing P by a single edge still requires the same success guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal lower-bound proposition. A positive answer requires one c and one \(n_0\) working for all the indicated graph properties and all \(n\ge n_0\). Its negation is: for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(N\ge 2\), there exist an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonconstant monotone graph property P on n vertices with \(R_{1/3}(P)<c n^2\). A refutation must establish this quantified failure, not just a constant-factor saving from querying every edge. A result only for zero-error randomized algorithms, deterministic algorithms, selected properties, or proximity testing does not by itself settle the bounded-error target.
context:
Connectedness is monotone: adding edges cannot disconnect a connected graph. It is also independent of how its vertices are named. The conjecture encompasses every property with these two formal features, including properties chosen separately at different graph sizes, rather than only a fixed list of familiar algorithmic problems.

Recognition asks for the actual membership bit on every graph. Property testing changes the required distinction by allowing graphs close to the property to have unconstrained answers. Goldreich’s discussion emphasizes this difference: constant-query proximity testers do not contradict a quadratic lower bound for recognition.

The saved manuscript only briefly describes randomized recognition. This card explicitly adopts the bounded-error convention already used in its working summary, corroborated by Buhrman and de Wolf’s Open Problem 6 and Grossman, Komargodski and Naor’s Conjecture 3.14. The no-error expected-cost question is a distinct weaker variant and is preserved as context, not silently conflated with this target.

For zero-error computation, every sampled deterministic tree is correct on every input and complexity is the largest, over inputs, expected query count. Chakrabarti and Khot prove \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) in that model. Their definition is narrower than algorithms allowed to give a wrong answer. The cited theorem is therefore not itself a proof of the same bound for this card’s larger algorithm class.

The deterministic Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture asks for the exact value \(\binom n2\) for every property at every size. Here the target allows a fixed multiplicative saving and concerns randomized algorithms. A quadratic randomized lower bound would not automatically establish the exact deterministic value. A quadratic deterministic lower bound alone does not exclude randomized savings.

The quantum analogue has a different scale. The 2020 result proves a universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query lower bound, and the property of having at least one edge admits \(O(n)\) quantum queries. Resolving that linear-scale analogue does not resolve the quadratic classical randomized conjecture.
why: This conjecture asks whether monotonicity and invariance under vertex names force essentially complete inspection even when random errors are allowed. It is a broad structural lower-bound question covering many graph recognition tasks at once. Its resolution would sharply delimit the power of randomized access to an exact graph property and explain why proximity testing can behave so differently.
status_note: The bounded-error conjecture is explicit in the checked 2002 and 2020 sources and is restated as open in the Winter 2025 notes. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. Original model definitions, not informal randomized-complexity labels, govern the reported lower bounds. The search is bounded and cited proofs were not independently verified.

working_summary: A monotone graph property is invariant under vertex renaming and cannot be destroyed by adding edges. The conjecture says every nonconstant such property needs a quadratic number of adjacency queries even with randomized error at most one third. The query bound is worst-case over graphs and random choices, while the error guarantee holds separately for each graph. title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
importance_reason: Separating majority from constant-depth modular circuits would cross a major explicit Boolean circuit lower-bound barrier.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.
context:
Jukna’s Research Problem 12.28 asks whether Majority lies outside ACC⁰. This is a lower bound for one concrete counting function, stronger in explicitness than separating a large uniform complexity class from the circuit class.

Prime-modulus lower bounds and the separation of nondeterministic exponential time from ACC⁰ concern different targets from the full majority question. In particular, results for prime moduli do not cover arbitrary composite moduli such as six.

Pago’s 2026 work proves lower bounds for computing AND using modular gates under syntactic symmetry assumptions. The permitted gate basis, target function and symmetry restriction differ from the unrestricted majority circuits in this card, so that result does not resolve this question.
why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.
status_note: The target is explicitly open in Jukna’s source. A 13 September 2026 small-text check of later modular-circuit work identified a symmetry-restricted AND result, not a solution for majority in unrestricted ACC⁰. No resolution was verified; status remains source_open.

title: Graph nonisomorphism in BPP
importance_reason: A central randomized-computation variant of graph isomorphism, distinguished from both the deterministic polynomial-time frontier and interactive proof membership.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that M halts on every binary input x and every random outcome within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions, and outputs the correct membership bit for \(\mathrm{GNI}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each x? The language \(\mathrm{GNI}\) consists of valid encodings of two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs. This asks whether \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\).
definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. At a randomized transition the machine may obtain one independent unbiased random bit, with this transition counted in its runtime. Success probability is over these internal bits for each fixed input, not over a distribution of graphs. BPP consists of binary languages for which such a machine has error at most \(1/3\) on every input and a polynomial worst-case clock over inputs and random outcomes. For \(\mathrm{GNI}\), acceptance is required with probability at least \(2/3\) when the encoding is valid and \(G\not\cong H\); it is at most \(1/3\) for isomorphic pairs and malformed strings. Distinct vertex counts form yes-instances for GNI. The output is only one membership bit, without a nonisomorphism certificate, quantum computation or interaction with another party. One machine and one polynomial must work at all graph sizes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\) or \(\mathrm{GNI}\notin\mathrm{BPP}\) in the model above. The positive case must supply one uniform polynomial-time bounded-error decider, or establish its existence, with the required probability bound on every input. The negative case must exclude every such randomized machine. Correctness only on typical graphs, an interactive verification protocol, a method with only expected polynomial time and no suitable clock conversion, or a restricted-model lower bound does not by itself settle this target.
context:
Graph nonisomorphism asserts that no bijection of the vertex sets preserves adjacency. An isomorphism is an easily checked witness for the opposite answer; a failed attempt to find one does not certify nonisomorphism. The target requires a bounded probability of error on every graph pair, including highly symmetric instances.

Goldreich’s footnote uses graph nonisomorphism to contrast an interactive proof with a problem not known to have a BPP algorithm. The verifier in such a proof receives messages from a computationally unbounded party. The question here removes that assistance and asks about the verifier’s own randomized computation.

BPP is closed under complement: reversing the answer preserves its error bound and runtime. After checking that the encoding is valid, an algorithm for nonisomorphism can therefore be turned into one for isomorphism, and conversely. Validity checking is needed because both graph languages reject malformed strings. Thus this is exactly the randomized polynomial-time question for ordinary graph isomorphism, with its answer polarity reversed.

The deterministic and randomized targets are related but distinct. A deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider supplies a positive answer here. A negative answer here would exclude a deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider and, since isomorphism has efficiently checkable permutation witnesses, would imply P differs from NP. A positive answer here does not automatically derandomize the computation.

The general quasipolynomial upper bound also applies to nonisomorphism by reversing a validated input’s answer. Its January 2017 correction matters when interpreting the original arXiv manuscript. Parameterized algorithms and typical-instance performance must separately account for their promises before they can be compared with an all-input polynomial clock.

The 2026 survey concerns the general deterministic frontier and parameterized progress. It does not prove that randomized polynomial-time algorithms are impossible. The BPP question remains a dated source-open question after the bounded later-work check recorded here.
why: This asks whether random computation alone can efficiently decide a canonical structural equivalence problem. Nonisomorphism has efficient interactive verification, but the help of an unbounded prover is an additional resource. Settling the BPP question would locate ordinary graph comparison more precisely between efficient deterministic algorithms, randomized algorithms and stronger forms of verification.

The corrected general upper bound and the full introduction of Neuen’s 2026 survey were checked, alongside targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026. No verified general BPP algorithm or separation was found. The 2026 deterministic-status statement is not being used as a theorem about BPP, and the bounded search is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

These parameter-dependent results do not supply an all-graph BPP decider.

title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
importance_reason: A central longstanding simultaneous time-space question for the complete problem of nondeterministic logspace, with a broad graph-algorithmic interpretation and a substantial gap between known upper bounds and the target.
formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
definitions:
For an integer \(v\ge1\), the directed graph \(G=([v],E)\) has \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and \(E\subseteq[v]\times[v]\). Loops are allowed, and repeated edges have no separate meaning. The graph may have cycles, arbitrary in- and out-degree and arbitrarily many paths. No planarity, acyclicity, uniqueness, few-path or connectivity promise is imposed. The marked vertices satisfy \(s,t\in[v]\).

Reachability means that for some integer \(\ell\ge0\) there are vertices \(u_0,\ldots,u_\ell\) with \(u_0=s\), \(u_\ell=t\) and \((u_i,u_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i<\ell\). The zero-edge path makes every vertex reachable from itself. Whenever reachability holds, a path with at most \(v-1\) edges also exists. The required output is one membership bit; a path itself need not be output.

Use the explicit binary encoding \(1^v0\), followed by the \(v^2\) adjacency-matrix bits in row-major order, followed by fixed-width binary encodings of \(s,t\). Each vertex field has \(b_v=\lceil\log_2(v+1)\rceil\) bits and must represent an integer between \(1\) and \(v\). The total length is
\[N=v+1+v^2+2b_v.\]
There are no trailing fields. Any binary string failing this format is rejected. The machine must also meet the same time and space bounds on malformed inputs, measured by their actual length. This representation is polynomially related to the vertex count; it is not a succinct circuit description of an exponentially large graph.

The machine has one two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of ordinary work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, initially blank. Each step changes the finite control, reads or writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the total number of steps until its accept/reject halt, in the worst case. Space is the maximum number of work-tape cells ever visited during the run, multiplied by a fixed number of bits sufficient to encode a tape symbol. In particular all counters, indices, remembered input bits and temporary data count toward space. Input storage and the finite control do not count. The single decision bit is the halting state, so no uncharged output tape can be used as working memory.

No random bits, nondeterministic choices, quantum register, oracle, advice, writable input or extra catalytic memory are available. The same finite program and constants work for all graph orders and all valid and malformed inputs. An algorithm may depend on the fixed encoding, but cannot be chosen separately for each graph. The input is read sequentially by its head rather than supplied as a unit-cost adjacency oracle; scanning it is charged to time.

For an ordinary language of binary strings, SC means decidability by a single uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound and a fixed-power logarithmic space bound as above. It differs from merely supplying one polynomial-time algorithm and another polylogarithmic-space algorithm. The exponent \(k\) is allowed to be any fixed positive integer; the target does not specifically demand logarithmic or squared-logarithmic space.

Equivalently, the question is \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{SC}\). Here NL consists of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine with logarithmic charged work space and a fixed polynomial clock on every branch, accepting an input exactly when at least one branch accepts. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions, and those reductions preserve membership in SC. In particular, \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{NL}\) would imply an affirmative answer, but this card asks only for the weaker simultaneous bounds and does not assert the converse.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the simultaneous-bound existence statement. An affirmative answer must give one exact deterministic decider for all directed graphs and prove its polynomial time and fixed-power logarithmic space bounds with constants independent of the instance. A negative answer must prove that no such decider exists: for every correct uniform decider and every proposed constants, some input violates at least one bound. Separate algorithms meeting separate bounds, a restriction to a special graph family, or a simulation with randomness, advice or catalytic memory is insufficient.
context:
Exercise 9 explicitly asks whether PATH is in SC and points out that Savitch’s theorem does not settle this. The small-space simulation uses superpolynomial time, while usual graph traversal uses much more than polylogarithmic space.

Barnes, Buss, Ruzzo and Schieber give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with space \(v/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log v})}\). This is sublinear but remains far larger than any fixed power of \(\log v\). Their introduction also separates lower bounds for restricted graph-exploration models from bounds for general Turing computation.

The 2025 paper studies quantum logspace on directed graphs with bounded path counts and reviews deterministic simultaneous bounds for such restricted instances. Its promises and computational model are different from an unrestricted deterministic reachability algorithm.

The February 2026 preprint trades ordinary workspace against an additional tape of catalytic memory. Catalytic storage is extra writable memory that must eventually be restored, and is absent from this card’s model; a small ordinary-workspace bound in that model is not the claimed SC containment.
why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

title: P versus NP intersect coNP
importance_reason: Tests whether two-sided efficiently checkable evidence guarantees efficient computation, with relevance to total search and cryptographic candidates.
formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
definitions: For a binary string \(x\), write \(n=|x|\). Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\) means that there are one polynomial \(q\) and two deterministic polynomial-time Boolean verifiers \(V_1,V_0\) such that, for every \(x\), \[x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_1(x,y)=1,\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_0(x,z)=1.\] In particular, no input has accepted certificates of both types and every input has an accepted certificate of one type. Verifier time is polynomial in the combined bit length. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decided on every input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^k\) steps for fixed constants \(C,k\). The proposed language must defeat every such machine and polynomial bound. Algorithms have no advice, oracle or random bits. This is a total language-class comparison, not a promise problem or a requirement to output certificates. Witness lengths and machines are uniform over all input lengths.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a language in \((\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP})\setminus\mathrm P\), including both verifiers and an unconditional uniform lower bound, or prove that every language satisfying the two verifier conditions belongs to \(\mathrm P\). An unproved hardness assumption, a promise-problem separation or hardness of finding witnesses alone does not decide this statement.
context:
A deterministic polynomial-time decision supplies trivial short certificates for either answer, so P is contained in NP ∩ coNP. The conjecture asks whether this containment is strict: efficiently checking either kind of answer need not give a method for deciding which kind exists.

Wigderson states this as Conjecture 3.9. The surrounding discussion uses problems such as linear programming and primality to illustrate that two-sided verification alone is not evidence of a separation; those problems have deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.

A strict separation would imply P ≠ NP, but the P versus NP question alone does not specify whether the intersection is larger than P. Search problems associated with finding certificates introduce another task and are not the language-class comparison asked here.
why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.
status_note: Conjecture 3.9 is open in the saved August 2019 draft. The formulation was checked against that source on 13 September 2026. The bounded related-literature check supplied no verified resolution or new status theorem, so the card remains source_open rather than claiming exhaustive current verification.

title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted threshold-of-threshold circuits
importance_reason: Unrestricted threshold-of-threshold lower bounds test the power of a basic shallow circuit model.
formal: Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), in the source’s sense \(\mathrm{NP}\), and constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\), such that every unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit computing \(f_n\) has at least \(2^{cn}\) gates for every \(n\geq n_0\)?
definitions: A threshold gate on Boolean inputs \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\) outputs one if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_i z_i\geq\theta\), where all weights \(w_i\) and the threshold \(\theta\) are arbitrary real numbers of either sign. An unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit on \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) consists of any finite number \(s\) of such gates applied to the original input bits, followed by one threshold output gate applied to their outputs. Arbitrary fan-in, fan-out and length-dependent weights are permitted; omitted inputs can have weight zero. Its size is \(s+1\), the number of threshold gates, not total weight magnitude or the number of bits encoding weights. Constants and direct input-to-output connections can be represented by additional threshold gates, changing size by at most \(n+1\), which does not alter exponential-size existence. Computation must agree with \(f_n\) on every input, with no approximation. The family is explicit in the definition of Section 1.5.1 of the source: there exist a polynomial \(q\) and a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \(f_n(x)=1\) precisely when some binary witness \(y\) with \(|y|\leq q(n)\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). Verifier cost is measured on a standard bit Turing machine. Neither circuit weights nor circuits are required to be uniform or polynomially bounded. The exponential target is interpreted as \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for all sufficiently large input lengths, with one fixed positive exponent coefficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof by specifying one uniform NP verifier defining the family and proving the stated exponential gate lower bound for every sufficiently large length, or prove that no such NP family and constants exist. A counting argument without an NP witness family, a bound on total weight, a restriction on signs or magnitudes, or a conditional complexity consequence does not meet the full target.
context:
Research Problem 11.40 asks for an exponential lower bound for unrestricted depth-two threshold circuits. The preceding discussion obtains strong bounds under restrictions on the weights; dropping such restrictions is the point of the question.

The source explicitly defines “explicit” in Section 1.5.1 through polynomial-time verification, corresponding to NP. Requiring the chosen function to lie in P would add a stronger condition that is not imposed here. Counting the existence of hard truth tables without this uniform verification condition would miss the intended explicit lower bound.

Chen’s 2018 paper describes even superpolynomial unrestricted depth-two threshold lower bounds for NEXP as a major frontier and develops conditional implications. Those implications do not supply the unconditional exponential lower bound for an NP family required by this card.
why: Depth-two threshold circuits are a basic model of two layers of weighted Boolean decisions. An exponential lower bound with unrestricted real weights would establish a strong limit on this expressive shallow architecture for an explicitly verifiable computational task.
status_note: The source states this challenge as open. The source-wide explicitness convention and circuit model were rechecked on 13 September 2026, together with the abstract of Chen’s subsequent work and a limited later-work search. No unconditional resolution was verified; this is not an exhaustive status review, and status remains source_open.

title: Black-Box Hypothesis
importance_reason: A broad foundational hypothesis about the computational value of program descriptions, implying a major complexity separation and supported by a continuing theory of restricted variants.
formal:
Is every semantic property of Boolean functions that is decidable in randomized polynomial time from a circuit description also decidable in randomized polynomial time from only input-output queries and a circuit-size bound?

More precisely, for every family of total predicates \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{2^n}\to\{0,1\}\), does
\[F\in\mathrm{wbBPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\in\mathrm{bbBPP}\]
hold under the definitions below? The reverse implication follows from polynomial-time circuit evaluation, so this is the usual equality formulation of the Black-Box Hypothesis. The property is defined on every truth table, and a white-box algorithm must be correct for every circuit description of that truth table.
question_excerpt: The main statement, which we will call here ‘the Black-Box Hypothesis’, remains open.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge0\), a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) has the length-\(2^n\) truth table \(\operatorname{tt}(f)\), ordered lexicographically by input. A property is an arbitrary family \(F=(F_n)_{n\ge0}\) of total Boolean predicates on these tables. It need not be invariant under permutations of the input variables or table positions. Its semantic character means that two circuits computing the same \(n\)-input function have the same required property value.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. Wires may share gate outputs; unrestricted depth is allowed. Unused designated input vertices are retained. Its size \(s(C)\) is the number of vertices plus wires, and its computed function is \(f_C\). Define \(s(f)=\min\{s(C):f_C=f\}\). Counting input vertices is a harmless explicit convention because the black-box resource bound includes \(n\).

Descriptions list all vertices in topological order, their types and earlier incoming indices, followed by the output index; integers use self-delimiting binary fields. This gives a polynomial-time parsable encoding of length polynomial in \(s(C)+1\), including all \(n\) input vertices. Any fixed encoding with these properties gives the same polynomial-time target. Malformed descriptions are rejected.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{wbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,k\) such that \(A\) halts on every input and every random-bit sequence within \(c(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is description length, and
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr[A(\operatorname{desc}(C))=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f_C))]\ge2/3.\]
The same machine must work across all sizes and arities and on every representation of a function, including padded or redundant circuits. The acceptance probabilities for different representations need not be equal; each must give the correct Boolean property value with the stated error bound.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{bbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(d,\ell\) such that \(B^f(1^n,1^m)\) halts within \(d(n+m+1)^\ell\) steps on every random-bit sequence, and
\[\forall n\ge0\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\ \forall m\ge1,\quad m\ge s(f)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[B^f(1^n,1^m)=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f))]\ge2/3.\]
Here \(m\) is an integer upper bound, not necessarily the minimum circuit size. Both parameters are in unary. A query consists of an explicitly written \(n\)-bit string \(x\); the oracle returns \(f(x)\) in one step. Writing and manipulating the query counts toward time. Invalid-length queries return a fixed zero bit. Queries may be adaptive, and all computation between queries also counts. Thus the bound is on running time, not merely the number of oracle calls. The same machine and polynomial work for all valid bounds \(m\). If \(m<s(f)\), no correctness is required, but the running-time bound remains.

Both machines use independent fair random bits, and all probabilities above are over those bits for each fixed input or oracle. They have no advice or other oracle. In the black-box case, \(f\) and the unary parameters are the only supplied information about the function; no circuit, truth table, distribution on circuits or special representation is given. The circuit-size promise in this definition does not turn \(F_n\) into a partial property: \(F_n\) is defined on every Boolean function.

The quantifiers allow \(A,B\) and their polynomial constants to depend on \(F\). The conclusion is existence of a suitable \(B\) for every white-box decidable property, not an additional requirement of an effective procedure that transforms arbitrary machine descriptions into black-box algorithms.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal implication. A proof must establish a uniform black-box algorithm with the stated total running-time and pointwise error guarantees for every total semantic property in white-box BPP. A refutation must specify one such property and a correct white-box BPP algorithm and prove that no black-box BPP algorithm decides it under the supplied-size-bound model. A property defined only on a promised family of circuits, a distinction between two encodings of the same function, or a lower bound only for nonadaptive queries does not alone meet this criterion.
context:
The 2017 source identifies this as the total-property form of the scaled-down Rice’s theorem conjecture originating in work on program obfuscation. It distinguishes the still-open hypothesis from conditional counterexamples to a promise version; those counterexamples do not decide a property on every circuit.

The authors prove consequences of particular kinds of hypothetical counterexamples, including ones with highly sensitive low-complexity functions. These are conditional implications for circuit satisfiability, rather than a general proof or disproof of the hypothesis.

The 2021 paper retains the original hypothesis as open and studies other combinations of analysts and represented computations. Its positive results for restricted circuit analysts, and its equivalence involving nondeterministic circuits as boxes, change the computational models and do not settle ordinary circuits with uniform BPP analysts.

The cost of black-box computation includes the unary circuit-size bound. This avoids demanding a polynomial-in-arity algorithm for properties of functions whose smallest circuits are already exponentially large, and makes the two kinds of access comparable.
why: The hypothesis asks whether reading an efficient program can reveal any efficiently decidable fact about its function that could not also be learned efficiently by running the function on selected inputs. It connects the limits of program analysis with circuit complexity and obfuscation. Its truth would imply that NP is not contained in BPP, while restricted failures have known consequences for the complexity of circuit satisfiability.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the 2017 conference paper Sections 2–3.1 and the 2021 paper introduction and results overview. The latter explicitly calls the original hypothesis open; its proved variants do not use the same pair of computational models. A bounded later-work search found no matching unconditional resolution. Conditional consequences quoted from these sources were checked for scope, not independently reproved.
progress: 2017-12-01: The publisher releases the MFCS formulation with explicit unary arity and size inputs, the wbBPP/bbBPP definitions and conditional consequences of particular counterexamples. | 2021-08-18: MFCS publishes a broader framework connecting several restricted black-box hypotheses to lower bounds while explicitly leaving the original hypothesis open.
working_summary: The Black-Box Hypothesis compares access to a Boolean circuit’s code with access to its input-output behavior. It concerns total semantic properties that a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm decides correctly on every circuit representation. The proposed black-box algorithm receives unary input length and circuit-size bounds and may make adaptive evaluations of the function. Its total running time, including queries, must be polynomial in those bounds with error at most one third on each input. Known restricted-model results and promise-property counterexamples do not settle this general hypothesis.

title: Does NP-hardness of MCSP imply circuit lower bounds for EXP?
importance_reason: Whether ordinary NP-hardness of circuit minimization entails exponential-time circuit lower bounds is a central connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.
formal: If the Minimum Circuit Size Problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, must \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly? The hypothesis uses unrestricted ordinary polynomial-time reductions, with no locality, uniform-\(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) or naturalness promise.
question_excerpt: We conjecture that the consequence of Theorem 1.3 can be strengthened to \(\mathrm{EXP} 6\subset  \mathrm{P}\)/poly , and that MCSP is (unconditionally) not NP-hard under uniform […]
definitions: An MCSP input is the complete truth table \(t\in \{0,1\}^{2^{n}}\) of a Boolean function on \(n\ge 1\) input bits, in lexicographic order, together with a nonnegative integer size threshold s in binary. It is accepted if some Boolean circuit of size at most s computes that function. Circuits are finite acyclic graphs over binary AND and OR, unary NOT, input variables and constants 0,1, with one designated output and unrestricted sharing. Size counts noninput gates, including constant gates. The total encoded input length counts the truth table, threshold and delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. NP-hardness means that for every language L in NP there is a deterministic polynomial-time map r such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(r(x)\in\)MCSP. NP consists of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup _{k\ge 1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{k}}); \mathrm{P}\)/poly consists of languages decided by families of Boolean circuits whose sizes are bounded by a polynomial in input length, with no uniformity condition on their construction. \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly means that some language in EXP has no such polynomial-size circuit family.
answer_criterion: Prove the conditional implication or its logical negation in these exact reduction and circuit models. Deriving only \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\) or \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly is a weaker consequence. A theorem for a restricted reduction class or for partial, promise or approximate circuit minimization does not prove the stated implication.
context:
MCSP tests whether an explicit truth table has a small circuit. An NP-hardness proof would relate efficient reductions to the same lower bounds that the output instances ask us to establish.

The source derives \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly, and consequently \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\), from ordinary polynomial-time NP-hardness. These statements do not assert that EXP itself lacks polynomial-size circuits.

The original source also discusses stronger restrictions on reductions. The retained card selects the general implication to \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly and does not combine it with the separate uniform-\(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) reduction conjecture.
why: Whether ordinary NP-hardness of circuit minimization entails exponential-time circuit lower bounds is a central connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.
status_note: The original conjecture and the 2017 journal consequences were checked. The stronger EXP nonuniform lower bound is not established by the weaker known consequence; no resolution was located in the bounded later-work search.
progress: 2017: The journal treatment records weaker consequences of polynomial-time NP-hardness; the stronger EXP nonuniform lower bound is the selected conjectural consequence.
working_summary: MCSP asks whether a fully listed Boolean function has a small circuit. The question concerns what proving its ordinary NP-hardness would force elsewhere in complexity theory. The proposed consequence is that some exponential-time language requires superpolynomial circuits. Existing consequences separate EXP from smaller intersections or randomized classes and do not yield that circuit lower bound. The target captures a major proposed connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.

title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
importance_reason: Connects the arithmetic nature of numbers to an elementary resource bound on computing their digits.
formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in\)[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b- 1; a\) terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(\mathrm{P}(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.
context:
For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.
why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked 2024 research paper and June 2026 thesis abstract. The May 2026 automata paper uses a different input representation. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. A June 2026 listing titled “FIS Application: Hartmanis-Stearns” supplied no theorem statement or full text at https://uvsmpublications.com/publications/fis-application-hartmanis-stearns/ and is not evidence of a resolution. Proofs were not independently audited.

working_summary: The question concerns a fixed machine that prints all digits of a real number with bounded delay between outputs. Every rational number permits this because its expansion is eventually periodic. The conjecture says that any irrational number generated this quickly must be transcendental. It quantifies over unrestricted deterministic multitape machines, beyond the restricted automata covered by known partial results.
