The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.
why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.
status_note: The checked primary bounds and the CMU Spring 2025 source leave expected linear-time sorting across all word lengths open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in \([n]\) concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.
progress: 2002: Han–Thorup achieve \(O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\) expected time and linear space for arbitrary word-sized integer keys. | 2004: Han’s journal paper gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) time and linear space, following STOC 2002. | 2014: Belazzougui–Brodal–Nielsen extend expected linear time to \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\). | 2025: The CMU integer-sorting lecture retains linear sorting for arbitrary word lengths as an open question and distinguishes polynomial-size universes.
working_summary: Integer sorting can inspect the bits of keys instead of treating them only as objects to compare. The question asks for one always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm taking expected linear time for every permitted word length. The constant must remain uniform when keys occupy much more than logarithmically many bits. Ordinary radix sorting handles smaller universes but its number of passes can grow. This tests whether powerful word operations can completely remove the asymptotic overhead of ordering an arbitrary list of machine words.

title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
importance_reason: A long-standing structured sorting question: only 2n real parameters generate n² values, yet converting known comparison savings into optimal total time remains unresolved. Documented geometric reductions and connections to convolution give the question significance beyond one sorting routine.
focus_reason: Sorting all pairwise sums is a classical structured comparison problem: the output is quadratic, but exploiting the inherited order with equally efficient total computation remains the target. It adds real-key comparison algorithms alongside word-RAM integer sorting and data structures.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.
context:
The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

For bounded-integer inputs on a word RAM, a linear-time algorithm for sorting arbitrary word-sized integers would also sort the explicitly generated pairwise sums in quadratic time, allowing a constant-factor increase in word length for the sums. The present target instead allows arbitrary exact real inputs, without floor or bit extraction. An integer-sorting result therefore does not automatically answer this real-RAM question.
why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The \(2017/2018\) decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.
progress: 1976: Fredman proves an \(O(n^{2})\) comparison bound for sorting \(X+Y\); this does not provide quadratic total running time. | 1992–1995: Lambert and Steiger–Streinu give algorithms combining \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons with \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total time. | 2014: The necklace/convolution paper explicitly retains quadratic-time sorting on the real RAM as open while proving faster algorithms for more limited convolution outputs. | 2017 / STOC 2018: Kane–Lovett–Moran obtain \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) depth using 8-sparse linear tests. The bound concerns decision-tree queries and excludes output and general computational costs.
working_summary: Given two lists of n numbers, form every sum consisting of one number from each list. The task is to sort these quadratically many sums as quickly as possible. They have substantial inherited order, so they are not an arbitrary collection of unrelated values. The source distinguishes having few comparisons from implementing those comparisons with equally small total running time. Removing avoidable overhead would improve both structured sorting and geometric problems whose events are ordered by pairwise sums.

title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
importance_reason: The question concerns the general power of sparsification, linear sketches, or adversary-robust summaries, which are widely reused algorithmic tools.
focus_reason: A universal cut-preserving reduction of hypergraphs to few weighted hyperedges is a broad compression target supporting many downstream algorithms. Its focus is the size of a combinatorial sparsifier, with no query-interface guarantee.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.
context:
A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.
why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.
status_note: The original source permits arbitrary weighted replacement hyperedges on the same vertex set. The reviewed general upper bound has a logarithmic factor; later sketching and streaming-space results do not themselves remove it. A bounded 13 September 2026 later-work search did not locate a matching existence theorem or refutation. Cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2012: Batson–Spielman–Srivastava achieve the graph edge-count benchmark through spectral sparsification. | 2018: Krauthgamer poses the \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) same-vertex hypergraph existence question. | 2020: Chen–Khanna–Nagda obtain \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges, eliminating the prior rank dependence. | 2024: Near-optimal sketching addresses bit complexity, with logarithmic factors retained. | 2025 / 2026: Insertion-only streaming space improves without proving the exact edge-count target.
working_summary: A hypergraph cut counts the total weight of hyperedges meeting both sides of a vertex partition. A cut sparsifier replaces the hypergraph by a smaller weighted hypergraph that approximately preserves every cut at once. The question asks whether O(n/epsilon squared) hyperedges always suffice for multiplicative error epsilon. This matches the natural target from ordinary graphs, while a hyperedge can involve arbitrarily many vertices. The size measure counts hyperedges rather than their total incidence size, making the project specifically about how many distinct multiway interactions must be retained.

title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
importance_reason: Relates directed reachability structure to near-linear algorithms and isolates a basic obstruction behind shortcutting and parallel graph computation.
focus_reason: A constant-factor estimate of the largest finite directed distance in near-linear time is a broad algorithmic target alongside sorting, sparsification and offline comparisons. It is the highest-ranked remaining candidate in this category; its saved importance score and statement are preserved.
formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least \(2/3\) in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving \(D(G)=0\) on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.
answer_criterion: Give a randomized algorithm and one absolute constant C meeting the displayed guarantee in near-linear time on every directed graph, or prove that no constant approximation is possible with that time bound.
context:
A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.

The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.
why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.
progress: 2026: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved. | 2026: Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.
working_summary: Reachability diameter measures the largest finite shortest-path distance in a directed graph. Unreachable ordered pairs are omitted so that disconnected directions do not make the answer automatically infinite. The question asks for a constant-factor estimate in near-linear time on every unweighted directed graph. Simple searches from arbitrary pivots can miss a long directed route. A successful method would summarize the extent of reachable routes without computing distances from every vertex or imposing strong connectivity.

title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
importance_reason: This asks whether a fundamental pseudopolynomial problem can be solved at essentially its actual input and output size, avoiding a large unused numerical universe.
formal: Do there exist a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(b\ge0\) that, given \(n\ge1\) positive integers \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\le t\) and an integer \(t\ge1\), output exactly the distinct values in \(S(X,t)=\{\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}:I\subseteq[n]\}\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}\) in at most \(C(n+|S(X,t)|)(\log(n+t+2))^{b}\) operations?
definitions: The input is an explicitly listed multiset; repeated values are allowed and each index can be selected at most once. The empty subset contributes zero. Output every attainable value once, in any order, with no requirement to list subsets or witnesses. Inputs exceeding the threshold can be discarded when represented in the same word model. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+t+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The word-size constant and all time constants are independent of both \(n\) and \(t\). The target permits polylogarithmic dependence on the numerical threshold, but no linear scan of its universe unless covered by the stated output bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Subset Sum may have very few attainable values below the threshold even when the threshold is huge. Output-sensitive complexity measures the set that must actually be produced, together with reading the input.

Bringmann and Nakos explicitly ask for near-linear time in the number of attainable sums. Their algorithm gives a four-thirds power dependence on the output size.

Chan derandomizes pseudopolynomial Subset Sum in 2026 and also derandomizes the \(\widetilde O(|S|^{4/3})\) and \(\widetilde O(|S|\sqrt n)\) output-sensitive bounds. Those results do not attain the stated near-linear output-sensitive endpoint.
why: This asks whether a fundamental pseudopolynomial problem can be solved at essentially its actual input and output size, avoiding a large unused numerical universe.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The explicit input-reading term, multiplicities, truncation and word length are fixed. Algorithms is the editorial home because the target is a basic pseudopolynomial computation measured by its support size, closely tied to convolution; it is not counting the number of solutions.
progress: 2021: An output-sensitive algorithm achieves \(\widetilde O(|S|^{4/3})\) time, with input-reading costs understood. | 2026: Known pseudopolynomial and output-sensitive bounds are derandomized, leaving the near-linear output endpoint unanswered.
working_summary: The input is a multiset of positive integers and a threshold. The task is to enumerate the distinct attainable subset sums at most that threshold. The question asks for near-linear time in the explicit input and the actual number of output values. Known pseudopolynomial algorithms and output-sensitive improvements do not reach this endpoint. The target avoids spending linear time on a large numerical universe containing few attainable sums.

title: Small Implicit Graph Conjecture
importance_reason: A named surviving implicit-representation conjecture that tests when global graph-class entropy supports logarithmic local labels.
formal: Does every hereditary small graph class \(\mathcal C\) admit an adjacency labeling scheme using at most \(K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits per vertex on every \(n\)-vertex graph in \(\mathcal C\), for some constant \(K\) depending only on \(\mathcal C\)?
question_excerpt: However, it is still unknown if all such classes admit an implicit representation (see [12] for more details on implicit representation of small classes).
definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under isomorphism; it is hereditary when every induced subgraph of every member also belongs to it. Write \(\mathcal C_n\) for its members with labeled vertex set \([n]\). Small means that there is a constant \(c\geq1\) with \(|\mathcal C_n|\leq n!c^n\) for every \(n\geq1\). A labeling scheme consists of an encoder and a decoder, fixed for the class and all input lengths. The encoder, given an adjacency-matrix encoding of \(G\in\mathcal C_n\), assigns one finite binary label to each vertex. The decoder receives only two labels and returns whether the corresponding distinct vertices are adjacent; it receives no graph description, class-membership oracle, additional table or external value of \(n\). Any size information needed by the decoder must be encoded within the labels. Both are deterministic algorithms, with no imposed time bound; encoding must halt on every graph in the class and decoding must halt on every pair of finite labels. Outside-class encoder behavior is unrestricted. All answers for pairs of vertices of an input member must be exact and simultaneous. Label length is the sole resource being bounded. No polynomial-time recognition of the class is assumed. Monotone, which is a stronger condition, means closed under deletion of both vertices and edges; this question assumes only hereditary closure.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a labeling scheme and a class-dependent logarithmic length constant for every hereditary small class, or exhibit such a class and prove that no scheme satisfying these conditions exists. No efficient encoding or decoding time is required beyond the source’s algorithmic definition. A result for monotone or weakly sparse classes alone does not settle the universal claim.
context:
The saved source proves logarithmic adjacency labels for monotone small classes and explicitly conjectures the extension to hereditary small classes. Its Conjecture 9 is the Small Implicit Graph Conjecture. The earlier draft title incorrectly described the already-treated monotone case.

The broader conjecture for all hereditary classes of factorial growth is false. The sharper small-class bound limits the number of labeled graphs to a factorial times a fixed exponential, leaving a distinct question.

The 2025 follow-up proves \(O((\log n)^3)\)-bit labels for every hereditary small class and logarithmic labels for small weakly sparse classes. Weak sparsity means excluding some fixed complete bipartite graph as a subgraph; that additional restriction is absent in the general conjecture.
why: A short global description of every graph does not by itself make adjacency locally decodable from two short vertex descriptions. The conjecture asks whether a precise growth restriction and induced-subgraph closure suffice to bridge this gap.
status_note: The hereditary small conjecture is explicit in the 2024 source and repeated in the 2025 follow-up. The later abstract and algorithmic labeling definition were checked on 13 September 2026; no full logarithmic result was verified. Status is source_open.
progress: 2024: The source proves the monotone small case and states the hereditary extension as Conjecture 9. | 2025: The follow-up gives \(O((\log n)^3)\)-bit labels for hereditary small classes, and logarithmic labels under additional weak sparsity.
working_summary: An adjacency labeling scheme assigns each vertex a short binary string from which adjacency can be determined using only two labels. The conjecture asks for logarithmic labels in every hereditary class with at most a factorial times a fixed exponential number of labeled graphs. Hereditary means closed under induced subgraphs, and is weaker than closure under all subgraphs. The monotone case is known, and a 2025 follow-up proves logarithmic-cubed labels for all hereditary small classes. The question isolates when low total information content permits efficient storage in locally decodable vertex descriptions.

title: Optimal size of four-additive graph spanners
importance_reason: The +4 additive-spanner regime is the classical remaining constant-error sparsity-exponent gap, making it a central distance-compression problem rather than a peripheral parameter choice.
formal: Determine \(s_{4}(n)=\max _{G} \min _{H} |E(H)|\) up to universal multiplicative constants for integers \(n\ge 2\), where G ranges over connected simple undirected unweighted graphs on n vertices and H ranges over their spanning subgraphs satisfying \(d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+4\) for all vertices u,v.
definitions: Each original edge has length one. \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path, with \(d_{G}(u,u)=0\). A spanning subgraph H has the same vertex set and a subset of G’s edges, with unchanged unit lengths. If u,v are disconnected in H put \(d_{H}(u,v)=\infty\), so the requirement forces H to be connected. The lower inequality \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) follows from being a subgraph. Both extrema exist because there are finitely many graphs on a fixed labeled vertex set and \(H=G\) is feasible. The cost is number of retained edges; neither construction time nor weights, shortcuts, missing vertices, terminal subsets or faults are part of the model. New weighted edges would be an emulator and are not allowed. Restricting to connected inputs only removes disconnected bookkeeping; applying a universal bound componentwise recovers its usual all-graph form.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\), constants \(a,A>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that a \(g(n)\le s_{4}(n)\le A g(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\). Prove a universal existence upper bound and a matching worst-case lower bound. Polynomial exponents alone do not settle this constant-factor target if a growing logarithmic gap remains. This is an asymptotic extremal-size question, not an additive 0.01 estimate of an integer function.
context:
The survey asks whether +4 error can be achieved with \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges, compared with the known exponent \(7/5\). This is a major gap in the sparsity of additive distance-preserving subgraphs.

The 2025 deterministic construction improves construction time while retaining the soft-\(O(n^{7/5})\) edge bound. The source does not supply an \(n^{4/3}\) upper bound.

Six-additive spanners achieve the \(4/3\) exponent, and general lower bounds obstruct beating that exponent for constant additive error. The +4 regime therefore asks whether a basic sparsity threshold can be reached with a smaller distance error.

The original \(O(n^{4/3})\) conjecture remains the candidate sharp upper bound; standard high-girth examples require \(\Omega (n^{4/3})\) edges. The retained question asks for the actual optimal size even if that conjecture fails. It is not asserted to be equivalent to the original yes/no question.

The question of how additive error must grow when only \(O(n)\) edges are allowed is separately retained as TCS-6785. This card keeps the important +4 regime, rather than bundling weighted, variable-error and failure-tolerant models.
why: The +4 additive-spanner regime is the classical remaining constant-error sparsity-exponent gap, making it a central distance-compression problem rather than a peripheral parameter choice.
status_note: The +4 sparsity gap remains in the 2025 primary source. The broader variable-error linear-size question is retained separately as TCS-6785.
progress: 2020: The survey lists the +\(4, O(n^{4/3})\) question in Section 8.4 as an open problem. | 2025: Qi retains the soft-\(O(n^{7/5})\) edge bound while improving construction time and determinism.

working_summary: An additive spanner keeps original graph edges while limiting the increase in every pairwise distance. This card fixes the increase to at most four and asks for the optimal worst-case number of edges. The target is the complete asymptotic function up to universal constant factors. The familiar candidate is \(n^{4/3}\), while recent constructions still have exponent \(7/5\) up to logarithmic factors. This gap is a fundamental unresolved regime of distance compression, and the variable-error linear-size tradeoff has its own card.

title: Quasipolynomial dependence on vertices for hypergraph isomorphism
importance_reason: A central isomorphism parameter-dependence question for general set systems, with consequences for symmetry algorithms using structural decompositions.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that decides isomorphism of two explicitly represented hypergraphs in time \[2^{C(\log_2(n+2))^{a}}\,N^{b},\] for fixed constants \(C,a,b\geq1\), where \(n\) is the maximum number of underlying vertices and \(N\) is the combined input bit length?
definitions: A hypergraph is a finite pair \((V,\mathcal E)\) with \(V=[n]\) and \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\). Empty hyperedges and isolated vertices are allowed; edges have no colors, order, weights or repeated copies. The input lists the vertices and every hyperedge explicitly by its incidence bit vector; vertex counts and list lengths are included in the binary encoding. Input length \(N\) therefore includes all incidences and at least \(n\) symbols. An isomorphism from \((V_1,\mathcal E_1)\) to \((V_2,\mathcal E_2)\) is a bijection \(\pi:V_1\to V_2\) with \(\{\pi(e):e\in\mathcal E_1\}=\mathcal E_2\). The algorithm must decide whether one exists and must be correct on every well-formed input; unequal vertex counts imply rejection. Time is worst-case bit time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice or oracle. Neither the hyperedge size nor the number of hyperedges is bounded polynomially in \(n\). All constants and exponents are uniform over both parameters. Replacing incidence vectors by explicit incidence lists changes length by at most a polynomial and preserves the requested two-parameter bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with fixed constants satisfying the displayed two-parameter bound, or prove that no such deterministic uniform algorithm exists. A quasipolynomial bound in the full incidence-graph size, or a polynomial exponent depending on the number of vertices or maximum hyperedge size, does not meet the target.
context:
The source distinguishes a quasipolynomial dependence on the number of vertices from a polynomial dependence on the possibly much larger collection of hyperedges. Encoding a hypergraph as a bipartite incidence graph does not automatically give that separation of dependencies.

Wiebking discusses a bound whose exponent on total hypergraph size depends polylogarithmically on the vertex count, and explicitly asks for the stronger bound in which the hyperedge-size exponent is constant. The same open question reappears in the outlook section.
why: This asks whether symmetry testing can depend quasipolynomially only on the underlying universe, while remaining polynomial in the amount of set-system data. It matters for hypergraphs with many large edges and for algorithms that encode structural graph information as set systems.
status_note: The stronger separated-parameter bound is explicitly open in the 2020 source. The source passages were checked on 13 September 2026; a bounded subsequent-work search supplied no verified resolution. Status is source_open.
progress: 2020: The paper explicitly separates a vertex-dependent exponent on total hypergraph size from the desired fixed polynomial dependence on the number of hyperedges, and leaves the stronger bound open.
working_summary: Hypergraph isomorphism asks whether a relabeling of vertices makes two explicitly listed set systems identical. The target running time is quasipolynomial in the number of vertices and polynomial in the full input size. The exponent on input size must be a fixed constant even when many hyperedges are listed. The source explains why a quasipolynomial bound in the larger incidence representation does not automatically provide this guarantee. A resolution would extend efficient symmetry testing to rich set systems over comparatively small universes.

title: Complexity of planar 3-edge-colorability
importance_reason: A fundamental unresolved planar edge-coloring decision problem at maximum degree three, closely tied to the boundary of Four-Color-Theorem consequences.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple planar graph \(G\), decides whether its edges can be properly colored with three colors?
question_excerpt: The computational complexity of the 3-Edge Colorability-problem for planar graphs remains open, while it is known to be NP-complete already for 3-regular, but not necessarily […]
definitions: The input graph is undirected, without loops or parallel edges, and encoded by an adjacency matrix on the labeled vertex set \([n]\). The planarity promise means it admits a crossing-free embedding in the plane; no embedding is required as input. A proper three-edge-coloring is a function \(\chi:E(G)\to\{1,2,3\}\) assigning different colors to any two distinct edges with a common endpoint. Graphs may be disconnected, have bridges or isolated vertices, and need not be regular. A vertex of degree greater than three forces rejection, but no other special degree pattern or augmentation promise is imposed. Running time is worst-case bit time \(C(n+1)^k\) for fixed constants on a deterministic Turing machine, with no advice, randomness or oracle. The answer must be exact on every planar input. A total-language version may reject nonplanar encodings, since planarity can itself be tested in polynomial time. This card asks for decision, not for a prescribed structural characterization of all colorable graphs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all planar inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. NP-hardness together with a Lean theorem conditional on P ≠ NP establishes conditional intractability and must be labeled as such; it is not by itself an unconditional refutation. Solving only cubic graphs or graphs admitting a particular augmentation is insufficient.
context:
The source poses this as Question 1 and explains why the Four-Color Theorem settles the cubic bridgeless case without settling all subcubic planar graphs. A graph with degree-two vertices need not lie in a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph.

The 2022 paper gives a polynomial-time test for augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph. Its concluding discussion keeps general planar three-edge-colorability open and states a stronger proposed structural characterization.

The expanded journal article, published online in November 2025 and appearing in Algorithmica’s 2026 volume, again poses planar three-edge-colorability as an open question. Its recognition results concern specified cubic supergraphs and do not identify that augmentation task with the full coloring decision problem.
why: This is a basic unresolved coloring decision problem on planar graphs with very small maximum degree. A resolution would clarify exactly how far the algorithmic consequences of the Four-Color Theorem extend beyond regular planar graphs.
status_note: The question is open in the 2022 source and explicitly retained in the journal version published online on 25 November 2025. These source statements were checked on 13 September 2026; no subsequent resolution was verified. Status is source_open.
progress: 2022: The source gives polynomial-time recognition of graphs admitting a cubic bridgeless planar augmentation while explicitly leaving general planar three-edge-colorability open. | 2025-11-25: The expanded journal version retains the general coloring question and distinguishes it from its polynomial and hardness results for specified supergraph recognition tasks.
working_summary: Three-edge-colorability asks whether the edges of a graph can receive three colors with different colors on every pair meeting at a vertex. The selected question asks for the computational complexity of this decision problem on planar graphs. The source studies a sufficient route through augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph, where three-edge-colorability follows from the Four-Color Theorem. It also discusses a conjectured characterization for two-connected planar graphs of maximum degree three. A full classification would determine whether the remaining planar cases admit an efficient coloring test or conceal an NP-hard obstruction.

title: Planarity dichotomy for induced subdivision detection
importance_reason: A broad fixed-pattern complexity classification linking planarity to induced-subdivision detection, beyond the known isolated hardness example.
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), is it true that for every fixed finite subcubic graph \(H\), detecting an induced subdivision of \(H\) in an arbitrary input graph belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if and only if \(H\) is planar?
definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Subcubic means maximum degree at most three; \(H\) need not be connected. A subdivision of \(H\) is obtained by replacing each edge by a path of positive length, with pairwise disjoint internal vertex sets, none of which contains a vertex of \(H\). An induced subdivision in \(G\) is a set \(W\subseteq V(G)\) such that the induced graph \(G[W]\) is isomorphic to a subdivision of \(H\). Equivalently, choose distinct branch vertices for all vertices of \(H\), including its isolated vertices, and replacement paths with exactly the prescribed edges and no additional edges anywhere among the selected vertices. For each fixed \(H\), the decision problem takes only \(G\), encoded by its binary adjacency matrix, and answers whether such \(W\) exists; no degree, planarity or connectivity promise is made on \(G\). Polynomial time means a deterministic Turing machine with running time \(C_H(|V(G)|+1)^{k_H}\) for constants depending on \(H\), but not on \(G\). An algorithm need not be uniform in the pattern \(H\), which is not part of the input. Planarity means admitting a crossing-free drawing in the plane. The complexity assumption uses the ordinary uniform deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial-time language classes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal equivalence under the stated P ≠ NP hypothesis, or a proof of its negation under that hypothesis. A counterexample must identify a fixed subcubic pattern and establish the failure of the corresponding direction. Proving hardness for one nonplanar pattern, or algorithms for only some planar patterns, does not settle the whole conjecture. NP-completeness of every nonplanar case would suffice for that direction but is not silently added as a stronger required conclusion.
context:
The source proposes planarity of a fixed subcubic pattern as the complete boundary for tractable induced-subdivision detection. Its assumption P ≠ NP is essential to the stated if-and-only-if claim.

The paper exhibits a fixed subcubic pattern whose induced-subdivision containment problem is NP-complete. This establishes an obstruction within low-degree patterns but does not classify every such pattern. Induced containment additionally forbids unwanted edges between the selected paths, unlike ordinary subdivision containment.
why: A resolution would give one structural explanation for the complexity of an entire family of induced pattern-detection problems. It asks whether the geometry of the fixed pattern, rather than just its bounded degree, controls tractability.
status_note: The published 2025 paper explicitly states Conjecture 5 under P ≠ NP. The statement and model were checked on 13 September 2026; the bounded subsequent-work search supplied no verified resolution. Status is source_open.
progress: 2025: The paper proves hardness for a particular fixed subcubic induced-subdivision pattern and states the general planarity characterization as Conjecture 5.
working_summary: For a fixed graph H, induced-subdivision detection asks whether an input graph contains a subdivided copy of H as an induced subgraph. Extra edges between selected vertices are forbidden. The conjecture concerns patterns H of maximum degree three and predicts tractability exactly for planar patterns, assuming P differs from NP. Existing algorithms and hardness constructions motivate the proposed boundary. This would classify a natural family of pattern-detection problems by a geometric property of the fixed pattern itself.

title: Isomorphism dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes
importance_reason: A general finite-description dichotomy for hereditary isomorphism, asking whether finite induced obstructions eliminate intermediate complexity.
formal: For every finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite graphs, is graph isomorphism restricted to graphs containing no induced copy of a member of \(\mathcal F\) either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or complete for general graph isomorphism under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
question_excerpt: However, this statement does not carry over to forbidden induced subgraphs and the question of the existence of intermediate graph classes characterized by finitely many […]
definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple, with binary adjacency-matrix encodings. The finite forbidden family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed, not part of the input. Let \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\) contain every graph with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of \(\mathcal F\). Its isomorphism task receives two members \(G_1,G_2\) and asks whether there is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. Polynomial time means worst-case deterministic bit time bounded by a polynomial in their combined encoding length; the machine and polynomial may depend on \(\mathcal F\). Graph-isomorphism completeness means that there is a deterministic polynomial-time map from any pair of arbitrary simple graphs to a pair in \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\), preserving the YES/NO isomorphism answer. The reverse reduction is the identity. Outputs of the hardness reduction must satisfy the class promise on both YES and NO inputs. Class membership can be checked in polynomial time for fixed finite \(\mathcal F\), so a total-language formulation may reject encodings outside the class. No algorithm deciding which side applies from an input description of \(\mathcal F\) is required. The alternatives need not be disjoint if general graph isomorphism is in P; the conjecture asserts their union covers every finite forbidden family.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal dichotomy, or exhibit a fixed finite forbidden family and prove that its restricted isomorphism problem has neither property. A complete proof may use a mathematically specified classification without an effective classifier for forbidden families. A two-pattern theorem alone, a result for ordinary subgraph exclusion, or NP-hardness terminology without the required graph-isomorphism reductions does not settle the target.
context:
Schweitzer’s Conjecture 1 asks for a polynomial-time versus general-isomorphism-complete dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes. Finiteness of the forbidden induced family is essential: the discussion distinguishes conditional intermediate examples requiring infinite descriptions.

The source obtains the dichotomy for all but finitely many two-forbidden-graph cases. A classification by forbidden ordinary subgraphs also does not settle the conjecture, because induced exclusions allow a broader range of structural behavior.
why: A finite list of forbidden induced patterns is a simple and widely used graph-class description. The conjecture asks whether such finite structural restrictions always make symmetry testing tractable or retain the full difficulty of unrestricted graph isomorphism.
status_note: Conjecture 1 is explicit in the 2015 source. Its quantifiers and partial theorem were checked on 13 September 2026; the limited later-work check supplied no verified resolution for arbitrary finite forbidden families. Status is source_open.
progress: 2015: The paper states the finite-family dichotomy as Conjecture 1 and establishes the polynomial-time versus isomorphism-complete alternatives for all but finitely many two-forbidden-pattern cases.
working_summary: Hereditary graph classes can be specified by finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs. The question asks whether graph isomorphism on such a class can have complexity intermediate between polynomial time and general graph-isomorphism completeness. The source establishes broad classifications and resolves most two-forbidden-pattern cases. Results for forbidden ordinary subgraphs do not immediately extend to induced exclusions. The project seeks a dichotomy explaining whether a finite structural prohibition always makes isomorphism substantially easier or leaves its full general difficulty intact.

title: Quadratic-size submodular hypergraph sparsifiers
importance_reason: A general quadratic compression conjecture for arbitrary submodular cut objectives, including asymmetric and unbounded-range splitting functions.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that every submodular hypergraph on \(n\geq1\) vertices and every \(0<\varepsilon<1\) admit a reweighted sub-hypergraph with at most \(C n^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}\) hyperedges that simultaneously approximates every cut value within factors \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(1+\varepsilon\)?
definitions: A submodular hypergraph \(H=(V,E,(g_e)_{e\in E})\) has a finite vertex set \(V\), \(|V|=n\), a finite set \(E\subseteq2^V\) of hyperedges, and, for each \(e\), a function \(g_e:2^e\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with \(g_e(\varnothing)=0\). Submodularity means \(g_e(A\cup B)+g_e(A\cap B)\leq g_e(A)+g_e(B)\) for every \(A,B\subseteq e\). Neither symmetry under complementation nor monotonicity, bounded positive-value ratios, integral values or bounded hyperedge rank is assumed; in particular \(g_e(e)\) need not vanish. A cut is any \(S\subseteq V\) and its value is \(F_H(S)=\sum_{e\in E}g_e(S\cap e)\). A reweighted sub-hypergraph chooses \(E'\subseteq E\) and one real scalar \(w_e>0\) for each retained edge, giving \(F_{H'}(S)=\sum_{e\in E'}w_e g_e(S\cap e)\). It must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)F_H(S)\leq F_{H'}(S)\leq(1+\varepsilon)F_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\), including exact preservation of zero-valued cuts. Size counts retained hyperedges, not total incidences, splitting-function descriptions or bits. This is an existence theorem: no input-oracle representation, construction time, coefficient bit bound or random failure probability is imposed. The constant \(C\) must be independent of every hypergraph parameter and of \(\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a universal constant and the stated simultaneous reweighted sparsifier bound, or prove its negation. A refutation must rule out every possible universal constant, not just one proposed bound. Bounds with additional logarithmic losses, a worse power of inverse accuracy, restricted splitting functions, or newly invented splitting functions do not establish the conjecture.
context:
Theorem 1.4 of Kenneth and Krauthgamer gives an \(O(n^3/\varepsilon^2)\) reweighted sparsifier for arbitrary nonnegative submodular splitting functions. Their Conjecture 1.14 asks whether the vertex dependence can be reduced to quadratic, while retaining the stated accuracy dependence and the original splitting functions.

A July 2026 preprint proves a \(\widetilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^4)\) bound when all functions take values in a fixed finite integer range. Its Theorem 1.5 and following discussion explicitly leave arbitrary nonnegative submodular functions outside that result.

An August 2026 preprint reports \(O(n/\varepsilon^2)\) sparsifiers for sums of symmetric submodular functions. Symmetry is an additional promise absent here; it does not cover arbitrary directed or asymmetric splitting costs.
why: The question asks whether rich higher-order cut objectives always have representations using quadratically many original terms, independent of their complexity and value ranges. Such a theorem would provide a general compression guarantee across submodular optimization models.
status_note: Conjecture 1.14 is explicit in the 2024 paper. On 13 September 2026 the later-work check verified the statement, but not the proof, of a July theorem restricted to bounded integral functions and the abstract of an August symmetric-function result. Neither states the full conjectured bound for arbitrary splitting functions; status remains source_open.
progress: 2024: The source proves a general cubic bound in \(n\) and poses Conjecture 1.14 for the quadratic bound. | 2026-07-17: Theorem 1.5 of the new preprint gives a nearly quadratic bound with inverse-fourth accuracy dependence for bounded integral submodular functions. The general nonnegative case remains outside its stated theorem. | 2026-08-04: A separate preprint reports linear-size sparsifiers for symmetric submodular sums. Its abstract was checked, but the proof was not independently verified.
working_summary: A submodular hypergraph assigns each hyperedge a flexible submodular cost for being split by a cut. A sparsifier retains and reweights hyperedges so that every cut value remains approximately correct. The conjecture proposes a quadratic-in-vertices size bound with inverse-squared accuracy dependence in the source's size measure. Preserving exponentially many cuts simultaneously is the main obstacle identified there. The project seeks a compression theorem extending beyond ordinary all-or-nothing hyperedge cuts to richer models used in optimization and learning.

title: Three disjoint directed shortest paths
importance_reason: The first unresolved fixed number of directed disjoint shortest-path pairs, isolating a basic barrier in exact multi-pair routing.
formal: Does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decide whether a directed graph with positive rational arc lengths and three prescribed source-target pairs contains three mutually vertex-disjoint paths, each individually shortest between its own endpoints?
question_excerpt: This is because while k-DSP is polynomial-time solvable for constant k in undirected graphs, it remains open whether even 3-DSP over directed graphs can be […]
definitions: The input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), with \(V=[n]\), no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair, together with a length \(\ell(a)\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) for each arc and three pairs \((s_i,t_i)\in V^2\), \(i=1,2,3\). Graph incidences and all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicitly encoded in binary. A directed path follows the arcs and has no repeated vertex; a zero-arc path is permitted when its endpoints coincide. Its length is the sum of its arc lengths. The distance \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum path length, or infinity when no path exists. A valid answer YES means there are paths \(P_i\) from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\), each of length \(d_G(s_i,t_i)\), with \(V(P_i)\cap V(P_j)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Disjointness includes all terminals. Repeated terminals across different pairs therefore force NO. Distances are measured in the original graph, not after deleting other paths; minimizing the total length of three disjoint paths is a different condition. Time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine bit time polynomial in the total encoding length, including lengths. No acyclicity or planarity promise, uniqueness of shortest paths, randomness, advice or oracle is allowed. Strict positivity follows the source preliminaries; allowing zero-length directed cycles is not part of this card.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the deterministic polynomial-time decision statement or its negation for the specified positive-rational-length model. An NP-hardness reduction is a conditional negative result under P ≠ NP and must be stated with that hypothesis. A randomized algorithm alone, an algorithm for two pairs or acyclic inputs, or a solution minimizing only total path length does not settle the exact statement.
context:
The source’s congested shortest-path task includes mutually vertex-disjoint shortest paths as the congestion-one case. It states that the directed three-pair problem remains open even though fixed numbers of pairs are tractable on undirected graphs and directed acyclic graphs.

A January 2026 paper improves randomized algorithms for two disjoint shortest paths in general directed graphs. Its Open Problem 6.3 again asks for polynomial-time solvability or hardness of the three-pair case. The two-pair theorem and the three-pair question must remain separate.
why: Three pairs form a small and sharply defined test of whether directed shortest-path constraints can be coordinated efficiently. A resolution would distinguish the difficulty of selecting individually optimal routes from ordinary shortest-path computation and from undirected routing.
status_note: The 2023 source and January 2026 follow-up both state the directed three-pair question as open. Those statements and the positive-weight model were checked on 13 September 2026. No later resolution was verified; status is source_open.
progress: 2023: The paper states the directed three-disjoint-shortest-paths problem as open and uses strictly positive edge weights throughout. | 2026-01-23: The later paper improves randomized two-pair algorithms and repeats the directed three-pair question as Open Problem 6.3.
working_summary: The input specifies three source-target pairs in a directed graph with positive arc lengths. Each selected path must be shortest for its own pair in the original graph, and no vertex may belong to two paths. The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the full binary input length. A 2026 paper improves randomized two-pair algorithms but explicitly leaves three pairs unresolved. A resolution would explain whether several individually optimal directed routes can be selected efficiently while avoiding all conflicts.

title: Optimal additive error of linear-size spanners
importance_reason: The general additive-distance loss forced by a linear edge budget is a central sparsity-versus-accuracy question for graph metrics.
formal: Determine the optimal worst-case additive error \(A_c(n)\) of a spanner with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges, up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), for every fixed real constant \(c\geq1\). The graph is arbitrary, undirected and unweighted; the edge budget is genuinely linear, without hidden factors depending on \(n\).
definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. A result up to constant factors supplies a nonnegative function \(a(n,c)\) and, for each fixed \(c\), constants \(0<L_c\leq U_c<\infty\) and \(n_c\) with \(L_c a(n,c)\leq A_c(n)\leq U_c a(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_c\). Constants may depend on \(c\), never on \(n\). This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked asymptotic determination of the defined family, with matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants for every fixed edge coefficient. The upper bound must cover every input graph and the lower bound must establish matching worst cases under the same edge budget. Determining only an exponent with an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic gap does not meet this precision; a numerical tolerance of 1/100 is not an additive error on asymptotic notation.
context:
The survey’s Section 8.4, item 3, asks how much additive error is unavoidable with \(O(n)\) retained edges. Its dated bounds leave a polynomial gap between what sparse subgraphs can achieve and what some input metrics force.

Bodwin and Hoppenworth subsequently establish an \(\Omega(n^{1/7})\) additive-error lower bound for linear-size spanners, improving the lower bound quoted in the survey. This is a lower bound, not a matching determination.

The later Almost-Optimal Sublinear Additive Spanners abstract reports \(O(n^{0.403})\) additive error with \(\widetilde O(n)\) edges. That edge budget hides logarithmic factors and cannot be substituted for a fixed \(cn\) budget in this question.
why: The linear edge regime compresses a graph to a constant number of retained edges per vertex. Determining its unavoidable distance loss would quantify a fundamental limit on how accurately arbitrary graph metrics can survive such strong sparsification.

title: Polynomial-time detection of fixed pivot- and vertex-minors
importance_reason: A general algorithmic counterpart to structural graph containment, connecting width theory with transformations used in quantum graph states.
formal: For each relation \(\rho\in\{\text{pivot-minor},\text{vertex-minor}\}\) and each fixed finite simple graph \(H\), does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple graph \(G\), decides whether some \(\rho\) of \(G\) is isomorphic to \(H\)?
definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and have no parallel edges. Local complementation at a vertex \(v\) toggles adjacency between each pair of distinct neighbors of \(v\), leaving all other adjacencies unchanged. If \(uv\) is an edge in the current graph, pivoting on \(uv\) means local complementation at \(u\), then \(v\), then \(u\). A vertex-minor is obtained by a finite sequence of local complementations and vertex deletions; a pivot-minor instead permits edge pivots and vertex deletions. A deletion removes the chosen vertex and all its incident edges. Isomorphism is a bijection preserving adjacency in both directions; target vertices have no prescribed locations in the host. The empty target is allowed. For each fixed pair \((\rho,H)\), the algorithm receives only \(G\), encoded by its vertex count and adjacency matrix in binary. There must be constants \(C_{\rho,H},a_{\rho,H}>0\) such that it always returns the correct bit in at most \(C_{\rho,H}(n+1)^{a_{\rho,H}}\) Turing steps on every \(n\)-vertex host. Its program and these constants may depend on the fixed target and relation. No uniform construction from an input \(H\), fixed-parameter bound, containment witness or host-width promise is required. There is no advice depending on the growing host.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the quantified polynomial-time decision algorithms for both relations and every fixed target, or a Lean refutation for some fixed target and relation. A result only for hosts of bounded width or a bound exponential in host size does not meet the assertion. A uniform fixed-parameter algorithm would be sufficient but is not required.
context:

title: Complexity of general vertex-connectivity augmentation
importance_reason: Exact unweighted augmentation with all links available isolates the unresolved complexity of general target vertex connectivity.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a simple undirected graph \(G\) and a target \(1\leq\lambda<|V(G)|\), computes the minimum number of new edges needed to make \(G\) \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected, when every missing edge is available at unit cost?
definitions: The graph is finite, undirected and simple, with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\geq2\), and an explicit binary adjacency matrix. The integer \(\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is part of the input, encoded in binary, and need not be fixed. The available links are exactly \(\binom{V(G)}{2}\setminus E(G)\). An augmentation is any subset \(F\) of these links; its cost is \(|F|\), and no new vertices are permitted. The graph \(G+F\) is \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected if deleting any set of fewer than \(\lambda\) vertices leaves a connected graph. The condition \(\lambda<n\) excludes ambiguous conventions on graphs with too few vertices. The optimum is finite because adding every missing edge produces a complete graph. The algorithm must output the exact minimum integer; equivalently it may decide, for a binary budget \(k\geq0\), whether some augmentation has \(|F|\leq k\). The two tasks are polynomial-time equivalent using the finite \(\binom n2\) budget range. Running time is worst-case bit time bounded by one fixed polynomial in the whole input length, with no exponent or multiplicative nonpolynomial dependence on \(\lambda\). The input graph may have arbitrary initial connectivity; there is no promise that the target increases connectivity by only one.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time exact algorithm for all target values, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An algorithm polynomial only for fixed target connectivity, a parameterized algorithm exponential in the target or budget, an approximation, or a one-increment result does not meet the guarantee. NP-hardness implies a negative answer only under an explicitly stated P ≠ NP hypothesis.

why: The question asks whether optimal resilience to vertex failures can be added efficiently when all new links have the same cost and are freely available. These simple input conditions isolate the difficulty of vertex connectivity itself from costly or forbidden links.
