title: A dichotomy for edge deletion with finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs
importance_reason: A broad structural classification across finite-forbidden hereditary graph modification problems, with a uniform conceptual reach beyond individual classes or parameterized bounds.
formal: For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is the following decision problem either in \(\mathrm P\) or \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\geq0\), decide whether there is \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) has no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of \(\mathcal F\).
definitions: A simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. For \(U\subseteq V\), its induced subgraph contains every edge of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). Graph isomorphism is an adjacency-preserving bijection of vertex sets. The class of \(\mathcal F\)-free graphs consists of all finite graphs with none of the forbidden induced subgraphs; it is hereditary, meaning closed under taking induced subgraphs. Deleting \(S\) retains all vertices and exactly the edges in \(E\setminus S\). Edges cannot be added, vertices cannot be removed, and every deleted edge costs one. The empty graph and the empty forbidden family are permitted. The input graph uses its adjacency matrix on numbered vertices; \(k\) is binary. The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before the input varies and is not part of the input to this decision problem. For each fixed family, its finite graph list may be built into the program, and polynomial exponents and constants may depend on it. A language is in \(\mathrm P\) if a deterministic Turing machine decides it in polynomial input length. It is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if polynomial-size certificates can be checked in polynomial time. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(K\) to \(L\) is one deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) on finite binary strings such that \(x\in K\) iff \(f(x)\in L\). NP-completeness means membership in NP and such a reduction from every NP language. Each problem here is in NP because a deletion set can be checked and all induced copies of the finitely many fixed forbidden graphs can be enumerated in polynomial time. The dichotomy is inclusive; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) nor its negation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite family \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the stated P-or-NP-complete alternative. Alternatively specify one finite family and prove in Lean that its decision problem is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated reductions. A theorem for a single forbidden graph or a fixed selection of graph classes is insufficient. No separate effective procedure for classifying the family \(\mathcal F\) is imposed by this proposition.
context:
The survey describes the absence of a general polynomial-time versus NP-hard classification for hereditary edge deletion. Editorial specialization: this card selects the finite-forbidden-induced-subgraph domain, giving the graph properties a finite description and ensuring that every resulting decision problem is in NP. The source’s broader direction also encompasses hereditary classes without such a finite forbidden list.

There are immediate tractable families. If the only forbidden graph is a single edge, all input edges must be removed. If the forbidden graphs are the three-vertex path and the triangle, every remaining component must be an isolated vertex or an isolated edge: maximizing the retained edges is maximum matching, which is polynomial-time solvable.

Deleting an edge can create a forbidden induced subgraph. For example, removing one edge from a triangle creates an induced three-vertex path. Consequently, eliminating all forbidden copies initially visible in the input need not produce a valid final graph.

The survey contrasts edge deletion with the classical broad hardness theorem for vertex removal into nontrivial hereditary properties. That contrast motivates a structural classification for edge operations; it does not transfer the vertex-removal theorem to the problem defined here.

The 2023 journal version still states the absence of a general edge-removal dichotomy. Its detailed tables also concern parameterized algorithms and kernelization. A bound depending arbitrarily on the deletion budget, or the existence of a polynomial kernel, addresses a different question from ordinary polynomial time in the entire input.

Completing the dichotomy would rule out NP-intermediate behavior inside this finite-description family, even if such behavior exists elsewhere in NP. Proving just that some cases are hard is weaker: every finite forbidden family must fall into one of the stated alternatives.
why: Edge deletion is a basic graph-repair operation whose tractability changes with the desired hereditary property. A dichotomy for every finite forbidden list would explain this variation across many graph classes and locate a general boundary between efficient repair and NP-completeness.

title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
importance_reason: A simple central offline counting task exposes a basic gap in the power of word-RAM algorithms, despite having only one output value and already rank-compressed input.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), computes \(\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\) exactly in \(O(n)\) worst-case time?
definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
An inversion counts an out-of-order pair in a ranking. The exact total is also the Kendall tau distance from the identity ordering and the minimum number of adjacent swaps needed to sort the permutation.

Chan and Pătraşcu give an \(O(n\sqrt{\log n})\) exact word-RAM algorithm and a linear-time constant-relative-error approximation. The latter does not compute the exact count.

The input is a permutation of small integers, so sorting those integers itself is already easy. Determining how many pairs were out of order is a separate offline aggregation problem.

The linear exact endpoint is an editorial formulation of the remaining gap. The September 2026 search found no general exact linear algorithm, but the status evidence relies mainly on older primary work and is weaker than for the other additions.
why: A simple central offline counting task exposes a basic gap in the power of word-RAM algorithms, despite having only one output value and already rank-compressed input.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The precise target fixes deterministic worst-case time on logarithmic words. The linear endpoint is editorial rather than an attributed conjecture; present-status review remains limited by older direct evidence.

working_summary: An inversion is a pair of positions that appear in the wrong relative order in a permutation. The task is to compute the exact total number of inversions. The question asks for deterministic linear time on a word RAM with logarithmic words. Linear approximation and faster algorithms for nearly sorted inputs do not give this exact worst-case guarantee. The current-status review is limited mainly to older primary evidence, and the card records that uncertainty.

title: Strongly polynomial planar minimum-cost flow
importance_reason: A significant algorithmic question under particular parameters or graph restrictions, with more specialized consequences than a general parameterized-complexity principle.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost flow in a planar directed graph whose worst-case number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is \(o(n^{2}\log(n+2))\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices? The algorithm must return an exact minimum-cost feasible flow, or correctly report infeasibility, for all rational capacities, costs and vertex supplies.
definitions: The input is a finite directed graph with vertex set \([n]\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. The underlying undirected graph is planar, and a combinatorial planar embedding is supplied. Thus the number of arcs is \(O(n)\). Each arc \(a\) has a finite rational capacity \(u_a\geq0\) and rational cost \(c_a\), and each vertex \(v\) has rational supply \(b_v\), with \(\sum_v b_v=0\). All numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; no magnitude bound is imposed. A feasible flow assigns rational \(f_a\) with \(0\leq f_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\text{ out of }v} f_a-\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a=b_v\) at each vertex. Its cost is \(\sum_a c_a f_a\). Strong polynomiality means a bound polynomial in \(n\) on exact rational arithmetic operations, comparisons and index/memory operations, independent of all numeric bit lengths, together with a polynomial bound in total input bit length on every intermediate number’s encoding length. Arithmetic uses addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values. The algorithm has finite uniform code and no advice, randomness or oracle. The little-o improvement means that there is a function \(T(n)\) bounding its operation count on every such \(n\)-vertex input with \(T(n)/(n^{2}\log(n+2))\to0\). The source’s instruction to beat the stated bound is interpreted as an asymptotic little-o improvement, not merely a smaller leading constant. The simple planar-network convention prevents arbitrarily many parallel arcs from hiding an unbounded input size in \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the exact flow guarantee, little-o operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths, or prove that no such deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm exists. A speedup for bounded numerical data, an approximation algorithm, or a lower leading constant at the same asymptotic order does not answer the stated question.
context:
Erickson’s question in the 2013 seminar report explicitly asks for a strongly polynomial algorithm improving the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound. The supply-and-capacity formulation is stated there; all-zero supplies give its minimum-cost circulation special case.

A 2022 preprint gives a nearly linear algorithm for planar minimum-cost flow with polynomially bounded integer costs and capacities. Those numeric restrictions are material: this result does not by itself answer the strongly polynomial question for arbitrary rational input data.
why: This asks how much planarity can accelerate exact flow optimization when numerical magnitudes cannot enter the operation count. It separates combinatorial graph structure from progress that relies on bounded capacities and costs.
status_note: The 2013 source states the strongly polynomial speedup as open. The model was recovered on 13 September 2026 and a bounded subsequent-work check found only a verified abstract for a different numeric regime, not a resolution of this target. Status is source_open; source proofs were not independently verified.

working_summary: Minimum-cost flow assigns capacity-respecting arc flows that meet prescribed supplies and minimize total cost. The question asks for an asymptotic improvement over the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound on planar graphs. The algorithm must be strongly polynomial, so numerical magnitudes cannot enter its arithmetic-operation bound. A later nearly linear algorithm for polynomially bounded integer data does not by itself meet that requirement. A resolution would show whether planar structure yields a faster exact algorithm independently of the size of the input numbers.

title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
importance_reason: A general multiplicative sparsification conjecture linking support size to a structural invariant, with consequences for cuts, codes and CSPs. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every family \(S\subseteq 2^{[m]}\), every weight vector \(w\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) and every \(0<\varepsilon <1\), there is a reweighting \(\tilde\{w\}\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) with at most \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) nonzero coordinates and satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\le \sum _{i\in A}\tilde\{w\}_{i}\le (1+\varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\) simultaneously for every \(A\in S\)?
definitions: Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\), and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is \(\{i:\tilde\{w\}_{i}>0\}\); coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as \(\sum w_{i}=1\) is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length \(\ell\) consists of distinct coordinates \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{\ell}\) and distinct sets \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{\ell}\in S\) with \(a_{i}\in A_{i}\) for every i and \(a_{j}\notin A_{i}\) whenever \(i<j\). \(CL(S)\) is the maximum possible \(\ell\), allowing \(\ell =0\). Equivalently, take the union-closure \(U(S)=\{\bigcup T:T\subseteq S\}\), including the empty union; \(CL(S)\) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from \(\varnothing\) in \(U(S)\). Thus \(CL(S)=0\) when S is empty or contains only \(\varnothing\). It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and \(\varepsilon\). The source allows \(\varepsilon >0\); values \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to \(0<\varepsilon <1\) preserves it.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.
context:
A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so \(CL(S)=m\). With unit original weights and \(\varepsilon <1\), every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

The paper gives support \(O(CL(S)\cdot \log ^{2}(CL(S)/\varepsilon )\cdot (\log  \log (CL(S)/\varepsilon ))^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.
why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.
status_note: Published definitions, main bound and Conjecture 23 checked through 11 September 2026, together with the related May 2026 report and subsequent searches. No matching logarithm-free universal bound or counterexample was located.
progress: 2026-07: The ICALP paper proves a universe-size-independent bound with logarithmic overhead and poses the \(O(CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2})\) bound as Conjecture 23. | 2026-05-15: A related CSP sparsification report still states its broad characterizations with polylogarithmic and accuracy factors; its abstract does not settle the sharper conjecture.
working_summary: A sparsifier retains and reweights a few coordinates while approximately preserving every set’s total weight. The conjecture asks for a support bound proportional to chain length divided by \(\varepsilon ^{2}\). Chain length is measured through the union-closure, so even an incomparable collection of singleton sets can have large chain length. The published upper bound has extra logarithmic factors, which are precisely the remaining loss in the question. A resolution would establish whether this structural parameter completely controls multiplicative sparsification up to a universal constant.

title: Complexity of directed detours
importance_reason: A canonical minimal detour question exposing the directed boundary between shortest-path computation and simple-path hardness. Existing score retained.
formal: Classify the worst-case complexity of the following decision problem on unrestricted finite directed graphs: given distinct vertices s and t, is there a simple directed s-to-t path with at least \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)+1\) edges? The requested distinction is polynomial-time solvability versus NP-completeness. This is the fixed \(k=1\) case of Longest Detour, not the problem with k supplied as part of the input.
definitions: The input is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n], n\ge 2\), no loops or parallel arcs, and distinguished \(s\ne t\). Both opposite arcs between two vertices are allowed. The graph is unweighted; every arc has length one. A simple s-to-t path is a sequence \(v_{0}=s,v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}=t\) of pairwise distinct vertices with \((v_{j- 1},v_{j})\in E\) for \(1\le j\le \ell\), and its length is \(\ell\). If t is reachable from \(s, \operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)\) is the minimum length of such a path. If t is unreachable, the instance is a no-instance. The input lists all vertices and arcs using binary vertex labels; N is the full encoding length. Polynomial time means one deterministic multitape Turing machine that decides every instance in at most \(C(N+1)^{a}\) steps for absolute constants C,a. NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions; in particular, a hardness proof can give a map from Boolean satisfiability instances to these graph instances that preserves yes/no answers. The decision problem is in NP: an at-most-n-vertex path is a polynomial-size certificate, and reachability distance and the path conditions can be checked in polynomial time. No planarity, acyclicity, connectivity or uniqueness of shortest paths is promised.
answer_criterion: Determine the problem’s complexity in the stated unrestricted directed, unweighted model. A deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm establishes tractability; a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SAT establishes NP-completeness, since membership in NP is known. The latter excludes a polynomial-time algorithm under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question does not assume a \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy in advance; any different established classification must explain the remaining boundary. Bounds only for planar graphs, or hardness when k is variable, do not classify the fixed \(k=1\) problem.
context:
The question asks for strictly greater length. A graph may have many different shortest s-to-t paths and still have no simple path longer than them. Finding a second distinct path therefore does not by itself decide the problem.

Allowing a walk to revisit a cycle would make it possible to add length without producing the required simple path. The distinct-vertex condition is essential to this complexity question.

Shortest paths are efficiently computable, but deciding whether their length can be exceeded by a simple path constrains which vertices can be reused. Here even one additional edge is the unresolved threshold.

The source gives a fixed-parameter algorithm for planar digraphs, and the 2023 follow-up gives an \(O(n^{2})\) algorithm for this \(k=1\) case. These results do not apply to arbitrary digraphs.

Longest Path Above Diameter asks for a path exceeding the graph’s diameter, rather than the distance between prescribed endpoints. Its \(k=1\) hardness theorem does not classify Directed Detour.
why: Pinpoints whether even the smallest departure from shortest-path length creates NP-complete difficulty under the simple-path constraint, a basic boundary in directed path algorithms.
status_note: Read the complete original target and the JCSS 2023 conclusion, and checked the planar follow-up. Exact-target searches through 12 September 2026 found no classification for arbitrary digraphs. A July 2026 second-shortest-simple-path abstract was also inspected, but did not establish a result for the strictly-longer-than-all-shortest-paths predicate here.
progress: 2022: The STACS paper gives a planar fixed-parameter algorithm and leaves the general \(k=1\) classification open. | 2023: The planar follow-up improves the \(k=1\) running time to \(O(n^{2})\). The JCSS version still explicitly retains the general-digraph question.
working_summary: The input is an unweighted directed graph with specified endpoints. The problem asks whether any simple path between them is longer than their shortest-path distance. Only one extra edge is required, and no path may repeat a vertex. Planar graphs have polynomial algorithms, but the general directed classification remains open in the checked sources. The NP-completeness of exceeding graph diameter concerns a different problem.

title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
importance_reason: A basic unresolved gap between feasibility and exact optimization for a fixed number of disjoint routes. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(\mathrm{P}_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(\mathrm{P}_{i})\cap V(\mathrm{P}_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A conditional negative answer must state its assumption and imply that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists for at least one fixed k. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.
context:
Disjointness can force one route away from its own shortest path. The optimization problem allows such detours and asks for the smallest total number of edges over all routes. An algorithm checking only whether all individual shortest distances can be attained cannot handle the remaining instances.

The source gives polynomial-time algorithms for individually shortest paths at every fixed k and cites a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for minimum total length when \(k=2\). It leaves the minimum-total-length extension open for \(k\ge 3\).

The 2024 grid result handles minimum-total-length routing on an infinite rectangular grid. Its geometric restriction does not give the requested algorithm on arbitrary undirected graphs.

The 2025 planar preprint requires every route to be individually shortest. That condition does not handle general minimum-total-length routing when disjointness forces detours.

The published 2025 cycle-packing paper explicitly states that Min-Sum Disjoint Paths remains open even for three pairs on planar graphs. Its own polynomial-time result packs cycles without prescribed terminal pairs, so it does not settle this routing problem.
why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.
status_note: Checked the original graph model and concluding question, the full 2025 cycle-packing discussion, and the exact scopes of the 2024 grid and 2025 planar results. Searches through 12 September 2026 identified no general fixed-k polynomial-time algorithm. Randomized bounded-error solvability is explicitly admitted as in the source’\(s k=2\) comparison.
progress: 2021: The source improves fixed-k algorithms for individually shortest disjoint paths and leaves minimum-total-length routing open for \(k\ge 3\). | 2024: Minimum-total-length routing is shown FPT in the special setting of an infinite rectangular grid. | 2025-10-07: The cycle-packing paper still lists the three-pair minimum-total-length routing problem as open, including on planar graphs.
working_summary: The graph is undirected and unweighted, with a fixed number k of prescribed terminal pairs. The task is to find vertex-disjoint routes with the smallest possible total number of edges, or report that routing is impossible. Individual routes may need to be longer than their own shortest paths to avoid the others. The source asks for polynomial time at every fixed \(k\ge 3\), allowing the exponent to depend on k. Recent grid and individually-shortest-path results do not settle the general problem, which a 2025 published paper still lists as open for three pairs.

title: Linear-time directed bottleneck paths and trees
importance_reason: An exact-complexity question for basic directed bottleneck optimization, separating comparison access from more powerful numerical models. Existing score retained.
formal: Do the directed bottleneck path and rooted bottleneck spanning-tree problems admit comparison-based algorithms with expected running time \(O(n+m)\) on every input, always returning an exact optimum? The input has \(n\) vertices and \(m\) weighted directed edges. Randomization is allowed; deterministic linear time would also answer positively. The source writes \(O(m)\) after the usual removal or treatment of irrelevant vertices. The requested guarantee is total running time, including graph processing and output, with weights accessible only through comparisons.
definitions:
In the bottleneck path problem (BP), the input is an explicit directed graph G=(V,E), a source s, a target t and a weight w(e) for every edge. Among all directed s-to-t paths P, output one minimizing max_{e∈P}w(e). Any optimal simple path is acceptable; ties require no prescribed choice. If t is unreachable, report that no path exists. When s=t the empty path is returned, with bottleneck conventionally −∞.

In the bottleneck spanning-tree problem (BST), the input is the same kind of directed weighted graph and a specified root s. Output an out-arborescence T spanning all vertices: s has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one in T, and there is a directed path in T from s to every vertex. Minimize max_{e∈T}w(e). If no such tree exists, report this. For a one-vertex graph, the empty tree has value −∞. This objective minimizes the single largest tree-edge weight, not the sum of weights. A tree minimizing that largest weight need not supply an individually optimal bottleneck path to every vertex.

Weights are arbitrary elements of a totally ordered set, such as arbitrary real numbers. They are opaque keys: they may be stored, copied and compared in constant time, but their digits, arithmetic values and integer ranks are not available for computation. Equal weights are allowed. The graph is given by adjacency lists with O(log(n+m+2))-bit vertex and edge indices; ordinary operations on these indices have unit cost. The algorithm is charged for all graph operations, comparisons, random sampling and writing its path or tree, not just the number of comparisons. There is no assumption that the weights are sorted, bounded integers, or machine words supporting bit operations.

The randomization convention is Las Vegas: on every fixed input the answer is exact, termination occurs with probability one, and the expected total work over the algorithm's internal random choices is at most C(n+m) for a universal constant C. This includes feasibility checks and output. A randomized algorithm with a small probability of an incorrect optimum would not meet this convention. For BP, isolated and unreachable vertices can be removed in O(n+m) work. A feasible nontrivial BST instance has m≥n−1. Thus O(n+m) makes the source's O(m) target meaningful also on degenerate explicit inputs without changing its substantive content.

The question asks for this guarantee for both tasks, but their expected-linear-time versions are equivalent through the reductions in Section 4 of the source. These reductions do not establish the corresponding deterministic equivalence: the BST-to-BP reduction uses randomness. The source's separate question about a deterministic O(mβ(m,n)) bound is not the target of this card. Neither all-pairs bottleneck paths nor finding every individual single-source bottleneck value is required.
answer_criterion: Give always-correct comparison-based algorithms with expected O(n+m) total work for both directed tasks, or use the source reductions to derive both guarantees from one. Alternatively, rule out such algorithms, stating any assumptions used. An undirected algorithm, a word-RAM algorithm inspecting weight representations, a bound on comparisons alone, or a faster algorithm only for sufficiently dense graphs does not settle the unrestricted target. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the permitted randomized algorithms.
context:
Theorem 3 gives expected O(mβ(m,n)) time, where β(m,n) is the least k≥1 for which the k-times iterated base-two logarithm of n is at most m/n, in the nondegenerate regime m≥n. This overhead grows very slowly, and the theorem is already linear when m≥n log^(k)n for any fixed k. The question includes sparse graphs where β is unbounded.

The source already obtains deterministic linear time in the word-RAM model and recalls linear-time algorithms for undirected graphs. Its open question concerns arbitrary directed graphs with opaque comparison-only weights.

Section 4 relates the two problems at the expected-linear scale. The spanning-tree objective is one global bottleneck; it should not be replaced with the stronger requirement to return every single-source optimal bottleneck path.

Gorbachev’s August 2026 preprint gives a counterexample to the 2016 paper’s claimed linear-time algorithm for deterministic graphical games and a linear reduction from directed BP to the designated-start game-value problem. It explicitly retains the BP question. This correction concerns the DGG claim, not the paper’s stated randomized BP/BST upper bound or its word-RAM result.
why: Determines the exact cost of fundamental directed min-max optimization when numerical information is available only by comparison. Removing the overhead would close a long-standing gap for sparse graphs; distinguishing the input model prevents an already-solved variant from being presented as open.
status_note: Checked the original definitions, Theorem 3, both reductions, the word-RAM result and the exact Section 7 questions, plus the August 2026 v2 preprint including its counterexample and reduction statement. The main target permits always-correct randomization, matching the preceding expected-time theorem; the separate deterministic near-linear question is not silently substituted. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The recent correction is a preprint and its proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2016: Theorem 3 improves the comparison-based expected time to O(mβ(m,n)); Section 5 separately gives deterministic linear time when word-RAM operations on weights are allowed. | 2026-08-06: The v2 preprint identifies a flaw in the claimed DGG algorithm and reduces directed BP to DGG value computation in linear time. It still states linear-time comparison-based BP as open.
working_summary: A bottleneck path minimizes its heaviest edge, and a rooted bottleneck tree minimizes the heaviest edge needed to reach all vertices. The open target is expected linear total time for exact solutions on arbitrary directed graphs using only comparisons of edge weights. The source already achieves a very slowly growing overhead and gives linear time in the stronger word-RAM model. The path and tree targets are equivalent at the expected-linear scale through the source reductions. An August 2026 preprint corrects a related graphical-games claim and continues to state the comparison-based path question as open.

title: Polynomial-time independent set under a forbidden forest
importance_reason: A major remaining tractability boundary for Maximum Weight Independent Set on hereditary classes, now with quasipolynomial algorithms across the conjectured polynomial side. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed finite forest \(H\) whose connected components each have at most three leaves, does Maximum Weight Independent Set on \(H\)-free graphs admit a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm? Precisely, must there exist an algorithm \(A_{H}\) and constants \(c_{H},C_{H}>0\) that, for every \(H\)-free vertex-weighted graph \((G,w)\) of encoding length \(L\), output a maximum-weight independent set in at most \(C_{H}(L+1)^{c_{H}}\) steps?
question_excerpt: However, we seem still far from proving it: not only we do not know how to improve the quasipolynomial bounds of \([15, 24]\) to polynomial […]
definitions:
Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A forest has no cycle. In a nontrivial tree, a leaf has degree one; an isolated vertex is allowed as a component. A tree with at most three leaves is a path or a subdivided claw. A subdivided claw \(S_{a,b,c}\), for integers \(a,b,c\geq1\), consists of three internally disjoint paths of respectively \(a,b,c\) edges sharing one endpoint. That common endpoint has degree three, and the other endpoints are the three leaves.

The graph \(G\) is \(H\)-free if no vertex subset induces a graph isomorphic to \(H\). An induced copy must preserve both edges and nonedges. If \(H\) is disconnected, all its components must occur together with no extra edges between their chosen vertices. Excluding the whole forest is therefore not the same as separately excluding every component.

The input explicitly lists \(G\) and nonnegative integer vertex weights \(w(v)\), encoded in binary. The length \(L\) includes the graph and all weight bits; zero weights and the empty independent set are allowed. An independent set \(I\subseteq V(G)\) contains no pair joined by an edge. Its weight is
\[w(I)=\sum_{v\in I}w(v).\]
The required output is a set \(I\) attaining the largest possible weight, not merely an inclusion-maximal set or an approximation.

The forbidden graph \(H\) is fixed before the input varies. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and multiplicative constant may depend on \(H\). The question does not require one exponent independent of \(H\), or fixed-parameter tractability when \(H\) is treated as a variable input. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity for each fixed class.

There is no bound on the maximum degree, clique size or biclique size of \(G\). No sparsity promise is imposed beyond the forbidden induced forest. Recognition of \(H\)-freeness can be done in polynomial time for fixed \(H\), but the optimization guarantee is required only on that class.

Computing the exact optimum value and outputting an optimum set are polynomial-time equivalent here by the usual self-reduction on induced subgraphs, which remain \(H\)-free. The primary source discusses the full family of forests; the symmetric long claws \(S_{t,t,t}\) are a central subfamily, not an unmentioned restriction of this formulation.
answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time solvability for every fixed forest in the stated family, or refute this assertion for at least one fixed forest. Any complexity assumption used for a negative result must be explicit. A quasipolynomial-time algorithm, an approximation scheme or a theorem requiring bounded degree or a forbidden biclique does not meet the full target.
context:
The sources recall that forbidding a fixed graph outside this forest family leaves Maximum Weight Independent Set NP-hard. Polynomial algorithms for every forest in the family would identify the tractable side of the classification for a single forbidden induced subgraph.

Theorem 1.3 of the September 2025 full version gives an algorithm for every such fixed \(H\), with graph-size running time \(n^{O_{H}((\log n)^{19})}\). This is major progress over the earlier subexponential and approximation results, but its exponent still grows with \(n\). Conjecture 1.1 in that same version retains the polynomial target.

The consolidated STACS 2024 source proves polynomial-time solvability when \(G\) excludes both an induced \(S_{t,t,t}\) and a fixed complete bipartite graph \(K_{s,s}\) as an ordinary subgraph. Its Conjecture 10 asks about replacing the biclique restriction by a clique restriction. Both restrictions are additional to the general question on this card.

The 2025 MFCS paper improves the structural theorem behind the quasipolynomial algorithms and simplifies polynomial algorithms in sparse cases. It still describes polynomial-time solvability for the full family as conjectural.
why: This conjecture would complete a natural complexity classification of a central optimization problem by forbidden induced structure. It asks whether the large family now admitting quasipolynomial algorithms actually permits polynomial-time exact optimization, including graphs of unrestricted density.
status_note: Read the original full-family paragraph, the consolidated 2024 sparse theorem and Conjecture 10, the September 2025 full quasipolynomial version, and the 2025 MFCS introduction. Checked the apparently broader polynomial manuscript on the author’s site: the linked PDF is explicitly bounded-degree. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial algorithm for the complete family.
progress: 2022: The source advances subexponential and approximation algorithms while retaining the full polynomial-time conjecture. | 2024: A quasipolynomial-time algorithm covers every forbidden forest in the conjectured tractable family. | 2025: A stronger structural theorem improves quasipolynomial bounds; the revised full algorithm paper retains Conjecture 1.1.
working_summary: Fix a forest whose components are paths or subdivided three-leaf claws. Given a graph with no induced copy of that forest, find an independent vertex set of maximum total weight. The question asks for polynomial time for every fixed forbidden forest, with the polynomial allowed to depend on that forest. The input graph may have arbitrarily large degree, cliques and bicliques. Quasipolynomial algorithms now cover the whole family, but known general results still fall short of polynomial time.

title: Near-linear-query reconstruction of bounded-degree graphs
importance_reason: A natural information-access boundary for exact sparse-network reconstruction, with a long-standing gap between nearly linear special-case bounds and the general three-halves exponent. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed integer \(\Delta\geq2\), is there a randomized exact reconstruction algorithm \(A_{\Delta}\) and constants \(C_{\Delta}>0\), \(k_{\Delta}\geq0\) such that every hidden connected simple unweighted undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) labeled vertices with maximum degree at most \(\Delta\) can be reconstructed using \[\mathbb E[Q(A_{\Delta},G)]\leq C_{\Delta}\,n(\log(n+2))^{k_{\Delta}}\] queries to an oracle that returns the shortest-path distance between one requested pair of vertices?
question_excerpt: Thus the open question from [27] of whether general graphs of bounded degree can be reconstructed using \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n)\) distance queries remains open and answering it […]
definitions:
The algorithm is given the entire vertex set, identified with \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the fixed degree bound. The edge set is hidden. The graph is fixed throughout the execution and is promised connected; no random input distribution is assumed.

A query supplies two named vertices \(u,v\) and receives the integer
\[d_{G}(u,v)=\min\{\text{number of edges on a path from }u\text{ to }v\}.\]
The answer contains no path, intermediate vertices or distances to other destinations. An edge has distance one. Computing all distances from one vertex by querying this oracle costs \(n-1\) queries, rather than one query.

The algorithm may choose each new query using all previous answers and its private random bits. Its output must be exactly the set \(E(G)\) on the given vertex labels. Isomorphism type, an approximate metric, a graph consistent with only some answers, or a sample of edges is insufficient.

The randomized convention is Las Vegas: the output is correct whenever returned, and the procedure terminates with probability one. The query bound is an expectation over its internal randomness for each fixed allowed graph. This is not average-case complexity over randomly generated graphs. Deterministic algorithms also qualify.

The constants may depend on the fixed \(\Delta\), but not on \(n\) or the particular graph. The displayed bound specifies the meaning of \(\widetilde O(n)\): a linear number of vertices times a fixed power of a logarithm. A bound \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) does not meet it.

Only calls to the distance oracle are charged in this query-complexity question. The algorithm must be an effective finite procedure, but no separate polynomial bound on local computation or memory is imposed. No restriction is placed on the number of adaptive rounds. There is no additional promise of bounded treewidth, treelength, cutwidth or a planar graph.

Simplicity matters because distances cannot reveal edge multiplicities or loops. Connectedness is also part of the source model: allowing a graph with just one hidden edge and otherwise isolated vertices would already force a quadratic search for that edge.
answer_criterion: Give algorithms with the displayed expected-query bound for every fixed degree bound, and prove exact reconstruction on every promised graph, or show that such bounds are impossible for at least one fixed degree bound. A lower bound against the source’s particular algorithm alone does not refute the general question.
context:
The original source compares its algorithm with the earlier \(\widetilde O_{\Delta}(n^{3/2})\)-expected-query reconstruction algorithm. The 2026 SWAT paper still identifies this as the best known general bound for connected bounded-degree graphs.

The source’s Theorem 1 gives \(\widetilde O(n)\) expected distance queries for uniformly random regular graphs of fixed degree. Its general-graph guarantee is weaker. The random-graph theorem averages over a restricted input distribution and therefore does not establish the per-graph bound asked here.

The concluding remark gives complete binary trees as a family requiring a superlinear number of queries for the particular Simple algorithm. That limitation does not apply to every possible reconstruction algorithm.

Kaudan and Nayyeri give deterministic \(O_{\Delta,\tau}(n\log n)\) reconstruction for graphs with bounded treelength and a supplied bound \(\tau\). Treelength means the minimum, over tree decompositions, of the largest graph-metric distance between vertices in one bag. The 2026 SWAT result instead gives deterministic subquadratic reconstruction for bounded cutwidth. Neither hypothesis follows from bounded degree alone.
why: The problem asks how much pairwise distance information is inherently needed to discover an entire sparse network. A near-linear worst-input guarantee would show that distances allow almost output-sized exact reconstruction despite hiding every edge, without relying on randomness in the network itself.
status_note: Read the original complete query model, theorem guarantees and open-question remark. Checked the March 2026 treelength theorem and the full SWAT 2026 graph-reconstruction section. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no near-linear expected distance-query algorithm for every connected graph of fixed maximum degree. The source’s expectation convention is retained as exact randomized reconstruction, not a random-input or stronger all-distances model.
progress: 2021: The source reaches near-linear expected queries on random regular graphs and retains the general bounded-degree question. | 2026-03-11: A full preprint gives deterministic linearithmic queries with a bounded-treelength promise. | 2026: The SWAT paper adds deterministic subquadratic reconstruction for bounded cutwidth and restates the general three-halves-exponent upper bound.
working_summary: All vertices of a connected bounded-degree graph are known, but its edges are hidden. One query returns only the shortest-path distance between two named vertices. The goal is to recover every edge using a linear number of vertices times polylogarithmically many expected queries. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for each fixed graph, and the returned answer must be exact. Near-linear results for random regular or bounded-treelength graphs do not cover every graph in the question.

title: Spanners matching Thorup–Zwick emulator tradeoffs
importance_reason: A central structural comparison between graph subgraphs and unrestricted metric compression, with a hierarchy of sharp distance guarantees and a concrete remaining gap after major recent progress. Existing score retained.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), do there exist constants \(C_{k},D_{k}>0\) such that every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge1\), has a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,E_{H})\), \(E_{H}\subseteq E\), satisfying
\[
|E_{H}|\le C_{k}n^{\,1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)}
\]
and, simultaneously for all distinct vertices \(u,v\) in the same connected component of \(G\),
\[
d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+D_{k}\,d_{G}(u,v)^{\,1-1/k}?
\]
The constants may depend on \(k\), but not on the graph, its size or the vertex pair. This is the fixed-\(k\) size and distance-error tradeoff achieved by Thorup–Zwick emulators, now required of an actual subgraph.
definitions:
The distance \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the number of edges on a shortest path in \(G\); it is \(+\infty\) if there is no path. A spanning subgraph keeps every vertex and may remove edges, but all retained edges still have unit length. It cannot insert shortcut edges or change weights. Consequently, \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) automatically.

The inequality for finite distances requires \(H\) to connect every pair originally connected in \(G\). Vertices in different components remain disconnected because \(H\subseteq G\). Equal vertices have distance zero in both graphs and need no separate distortion inequality. For distinct connected vertices, \(d_{G}(u,v)\ge1\), so the power is defined even at \(k=1\), where it equals 1.

There is one subgraph \(H\) for the entire graph and fixed \(k\). It must satisfy the bound for every distance scale and every pair simultaneously. The quantifier order is
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_{k},D_{k}>0\ \forall G\ \exists H\ \forall u,v.
\]
The size bound has no hidden logarithmic factor in \(n\), no \(n^{\delta}\) loss for positive \(\delta\), and no additional accuracy parameter affecting the selected subgraph. Dependence on a growing \(k=k(n)\) is not requested.

For \(k>1\), the allowed additive error is sublinear in the distance because \(d^{1-1/k}/d=d^{-1/k}\) tends to zero. It need not be a constant independent of distance. For example, \(k=2\) asks for \(O(n^{8/7})\) edges with additive error \(O(\sqrt d)\). The \(k=1\) case asks for \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges and constant additive error.

An emulator is a weighted graph on the same vertex set that may contain edges absent from \(G\). A shortcut between \(u,v\) can receive weight \(d_{G}(u,v)\), preserving the prohibition on underestimating original distances. A spanner must instead use only original edges. Replacing shortcuts by their full original paths can increase the number of retained edges and does not automatically preserve the size bound.

The main assertion is existential: it asks for the same structural tradeoff, not a prescribed transformation of a supplied emulator or a specified construction running time. A construction establishing these bounds qualifies. This follows the size/stretch question in the source; bounds on construction time are separate from this target.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence assertion for every fixed integer \(k\), or refute it by showing that for some fixed \(k\) no constants \(C_{k},D_{k}\) work for all graphs. A counterexample to one proposed construction is insufficient. A family with the stated edge exponent plus any fixed positive slack, or different spanners for different accuracy parameters, does not establish the exact target.
context:
Thorup and Zwick’s Theorem 4.1 gives emulators with the required sublinear distance error and \(O(k n^{1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)})\) edges after shifting their parameter by one. For fixed \(k\), the factor \(k\) is absorbed into the size constant. The tutorial asks whether actual subgraphs can match this tradeoff.

The 2018 hierarchy paper emphasizes that a sublinear-error spanner has corresponding near-additive guarantees for all accuracy choices on the same graph. A construction whose size or chosen edge set depends on a separately supplied \(\varepsilon\) does not automatically give this simultaneous property.

Tan and Zhang’s Theorem 1.1 proves that for every fixed \(k\ge2\) and \(\delta>0\), there is a spanner with \(O(n^{1+(1+\delta)/(2^{k+1}-1)})\) edges and error \(C(k,\delta)d^{1-1/k}\). This is a major improvement over the bounds recorded by the tutorial, but still has positive exponent slack.

The later theorem permits its constants to depend on \(\delta\). Its Section 4 bound explicitly allows the stretch coefficient to grow as \(\delta\) decreases. Thus taking smaller fixed slack, or choosing slack as a function of \(n\), does not supply a fixed \(D_{k}\) and the exact required edge bound.

The known additive-six spanner on \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges settles \(k=1\). The unresolved hierarchy begins with the square-root distance error at \(k=2\) and continues through the higher fixed levels.
why: Spanners retain real routes in the original network, while emulators can encode long routes as weighted shortcuts. Matching their size/error tradeoffs would establish that this structural restriction costs only constant factors at every fixed level of sublinear distance accuracy. The later almost-matching theorem makes the exact remaining loss especially concrete.

title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
importance_reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.
focus_reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.
context:
This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts \(T(n)=(n- 1)^{2}\). Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.
why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.
status_note: Szykuła’s survey posted 25 August 2026 explicitly states the unrestricted conjecture as open and records the cubic upper bound. Sources and later work were checked on 11 September 2026. The July one-cluster preprint is a restricted-class claim whose proof was not independently verified.

working_summary: A reset word drives a finite automaton to one common state regardless of its initial state. The target is the maximum shortest reset-word length among all complete synchronizing n-state automata. A real-valued approximation with Lean-certified absolute error at most 0.01 for every n meets the benchmark criterion. The Černý conjecture proposes the formula \((n- 1)^{2}\). Arbitrary finite alphabets are permitted, and no endpoint, connectivity or algorithmic restriction is added.

title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
importance_reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.
focus_reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.
formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.
why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.
status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.
