It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap. | 2011–2014: Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice. | 2025: Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages. | 2026-02-25: Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open. | 2026-07-06: Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ revised preprint establishes a quadratic 2DFA state lower bound for one-way liveness and the resulting NFA-to-2DFA conversion. This does not exclude a polynomial determinization bound.
working_summary: Two-way finite automata can reread their input by moving their head in either direction. This project asks whether every n-state nondeterministic machine has an equivalent deterministic two-way machine with polynomially many states. Both machines must agree on all finite words, with no restriction on input length. Rereading sometimes replaces exponentially much one-way memory, but that observation does not supply a general simulation. Resolving the question would quantify how much finite-state succinctness comes from nondeterministic choice once unrestricted revisiting of the input is available.

title: Generalized star-height problem
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.
focus_reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.
formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \Sigma\)* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
definitions: \(\Sigma\)* is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in \mathrm{L}(E)\) and \(v\in \mathrm{L}(F), \Sigma *\setminus \mathrm{L}(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(\mathrm{L}(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{h(E):\mathrm{L}(E)=\mathrm{L}\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
context:
Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma *ab\Sigma *)^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma\)* by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)\)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.
why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.
status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.
progress: 1965: Schützenberger characterizes generalized height zero by aperiodic syntactic monoids; height one is already necessary for simple parity languages. | 1992: Pin–Straubing–Thérien prove additional height-one classes and remove a proposed height-two candidate. | 2016-09-27: Bourne–Ruškuc’s revised manuscript establishes height-one bounds for specified factor-counting languages and Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. | 2018: Daviaud–Paperman give effective characterizations of restricted classes generated by stars of individual words. | 2025: Cotumaccio’s automata/compression survey still identifies generalized star height among the open structural questions.
working_summary: Generalized regular expressions describe regular languages using concatenation, Boolean operations and arbitrary finite repetition. Their star height counts nested repetitions while allowing complementation without an additional height charge. The question asks for a language whose every such description needs at least two nested stars. Ordinary examples with complicated repetitions may simplify drastically when complements are allowed, so inspecting one expression proves little. Establishing a separation beyond height one would reveal a further intrinsic layer of repetition complexity within regular languages.

title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
importance_reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.
focus_reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(\mathrm{L}_{0}a_{1}\mathrm{L}_{1}\cdots a_{r} \mathrm{L}_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(\mathrm{L}_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(\mathrm{L}(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(\mathrm{L}(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.
context:
Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA\)* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.
why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.
status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. Place–Zeitoun’s full-level-three decidability theorem remains distinct from the all-level target. The January 2025 alternation-hierarchy announcement is still explicitly withdrawn because of a fatal flaw in Lemma 19. No corrected result settling every fixed full dot-depth level was located.

working_summary: The dot-depth hierarchy sorts star-free regular languages by how repeatedly concatenation and Boolean operations must be combined. Given a finite automaton and a fixed level, the project asks whether membership in that level can always be decided. The relevant level concerns the simplest possible description of the language, rather than the syntax initially supplied. Deciding star-freeness only establishes membership somewhere in the hierarchy and does not identify a prescribed level. An effective test for every level would connect automaton behavior to precise bounds on logical descriptive complexity.

title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
importance_reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.
focus_reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.
formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
context:
A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.
why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.
status_note: Primary-source review and a later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no decider or undecidability theorem for the unrestricted model stated here. The inspected 2025–2026 papers classify shape, growth or expressive power. Their claims do not decide ordinary functional equivalence of arbitrary pairs.

working_summary: Deterministic macro tree transducers are recursive programs that turn finite ordered trees into other trees. Parameters carry intermediate output pieces, which rules may pass onward or duplicate during processing. The project asks whether two such programs define exactly the same partial transformation on every finite input tree. Testing examples can reveal a disagreement but cannot certify universal agreement without a completeness argument. A general decision procedure would provide an exact equivalence test for an expressive model of structured-data transformation, including cases with very large outputs.

title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
importance_reason: A central equivalence problem joining higher-order functional computation, infinite-tree semantics, and deterministic collapsible pushdown automata.
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, on every pair of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes G,H over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether their possibly infinite value trees are exactly equal, including divergence leaves?
definitions: Types are generated by o and \(\tau \to \sigma\). A terminal a of rank r has type \(o\to \cdots \to o\) with r arguments. A scheme has finitely many typed nonterminals, a start S:o, and exactly one rule \(F x_{1}\cdots x_{k}\to t\) for each \(F:\tau _{1}\to \cdots \to \tau _{k}\to o\). The distinct parameters \(x_{i}\) have the indicated types; t:o is a well-typed applicative term made from terminals, nonterminals and those parameters. There is no pattern matching, test on constructor values, nondeterministic choice, or restriction called safety. To obtain the value at a node, unfold the head nonterminal with substitution until a terminal a is exposed, then repeat for its r ordered arguments. If no terminal is ever exposed, that node is a nullary ⊥ leaf. This defines a tree over the alphabet extended with ⊥. Equality means identical node domains and labels at every finite address in the ordered tree; evaluation-step counts are ignored. The order of o is 0 and \(ord(\tau \to \sigma )=\max\)(\(ord(\tau )+1,ord(\sigma )\)); the maximum nonterminal order is finite but part of the input. Inputs may have different orders. No time bound is imposed beyond halting on every valid pair.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer is a single effective decision procedure for all finite input orders, with a proof of termination and correctness on equal as well as unequal trees. A negative answer proves this decision problem undecidable. Decidable model checking of one generated tree, a bounded-order subclass, or a conditional reduction to another open problem is not a full resolution.
context:
A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule \(S\to a S\), for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system \(S\to a T\) and \(T\to a S\) describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation \(plus(0,x)=x\). Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule \(S\to S\) generates ⊥, while \(S\to a S\) generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme \(S\to b S c\), with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, the generated trees are regular and equality can be checked by comparing finite state descriptions. At order one, the problem connects to deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. Allowing higher-order parameters makes the finite description much more expressive. The inherited Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre paper identifies equivalence as a central remaining question.

That paper’s positive equivalence theorem concerns two kinds of representation: higher-order recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata generate the same tree class, with effective translations. It transfers the problem to language equivalence for deterministic collapsible pushdown automata. It does not give an algorithm that compares arbitrary trees represented in either formalism. The difference between representation equivalence and instance equivalence is essential here.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems supplies a route through coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses. The translation represents the generated tree using predicates interpreted through a greatest model and creates separate positive and negative instances. A suitable semidecision procedure for the resulting coinductive problems would yield a decision procedure by interleaving the two searches. The needed semidecidability is left open, so this is a reduction rather than a completed decision algorithm.

The same work handles divergence constructively: it transforms a scheme so that each ⊥ leaf is replaced by an infinite chain over a fresh unary symbol. Equality is preserved and reflected. Thus treating divergence carefully need not restrict the question to an informal assumption that every program is productive. The present formulation keeps divergence explicit so readers can compare two given schemes without an unstated promise.

Recent results with similar terminology concern other targets. Bojańczyk–Fabiański–Stefański’s April 2026 undecidability theorem compares functions at higher-order types in the polyregular \(\lambda\)-calculus, a language with list-processing operations and extensional input/output semantics. Its theorem is not a stated undecidability result for the closed constructor-tree generators defined above. No reduction identifying the two decision problems is assumed here.

Dal Lago–Fiorillo–Pistone’s LICS 2026 work instead decides almost-sure termination for a typed subclass of probabilistic recursion schemes, using algebraic generating functions. That achievement concerns termination probabilities under additional type restrictions. The inherited question asks exact equality of deterministic value trees at unrestricted finite orders, and remains separate.
why: A fundamental decidability boundary for comparing higher-order recursive computations: expressive tree generators admit strong verification procedures, while exact equality of two generated behaviors remains unresolved.
status_note: Open for unrestricted finite-order deterministic schemes with the exact tree semantics stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Conditional Horn reductions, model checking, probabilistic termination and higher-order polyregular functional equivalence do not by themselves settle it.
progress: 1997–2002: Sénizergues establishes deterministic pushdown equivalence, giving the order-one recursion-scheme boundary described in the inherited survey. | 2008–2017: Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre give effective translations between recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata; the journal article explicitly retains instance equivalence as open. | 2021-03-02: Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre’s revision develops effective logical reflection, selection and model checking. | 2021: Jochems reduces scheme equivalence to an open coinductive-Horn semidecidability problem and gives an equality-preserving removal of divergence leaves. | 2026-04-13: Higher-order polyregular functional equivalence is proved undecidable in a different model and semantics. | 2026: LICS work gives almost-sure termination decidability for a typed probabilistic subclass, not unrestricted deterministic tree equivalence.
working_summary: A higher-order recursion scheme is a finite system of typed recursive rules that unfolds into a possibly infinite labeled tree. The project asks whether two deterministic schemes always admit an effective test for equality of their complete value trees. Equality includes divergence leaves and compares labels at every finite address, irrespective of internal evaluation steps. Functions passed as arguments make the generators much richer than finite-state descriptions. Solving this comparison problem would extend our ability to verify higher-order recursive behavior beyond properties of one generated tree at a time.

title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
importance_reason: The tree analogue of effective first-order definability for regular word languages.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a finite bottom-up automaton A for finite unranked ordered labeled trees, always halts and decides whether some first-order sentence \(\varphi\) using label predicates, strict descendant and sibling order satisfies A accepts t if and only if \(t\models \varphi\) for every finite input tree t?
definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word \(\varepsilon\), closed under prefixes, and such that \(ui\in T\) implies \(uj\in T\) for \(1\le j\le i\). Its root is \(\varepsilon\); the children of u are \(u1,\ldots ,uk\) in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). There is no fixed bound on k. \(Desc(x,y)\) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. \(Sib(x,y)\) means \(x=ui\) and \(y=uj\) for the same parent u with \(i<j\); it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates \(\mathrm{P}_{a}(x)\), one per label \(a\in \Sigma\), complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if \(Desc(x,y)\), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making \((Q,\oplus ,0) a\) monoid, a table \(\delta _{a}:Q\to Q\) for each \(a\in \Sigma\), and an accepting subset \(F\subseteq Q\). A node labeled a with ordered child states \(q_{1},\ldots ,q_{k}\) receives state \(\delta _{a}(q_{1}\oplus \cdots \oplus q_{k})\); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence \(\varphi\) may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.
context:
An automaton combines finitely many states from the children and passes one state to their parent. A first-order sentence instead describes relationships between named nodes. For instance, “every a-labeled node has a b-labeled descendant” is the sentence \(\forall x\)(\(\mathrm{P}_{a}(x)\Rightarrow \exists y\)(\(Desc(x,y)\land \mathrm{P}_{b}(y)\))). The question asks whether the entire language recognized by a given automaton has some description of this logical kind.

A two-state bottom-up computation can track whether the total number of nodes is even or odd: combine child parities and then count the parent. First-order logic with order cannot express arbitrary parity even on trees that are single paths. Thus finite-state recognition is strictly more expressive. The task is to tell, from an automaton’s finite description, on which side of that expressiveness boundary its language lies.

A descendant relation permits a sentence to refer directly to nodes arbitrarily far below another node. A child relation concerns just one edge. Decidability results for the child-only vocabulary therefore do not settle this card. Order among siblings is also part of the input structure: permuting subtrees can change the truth of a formula. The chosen vocabulary matches the ordered ancestor-plus-lexicographic setting of the source rather than an unordered or purely local variant.

Bojańczyk and Segoufin decide definability in \(\Delta _{2}\), the languages having both an existential-then-universal and a universal-then-existential definition. They do not decide arbitrary first-order definability. Blumensath’s 2024 finite-tree work supplies decidable necessary and sufficient conditions separately, but no one condition that is both. A necessary condition can fail to reject every nondefinable language, while a sufficient condition can fail to accept every definable language. The remaining gap is a complete test.

The 2025 automata characterization studies first-order logic over unordered infinite trees. The August 2026 result decides a common fragment of particular branching-time and linear-time temporal logics. Their domains or logical restrictions differ from the full finite ordered-tree question. They do not supply the all-input terminating test requested here. A solution would turn an expressiveness boundary into a mechanically checkable property of finite-state tree specifications.
why: The tree analogue of effective first-order definability for regular word languages.
status_note: The 2024 primary finite-tree study explicitly retains the general first-order-definability problem. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established decision or undecidability theorem for this ordered finite-tree target. The 2025 infinite-tree and 2026 restricted temporal results are distinguished.
progress: 2010: An effective characterization is proved for \(\Delta _{2}\) over finite ordered trees, including the ancestor-plus-lexicographic signature. | 2024-07: New effective necessary and sufficient tests in a finite-tree algebra setting remain separate rather than forming a full criterion. | 2025-09: A first-order automata characterization is obtained for unordered infinite trees, a different semantic domain. | 2026-08: A temporal-logic common-fragment decision theorem does not decide unrestricted FO-definability on finite ordered trees.
working_summary: Can one decide whether a regular language of finite ordered trees has a first-order definition? The automaton is finite input, while the sought sentence must describe its language on trees of every finite size. The logic can inspect labels, descendants and sibling order but cannot quantify over sets of nodes. Known fragment tests and separate necessary or sufficient algebraic conditions leave the full decision problem unresolved. Recent infinite-tree and restricted temporal-logic characterizations do not establish this finite ordered-tree test.

title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
importance_reason: A longstanding decidability boundary for language equivalence under the fundamental unique-parse restriction.
formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. A result for deterministic pushdown presentations, comparison with only a finite automaton, or a semidecision procedure for inequivalence does not settle the complete two-grammar question.
context:
Each generated word has a unique parse in an unambiguous grammar, but the grammar need not make deterministic parsing choices. The question compares two languages under that promise.

The author’s problem list separates this question from the stronger problem of comparing arbitrary derivation multiplicities.
why: This basic equivalence problem tests the algorithmic power of unique parsing beyond deterministic context-free language descriptions.
status_note: The checked author page records this as open, last seen open in 2025. Read on 13 September 2026; its date is reported faithfully rather than treated as a new 2026 theorem. No exhaustive subsequent-result audit is claimed.
progress: 2025: The author’s problem list records 2025 as the last year in which this equivalence question was seen open.
working_summary: An unambiguous context-free grammar has at most one parse tree for every generated word. Two such grammars are given with the promise of unambiguity. The task is to decide whether they generate exactly the same finite words. No deterministic-pushdown or regular-language restriction is imposed. The question asks for a terminating decision procedure without any prescribed complexity bound.

title: Decidability with two parametric clocks and arbitrarily many integer parameters
importance_reason: Resolve a longstanding decidability boundary in timing-parameter synthesis.
formal: Is reachability decidable for discrete-time parametric timed automata with at most two parametric clocks and an arbitrary finite number of nonnegative integer parameters?
definitions: An input has finitely many locations, clocks initially zero, parameter symbols, guarded transitions and an initial and target location. A time-elapse step adds the same nonnegative integer to every clock. A transition guard is a conjunction of comparisons \(x\bowtie c\) or \(x\bowtie p\), where c is a nonnegative integer, p a parameter and \(\bowtie\in\{<,\le,=,\ge,>\}\); the transition may reset designated clocks to zero. Other clocks are unchanged. At most two clocks appear in comparisons to parameters; arbitrarily many clocks compared only with constants are allowed. A parameter valuation assigns a nonnegative integer to every parameter once for the entire run. The algorithm must halt on every finite binary encoding and answer whether some valuation permits a finite run to the target. This transition-guard presentation has no extra diagonal or parameter-arithmetic guards.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Parametric clocks describe systems whose timing constants are not fixed in advance. Decidability asks whether some assignment of those constants can make a target behavior reachable.

Göller and Hilaire establish EXPSPACE-completeness with two parametric clocks and one parameter in discrete time. They explicitly leave arbitrary numbers of parameters open. Dense-time results and infinite-word acceptance questions use different semantics and cannot be substituted for this finite-reachability target.
why: Resolve a longstanding decidability boundary in timing-parameter synthesis.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2023: The source settles one parameter and explicitly leaves the multiple-parameter case open.

title: Containment of finitely ambiguous probabilistic automata
importance_reason: Exact containment for bounded-ambiguity stochastic automata is a basic decidability frontier, separating fixed finite accepting multiplicity from a linearly ambiguous model with undecidable comparison. Its arithmetic obstruction reaches beyond one construction or parameter improvement.
formal: Is quantitative containment decidable for pairs of finitely ambiguous probabilistic automata? Given two rational probabilistic automata \(A,B\) over the same finite alphabet, each promised to admit its own uniform finite bound on the number of positive accepting runs per word, decide whether \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\). Neither automaton is required to be unambiguous, and the sought algorithm is unconditional.
definitions: ['A probabilistic automaton is \\(A=(\\Sigma,Q,\\delta,\\iota,F)\\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \\(\\Sigma\\), a finite nonempty state set \\(Q\\), accepting states \\(F\\subseteq Q\\), nonnegative rational initial weights \\(\\iota(q)\\) satisfying \\(\\sum_q\\iota(q)\\leq1\\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \\(\\delta(q,a,p)\\) satisfying \\(\\sum_p\\delta(q,a,p)\\leq1\\) for each state \\(q\\) and letter \\(a\\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.', 'For \\(w=a_1\\cdots a_m\\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \\(q_0,\\ldots,q_m\\) with \\(q_m\\in F\\) and \\(\\iota(q_0)\\prod_{i=1}^{m}\\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\\). Its weight is this product. Let \\(p_A(w)\\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \\(p_A(\\varepsilon)=\\sum_{q\\in F}\\iota(q)\\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.', 'Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \\(K\\geq0\\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \\(K\\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.', 'Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \\(p_A(w)\\leq p_B(w)\\) for every finite word \\(w\\in\\Sigma^{*}\\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.', 'Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every pair under the two finite-ambiguity promises, or a Lean-checked proof that this promise problem is undecidable. The proof must be unconditional. Restricting one side to unambiguous automata, approximating probabilities, or assuming a numerical gap does not settle this question.
context:
The primary paper leaves containment open when both input automata have uniformly bounded accepting ambiguity. The individual bounds may differ and need not be fixed across instances.

The journal version maintains that question. It proves unconditional decidability when the right side is unambiguous and conditional decidability, using Schanuel’s conjecture, when only the left side is unambiguous. Neither result covers arbitrary finite ambiguity on both sides.

The same journal paper proves undecidability when ambiguity may grow linearly with word length. A finite word-independent bound is therefore a substantive proposed decidability boundary. The narrower conjecture-removal target is TCS-0133.
why: Pointwise probability comparison is a basic refinement test for stochastic finite-state descriptions. Resolving this case would determine whether a constant bound on accepting multiplicity suffices to make exact comparison effective, just below a model in which linear growth of that multiplicity already permits undecidability.
status_note: The 2018 conference paper and 2021 journal conclusion explicitly leave this exact containment problem open. A bounded later-literature check on 13 September 2026 found no decision or undecidability theorem for both finitely ambiguous inputs. Source proofs were not independently verified and the status is not an exhaustive certification.
progress: 2018-07-04: The ICALP paper explicitly leaves the two-finitely-ambiguous containment problem open. | 2021-02-10: The journal version retains the open problem, distinguishes the directional partial results, and gives undecidability for linearly ambiguous automata.
working_summary: Two probabilistic automata assign acceptance probabilities to every finite input word. Each machine has a fixed finite bound on its positive accepting runs, but either bound can be greater than one. The question asks for an unconditional terminating test of whether the first probability never exceeds the second. Existing results with an unambiguous side do not settle the general case, and allowing linearly growing ambiguity already gives undecidability. The benchmark requires a Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proof for exact comparison without a gap promise.

title: Primitive words and context-freeness
importance_reason: A canonical elementary language whose grammar expressibility remains a fundamental question in combinatorics on words and automata theory.
formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with \(|\Sigma|\ge2\), is the language \[\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)=\{w\in\Sigma^+ : \text{there are no }u\in\Sigma^+,\ k\ge2\text{ with }w=u^k\}\] not context-free?
definitions: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of symbols; \(\Sigma^*\) includes the empty word and \(\Sigma^+\) excludes it. The power \(u^k\) is the concatenation of \(k\) copies of \(u\), where \(k\) is an integer. All one-letter words are primitive. A context-free grammar consists of a finite set \(V\) of nonterminals disjoint from \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of rules \(A\to x\) with \(A\in V\) and \(x\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Its language is the set of all terminal words derivable from \(S\) by finitely many applications of rules. Empty productions, unit productions and ambiguity are allowed. The assertion is that no such grammar has language exactly \(\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)\), for every allowed alphabet. It concerns all word lengths, with no algorithmic size or running-time parameter. Nonprimitive words are excluded even when their repeated root is itself nonprimitive.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that the primitive-word language is non-context-free for every finite alphabet of size at least two, or a Lean counterexample consisting of an allowed alphabet and a context-free grammar generating exactly its primitive words. Excluding only unambiguous grammars, deterministic grammars or grammars of bounded size is insufficient.
context:
Primitivity excludes every nontrivial repetition of a shorter word. The question asks whether a context-free grammar can express that condition over all lengths.

The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains context-freeness of primitive words as open while proving a result about probabilistic membership.
why: The primitive-word language is a basic boundary case linking periodicity of words with the expressive power of context-free grammars.
status_note: Explicitly open in the STACS 2026 introduction and retained on the checked author problem list. Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the probabilistic-membership result is a different target and no general context-freeness resolution was identified.
progress: 2026-02-25: The STACS paper treats context-freeness of primitive words as a longstanding open question; its probabilistic-membership theorem does not resolve it.
working_summary: A primitive word is nonempty and is not a power of any shorter nonempty word. The language contains all such words over a fixed finite alphabet with at least two symbols. The conjecture says that no context-free grammar generates exactly this language. Grammars may be ambiguous, so unique-parse limitations would not settle the question. A 2026 paper still states this grammar-expressibility question as open.

title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
importance_reason: Determine the intrinsic sequential cost of a canonical finite-state operation, beyond the limitations of its classical algorithmic framework.
formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 2\), is there a deterministic word-RAM algorithm that minimizes every complete n-state DFA over \([a]\) in \(O(n)\) worst-case time?
definitions: Use a uniform word-RAM with word length w, addressed word memory, addition and subtraction modulo \(2^{w}\), multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by less than w, comparisons and conditional branches, each costing one step. No nonuniform tables are supplied; initialization and preprocessing are charged. Here \(w=\lceil 2 \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\). The input gives n, a transition table \(\delta :[n]\times [a]\to [n]\), an initial state and n accepting-state bits. A word is accepted when its successive transitions from the initial state end in an accepting state. The output is a complete DFA for exactly the same language with the fewest possible states. Unreachable states may be removed. The time constant may depend on a; it cannot depend on n or the automaton.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Minimization asks for the smallest deterministic recognizer of a regular language, a basic operation in language processing and finite-state verification. Hopcroft’s algorithm gives \(O(n \log  n)\) time for a fixed alphabet.

The remaining question concerns unrestricted sequential algorithms in an explicit RAM model. Lower bounds for a particular partition-refinement framework do not establish a lower bound for every such algorithm. The unary-alphabet special case does not resolve the fixed alphabet of size at least two.
why: Determine the intrinsic sequential cost of a canonical finite-state operation, beyond the limitations of its classical algorithmic framework.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2014: The paper uses Hopcroft’\(s O(a n \log  n)\) algorithm as the classical baseline and distinguishes symbolic alphabets from ordinary finite alphabets.

title: Separating words problem
importance_reason: A basic state-complexity problem measuring finite automata’s ability to distinguish arbitrary strings and connecting to reconstruction questions.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), \[s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}\min\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\}.\]
definitions: The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton. A proposed positive comparison function \(f\) determines the requested asymptotic scale when constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) exist with \(a f(n)\le s(n)\le b f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). The source’s conjectured endpoint is \(s(n)=O(\log n)\); the card explicitly asks for the underlying worst-case scale rather than asserting this endpoint.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function \(f(n)\) and a Lean proof of both constant-factor inequalities in the definitions. A universal small-DFA upper bound must be accompanied by a matching worst-case lower bound. This is asymptotic state complexity; the numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to big-O bounds. Results for random words or selected families of pairs do not determine the unrestricted maximum.
context:
The original problem asks whether logarithmically many states always suffice to distinguish two equal-length binary words. This card develops that threshold question into determination of the worst-case state function.

The August 2026 primary abstract reports a general \(\widetilde O(n^{1/3})\) upper bound and studies a stronger result only when one word is random. The September preprint supplies another proof at the general one-third exponent, not a logarithmic universal bound.
why: Determining this scale would quantify how little finite-state memory suffices to distinguish an arbitrary pair of long binary strings.
status_note: The checked 2026 preprints retain a general one-third-power upper-bound scale and do not give matching asymptotics or a universal logarithmic bound. Read on 13 September 2026; proofs were not independently verified and the literature search was bounded.
progress: 2019: The source poses a logarithmic upper-bound target and mentions a one-third-power bound as an intermediate scale. | 2026-08-28: Bathie reports the general one-third-power upper-bound frontier and proves a different guarantee for a random word against an adversarial comparison word. | 2026-09-08: Xu’s preprint abstract gives an elementary proof of an \(O(n^{1/3}(\log n)^{7/3})\)-state upper bound.
working_summary: The problem measures the smallest deterministic automaton that distinguishes two binary words of equal length. A different automaton may be chosen for each pair and its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The target is the worst-case number of states as a function of the common word length. The original question proposes a logarithmic upper bound, while recent general bounds have a one-third power with logarithmic factors. The benchmark asks for matching constant-factor asymptotics across all pairs, not a random-input guarantee.

title: Polynomial-time universality for unambiguous context-free grammars
importance_reason: Universality for unambiguous context-free grammars is a canonical complexity question about a major language class.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that decides whether \(L(G)=\Sigma^{*}\) for every context-free grammar \(G\) promised to be unambiguous, in time polynomial in the bit length of its explicit description? The algorithm must have one polynomial running-time bound on all input strings; correctness is required on the promised grammars. The terminal alphabet is part of the input. This card selects the polynomial-time endpoint of the source’s broader question about the exact complexity.
definitions: ['A context-free grammar is a finite tuple \\(G=(V,\\Sigma,P,S)\\), where the finite sets of nonterminals \\(V\\) and terminals \\(\\Sigma\\) are disjoint, \\(S\\in V\\), and \\(P\\subseteq V\\times(V\\cup\\Sigma)^{*}\\) is a finite set of production rules. The alphabet is finite and nonempty. All symbols, productions and right-hand-side strings are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices; repeated identical rules are treated as a single rule. Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed.', 'A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \\(S\\). Each nonterminal node expands according to one production, with its children in the right-hand-side order; an empty production contributes no terminal. Its yield is the terminal string read from left to right. \\(L(G)\\) is the set of yields. The unambiguity promise says that each word has at most one such parse tree, including the empty word. It is a promise on the given grammar, not merely on its language.', 'Universality includes every finite word, including \\(\\varepsilon\\). Polynomial time means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine and constants \\(C,d\\geq1\\) whose runtime on every string of length \\(N\\) is at most \\(C(N+1)^{d}\\). It outputs a bit. On every well-formed unambiguous grammar this bit is 1 exactly for universal grammars; on other inputs either answer is allowed.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the specified uniform polynomial-time promise algorithm, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A faster superpolynomial algorithm, a conditional lower bound alone, or an algorithm limited to deterministic grammars does not meet this criterion.
context:
The 2019 problem asks to close the complexity gap for universality with a unique-parse promise. The benchmark’s yes/no polynomial-time endpoint is an editorial choice; a negative answer would leave finer complexity classification open.

Clemente’s 2020 paper proves a polynomial-space upper bound (Theorem 10). Its quantitative coin-flip-measure hardness theorem concerns a different problem and does not establish an equivalent hardness result for universality.

The 2023 paper improves the checked upper bound to \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\): randomized polynomial time with one-sided error and access to an oracle for majority acceptance of polynomial-time nondeterministic computations. This oracle-assisted bound does not provide the deterministic polynomial-time algorithm asked for here.
why: Unique parse trees suffice to make universality decidable, but they do not give deterministic control of parsing. A polynomial-time procedure, or a proof excluding one, would locate the computational cost of this fundamental coverage test between finite-state reasoning and general context-free behavior.
status_note: The 2019 question asks to close the complexity gap. Primary papers from 2020 and 2023 give successively stronger upper bounds, the latter in coRP with a PP oracle. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no resolution of the deterministic polynomial-time endpoint; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2019-07-01: The problem list asks for improved upper or lower complexity bounds under the unambiguity promise. | 2020-08-07: Theorem 10 gives a polynomial-space algorithm; the discussion leaves exact universality complexity open. | 2023-04-27: Corollary 4 and its stated consequence place universality of arbitrary-alphabet unambiguous grammars in \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\), improving the polynomial-space bound.
working_summary: An unambiguous context-free grammar gives each accepted word a unique parse tree. This card asks whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can test if such a grammar generates every finite word over its alphabet. Unambiguity is promised for the supplied grammar, and the alphabet and complete production rules are part of the input. The checked upper bound uses randomized polynomial time with a PP oracle; it does not yield the unconditional deterministic polynomial-time procedure sought here. The polynomial-time endpoint is an explicit editorial specialization of the source’s broader complexity question, with either answer requiring a Lean-checked proof.

title: Decidability of discounted-sum universality over infinite words
importance_reason: A central decision problem for quantitative automata with direct connections to verification and exact discounted-sum representability; the rational infinite-word case goes beyond established restricted algorithms.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a complete nondeterministic discounted-sum automaton \(\mathcal A\) with rational weights and a rational discount factor \(0<\lambda<1\), and a rational threshold \(t\), decides whether \(\mathcal A(w)\leq t\) for every infinite word \(w\in\Sigma^\omega\)? Here \(\mathcal A(w)\) is the infimum of the discounted sums of its runs on \(w\).
definitions: The input contains a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), finite nonempty state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and weight map \(g:E\to\mathbb Q\). Completeness means every state has at least one outgoing transition for each letter. There are no epsilon transitions, final-state restrictions or fairness conditions: every infinite run is eligible. On \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run is an infinite state sequence \(q_0,q_1,\ldots\) with \(e_i=(q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\in E\). Its value is \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i)\); finite weights and \(0<\lambda<1\) ensure absolute convergence. The word value is \(\mathcal A(w)=\inf\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i): (e_i)_{i\geq0}\text{ is a run on }w\}\). The run set is nonempty and finitely branching, and this infimum is attained, so universality is equivalently \(\forall w\,\exists r\) with run value at most \(t\). Different words may use different runs; a run is not required to be chosen by an online strategy. One common discount factor applies to every transition. It is an input rational, not restricted to the reciprocal of an integer. All finite sets and tables are explicit; rational numerators and positive denominators are binary integers. An algorithm means one ordinary deterministic Turing machine that halts on every encoded valid instance and answers the exact non-strict threshold question. No finite-word truncation, approximation tolerance or bound on running time is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for the stated infinite-word, non-strict universality problem, including its correctness on every rational input. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A procedure for deterministic or functional automata, integer-reciprocal discount factors, finite words, strict inequalities alone or thresholds separated by a promised positive gap does not meet this full target without a proved reduction.
context:
Discounting reduces the influence of distant transitions while retaining their exact contribution. For instance, an infinite run of weight one at every step has value \(1/(1-\lambda)\). A finite prefix determines an approximation, but equality to a rational threshold can depend on the entire continuation.

The 2014 source mentions universality as an unresolved problem related to exact-value discounted-sum games. This card fixes the standard non-strict infimum convention from the cited discounted-automata literature. The games problem is related but has different quantifiers and is not substituted for automaton universality.

Boker and Henzinger define universality by comparing every word value to a constant threshold. Their discount parameter is greater than one and divides the weight at each successive position; the present multiplier is its reciprocal. Their integral-parameter determinization result therefore covers integer-reciprocal multipliers, not all rational multipliers.

Nondeterminism is resolved separately for each complete word. Requiring one strategy to choose transitions from prefixes would impose an additional online restriction. Similarly, finding one favorable path in the underlying weighted graph would ignore the requirement to handle every input word.

The 2025 target-sum paper distinguishes strict from non-strict universality and finite from infinite words. Its universality and inclusion decidability theorem for functional automata appears in the finite-word part. Functional means that all accepting runs of each word have the same value; this is an additional restriction absent here.

For infinite words, the same paper develops connections to exact target discounted sums, including a hardness implication for strict universality and a result for instances where the corresponding generalized target sum has no solution. These are useful delineations of the remaining difficulty, rather than a decision theorem for every instance in this card.
why: Universality asks whether a quantitative finite-state specification can keep every possible infinite input below a threshold. Its decidability is a basic unresolved boundary for verification with rational discounting, where arbitrarily small tail contributions can still decide exact threshold equality.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2014 source records the general universality difficulty, and the November 2025 follow-up still separates finite-word functional results from the infinite-word problem. No general decision or undecidability theorem for the precise non-strict rational model was located in the bounded later-work check. The infimum and non-strict convention are made explicit rather than inferred from the isolated 2014 sentence.
progress: 2011: Integral divisor discount factors admit the determinization result of Boker and Henzinger; in the multiplier convention this means integer-reciprocal factors. | 2014: Hunter and Raskin identify discounted-sum universality as unresolved in their discussion of exact-value games. | 2025-11-28: Boker, Henzinger and Otop give finite-word functional-automaton universality results and separate partial connections for infinite words in Section 6.
working_summary: The input is a finite nondeterministic automaton whose transitions carry rational discounted costs. Each infinite word receives the minimum cost among its runs, using one rational discount multiplier. The problem asks whether every infinite word has value at most a supplied rational threshold. The chosen run may depend on the entire word, and threshold equality must be decided exactly. Known restricted discount factors and recent finite-word functional results do not supply the general algorithm requested here.

title: Zeroness of rational weighted context-free grammars
importance_reason: Zero and universality questions are basic algorithmic tests for the power of automata representations.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides whether \(f_G(w)=0\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), given a context-free grammar in the weighted normal form below with rational production weights? Here \(f_G(w)\) is the sum, over all parse trees with yield \(w\), of the product of their production weights. Rational weights may be negative. This card selects the rational weighted-grammar case of the source’s broader zeroness agenda.
definitions: ['The input has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \\(V\\) and terminals \\(\\Sigma\\), with \\(\\Sigma\\ne\\varnothing\\), a start nonterminal \\(S\\in V\\), and finitely many productions. Every production has one of the forms \\(A\\to BC\\) or \\(A\\to a\\), with \\(A,B,C\\in V\\) and \\(a\\in\\Sigma\\); additionally \\(S\\to\\varepsilon\\) is allowed. The start symbol never occurs on a right-hand side. Each production has a rational weight, explicitly encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. At most one production with each left- and right-hand side is listed. There are no unit productions or other empty productions. Zero weights are allowed.', 'A parse tree is a finite ordered tree rooted at \\(S\\). Each nonterminal node expands by a listed production; the terminal leaves in order give its yield, and the empty start production gives the empty yield. The weight of a tree is the product of all weights of the productions used at its nonterminal nodes. The same production used at several nodes contributes one factor for every occurrence.', 'For a nonempty word of length \\(m\\), a parse tree in this form has \\(m\\) terminal-producing nodes and \\(m-1\\) binary-producing nodes. Thus there are only finitely many parses for each word, even when the grammar is ambiguous. Their rational weights are summed to define \\(f_G(w)\\); an empty sum is zero. For the empty word the value is the weight of \\(S\\to\\varepsilon\\), or zero if that production is absent. No analytic convergence or infinite sums of derivations are involved.', 'Terminal order is preserved: words with the same numbers of letters can have different values. Zeroness concerns the full function on words, not its commutative generating function or sums over word lengths. Cancellation between positive and negative tree weights is part of the semantics; there is no nonnegativity or probabilistic normalization promise.', 'All symbols and productions are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices. The algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on finite descriptions, halting on every well-formed input and returning yes exactly for identically zero functions. No time bound is imposed; malformed descriptions can be rejected. The explicit binary normal form and coefficient field \\(\\mathbb{Q}\\) are editorial choices fixing one benchmark variant.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for this rational weighted-grammar zeroness problem, or a Lean-checked undecidability proof. Testing finitely many sampled words, deciding zero only on a unary or bounded language, or deciding a commutative generating-series identity does not settle the stated word-by-word problem.
context:
The seminar’s question lists several separate models: weighted grammars over a field, unary polynomial automata, weighted Parikh automata and weighted vector addition systems. This benchmark retains the grammar branch with rational coefficients and an explicit finite-parse normal form. It does not claim that solving this selected variant settles the other listed models.
