Clemente’s 2024 paper still identifies rational weighted context-free grammar zeroness as beyond known techniques. It obtains decidability for weighted basic parallel processes, whose interleaving composition is different from sequential grammar concatenation.

The 2023 algebraic-series results concern commuting variables and multiplicity comparisons on restricted languages. Those results do not determine cancellation separately for every ordered word in an unrestricted alphabet.
why: This is an identity test for recursive numerical descriptions, extending finite-state weighted equivalence to context-free composition. It isolates the difficulty of exact cancellation across arbitrarily deep but finitely parsed derivations, a basic obstacle behind comparing quantitative grammars and counting their parses.
status_note: The 2021 seminar direction and 2024 primary paper identify weighted context-free zeroness as unresolved. The 2023 results concern commutative series or restricted word languages. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no decision theorem for the selected rational finite-parse grammar model; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2022-04-11: The seminar report lists weighted-grammar zeroness among the unresolved algorithmic questions. | 2023-04-27: The algebraic-series paper gives counting-hierarchy upper bounds for commuting-variable series and restricted multiplicity comparisons. | 2024-07-04: The weighted-parallel-process paper distinguishes its new decidability result from the still-unresolved weighted context-free grammar case.
working_summary: A weighted context-free grammar assigns each word the sum of the weights of its parse trees. This card asks whether an algorithm can always decide if that value is zero for every finite word. Production weights are signed rationals, and an explicit normal form ensures every word has only finitely many parses. The challenge is cancellation for each ordered word; results on commuting-variable series and weighted parallel processes address different models. The rational grammar variant is an explicit editorial choice from a broader source agenda, with decidability or undecidability to be proved in Lean.

title: A \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) dichotomy for visibly pushdown languages
importance_reason: A structural circuit-complexity classification for an established automaton model; its scope connects language theory with the unresolved boundary between threshold and logarithmic-depth circuits.
formal: For every visibly pushdown language \(L\) of well-matched finite words, is \(L\in\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) or is \(L\) complete for \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under constant-depth truth-table reductions? The circuit families and reductions are nonuniform, as defined below; the alternatives are inclusive.
definitions: The alphabet is a fixed finite disjoint union \(\Sigma=\Sigma_{\mathrm{call}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{ret}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{int}}\). A word is well-matched when every prefix has at least as many calls as returns and the whole word has equally many. A deterministic visibly pushdown automaton has finite control states, a finite stack alphabet with a bottom marker, an initial state and designated final states. It reads one letter per step, starting with just the bottom marker. A call pushes one non-bottom symbol, a return pops one symbol, and an internal letter leaves the stack unchanged; the finite transition table may inspect the state, letter and stack top. Acceptance requires a final control state and a stack containing just the bottom marker. Words that are not well-matched are rejected. Missing transitions reject. A language recognized by such an automaton is a visibly pushdown language (VPL); the automaton is fixed, while word length grows. Letters use a fixed-length injective binary code, and invalid codes are rejected. A nonuniform circuit family has one Boolean circuit for each input length, with no requirement that a machine generate the circuits. In \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), circuits have polynomial size and constant depth and may use NOT and unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and majority gates. A majority gate returns one precisely when more than half its inputs are one. In \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\), circuits have polynomial size, depth \(O(\log(n+2))\), and AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two, together with NOT gates. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on the fixed language. The reduction \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) consists of nonuniform constant-depth polynomial-size Boolean circuits with AND, OR and NOT gates and polynomial-length oracle gates for membership in \(L\). No directed path goes from an oracle output to an oracle input. The circuit decides \(K\), and its size includes the oracle-query wires. Completeness means \(L\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) and \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) for every \(K\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated alternative for every VPL. Alternatively specify a VPL and prove in Lean both that it is outside \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) and that it is not \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-hard under the stated reductions. The target does not additionally require an algorithm assigning automata to the alternatives. A classification using a different reduction or uniformity convention must establish that it implies this proposition.
context:
The input itself prescribes when the machine uses its stack. Nested calls can therefore carry information that finite-state machines cannot store, while the matching structure remains visible before the control computation is performed. Well-matched words can nest arbitrarily deeply; the question does not impose a depth bound.

Every VPL is in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The unresolved issue is whether any VPL occupies an intermediate position: requiring more than constant-depth threshold computation while failing to represent every logarithmic-depth bounded-fan-in computation. The known upper bound makes hardness and completeness equivalent here.

The 2024 paper classifies many VPLs relative to \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\), the constant-depth class without majority gates, and isolates a family whose \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) membership remains unresolved. That three-way outcome does not decide the present \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) question.

A lower bound against \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) is insufficient: majority and modular counting can require gates absent from \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) but still lie in \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Conversely, knowing that a language has a logarithmic-depth circuit is only an upper bound, not a completeness proof.

The source separately asks whether membership in the threshold-circuit class can be decided from an automaton. This card selects the stated dichotomy proposition itself, preserving that distinction. It also retains the source’s constant-depth truth-table reductions, which allow several parallel oracle queries, rather than silently strengthening completeness to a single-query many-one reduction.

The two classes are not assumed to be different. If they coincide, the first alternative holds for every VPL. A negative answer would in particular separate them, so a conjectural class separation cannot be used as an unstated premise.
why: This asks whether visible stack structure admits a complete boundary between constant-depth threshold computation and general logarithmic-depth circuits. Such a theorem would explain parallel complexity across an infinite language family, beyond deciding individual automata or proving one circuit lower bound.
status_note: The 2024 primary source explicitly poses this dichotomy with its own circuit and reduction conventions. A bounded subsequent-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a resolution. This is source-backed open status, not an independent certification of the entire literature.
progress: 2024: Göller and Grosshans establish a partial effective \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) classification and pose the \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) dichotomy in Section 6.
working_summary: A visibly pushdown automaton reads finite words whose letters prescribe its stack operations. The target concerns well-matched inputs and nonuniform Boolean circuit families. It asks whether every recognized language is either in constant-depth threshold circuits or complete for logarithmic-depth bounded-fan-in circuits. Hardness uses constant-depth truth-table reductions, and the alternatives may overlap. The source’s partial classification for the weaker class AC0 does not settle this dichotomy.

title: Universality of unambiguous register automata over ordered integers
importance_reason: A general decidability boundary for data, timed, or hyperproperty formalisms would affect the corresponding verification model.
formal:
Is universality decidable for unambiguous register automata with guessing over \((\mathbb Z,<,=)\) and finitely many named integer constants? Given a finite automaton description in the model below, promised to have at most one accepting run on every finite data word, must there be an algorithm deciding whether
\[L(\mathcal A)=(\Sigma\times\mathbb Z)^*?\]
The finite alphabet, number of registers, control states, guards and binary-encoded constants are all part of the input. This card makes the guessing convention explicit, using the relational register model discussed in the cited literature. Its main target is the decidability part of the source question; a tight complexity classification is a further question if the answer is positive.
definitions:
The automaton has a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite set of control states \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a set \(F\subseteq Q\) of accepting states, and \(k\ge0\) registers with values in \(\mathbb Z\). All registers initially contain zero. This fixed initialization is part of the selected convention; integer constants, including zero, are available in guards. A data word is any finite sequence \((a_1,z_1)\cdots(a_m,z_m)\), where \(a_i\in\Sigma\) and \(z_i\in\mathbb Z\). The empty word is included.

For each control-state pair and input letter, the transition table specifies a quantifier-free Boolean formula \(g\) built using true, negation and conjunction from atoms \(u=v\) and \(u<v\). Terms \(u,v\) are the current input datum, an old register value \(r_i\), a proposed new register value \(r'_i\), or one of the finitely many integer constants in the description. Disjunction can be expressed using negation and conjunction. There is no addition, successor, multiplication or arbitrary numerical predicate in a guard. Parallel descriptions of the same transition relation are combined by disjunction.

From state \((q,\bar r)\) on input \((a,z)\), the automaton may move to any \((q',\bar r')\) for which the corresponding guard is true over the ordinary integers. Thus new register values may be nondeterministically guessed; they are not required to be copies of the input or old values. The transition relation may have infinitely many successors. Each transition consumes exactly one input letter, with no epsilon moves. A run is its sequence of control states and register tuples, starting at \((q_0,0,\ldots,0)\). It accepts if its control state after the last input letter is in \(F\). Acceptance depends on the existence of such a run, and no condition is imposed on final register contents. Different syntactic guard clauses producing the same sequence are not counted as different runs.

Unambiguity means that every word has at most one initialized accepting run, including all guessed values. There may be many rejecting or partial runs. In particular, a universal unambiguous automaton has exactly one accepting run for every word. This is a semantic promise on the supplied description, not a claim that all transition choices are unique.

Descriptions use finite binary encodings of states, letters, register indices, guard syntax and signed integer constants. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine that halts and returns the correct universality answer on every description satisfying the promise. Its behavior on ambiguous or malformed descriptions is unrestricted, and it need not verify the promise. There is no complexity bound, bound on the number of registers, or bound on constant magnitudes beyond finiteness.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of decidability in this promised class, or prove that no such decision procedure exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary finite register counts and named integer constants, with the specified guessing transitions. An undecidability reduction must produce unambiguous automata. Algorithms over rational data, over equality alone, or for a fixed restricted register model do not settle this integer-order target.
context:
The source explicitly names the integers, their order and constants. Replacing them by the rationals changes the available values between two named constants. In addition, equality of control states does not identify runs with different guessed register tuples.

The relational guard convention follows the standard guessing model: guards constrain both old and new register values. Requiring every update to copy a previously seen datum would remove this feature. The card records this modeling choice explicitly because register-automaton terminology varies across papers.

Czerwiński, Mottet and Quaas establish decidability bounds in equality-based cases and for a one-register dense-order case. Their results do not state the general integer-order-with-constants theorem asked here.

The later vector-space approach gives exponential-time equivalence for unambiguous register automata with guessing over equality atoms and ordered atoms, and polynomial time at fixed register count. Its ordered atoms are the dense rational order. An appeal to that theorem alone does not establish universality over the discrete integer domain.
why: Unambiguity often preserves much of nondeterministic expressive power while recovering decidable equivalence or universality. This question tests that phenomenon over discrete ordered data with constants and guessed register values. Its resolution would identify how far the successful algorithms for equality and dense order extend toward integer-valued verification models.
status_note: The seminar’s Section 5.9 question, the 2021 relational register-automaton definitions and the published 2024 orbit-finite equivalence theorem were checked on 2026-09-14. The selected guessing and initialization conventions are explicit. A bounded later-work search identified no decision procedure or undecidability theorem for the full selected integer-order-with-constants class.
progress: 2021: The ICALP paper develops universality and containment techniques for equality data and restricted dense-order cases. | 2021: Quaas poses the integer-order-with-constants question at Dagstuhl Seminar 21452; the report is published in April 2022. | 2024: The published orbit-finite vector-space work provides stronger equivalence algorithms with guessing for equality atoms and the rational order.
working_summary: A register automaton reads letters paired with integer data and retains finitely many integer values. Its transitions may compare stored values, input values and named constants, and may guess new values. Unambiguity promises at most one accepting run for every word. The question asks whether one can decide that every finite data word is accepted. Known algorithms over equality or dense rational order do not by themselves settle the selected discrete-integer model.

title: Deterministic separability of nondeterministic timed languages
importance_reason: A general decidability boundary for data, timed, or hyperproperty formalisms would affect the corresponding verification model.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given two nondeterministic timed automata \(A,B\) with epsilon transitions over the same finite alphabet, always halts and decides whether there exists a deterministic timed automaton \(S\) such that \(L(A)\subseteq L(S)\) and \(L(S)\cap L(B)=\varnothing\)? Languages contain finite timed words. The separator may use any finite number of clocks and any finite integer constants: no resource bound is supplied or fixed in advance.
definitions: ['A finite timed word over a finite alphabet \\(\\Sigma\\) is \\((a_1,t_1)\\cdots(a_n,t_n)\\), where \\(n\\geq0\\), \\(a_i\\in\\Sigma\\), and \\(0\\leq t_1\\leq\\cdots\\leq t_n\\) are real timestamps. Equal timestamps and the empty word are allowed.', 'A timed automaton has finite sets of locations \\(Q\\), clocks \\(X\\), initial locations \\(I\\subseteq Q\\), final locations \\(F\\subseteq Q\\), and transitions \\((p,a,\\phi,Y,q)\\). Here \\(a\\in\\Sigma\\cup\\{\\varepsilon\\}\\), \\(Y\\subseteq X\\), and \\(\\phi\\) is a Boolean combination of true, false, \\(x\\mathrel{\\sim} z\\), and \\(x-y\\mathrel{\\sim} z\\), with clocks \\(x,y\\), integer \\(z\\), and \\(\\sim\\in\\{=,<,\\leq,>,\\geq\\}\\). There are no location invariants. All sets, transitions and guard formulas are explicitly encoded, with signed binary integer constants.', 'A run starts at time 0 in an initial location with all clocks zero. Time may advance by any nonnegative real amount, adding that amount to every clock. A transition can then fire when its guard is true; it changes the location and resets precisely the clocks in \\(Y\\) to zero. Its label and absolute firing time form an event. A finite run is accepting when its final location belongs to \\(F\\). The language \\(L(A)\\) consists of the timed words obtained from accepting runs by deleting all epsilon-labeled events and preserving the timestamps of all other events. Arbitrarily many but finitely many epsilon steps, including before the first and after the last visible event, are allowed.', 'A deterministic separator has exactly one initial location, no epsilon transitions, and at most one enabled transition for each location, input letter and clock valuation. Incomplete transition relations are permitted and a missing transition rejects. Equivalently one can merge overlapping guards when their target location and reset set coincide. The number of locations, number of clocks and magnitudes of constants can all depend on the input pair.', 'The decision algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions and must halt on every valid pair; no complexity bound or disjointness promise is imposed. A pair with intersecting languages necessarily has answer no. Malformed descriptions can be rejected.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for this input model and unrestricted finite separators, or a Lean-checked proof of its undecidability. Decidability for each fixed clock bound does not supply a decision algorithm for the unrestricted problem; the algorithm must also terminate on negative instances.
context:
The problem asks whether two nondeterministically specified timed behaviors can be classified by a deterministic timed language. The accepted and rejected sets may leave other timed words unconstrained.

Theorem 1.1 of Clemente, Lasota and Piórkowski establishes decidability when the separator’s number of clocks is fixed, including when its largest constant is unrestricted. Their concluding section leaves unbounded-clock separability open. The paper’s undecidability theorem for unbounded timed synthesis is a separate game problem.
why: Deterministic timed descriptions support complement and monitoring operations that arbitrary nondeterministic descriptions do not. Settling unrestricted separability would identify whether the existence of such a classifier can be decided without an advance bound on the memory of time represented by clocks.
status_note: The primary 2020 paper and original problem page explicitly leave unrestricted deterministic separability open. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a later resolution; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.
progress: 2020-04-27: The primary paper establishes the fixed-clock decidability results and explicitly leaves the unrestricted separator question open.
working_summary: The input is a pair of nondeterministic timed automata describing finite event sequences with real timestamps. The question is whether a terminating algorithm can decide the existence of a deterministic timed separator accepting the first language and rejecting the second. Input automata may use invisible epsilon steps, while the separator has no such steps and may use any finite number of clocks. The known decidability theorem fixes the separator’s clock count and therefore does not answer this unrestricted question. Either a general decision procedure or an undecidability proof must be checked in Lean for the stated timed-word model.

title: Deciding first-order definability of orbit-finite automata
importance_reason: A foundational definability boundary for nominal automata, connecting effective algebra and infinite-alphabet language theory while isolating the deterministic finite-orbit restriction.
formal: Is it decidable, given a finitely presented deterministic orbit-finite automaton over an infinite equality-only data alphabet \(D\), whether its language \(L\subseteq D^*\) is definable by a first-order sentence using the order of word positions and equality of their data values?
definitions: Fix a countably infinite set \(D\), whose elements have no structure except equality. A data word is a finite sequence \(w=d_1\cdots d_n\), including the empty word. A data permutation is a bijection \(D\to D\). The automaton consists of a state set \(Q\) acted on by all data permutations, an initial state \(q_0\) fixed by every permutation, a set of final states \(F\), and a total deterministic transition function \(\delta:Q\times D\to Q\). Both \(F\) and \(\delta\) are equivariant: renaming all data values preserves finality and commutes with transitions. Every state has finite support, meaning a finite set of data values whose pointwise fixation fixes the state. Orbit-finite means that renaming data partitions \(Q\) into finitely many equivalence classes. Acceptance starts at \(q_0\), follows the unique transition sequence and tests finality after the last letter. The finite input presentation is as follows. Each state orbit has an integer arity \(r\geq0\) and a finite subgroup \(H\) of the permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Its states are injective \(r\)-tuples of data, identified under coordinate permutations from \(H\). The presentation lists the orbit tags, arities, groups, final tags and a zero-arity initial tag. A finite transition table gives a target tag and a tuple of selectors from the old coordinates and current input datum for each possible equality case between that datum and the coordinates. Selected output coordinates must be distinct, and the rules must be compatible with the stated coordinate identifications. These finite consistency conditions ensure a well-defined equivariant function; no unseen data value may be generated. Thus unordered stored data sets as well as ordered registers are represented, without an infinite transition table. A first-order formula quantifies only over the positions \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), has the usual Boolean operations and quantifiers, position equality and order \(<\), and the relation \(i\sim j\) interpreted as \(d_i=d_j\). There are no named data constants, data-order tests, predicates for arithmetic on positions or quantifiers over sets. Definability means that one finite sentence accepts exactly the language for all word lengths and all data values. Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine halting on every valid finite automaton presentation; no complexity bound is specified.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm deciding this first-order definability question for every valid presented automaton. Alternatively prove in Lean that the decision problem is undecidable. An algebraic characterization counts as a decision procedure only with an effective test for its condition on these inputs. A theorem assuming that the syntactic monoid itself is orbit-finite covers only a restricted class.
context:
An orbit represents all states that differ only in the actual names of stored data. Remembering one datum requires infinitely many concrete states but only one such state orbit. Finite orbit count bounds the shape of memory without bounding the number of possible input data values.

The source’s example “the first datum appears again later” is recognized by a deterministic orbit-finite automaton: it can retain the first datum and remember whether another occurrence has appeared. The same property is first-order definable by selecting the first position and a later position carrying equal data.

The 2011 theorem characterizes first-order definability when the syntactic data monoid is orbit-finite. The source explicitly asks to extend decidability to orbit-finite deterministic automata, whose syntactic monoids need not have finitely many orbits. The first-datum example already demonstrates the difference between these hypotheses.

The syntactic monoid identifies words \(u,v\) when \(xuy\in L\) iff \(xvy\in L\) for every pair of context words \(x,y\); multiplication is concatenation of equivalence classes. A monoid is aperiodic when each element \(m\) satisfies \(m^k=m^{k+1}\) for some integer \(k\geq1\). In an infinite monoid this definition does not silently impose one common exponent for all elements.

The author conjectures aperiodicity as the appropriate condition in the larger deterministic-automaton class. It is a candidate characterization, not an established algorithm in the source. The paper also gives a language outside the relevant restricted setting for which aperiodicity does not imply first-order definability.

Undecidability for first-order definability from nondeterministic register automata is a different input problem. The present automata have one unique run. Likewise, deciding a first-order property of the automaton’s state structure is different from deciding whether some first-order sentence defines its entire word language.
why: Over finite alphabets, first-order definability has a classical effective algebraic characterization. This problem asks whether that connection remains decidable when finite memory stores data from an infinite set, beyond the narrower orbit-finite-monoid setting.
status_note: The 2011 paper and its 2013 journal version explicitly leave the deterministic orbit-finite-automaton problem open. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a resolution. The finite presentation makes the input model explicit; newer decidability results for first-order properties of orbit-finite structures are not treated as answers to this language-definability question.
progress: 2011: Bojańczyk proves the first-order/aperiodicity characterization for orbit-finite syntactic data monoids and poses decidability for the larger deterministic orbit-finite-automaton class. | 2013: The journal version, Nominal Monoids, retains the deterministic-automaton definability question and the proposed aperiodicity criterion.
working_summary: The alphabet consists of infinitely many data values that can only be compared for equality. The deterministic automaton has finitely many kinds of state up to renaming stored data. The target is an algorithm deciding whether a sentence about position order and data equality defines its entire language. The known orbit-finite-monoid characterization applies to a smaller class than the automata in this question. A proposed aperiodicity characterization would need an effective test before it could establish decidability.

title: Periodic configurations in low-complexity two-dimensional shifts of finite type
importance_reason: A substantial periodicity and tiling-decidability question with a sharp pattern-count threshold and a specific unresolved extension beyond convex shapes.
formal: For every finite nonempty alphabet \(A\), finite nonempty shape \(D\subset\mathbb Z^2\), and set of allowed patterns \(P\subseteq A^D\) with \(|P|\leq|D|\), let \(X(D,P)=\{x:\mathbb Z^2\to A:\ (d\mapsto x(t+d))\in P\text{ for every }t\in\mathbb Z^2\}\). If \(X(D,P)\neq\varnothing\), must there exist \(x\in X(D,P)\) and a vector \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\) such that \(x(t+v)=x(t)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z^2\)?
definitions: A configuration assigns one alphabet symbol to each lattice cell. A \(D\)-pattern is a function from \(D\) to \(A\), and distinct functions count as distinct patterns. The same allowed list \(P\) is enforced at every translate of \(D\); its entries need not all occur in a valid global configuration. The shape is arbitrary: it may be disconnected, nonconvex or contained in a proper sublattice. No rectangle, nearest-neighbor, connectedness or convexity assumption is imposed. A shift of finite type (SFT) is a set of configurations specified by finitely many forbidden finite patterns and all their translates. In the displayed presentation, the forbidden patterns are exactly \(A^D\setminus P\). The low-complexity restriction is on this finite allowed presentation, \(|P|\leq|D|\), not merely on the number of patterns observed in one chosen configuration. Periodic means invariant under at least one nonzero translation; two independent periods are not required in the proposition. An aperiodic SFT in the source’s terminology is nonempty and contains no configuration with even one nonzero period. All configurations and periods in the conclusion may depend on \(A,D,P\); no bound on a period’s size or running time of a construction is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every nonempty \(X(D,P)\) satisfying \(|P|\leq|D|\) contains a periodic configuration. Alternatively give explicit finite \(A,D,P\), prove the pattern-count bound and nonemptiness in Lean, and prove that every configuration in \(X(D,P)\) has no nonzero translation period. A nonperiodic member alone is not a counterexample, and a theorem restricted to convex shapes does not resolve the stated quantification.
context:
A small set of local patterns can force large-scale regularity. If the shape consists of one cell, the bound permits at most one symbol, so every nonempty system is constant and periodic. Larger shapes can impose interacting constraints despite using at most as many allowed patterns as cells.

Kari and Moutot prove the implication for rectangular shapes in Corollary 5. Their conclusion extends the result to finite convex lattice shapes, meaning shapes containing all lattice points in their convex hull. The remaining question explicitly allows arbitrary shapes.

For the rectangular case, the existence of a periodic configuration also yields decidability of whether the finite local constraints admit any configuration; this is Corollary 6. General two-dimensional finite local constraints do not have this decidability property. The present card keeps periodic existence as its single main target.

Nivat’s conjecture makes a stronger demand about each individual configuration with few rectangular patterns: that configuration should itself be periodic. Here only one periodic member of the entire allowed system is required. An SFT can therefore satisfy this card even if it also has nonperiodic members.

The source describes why arbitrary scattered shapes are delicate. Such a shape may inspect only one parity class of lattice cells, allowing different sublattices to carry incompatible directions of periodicity. Known failures of an orbit-closure periodicity assertion for these shapes do not automatically supply a finite-type system with no periodic member.

The quantifier over all lattice cells matters. A collection of finite patches or a large computer-generated tiling does not by itself establish nonemptiness of an aperiodic SFT, nor does a search with no small period exclude every possible period.
why: This is a boundary question for how little local diversity can still enforce complete absence of global repetition. It links symbolic dynamics with the decidability of planar tiling constraints and isolates the arbitrary-shape obstruction beyond the established convex case.
status_note: The 2020 source explicitly conjectures periodic existence for arbitrary shapes, and its extended-version abstract continues to distinguish the convex result. A bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of the arbitrary-shape statement. Recent crawl dates of the October 2020 talk were not treated as new research dates.
progress: 2020: Corollaries 5 and 6 establish periodic existence and decidability for the rectangular low-complexity presentation; Section 6 extends the results to convex shapes and conjectures the arbitrary-shape case. | 2020-10: A problem presentation attributed to Jarkko Kari restates the low-complexity aperiodic-SFT question.
working_summary: A finite list of local patterns defines all legal colorings of the integer plane. The list is low-complexity when it has at most as many patterns as cells in its finite shape. The question asks whether every nonempty such system admits at least one coloring with a nonzero translation period. Rectangular and convex shapes are covered by the cited theorem, while arbitrary scattered shapes remain the stated target. This asks for one periodic global coloring, rather than requiring every legal coloring to be periodic.

title: State complexity of complementing unambiguous automata
importance_reason: The cost of unambiguous automata representations measures a basic tradeoff between ambiguity and succinctness.
formal: For each integer \(n\geq1\), define \[C(n)=\max_{A}\ \min\{\lvert Q_B\rvert: L(B)=\{0,1\}^{*}\setminus L(A)\},\] where \(A\) ranges over all unambiguous finite automata with between 1 and \(n\) states over the binary alphabet, and \(B\) ranges over nondeterministic finite automata over that alphabet with at least one state. Determine the asymptotic growth of \(C(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors. The output automaton is allowed to be ambiguous.
definitions: ['Both kinds of automaton are finite tuples \\((Q,\\{0,1\\},\\Delta,I,F)\\), where \\(Q\\) is the state set, \\(I,F\\subseteq Q\\) are the initial and final state sets, and \\(\\Delta\\subseteq Q\\times\\{0,1\\}\\times Q\\) is a transition relation. Multiple initial states, missing transitions, unreachable states and empty initial or final sets are allowed. There are no epsilon transitions or duplicate parallel transitions.', 'An accepting run on a word \\(a_1\\cdots a_m\\) is a state sequence \\(q_0,\\ldots,q_m\\) with \\(q_0\\in I\\), \\(q_m\\in F\\), and \\((q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)\\in\\Delta\\) for every \\(1\\leq i\\leq m\\). A word belongs to the language if it has an accepting run. For the empty word the accepting runs are the states in \\(I\\cap F\\). The input automaton is unambiguous when each word has at most one accepting run; there is no restriction on the number of rejecting runs.', 'Only the number of states is charged, not transitions, the alphabet description or computation used to construct the automaton. Up to state renaming there are finitely many eligible inputs. Determinization and complementation give an output with at most \\(2^{n}\\) states, so the minimum and maximum defining \\(C(n)\\) exist.', 'The target is a positive real-valued comparison function \\(g\\) on the positive integers, together with constants \\(c_1,c_2>0\\) and an integer \\(n_0\\geq1\\), such that \\(c_1g(n)\\leq C(n)\\leq c_2g(n)\\) for every \\(n\\geq n_0\\). Matching only the order of \\(\\log C(n)\\) is weaker than this criterion. The function must specify an asymptotic rate rather than restate the defining automaton optimization.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds within constant factors for \(C(n)\) as defined. The upper bound must cover every eligible input automaton; the lower bound must give a worst-case input for every sufficiently large size bound. No efficiency requirement is imposed on the conversion algorithm. Bounds only for one particular conversion, unary inputs, or unambiguous outputs do not supply the required matching result.
context:
Section 5.11 asks for better bounds on the number of states needed to complement unambiguous automata, emphasizing the gap for binary and larger alphabets. This benchmark makes the binary-alphabet extremal state count the single target and asks for matching multiplicative bounds.

The consolidated 2018 source also asks whether general-alphabet complementation can require an exponential number of states. That endpoint motivates the gap but is not equivalent to determining the entire asymptotic rate.

Göös, Kiefer and Yuan prove a binary-alphabet lower bound \(n^{\widetilde{\Omega}(\log n)}\) even when the complement may be represented ambiguously. Here the tilde suppresses powers of \(\log\log n\) in the exponent.

Indzhev and Kiefer give a complement with at most \(\sqrt{n+1}\,2^{n/2}\) states even with an unambiguous output. Their matching analysis of that specific conversion does not prove an exponential lower bound on the smallest possible complement.

The later unary-alphabet result gives quasipolynomial complementation there and still distinguishes the much wider binary-alphabet gap.
why: Unambiguity limits the number of positive certificates without directly describing negative certificates. The optimal cost of complementing this representation measures how much succinctness is lost under logical negation and tests the reach of communication-based lower bounds for finite-state models.
status_note: Primary 2022 papers and the 2025 unary-language paper describe a gap between quasipolynomial lower and exponential upper bounds for binary alphabets. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no matching general bound. Source claims and preprint statements have not been independently proof-verified.
progress: 2018-07-04: Raskin proves a superpolynomial lower bound using unary automata. | 2022-02-12: The revised binary construction gives the stronger lower bound \(n^{\widetilde{\Omega}(\log n)}\). | 2022-03-15: The revised upper-bound paper proves \(\sqrt{n+1}\,2^{n/2}\) states suffice for every input UFA. | 2024-12-13: The updated unary-language paper gives quasipolynomial unary complementation; it was subsequently published in 2025. This does not close the binary gap.
working_summary: An unambiguous finite automaton has at most one accepting run for each word. For a binary alphabet, this card asks for the worst-case number of states in a smallest nondeterministic automaton accepting its complement. The input has at most n states, while the output may be ambiguous and may have multiple initial states. Known binary lower bounds are quasipolynomial and known general upper bounds are exponential; stronger unary results concern a different alphabet. The requested answer gives matching multiplicative constant-factor bounds on the state count, proved in Lean.

title: Does adding modular predicates preserve decidable first-order definability?
importance_reason: A broad but model-sensitive meta-decidability question connecting word logic and algebraic language classification; the explicit fragment framework makes its intended transfer claim testable.
formal: For every effective first-order fragment \(\mathcal F\) satisfying the closure conditions below, does decidability of \(\mathcal F[<]\)-definability of regular finite-word languages imply decidability of \(\mathcal F[<,\mathrm{MOD}]\)-definability? Each decision algorithm takes a finite alphabet and a deterministic finite automaton as input; the fragment is fixed.
definitions: A word \(w=a_1\cdots a_n\) over a finite nonempty alphabet \(A\) is the finite structure on positions \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with position equality, order \(<\), and a unary letter predicate \(Q_a(i)\) for each \(a\in A\), true exactly when \(a_i=a\). Empty words have no positions. First-order formulas have Boolean connectives and quantifiers over positions only. The modular signature adds unary predicates \(M_{d,r}(i)\) meaning \(i\equiv r\pmod d\), and nullary predicates \(N_{d,r}\) meaning \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), for all integers \(d\geq1\) and \(0\leq r<d\). A formula uses finitely many of them, but there is no global modulus bound. These are position and length congruences, not quantifiers counting the number of positions satisfying a subformula. A fragment fixes either finitely many variable names or a countable list of names, and for every finite relational signature \(S\) specifies a set \(\mathcal F[S]\) of first-order formulas using those names. It contains all quantifier-free formulas on those variables and signatures, is closed under conjunction and disjunction, and is closed under quantifier-free substitution of relation atoms by formulas with the same available free variables, with bound variables renamed to avoid capture. Effectiveness here means one terminating procedure decides syntactic membership of a finite formula in \(\mathcal F[S]\) when its finite signature and formula are given. The names and arities of predicates and modular integers have ordinary finite encodings. For a signature with infinitely many available modular predicates, membership is read on the finite signature actually used. The notation \(\mathcal F[<]\) includes the letter and equality predicates, and \(\mathcal F[<,\mathrm{MOD}]\) also permits the modular predicates just defined. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is an explicit finite state set, initial state, final-state subset and total transition table on \(A\); it recognizes a regular language \(L\subseteq A^*\). Definability asks whether some sentence in the specified fragment has exactly language \(L\), for all finite words. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine halting on every DFA/alphabet input. Its program may depend on the fixed fragment; no uniform transformation from base deciders to enriched deciders or running-time bound is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every effective fragment satisfying the specified closure conditions. Alternatively define a particular such fragment, prove its effectiveness and closure properties in Lean, give a Lean-verified algorithm for its base definability problem, and prove in Lean that the enriched definability problem is undecidable. Results about satisfiability, fixed moduli, separation given as an additional oracle, or only selected standard fragments do not decide this full implication.
context:
The 2013 paper poses a general transfer question for fragments without providing one formal universe of admissible fragment descriptions. Editorial convention: the target above uses the quantifier-free-substitution closure framework made explicit in the 2019 follow-up literature, and additionally requires decidable syntax. This states a concrete transfer proposition; it is not presented as a verbatim formal theorem from the original concluding paragraph.

Adding congruence tests can increase expressive power while preserving regularity. For example, a nullary length predicate can require the whole word to have even length, and a unary predicate can restrict which letters occur at positions of a given parity. The question concerns whether a supplied regular language can be described at all, not whether an individual sentence has a model.

The 2013 theorem establishes decidability for two-variable first-order logic with modular predicates. Two-variable logic allows reusing two position-variable names under nested quantifiers. This important instance does not imply the universal transfer proposition for all admissible fragments.

Place, Ramanathan and Weil develop a generic transfer theorem for separation and covering when the underlying language classes already include an appropriate enrichment by local predicates such as successor. Their statement both assumes a stronger decision problem and uses structural hypotheses beyond the bare decidable-membership premise here.

Separation takes two regular languages and asks for a language of the fragment containing the first and disjoint from the second. There is also a difference between allowing any finite collection of moduli in the defining sentence and fixing that collection in advance. title: Unconditional containment of unambiguous probabilistic automata
importance_reason: A substantive complexity or decidability question for a standard quantitative, timed, string, or language model.
formal: Is quantitative containment decidable when the left automaton \(A\) is unambiguous and the right automaton \(B\) is finitely ambiguous? In other words, does a single unconditional terminating algorithm decide \(\forall w\in\Sigma^{*},\ p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every promised pair of rational probabilistic automata as defined below? This selects the direction of bounded-ambiguity containment whose known decidability proof uses Schanuel’s conjecture; the reverse direction is already decidable unconditionally.
definitions: ['A probabilistic automaton is \\(A=(\\Sigma,Q,\\delta,\\iota,F)\\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \\(\\Sigma\\), a finite nonempty state set \\(Q\\), accepting states \\(F\\subseteq Q\\), nonnegative rational initial weights \\(\\iota(q)\\) satisfying \\(\\sum_q\\iota(q)\\leq1\\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \\(\\delta(q,a,p)\\) satisfying \\(\\sum_p\\delta(q,a,p)\\leq1\\) for each state \\(q\\) and letter \\(a\\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.', 'For \\(w=a_1\\cdots a_m\\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \\(q_0,\\ldots,q_m\\) with \\(q_m\\in F\\) and \\(\\iota(q_0)\\prod_{i=1}^{m}\\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\\). Its weight is this product. Let \\(p_A(w)\\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \\(p_A(\\varepsilon)=\\sum_{q\\in F}\\iota(q)\\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.', 'Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \\(K\\geq0\\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \\(K\\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.', 'Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \\(p_A(w)\\leq p_B(w)\\) for every finite word \\(w\\in\\Sigma^{*}\\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.', 'Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.']

title: Determinacy of Wadge games for Muller tree languages
importance_reason: A foundational question linking finite automata, infinite games and the axiomatic strength of descriptive language complexity. Existing score retained.
formal: Let \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) be the statement that, for every pair \(A,B\) of finite nondeterministic Muller automata on infinite full binary labeled trees, the Wadge game \(W(L(A),L(B))\) is determined. Is \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) provable in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice, ZFC? The target is provability from these axioms, not an algorithm for finding the winning player.
definitions:
For a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a full binary labeled tree is a function \(t:\{0,1\}^*\to\Sigma\). The empty word is the root and the children of node \(u\) are \(u0,u1\). All branches are infinite.

A nondeterministic Muller tree automaton consists of a finite state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\times Q\), and an acceptance family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^Q\). A run assigns a state to every node, starting with \(q_0\), and respects the transition relation at every node and its two children. It is accepting if, on each infinite branch, the set of states occurring infinitely often belongs to \(\mathcal F\). The language \(L(A)\) contains exactly the trees admitting at least one accepting run. No determinism, unambiguity or Borel-language promise is imposed.

In the Wadge game, Player I builds a tree over the alphabet of \(A\), and Player II builds one over the alphabet of \(B\). Both initially have empty finite trees. In each round I appends one or more complete levels, with all their labels, to I's own tree. II sees that move and appends finitely many complete levels to II's tree, or skips. Earlier labels cannot be changed. I therefore produces an infinite tree \(t\). II loses if II's output has only finitely many levels; otherwise it defines an infinite tree \(u\), and II wins exactly when
\[
t\in L(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in L(B).
\]
I wins in every other case. II may skip infinitely often, but must also extend the output infinitely often.

This is a perfect-information, length-\(\omega\), zero-sum game. A strategy specifies a legal move after every finite play history at which that player acts. A winning strategy succeeds against every legal opposing play. Strategies are arbitrary set-theoretic functions, with no computability, finite-memory or resource restriction. “Determined” means that one of the two players has a winning strategy.

The tree space has the product topology of discrete node labels: finitely many fixed levels specify basic neighborhoods. The tree-level version is the usual Wadge game; II has a winning strategy exactly when a continuous map \(F\) satisfies \(L(A)=F^{-1}(L(B))\). This equivalence explains the connection to language complexity, but does not assume determinacy.

The single sentence \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) universally quantifies over the finite automaton descriptions and asserts the existence of a winning strategy for each pair. The question asks whether ZFC proves that sentence. It does not assert that merely adding some stronger axiom is a negative resolution: such an axiom can prove statements already provable in ZFC.
answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a ZFC proof of determinacy for every pair in the specified class. A negative answer establishes nonprovability, for example by a relative-consistency or model construction yielding ZFC together with a failure of this universal determinacy statement; any metatheoretic consistency assumption must be stated explicitly. A theorem assuming a stronger determinacy principle without a nonprovability argument, or a proof for a restricted subclass, does not answer the ZFC-provability question.
context:
The source proves independence phenomena for Wadge games involving one-counter automata on infinite words. Its conclusion separately leaves the finite-state Muller tree case open; replacing one model with the other would misstate the result.

When both tree languages are Borel, determinacy follows from the Borel theorem. Regular infinite-tree languages can be non-Borel, so this observation does not cover arbitrary Muller automata.

The 2016 workshop paper constructs families of regular tree languages of high Wadge complexity without assuming an additional determinacy principle. Establishing comparisons within such families does not prove that every pair of regular tree languages yields a determined game.

Later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of ZFC-provability for all Muller tree language pairs. Word-game independence, Borel determinacy and special hierarchy constructions were not treated as resolutions.

title: Positivity problem for linear recurrences
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.
focus_reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.
formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer \(d\ge 1\), integer initial values \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{d- 1}\), and integer coefficients \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{d- 1}\), halts and decides whether \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for every \(n\ge 0\), where \(u_{n+d}=\sum _{i=0}^{d- 1}a_{i} u_{n+i}\)? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from \(u_{0}\) onward and allows zero terms. Coefficients may be zero, including \(a_{0}\); the decision procedure must accept these inputs as well. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that nonnegativity of every term is decidable for integer linear recurrences of arbitrary input order, by a machine halting on both positive and negative instances, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. The property is \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for all \(n\ge 0\), including the initial values.
context:
A recurrence is a finite description of an infinite trajectory. One can compute any requested term exactly, but checking every term asks for a finite justification covering unbounded time. This makes positivity a basic test case for the limits of algorithmic verification. The July 2026 survey still lists its general decidability among the central unresolved problems. The word positivity is conventional here: the inequality is non-strict.

The connection to linear dynamics is direct. Store d consecutive values in a vector \(x_{n}\). A fixed integer companion matrix M then gives \(x_{n+1}=Mx_{n}\), and the first coordinate of \(M^{n} x_{0}\) is \(u_{n}\). The question is whether that coordinate ever enters the negative half-line. Even though the transition is linear and deterministic, the trajectory can combine growth, decay and oscillation through its characteristic roots.

No universal finite amount of simulation certifies the desired answer. For any chosen integer N, the sequence \(u_{n}=N- n\) satisfies \(u_{n+2}=2u_{n+1}- u_{n}\), is nonnegative through index N, and becomes negative afterward. Of course this particular family is easy to analyze. Its role is to distinguish sampling a long prefix from proving a bound that is computed from an arbitrary input and is sufficient for that input.

Ouaknine and Worrell decide positivity for all sequences of order at most five. Their analysis combines effective estimates from Diophantine approximation with decision procedures for real algebraic conditions. At order six, decidability would already imply that certain approximation constants associated with transcendental numbers are computable. This is a precise mathematical consequence, rather than a proof that no algorithm can exist.

Removing repeated characteristic roots improves the known frontier: positivity is decidable for simple sequences through order nine.

A separate theorem decides ultimate positivity for simple sequences of every order, in polynomial space. Ultimate positivity asks whether some finite prefix contains all negative terms. The algorithm need not provide an effective cutoff beyond which the terms are nonnegative. Without such a cutoff, the theorem cannot be turned into a positivity decider by checking the remaining prefix.

There are larger decidable orders under a different structural promise. An integer recurrence is reversible when its extension to all negative indices also has integer values. Kenison and coauthors decide positivity through order eleven for reversible sequences, and through order seventeen when they are also simple. The extra integrality in backward time matters; these bounds do not apply to arbitrary integer recurrences of those orders.

A general solution would also decide the Skolem problem, which asks whether an integer recurrence ever equals zero. Integer recurrence sequences are effectively closed under termwise products and subtraction of a constant. Thus \(w_{n}=u_{n}^{2}- 1\) is another such sequence, and it is nonnegative at every index exactly when u has no zero. Negating the answer to a positivity decider would decide Skolem. This reduction explains why positivity has consequences beyond sign analysis itself.
why: A basic infinite-time safety question for finite linear descriptions. Its resolution would establish a major decidability boundary connecting verification, discrete dynamical systems and effective number theory, and would also settle general Skolem decidability.

Low-order, simple-root, reversible and ultimate-positivity theorems have separate hypotheses and do not settle this arbitrary-order question.

The positivity problem asks whether every term is nonnegative, with the recurrence order included in the input. Computing a long prefix cannot certify the answer because a negative term may appear arbitrarily late. Characteristic roots can combine growth and oscillation, making exact sign control depend on subtle arithmetic relationships. A terminating decision procedure would provide a basic verification tool for linear discrete dynamics, while a negative result would establish limits even in this elementary setting.

title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
importance_reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.
focus_reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.
formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
context:
This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.
why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.
status_note: Rechecked on 11 September 2026. The inspected 2026 work on iteration and stopping ladder games does not give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for all exact threshold instances. No resolution was located in the later-work search.
progress: 1992: Condon establishes \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership for the stochastic-game decision problem and the foundational positional-strategy framework. | 1995: Ludwig gives a randomized subexponential algorithm requiring an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations. | 2025-08-18: Berthon, Katoen and Zhou publish a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games with binary probability encodings. | 2025-09-17: Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger present sound value iteration for stochastic games, including end components, with certified approximation bounds. | 2026-01-22: Baldan and coauthors extend fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. This convergence result does not give a general exact polynomial-time threshold decider. | 2026-05-15: Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang solve stopping binary SSGs on ladders in polynomial time; their introduction explicitly retains the general P question as open.
working_summary: A simple stochastic game combines choices of a maximizing player, choices of a minimizing player and fair random branching. The project asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether the optimal probability of reaching a target exceeds a given rational threshold. Optimal positional strategies provide short certificates, but finding them may require navigating exponentially many combinations. Cycles also mean that solving local value equations without the correct reachability interpretation can give misleading answers. Progress would clarify the computational cost of exact planning against both adversarial and random uncertainty.

title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
importance_reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.
focus_reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.
formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.
context:
Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type \(A_{0}\) of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, \(A_{1}\) gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—\(A_{2}\) gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.
why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.
status_note: The original question and the May 2026 two-level revision were rechecked on 11 September 2026. No construction in the specified theory T, or nondefinability theorem for T, was located. Results with outer strict equality or display primitives use additional structure and are recorded separately.
progress: 2013: The HoTT book supplies the ordinary dependent-type, univalence and higher-inductive framework fixed for this card. | 2018: Kraus states the uniform finite-level semisimplicial family problem and explains its connection to higher categories and internal metatheory. | 2023: Annenkov and coauthors develop the two-level framework and distinguish outer-indexed constructions from inner semisimplicial universes. | 2025: Chen’s thesis develops internal-model methods but explicitly marks the classifier construction incomplete and the unrestricted ordinary-HoTT problem open. | 2025-12-17: The journal version of Displayed Type Theory gives semisimplicial types using additional modal/display primitives; the preprint dates from 2023–2024. | 2026-05-26: Two-Level Type Theory v5 updates typos and references while retaining the distinction between ordinary HoTT and enriched constructions.
working_summary: Semisimplicial types organize vertices, edges, triangles and higher-dimensional fillers with compatible shared boundaries. Ordinary homotopy type theory can describe any fixed finite collection of these stages externally. The project asks for one internal family indexed by natural numbers, together with compatible maps forgetting the highest stage. Higher identities carry data, so specifying all coherence requirements uniformly is harder than listing equations in ordinary set-based mathematics. Such a construction would provide an internal foundation for important higher-dimensional structures without extending the stated type theory.

title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory \(\lambda \beta\)
importance_reason: The classical completeness question of whether denotational semantics can capture exactly the syntactic equality of a basic programming model.
focus_reason: The classical completeness question of whether denotational semantics can capture exactly the syntactic equality of a basic programming model.
formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to [D\to D]\) and \(\mathrm{L}:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction \(\lambda x\).M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (\(\lambda x\).M)\(N=M[N/x]\), with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. \([D\to D]\) consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as \(\rho (x), MN\) as F(⟦M⟧\(\rho\))(⟦N⟧\(\rho\)), and \(\lambda x\).M as L(\(d\mapsto\)⟦M⟧\((\rho [x:=d])\)). The desired condition is \(\forall M,N\): (\(\forall \rho\), ⟦M⟧\(\rho\)=⟦N⟧\(\rho\)) ⇔ \(M=\beta N\). Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.
