answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.
context:
The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates \(\lambda x\).f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly \(\lambda \beta\) or \(\lambda \beta \eta\). They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly \(\lambda \beta\). Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.
why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?
status_note: The exact question is explicit in Honsell’s primary statement. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of its \(\lambda \beta\) alternative. The inspected 2025–2026 filter-model papers study unsolvables and other equational theories. Proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2007: Honsell records the exact \(\lambda \beta\) and \(\lambda \beta \eta\) continuous-model questions, tracing discussion to the 1980s. This card asks the \(\lambda \beta\) alternative. | 2007: Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra rule out exact \(\lambda \beta\) and \(\lambda \beta \eta\) theories for their class of effective models. | 2025: Dezani-Ciancaglini, Giannini and Honsell analyze nontrivial interpretations of unsolvable terms in filter models. | 2026-04-15: Lambda Galore constructs sensible continuously complete filter models not extending Böhm-tree theory; sensibility prevents these constructions from realizing exactly \(\lambda \beta\).
working_summary: Scott's continuous semantics interprets untyped lambda terms using mathematical domains and continuous functions. The project asks whether some model identifies exactly the pairs of terms related by beta-conversion. Beta-conversion expresses equality generated by applying functions to arguments and substituting those arguments into their bodies. Many semantic constructions validate additional equations, so soundness for beta-reduction alone does not answer the question. An exact model would show whether this influential notion of continuous meaning can distinguish every pair of terms that the basic operational equations keep separate.

title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
importance_reason: Asks whether the existence of a terminating reduction for every typable term forces every reduction of every such term to terminate.
focus_reason: Asks whether the existence of a terminating reduction for every typable term forces every reduction of every such term to terminate.
formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
definitions: S is a set of sorts, \(A\subseteq S\times S\) is a set of axioms, and \(R\subseteq S\times S\times S\) is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions \(t ::= x | s | t u | \lambda x:B\).\(t | \Pi x:B\).C, with \(s\in S\) and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) generated by the following rules. Axiom: \(\varnothing \vdash s:t\) when \((s,t)\in A\). Start: \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash x:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s\) and x is fresh. Weakening: \(\Gamma ,x:C\vdash t:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and x is fresh. Product: \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).\(C:s_{3}\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s_{1}, \Gamma ,x:B\vdash C:s_{2}\) and \((s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})\in R\). Abstraction: \(\Gamma \vdash \lambda x:B\).\(t:\Pi x:B\).C when \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).C:s for a sort s. Application: \(\Gamma \vdash t u:C[u/x]\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:\Pi x:B\).C and \(\Gamma \vdash u:B\). Conversion: \(\Gamma \vdash t:C\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and \(B=\beta C\). All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (\(\lambda x:B\).t)u to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =\(\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) for some finite \(\Gamma ,B\). Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.
context:
A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let \(\Omega\)=(\(\lambda z\).zz)(\(\lambda z\).zz). The term (\(\lambda x\).y)\(\Omega\) reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce \(\Omega\) forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.
why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.
progress: 1993–1995: The conjecture appears in Geuvers’ thesis and is circulated by Barendregt; the TLCA list records it as Problem 9. | 1997: Sørensen proves the implication for specified typed calculi and generalized non-dependent systems under additional hypotheses. | 2001: Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend the known non-dependent class, recorded as a partial result in the problem statement. | 2023-07-28: Mull’s TYPES 2022 proceedings paper extends the known class to some systems with dependent rules, retaining the general conjecture.
working_summary: A pure type system specifies a typed lambda calculus through a uniform collection of formation rules. Weak normalization means that every well-typed term has some terminating reduction path. The conjecture asks whether that global property forces every reduction path of every well-typed term to terminate. A term may have both a normalizing route and a divergent route in less constrained rewriting settings, so the type-system hypothesis is essential. A proof would connect existence of normal forms with unrestricted evaluation termination across a broad family of typed calculi.

title: Parity games in polynomial time
importance_reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. Its former rank came from a provisional unassessed score, not a low-significance assessment. The score does not certify the correctness or failure of the located solution claim.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input length defined below?
definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(L\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.
context:
The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.
why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).
status_note: Current status unverified as of 14 September 2026. arXiv:2511.03752v1 (4 November 2025) claims a full polynomial-time solution; the checked record has no later version. Suilen–Pérez arXiv:2604.26748v2 (24 June 2026, accepted at CONCUR) still treats the question as open. The review did not independently establish the claimed proof or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution, and later open-problem language is not itself a refutation. The mathematical formulation is complete; the card remains uncertain.
progress: 2017: Calude and coauthors give a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm for general parity games. | 2018-11-02: The second preprint version of the separating-automata work gives a quasipolynomial size barrier for the specified strong separating safety automata; the paper later appeared at SODA 2019. | 2025-11-04: Van der Heijden posts a claimed polynomial-time solution, with correctness and time bound asserted in Theorems 5, 7 and 8. This review has not independently verified that claim. | 2026-06-24: Suilen and Pérez’s revised CONCUR paper still treats polynomial-time parity-game solving as open and gives a reduction to robust discounted reward. This does not constitute a refutation of the earlier claim.
working_summary: A parity game is a finite arena in which two players choose an infinite path, and the least priority recurring infinitely often decides the winner. The target asks whether one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decides the winner from every specified starting vertex. The card specifies arbitrary vertex ownership, full-history strategies, binary priorities and the complete bit-cost model. Quasipolynomial algorithms are established, while known separating-automaton lower bounds concern restricted methods. A November 2025 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution, but its correctness remains unverified in this review despite later literature continuing to call the problem open.

title: Skolem problem
importance_reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every input \(k\ge 1, c_{0},\ldots ,c_{k- 1}\in Z\) and \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{k- 1}\in Z\), and correctly decides whether the sequence defined by \(u_{t+k}=\sum _{j=0}^{k- 1}c_{j} u_{t+j}\) for all \(t\ge 0\) has \(u_{t}=0\) for some integer \(t\ge 0\)?
question_excerpt: Although the Skolem-Mahler-Lech Theorem is almost 90 years old, decidability of the Skolem Problem remains open.
definitions: All integers, including k, are given in binary with signs and delimiters; the input explicitly lists exactly k coefficients and k initial values. These data uniquely define the infinite integer sequence. The order k is unrestricted and is part of the input, not a fixed parameter. Coefficients may vanish, the supplied recurrence need not be of minimal order, and no simplicity, non-degeneracy or nonzero-leading-product promise is imposed. The search includes the given initial terms and all subsequent nonnegative indices. There is no supplied upper bound on t. The required output is YES exactly when a zero occurs and NO otherwise; only termination and correctness are demanded, without a time or space bound. This is the discrete recurrence problem over integers, not the continuous-time Skolem problem or the question whether every term is nonnegative.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
A short recurrence determines infinitely many exact integer values. Testing any particular term is effective, but deciding that no term will ever be zero requires a terminating procedure for a global property. Even this elementary linear evolution leaves an unresolved boundary between arithmetic structure and algorithmic decision.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem constrains zero sets to a finite union of arithmetic progressions together with a finite exceptional set. That qualitative description is not, by itself, an algorithm that determines all exceptional zeros from the input. The distinction explains why a structural theorem about the sequence does not automatically settle the decision question.

Bilu and coauthors study simple recurrences and relate termination of their proposed procedure to transcendence conjectures. The arbitrary integer recurrence in this card also allows repeated characteristic roots and other cases outside the simple setting. Conditional termination for a subclass therefore has a different scope from an unconditional decision algorithm for the full input domain.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell improve the complexity of low-order and bounded-index versions. Their July 2026 revision places the unrestricted order-at-most-four problem in coRP. A bounded index range is additional input, and an order bound of four excludes general recurrences; neither restriction answers the unrestricted decision problem.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 paper obtains general decidability conditionally on a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture. Its unconditional density results for possible large zeros do not guarantee a decision for each individual recurrence. The new review preserves TCS-5773 and its original 2022 source rather than creating a second general Skolem entry.
why: Locate the decidability boundary for exact zero reachability in discrete linear dynamics.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026, including the July 2026 general conditional result and the corrected low-order revision. No unconditional decision procedure or undecidability theorem for arbitrary integer recurrences was found.
progress: 2022: Skolem Meets Schanuel studies simple recurrences and conditional termination without resolving arbitrary integer recurrences. | 2026-07-17: The low-order paper’s corrected third version gives coRP for order at most four and distinguishes the bounded-index task. | 2026-07: The new general decidability result remains conditional on a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture.
working_summary: The Skolem problem asks whether an integer linear recurrence ever has a zero term. Its order, coefficients and initial values form a finite binary input, with no restriction to simple or non-degenerate sequences. The classical structural theorem about zero sets does not provide an unconditional decision procedure for every recurrence. The reviewed July 2026 results establish stronger low-order bounds and a general conditional decidability theorem, leaving the unrestricted unconditional target unresolved. The completed card preserves the original identifier and source while spelling out the exact discrete recurrence model.

title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
importance_reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in the total input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E), a\) partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), integer edge weights \(w:E\to Z\), and a start vertex s, determine whether Max has a strategy \(\sigma\) such that every strategy \(\tau\) of Min produces a play \(s=v_{0},v_{1},\ldots\) satisfying \(\liminf _{T\to \infty}(1/T) \sum _{t=0}^{T- 1} w(v_{t},v_{t+1})\ge 0\).
definitions: The graph, its ownership partition, its start vertex and all weights are represented explicitly; weights use signed binary. Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge, so plays are infinite. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge with full knowledge of the finite history. Strategies are arbitrary deterministic functions of this history. There are no chance vertices, simultaneous moves, hidden observations or multiple payoff coordinates. Max seeks a nonnegative lower limit of average accumulated weight; equality zero is winning. No bound is imposed on intermediate losses or on the size \(\mathrm{W}=\max (1,\max _{e} |w(e)|)\). The running-time requirement concerns ordinary bit operations, so a polynomial dependence on W is not sufficient. Zero threshold loses no generality: a binary rational threshold \(a/b\) with \(b>0\) can be absorbed by replacing \(w(e)\) with \(b w(e)- a\), with polynomial growth of the encoding.
answer_criterion: Prove that this exact winner-decision language is in P, or prove that it is outside P. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a smoothed or average-case guarantee, or a lower bound for one strategy-improvement rule does not settle the unrestricted worst-case question. Strongly polynomial time would suffice but is a stronger requirement than this card asks for.
context:
Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight \(2^{b}\) takes only \(b+1\) binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

A July 2026 preprint by Adenwalla and coauthors connects tropical inequality systems and mean-payoff games with deciding chromatic boundedness for certain classes of graphs defined by equality patterns. Its reverse encoding uses a specified succinct representation. This creates another setting in which a solver would be useful. The paper explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open, and its graph-class reduction should not be mistaken for a polynomial algorithm for games.
why: A foundational complexity question for long-run adversarial optimization. It connects finite graph games, quantitative verification, resource reasoning and tropical algebra, with short optimal strategies but no known polynomial-time method to find the winner on arbitrary binary-weighted inputs.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly states that polynomial-time solution with binary weights remains open. The card fixes a single deterministic mean-payoff objective with a nonnegative liminf threshold. Pseudopolynomial, ergodic smoothed-analysis and framework-specific results do not resolve arbitrary worst-case inputs.
progress: 1995–1996: Zwick and Paterson give pseudopolynomial algorithms, establish the complexity framework, and reduce mean-payoff games to simple stochastic games. | 2011: Brim, Chaloupka, Doyen, Gentilini and Raskin obtain O(nmW) arithmetic-operation bounds for threshold decision and winning-strategy synthesis via energy games. | 2020-08-18: Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann derive tight bounds for value iteration using universal graphs, a restricted algorithmic framework. | 2024-07-02: Loff and Skomra publish smoothed polynomial guarantees for games on ergodic graphs with independently perturbed rewards. The published theorem includes the ergodicity restriction omitted from the earlier arXiv abstract. | 2025-09-19: Maat’s preprint gives direct connections between strategy improvement and simplex variants under nondegeneracy assumptions, without a general polynomial iteration bound. | 2026-07-26: Adenwalla and coauthors give connections to graph-class chromatic boundedness and explicitly retain the general polynomial-time question in §3.7.2.
working_summary: In a mean-payoff game, two players move a token through a finite weighted directed graph. The maximizing player wants the limiting lower average weight to be nonnegative against every opposing strategy. The project asks whether this threshold question has a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the full binary input length. Algorithms polynomial in the numerical magnitude of weights do not suffice because a large weight can have a short encoding. An efficient solution would settle a central exact optimization problem for systems with long-run rewards and adversarial control.

title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
importance_reason: A longstanding central question of real model theory with direct relevance to symbolic reasoning about exponential expressions. The explicit 2026 conditional result confirms continuing specialist interest without settling the unconditional target.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which, on every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in the language \(\{0,1,+,- ,\times ,<,\exp\}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(\varphi\) is true in \((R,0,1,+,- ,\times ,<,x\mapsto e^{x})\)?
definitions: Sentences have finite syntax and no free variables. Terms are formed from variables, 0,1, the unary symbols − and exp, and binary + and ×; atomic formulas are equalities or strict inequalities of terms. Formulas use Boolean connectives and first-order quantifiers, all ranging over R. Equality has its usual logical interpretation. Inputs are finite parenthesized strings over a fixed finite alphabet, with variable indices written in binary; any fixed effectively interconvertible syntax encoding gives the same decidability question. No arbitrary real constants or oracles for real numbers are allowed. The symbol exp denotes the standard real exponential function on all of R, not a restricted function or an unspecified solution in another structure. There is no time or space bound beyond termination. A positive resolution must be unconditional, rather than assuming an unresolved transcendence conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
First-order arithmetic over the real numbers can describe polynomial equalities, inequalities and quantifier alternation. Adding the exponential function permits expressions involving growth and decay that are unavailable in the polynomial language. The target is exact truth of every sentence, including cases in which a numerical approximation alone cannot distinguish equality from a very small nonzero quantity.

The syntax is finite even though the quantified domain is infinite. An algorithm receives a formula such as an existential statement about real solutions; it does not receive an arbitrary real constant as an infinitely long input. Fixing the standard exponential function and excluding such parameters prevents representation choices from changing the decision problem.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability under Schanuel’s conjecture. Berarducci and Gallinaro’s 2026 paper obtains an axiomatization under the same assumption and recovers that conditional decidability result. Its unconditional result for a related restricted exponential setting does not settle the unrestricted theory on this card.

This question is not the task of efficiently evaluating \(e^{x}\) to a specified error. Exact logical decision also includes formulas with arbitrary quantifier patterns and exact equalities. Conversely, the card imposes no polynomial running-time demand. An unconditional terminating algorithm of any complexity would answer it affirmatively.

The catalogue already contains individual questions about linear recurrences and linear dynamical systems. TCS-6265 concerns safety exactly at a specific robustness threshold, not the full elementary theory of the real exponential field. The new card supplies a broader, distinct boundary for algorithmic reasoning with real analytic operations.

The weighted-automata source also invokes decidability of the first-order real field with exponentiation. It supplies an application of the same real-exponential theory question; the conditional role of Schanuel’s conjecture does not constitute an unconditional decision procedure.
why: Locate a fundamental decidability boundary beyond polynomial real arithmetic, where exact reasoning interacts with transcendence.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. The June 2026 revision remains conditional for the full theory, and no unconditional decision procedure or undecidability result was found.
progress: 1996: Macintyre–Wilkie obtain conditional decidability from Schanuel’s conjecture, as recalled by the 2026 primary source. | 2026-06-23: Berarducci–Gallinaro v2 retains the Schanuel assumption for the full real exponential theory.

title: Continuous Skolem problem
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary for verification of linear differential systems, with a precisely finite rational input and an unrestricted exact reachability target.
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension \(d\ge 1\), rational matrix \(A\in Q^{d\times d}\), and rational column vectors \(b,c\in Q^{d}\), always halts and correctly decides whether \(c^{T}\exp (tA)b=0\) for some real \(t\ge 0\)?
definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is \(\exp (tA)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t^{j} A^{j}/j!\), and \(x(t)=\exp (tA)b\) is the unique real solution of \(x' (t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b\). The target is the hyperplane \(\{x:c^{T}x=0\}; c=0\) is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at \(t=0\) counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit \(t\to \infty\), the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
answer_criterion: Give an unconditional always-halting decision algorithm for every rational input, or prove that no such Turing algorithm exists. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may run forever on some inputs, or a certified answer only under a nonzero distance promise is partial progress. An undecidability theorem allowing more general coefficients or nonlinear differential equations must be reduced to this rational linear model to refute the proposition.
context:
Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output \(c^{T}x(t)\) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system \(x' =- x, x(0)=1\) has output \(e^{- t}\), which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial \((t- 1)^{2}\) touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is \(c^{T}b=0\). By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when \(c^{T}A^{j} b=0\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,d- 1\). These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all \(t\ge 0\).

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at \(\pi /2\). The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.
why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.
status_note: No unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof for this rational linear model was found through 11 September 2026. Bounded conditional results, low-order recurrence algorithms, approximate/robust verification and nonlinear-system hardness do not settle the unbounded exact question.
progress: 2010: Bell and coauthors establish the continuous Skolem framework, equivalent formulations and decidable special cases. | 2016: Chonev–Ouaknine–Worrell obtain conditional bounded decidability and reductions for restricted frequency patterns. | 2016: Their recurrent-reachability work decides infinitely many zeros at differential order at most seven and supplies effective last-zero bounds in that regime. | 2025-11: Platzer–Qian explain why exact closed-target reachability is not covered by their completeness results for open properties. | 2026-07-26: The Skolem/Positivity survey records continuous analogues and their distinct analytic obstacles.
working_summary: A rational linear differential system evolves as a matrix exponential applied to its initial state. Continuous Skolem asks whether a specified linear observation of that trajectory is exactly zero at some nonnegative real time. The dimension is unrestricted, and the project seeks decidability without a time horizon. Approaching zero or changing sign are inadequate substitutes because trajectories may approach without hitting or touch zero without crossing it. A resolution would establish the limits of exact reachability verification even for continuous systems with linear, fully specified dynamics.

title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic
importance_reason: A basic decidability boundary linking proof theory to branching vector addition systems.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite propositional MELL sequent \(\Gamma\) in the calculus below, halts and answers yes exactly when \(\vdash \Gamma\) has a finite derivation? There is no promised bound on formula size or exponential nesting and no requested time bound beyond termination on every input.
definitions: Use atoms \(p_{i}\) and their distinct dual literals \(p_{i}^{\perp}\) for integers \(i\ge 0\). Formulas are finite syntax trees generated by \(A ::= p_{i} | p_{i}^{\perp} | 1 | \perp  | (A\otimes A) |\) (A⅋A) | !A | ?A. A sequent \(\Gamma\) is a finite multiset of formulas; commas denote multiset union, retaining multiplicity. The following rules, read from premises to conclusion, define derivations. Identity has no premises and concludes \(\vdash p_{i},p_{i}^{\perp}\). The unit rule has no premises and concludes \(\vdash 1\). Tensor takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) and \(\vdash \Delta ,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\Delta ,A\otimes B\). Par takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\)⅋B. The other unit rule takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\perp\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Weakening takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Contraction takes \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A,?A to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Promotion takes \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,!A\), where every formula in ?\(\Gamma\) has outermost symbol ?. Contexts may be empty, and all displayed formula and context choices are arbitrary subject to these conditions. A derivation is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are the two nullary rules and whose internal nodes are instances of the other rules. There are no further rules; exchange is implicit in multisets. This is the cut-free presentation of classical commutative MELL, whose usual cut rule is admissible. Inputs explicitly list formula trees with constructor delimiters and binary atom indices; malformed strings are rejected. Formulas contain neither additives nor quantifiers, and there is just one pair of exponential modalities ! and ?.
answer_criterion: Prove that the provable sequents of this calculus form a decidable language, or prove that no algorithm can decide that language. A procedure that terminates only on provable sequents does not establish decidability.
context:
Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of \(p\to p\otimes p\) asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

Branching vector addition systems describe trees of computations with nonnegative integer resources. Their general reachability problem is inter-reducible with MELL provability. The 2025 result in the original reference establishes decidability for two-dimensional systems, so its dimension restriction cannot be omitted.

Status update: the July 2026 preprint claims decidability of general branching vector addition systems and explicitly states that MELL provability follows. This reaches the full decision question, unlike the earlier low-dimensional result. This card records the claim with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified here.
why: MELL combines resource-sensitive composition with controlled reuse. Its decision problem connects automated proof search to branching counter systems and tests a fundamental boundary of algorithmic reasoning about resources.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026: the MFCS 2025 source described the general problem as open. Bizière, Leroux and Sutre, arXiv:2607.09558v1 (10 July 2026), now claim decidability for general BVAS reachability and explicitly deduce MELL decidability. The exact claimed consequence and Theorem 3.3 were read, but the proof was not independently verified; this is an uncertain claimed resolution, not a certified open or resolved benchmark.
progress: 2019: Straßburger identifies gaps in the earlier proposed MELL decision procedure and distinguishes it from the decidable logic with unrestricted contraction. | 2025: Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability of reachability for two-dimensional branching VASS; their introduction still leaves general dimension open. | 2026-07-10: Bizière, Leroux and Sutre state a general decidability result and its MELL consequence. Theorem 3.3 supplies the claimed separation property. The proof is not independently verified in this review.
working_summary: MELL asks whether provability in a resource-sensitive propositional logic can always be decided. Its multiplicative connectives combine resources, while exponential modalities permit controlled reuse. The card specifies the entire finite proof calculus, including units and the conditions on contraction and promotion. Proof checking alone does not guarantee that a search can terminate on an unprovable input. A July 2026 preprint claims a positive resolution through general branching vector addition systems, which is recorded here without independent proof verification.

title: Unconditional decidability of exact time-bounded CTMDP reachability
importance_reason: Settle a foundational exact-verification question for continuous-time controlled stochastic systems.
formal: Is there an unconditional terminating algorithm that, for every finite rational-rate continuous-time Markov decision process with an absorbing state \(\mathrm{good}\), rational deadline \(T>0\) and rational threshold vector \(r\), decides whether \[\forall s\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \sup_{\pi\in\Pi_T}\Pr_s^\pi[\text{reach }\mathrm{good}\text{ by time }T]>r_s,\] where \(\Pi_T\) consists of the measurable timed positional policies defined below?
definitions: The input lists a finite state set \(S=\{1,\ldots,n\}\sqcup\{\mathrm{good}\}\), with \(n\ge1\); a nonempty finite action set \(A_{s}\) for each state; nonnegative rational rates \(q(s,a,t)\) for \(t\ne s\); \(T\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\); and \(r\in([0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q})^{n}\). Integers and rational numerators/positive denominators are binary encoded. All rates out of good are zero, and the diagonal generator entry is \(q(s,a,s)=- \sum_{t\ne s}q(s,a,t)\). A decision vector d chooses one action \(d(s)\in A_{s}\) at each state. A policy is a Lebesgue-measurable map \(\pi :[0,T]\to \prod _{s} A_{s}\): at elapsed time u in state s the instantaneous generator row is \(q(s,\pi (u)(s),\cdot )\). Actions may change while the process remains in the same state, not only at jumps. Policies are deterministic and may depend on time and current state, with no computability restriction. For a fixed policy and initial state s, its probability law is the finite-state inhomogeneous Markov jump law with this bounded measurable generator. Equivalently its row distribution \(\rho _{s}(u)\) is the unique absolutely continuous solution of \(\rho _{s}(0)=e_{s}\) and \(\rho _{s}' (u)=\rho _{s}(u)Q^{\pi (u)}\) for almost every u. Bounded rates ensure nonexplosion. Since good is absorbing, the probability of reaching it at some time in \([0,T]\) equals \(\rho _{s}(T)_{\mathrm{good}}\). The supremum is taken over all such policies separately for each initial state. This defines the value without an attainment assumption; the source also proves existence of an optimal piecewise-constant timed positional policy. The decision uses strict > in every coordinate, so equality to any threshold requires NO. The algorithm is a deterministic Turing machine that halts with the correct YES/NO result on every valid encoding; there is no requested complexity bound and no number-theoretic oracle or unproved premise. Invalid encodings may be rejected.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of an unconditional, total exact decision procedure for the specified strict vector-threshold language, or a Lean proof that it is undecidable. Approximation, termination only away from equality, or a result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic conjecture does not settle the target.
context:
A continuous-time decision process combines random event times with choices that can vary with elapsed time. The question concerns exact comparison of the best probability of reaching a target before a deadline.

Majumdar, Salamati and Soudjani define the strict vector-threshold question and prove its decidability assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. Their result does not give an unconditional decision procedure, and numerical approximation alone does not decide equality at the threshold.
why: Settle a foundational exact-verification question for continuous-time controlled stochastic systems.
status_note: Open in the 2020 primary source; its decidability theorem assumes Schanuel’s conjecture. The source and a bounded later-work search were checked on 13 September 2026 without finding an unconditional resolution. This does not certify that no later resolution exists.
progress: 2020: The source proves decidability under Schanuel’s conjecture and identifies an unconditional decidability barrier.
working_summary: The input describes a finite controlled stochastic process whose transitions occur in continuous time. A policy chooses actions from the current state and elapsed time, including between jumps. The target is exact comparison of the optimal deadline-reachability probability with rational thresholds for every initial state. The cited theorem decides this question assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. The card asks whether the same strict-threshold language is decidable unconditionally.

title: TOWER-hard reachability with seven nonnegative counters
importance_reason: Low-dimensional VASS reachability is a central test of how dimension controls the complexity of infinite-state verification.
formal: Is reachability in unary-encoded seven-dimensional vector addition systems with states (7-VASS) \(\mathrm{TOWER}\)-hard under elementary-time many-one reductions?
definitions: A \(d\)-VASS has a finite nonempty control-state set \(Q\) and a finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\mathbb Z^d\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,x)\in Q\times\mathbb N^d\), where \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q^{\prime})\) takes \((q,x)\) to \((q^{\prime},x+a)\) exactly when every coordinate of \(x+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests, counter resets, unrestricted signed counters, stacks or fractional updates. An instance gives \(Q,E\) and source and target configurations; reachability asks for a finite transition sequence between them, possibly of length zero. For the target \(d=7\) is fixed, but the control graph, vectors and endpoint configurations are inputs. They are listed explicitly. Every integer magnitude in a displacement or endpoint is unary, with a separate sign where necessary; state identifiers use a finite binary encoding. Let \(e_0(n)=n\) and \(e_{j+1}(n)=2^{e_j(n)}\). An elementary time bound is bounded by \(e_k(n^c+c)\) for fixed nonnegative integer \(k\) and positive integer \(c\). Define \(T(0)=1\), \(T(h+1)=2^{T(h)}\). The class \(\mathrm{TOWER}\) consists of languages decidable by deterministic Turing machines in time \(O(T(f(n)))\) for some elementary-time computable nonnegative integer function \(f\). A many-one reduction from a binary language \(K\) to VASS reachability is a total computable function mapping each input string to a valid VASS instance, preserving yes and no answers. Elementary-time reductions must obey one elementary time bound for each fixed source language. TOWER-hardness quantifies over every language in TOWER; it does not additionally assert that the target problem belongs to TOWER.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of TOWER-hardness in exactly the stated seven-counter, unary-encoded model and reduction convention. Alternatively prove in Lean that this problem is not TOWER-hard under those reductions. An elementary algorithm would imply a negative answer, but the target does not require that stronger conclusion. Results using eight counters or additional signed counters do not establish the required lower bound.
context:
The original 2025 question asks whether the known eight-counter hardness can be attained in a lower dimension. This is exactly captured by testing seven counters: a lower-dimensional VASS can be padded with permanently zero counters, without changing reachability.

Czerwiński and Orlikowski prove TOWER-hardness already with eight counters and unary displacement encoding. Their result therefore cannot be explained solely by exponentially succinct binary counter values. The elementary reduction convention is significant for this nonelementary complexity class.

A fixed-height tower, such as a double or triple exponential, is an elementary bound. TOWER allows the tower height itself to grow with the input. Hardness for every fixed-height exponential class does not on its own supply the single TOWER-hardness statement.

The 2026 work on VASS extended with signed integer counters reports the ordinary three-counter reachability problem as elementary and the ordinary TOWER lower bound as known in dimension eight. Its new three-counter hardness counts only the nonnegative counters and permits additional unrestricted integer counters. Those extra counters are absent from the present model.

The number of counters stays fixed but the finite control graph can grow. This differs from fixing the entire VASS and varying only its endpoints. It also differs from requiring a long run in a particular example: a complexity lower bound must reduce every problem in the hardness class.

The source separately discusses geometric dimension, defined using the span of cycle effects. That structural parameter is not substituted for the seven actual nonnegative counters in this card; its associated question remains a distinct direction.
why: This seeks the dimension at which a small collection of nonnegative counters can already encode nonelementary computational difficulty. Reducing the eight-counter frontier would sharpen the low-dimensional boundary between tractable geometric behavior and extreme reachability complexity.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2025 question and LICS 2026 paper retain eight as the known ordinary-VASS TOWER-hard dimension. The latter’s hardness with three nonnegative counters also uses signed counters and does not settle the present target. No seven-counter resolution was located in the bounded subsequent-work check.
progress: 2022-03-08: Czerwiński and Orlikowski establish TOWER-hardness for unary 8-VASS. | 2025-07-01: Orlikowski asks whether the eight-counter TOWER lower bound can be achieved in smaller dimension. | 2026: The LICS 2026 signed-counter extension still identifies dimension eight as the ordinary-VASS TOWER-hardness frontier; its smaller-dimensional result uses extra signed counters.
working_summary: A VASS combines finite control with nonnegative integer counters updated by fixed transition vectors. The question asks for TOWER-hard reachability using only seven counters and unary-encoded numbers. Seven counters capture the source’s request for any improvement below the known eight-counter bound, by padding unused coordinates. TOWER-hardness uses elementary-time reductions and is stronger than a collection of unrelated fixed-height exponential lower bounds. Recent lower bounds with extra signed counters concern a different computational model.

title: Decidability of branching-VASS reachability
importance_reason: A core decidability question for a major extension of vector addition systems, left open beyond recent low-dimensional progress and closely connected to resource-sensitive computation.
formal: Is there an algorithm deciding reachability in branching vector addition systems with states when the dimension is part of the input? Given a finite system \(B\) as defined below and a target configuration \(q(x)\), decide whether \(q(x)\) is the root of a finite valid derivation tree of \(B\).
definitions: The input dimension is an integer \(d\geq1\). A \(d\)-dimensional branching vector addition system with states (\(d\)-BVASS) has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\) and finite rules \((S,a,q)\), where \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\) and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) consists of a state \(q\) and vector \(x\in\mathbb N^d\). A rule with \(S=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\) combines one configuration \(q_i(x_i)\) for each input state into \(q(a+x_1+\cdots+x_k)\), provided all coordinates of this output are nonnegative. All child configurations must themselves have nonnegative coordinates. Input states in one rule are distinct, following the source’s set convention. When \(S\) is empty, the rule supplies the initial configuration \(q(a)\) if \(a\geq0\) coordinatewise. A derivation is a finite rooted tree: each node uses one rule, has exactly its rule’s specified children, and its label is obtained by the preceding sum. Leaves therefore use empty-input rules. A target is reachable if some such tree has that target as root. Derivations may use the same rule any finite number of times; there is no global stock of initial tokens shared between different branches. The number of children and the dimension are unbounded input parameters. States, rules, child-state sets and target are listed explicitly, with signed binary integers for displacement coordinates and binary nonnegative target coordinates. There are no equality or zero tests, resets, counter multiplication, probability or additional acceptance conditions. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine that halts and answers correctly on every valid finite encoding, with no running-time bound requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm for the stated arbitrary-dimensional finite-tree reachability problem, or prove in Lean that it is undecidable. A dimension-dependent result covering only some fixed dimensions, a coverability algorithm, or a procedure that terminates only on reachable targets does not decide this problem. Finite derivation trees must satisfy every branch and every exact target coordinate.
context:
A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.
why: Branching VASS extend the Petri-net style of counter computation to recursive combinations of resources. Settling exact reachability in arbitrary dimension would identify a central decidability boundary between path computations and branching derivations in infinite-state verification.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper proves decidability for dimension two and explicitly leaves arbitrary-dimensional BVASS reachability open. No general resolution was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 check. A repository contribution formalizing the conjecture was not treated as a proof of it.
progress: 2025: Theorem 3.3 establishes a computable semilinear reachability set for 2-BVASS; the conclusion retains arbitrary-dimensional decidability as open.
working_summary: A branching vector addition system combines finite control with nonnegative integer resources. Rules can combine several already derived configurations by adding their resource vectors and a fixed displacement. Reachability asks whether a finite valid derivation tree produces exactly a supplied target. The dimension is part of the input, and every branch must be fully justified. The 2025 two-dimensional decidability theorem does not settle the arbitrary-dimensional problem.

title: Linear-length witnesses for reachability in each fixed vector addition system
importance_reason: The complexity of fixed VAS reachability isolates a basic source of difficulty in an important infinite-state model.
formal: For every integer \(d\geq1\) and finite set \(V\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\), does there exist a constant \(C_V\geq1\) such that every reachable pair \(s,t\in\mathbb N^d\) has a run of length at most \(C_V(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\)?
definitions: A vector addition system (VAS) is the finite set \(V\) of allowed displacement vectors; there is no control-state graph. Its configurations are vectors in \(\mathbb N^d\), where zero coordinates are allowed. A run from \(s\) to \(t\) is a finite sequence \(c_0=s,c_1,\ldots,c_m=t\) with \(c_i\in\mathbb N^d\) and \(c_i-c_{i-1}\in V\) for all \(1\leq i\leq m\). Its length is the number \(m\) of transitions, not the magnitude of its largest counter. Empty runs of length zero are permitted, so every configuration reaches itself. The norm is \(\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d |x_j|\). The whole system, including its dimension, number of updates and their integer magnitudes, is fixed before \(C_V\) is chosen. The constant must then work for all source and target vectors in that system. There are no tests except the requirement that updated coordinates remain nonnegative. No algorithm for computing \(C_V\), finding a short run or deciding reachability in a specified time is required. The bound measures numerical endpoint magnitudes, not their binary encoding lengths. Choosing another fixed norm would change only the system-dependent constant. The non-strict inequality includes the zero-to-zero empty run; the source’s strict wording otherwise has an artificial zero-endpoint exception. For positive endpoint norm sums, strict and non-strict versions are equivalent after enlarging \(C_V\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal system-dependent linear witness bound. Alternatively give one explicit finite VAS \(V\) and prove in Lean that for every \(C\geq1\) there are reachable endpoints \(s,t\) for which every run has length greater than \(C(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\). Letting the update system vary with \(C\), using binary bit length instead of endpoint magnitudes, or merely displaying one unnecessarily long run does not refute the proposition.
context:
For a one-counter system allowing increments and decrements by one, the shortest run has length \(|s-t|\), which meets the desired bound. The conjecture says that more involved interactions among a fixed finite collection of counters never force a superlinear shortest detour as the endpoints grow.

Jecker’s source formulates a short-witness conjecture, despite the entry’s broad complexity title. The present title and criterion expose that actual mathematical claim. The choice of a non-strict bound simply handles the permitted empty run at zero rather than turning a wording defect into a counterexample.

A fixed system can contain very large displacement constants, and the allowed multiplicative constant may be correspondingly large. Exhibiting a family of larger and larger systems with hard instances would not disprove this conjecture: a counterexample must keep one finite update set for every endpoint pair.

The 2024 fixed-VASS paper discusses Jecker’s conjecture and reports that its lower-bound constructions give no evidence against it. It proves PSPACE-hardness for a fixed five-counter VASS when initial counter values are binary and explains the PSPACE upper-bound implication of the proposed short-path property.

There is no conflict between a path linear in endpoint magnitudes and a high complexity measured in binary digits. A counter value with a short binary encoding can be exponentially larger than that encoding, so writing out such a path may already take exponentially many steps.

A positive answer would constrain how much of the infinite configuration graph is needed to witness each reachable pair once the system is fixed. It would not make all VAS reachability uniformly linear-time, since the constant carries the entire fixed system and the target is existential.
why: The conjecture isolates whether unbounded shortest-run growth is caused by changing the transition system or can already occur within one fixed system. This structural distinction is fundamental for understanding the complexity of reachability when only numerical configurations vary.
status_note: The 2022 source and 2024 fixed-VASS paper retain the linear shortest-run conjecture. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a proof or a fixed-system counterexample. The zero-endpoint inequality convention is an explicit editorial repair of the literal strict source wording, not a claimed research resolution.
progress: 2022-07-01: Jecker poses the system-dependent linear shortest-run conjecture. | 2024: Draghici, Haase and Ryzhikov establish fixed-VASS lower bounds, explain the conjecture’s PSPACE consequence with binary endpoints, and report no counterevidence from their constructions.
working_summary: A fixed vector addition system supplies a finite collection of updates on nonnegative integer vectors. The conjecture asks whether every reachable pair has a run linear in the numerical sizes of its endpoints. The multiplicative constant may depend on the entire fixed system, while the endpoints vary freely. The non-strict bound includes the zero-length run from zero to itself. This structural witness bound would have complexity consequences, but it is not a linear-time algorithm in binary input length.

title: Elementary-time reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled VAS
importance_reason: A significant complexity boundary for the basic combination of pushdown control and one nonnegative counter, sharpened by recent decidability and thin-grammar results.
formal: Can reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition systems be decided in elementary deterministic time? More explicitly, do there exist fixed integers \(h\geq0\), \(c\geq1\) and one deterministic Turing machine deciding every instance of bit length \(n\) within \(O(e_h(n^c+c))\) steps, where \(e_0(z)=z\) and \(e_{j+1}(z)=2^{e_j(z)}\)?
definitions: A one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition system (1-GVAS) is a finite context-free grammar with nonterminal set \(N\), distinguished start nonterminal \(S\), and finitely many productions \(X\to\alpha\) with \(X\in N\) and \(\alpha\) a finite sequence of nonterminals and integer terminals. There is no restriction on recursion or on the number of nonterminals occurring in a sentential form. The empty right-hand side is allowed. A terminal word \(a_1\cdots a_m\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\), is generated when a finite sequence of production applications transforms \(S\) into that word. Given starting and target counters \(s,t\in\mathbb N\), the word witnesses reachability if \(s+\sum_{i=1}^j a_i\geq0\) for every \(0\leq j\leq m\), and \(s+\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=t\). The terminal order is the left-to-right order in the generated word, not the order in which productions were expanded. An empty terminal word witnesses exactly \(s=t\), if generated. There is one nonnegative counter, no test for zero except through inability to take a negative update, and no restriction on stack depth implicit in the grammar. The whole grammar, both counters and all production sequences are explicit inputs. Integer terminals use signed binary encodings, and \(s,t\) use binary nonnegative encodings; their digits and every symbol occurrence contribute to input length. The tower height \(h\), polynomial exponent \(c\), hidden multiplicative constant and program must be independent of the grammar and both counters. Correctness concerns exact reachability, not coverability or an approximation of the reachable set.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic decision algorithm with one fixed elementary time bound for all instances, or prove in Lean that no elementary-time decider exists. A bound whose tower height depends on the input grammar or a theorem only for structurally restricted grammars does not establish the positive answer. The output need only decide reachability; it need not print a potentially enormous derivation.
context:
The 2024 survey asks broadly for the complexity of 1-GVAS reachability and at that time describes an unconfirmed decidability argument. Editorial specialization: this card selects the elementary-time boundary, explicitly conjectured in the subsequent complete decidability paper. It does not claim that answering this boundary alone determines the exact complexity class.

The counter constrains prefixes, not just the final sum. A generated word \((-1),1\) has total effect zero but is invalid from counter zero. A word \(1,(-1)\) with the same total effect is valid from zero. A grammar’s ordering constraints and counter nonnegativity therefore interact.

Bizière and Czerwiński’s November 2024 paper proves reachability decidable for general 1-GVAS. It constructs a thin grammar with the same reachability relation. A nonterminal is thin if no derivation from it can produce a sentential form containing two copies of that same nonterminal; a grammar is thin when all its nonterminals are thin.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 show that an elementary algorithm for thin grammars would imply an elementary algorithm for all 1-GVAS. Thin grammars are already a subclass, so the elementary-time question has the same yes/no answer in the two settings. This is a preservation theorem for the complexity boundary, not an existing elementary bound.

The February 2026 thin-GVAS preprint improves an upper bound parameterized by its structural index and continues to leave an elementary upper bound open. Since that index can grow with the grammar, its stated fast-growing bound does not supply a fixed-height exponential tower for every input.

The survey illustrates small grammars with extremely large finite reachable sets. Such cardinality alone does not prove a matching lower bound for deciding whether one supplied counter value is reachable. Conversely, merely finding short derivations in a collection of examples does not give a uniform decision algorithm.
