why: This asks whether one nonnegative counter interacting with context-free control can still be analyzed within a fixed-height exponential time bound. It separates existence of a decision algorithm from a meaningful complexity boundary and tests whether enormous reachable sets force equally enormous decision time.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. General 1-GVAS decidability is established by the later Bizière–Czerwiński paper, superseding the survey’s provisional wording. The selected elementary-time question is explicitly left open there and remains distinguished from the 2026 index-dependent thin-grammar bound. These proof texts were checked for statements and scope, not independently formalized in Lean.
progress: 2024: The MFCS survey distinguishes an anticipated decidability proof from the unresolved complexity of 1-GVAS reachability. | 2024-11-04: Bizière and Czerwiński prove decidability and show that an elementary algorithm for thin 1-GVAS would extend to all 1-GVAS. | 2026-02-05: Xue and Fu improve a structural-index upper bound for thin 1-GVAS while retaining the elementary-time question.
working_summary: A context-free grammar specifies integer update sequences for a single nonnegative counter. Reachability requires a generated sequence that stays nonnegative at every prefix and ends at the exact target value. General decidability is now established, and this card selects the still-open elementary-time boundary. The algorithm must have one fixed-height exponential bound for all binary-encoded grammars and endpoints. A later reduction preserves this elementary-time question between general and thin grammars.

title: Consistency of excluded middle and Church’s thesis in Coq
importance_reason: A foundational compatibility question for classical synthetic computability in dependent type theory, testing the exact role of impredicative propositions, large elimination and choice; a full result would justify a broad axiomatic development beyond known fragments.
formal:
Is \(\mathcal T+\mathrm{LEM}+\mathrm{CT}\) logically consistent, where \(\mathcal T\) is Coq's ordinary cumulative inductive core calculus specified below, and the two added propositional axioms are
\[\mathrm{LEM}:\quad\forall P:\mathrm{Prop},\ P\lor\neg P,\]
\[\mathrm{CT}:\quad\forall f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N,\ \exists e:\mathbb N,\ \forall x:\mathbb N,\ \exists s:\mathbb N,\ T(e,x,s)=\mathrm{Some}(f(x))?\]
Here \(T\) is the fixed bounded evaluator for ordinary register-machine programs defined below. Consistency means that there is no finite well-typed closed proof term of \(\mathrm{False}\) in the extended calculus. The existence quantifiers in CT are in Prop; they are not computational dependent pairs.
definitions:
The base \(\mathcal T\) is the Prop/Set/Type calculus of inductive constructions in the Coq 8.11 reference manual, with predicative Set and cumulative predicative universes \(\mathrm{Type}_i\) above it. This fixes the source's full inductive-calculus setting rather than only the arithmetic fragment used in some consistency models. The optional separate SProp sort and the impredicative-Set extension are outside this selected core. Terms include variables, universe sorts, dependent products \(\Pi x:A.B(x)\), abstractions, applications, local definitions, inductive constructors, pattern matching and guarded recursive or co-recursive definitions. Definitions and conversion follow the cited calculus: function application reduces by substitution, pattern matching computes on constructors, local definitions unfold, and recursive/co-recursive unfolding obeys the guardedness rules. Universe constraints must have a well-founded assignment to levels. Arbitrary mutual inductive and coinductive declarations satisfying its positivity and universe conditions are permitted; not just a fixed list of natural-number and list types.

Prop is the impredicative universe of propositions: a proposition may quantify over a type at any universe level and remain in Prop. Ordinary data live in Set or Type. Propositional disjunction and existential quantification are inductive propositions. Their proofs generally cannot be pattern-matched to produce arbitrary computational data. The standard exceptions for empty and singleton inductive propositions remain allowed, including elimination of False into any type. Singleton elimination is the calculus's syntactic constructor rule, not a new assumption that every inhabited proposition has one proof. Identity is the usual inductive equality with reflexivity and its permitted elimination rule. Equality reflection, functional or propositional extensionality, univalence, unrestricted choice and proof irrelevance are not added as axioms.

Natural numbers have constructors zero and successor. Fix a computable, effectively decodable Gödel numbering of finite deterministic register-machine programs. Registers hold natural numbers. A program consists of labelled increment-and-jump instructions, decrement-with-zero-test-and-jump instructions, and halt instructions. It starts with register zero containing \(x\), all other registers zero, and its initial program counter at the first instruction; on halting it outputs register zero. The selected model is Turing complete. The total, structurally recursive function \(T(e,x,s)\) simulates the program coded by \(e\) for at most \(s\) transitions, returning \(\mathrm{Some}(y)\) if it has halted with output \(y\), and \(\mathrm{None}\) otherwise. Invalid codes are interpreted as nonhalting programs. The numbering and evaluator are fixed before adding either axiom; CT does not assert the existence of an unspecified oracle evaluator. Standard effectively intertranslatable program codings yield equivalent CT assertions.

The symbol \(\neg P\) means \(P\to\mathrm{False}\), where False is the proposition with no constructors. Add opaque proof constants of the displayed LEM and CT types and no computational reduction equations for them. The quantifier over \(f\) ranges internally over all functions of the extended theory, not merely functions in a chosen list of already written programs. A contradiction would be a closed derivation of False using finitely many permitted declarations and these constants. The question concerns the mathematical inference rules, not bugs in a proof-assistant executable.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that the extended formal calculus has no closed proof of False, or exhibit such a proof and verify its typing. A semantic construction must include soundness for the selected universes, general permitted inductive/coinductive declarations and elimination rules; modeling only a restricted arithmetic fragment is insufficient. A proof of consistency for CT alone, for a different type theory, or after replacing propositional existentials by a different assertion does not settle this joint-consistency target.
context:
Classical set-theoretic reasoning commonly turns an existence statement into a function by choice. Combining such a choice principle with excluded middle produces noncomputable numerical functions and contradicts CT. The source explains that the corresponding choice principle is not derivable merely from Coq’s Prop-level excluded middle.

CT asserts that a program index exists propositionally. It does not provide an operation that extracts an index from an arbitrary function. Likewise, LEM is a propositional disjunction, not a Boolean decision procedure for every proposition. These distinctions are essential to the conjecture.

Forster explicitly conjectures joint consistency at the end of Section 7. Earlier consistency results for Church’s thesis in other constructive type theories do not automatically establish this particular combination of classical logic, impredicative propositions and Coq’s elimination rules.

Putrle’s 2023 thesis proves consistency of the fCIC fragment used for a synthetic computability development, with stronger synthetic computability assumptions and selected large-elimination rules. Its Definition 6.4 and following text explicitly restrict general inductive types. This is substantial partial progress but does not by itself model the full core selected here.
why: This would clarify whether classical reasoning about propositions can coexist with the claim that every internal numerical function is computable, while retaining a rich dependent type theory. The distinction matters for synthetic computability developments that use Church’s thesis as an axiom and for the foundational role of separating propositions from computational data.
status_note: Forster’s Section 7 conjecture, the Coq 8.11 calculus documentation and Putrle’s 2023 consistency theorem were checked on 2026-09-14. The latter explicitly covers a fragment without general inductive types. A bounded later-work search did not identify a consistency model or contradiction for the full ordinary core with exactly the selected two axioms.
progress: 2021: Forster separates propositional Church’s thesis from stronger data-producing formulations and conjectures its compatibility with Prop-level excluded middle in Coq. | 2023: Putrle proves a joint-consistency result for the explicitly restricted fCIC fragment and explains the scope of its realizability interpretation.
working_summary: Church’s thesis says that every internal function from natural numbers to natural numbers is computable. The law of excluded middle gives classical reasoning about propositions. The question asks whether adding both propositional axioms to Coq’s ordinary cumulative inductive core can produce a contradiction. The distinction between propositional existence and computable witness extraction is essential. A 2023 thesis proves consistency for a restricted fragment, leaving the selected full-calculus target beyond that result.

title: Shortest runs in 3-D VASS
importance_reason: Sharp bounds for reachability or coverability in restricted counter systems would refine core infinite-state verification complexity.
formal: Is there no single-exponential bound on shortest runs in binary-encoded three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Precisely, is it true that for every integer \(k\ge 1\), every real \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\ge 1\), there is a reachable instance I of encoding length \(N\ge N_{0}\) whose shortest source-to-target run has more than \(2^{C N^{k}}\) transitions?
definitions: A three-dimensional vector addition system with states (3-VASS) is a finite set Q of control states and a finite transition set \(T\subseteq Q\times \mathbb{Z} ^{3}\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,u)\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(u\in \mathbb{N} ^{3}\), where \(\mathbb{N}\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q' )\) sends \((q,u)\) to \((q' ,u+a)\) only when every coordinate of \(u+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests or counter bounds. A reachability instance I consists of Q,T and two configurations s,t. It is reachable if some finite sequence of enabled transitions sends s to t. Its shortest-run length \(\ell\)\((I)\) is the minimum number of transitions in such a sequence; the empty run is allowed, and \(\ell\)\((I)=0\) when \(s=t\). Unreachable instances are excluded from the quantified claim. N is the bit length of an explicit description: states are numbered, the transition list and the source and target are given explicitly, and all integer coordinates are written in signed binary (nonnegative binary for configurations), with delimiters and state indices included. Usual explicit binary-list encodings differ by polynomial factors, which do not affect existence of a \(2^{N^{O}(1)}\) bound. The dimension is always exactly three, while the number of states, transitions and counter magnitudes may grow. No finite-reachability-set promise or effective construction of the hard instances is required. The single-exponential convention and binary encoding follow the explicit later formulation in Section 7 of the 2025 source.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed unboundedness beyond every \(2^{C N^{k}}\), or refute it by proving that there are fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge 1\) for which every reachable binary 3-VASS instance I has \(\ell\)\((I)\le 2^{C |I|^{k}}\), after adjusting C to include the finitely many small sizes. A long run alone is insufficient: the lower bound concerns the shortest run between the chosen configurations. Neither a lower bound with a growing number of counters nor the mere existence of many reachable configurations establishes this target.
context:
The control graph is finite, but each counter may become arbitrarily large. A transition can consume tokens from one counter and produce tokens in another, provided it never makes a counter negative. Reachability asks whether a target configuration can be obtained from a given start through legal transitions.

Consider one state and the single transition \((- 1,+1,0)\), from counters \((2^{r},0,0)\) to \((0,2^{r},0)\). Every successful run has exactly \(2^{r}\) steps, although the instance uses only \(O(r)\) bits. This gives exponential length in the input description. The question asks whether shortest runs can exceed every bound \(2^{N^{k}}\), with fixed k, rather than merely whether exponential runs occur.

A reachable target may have many very long runs leading to it. Only the minimum length is relevant here. A single-exponential shortest-run upper bound would allow the binary reachability problem to be decided in polynomial space, as the 2025 source explains. A lower bound on the number or largest size of reachable configurations is a different assertion.

The 2019 question mentioned a tower-type upper bound. The ICALP 2025 work gives a triple-exponential bound on shortest runs, and the July 2026 preprint states an improvement to a doubly-exponential bound. These upper bounds do not establish that any shortest run actually needs more than single-exponential length.
why: Isolates how much witness complexity three unbounded counters can force. Resolving the single-exponential threshold would clarify the gap between low-dimensional reachability and the much more expensive behavior possible when the number of counters grows.
status_note: Original question and the 2025 explicit binary formulation checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint improves the upper bound but does not resolve whether single-exponential shortest runs always suffice. No resolution of that threshold was located; proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2019-07: Czerwiński asks for a three-counter shortest-run lower bound beyond the exponential scale; the upper-bound discussion is historical. | 2025: The ICALP paper obtains a triple-exponential shortest-run upper bound and 2-EXPSPACE membership. Section 7 retains the question whether single-exponential runs suffice for binary 3-VASS. | 2026-07-16: Chen and coauthors state a doubly-exponential shortest-run upper bound and EXPSPACE membership in a new preprint. This review checked the model and theorem statements, not the full proof; the result does not supply the requested super-single-exponential lower bound.
working_summary: A three-dimensional VASS is a finite-state system with three nonnegative integer counters. The source asks whether some reachable instances require shortest runs longer than every single-exponential bound in their binary input length. Encoding a large initial counter in binary already permits exponentially many necessary steps, so a stronger growth rate is required. A July 2026 preprint states a doubly-exponential upper bound, improving the triple-exponential bound from 2025. The remaining threshold question measures how much reachability-witness complexity three counters can force.

title: Relative completeness of Kleene induction for the positive calculus of relations
importance_reason: A substantial algebraic completeness question for relational reachability, sharpening the distinction between deciding identities and explaining them through reusable finitary proof principles.
formal: Is every equation valid in binary relations with union, intersection, composition, converse, constants \(0,1,\top\), and reflexive-transitive closure derivable from all valid closure-free equations in these operations together with the Kleene algebra axioms and induction rules specified below?
definitions: Expressions are finite terms over countably many relation variables using binary operations \(+\) (union), \(\cap\) (intersection), \(\cdot\) (composition), unary converse \((-)^{\circ}\), unary closure \((-)^*\), and constants \(0,1,\top\). On any set \(X\), variables denote arbitrary subsets of \(X\times X\). The constants denote the empty relation, the identity relation and \(X\times X\). Composition is \(R\cdot S=\{(x,z):\exists y\in X,\ (x,y)\in R\text{ and }(y,z)\in S\}\). Converse reverses each ordered pair. Closure is \(R^*=\bigcup_{n\geq0}R^n\), with \(R^0=1\) and \(R^{n+1}=R\cdot R^n\); it contains paths of every finite length, including zero. Complements and tests are absent. An equation is valid if it holds for every set \(X\), finite or infinite, and every assignment of its relation variables. Define \(u\leq v\) as the equation \(u+v=v\). The base axiom scheme consists of every valid equation whose expressions have no occurrence of \((-)^*\); it includes the interactions between union, intersection, converse and the constants. The Kleene algebra axioms make \((+,\cdot,0,1)\) an idempotent semiring: addition is associative, commutative and idempotent with identity zero; multiplication is associative with identity one, distributes over addition on both sides and has absorbing zero. The closure axioms are \(1+xx^*\leq x^*\) and \(1+x^*x\leq x^*\). The left induction rule infers \(x^*y\leq z\) from \(y+xz\leq z\); the right rule infers \(yx^*\leq z\) from \(y+zx\leq z\). Proofs are finite derivations using these schemes and rules, equality reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, congruence for every operation, and uniform substitution of arbitrary expressions for variables. In particular, closure-bearing expressions may be substituted into closure-free axiom schemes. No other closure axiom, infinitary rule, relational-validity oracle for closure-bearing expressions or auxiliary operation is permitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that this specified derivation system proves every relationally valid equation. Alternatively exhibit a valid equation and prove in Lean that it is not derivable in this system, for example using a model of all the axioms that refutes it. Decidability of relational validity alone, or a complete axiomatization of a proper signature fragment, does not establish completeness of these particular rules.
context:
The source asks for axiomatizations and suggests adding Kleene algebra axioms to a complete closure-free relational calculus. Editorial specification: this card uses all valid closure-free laws in the full positive signature as the base. This explicitly includes interactions between union and intersection rather than leaving the interface between separate axiom systems ambiguous.

Without the specified base and rules, asking for an axiomatization would be too loose: declaring every valid equation an axiom gives no structural explanation. The target instead asks whether ordinary finitary Kleene induction accounts for all additional identities created by closure once the closure-free theory is available.

Intersection requires the same pair of endpoints to satisfy two relational conditions. It cannot generally be pushed through composition: \(R\cdot(S\cap T)\subseteq (R\cdot S)\cap(R\cdot T)\), but the reverse inclusion can fail because the two right-hand paths may use different intermediate points. Such interactions make relational closure more subtle than independent word-language iteration.

The 2018 paper records complete axiomatizations for important smaller signatures and explains why finite axiomatization of representable allegories is already delicate without closure. The target here deliberately permits an infinite closure-free axiom scheme and asks for relative completeness, rather than promising a finite list of all relational axioms.

Nakamura’s December 2025 journal article proves EXPSPACE-completeness of validity for the full positive signature, including identity, top, converse and closure. Its final discussion still distinguishes axiomatizability from the decision procedure. Thus an effective validity test does not by itself verify the relative proof system specified here.

The same later article cites a finite axiomatization for identity-free Kleene lattices. That result omits operations present in this card. It is retained as a boundary of known completeness results, not generalized to the full signature.
why: This asks whether standard induction for iteration remains complete when programs can also be intersected and reversed as binary relations. A positive theorem would give a principled relative proof calculus for graph reachability expressions; a negative result would isolate an additional law of relational iteration.
status_note: The 2018 source poses relative axiomatization as an open direction, and the December 2025 paper continues to distinguish axiomatization questions from its decidable full-signature theory. This card explicitly fixes a closure-free full-signature base and finitary induction rules as the concrete editorial variant. No completeness or incompleteness theorem for that exact system was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 check.
progress: 2018: Pous poses the axiomatization question and the suggested addition of Kleene algebra axioms to a complete closure-free relational theory. | 2025-12-08: Nakamura establishes EXPSPACE-completeness for the full positive calculus and separately discusses the remaining axiomatization questions.
working_summary: Expressions denote binary relations using positive operations, converse and finite-path closure. The target asks whether every relationally valid equation follows from a specified proof system. That system contains all valid closure-free equations and ordinary left and right Kleene induction. The closure-free base is an explicit editorial choice that fixes interactions among the operations. The later EXPSPACE validity algorithm and completeness of smaller fragments do not prove this relative-completeness claim.

title: Word problem for the S-combinator
importance_reason: The word problem for a basic combinator tests the decidability frontier of elementary computational formalisms.
formal: Is convertibility of closed S-combinator terms decidable? Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the least set with \(S\in\mathcal{T}\) and \((uv)\in\mathcal{T}\) whenever \(u,v\in\mathcal{T}\). The sole rewrite rule, applicable inside any term context, is \[(((Sx)y)z)\longrightarrow ((xz)(yz)),\qquad x,y,z\in\mathcal{T}.\] Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that halts on every pair \(p,q\in\mathcal{T}\) and decides whether they are connected by a finite sequence of forward or backward applications of this rule?
definitions: ['A term is a finite ordered binary application tree whose leaves are all the one constant \\(S\\). Application is not associative; by convention \\(uvw\\) abbreviates \\(((uv)w)\\). There are no object-language variables, other combinator constants, lambda abstractions, types or infinitary terms. The letters \\(x,y,z\\) in the rule range over entire closed terms.', 'A one-hole context is built from a hole \\(\\square\\) by repeatedly forming \\((Ct)\\) or \\((tC)\\), where \\(t\\in\\mathcal{T}\\) and \\(C\\) is a one-hole context. Write \\(C[t]\\) for replacing its hole by \\(t\\). A forward step is exactly \\(C[(((Sx)y)z)]\\to C[((xz)(yz))]\\). Both appearances of \\(z\\) on the right are copies of the same finite tree.', 'Terms \\(p,q\\) are convertible when there exist \\(m\\geq0\\) and closed terms \\(t_0=p,\\ldots,t_m=q\\) such that, for each \\(i<m\\), either \\(t_i\\to t_{i+1}\\) or \\(t_{i+1}\\to t_i\\). This is the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of the contextual rewrite relation. No extensionality, eta law or identification merely by an infinitary semantic tree is added.', 'The two input trees are written explicitly, for example using prefix encodings \\(\\operatorname{enc}(S)=0\\) and \\(\\operatorname{enc}(uv)=1\\operatorname{enc}(u)\\operatorname{enc}(v)\\) with a delimiter between the two trees. A decider is one deterministic Turing machine halting on all valid pairs and outputting yes exactly on convertible pairs; malformed descriptions can be rejected. No time bound and no normalization promise are imposed.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for all pairs of closed S-terms under this conversion relation, or a Lean-checked proof of undecidability. Deciding whether individual terms have normal forms, deciding only pairs of normalizing terms, or comparing a coarser semantic invariant is insufficient.
context:
RTA Problem 97, attributed to Barendregt in 1975, asks for this exact word problem on ground terms built solely from S and application. Rule direction can be reversed during conversion, even though operational reduction has a forward direction.

The 2023 Satellite account reports decidability of normalization and of head-reduction termination for this fragment, but explicitly leaves interconvertibility open. It also distinguishes convertibility from equality of certain infinitary semantic trees.
why: The S-only fragment retains duplication and nonterminating behavior with just one combinator. Its word problem tests whether symbolic equality becomes decidable after removing the other primitives of combinatory logic, beyond the already-known ability to recognize normalizing terms.
status_note: The original RTA list and the 2023 primary Satellite account leave this convertibility problem open. A bounded later-literature check on 13 September 2026 did not find a decision or undecidability theorem. Normalization results do not resolve this target; no exhaustive present-day certification is claimed.
progress: 1998: Waldmann proves decidability of whether a closed S-term has a normal form, as recorded in the original list and the later Satellite account. | 2023: The Satellite account explicitly retains decidability of interconvertibility as an open question.
working_summary: Closed S-terms are finite application trees using only the combinator S. The rule sends S applied to x, y and z to the application of xz to yz, and can be used inside any subterm. The word problem asks whether two such trees are connected by finitely many forward or backward rule applications. Normalization is decidable for this fragment, but the 2023 source still leaves general convertibility open. A solution supplies a Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proof covering nonnormalizing terms as well.

title: Exact finite-iteration reachability for Bellman operators
importance_reason: A precise decidability boundary for structured piecewise-affine dynamics, motivated by finite termination of quantitative value iteration and multiple optimal actions.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a finite rational Markov decision process with no end components, its reachability Bellman operator \(\Phi:[0,1]^d\to[0,1]^d\), and rational vectors \(s,t\in[0,1]^d\), decides whether \(\Phi^n(s)=t\) for some integer \(n\geq0\)? The dimension is unbounded and several actions may be available, including several actions tight at the fixed point.
definitions: A Markov decision process (MDP) has finitely many states, a designated target sink \(g\), and a finite set of available actions at each other state. Sinks have no actions. Each available action \(a\) at state \(i\) has rational probabilities \(p(i,a,j)\geq0\), summing to one over all states \(j\). An end component consists of a nonempty state subset \(U\) and a nonempty choice of available actions at each state in \(U\), such that all their positive-probability successors stay in \(U\), and the directed graph of these chosen positive-probability transitions is strongly connected. The input promise excludes all such end components. Let \(Q=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) consist of the non-target states from which a path of positive-probability transitions to \(g\) exists. Other non-target states have reachability value zero and are omitted from the vector coordinates. For every \(i\in Q\), define \(L_{i,a}(x)=p(i,a,g)+\sum_{j\in Q}p(i,a,j)x_j\) and \(\Phi(x)_i=\max_{a\in\mathrm{Act}(i)}L_{i,a}(x)\). Each such action set is nonempty. The maximum is coordinatewise: different coordinates may attain it at different actions. All probabilities, the explicit transition tables and the vectors \(s,t\) are inputs with binary rational encodings; \(d\) is the number of retained coordinates. Iteration is \(\Phi^0(s)=s\) and \(\Phi^{n+1}(s)=\Phi(\Phi^n(s))\). Equality means equality of every rational coordinate at one finite iteration, without a numerical tolerance. An action is tight at a fixed point \(u\) when \(L_{i,a}(u)=u_i\). The no-end-component promise gives a unique fixed point and convergence of all iterations to it; no uniqueness of tight actions is assumed. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine halting on every valid input; no time bound or bound on the witnessing \(n\) is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating exact reachability algorithm on this entire promised class, or prove in Lean that the decision problem on this class is undecidable. Merely computing or approximating the fixed point, deciding whether a limit equals the target, or solving unrestricted matrix-semigroup reachability does not decide finite-iteration reachability of the specified Bellman operator.
context:
Convergence does not imply that an iteration ever attains its limit. For \(\Phi(x)=(x+1)/2\), starting at zero produces \(1-2^{-n}\); the fixed point one is approached forever and never reached at a finite step. This scalar map is a valid reachability Bellman operator for a state that either repeats or reaches the target, each with probability one half.

The source proves decidability in arbitrary dimension when the requested vector differs from the unique fixed point. It also handles a fixed-point target when the starting vector is comparable to it coordinatewise, meaning all coordinates lie on the same side of their respective target values.

In dimension two, the paper resolves the remaining incomparable case as well. Thus the outstanding general question permits higher-dimensional starts with some coordinates above and others below their target values, and permits several tight actions.

If every coordinate has a unique tight action, the local fixed-point dynamics reduce to powers of one rational matrix. Proposition 27 gives a finite bound for testing whether these powers send a difference vector to zero. With multiple tight actions, the maximizing matrix can change during the iteration.

The associated matrices have nonnegative entries and row sums at most one. Their available rows can be chosen independently at each coordinate, forming the source’s product family. The resulting map takes coordinatewise maxima; it does not permit an arbitrary favorable sequence of matrices irrespective of those maxima.

The exclusion of end components is part of the target, not an incidental computational convenience. An MDP transformation preserving the least fixed point need not preserve the exact sequence of iterates from a supplied vector. General piecewise-affine undecidability results therefore require an actual reduction into this promised Bellman class before they could answer the question.
why: Exact attainment is a sharper verification property than convergence of value iteration. Resolving it for Bellman operators would locate how much decidability survives the structured maxima of affine probability updates, beyond the already solved two-dimensional and single-policy cases.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves arbitrary-dimensional BOR open under its no-end-component promise. A bounded 13 September 2026 later-work check did not locate a resolution. The source’s general-semigroup remark is retained only within its Bellman/product-family setting; general matrix-semigroup undecidability is not treated as a solution.
progress: 2025: Varonka and Watanabe prove decidability for non-fixed-point targets, comparable starting vectors, unique tight actions and all two-dimensional instances; unrestricted dimension with multiple tight actions remains open.
working_summary: The input describes a finite rational Markov decision process and two rational value vectors. Its Bellman operator updates each coordinate by the best available affine probability expression. The question asks whether exact iteration reaches the target vector after finitely many steps. The source assumes no end components but allows several actions tight at the fixed point. Convergence and the known two-dimensional decision procedure do not settle the general finite-attainment problem.

title: Computable one-step normalization for finite confluent term rewriting
importance_reason: A structural normalization question separating confluence from effective one-step evaluation; the existing score is retained while the rationale is made specific to the strategy model.
formal: Does every finite, full, confluent first-order term-rewriting system \(R\) have a total computable one-step strategy \(F_R\) that reaches a normal form from every term having a normal form? The strategy depends only on the current term, may depend on the whole fixed system \(R\), and must also return a step on terms that have no normal form.
definitions: A finite ranked signature \(\Sigma\) is a finite collection of function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are all finite ordered trees built from these symbols and a countably infinite set of variables; a variable is a leaf. “Full” means this entire term set is admitted, without a type, language or reachability restriction. A rule \(\ell\to r\) consists of terms, with \(\ell\) not a variable and every variable of \(r\) occurring in \(\ell\). The system \(R\) has finitely many rules. A substitution replaces variables by finite terms; a context is a term with one designated hole. One step \(C[\ell\sigma]\to_R C[r\sigma]\) contracts a single occurrence of a rule instance at any position. No simultaneous contractions, equations modulo which to match, or variable binding are included. Write \(\to_R^*\) for zero or more steps. Confluence means that whenever \(u\to_R^*v\) and \(u\to_R^*w\), there is \(z\) with \(v\to_R^*z\) and \(w\to_R^*z\); this is equivalent to the Church–Rosser property in the source. A normal form has no outgoing rewrite step. A term has a normal form if it reaches one by finitely many steps. The strategy \(F_R\) is a function on all terms, computable by an ordinary Turing machine from a finite tree encoding with numbered variables. It fixes every normal form and satisfies \(u\to_R F_R(u)\) for every other term, even when a permitted rewrite has identical input and output. It is total: computing the next step halts for every finite term. Normalization requires that for every term \(u\) having a normal form there is \(n\geq0\) such that \(F_R^n(u)\) is a normal form. There is no persistent history input or extra state carried between successive applications of \(F_R\). No time bound is required. The quantifiers are \(\forall R\,\exists F_R\,\forall u\); an algorithm synthesizing \(F_R\) uniformly from \(R\) is not additionally required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every system satisfying the hypotheses admits such a total computable strategy. Alternatively exhibit a finite full confluent first-order system and prove in Lean that every total computable valid one-step strategy fails to normalize at least one term that has a normal form. A partial procedure that waits indefinitely on non-normalizable terms, a strategy with external memory, or a strategy allowed several contractions per output does not meet the stated conditions.
context:
Confluence ensures that a term cannot have two different normal forms, but an arbitrary choice of reductions can still run forever. For example, the rules \(f(x)\to a\) and \(b\to b\) form a confluent system; \(f(b)\) has normal form \(a\), while repeatedly contracting its occurrence of \(b\) never reaches it.

A search can eventually discover a reduction to a normal form when one exists. That observation does not immediately produce the required total next-step function: on a term without a normal form, the strategy must still choose and return an available step in finite time.

Kennaway’s question combines finite generation, fullness and Church–Rosser confluence. The source reports counterexamples when these restrictions are dropped. This card selects its first-order term-rewriting formulation; the parenthetical extension to calculi with bound variables is not silently included.

The source records a positive result for weakly orthogonal systems: rules are left-linear, and nonvariable overlaps of rule instances give the same immediate reduct. The general question permits nontrivial overlaps, so that result does not establish the full proposition.

One-step and dependence only on the current term are substantive conditions. A procedure that remembers previously explored branches has a larger input state, while outputting a whole discovered reduction sequence changes the required interface. The question asks whether confluence always suffices under the more restrictive interface.

The RTALooP entry cites the later 1996 work on sequential reduction strategies. The source does not mark the general problem solved. Its historical dates identify the provenance of the question rather than certify the entire subsequent literature.
why: This asks whether semantic uniqueness of outcomes guarantees an effective local way to reach an outcome whenever one exists. It isolates the interaction of confluence, finite syntax and memory-free evaluation beyond familiar orthogonal rewriting models.
status_note: The source leaves the first-order formulation open and records the weakly orthogonal result as a special case. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The source’s optional extension with bound variables is distinguished from the explicit first-order target here.
progress: 1989: The source attributes the positive weakly orthogonal case to Kennaway’s work on sequential evaluation strategies. | 1991-04: Kennaway poses the finite full Church–Rosser strategy question in RTALooP. | 1996: The source adds Antoy and Middeldorp’s work on sequential reduction strategies as related progress.
working_summary: The system has finitely many first-order rewrite rules and admits every term over its finite signature. Confluence makes normal forms unique when they exist. The question asks for a computable strategy that chooses exactly one available contraction from the current term. The next-step computation must halt even on terms that never reach a normal form, without retaining an external history. The strategy must nevertheless normalize every term for which some terminating reduction exists.

title: Decidability of termination for one left- and right-linear term rule
importance_reason: A precise minimal-syntax decidability boundary for rewriting, retaining the existing score while distinguishing variable-linearity from restrictions on termination proof methods.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given one first-order rewrite rule \(\ell\to r\) over a finite ranked signature, with both \(\ell\) and \(r\) linear, decides whether its unrestricted rewrite relation terminates on every finite term?
definitions: A ranked signature \(\Sigma\) consists of finitely many function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are finite ordered trees over \(\Sigma\) and a countably infinite set of variables. A term is linear if each variable occurs at most once in that term; occurrences are counted separately on the two sides of a rule. The left side \(\ell\) must not be a variable and every variable of \(r\) must occur in \(\ell\); variables may be erased, but may not be duplicated on either side or newly introduced on the right. A substitution maps variables to finite terms. A one-step rewrite replaces one occurrence of \(\ell\sigma\) by \(r\sigma\) inside an arbitrary term context, for some substitution \(\sigma\). The same single rule may be used at any position and any number of times. Matching is syntactic; no equations, types, binding operations or restrictions such as innermost-only rewriting are present. Termination means there is no infinite chain \(u_0\to u_1\to u_2\to\cdots\) starting from any finite term, including terms with variables. It is not only existence of one terminating reduction, termination from one designated input, or absence of short cycles. If a rewrite returns the same term, it is still a step and can witness nontermination by repetition. The finite signature, symbol arities, variables and both finite term trees are explicitly encoded and form the algorithm’s input. A decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid input rule and answers the global termination question exactly; no complexity bound is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every valid rule linear on both sides, or prove in Lean that this restricted global termination problem is undecidable. A single nonterminating example does not prove undecidability. A decision procedure for string rules, a bounded search for loops, or a test for whether one specific interpretation proves termination does not settle the full proposition.
context:
Linearity controls variable repetition, not the number of function symbols. Both \(f(x)\to x\) and \(f(x)\to f(f(x))\) are linear on each side. The first decreases term size at every step and terminates; the second can grow forever. Thus the input class includes both possible answers even with unary function symbols.

Dauchet’s 1991 question explicitly requires both left and right linearity. The source cites undecidability for one rule with only left linearity, so omitting the right-side restriction would replace the open question by a known harder model.

One-rule string rewriting is a special case, represented by unary function symbols with a shared tail variable. Its unresolved termination question is therefore related but does not cover the branching first-order terms admitted here. The source separately discusses confluence, which is another property and is not part of the present target.

The 2024 paper Linear Termination is Undecidable studies whether termination can be certified by linear polynomial interpretations. Here “linear” describes the proof interpretation, whereas this card uses it for occurrence of variables in a rule. The paper’s undecidability result is not a resolution of the question merely because the titles share the word linear.

Indeed, that paper can make the interpretation-existence question undecidable even within systems already known to terminate by another polynomial interpretation. This emphasizes the difference between deciding actual termination and deciding whether a particular proof method succeeds.

title: A coanalytic upper bound for fair almost-sure termination
importance_reason: The existing specialist score is retained for this precise strong-fairness model; its specific significance is the logical complexity of probability-one termination under unrestricted history-dependent schedulers.
formal: Does fair almost-sure termination for finitely branching probabilistic nondeterministic Turing machines admit a computable many-one reduction to well-foundedness of primitive-recursive trees on \(\mathbb N\)? That is, is there one total computable map sending each machine/input pair \((M,w)\) to such a tree \(T_{M,w}\) with \(M\) terminating with probability one under every fair scheduler exactly when \(T_{M,w}\) has no infinite branch?
definitions: A machine has a finite control, a finite tape alphabet with a blank symbol, one unbounded tape initially containing the finite input \(w\), and a head position. Nonhalting control states are probabilistic or nondeterministic. Each has a fixed finite nonempty set of actions. An action is a total finite table indexed by the currently scanned symbol, prescribing a symbol to write, a head move by at most one cell and the next control state. Thus an available action is enabled whenever its origin control state is visited. A probabilistic state also has a fixed rational distribution of strictly positive probabilities over its actions; these choices are sampled independently conditional on the execution history. Deterministic behavior is represented by a single action of probability one. Halting states have no actions. A scheduler is any function from finite execution histories ending at a nondeterministic state to an available action. Histories include the configurations and actions taken. Schedulers are deterministic but need not be computable and may use the entire history. A scheduler is fair from the given initial configuration if, on every infinite execution consistent with it and the probabilistic action supports, every nondeterministic action whose origin state occurs infinitely often is itself taken infinitely often. This is pathwise strong fairness, including individual infinite paths of probability zero. The scheduler induces the usual probability measure on executions, with finite-prefix probabilities given by products of the rational choices. Fair almost-sure termination (FAST) means that every fair scheduler gives probability one to reaching a halting state. It imposes no bound on expected running time. Machine tables, rational probabilities and input words have finite binary encodings. A tree on \(\mathbb N\) is a prefix-closed subset of finite sequences of natural numbers. It is presented by a primitive-recursive membership predicate: a finite expression built from zero, successor and projections using composition and primitive recursion, with a fixed effective encoding of sequences. An infinite branch is a function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) whose every finite prefix belongs to the tree. Well-foundedness means no such branch exists. Branching is not restricted to two children or any fixed finite bound. The reduction must halt on every valid machine/input pair and output a valid predicate for a prefix-closed tree; no resource bound on the reduction is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a total computable reduction satisfying the displayed equivalence for all machine/input pairs, or prove in Lean that no such reduction exists. Requiring computable schedulers, fairness only with probability one, weak fairness, finite expected time, or finitely branching witness trees changes the problem. Sound proof rules for selected program classes alone do not establish this universal reduction.
context:
The source asks both for the recursion-theoretic complexity of FAST and for sound complete reasoning techniques. Editorial specialization: this card selects the coanalytic upper-bound question, expressed concretely as a reduction to tree well-foundedness. It does not present a conjectured upper bound as a theorem or claim that this choice already supplies a Hoare-style proof system.

Fairness rules out indefinitely ignoring an action at a control state revisited infinitely often. It still permits arbitrarily long finite postponements. Requiring this property on every supported infinite execution is stronger than requiring that unfair executions merely have probability zero.

The source reports \(\Pi^1_1\)-completeness for the corresponding non-probabilistic fair-termination problem. Well-foundedness of recursive, arbitrarily branching trees is the standard complete problem at that coanalytic level; the reduction target makes the prospective upper-bound question precise.

Probability-one termination permits exceptional nonterminating executions of probability zero. It is therefore weaker than termination on every path, even though the scheduler’s fairness requirement in this card quantifies over every supported infinite path. These two uses of quantification must not be conflated.

The 2023 positive-almost-sure-termination work proves a \(\Pi^1_1\)-complete classification for a different property: finite expected runtime for each scheduler, without the same fair-scheduler restriction. That theorem does not automatically classify FAST.

Those applications are important evidence of useful techniques, but its stated soundness and fairness convention do not prove the universal strong-fairness reduction requested here.

title: P versus NC
importance_reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.
focus_reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
context:
Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.
why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.
status_note: The primary P-completeness monograph and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No unrestricted resolution of P versus logspace-uniform NC was found. The \(2025/2026\) matching lower bound concerns monotone circuits and therefore does not resolve the stated \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) model.
progress: 1975: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization. | 1995: Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations. | 1999: Raz and McKenzie prove monotone \(\mathrm{NC}\ne\)monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits. | 2025–2026: Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size \(2^{n^{\Omega (1)}}\), improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.
working_summary: NC describes computations with polynomial total circuit size and only polylogarithmic dependency depth, under a uniformity requirement. The question asks whether every problem solvable in polynomial sequential time belongs to this parallel class. Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem: given a circuit and its input, compute the designated output. An NC algorithm for circuit evaluation would therefore parallelize every problem in P. The challenge is to distinguish a long chain in the supplied circuit from an unavoidable chain in every possible algorithm for evaluating its behavior.

title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
importance_reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.
focus_reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.
formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
context:
Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most \(n- 1\) scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc \((u,v)\) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes require \(n^{2- o(1)}\) space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.
why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.
status_note: The primary survey, cited multipass bounds and the revision of 9 September 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. The recent paper explicitly retains the \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass upper benchmark. No polylogarithmic-pass algorithm or lower bound ruling out every polylogarithmic pass bound in the stated memory model was found. This check covers decision with adversarial fixed order, rather than a changed stream or a path-output requirement.
progress: 2013–2016: Guruswami–Onak establish multipass superlinear space lower bounds for directed reachability decision; these imply \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes in semi-streaming space. | 2019: Jambulapati–Liu–Sidford develop nearly linear-work, approximately square-root-depth parallel reachability and its sparse shortcut construction. | 2021: Chen and coauthors prove almost-quadratic space is necessary for \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes, strengthening the few-pass space tradeoff. | 2022: Assadi and coauthors state and explain the \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming implementation, including path recovery, in Proposition 4. | 2023-09: Assadi’s survey records the gap and explains the transition from search lower bounds to reachability-decision lower bounds. | 2026-09-09: The revised streaming-monotonicity paper retains the square-root reachability benchmark and reduces faster approximation to faster reachability.
working_summary: Directed reachability in a stream asks whether one vertex can reach another when graph edges arrive in an adversarial order. Nearly linear memory in the vertex count cannot store every edge of a dense graph. The question asks for a randomized algorithm using only polylogarithmically many passes and n times a polylogarithmic number of memory bits. Simple repeated scans can propagate reachability one step at a time, taking many passes on badly ordered paths. The project is to combine a small memory footprint with far fewer scans without relying on favorable edge order.

title: Perfect matching in NC
importance_reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.
focus_reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the stated logspace-uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth search circuits on all simple undirected graphs, or prove that no such family exists. A negative answer rules out every fixed choice of the size and depth exponents and constants. An algorithm only for bipartite graphs, or one using quasipolynomial circuit size or catalytic auxiliary memory, does not meet the specified positive criterion.
context:
A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.
why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.
progress: 1987 / background: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it. | 2017: Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap. | 2026-06-01: Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC. | 2026-06 / revised 2026-07-15: The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.
working_summary: Perfect matching seeks pairwise disjoint edges that cover every vertex of a graph. The question asks for a deterministic parallel algorithm on general graphs with polynomially many processors and polylogarithmic running time. Sequential polynomial-time algorithms do not supply this bound because their matching updates may depend on earlier choices. General graphs also contain odd cycles, which require coordination beyond the constraints that suffice in bipartite graphs. The saved card distinguishes this target from the nearby bipartite advance and asks whether compatible matching decisions can be organized efficiently in parallel without randomness.

title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
importance_reason: The bounded-degree distributed LLL is a central conflict-resolution primitive and a benchmark for the randomized LOCAL complexity hierarchy. Its connection to locally checkable labeling and its use in coloring algorithms give a precise reason to seek the log-logarithmic bound.
focus_reason: A canonical obstacle to resolving local conflicts rapidly, with consequences for many distributed graph algorithms.
formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge 2, a\) uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.
context:
The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.
why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.
status_note: The original conjecture, primary distributed bounds, the 2025 locality result and the August 2026 resilient-LLL paper were checked on 11 September 2026. No result settling the exact bounded-degree \(O(\log  \log  n)\) worst-case target was found. The fixed factor \(1/2\) and order of slack/degree quantifiers preserve the saved precise interpretation. Node averages and results for stronger communication models are not substituted for this guarantee.
