progress: 2016: Brandt and coauthors prove \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) lower bounds for sinkless orientation and distributed LLL under the stated criterion hypotheses. | 2017: Fischer–Ghaffari obtain \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  \log  n})}\) rounds at low dependency degree under polynomial slack and explicitly record the Chang–Pettie \(O(\log  \log  n)\) conjecture. | 2023: Davies gives \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) rounds under polynomially strengthened criteria, with a broader probability-versus-degree tradeoff. | 2025: Davies-Peck improves node-averaged LOCAL complexity and complexity in other models; Theorem 3 retains a separate, larger worst-case LOCAL bound. | 2026-08: Davies-Peck and Zhang extend efficient resilient-LLL applications to triangle-free coloring. Their general-degree discussion does not resolve the fixed-degree linear-log-log target.
working_summary: The distributed Lovasz Local Lemma seeks an assignment avoiding many bad events, each depending on only a bounded number of other events. Processors know local portions of this dependency structure and communicate in synchronous LOCAL rounds. The question asks for \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds with high probability when the dependency degree is constant and the probability criterion has sufficiently strong constant polynomial slack. The guarantee must bound the worst finishing time over all nodes. An algorithm that achieves only a small average finishing time would leave the central coordination issue unresolved for the last remaining bad events.

title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
importance_reason: Exact weighted distances are a basic distributed optimization primitive. Matching the bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark, or proving an additional obstacle, would resolve a central gap between exact algorithms and communication lower bounds, with consequences for other distributed graph constructions.
focus_reason: A basic distributed graph primitive with an unresolved gap between algorithms and communication lower bounds.
formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.
context:
Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.
why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.
progress: 2011 / 2012: Das Sarma and coauthors establish randomized communication lower bounds for exact and approximate distance problems, giving the \(\tilde\{\Omega\}(\sqrt{n}+D)\) lower-bound benchmark. | 2020 / 2022: Chechik–Mukhtar obtain \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\) rounds for exact weighted SSSP. | 2022: Rozhoň and coauthors give near-optimal deterministic distributed algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances, with accuracy-dependent complexity. | 2023: Cao–Fineman give \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\) rounds for polynomially bounded weights, including an improvement in the intermediate-diameter comparison. | 2026-04-18: The programmable-matter article retains a CONGEST gap in related work. Its own communication model and theorems are different, and that summary does not include the 2023 bound above.
working_summary: Single-source shortest paths asks every vertex to learn its exact distance from one source in a weighted network. In CONGEST, each edge carries only a logarithmic number of bits per communication round. The target is a randomized algorithm using roughly \(\sqrt{n}\) plus the hop diameter D rounds, ignoring polylogarithmic factors. The graph is undirected and connected, with nonnegative polynomially bounded integer edge weights. Achieving this bound would combine global distance propagation with the bandwidth limits of the network at the scale identified by the saved problem statement.

title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
importance_reason: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(\mathrm{P}(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.
context:
Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.
why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
status_note: The checked primary literature leaves explicit superconstant unicast bounds as a central challenge. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this polynomial-time, one-bit target. The latest checked revision of the one-round MST result is January 2024; it is not presented as a new 2026 status theorem.
progress: 2014: Circuit simulations explain barriers to explicit lower bounds and separate unicast from broadcast communication. | 2018: A uniform congested-clique time hierarchy is proved through hard-function selection, without the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time guarantee. | 2023 / 2024: The MST lower bound excludes one round with logarithmic link bandwidth; it does not establish a diverging lower bound for a one-bit graph predicate.
working_summary: Can a graph predicate that is easy to compute centrally require a number of congested-clique rounds tending to infinity? Each processor initially knows its incident graph edges and can send a different logarithmic-size message to every other processor in each round. Only one decision bit is required, and local computation is unrestricted. Known hard-function counting and hierarchy arguments do not provide the required centrally polynomial-time predicate. Broadcast bounds and the known two-round MST limitation do not resolve this unicast one-bit target.

title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
importance_reason: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.
formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), is there a uniform bounded-error randomized parallel algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in any directed graph with integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots,n^{a}\}\), using \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Output integral arc flows. Use a synchronous priority CRCW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed; if several processors write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes one word-RAM instruction per round, with the instructions and word length specified below. Work is the total number of executed processor instructions, including activation, input access and output; depth is the number of rounds. Processor IDs and addresses fit in words. All processors run a fixed finite program with their IDs; there is no advice or free preprocessing. Independent uniform random words cost one instruction each. The entire output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Both resource bounds hold on every execution. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. With \(N=m+n\), require a function \(h_{a}:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h_{a}(N)/\log N=0\), such that work is at most \(C_{a}Nh_{a}(N)\) and depth at most \(C_{a}h_{a}(N)\). The program, \(d\), \(C_{a}\) and \(h_{a}\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph. Initially the explicit input is in shared memory; all subsequent computation is charged.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Sequential almost-linear time does not imply that the same computation can be completed with very few dependent stages. This target asks for both near-optimal total work and subpolynomial parallel depth.

Haeupler, Jiang and Saranurak explicitly identify almost-optimal parallel exact maximum flow as a major open problem. Their DAG Projections paper gives efficient reductions between exact directed flow and approximation problems on directed acyclic graphs.

The reductions classify the difficulty of several parallel tasks; they do not establish the requested work and depth. The capacity restriction makes each numerical input occupy logarithmically many bits.
why: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The sourced work/depth endpoint is fixed to a uniform priority CRCW word PRAM, bounded error and worst-case resources. Subpolynomial depth is retained; polylogarithmic depth is not added as a stronger requirement.
progress: 2026: Efficient parallel reductions relate exact directed maximum flow to approximate flow on DAGs; the almost-optimal parallel algorithm remains an open target.
working_summary: The task is exact maximum flow in a directed graph with polynomially bounded integer capacities. The question asks for almost-linear total parallel work and subpolynomial depth. Bounded-error randomization is allowed in a uniform shared-memory parallel model. Sequential almost-linear algorithms do not provide the requested bound on dependent stages. DAG projection reductions connect several versions of this open parallel flow problem.

title: Work-efficient parallel directed reachability
importance_reason: Combining near-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for directed reachability would resolve a major barrier in efficient parallel graph algorithms.
formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm meeting the work, depth, and error guarantees simultaneously on all directed inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the specified PRAM model. Work measured by transitive-closure size is insufficient.
context:
A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”
why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 closure-sensitive algorithm. Near-linear input work with polylogarithmic depth remains the target.
progress: 2019: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability. | 2026-05: Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density. | 2026-08: Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.
working_summary: A parallel reachability algorithm must identify every vertex reachable from a source in a directed graph. The target combines nearly linear total work in the input size with polylogarithmic depth, using randomization and high-probability correctness. Ordinary graph search does little work but can expose a long sequence of dependent frontiers. Highly parallel transitive-closure methods may perform far more work than this one-source task requires. The question is whether shortcuts or another representation can remove long dependencies while accounting for the cost of constructing all auxiliary information.

title: Depth-first search in NC
importance_reason: Asks whether the search structure produced by an apparently sequential graph traversal can be computed efficiently in parallel.
formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.
context:
Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.
why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The FSTTCS 2025 paper explicitly leaves deterministic NC construction for general graphs open while proving results for restricted classes. Targeted searches found no later general resolution. Randomized NC, deterministic quasipolynomial resources, and the 2023 near-linear-work algorithm have distinct guarantees. The cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 1988: Aggarwal and Anderson give a randomized NC algorithm for undirected DFS, as documented in the 2025 paper’s introduction. This permits randomness. | 2023: Ghaffari, Grunau and Qu give a randomized algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) work and \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\) depth; this addresses work efficiency with a larger depth bound. | 2025-12-09: Chauhan, Datta and Praveen prove deterministic parallel bounds for bounded-genus and undirected single-crossing-minor-free graphs, and a logspace bound for bounded treewidth. The general question remains open in their statement.
working_summary: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration. For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors. The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth. Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target. A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.

title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in \(o(\log * n)\) rounds
importance_reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.
formal: Is there a uniform quantum-LOCAL algorithm that, for every \(n\ge 3\) and every identifier assignment to an n-cycle, outputs a proper 3-coloring with global probability at least \(1- 1/n\) in $T(n)=o(1+\log^* n)$ communication rounds? Every node is given n, its own identifier from \([n^{2}]\), and a consistent clockwise/counterclockwise orientation. Initial quantum registers are unentangled across nodes.
definitions: The network is a simple cycle; the orientation only identifies predecessor and successor, and communication is allowed in both directions. Nodes do not receive their numerical position in the cycle, a leader, or the list of other identifiers. They run one finite classical control program which may perform arbitrary finite local quantum computations, then exchange finite but unbounded numbers of qubits with each neighbor in each synchronous round. For a concrete uniform model, local quantum operations are finite circuits over H, T, and CNOT, fresh |\(0\rangle\) ancillas, and computational-basis measurements with adaptive classical control. Register size, message size, and local computation time are not charged, but are finite on every branch. Initially the joint quantum state is a product of local |\(0\rangle\) registers; the given classical local input may affect subsequent operations. No shared randomness, initial entanglement, or graph-dependent advice is supplied. The protocol may generate entanglement by sending qubits during its counted rounds. Every node eventually outputs one color in \(\{1,2,3\}\). Success means that every cycle edge has differently colored endpoints, simultaneously. \(T(n)\) bounds all branches of the protocol, not its expected time. The little-o condition is \(T(n)/(1+\log * n)\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty ; \log\)* counts iterated base-2 logarithms down to at most 1. This card fixes the standard directed-cycle input variant, while allowing communication in either direction.
answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol with a proof of its worst-case round bound and global success probability, or prove that no such protocol exists. A constant-round protocol would answer yes. An anonymous zero-error lower bound, a two-color lower bound, or a lower bound using unbounded-degree trees does not by itself answer this high-probability three-color cycle question.
context:
A cycle is the simplest network in which many nearby choices must be coordinated. Two colors encode a global parity constraint, but three colors allow a much more local solution. In classical distributed computing, the exact deterministic cost of this symmetry breaking is \(\Theta (\log * n)\).

Naor’s lower bound shows that classical randomization with high-probability correctness still needs \(\Omega (\log * n)\) rounds. Quantum messages can create correlations unavailable to classical messages, but a coloring algorithm still has to return ordinary classical colors. The question is whether those correlations allow neighboring processors to agree on a valid local pattern faster than the classical symmetry-breaking threshold. The orientation and identifiers are explicit inputs, so no lower bound may rely on their absence.

There is a fundamental obstacle to arguments based only on causality. Finitely dependent proper colorings exist: far-separated sets of outputs can be independent while all adjacent colors differ. Consequently, the output distribution of a hypothetical constant-round quantum coloring algorithm need not violate a general no-signaling or finite-dependence constraint. Existence of such a distribution does not provide a quantum protocol that samples it.

The August 2026 result attacks the quantum implementation itself using matrix-product-state structure and a teleportation-based reduction. It proves a linear lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that must always succeed. Its Section 1.4 explicitly identifies the extension to high-probability correctness as the remaining problem. That is precisely the error regime retained on this card.

A separate July 2026 paper proves a log-star lower bound for 3-coloring rooted trees through growing-degree instances, and a linear lower bound for 2-coloring even cycles. Neither theorem handles the combination here: degree exactly two, three available colors, and small nonzero failure probability.
why: This is a canonical test of quantum advantage for a natural distributed symmetry-breaking task. A faster protocol would improve one of the basic local coordination primitives; a lower bound would have to explain a limitation of quantum realizability that mere causal consistency does not capture.
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves high-probability cycle 3-coloring open. Its new theorem is for anonymous nodes and success probability exactly 1, so it is not recorded as resolving this identified, bounded-error protocol question. No later resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 1980s–1990s: Cole–Vishkin and subsequent algorithms give \(O(\log * n)\) classical coloring. Linial proves a matching deterministic lower bound. These classical bounds also give a quantum upper bound by running a classical protocol. | 1991: Naor proves the classical randomized ring-coloring lower bound, preserving the log-star obstruction when small failure probability is allowed. | 2016: Holroyd and Liggett construct finitely dependent colorings. These establish the barrier to deriving the desired quantum lower bound solely from finite dependence or causality. | 2026-07: Fraigniaud, Magniez, and Ziccardi give quantum lower bounds for rooted-tree 3-coloring and even-cycle 2-coloring. Their rooted-tree lower bound uses degree as a growing parameter. | 2026-08: Coiteux-Roy and coauthors prove that for any fixed \(c\ge 3\), anonymous quantum-PN c-coloring of an even directed n-cycle with probability 1 needs more than \(\operatorname{floor}(n/2)- 2\) rounds. They explicitly leave high-probability correctness open.
working_summary: Processors arranged on an oriented cycle must choose three classical colors so that adjacent processors receive different colors. The question allows quantum communication and asks for a round bound asymptotically smaller than log-star n. Nodes have distinct identifiers and know the cycle size, while their initial quantum registers are unentangled. The complete coloring must be valid with probability at least one minus one over n. A successful algorithm would beat the classical symmetry-breaking threshold, whereas a lower bound must handle quantum correlations without relying only on coarse causality constraints.

title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
importance_reason: A basic randomized symmetry-breaking question on arbitrary graphs whose resolution would sharpen the global locality frontier.
formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.
answer_criterion: Give one randomized LOCAL algorithm with a uniform \(o(\log  n)\) round bound and the stated success probability on all graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A degree restriction does not settle the proposition.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?
why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. General-graph sublogarithmic elapsed-round complexity remains open in the checked literature; awake-time and high-girth results have different guarantees.
progress: 2016: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$. | 2025: Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier. | 2025: Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.
working_summary: A maximal independent set contains no adjacent vertices and leaves every unselected vertex next to a selected one. The question asks for a randomized LOCAL algorithm that finds such a set in \(o(\log  n)\) rounds on every graph with high probability. Message sizes and local computation are unrestricted, so the resource measures the distance over which decisions must be coordinated. The running-time improvement must hold uniformly even for graphs of very large degree. Degree-sensitive algorithms already improve some cases, but the target requires a mechanism that also avoids logarithmically many phases on unrestricted graphs.

title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
importance_reason: A small connectivity promise problem serves as a basic round-complexity benchmark for low-memory massively parallel computation.
formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint \((n/2)\)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is \(O(n)\) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.
answer_criterion: Prove the logarithmic lower bound for every fixed sublinear-memory exponent and every admissible randomized algorithm, or refute that universal lower bound. An \(o(\log  n)\)-round algorithm for one fixed exponent would suffice for a refutation.
context:
Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.
why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The lower bound is conjectural. Constant-round results for geometric graphs or larger local memory do not establish this variant.
progress: 2022: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here. | 2025: Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.
working_summary: The one-cycle-versus-two problem distinguishes a single n-vertex cycle from two disjoint cycles of half that size. In the low-memory MPC model, edges are spread across machines with sublinear local memory and linear total memory. The conjecture says randomized algorithms require \(\Omega (\log  n)\) communication rounds under these resource bounds. Both input types have identical vertex counts, edge counts, and degrees, so only their global connectivity distinguishes them. A lower bound must handle arbitrary communication between machines and arbitrary encodings, rather than assuming information can travel only along graph edges.

title: Deterministic LOCAL MIS in \(O(\log  n)\) rounds
importance_reason: Matching a logarithmic deterministic bound for MIS would settle a central gap in local symmetry breaking.
formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be \(O(\log  n)\) uniformly over degrees.
answer_criterion: Give one deterministic LOCAL algorithm with a uniform \(O(\log  n)\) bound over all graphs and valid identifiers, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Constants must not depend on maximum degree.
context:
Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.
why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An \(O(\log  n)\) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is solved; the \(O(\log  n)\) target remains open in the checked literature.
progress: 2019: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor. | 2020: Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS. | 2024: Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$. | 2026: Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve \(\Delta\)-coloring; their result does not give an \(O(\log  n) \mathrm{MIS}\) algorithm.
working_summary: Deterministic maximal independent set algorithms must coordinate their choices using the graph and vertex identifiers alone. The question asks whether \(O(\log  n) \mathrm{LOCAL}\) rounds suffice on every graph and every valid identifier assignment. The output must be independent and dominate all unselected vertices, without requiring maximum cardinality. Network decomposition already supports polylogarithmic deterministic algorithms, so the target is a sharper dependence on network size. Reaching the logarithmic bound would require organizing deterministic progress efficiently even when identifier patterns defeat simple greedy local rules.

title: Fast merging of summaries for symmetric streaming computations
importance_reason: The existing high importance is retained for the broad conversion from sequential summaries to efficiently mergeable computation; the unresolved resource is explicitly time, after the known space simulation.
formal: Does every total, order-invariant Boolean stream function computable deterministically in polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per item also admit a deterministic summary scheme with polylogarithmic message size, working space, and time per merge, correct for every binary merge tree? The uniform families, input lengths and costs in this question are specified below.
definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.
context:
The workshop page asks broadly whether good streaming algorithms yield good sketches and compares one-way with simultaneous communication. Editorial specialization: this card selects the deterministic, total-function question with efficient merging. This is the time-sensitive refinement motivated by the paper cited on that page, rather than a claim that the already established space-only simulation remains unknown.

Feldman, Muthukrishnan, Sidiropoulos, Stein and Svitkina show that symmetric deterministic streaming computation can be distributed through a binary aggregation tree with comparable message size and polynomially related space. Their simulation uses reachability search and can take superpolynomial time. The retained target asks whether that time cost can always be avoided.

A sequential chain of merges is itself a streaming computation. The converse must support balanced trees and every other arrangement, even when the stream algorithm’s intermediate states record order-dependent information that disappears from the final answer.

The cited paper also gives failures of analogous comparisons for promises, multiple permissible outputs and private randomness. This card removes those routes to a separation by requiring a total Boolean function and deterministic exact computation. The malformed final sentence on the workshop page is not used as a theorem statement.

Associativity of the summary representation is not required: two different trees can leave different internal summaries provided both decode correctly. Demanding identical summaries would strengthen the problem beyond the aggregation model used here.

Recent turnstile-to-linear-sketch simulations address algebraic update streams and space preservation. Their hypotheses and conclusions do not provide this uniform polylogarithmic-time merging theorem for arbitrary insertion streams and arbitrary total symmetric functions.
why: Fast merging would allow any efficiently maintained order-independent statistic to be computed from independently processed pieces without an expensive reconstruction step. A separation would expose an inherent computational cost of parallel aggregation even when communication and memory are small.
status_note: The cited paper establishes a space-preserving simulation but explicitly identifies its high running time as a limitation. This card selects a precise uniform polylogarithmic-time refinement, with no promise or randomness. No matching general simulation or separation was located in the bounded September 2026 check; the literal malformed source sentence is not treated as evidence.
progress: 2006: Sivakumar asks the general streaming-versus-sketching question. | 2008: Feldman and coauthors give the aggregation simulation, discuss its large running time, and identify time as the remaining possible source of separation. | 2026-04-23: A later turnstile simulation treats polynomial-length integer update streams, a different model from the one fixed here.
working_summary: The input statistic is a total Boolean function invariant under reordering the stream. A streaming program computes it using polylogarithmic memory and time per item. The selected question asks for equally efficient local summaries and merging on every binary aggregation tree. A known simulation preserves small space but can use superpolynomial merge time. The target excludes promise and randomness separations and does not require identical intermediate summaries.

title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
importance_reason: The queue question tests whether consensus number alone captures the strength of basic concurrent data types, and whether weak primitives can provide per-process progress.
formal: For every fixed integer \(n\ge3\), is there a deterministic linearizable wait-free implementation of an unbounded FIFO queue for \(n\) asynchronous processes using only atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set objects?
definitions: Processes have distinct identifiers, arbitrary private memory and no timing information. The shared primitives are atomic registers supporting Read and Write of finite values, and test-and-set bits initially zero: TAS returns the old bit and sets it to one. An unbounded supply of fresh primitives is permitted; stronger atomic operations are not. Each process can repeatedly invoke either Enqueue(v), for any finite binary string \(v\), or Dequeue(). Sequential queue semantics append at the tail, remove and return the oldest item at the head, and return a distinguished empty marker immediately when empty. Linearizability requires each concurrent history to admit a sequential ordering of completed operations and a subset of pending operations that obeys these semantics and respects real-time precedence of nonoverlapping operations. Wait-freedom requires every operation of a process that continues taking steps to complete after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of delays or crashes of others. There is no restriction to designated enqueuers or dequeuers and no bound on the number of operations. Algorithms may depend on \(n\); they receive no random coins.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
Stacks belong to Common2, but this does not give a queue implementation. Restricted one- or two-enqueuer/dequeuer queues leave the unrestricted many-process interface unresolved.

The source explicitly identifies the open question with an n-process linearizable wait-free queue built from test-and-set and registers. Lock-free system-wide progress is a weaker guarantee.
why: The queue question tests whether consensus number alone captures the strength of basic concurrent data types, and whether weak primitives can provide per-process progress.
status_note: Explicitly open in the cited primary source. The bounded 13 September 2026 literature search found no later general resolution; the source date is retained rather than presented as a 2026 theorem.
progress: 2015: The source explicitly retains Common2 membership of a fully accessible FIFO queue as open.
working_summary: Several processes concurrently insert and remove items from a FIFO queue. Every continuing process must complete its own operation despite arbitrary delays of others. Only read/write registers and test-and-set primitives are available. Known restricted queue implementations do not cover the full interface. The question separates the synchronization power of a queue from that of weaker shared objects.

title: Deterministic volume gap
importance_reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.
formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with \(V_{A}(n)=o(n)\) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with \(V_{B}(n)=O(1+\log * n)\)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots ,|V(G)|^{2}\}\). Here \(V_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed \(\Delta \ge 2, a\) fixed verification radius \(r\ge 1\), finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, \(\Pi\) and the exact |\(V(G)|\), and visited set \(\{v\}\). It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. \(\log * n\) is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no \(O(\log * n)\)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every \(C>0\) and every \(n_{0}\), some \(n\ge n_{0}\) satisfies \(V_{B}(n)>C(1+\log * n)\). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
context:
A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.
why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.
status_note: The July 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the deterministic gap as open. The new constructions are randomized; no deterministic resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2020: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume. | 2021: Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) can be sped up to deterministic \(O(\log * n)\). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL. | 2022: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above \(\log * n\) remains the issue here. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear. | 2026-07: Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity \(\Theta (\log ^{k} n)\) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.
working_summary: The VOLUME model measures how many graph vertices an adaptive local algorithm inspects to determine one requested output. Outputs from separate queries must still fit together into a single valid labeling. The conjecture says every deterministic locally checkable problem with sublinear worst-case volume actually has O(log-star n) volume. It concerns fixed bounded-degree graph families with exact size information and polynomially bounded identifiers. Proving the collapse would eliminate an entire intermediate range of deterministic local information complexity, despite the richer range available to randomized algorithms.

title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.
formal: Is the following decision problem in logspace-uniform NC? An input gives positive integers W,H, an explicit W-by-H array c with entries in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), and two cells p,q in that rectangle. Extend c by zero to the whole integer square lattice and add one grain at p. Answer YES exactly when q eventually topples under the four-neighbor parallel sandpile dynamics defined below. The input length N includes every array entry, not a compressed representation.
definitions: The four neighbor displacements are \(E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\}\). Set \(c_{0}(v)=c(v)+1\) if \(v=p\), and \(c_{0}(v)=c(v)\) otherwise. At each integer time \(t\ge 0\) every vertex v with \(c_{t}(v)\ge 4\) topples once, losing four grains and sending one to each neighbor. Equivalently, \(c_{t+1}(v)=c_{t}(v)-4 I[c_{t}(v)\ge 4]+\sum\)_{e in E} \(I[c_{t}(v-e)\ge 4]\), where I is the indicator. The question is whether \(c_{t}(q)\ge 4\) for some \(t\ge 0\). The array is row-major with binary dimensions and cell coordinates; invalid encodings are rejected. The zero extension is an infinite lattice, not a periodic boundary or a boundary that absorbs grains. A supplied rectangle may contain extra zero rows or columns to include p and q. Finite initial mass eventually stabilizes. NC here means that for some fixed integers a,k the decision has Boolean circuits of size \(O(N^{a})\) and depth \(O((\log  N)^{k})\), with fan-in at most two, whose description is generated from \(1^{N}\) in \(O(\log  N)\) work space. There is no requested time t in the input and the answer is exact, without random error.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute membership of the specified language in logspace-uniform NC. Any complexity assumption used in a negative result must be stated explicitly.
context:
The initial configuration is stable, so all activity comes from the extra grain. The requested output is a single eventual-toppling bit; computing the entire final configuration or a toppling at a specified time are related but different tasks.

The classical dimension-dependent results provide efficient parallel prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three. They leave the planar case as a distinct question.

Recent work still separates the standard four-neighbor lattice from weighted or nonuniform grids. NC membership and P-completeness are not an unconditional exclusive dichotomy: a P-completeness result rules out NC only under \(\mathrm{NC} \ne  \mathrm{P}\).
why: A local deterministic physical process can have a long cascade after a single perturbation. This problem asks whether its outcome permits an efficient parallel computation, addressing the boundary between prediction and sequential evolution.
status_note: The 2025 primary source and the introduction of the 25 June 2026 preprint explicitly leave the standard planar case open. Checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 preprint is used for dated status and variant separation, not as an independently verified proof. This card fixes the NC-membership side of the proposed parallel-complexity question.
progress: 1998 / 1999: Moore and Nilsson obtain \(\mathrm{NC}^{3}\) prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three, leaving dimension two open. | 2025-06-26: Concha-Vega and Perrot explicitly define single-grain eventual prediction on the infinite lattice and retain the von Neumann-neighborhood problem as open. | 2026-06-25: A new preprint studies weighted and nonuniform crossing constructions and continues to state the standard two-dimensional complexity question as open.

title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
importance_reason: A unifying classification problem for streaming dissimilarity estimation, extending both norm-based geometry and the known one-variable aggregation framework.
formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. Equivalently, determine the classification function \(\chi(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\), equal to one exactly for functions with such algorithms.
definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.
context:
The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset.
