This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.
why: A full classification would explain which local comparisons of large frequency vectors retain enough structure for accurate compression under deletions. It would connect individual distance estimators and impossibility results through a general mathematical criterion, including dissimilarities that are not norms or even metrics.
status_note: The source asks for a broad characterization. This card explicitly fixes an effective separable streaming variant rather than attributing every resource convention to the source. The 2016 one-variable result is only a partial classification, and the later metric counterexample concerns another model. No full characterization for the specified domain was located in the bounded September 2026 check.
progress: 2006: Guha and Indyk pose the broad distance-sketchability question and discuss separable coordinate costs. | 2016: Braverman and coauthors classify nearly all one-variable frequency aggregates and explicitly identify the result as a partial answer for difference-based dissimilarities. | 2019: Khot and Naor show that the norm-sketchability characterization does not extend to arbitrary metrics.
working_summary: A local nonnegative cost φ defines a dissimilarity by summing over corresponding frequency coordinates. The stream may insert and delete frequencies while keeping both vectors nonnegative. The selected task classifies exactly which effectively evaluable costs admit polylogarithmic-space relative approximations. The criterion must cover the entire specified domain and include both algorithms and impossibility proofs. Known offset obstructions, difference-based aggregate classifications and norm-sketching results cover only parts of this domain.

title: Maximum independent set in the congested clique
importance_reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.
definitions: There is one processor for each vertex in \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |\(S| \ge  |I|\) for every independent set I of the input graph. Define \(T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)\) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.
answer_criterion: Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function \(f(n)\), construct protocols taking \(O(f(n))\) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires \(Omega(f(n))\) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.
context:
The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.

A simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take \(O(n / \log  n)\) rounds for \(n \ge  2\). Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. This is an elementary upper bound for the stated model, rather than a claim that centralizing the graph is optimal.

The unlimited local computation is essential to interpreting this baseline. The exponential subset enumeration has no communication cost. Conversely, a faster centralized algorithm does not by itself reduce the number of rounds needed to assemble the input. The question isolates information movement from the ordinary running-time difficulty of exact independent set.

Lower bounds are especially delicate in the unicast clique. Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman relate this model to powerful circuit computations, explaining why familiar sparse-network bottleneck arguments do not transfer directly. Chechik nevertheless identifies exact maximum independent set as a concrete round-complexity question. The catalogue has a separate constant-round question for a maximal independent set; that weaker output requirement must not be substituted here.
why: This places a canonical exact graph optimization problem in a model where computation is free but communication is limited. Understanding its round complexity would help distinguish the benefit of distributing information from merely gathering the graph at one processor.
status_note: The 2025 seminar source asks for the optimal round complexity. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate matching bounds for this exact task. Randomness and bandwidth are fixed explicitly here; results for maximal MIS, broadcast cliques, or edge-restricted CONGEST do not resolve this formulation.
progress: 2014: Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman establish circuit-simulation connections and distinguish unicast from broadcast congested cliques. Their work supplies model context, not a tight bound for the present task. | 2025: Chechik explicitly asks for the communication rounds necessary to compute a maximum independent set in the congested clique.
working_summary: Maximum independent set asks for a largest collection of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Here each vertex is a processor in a congested clique, whose communication links exist even between nonadjacent input vertices. The question asks for the optimal deterministic number of rounds, with unlimited local computation and storage. Collecting the full graph at one processor gives an elementary upper bound, after which even exhaustive local optimization costs no communication rounds. The challenge is to determine how much information must move to identify an exact optimum, independently of the usual centralized NP-hardness barrier.

title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
importance_reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) and one deterministic VOLUME algorithm that computes a maximal matching on every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), inspecting at most \(C(\Delta +1)^{k}\) distinct vertices per queried vertex, independently of the number n of graph vertices? A proper input two-coloring specifying the bipartition is supplied. Answers to all vertex queries must describe the same matching.
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph, arbitrary local port orders, a supplied proper two-coloring, distinct identifiers in \([n^{2}]\), and known integers n and \(\Delta \ge 1\) bounding its size and degrees as stated. A query at v must output either ⊥ for unmatched or the local port of its matching edge. If v names u then u must name v. Every edge must have at least one matched endpoint, which is equivalent to maximality by inclusion. Initially the algorithm sees only v’s identifier, degree, color, ports, n, and \(\Delta\). It may adaptively follow a port at any already visited vertex; doing so reveals the neighbor’s identifier, degree, color, and reciprocal port. Count all distinct visited vertices, including v. The explored set is connected: arbitrary jumps to identifiers are forbidden. Each query starts afresh, with no preprocessing or memory retained between queries. Repeating a query must give the same answer regardless of other queries or their order. Local computation and temporary memory are unrestricted but finite, and only the number of distinct visited vertices is charged. One finite deterministic program must work for all \(n, \Delta\), graphs, identifiers, and port orders; the constants C,k are universal. There is no additional log n or \(\log * n\) term in the allowed volume.
answer_criterion: Construct the uniform polynomial-in-\(\Delta\) algorithm with globally consistent matching answers, or prove that every correct deterministic algorithm violates every such polynomial bound on some valid input and query. A randomized bound, expected volume, an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal, or a polynomial bound containing a factor depending on n does not settle this formulation.
context:
A matching is maximal when there is no edge that can be added while keeping its endpoints disjoint from the current matching. It can be much smaller than a maximum matching. The local output is only one port or an unmatched symbol, so the difficulty is the information needed to make this small answer consistent with answers elsewhere.

The supplied bipartition lets the two sides play different roles. A simple distributed procedure has unmatched vertices on one side propose along a new incident edge, while vertices on the other side accept at most one proposal and remain matched thereafter. After \(O(\Delta )\) rounds this yields a maximal matching. Gathering a whole neighborhood to simulate those rounds can inspect \(\Delta\) raised to a linear-in-\(\Delta\) power many vertices.

Volume asks whether that exploration can be made much narrower. A vertex may follow a few carefully chosen dependencies far into the graph, instead of collecting every branch of a large ball. But it cannot simply choose a convenient partner in isolation: when that partner is queried separately, the answers must agree. The lack of shared mutable query state makes this coordination part of the algorithm itself.

The independence from n is essential. For each fixed \(\Delta\), even an enormous function such as \(\Delta ^{2\Delta}\) is constant as n grows. This question compares those constants uniformly as \(\Delta\) grows, asking for a single polynomial. It is therefore different from obtaining logarithmic dependence on n for fixed degree or from studying only a single fixed-degree LCL.

Known round lower bounds force at least linear dependence on \(\Delta\) when n is sufficiently large. They leave a large interval between that obstruction and full-neighborhood simulation. Suomela conjectures an exponential degree dependence for volume, so even deciding whether a polynomial is possible would determine which side of that major gap is achievable.
why: This is a basic test of whether a fast distributed symmetry-breaking algorithm can be evaluated locally without exploring an exponentially branching dependency structure. A polynomial bound would give a small deterministic oracle for a fundamental graph primitive; a superpolynomial lower bound would expose an information cost that round complexity alone does not capture.
status_note: Explicitly open in the February 2026 primary problem list. Review through 10 September 2026 found no deterministic degree-only polynomial-volume algorithm or superpolynomial lower bound. The bipartition, connected probes, stateless consistency, and worst-case deterministic guarantee are fixed explicitly.
progress: 2020: rounds: Brandt and Olivetti sharpen the degree dependence of bipartite maximal matching in LOCAL. In the identifier model, the deterministic \(\Omega (\min \{\Delta ,\log  n/\log  \log  n\})\) lower bound gives an \(\Omega (\Delta )\) obstruction to any degree-only volume bound by choosing sufficiently large n. | 2020: volume model: Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive exploration and explain why an f-round LOCAL algorithm gives a \(\Delta ^{O}(f)\)-volume algorithm. Combining this with the bipartite \(O(\Delta )\)-round procedure gives the baseline \(\Delta ^{O}(\Delta )\) volume. | 2026-02: Suomela explicitly asks whether bipartite maximal matching admits polynomial volume in \(\Delta\), and conjectures \(2^{\Theta}(\Delta )\) as the correct dependence. The conjecture is not a proved lower bound.
working_summary: A maximal matching is a collection of disjoint edges to which no further edge can be added. The question asks for a deterministic local-query algorithm on bipartite graphs whose inspected volume is polynomial in the maximum degree and independent of graph size. A proper two-coloring identifying the bipartition is supplied. Simulating a distributed proposal algorithm by exploring whole neighborhoods can incur an exponential dependence on degree. The project is to follow a much smaller dependency structure while ensuring that separately answered vertex queries describe the same matching.

title: Lifting CSP sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
importance_reason: A broad proposed transfer of approximation resistance across both models and space thresholds, with implications for the classification of streaming CSPs.
formal: For every finite family \(\Pi\) of Boolean predicates of a fixed arity, does the following implication hold? If no \(o(\sqrt n)\)-bit sketching algorithm nontrivially approximates Max-CSP(\(\Pi\)), then no \(o(n)\)-bit single-pass streaming algorithm nontrivially approximates it. Nontrivial approximation, sketching and the polynomial stream-length convention are defined below.
definitions: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\) and a nonempty finite family \(\Pi\subseteq\{\pi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\}\). A constraint on \(n\geq k\) variables consists of a predicate \(\pi\in\Pi\) and an ordered tuple of \(k\) distinct indices in \([n]\). An instance \(\Phi\) is a nonempty list of such constraints; repetitions are allowed and every occurrence has unit weight. For an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), its value is the fraction of constraint occurrences it satisfies, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) is the maximum over assignments. Let \(\rho(\Pi)=\inf_{n\geq k,\Phi}\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\). Padding with unused variables makes this the limiting trivial approximation threshold. A nontrivial approximation has a fixed \(\delta>0\), with \(\rho(\Pi)+\delta\leq1\), and outputs a value \(v\) satisfying \((\rho(\Pi)+\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\leq v\leq\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance and order. The algorithm need not output an assignment. A deterministic streaming algorithm has a finite state represented by \(s\) bits, a fixed initial state, an update map taking the current state and next constraint, and a final output map. It reads the constraint list once in an adversarial order. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic algorithms, chosen independently of the list. Local computation and the choice of this distribution are unrestricted; this is the nonuniform randomness model used for the source’s lower bounds. A sketching algorithm additionally has a state map \(K\) on lists and a binary combination map \(H\), with \(K(\sigma\tau)=H(K(\sigma),K(\tau))\) for every pair of lists whose concatenation is allowed; its updates append a singleton through this map, and its output depends only on the sketch. Randomized sketches are distributions over such deterministic schemes. Commutativity and linearity of the sketches are not separately required. Editorial length convention: an algorithmic space regime must handle every fixed polynomial length bound. Precisely, to admit nontrivial approximation in \(o(b(n))\) space means that there is one fixed \(\delta>0\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), there is an algorithm family for all lists of length at most \(n^d\), with worst-case state size \(s_d(n)\) satisfying \(s_d(n)/b(n)\to0\). The algorithm may depend on \(\Pi,d,\delta,n\), but not on the input list; the ratio improvement \(\delta\) does not depend on \(n\) or \(d\). The two occurrences of “no” in the conjecture negate this full definition.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every predicate family in the stated model, or give a fixed family that is resistant to nontrivial o(√n)-space sketching and a nontrivial o(n)-space streaming approximation for that family. Both parts of a counterexample need proofs. A faster approximation for a family already admitting nontrivial small sketches, or a lower bound under an additional condition not proved for all families in the premise, is insufficient.
context:
This is Conjecture 8 of Singer’s column. It simultaneously enlarges the algorithm class and the permitted memory, while asking only whether any fixed improvement over the trivial ratio is possible. It does not claim that every approximation threshold of every CSP stays unchanged as space increases.

The sketching dichotomy gives polylogarithmic-space algorithms or square-root-space lower bounds, with a small slack in the approximation thresholds. Its definition of a sketch permits general mergeable summaries; restricting the premise to linear sketches would be a different statement.

Max-DiCut illustrates why the premise matters. Its trivial ratio is one quarter, while small sketches already give a ratio approaching four ninths. Better streaming approximations using more memory therefore do not by themselves refute the resistance implication in this card.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy’s April 2026 manuscript proves linear-space lower bounds from integrality gaps of the basic linear programming relaxation. That relaxation assigns a distribution of local assignments to each constraint and requires consistent one-variable marginals on shared variables. Its ratio is not defined by the sketching premise in this card.

The same manuscript gives a tight classification for bounded-degree instances and explicitly continues to distinguish general sketching lower bounds from streaming lower bounds. Applying its theorem to Conjecture 8 requires a theorem connecting every resistant predicate family to the needed LP gap. This review does not claim that such a connection has been proved or disproved.
why: A universal implication would upgrade a broad sketching classification to a fundamental limitation on all small-memory streaming algorithms. A counterexample would show that some CSPs admit an informative sequential summary even though every substantially smaller mergeable summary is approximation resistant.
status_note: The 2025 source states this as a conjecture. A substantial April 2026 theorem now gives LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, but the checked text does not explicitly establish or refute Conjecture 8 for every sketching-resistant family. Status remains uncertain rather than certifying that the 2025 question survives that theorem. The card’s mathematical statement is complete, and its polynomial-length convention is identified explicitly.
progress: 2024: Chou, Golovnev, Sudan and Velusamy publish the finite-CSP sketching dichotomy. | 2025: Singer poses the lifting implication as Conjecture 8 and explicitly allows that counterexamples may exist. | 2026-04-09: Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy establish LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, creating a stronger framework that must be compared with the conjecture’s premise.
working_summary: Each fixed predicate family defines a maximum constraint-satisfaction problem. A nontrivial approximation beats the best constant lower bound on the optimum by a fixed amount. The conjecture lifts resistance to small mergeable sketches into resistance to all sublinear-space streaming algorithms. Both the algorithm model and the space threshold change in the implication. The 2026 LP-gap lower bounds are recorded without claiming a verified resolution of this exact lifting statement.

title: Register space of obstruction-free set agreement
importance_reason: This measures a basic memory cost of synchronization and exposes a large gap between known impossibility arguments and protocols.
formal: For every pair of integers \(n>k\ge1\), determine \(R(n,k)\), the minimum number of atomic read/write registers sufficient for deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set agreement among \(n\) processes with inputs in \([n]\). Supply the resulting function with pointwise absolute error at most \(1/100\) registers.
definitions: An asynchronous shared-memory system has named processes \(1,\ldots,n\), each with one input value, unbounded private computation and private storage, and at most \(r\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers. Each register may hold any finite value; register width is not charged. A shared step is an atomic Read or Write, and no stronger primitive or random choice is available. Every decision must be an input proposed by a participating process, and across an execution at most \(k\) distinct values may be decided. Safety must hold under every schedule, including process crashes. Obstruction-freedom means that from every reachable configuration, a process that thereafter runs alone for sufficiently many own steps decides, regardless of whether other processes ever resume. Each process invokes the task at most once. \(R(n,k)\) is the minimum integer \(r\ge0\) for which such a protocol exists; a protocol may depend on \(n,k\). Inputs, private memory and local computation are uncharged; all shared registers are counted.
answer_criterion: Supply a real-valued function \(g\) on all integer pairs \(n>k\ge1\), and prove in Lean that \(|g(n,k)-R(n,k)|\le1/100\) throughout the domain, in registers. The approximation need not be integer-valued. A finite table or bounds that do not reach this precision do not determine the function.
context:
Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu prove \(R(n,k)\ge\lceil n/k\rceil\). A known protocol gives \(R(n,k)\le n-k+1\). The endpoints coincide for consensus but can be far apart as \(k\) grows.

The 2025 source continues to state these register bounds. Bounds for swap objects concern a stronger primitive and do not determine this read/write-register function.
why: This measures a basic memory cost of synchronization and exposes a large gap between known impossibility arguments and protocols.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2024: The journal paper proves the \(\lceil n/k\rceil\) register lower bound. | 2025: The OPODIS paper retains the gap to the n-k+1 register upper bound.
working_summary: Processes must decide on at most k of their proposed values. A process is guaranteed to finish if it eventually runs alone. The resource being minimized is the number of shared read/write registers. Known lower and upper bounds are the ceiling of n/k and n-k+1. The benchmark requests the full register-space function over all n greater than k.

title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
importance_reason: Triangle detection is a basic distributed subgraph task. Its exact round complexity calibrates techniques used for many larger patterns.
formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.
answer_criterion: Determine a function \(f(n)\) with an \(O(f(n))\)-round randomized algorithm and an \(Omega(f(n))\) worst-case lower bound for every randomized algorithm in the stated model, up to constant factors. Either a faster algorithm or a stronger lower bound alone is partial progress.
context:
Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.
why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2025 multi-round lower bound is included; the detection/listing distinction is essential.
progress: 2021: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound. | 2025: Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round. | 2025-10: Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.
working_summary: Triangle detection asks a distributed network to report whether any three vertices are pairwise adjacent. In CONGEST, each edge transmits only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per round, even though vertices initially know all their own neighbors. The saved card asks for the optimal randomized round complexity between the stated doubly logarithmic lower bound and roughly \(n^{1/3}\) upper bound. Detection needs only one positive witness somewhere in the network, unlike listing every triangle. The challenge is to exploit that smaller output requirement while still communicating enough information to discover an edge between two neighbors.

title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
importance_reason: A general space-versus-approximation barrier for a central geometric connectivity objective, separating polynomially small summaries from polylogarithmic ones as dimension grows.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm A and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of n distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), A uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate Z satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
definitions:
The point set X consists of the n distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters n,d and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, private independent fair random bits, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, random seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer b and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows d to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in d does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite C. Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing C. Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.
context:
Pavel Veselý proposed the insertion-only, one-pass, constant-factor question through the Atlas website. The requested output is the cost of the Euclidean minimum spanning tree, with memory polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in the number of points. This card adds the finite-coordinate, randomness and output conventions needed to make that request precise.

The STOC 2023 paper obtains constant-factor estimation using \(n^{O(\varepsilon)}\) space for a fixed positive parameter \(\varepsilon\). Its sketches support insertions and deletions. This leaves a gap to polylogarithmic memory even in the insertion-only model selected here.

The same paper rules out one-pass space \(o(\sqrt n)\) for approximation better than 1.1035 in sufficiently high dimension. This near-one barrier does not exclude every absolute approximation constant. Its multiple-pass improvements also do not settle the one-pass target.

title: Optimal measurements and near-linear decoding for universal ℓ₂/ℓ₁ sparse recovery
importance_reason: A central universal compressed-sensing tradeoff between measurement count, robust mixed-norm error and decoding time; explicit matrix generation is a separate issue.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,B>0\), \(a\geq0\), and a deterministic recovery scheme such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and \(1\leq k\leq n\), one fixed matrix \(A_{n,k}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\leq Bk\log_2(en/k)\) permits recovery from \(A_{n,k}x\) in at most \(Bn\log_2^a(n+2)\) operations, with \[\|x-\widehat x\|_2\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\min_{z:\,|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\leq k}\|x-z\|_1\] simultaneously for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)?
definitions: The support of a vector is the set of its nonzero coordinates; a vector is \(k\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(k\). The norms are \(\|v\|_1=\sum_i|v_i|\) and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum in the statement is the sum of absolute values outside the \(k\) largest-magnitude coordinates of \(x\); ties may be broken arbitrarily. The decoder receives \(n,k\), the exact real measurement vector \(y=A_{n,k}x\), and read-only access to the fixed description of the scheme. It receives neither \(x\) nor its support, and must output all \(n\) coordinates of \(\widehat x\). The output need not itself be sparse. Measurements are linear and selected independently of the unknown signal. We use the real-arithmetic model: real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, square root of a nonnegative number, comparison, and access to an addressed stored entry each cost one operation; ordinary integer index operations cost one as well. The decoder is one fixed algorithm, with polynomial-size read-only advice depending only on \(n,k\), including the matrix and any preprocessing data. Reading advice is charged. Advice generation and forming the original measurement vector are outside the requested decoding bound. No polynomial-time explicit matrix construction is required. Once the scheme is fixed its decoder is deterministic and the guarantee holds for all real signals; a matrix chosen by the probabilistic method is admissible only if a single fixed choice works for all signals. Constants, the polynomial advice exponent and the decoding exponent are independent of \(n,k,x\). Measurements are noiseless; no additional post-measurement perturbation is included.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction or existence proof of a scheme meeting both resource bounds and the universal mixed-norm error guarantee in the specified arithmetic model, or prove that no such scheme exists. A guarantee holding with high probability separately for each input, an ℓ₁/ℓ₁ error bound, or optimal row count with slower decoding is insufficient.
context:
The source’s “deterministic” target is universal recovery from one matrix: the same measurements must work for every signal. Editorial model convention: this card makes the arithmetic-operation and preprocessing conventions explicit, without adding the separate challenge of efficient deterministic matrix generation. It also uses \(\log(en/k)\) and \(k\geq1\) to remove the source formula’s undefined or zero endpoint expressions.

For exactly \(k\)-sparse signals the right-hand side is zero, so the scheme must recover them exactly. For nonsparse signals, recovery quality depends on the entire tail and gains a factor \(1/\sqrt{k}\). Merely outputting a plausible support does not establish this robust guarantee.

The original question emphasizes achieving optimal measurement count and fast reconstruction together. Classical constructions achieve the two features separately for this error criterion, whereas some fast optimal-measurement schemes use a different norm on the reconstruction error.

The later for-all sparse-recovery work of Gilbert, Li, Porat and Strauss improves measurements and decoding for the ℓ₁/ℓ₁ formulation, and explicitly lists mixed-norm recovery as a remaining direction. Its use of a matrix fixed for all signals is compatible with a nonconstructive probabilistic existence proof.

The inequality \(\|v\|_2\leq\|v\|_1\) does not convert an \(\ell_1/\ell_1\) theorem into the requested result: it loses the essential \(1/\sqrt{k}\) factor. Likewise, an input-dependent success probability does not imply that one random seed works simultaneously over the uncountable set of all real inputs.

When \(k\) is comparable to \(n\), storing the full vector is consistent with the measurement bound. The compression challenge lies in the sparse regime. Counting the output cost explains why near-linear decoding remains a meaningful target even when the number of measurements is much smaller than \(n\).
why: The target combines information-efficient sensing with fast, uniformly reliable reconstruction for arbitrary signals. Resolving it would show whether the strongest standard universal mixed-norm guarantee can be obtained without sacrificing near-optimal compression or practical asymptotic decoding time.
status_note: The 2009 source poses this universal mixed-norm tradeoff, and the checked later for-all recovery paper still distinguishes it from its ℓ₁/ℓ₁ result. No matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check. The arithmetic/preprocessing convention is explicit; efficient explicit matrix generation is not asserted to be part of the original target.
progress: 2009: Indyk poses the simultaneous optimal-row-count and near-linear-decoding question for the ℓ₂/ℓ₁ guarantee. | 2014: Gilbert, Li, Porat and Strauss improve for-all ℓ₁/ℓ₁ recovery and separately identify mixed-norm recovery as an open direction.
working_summary: A fixed matrix compresses every real signal to a short vector of linear measurements. The decoder must work for all signals with error controlled by the best k-sparse ℓ₁ tail divided by √k. The conjecture combines O(k log(en/k)) measurements with near-linear deterministic decoding. The arithmetic model permits input-independent polynomial preprocessing but charges decoding accesses. Faster results with an ℓ₁ reconstruction error or only per-input randomized success do not meet this target.

title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
importance_reason: Asks whether all-to-all communication suffices for constant-round symmetry breaking, sharply testing the congested-clique model.
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in \(O(1)\) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.
answer_criterion: Construct one randomized algorithm whose round bound is constant on every input graph, with the stated high-probability guarantee, or prove that constant rounds cannot suffice for all graphs in this model.
context:
This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.
why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Constant-round MIS on arbitrary input graphs remains open in the checked literature.
progress: 2018: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović, and Rubinfeld obtain the $O(\log\log\Delta)$-round MIS bound using sparsification. | 2023: Cambus, Kuhn, Pai, and Uitto obtain constant rounds for the 2-ruling-set relaxation. | 2025: Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin, and Halldórsson obtain constant rounds, for example, when average degree is at most $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. They also identify graph families on which existing sparsification methods require $\Omega(\log\log n)$ iterations. That restriction applies to those methods, not to all Congested Clique algorithms.
working_summary: A maximal independent set is independent and places every excluded vertex next to a selected one. In the congested clique, processors can send separate short messages directly to every other processor. The question asks whether a randomized algorithm can solve this task in a constant number of rounds on every input graph with high probability. Collecting all edges at one leader is too expensive, but the algorithm need not reconstruct the entire graph to choose a valid set. The target is to replace repeated sparsification and degree-reduction phases with a bounded amount of globally coordinated communication.

title: Constant-pass weighted matching with O(n log n) bits
importance_reason: A precise resource question for a fundamental graph optimization task; its historical RAM and broad semi-streaming components are separated from the stricter bit-space endpoint.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and fixed integer \(c\geq1\), is there a randomized insertion-only streaming algorithm that, on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with integer edge weights in \([1,n^c]\), outputs a matching of weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p_{\varepsilon,c}\) passes and \(B_{\varepsilon,c}n\log_2(n+2)\) bits of memory, where \(p_{\varepsilon,c},B_{\varepsilon,c}\) do not depend on \(n\)?
definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\). A matching is a subset of edges with no shared endpoint, its weight is the sum of its edge weights, and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the largest such sum over all matchings of the graph. The input is a list of distinct edges, each represented by two binary vertex identifiers and its positive binary integer weight. The algorithm knows \(n,\varepsilon,c\). It reads the list sequentially in an arbitrary order selected independently of its random choices. A pass reads the same complete list in that same order; no deletions, changes of order, random access to earlier items, or requests for selected edges are allowed. The algorithm may stop after any number of passes up to the stated bound. At the end it must output the actual edges of a matching, not merely an estimate of its value. The empty graph has optimum zero and admits the empty output. All stored bits, including edge identifiers, weights, random seeds retained for reuse, counters and temporary working memory, count toward space. A final write-only output tape is permitted, but cannot be used as storage during the passes. The bound is worst case over inputs and random choices; success is required for each input and order. Local computation time is unrestricted, and the finite algorithm may depend on the fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Equivalently the space target is O(n) words of O(log n) bits for each fixed pair of parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is required for the pass count or space constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the approximation, actual matching output, pass and bit-space guarantees for every fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Alternatively prove that this family of guarantees is impossible, for some fixed parameters. A constant-pass algorithm with extra logarithmic factors in bits, an algorithm for bipartite graphs only, or a RAM approximation algorithm does not establish the displayed statement.
context:
The 2006 page contains two questions: a constant-pass streaming approximation with O(n log n) space, and a linear-time RAM approximation scheme. This card keeps the streaming question as its single target. Editorial convention: space is measured explicitly in bits and weights have polynomially bounded integer encodings, removing an ambiguity in the historical page.

Duan and Pettie resolved the RAM direction with running time \(O(m\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})\) for maximum-weight matching. That algorithm can access and store the graph in ways unavailable to the streaming model. The old RAM question is therefore recorded as solved context rather than repeated as an open demand.

Gamlath, Kale, Mitrović and Svensson obtained arbitrarily accurate weighted matching in a number of passes depending only on accuracy, using memory linear in n up to polylogarithmic factors. This settles the broader constant-pass semi-streaming objective, but the stated space guarantee alone does not supply the exact bit bound retained here.

Huang and Su improve the number of passes to a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). Their Theorem 1.2 states \(O(n\log W\,\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) words, where \(W\) is the weight ratio. Under the present weight encoding this can be \(O_{\varepsilon,c}(n\log^2 n)\) bits. One must account for word size before comparing it with the target.

The 2025 overview distinguishes general weighted graphs from bipartite and unweighted cases and tabulates their different pass-space guarantees. Strong bounds for one of those restrictions cannot be silently substituted for the graph class here.

For weighted matchings, improving the objective can involve both alternating paths and alternating cycles. Retaining enough information to coordinate such improvements while storing only a linear number of words is the specific resource issue in this formulation.
why: The question asks whether near-optimal weighted matchings can be found with memory comparable to the explicit output and a fixed number of scans of a dense graph. It isolates the remaining strict memory requirement from the already established existence of constant-pass algorithms with polylogarithmic overhead.
status_note: The broad historical question is substantially resolved: linear-time RAM approximation and constant-pass near-linear-space streaming algorithms exist. This card explicitly retains the stricter O(n log n)-bit streaming variant with polynomially bounded integer weights. The checked general-graph theorems and 2025 overview do not state that precise memory endpoint; no matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check.
progress: 2006: McGregor poses the streaming approximation and separate RAM-time questions. | 2014: Duan and Pettie give a linear-time approximation scheme in the RAM model. | 2019: Gamlath and coauthors obtain constant-pass weighted approximation with near-linear memory. | 2023: Huang and Su obtain polynomial-in-accuracy pass complexity; Theorem 1.2 records its word-space dependence on the weight ratio. | 2025: Assadi’s journal overview compares the available pass-space tradeoffs for weighted and unweighted matching.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary-order insertion stream of a positively weighted general graph. The algorithm must output a nearly maximum-weight matching after a number of passes independent of graph size. The retained space target is O(n log n) bits with polynomially bounded integer weights. Linear-time RAM approximation and broader constant-pass semi-streaming results are already known. The card distinguishes those achievements from the exact bit-space endpoint it asks to settle.

title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
importance_reason: Breaking the square-root degree barrier for the canonical coloring task would improve a broadly reused distributed primitive.
formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.
why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is deterministic and uniform in both degree and graph size; fast randomized coloring is not a resolution.
progress: 2020: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence. | 2026-01: The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.
working_summary: A proper coloring with Delta plus one colors always exists for a graph of maximum degree Delta. The question asks for a deterministic LOCAL algorithm running in O(\(Delta^{0.499}\) plus log-star n) rounds. The degree exponent deliberately lies just below one half, while the network-size dependence retains the small symmetry-breaking term. Processors must reduce a large identifier-based palette without causing conflicts among adjacent vertices acting simultaneously. Crossing this degree threshold would improve the coordination of dense local neighborhoods without paying a larger dependence on the total number of vertices.

title: Randomized parity sketches versus one-way communication for XOR functions
importance_reason: A broad structural comparison between randomized communication and parity measurements, with consequences for transferring sketching lower bounds to unrestricted one-way protocols.
formal: Are there universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\geq0\) such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{0,1\}\), \[R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\leq C\bigl(1+R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\bigr)\log^a(n+2),\qquad f^+(x,y)=f(x+y)?\] Here the two complexities use worst-input error and shared randomness as defined below. This fixes the polylogarithmic-loss convention in the source’s conjecture.
definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_2\) has elements zero and one, with addition modulo two; vector addition is bitwise XOR. A randomized parity sketch of length \(k\) consists of a jointly sampled matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{k\times n}\) and a decoder \(g\). Their joint distribution is fixed in advance, independently of the input \(z\). The sketch is the \(k\)-bit vector \(Az\); the decoder knows the sampled matrix and all shared coins, and may depend on \(f\) and \(n\). For each fixed \(z\), its probability of outputting \(f(z)\) must be at least \(2/3\). The minimum possible \(k\), including zero, is \(R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\). Each row of \(A\) specifies a subset of input coordinates whose parity is measured. Rows are chosen before seeing any measurement outcome: adaptive parity queries are not allowed. In the communication model Alice knows \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\), Bob knows \(y\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and both know \(f,n\) and a public random string independent of their inputs. Alice sends one message; Bob must output \(f(x+y)\). For every fixed pair \((x,y)\), success probability is at least \(2/3\). The cost is the largest message length over inputs and coin outcomes; variable-length messages can be padded. Its minimum is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\). Local computation, the description of \(f\), and shared randomness are free in both models. No uniform polynomial-time construction of optimal protocols is required. Logarithms are base two. The constants in the proposed inequality are independent of the truth table of \(f\), the dimension and its communication complexity. The additive one handles zero-cost constant functions without imposing a convention for logarithms of zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed inequality with fixed universal constants, or prove its negation: for every proposed constants there is a dimension and Boolean function violating the bound. A superpolylogarithmic separation family suffices for a negative answer. Equality for deterministic protocols, average error under the uniform input distribution, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not settle this target.
context:
The source asks whether randomized linear sketching and randomized one-way communication of the associated XOR function agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The card spells out the usual dimension-based interpretation at error one third; it does not request exact equality of the two integer complexities.

The easy comparison is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\leq R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\): Alice sends \(Ax\), and Bob forms \(Ax+Ay=A(x+y)\) before using the decoder. The question is whether an arbitrary message can always be replaced, with the stated loss, by information of this linear form.

For deterministic exact computation the complexities agree. The randomized case allows a different error set for each choice of coins, so the deterministic statement does not give the desired simulation by simply fixing a seed.

Kannan, Mossel, Sanyal and Yaroslavtsev prove an analogue under uniformly distributed inputs, with an adjustment of the error constant, and analyze several function classes. Worst-input correctness is stronger: a protocol cannot ignore even a very small exceptional set of pairs.

The 2026 turnstile simulation paper concerns streams of integer-coordinate insertions and deletions. Its discussion treats modular and XOR updates as a separate line of work. A simulation for algorithms that already process long streams does not itself convert a single arbitrary Alice-to-Bob message into a parity sketch.
why: A positive result would justify proving lower bounds for arbitrary one-way XOR protocols by analyzing linear summaries, a much more structured class. A separation would identify Boolean information that a short nonlinear message preserves more effectively than nonadaptive random parities.
status_note: The primary CCC 2018 paper leaves the worst-input randomized comparison open. The checked April 2026 simulation is for a different streaming model and does not claim this one-way communication theorem. No matching resolution was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 check; the precise polylogarithmic-loss convention is stated explicitly.
progress: 2017: Yaroslavtsev presents the conjecture at the Banff workshop. | 2018: The CCC paper proves the uniform-distribution comparison and records the general randomized conjecture. | 2026-04-23: Jiang, Liu and Yu give a polynomial-length integer-turnstile simulation and distinguish prior XOR-stream results from that model.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary Boolean function on a binary vector space. A parity sketch measures a fixed random collection of linear forms and then decodes their bits. A one-way protocol may instead send any randomized message about Alice’s vector to Bob. The conjecture asks whether parity sketches lose only a universal polylogarithmic factor for the associated XOR function. Known deterministic and uniform-input comparisons do not establish the required worst-input randomized bound.

title: Wait-free exact FIFO queues in Common\(_{2}\)
importance_reason: A longstanding test of whether consensus power characterizes implementation strength for a fundamental concurrent object. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed number \(n\ge 2\) of asynchronous processes, is there a deterministic wait-free linearizable implementation of an initially empty, unbounded FIFO queue using only atomic read/write registers and atomic Test&Set bits? Every process may perform both Enqueue and Dequeue, repeatedly and in any order. The implementation must satisfy exact FIFO semantics in every execution, including executions with arbitrary delays and crashes. This is the source’s Common\(_{2}\) question; “some objects with consensus number two” is not a free choice of base types that could include the desired queue itself.
definitions: There are n sequential processes with distinct identifiers \(1,\ldots ,n\). Each invokes a new high-level operation only after its previous one returns. The scheduler interleaves atomic shared-memory steps arbitrarily; a process may stop forever at any point. A register stores a finite value and supports atomic Read and Write. A Test&Set object is a bit initially 0 whose atomic operation returns the old bit and sets it to 1; arbitrarily many initially fresh objects and registers are available. Private computation and storage are allowed. No bound on memory growth or on the number of operations in a history is imposed, but every performed step manipulates finitely represented data. No Compare&Swap, stronger atomic multi-object operation, or queue base object is supplied. Sequential queue state is a finite sequence of values from \(\{0,1\}\)*. \(Enqueue(v)\) appends a new occurrence of v and returns an acknowledgement. Dequeue removes and returns the first occurrence if one exists; otherwise it returns a distinguished EMPTY symbol outside the value set and leaves the queue empty. Equal values may be enqueued multiple times, but each enqueue occurrence may be removed only once. Linearizability means that each finite concurrent history can be completed by responses to some pending invocations and deletion of the others, so that its completed operations have a legal sequential FIFO order preserving each process’s order and real-time order: an operation that returns before another is invoked precedes it. Wait-freedom means that any invoked operation whose process continues taking steps returns after finitely many of that process’s own steps, regardless of other processes’ speeds or failures. No promise that another process will take a step is available. The algorithm may depend on the fixed n; the question does not require one implementation for infinitely many simultaneously participating processes. Common\(_{2}\) denotes types implementable for every finite n from registers and two-process-consensus power; the cited model paper states the queue question equivalently using Test&Set. Equal consensus numbers alone do not assert mutual implementability.
answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct such a deterministic implementation for every finite n, or prove impossibility for some finite n in this model. Both exact linearizability and individual wait-free progress are required. A lock-free implementation that permits starvation, a restriction on the number of enqueuers or dequeuers, duplicated removal of an occurrence, weak-empty responses, bounded histories, or a stronger atomic base type does not meet the target. An impossibility result only for strong linearizability does not rule out ordinary linearizability.

title: Deterministic linearizable objects for set agreement
importance_reason: A structural question about whether deterministic linearizable abstractions can express exactly the power of set agreement; relevant to classifications of shared-object coordination power. Existing score retained.
formal: Is it true that, for every pair of integers \(n>k>2\), no deterministic linearizable \((n,k)\)-set agreement object is computationally equivalent to the \((n,k)\)-set agreement task? The quantifier includes every proposal domain I with at least n values and every n-ported object satisfying the definitions below. Equivalence means mutual implementation with atomic read/write registers by deterministic wait-free algorithms. The object may depend on n,k and I, may use the chosen port in determining a response, and may be invoked repeatedly; it is not restricted to one call per port.
definitions: The system consists of asynchronous processes with distinct identities communicating through shared objects and atomic read/write registers. A process can crash by stopping permanently. Algorithms must be correct for every schedule and every pattern of such crashes. Wait freedom means each operation or task invocation of a process that continues taking steps completes after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of the speeds or failures of other processes; no fixed complexity bound is requested. Reductions are deterministic: randomization is not available. The one-shot task \(T(n,k,I)\) has at most n participating processes, each supplying an input in I and deciding once. Every decision is an input supplied by a participant, at most k distinct values are decided, and every participant that continues taking steps must decide. No sequential ordering constraint is added to these task guarantees. An \((n,k)\)-set agreement object O has ports \(1,\ldots ,n\) and an operation \(ProposeSA(v), v\in I\). Each process chooses a port for each call and waits for its response before making another call. Access is well formed if no two pending calls use the same port. Ports are not permanently assigned to process identities; arbitrarily many processes may use the object over its lifetime, but at most n calls may be pending simultaneously. Only well-formed access is required to be implemented. On every such execution, each response is the current call’s proposal or a proposal of a previously invoked call, and across the entire execution at most k distinct values are returned. This agreement bound does not reset after a round or after all processes become idle. All invocations are supported and are wait-free. A finite sequential history S is a sequence of completed triples (port,proposal,response). Determinism requires that for every allowed S, port p and proposal v there is a unique response extending S by a call at p with v; different histories or ports may give different responses. Linearizability requires every concurrent history to admit an ordering of its operations that obeys this sequential specification and preserves real-time precedence: an operation whose response precedes another’s invocation must come first. Incomplete calls may be discarded or assigned responses before ordering them. To implement an object means to produce only its allowed histories, with the required termination, for all well-formed client executions; reproducing every allowed history is unnecessary. O and T are computationally equivalent when copies of O and registers can solve T, and O can be implemented from registers and instances of any correct solver for T. A task instance has n one-shot participant roles; separate instances have independent state, and the implementation must rely only on the task guarantees, not on additional agreement power a particular solver might possess. This is the source’s equivalence to the black-box set agreement task. Any number of fresh instances and registers is allowed; a completed operation uses finitely many steps. The object’s specified initial state is fixed independently of client inputs. O already solves T by one proposal per participant on distinct ports, so the substantive issue is whether a reduction from the task to O can exist.
answer_criterion: Prove that no such object and reverse wait-free implementation exist for every \(n>k>2\), or refute the statement by giving a pair \(n>k>2, a\) proposal domain with at least n values, a deterministic linearizable object and a correct wait-free implementation from the set agreement task and registers. A positive proof need not exhibit a stronger set agreement task: that is an additional conjectured explanation in the source, not a required proof method. Restricting objects to port-independent behavior or proving only some parameter pairs does not establish the universal claim.

Set agreement allows several proposed values to be decided. A linearizable object must additionally behave like an ordered sequence of operations. Computational equivalence asks whether these constraints change implementation power, even though the permitted histories differ.

The 2017 paper gives a linearizable object equivalent to the task, but its sequential specification allows nondeterministic choices. The OPODIS paper gives a deterministic equivalent object whose concurrent behavior is not linearizable. Requiring both properties is the remaining issue.

It also proves the \(n=3\) case for objects whose sequential behavior is independent of the port. These theorems do not cover \(k>2\).

The 2020 journal paper constructs deterministic linearizable objects whose full set agreement power is insufficient to implement them. This demonstrates limitations of classifying objects by agreement tasks, but does not establish the claimed separation for every deterministic linearizable \((n,k)\)-set agreement object.

Each knows n, H, its own distinct identifier and the identifiers of its neighbors; identifiers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, and the guarantee must hold for every valid assignment of identifiers. Local edges have identifiable ports. In each synchronous round a node may send a different message of at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to each neighbor, for a fixed constant B independent of n. Messages are received before the next round, and later messages may depend on everything received so far. No communication is allowed across nonedges. Local computation and memory are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. This is ordinary CONGEST, with distinct messages permitted on distinct edges, not broadcast CONGEST or the congested clique.

The algorithm is a uniform distributed procedure fixed with H; it may use independent private random bits at the nodes. Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. It halts within a worst-case bound \(T_{H}(n)\) on every network, identifier assignment and random tape. The success event concerns the joint vector of all node outputs, with probability over all random bits. In an H-free network all outputs must be NO simultaneously; in a network containing H one YES anywhere suffices. There is no requirement that the detecting node belong to a copy, identify its vertices, list all copies, or notify distant nodes. Disconnected networks are permitted and the same global output convention applies.

The required bound \(n^{o(1)}\) means that one such algorithm exists with \(\log (\max \{2,T_{H}(n)\})/\log  n\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty\). Equivalently, for every fixed \(\delta >0\) its worst-case round bound is at most \(n^{\delta}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants and the threshold length may depend on H and \(\delta\). A family of different algorithms, one for each \(\delta\), is not silently identified with that single-algorithm claim. A bound \(n^{\alpha _{H}}\) with a fixed positive \(\alpha _{H}\), even a very small one, is not subpolynomial. The size of H is a constant, not another growing complexity parameter.

The source also asks whether every 2-connected pattern instead requires a polynomial number of rounds. A theorem giving each fixed H a lower bound \(\Omega (n^{\delta _{H}})\) for some \(\delta _{H}>0\) would refute the existence question, but this stronger growth dichotomy is not assumed to be its logical negation. A negative answer here only needs to exclude the stated \(n^{o(1)}\) algorithms for every eligible H.
answer_criterion: A positive answer provides one fixed eligible H and proves a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm with the stated global success probability and \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case rounds. A negative answer rules out such an algorithm for every fixed eligible H. A lower bound for only one pattern, or a fast algorithm for induced copies, promised-far graphs, listing in another model or a pattern that grows with n, does not settle this existence question.

title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
importance_reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.
focus_reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most \(p(m+n)\) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most \(q(N)\)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.
definitions: A is in \(\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), b in \(\mathbb{Q}^{m}\), and c in \(\mathbb{Q}^{n}\), with \(m,n\ge 1\). All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of \(c^{T} x\) is minus infinity. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.
why: This isolates whether the combinatorial dimensions of a linear program suffice to control its arithmetic complexity. A resolution would clarify the relation between numerical precision, polyhedral structure, and the complexity of one of optimization’s basic models.
status_note: The standard problem remains listed as open, but a direct claimed solution exists in Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision. This card records it without treating it as established: correctness, the iteration bound, and the full strongly polynomial guarantee have not been independently validated in this review. Checked through 10 September 2026.

The question asks whether every rational instance can be solved using a number of arithmetic operations polynomial only in its numbers of variables and constraints.
