title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
importance_reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.
focus_reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.
formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices \(A_{0},A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\in Q^{n\times n}\) for which there exists a real vector \(x\in R^{m}\) satisfying \(A_{0}+\sum _{i=1}^{m} x_{i} A_{i}\succeq 0\)? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size \(n\ge 1\). A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written \(M\succeq 0\), when \(z^{T}Mz\ge 0\) for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real \(n\times n\) matrix Y and impose \(A_{0}+\sum _{i} x_{i} A_{i}=YY^{T}\). These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix \(M(t)\) with rows \((0,1)\) and \((1,t)\) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue \((t- \sqrt{t^{2}+4})/2\) tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks \([[x,2],[2,2x]]\) and \([[2,x],[x,1]]\). The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x\ge \sqrt{2}\), and the second when |\(x|\le \sqrt{2}\). The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at \(x=\sqrt{2}\). All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions \(x_{1}\ge 2\) and \([[x_{i+1},x_{i}],[x_{i},1]]\succeq 0\) force \(x_{i+1}\ge x_{i}^{2}\), hence \(x_{k}\ge 2^{2^{k- 1}}\). A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.

Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.
why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.
progress: 1997: Ramana constructs an exact dual without regularity assumptions and proves simultaneous \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{coNP}\) membership in the Turing model, without proving membership in either class. | 2016-09-21: De Klerk and Vallentin establish Turing-model polynomial approximation complexity for a short-step interior-point method under their stated assumptions. | 2018–2021: Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop symbolic homotopy for degenerate feasible sets. Generic auxiliary choices and objectives remain in their algorithmic analysis; fixed-parameter arithmetic bounds are not a general polynomial bit bound. | 2024-03-08: Pataki and Touzov publish a structural analysis of exponentially large feasible solutions and partial approaches to representing them compactly. | 2025-10-08: Pataki’s preprint gives a combinatorial treatment of Ramana’s exact dual and its feasible set, preserving the unresolved Turing-model complexity distinction. | 2026 — STOC: Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer prove polynomial bit-length bounds for approximate optima of convex polynomial minimization over polyhedra. The result does not cover exact feasibility of arbitrary linear matrix inequalities.
working_summary: A semidefinite feasibility instance asks whether some real assignment makes an affine combination of rational symmetric matrices positive semidefinite. The target is an exact yes-or-no decision in polynomial time in the ordinary bit model. Numerical approximation does not settle this question because an infeasible affine space can approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. Feasible rational inputs can also require irrational or very large witnesses. The challenge is to decide arbitrary degenerate instances efficiently without adding regularity assumptions that make approximation algorithms easier to analyze.

title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
importance_reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.
focus_reason: The packing versus max-flow min-cut conjecture adds a fundamental combinatorial integrality question alongside continuous optimization and numerical computation.
formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
definitions:
A clutter C on a finite ground set E is a family of subsets of E, no one properly containing another. In the original instance all members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover \(T\subseteq E\) meets every member, and \(	au (C)\) is the smallest cover size. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members, with maximum size \(
u (C)\). Deleting e removes e from the ground set and discards all members containing e. Contracting e removes it from the ground set and from every member, and retains only inclusion-minimal resulting members. A minor results from any sequence of these operations. The packing property means \(	au (C' )=
u (C' )\) for every minor \(C'\). For the empty family both values are zero; for a minor containing the empty set both are defined as +∞, with the empty member permitted arbitrarily many times in a packing. For \(w\in \mathbb{Z} _{\ge 0}^{E}\), let \(	au _{w}(C)=\min\){\(\sum_{e\in T}w_{e}:T\) covers C}. Let \(
u _{w}(C)\) be the maximum of \(\sum_{F\in C}y_{F}\) over nonnegative integers \(y_{F}\) satisfying \(\Sigma\)_{F∋e}\(y_{F}\le w_{e}\) for every \(e\in E\). Thus a weighted packing may use a member repeatedly, subject to capacities w. The max-flow min-cut property is \(	au _{w}(C)=
u _{w}(C)\) for every such w. The original nonempty-member assumption makes these weighted optima finite.
answer_criterion: Prove that the packing property implies \(\tau _{w}=\nu _{w}\) for every finite clutter and every nonnegative integer weight vector, or give a finite clutter and weight vector with the packing property and \(\tau _{w}>\nu _{w}\). A counterexample must verify equality for all minors, not merely for the original unweighted clutter. Finite searches, proofs for a proper subclass, or fractional optimality alone do not resolve the universal statement.
context:
Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

If A is the member-by-element incidence matrix, the associated linear programs are \(\min  w^{T}x\) subject to \(Ax\ge 1\) and \(x\ge 0\), and \(\max  1^{T}y\) subject to \(A^{T}y\le w\) and \(y\ge 0\). Equality of the two integer optima forces their values to agree with the fractional optimum by weak and strong duality. This is the standard MFMC integrality requirement.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.
why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.
status_note: No general resolution was found through 11 September 2026. The checked July 2026 manuscript explicitly retains the conjecture. Its reported finite computations and subclass results are recorded as progress; their proof artifacts were not independently rechecked in this editorial review.
progress: 2003: Schrijver lists the packing-to-Mengerian implication as Survey Question 68. | 2026-07-09: Abdi–Schwarcz v2 reports finite verification through ten ground-set elements and an improved finite-weight test, while leaving the universal conjecture open.

title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
importance_reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.
focus_reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_{c}\) with the following guarantee? Given \(n\ge 2, a\) nonsingular rational \(n\times n\) matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer \(1\le p\le c\cdot \operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||\(A\hat\{x\}- b||_{2}\le 2^{- p}||b||_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most \(c\cdot \operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) binary digits, and the spectral condition number \(\kappa _{2}(A)\) is promised at most \(n^{c}\). The worst-case running time must be \(O_{c}(m \log ^{d_{c}}n)\) for some constant \(d_{c}\) independent of the input.
definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence \(n\le m\le n^{2}\). The Euclidean norm is ||\(v||_{2}=(\sum_{i} v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\), and \(\kappa _{2}(A)=\sigma _{\mathrm{max}}(A)/\sigma _{\mathrm{min}}(A)\), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Solving \(Ax=b\) is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all \(n^{2}\) matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If \(x*=A^{-1}b\), the elementary inequality ||\(\hat\{x\}- x*||_{2}/||x*||_{2}\le \kappa _{2}(A)\cdot ||A\hat\{x\}- b||_{2}/||b||_{2}\) relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, \(A=diag(1,\delta ), b=(1,\delta )\) and \(\hat\{x\}=(1,0)\) have residual \(\delta\) while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m^{(\omega - 2)/(\omega - 1)}n^{2})\) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For \(m=\widetilde{O} (n)\), this becomes \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{(3\omega - 4)/(\omega - 1)})\). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of \(\omega\). Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular \(n\times n\) input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.
why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. This is an editorial, fully specified near-linear target in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime, not a named positive conjecture. The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.
progress: 2004–2014: Spielman and Teng develop nearly linear algorithms for graph-structured and symmetric diagonally dominant systems; the expanded solver paper appears in SIAM J. Matrix Analysis and Applications in 2014. | 2020–2021: Peng and Vempala give a finite-precision general sparse-system algorithm faster than matrix multiplication; the July 2020 preprint is presented at SODA 2021. | 2021–2022: Nie strengthens matrix anti-concentration and improves the block Krylov solver. The November 2021 preprint, revised in December, appears at STOC 2022. | 2022-06-28: Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang publish a sparsity-preserving reduction from general equations to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes. | 2026-08-21: The Simons workshop report is revised to reflect status through 20 August, retaining questions about extending scalable solvers and understanding finite-precision iterative methods. It does not give a universal nearly linear algorithm.
working_summary: A sparse linear system stores only the nonzero entries of its coefficient matrix, making matrix-vector multiplication relatively cheap. The question asks whether solving every well-conditioned rational system approximately can take nearly linear time in that sparse input size. The saved formulation bounds coefficient lengths, conditioning, and requested residual accuracy to avoid hiding excessive numerical costs. It seeks an explicit solution vector with high enough success probability from a randomized classical algorithm. Such a result would extend the efficiency of structured Laplacian solvers to general sparse matrices, where sparsity alone currently provides much less algorithmic structure.

title: Smale’s seventh problem
importance_reason: Smale's seventh problem asks for efficient construction of globally near-optimal configurations.
focus_reason: Smale's seventh problem asks for efficient construction of globally near-optimal configurations.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.
context:
Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance \(C\ln N\) is an additive error in the total energy. The minimum has leading terms \(E_N^{\ast}=(1/2-\ln2)N^2-(N/2)\ln N+O(N)\). An approximation that only matches these leading terms may still have error proportional to \(N\), much larger than the requested logarithmic excess.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an \(O(\sqrt{N} \ln  N)\) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least \(1- \exp (- N \ln  N)\). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the \(\sqrt{N}\) scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?
why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No general deterministic polynomial-time construction with logarithmic total-energy excess was located. The March 2026 finite-cardinality classification and existing distributional energy guarantees do not establish the uniform algorithmic target. This source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.
progress: 1998: Smale specifies polynomial time in N in the real-number model and universal logarithmic excess energy. | 2018: The low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution attains logarithmic excess in expectation and with high probability; efficient generation is a separate issue. | 2022 / 2023: The generalized Diamond ensemble covers every N with an explicit asymptotic expected-energy estimate. | 2023 / 2024: A central limit theorem identifies \(\sqrt{N}\) energy fluctuations for random polynomial zeros. | 2026-03-22: Revised algebraic classification handles at most six points in all dimensions and a restricted seven-point case.
working_summary: Smale's seventh problem concerns placing N points on the unit sphere so that their logarithmic interaction energy is nearly minimal. The target is an algorithm running in time polynomial in N. Its output energy may exceed the global minimum by only a universal constant times log N. This is an additive energy guarantee, which requires more precise control than merely producing visually well-distributed points. A construction with a rigorous bound would connect efficient computation with the equilibrium behavior of many mutually repelling particles on a curved surface.

title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program \(\max \{c^{T}x: Ax=b, x\ge 0\}\) with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis \(B_{0}\), the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and \(B_{0}\), and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
definitions:
A has m rows and n columns with \(1\le m\le n\); all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible \(A_{B}\). Its basic solution is \(x_{B}=A_{B}^{-1}b\) and \(x_{j}=0\) for \(j
otin B\), and feasibility means \(x_{B}\ge 0\). An entering column \(j
otin B\) must have reduced cost \(r_{j}=c_{j}- c_{B}^{T}A_{B}^{-1}A_{j}>0\). Put \(a=A_{B}^{-1}A_{j}\). Choose a leaving basic index i attaining \(	heta =\min _{k\in B:a_{k}>0}x_{k}/a_{k}\), and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; \(	heta =0\) is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to \(p(\mathrm{L})\). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from \(B_{0}\): it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition \(r_{j}\le 0\) for all \(j
otin B\) certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
context:
Linear programming already has algorithms with polynomial bit complexity, including ellipsoid and interior-point methods. The unresolved question is whether the same guarantee can be achieved while moving through bases by the simplex method. A pivot rule determines which improving direction to expose next and how to break ties. The STACS 2026 paper on ranking-based rules states that the general question remains open.

There are two obstacles to a polynomial guarantee. First, a short route to an optimal basis must exist under the permitted improving moves. Second, the rule must discover such a route efficiently. Knowing the optimum from another computation does not authorize skipping the route: every intervening basis exchange is still required. Likewise, a short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short path along improving edges.

The bit-complexity requirement is deliberately weaker than strongly polynomial simplex. It permits the running time to depend polynomially on the number of bits in coefficients. A strongly polynomial rule would instead bound its arithmetic work polynomially in m and n, together with appropriate bounds on the sizes of numbers used. Therefore this card does not assert that a positive answer alone settles Smale’s strongly polynomial LP problem or a diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy means several bases can describe the same vertex. A legal pivot with \(\theta =0\) changes the basis without improving the objective value, so an algorithm can stall even if the geometric route is short. Kukharenko and Sanità’s March 2026 paper bounds a block of consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n- m- 1\), given an improving feasible direction. Such a direction can be obtained using an LP solver. This controls local stalling, but does not bound how many different nonoptimal vertices the method must visit.

Positive average-case results are also substantial. Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm under random perturbations of the input. Smoothed analysis studies the expected behavior around an arbitrary instance as a function of perturbation size. It helps explain good practical performance, but does not give a deterministic worst-case guarantee on every exact rational instance.

The 2026 ranking-based lower bounds exclude broader families than a single greedy rule. One result covers index-ranking rules with a specified limit on their memory states; another covers memoryless rules using rankings by index, reduced cost and objective improvement. Full access to numerical data and unrestricted polynomially bounded history are allowed in this card, so those lower bounds do not cover every candidate.

A striking neighboring result does exclude every pivot rule for the active-set method with a nonlinear objective. Disser and Mosis first use higher-degree polynomial objectives on the hypercube. Bach and coauthors then obtain the phenomenon for maximizing a convex quadratic function, published at SODA 2026. The direction of optimization matters: this is convex maximization. Their construction does not have a linear objective, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a general simplex lower bound.
why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The STACS 2026 and March 2026 primary publications retain the general polynomial simplex question as open. This card fixes deterministic total bit complexity for legal improving primal-simplex pivots from any supplied feasible basis on a finite-optimum rational LP. Strongly polynomial algorithms, nonlinear active-set bounds and distributional performance are distinct formulations.
progress: 2004: Spielman and Teng establish polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm; this is a distributional guarantee rather than worst-case polynomial bit complexity. | 2025: Disser and Mosis give an unconditional active-set lower bound using a nonlinear polynomial objective on a hypercube; the linear-objective question remains open. | 2026 — SODA: Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen the all-rules active-set lower bound to convex quadratic maximization. The latest preprint version is dated 22 October 2025. | 2026-02-25: Disser, Loho, Maat and Mosis publish superpolynomial lower bounds for specified ranking-based classes, with explicit information and memory restrictions. | 2026-03-23: Kukharenko and Sanità publish an antistalling rule bounding consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n- m- 1\), given an improving feasible direction. It leaves the global pivot count open.
working_summary: The simplex method solves a linear program by moving between feasible bases through legal pivots. This question asks for a deterministic pivot algorithm whose total bit complexity is polynomial for every rational input and supplied feasible starting basis. Finding the optimum by another method does not suffice unless the required sequence of pivots can also be followed efficiently. Degenerate pivots complicate progress because they may change the basis without changing the objective value. A positive answer would provide a worst-case polynomial guarantee for simplex itself, without automatically establishing the stronger arithmetic bound of strongly polynomial linear programming.

title: Komlós conjecture
importance_reason: A defining vector-balancing conjecture with consequences for rounding, approximation and the geometry of linear constraints.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for all integers \(m,n\ge 1\) and every real matrix \(A\in \mathbb{R} ^{m\times n}\) with \(\sum _{i=1}^{m} A_{ij}^{2}\le 1\) for each column j, there is a vector \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\) satisfying \(\max _{1\le i\le m}|\sum _{j=1}^{n} A_{ij}x_{j}|\le C\)?
definitions: All matrices are finite. Columns may have arbitrary real entries, including negative entries. The sign vector may depend on the entire matrix; C may not depend on the dimensions or entries. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic or input-encoding requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Discrepancy measures how accurately a fractional choice can be replaced by signs while controlling many linear constraints simultaneously. Komlós asks whether normalizing every column in Euclidean norm suffices to bound every coordinate of the signed sum by an absolute constant.

The 2025 improvement gives a polylogarithmic bound smaller than the classical square-root-logarithmic bound, but does not reach a constant. Komlós implies the Beck–Fiala conjecture after scaling an incidence matrix; the converse is not known. Both are retained as established landmarks with different hypotheses, rather than as unrelated questions.
why: A defining vector-balancing conjecture with consequences for rounding, approximation and the geometry of linear constraints.
status_note: Open target supported by the dated sources. Literature was checked on 11 September 2026, with the limits recorded here; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The companion Beck–Fiala target is a documented consequence, not a duplicate. No algorithmic construction requirement is added.
progress: 2025: The authors improve the general Komlós upper bound to roughly a fourth power of log n, with additional logarithmic factors; a universal constant is not obtained.

title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
importance_reason: A longstanding general optimization question with a strong total-search interpretation and continuing work on both structural and algorithmic restrictions. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity, distinct from strong polynomiality of LP and exact SDP feasibility.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given \(n\ge 1, a\) rational P-matrix \(M\in Q^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in Q^{n}\), outputs rational vectors \(z,w\ge 0\) satisfying \(w=Mz+q\) and \(z^{T}w=0\)?
definitions: A principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) uses the same nonempty index set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}\) for rows and columns. M is a P-matrix when \(\det  M[S,S]>0\) for every such S. All matrix and vector entries are explicitly listed as binary signed numerators and positive denominators; N denotes their total bit length including dimensions and separators. The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine whose running time, including output, is at most one polynomial \(p(N)\) independent of n and the entries. It must terminate within that bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs, but its output is required to satisfy the equations only when M is a P-matrix. No P-matrix recognition or certificate is supplied or required. Inequalities are coordinatewise, and \(z^{T}w=\sum_{i} z_{i} w_{i}\). There is no symmetry, positive-definiteness, sparsity, nondegeneracy or coefficient-size promise beyond rational encoding and the P-matrix condition. A numerical approximation alone is not an output solution.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
Complementarity combines linear constraints with a discrete choice: in each coordinate, at least one of \(z_{i}\) and \(w_{i}\) must vanish. For example, when M is the identity, a negative entry of q is compensated by a positive z entry, while a positive q entry remains in w. For a general matrix the coordinates interact, so the zero pattern cannot be chosen independently.

The P-matrix condition guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side q. This removes failure of existence and ambiguity of the answer, yet does not supply a polynomial-time method to find that answer. The distinction is a central example of total search: a mathematical existence theorem can be much easier to state than a fast algorithmic realization.

Exact rational output is meaningful in the bit model. Once a complementary zero pattern is fixed, the remaining coordinates satisfy a nonsingular rational linear system on a principal submatrix. Determinant bounds give polynomial bit length for the solution. Thus the question does not hide an unavoidable exponentially long output.

Several matrix subclasses admit polynomial algorithms. Results for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrices demonstrate how additional structure can make the problem tractable. Such restrictions are absent from this card. Likewise, a polynomial iteration count involving a condition-dependent parameter does not give a polynomial bound in the full input length without a bound on that parameter.

ETH’s 2025 research report identifies general P-matrix LCP as a major unresolved optimization question and relates it to unique-sink orientations. The current target concerns solving rational LCP instances, not recognizing the P-matrix promise and not solving every abstract orientation problem. It complements the existing cards for linear programming and exact semidefinite feasibility.
why: Test whether uniqueness and complementary linear structure suffice for polynomial-time exact solution of a central optimization search problem.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. The general rational P-matrix problem remains listed as open in the latest checked institutional research report; subclass results do not settle it.
progress: 1972: The P-matrix condition characterizes uniqueness of the LCP solution for every right-hand side. | 2011–2013: Polynomial algorithms are established for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrix restrictions. | 2025: ETH’s research report still lists general P-matrix LCP in polynomial time as unresolved.

title: Beck–Fiala conjecture
importance_reason: A central discrepancy conjecture governing how local incidence restrictions control global rounding error.
formal: Is there a universal \(C>0\) such that, for all integers \(m,n,t\ge 1\) and every \(A\in \{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) having at most t ones in each column, some \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\) satisfies \(\max _{i} |\sum _{j} A_{ij}x_{j}|\le C\sqrt{t}\)?
definitions: The matrix is the incidence matrix of a finite set system: its columns are elements and its rows are sets. Thus each element belongs to at most t sets. Empty sets and unused elements are allowed. The bound is independent of the number of elements and sets. The question asks for existence of a signing, without an algorithmic time requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Bounded element frequency is a basic sparsity assumption in rounding problems. The conjecture asks whether its discrepancy cost is proportional to the square root of the frequency even when the system is arbitrarily large.

Recent results prove this scale for substantial ranges of t relative to the size of the system. The full statement includes all frequencies and remains stronger than those range-restricted results. The separate Komlós conjecture implies this statement by rescaling each incidence column.
why: A central discrepancy conjecture governing how local incidence restrictions control global rounding error.
status_note: Open target supported by the dated sources. Literature was checked on 11 September 2026, with the limits recorded here; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. TCS-5224 concerned a particular route to a known range of Beck–Fiala, not the full conjecture admitted here.
progress: 2025: The square-root bound is established in the paper for a high-frequency range, not uniformly for every t. | 2026: A July 2026 preprint further extends the covered sparsity range. Its lower threshold still leaves the unrestricted conjecture open.

title: Single-exponential dependence on dimension for integer programming
importance_reason: Close the central dimension-dependence gap in a general-purpose optimization primitive used throughout parameterized algorithms.
formal: Do constants \(C,c>0\) and a deterministic algorithm exist that decide whether \(Ax\le b\) has an integer solution \(x\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\) in at most \(2^{Cn}(\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) bit operations, for every rational matrix A and vector b?
definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A has m rows and n columns, both dimensions are part of the input, and the system need not be bounded. No limit on coefficient size, number of constraints or lattice width is promised. This target concerns feasibility.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Integer programming is polynomial-time solvable in every fixed dimension, but the dependence on dimension determines how far that tractability extends. The single-exponential target would make the geometric dimension cost comparable to exhaustive search over a constant-size choice per variable.

The 2025 survey records the Reis–Rothvoss bound \((\log  n)^{O(n)}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L})\) and explicitly identifies \(2^{O(n)}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L})\) as open. Here n is the number of integer variables, not the coefficient bit length. The question applies to unrestricted systems rather than one block-structured subclass.
why: Close the central dimension-dependence gap in a general-purpose optimization primitive used throughout parameterized algorithms.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2025: The survey reports \((\log  n)^{O(n)}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L})\) and distinguishes the unresolved single-exponential bound.

title: Superpolynomial semidefinite extension complexity of perfect matching
importance_reason: Identify a fundamental limitation of exact semidefinite optimization representations.
formal: For every \(C,c>0\), does some even \(n\ge 2\) satisfy \(xc_{\mathrm{SDP}}(\mathrm{P}_{n})>Cn^{c}\), where \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is the perfect-matching polytope of \(K_{n}\)?
definitions: \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\subseteq \mathbb{R}\)^(n choose 2) is the convex hull of the zero-one incidence vectors of all perfect matchings of the complete graph on n labeled vertices. A size-r semidefinite lift is an affine subspace L of the real symmetric \(r\times r\) matrices and an affine map \(\pi\) into \(\mathbb{R}\)^(n choose 2) such that \(\mathrm{P}_{n}=\pi (\mathrm{L}\cap S_{+}^{r})\), where \(S_{+}^{r}\) consists of positive semidefinite matrices. \(xc_{\mathrm{SDP}}\) is the smallest such integer r. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers and need not be efficiently generated. The representation is exact; approximate relaxations and linear lifts are different notions.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Perfect matching can be optimized in polynomial time, yet exact linear descriptions in higher-dimensional spaces can require exponentially many inequalities. The question asks whether positive semidefinite constraints also suffer a superpolynomial representation barrier.

A linear extension-complexity lower bound is not a semidefinite one. Allowing an arbitrary affine slice of a positive semidefinite cone makes the model substantially stronger. A lower bound here would separate efficient optimization from compact exact SDP representation for a canonical tractable polytope.
why: Identify a fundamental limitation of exact semidefinite optimization representations.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2018: The source distinguishes the known linear extension lower bound from the open semidefinite target.

title: Woodall’s conjecture
importance_reason: A longstanding min–max conjecture in combinatorial optimization, singled out in Schrijver’s survey and the focus of recent approximation and integrality research. The direct packing/covering and algorithmic connections justify inclusion within optimization.
formal: For every finite weakly connected loopless directed multigraph D that is not strongly connected, let \(\tau (D)\) be the minimum size of a directed cut. Must D contain \(\tau (D)\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins?
definitions:
A directed multigraph has a finite vertex set V and a finite set A of individually distinguished arcs; parallel arcs are allowed and loops are excluded. Weak connectivity means connectivity after forgetting arc directions. Strong connectivity means that every ordered pair of vertices is joined by a directed path. For \(\varnothing 
e U\subsetneq V\), let \(\delta ^{+}(U)\) be the arcs with tail in U and head outside U, and \(\delta ^{-}(U)\) the arcs entering U. A directed cut, or dicut, is \(\delta ^{+}(U)\) with \(\delta ^{-}(U)=\varnothing\). Under the stated graph assumptions the family of dicuts is nonempty and each dicut has positive size, so \(	au (D)=\min \{|\delta ^{+}(U)|:\varnothing 
e U\subsetneq V, \delta ^{-}(U)=\varnothing\}\) is a finite positive integer. A dijoin is a subset \(J\subseteq A\) meeting every dicut. Pairwise arc-disjoint means \(J_{i}\cap J_{j}=\varnothing\) for \(i
e j\). Every arc has unit capacity; no zero-capacity arcs or other weights are included.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(\tau (D)\) pairwise disjoint dijoins for every stated D, or give a finite D satisfying the assumptions and prove that its maximum packing is smaller than \(\tau (D)\). Since each dijoin must meet a smallest dicut, \(\tau (D)\) is always an upper bound. An approximation by a constant fraction of \(\tau , a\) fractional packing, or a theorem confined to a proper graph subclass is partial progress.
context:
A dijoin selects arcs that collectively intercept every one-way boundary of a digraph. Packing dijoins asks how many separate selections can provide this complete coverage without sharing an arc. The smallest one-way boundary is an immediate bottleneck. Woodall’s conjecture says that this visible bottleneck is the only obstruction.

Schrijver lists this exact min–max equality as Survey Question 34. The adjacent Question 33 asks for a polynomial-time algorithm finding a maximum packing. The equality is the structural target here; no efficient construction is demanded as part of a positive answer.

The absence of weights matters. The stronger Edmonds–Giles statement permits arcs of capacity zero as well as one and is false. Deleting a zero-capacity arc can change which sets are dicuts, so it cannot generally turn a weighted counterexample into an unweighted one. The current formulation avoids that false strengthening.

Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi prove that at least \(\lfloor \tau /6\rfloor\) disjoint dijoins can be constructed in polynomial time. Their argument connects dijoin packing to nowhere-zero flows in the underlying undirected graph. This supplies a constant-factor guarantee while retaining the exact Woodall equality as open.

Weakly disconnected graphs have a zero-size cut and give a trivial zero-packing case. Strongly connected graphs have no dicuts, making the empty set a vacuous dijoin. Restricting the statement to the nontrivial case fixes the meaning of the minimum and maximum without changing the substantive conjecture.

This belongs to combinatorial optimization through the relation between packing and covering, integrality and constructive approximation. It is distinct from a minimum-cost dijoin problem or from maximum directed cut: those optimize different objects, even though some of the vocabulary overlaps.
why: Determine whether the minimum directed-cut capacity exactly characterizes the number of independently usable directed-cut covers, extending the reach of integral packing–covering duality.
status_note: The unweighted general conjecture remains open in the primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The false weighted Edmonds–Giles conjecture is a different statement. The checked 2025 constant-factor packing theorem does not imply equality.
progress: 2003: Schrijver’s survey lists the exact dijoin-packing equality as Question 34. | 2025-06-02: The Combinatorica paper proves a polynomial-time \(\lfloor \tau /6\rfloor\) packing guarantee and retains the exact conjecture.

title: Log-squared query complexity for fixed-dimensional Tarski
importance_reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.
formal: Let \(Q(n,k)\) be the minimum worst-case number of adaptive deterministic value queries needed to find any fixed point of an unknown monotone function $f:[n]^k\to[n]^k$, where \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and monotonicity is with respect to coordinatewise order. A query at x reveals the entire vector \(f(x)\). Is it true that for every integer \(k\ge 1\) there is a constant \(C_{k}\) such that $Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2$ for every \(n\ge 2\)? Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. Constants may depend on k but not on n or f. This asks for an exponent independent of the fixed dimension, not a polynomial bound on \(C_{k}\).
definitions: For x,y in the grid, \(x\le y\) means \(x_{i}\le y_{i}\) for every coordinate i. The oracle is promised to satisfy \(x\le y\) implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). A valid output is any x with \(f(x)=x\); no minimum or maximum fixed point is required. An adaptive query procedure can choose each query using all earlier queries and answers, and must terminate correctly for every promised oracle. Equivalently, \(Q(n,k)\) is the minimum depth of a finite deterministic oracle decision tree whose leaves output valid fixed points for every monotone function consistent with that leaf. Neither a circuit description nor the table of f is part of the input. Query cost is one per returned vector, and places no restriction on the bit complexity of choosing the next query. The finite product grid is a complete lattice, so a fixed point always exists.
answer_criterion: Prove the bound for every fixed k, or show that there is a fixed k for which \(Q(n,k)/(1+\log _{2} n)^{2}\) is unbounded as n grows. A growing factor depending only on k is permitted. A bound whose logarithmic exponent grows with k does not answer yes. A lower bound obtained only by letting k grow with n does not answer no unless it implies failure at some fixed k.
context:
Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have \(Theta(\log ^{2} n)\) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is \(O(\log ^{\operatorname{ceil}((k-1)/3)+1} n)\) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form \(f(k) \log ^{2} n\), which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.
why: This probes the information cost of finding a guaranteed fixed point under monotonicity, a basic organizing principle in algorithms, semantics, and equilibrium computation. The same sharp bound in dimensions two, three, and four makes the dependence on dimension a substantive structural mystery rather than just a loose analysis of one algorithm.
status_note: The broad 2022 question has substantial later progress: dimension four is settled by the 2026 preprint. The displayed all-fixed-dimensions target is explicitly discussed as open in that paper’s conclusion. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution.
progress: 2020: Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein, and Yannakakis prove an \(Omega(\log ^{2} n)\) lower bound already in two dimensions, including for randomized algorithms; the 2022 seminar records this starting point. | 2021 / 2022 journal: Fearnley, Pálvölgyi, and Savani give an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-query algorithm in three dimensions, matching the two-dimensional lower bound. | 2025-07-13: Brânzei, Phillips, and Recker prove randomized query lower bound \(Omega(k \log ^{2} n / \log  k)\) for \(n,k\ge 2\). For fixed k this remains quadratic in log n, so it does not rule out the card’s target. | 2026-03-31: Chen, Li, and Yannakakis obtain \(O(\log ^{2} n)\) queries in four dimensions and improve the exponent in every fixed dimension. Section 9 proposes the possibility of a generic dimension-dependent constant times \(\log ^{2} n\).
working_summary: A monotone function on a finite multidimensional grid is guaranteed to have a fixed point. The project asks whether one can find any such point using only a squared-logarithmic number of value queries in the grid side length. The dimension is fixed, and the multiplicative constant may depend arbitrarily on it. Incomparable grid points complicate the interval-discarding ideas that make one-dimensional search efficient. A positive answer would show that higher fixed dimensions need not increase the logarithmic query exponent, independently of the computation performed between queries.

title: Constant-factor entrywise \(\ell_1\) rank-\(k\) approximation with variable \(k\)
importance_reason: Determine whether robust low-rank compression remains computationally tractable with unrestricted target rank.
formal: Do a uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm \(A\) and an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) exist such that, for every rational matrix \(M\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and input integer \(0\le k\le\min(m,n)\), \(A\) returns rational factors \(U\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb{Q}^{k\times n}\) satisfying \[\|M-UV\|_1\le C\operatorname{OPT}_k(M),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(M)=\min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}}\|M-B\|_1,\] with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input?
definitions: \(m,n\ge 1\); dimensions, k and each signed rational numerator and positive denominator are explicitly encoded in binary. The input length L counts the whole dense matrix description. \(\|W\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|W_{ij}|\) is the entrywise norm; rank is matrix rank over \(\mathbb{R}\). The optimum is over all real \(m\times n\) matrices of rank at most k and is attained, since a minimizing sequence can be confined to a bounded closed sublevel set. The output consists of binary rational entries of U and V; for \(k=0\) their product denotes the zero matrix. There is a single polynomial P such that A halts within \(P(L)\) Turing-machine steps on every input and every random tape, including the time to write its factors. Therefore the factors have polynomial total encoded length; no unit-cost exact real arithmetic or implicit algebraic-number oracle is available. The approximation factor C and polynomial exponent are independent of m,n,k and entry magnitudes. The probability is over independent fair algorithm coins for each fixed input. Only the displayed multiplicative error is allowed. In particular, when \(\operatorname{rank}(M)\le k\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k}(M)=0\), success requires exact equality \(UV=M\). When the optimum is positive the output need not be an exact real minimizer: the task asks for rational factors meeting the constant-factor inequality. This is the explicit rational bit-model completion of the imported approximation question, not a claim that optimal real factors are rational or efficiently computable.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such an algorithm and absolute factor exist with the stated uniform bit bounds, or a Lean proof of their nonexistence. A factor depending on the rank, a polynomial exponent depending on the rank, output rank above the requested rank, or uncharged exact-real computation does not meet this criterion.
context:
Entrywise absolute error is a standard robust alternative to squared reconstruction error. Exact rank control and a constant independent of k distinguish the target from bicriteria or rank-dependent guarantees.

The existing TCS-7008 asks for a near-optimal relative approximation and does not resolve the weaker but separately significant constant-factor tractability threshold with growing rank. Known fixed-k schemes permit a polynomial exponent depending on k and therefore do not meet this target.
why: Determine whether robust low-rank compression remains computationally tractable with unrestricted target rank.
status_note: Source-backed variable-rank p=1 question. Checked the 2021 full version and the 2026 fixed-rank, even-p abstract; neither resolves this target. The bounded later-work review through 13 September 2026 is not exhaustive.
progress: 2019: The source gives a relative approximation scheme whose dependence on rank does not meet a polynomial bound jointly in the input and k. | 2026-04-27: The later paper gives a PTAS for fixed rank and even \(p>2\); its abstract does not give the variable-rank \(p=1\) guarantee asked for here.
working_summary: The task compresses a rational matrix while measuring error by the sum of absolute entrywise differences. The output must have rank at most the supplied rank and approximate the best real matrix of that rank. Both the approximation factor and polynomial-time exponent must remain independent of the rank. Known fixed-rank approximation schemes do not meet this joint polynomial-time requirement. The question asks whether an absolute constant-factor guarantee is possible with explicit rational output.

title: Input-sparsity relative spectral low-rank approximation
importance_reason: A central runtime frontier in randomized numerical linear algebra, separating worst-direction compression guarantees from aggregate-error guarantees for arbitrary sparse matrices.
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm and absolute constants \(C,b>0\) that, for every real \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), integer \(1\leq k<n\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), returns \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) with orthonormal columns such that \[\|A-ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\|_2\leq(1+\varepsilon)\min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq k}\|A-B\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C\operatorname{nnz}(A)+Cn(k/\varepsilon)^b\) operations?
definitions: The matrix is given as a list of its nonzero entries, each with its row index, column index and real value; unspecified entries are zero and index pairs do not repeat. The integer \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) is the length of this list. The spectral norm is \(\|D\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Dx\|_2\). For singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n(A)\geq0\), the optimum on the right is \(\sigma_{k+1}(A)\). Orthonormality means \(Z^{\mathsf T}Z=I_k\), so \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) is an orthogonal projection of rank \(k\). The output is the explicit matrix \(Z\); forming the generally dense product \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\) is not required. All real input matrices are included, with no gap, conditioning, spectral-decay, positivity or distributional promise. If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq k\), the required residual is exactly zero on a successful run. The selected arithmetic model is a uniform real RAM with unit-cost addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root of a nonnegative value, real comparison, and indexed memory access. Registers store exact reals or integer indices; integer indexing arithmetic is charged, and no real-to-integer floor or bit extraction is a free primitive. Independent fair random bits and independent standard normal real samples are available at unit cost. This explicitly adopts the ideal arithmetic and sampling convention used in randomized numerical linear algebra; bit complexity is not the target. The operation bound includes reading the input, all preprocessing, random sampling and writing the output, and must hold on every random run. Only correctness may fail with probability at most one third, separately for each fixed input. A single algorithm and the same constants work for all parameters; \(n\geq2\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of its probability guarantee and stated arithmetic running time, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The coefficient of the nonzero-entry term must be an absolute constant: multiplying that term by k, inverse accuracy or logarithms of n misses the target. Frobenius-norm error, additive spectral error, extra output rank, or a bound conditional on a singular-value gap does not establish the displayed claim.
context:
Woodruff’s Open Question 1 asks whether the input-sparsity bound for relative Frobenius approximation can also give the relative spectral projection guarantee in Equation (65). The card makes the arithmetic model, success probability and output representation explicit; it retains the square-matrix target.

The Frobenius norm sums squared errors over all entries, whereas the spectral norm controls the largest error in a unit direction. A relative Frobenius guarantee therefore need not provide a relative spectral guarantee when many small singular values contribute to the total tail energy.

The survey presents a spectral approximation based on repeated matrix products, but its dependence on repeated passes and the target rank does not have the requested additive input-sparsity form. Its Frobenius result already achieves that form.

Bakshi, Bhattacharyya, Kannan, Woodruff and Zhou’s 2021 latent-simplex algorithm obtains input-sparsity time under a spectral-mass assumption. Their paper connects removal of that assumption to a breakthrough for spectral low-rank approximation, rather than claiming to solve the unrestricted matrix problem.

A bound of the form input size plus a polynomial in rank and accuracy times n matters especially when a large sparse matrix can be read once but cannot cheaply be multiplied by many vectors. The additive second term also accommodates the n-by-k output. No explicit n-by-n projection is requested.
why: Relative spectral approximation protects every direction of a compressed linear operator, making it useful where a small average error is insufficient. Resolving the question would determine whether this stronger guarantee can share the basic input-reading cost of fast Frobenius approximation, without rank or accuracy multiplying the sparse-data term.
status_note: Open in Woodruff’s 2014 survey and explicitly connected to an algorithmic frontier by the checked 2021 work. A bounded primary-source search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a resolution for arbitrary matrices with the stated strict running time; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.
progress: 2014: Woodruff poses the additive input-sparsity spectral approximation question in the survey’s concluding open problems. | 2021: The latent-simplex result establishes a related fast algorithm under additional spectral structure and explains its connection to the unrestricted low-rank question.
