working_summary: Spectral low-rank approximation seeks a rank-k representation whose largest directional error is near the best possible. The source asks for a relative-error guarantee in time equal to reading the nonzero matrix entries plus a term linear in n and polynomial in k over epsilon. That speed is available in the cited comparison for Frobenius error, which aggregates squared errors instead of controlling the worst direction. The spectral target is therefore substantially stronger. A solution would make sparse-matrix compression fast while protecting against a large error concentrated in one singular direction.

title: Superlinear randomized query lower bounds for submodular minimization
importance_reason: A fundamental information lower-bound gap for general submodular minimization, separating randomization from the first known superlinear deterministic obstruction.
formal: Let \(R(n)\) be the minimum worst-case number of value-oracle queries needed by a randomized algorithm to find an exact minimizer of every real-valued submodular function on \(n\) elements, with success probability at least \(2/3\). Is \(R(n)=\omega(n)\), meaning \(R(n)/n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
question_excerpt: We leave proving a super-linear lower bound on the query complexity of randomized algorithms for SFM as an open question.
definitions: The ground set is \([n]\), and a function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if \(F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B)\) for all subsets \(A,B\). No monotonicity, nonnegativity, symmetry or normalization is promised. A query specifies any subset \(S\) and receives its exact real value \(F(S)\). The algorithm may adapt later queries to all previous values and its own random choices. Its final answer is a subset \(S_*\) satisfying \(F(S_*)\leq F(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq[n]\); any minimizer is acceptable, including the empty or full set. For every fixed valid oracle \(F\), the probability of a correct output is at least \(2/3\). In the definition of \(R(n)\), a cost bound \(q\) requires at most \(q\) oracle calls on every input and every outcome of the random choices, not just in expectation. Arbitrary finite local computation and exact operations on the oracle answers are free. The algorithm has no direct access to a formula, table or circuit for \(F\). We use classical randomized query complexity: for each dimension, random coins select a deterministic adaptive query procedure, independently of \(F\); the maps and distributions must define measurable success events. An algorithm may depend on \(n\), so lower bounds also apply to nonuniform choices. The value magnitudes and their bit encodings do not enter the query cost. Exhaustively querying all \(2^n\) subsets shows that \(R(n)\) is finite. A superlinear lower bound means that for each real constant \(C>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(R(n)>Cn\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked superlinear lower bound in the specified randomized bounded-query model. Alternatively prove the negation of that growth statement: a fixed constant C and infinitely many dimensions admit correct algorithms using at most Cn queries. An O(n)-query algorithm for all dimensions would suffice for a negative answer but is stronger than the logical negation. A deterministic lower bound, a lower bound on parallel rounds, or hardness only for finding a nonempty proper minimizer does not establish the target.
context:
The source proves an Ω(n log n) deterministic query lower bound and explicitly asks for a superlinear randomized one. The selected target is any unbounded multiplicative improvement over n, rather than a demand for the same n log n expression.

In the deterministic construction, an adversary can exploit the algorithm’s fixed queries to delay discovery of a hidden set. The paper explains why random subsets can defeat the local obstruction used for that logarithmic factor. Transferring the deterministic proof without a new randomized argument is therefore insufficient.

The paper also proves a nearly linear lower bound on the number of adaptive parallel rounds when each round permits polynomially many queries. This measures how often answers must be used to choose the next batch. It does not imply a superlinear lower bound on the total number of sequentially adaptive queries.

Earlier lower bounds include a linear bound for general minimization and stronger statements for nontrivial minimizers of certain function classes. The requirement to exclude the empty and full sets changes the optimization problem; this card allows both and asks for the usual unconstrained minimum.

Exact oracle values can reveal more than comparisons between candidate subsets. A lower bound in this model must survive that extra information and cannot assume a bounded numeric range unless it constructs hard functions within that range. Conversely, bit complexity of evaluating an oracle is outside the target.

Strongly polynomial query upper bounds do not depend on the range of function values. The source compares algorithms with different amounts of local computation, including exponential local time; the lower-bound target here deliberately imposes no polynomial-time restriction.
why: Submodular minimization is a central tractable optimization problem, yet its information requirements remain far from its best general algorithms. A superlinear randomized lower bound would establish that even unlimited computation and adaptive random querying cannot reduce exact minimization to a linear amount of oracle information.
status_note: The 2022 source explicitly leaves superlinear randomized query lower bounds open and explains why its deterministic argument does not transfer. No matching resolution for the bounded-query exact-minimization model was located in the bounded September 2026 check.
progress: 2020: Graur and coauthors improve general and restricted minimization lower bounds in the value-oracle model. | 2022: Chakrabarty and coauthors prove Ω(n log n) for deterministic algorithms and a separate nearly linear parallel-round lower bound, leaving randomized total-query superlinearity open.
working_summary: A value oracle answers exact evaluations of an unknown submodular set function. The randomized algorithm must find a true global minimizer on every input with constant success probability. The question asks whether the worst-case query requirement grows faster than every constant multiple of the ground-set size. Neither numeric evaluation cost nor local computation is charged. Known deterministic and parallel-round lower bounds do not settle this randomized total-query question.

title: Limited-memory convex optimization
importance_reason: A fundamental tradeoff between two distinct resources in first-order optimization, with major endpoint lower bounds and substantial unresolved parameter ranges.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the deterministic first-order oracle complexity \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)\) of minimizing a globally convex, Euclidean \(1\)-Lipschitz function with a global minimizer in the unit ball, when only \(M\) bits can be retained between queries. The target is the entire tradeoff for integers \(d\geq1\), \(M\geq0\) and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/4\), including the parameters for which \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\infty\).
definitions: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) contain all convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\|x-y\|_2\) for every \(x,y\), and such that some global minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies \(\|x_*\|_2\leq1\). A subgradient at \(x\) is a vector \(g\) with \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\). A query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),g)\) for any valid subgradient; correctness is required for every sequence of such choices. An \(M\)-bit, \(t\)-query algorithm consists of deterministic maps \(\phi_i:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\psi_i:\{0,1\}^M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to\{0,1\}^M\) for \(1\leq i\leq t\), and \(\zeta:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\). Starting with \(s_0=0^M\), it queries \(x_i=\phi_i(s_{i-1})\), receives \((f(x_i),g_i)\), and sets \(s_i=\psi_i(s_{i-1},f(x_i),g_i)\). Its final output is \(\zeta(s_t)\); for \(t=0\) it is \(\zeta(s_0)\). All maps may depend on \(d,M,t,\varepsilon\), but not on the unknown function. They are unrestricted mathematical maps: computing an update can use arbitrary real operations and temporary memory. Only the retained state is limited; there is no runtime, uniformity or computability requirement on these maps. The iteration index is implicit in the maps and is not charged to memory. Define \(R(d,M,t)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d,\,(g_i)}[f(\zeta(s_t))-\min_x f(x)]\), and \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:R(d,M,t)\leq\varepsilon\}\), with the minimum of the empty set equal to infinity. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained: \(R\leq\varepsilon\) means that for every \(\eta>0\) some algorithm has worst-case error at most \(\varepsilon+\eta\). Queries and outputs are not restricted to the unit ball.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular characterization \(G(d,M,\varepsilon)\in[0,\infty]\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG\leq T\leq CG\) throughout the stated domain, for fixed \(c,C>0\). Prove exactly which parameters have infinite complexity. The memory argument and requested accuracy must be those stated, without an unstated constant enlargement of memory or accuracy. Upper bounds must respect the infimum convention. Resolving only optimal-query memory requirements or one accuracy regime is not a characterization of the full tradeoff.
context:
This is Question 1 of Woodworth and Srebro’s 2019 contribution, with its preferred constant-factor accuracy selected explicitly. The source also permits a weaker polylogarithmic characterization and poses several subsidiary endpoint questions; those alternatives are not the acceptance criterion here.

The normalization loses no scale parameter: a Lipschitz constant \(L>0\) and a known minimizer radius \(B>0\) replace the accuracy by \(\varepsilon/(LB)\). The formal target retains the source’s global-function model and its bottleneck-memory convention, rather than total machine space.

The source exhibits gradient descent with \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) queries and \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) retained bits, and a discretized center-of-mass method with \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and \(O(d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) bits. These are achievable resource pairs; neither states the optimal query rate in every dimension and accuracy regime.

Blanchard, Zhang and Jaillet’s 2023 work establishes a nearly quadratic memory barrier for optimal query complexity in convex minimization over the unit ball. This addresses a source endpoint question, not the complete three-parameter tradeoff. Their separate recursive cutting-plane work gives additional memory-query upper bounds, including a high-accuracy regime.

Menart, Nikolov and Shamir’s July 2026 preprint strengthens deterministic and randomized lower bounds and reports a sharp transition near quadratic memory. Its stated model restricts queries to the feasible unit ball. No transfer of its numerical bounds to the global, unrestricted-query model above is assumed by this card.

A real-valued oracle answer can carry unlimited precision, but retaining it requires encoding it in the next finite state. Conversely, restricting temporary arithmetic would create a different problem. These distinctions are central to what a memory lower bound establishes.
why: The tradeoff separates acquiring information about a convex objective from retaining that information for later decisions. A full answer would quantify when nearly linear storage can preserve fast convergence and when the geometry needed for a small number of queries forces substantially larger memory.
status_note: The full tradeoff is open in the 2019 source. A review on 13 September 2026 found substantial later endpoint and partial-tradeoff results, but no complete characterization in the precise source model. The bounded later-work check is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2019: Woodworth and Srebro define the finite-state oracle model and ask for its full minimax tradeoff. | 2023: Blanchard, Zhang and Jaillet prove a nearly quadratic memory barrier at the optimal-query endpoint for unit-ball optimization. | 2023: Recursive cutting-plane algorithms give additional upper bounds, particularly at very high accuracy. | 2026-07-21: Menart, Nikolov and Shamir post stronger lower bounds in the bounded-query optimization model; these do not themselves characterize the full function on this card.
working_summary: First-order convex optimization learns about an objective through queries returning its value and a subgradient. The source asks how the number of queries needed for a prescribed accuracy changes when the algorithm has limited working memory. It highlights methods with strong oracle complexity whose stored geometric information can require quadratic space in dimension. The question is whether that memory cost is inherent or can be traded away without losing the optimal query rate. A sharp tradeoff would distinguish information acquired from the oracle from information that must remain available between optimization steps.

title: Smooth convex optimization with different domain and smoothness norms
importance_reason: A foundational oracle-complexity question connecting smoothness, feasible geometry and structured regression, with a substantial gap already in the canonical ℓ1-domain/Euclidean-smoothness case.
formal: For each fixed \(1\leq p<q\leq\infty\) and \(1<\kappa\leq2\), determine the optimal worst-case error \(\mathcal R_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)\), up to constant factors, of deterministic algorithms making \(T\) exact first-order queries to minimize a convex function whose gradient is Hölder continuous in the \(\ell_q\) geometry over the unit \(\ell_p\) ball. The target covers every integer \(n\geq2\) and \(1\leq T\leq n\).
definitions:
For \(1\leq s<\infty\), put \(\|x\|_s=(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^s)^{1/s}\), and put \(\|x\|_\infty=\max_i|x_i|\). Write \(B_p^n=\{x:\|x\|_p\leq1\}\). The conjugate exponent \(q_*\) is defined by \(1/q+1/q_*=1\), with \(1/\infty=0\). Let \(\mathcal F_{q,\kappa}^n\) be the class of all continuously differentiable convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) such that \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_{q_*}\leq\|x-y\|_q^{\kappa-1}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).\] There is no bound on the affine part of \(f\), no strong-convexity assumption and no promise of a sparse minimizer. One oracle query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),
abla f(x))\). A deterministic algorithm chooses each query as a function of the parameters and previous answers, and after at most \(T\) queries outputs \(\widehat x\in B_p^n\). It receives no explicit formula, data matrix, decomposition, proximal oracle or higher derivative. All computation between queries is free and unrestricted; arbitrary deterministic decision maps depending on \(n,T,p,q,\kappa\) are allowed, with no uniformity or bit-precision restriction. Its error is \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in B_p^n}f(x)\). Define \(\mathcal R_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_{q,\kappa}^n}[f(\widehat x_A(f))-\min_{B_p^n}f]\). Allowing an output outside the ball with error infinity gives the same definition. The minimum of each function exists because the ball is compact. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained. A Hölder bound with constant \(L>0\) and a feasible ball of radius \(R>0\) scales this risk by \(LR^\kappa\).
answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(c_{p,q,\kappa}G\leq\mathcal R\leq C_{p,q,\kappa}G\) over the entire stated domain, with positive constants independent of \(n,T\). The upper bound may be approached arbitrarily closely if the minimax infimum is not attained. Both the query and dimension dependence, including any logarithmic factors needed for constant-factor matching, must be established. A result for one pair of norms or for a stronger oracle alone does not characterize this family.
context:
Guzmán’s 2015 Open Problem 1 asks for large-scale minimax rates when the feasible ball and the smoothness norm differ. This card explicitly selects the vector case \(p<q\), where the reported gaps are substantial, and exact value-and-gradient access. The source also discusses matrix Schatten norms and a more general class of local oracles; those are related extensions rather than additional requirements.

When \(p<q\), the unit \(\ell_p\) ball is contained in the unit \(\ell_q\) ball. The source asks whether algorithms can exploit this smaller feasible geometry more effectively than methods analyzed only in the smoothness norm.

For \(p=1,q=2,\kappa=2\), the source compares an accelerated \(O(T^{-2})\) upper bound with a lower bound of order \(T^{-3}\), up to logarithmic factors, in its large-scale regime. These are dated nonmatching bounds, not a claimed present-day formula for the minimax risk.

Convex regression over a norm-constrained predictor class motivates the problem. Access to the complete regression data can supply structure unavailable to a first-order black box, so a faster algorithm for one explicit regression loss does not automatically determine this oracle complexity.

Adil, Bullins, Jambulapati and Sidford’s 2026 work studies stronger norm-dependent proximal oracles that solve a regularized minimization problem in one call. Its accelerated rates and matching span-restricted lower bounds concern that different information model.

The precision requested here concerns asymptotic error rates as the query budget and dimension vary. It is not an additive numerical tolerance on the risk. Constants may depend on the fixed norm and smoothness exponents; dependence on dimension cannot be hidden there.
why: The problem isolates whether the geometry of a constrained model can improve the fundamental convergence rate when smoothness is measured differently. Matching bounds would explain which gains in sparse and structured regression follow from geometry alone and which require access to additional problem structure.
status_note: The selected cross-norm problem is open in the 2015 source. Later-work checks on 13 September 2026 did not identify matching rates for the full first-order family; the 2026 proximal-oracle result uses different access. This is a dated source-backed status, not an exhaustive proof of current openness.
progress: 2015: Guzmán poses the cross-norm minimax problem and documents gaps for p below q. | 2026: Adil and coauthors give improved and optimal rates for stronger norm-dependent proximal access; this does not by itself determine the first-order cross-norm risk.
working_summary: Smooth convex optimization is often analyzed when the objective's regularity and the feasible region use compatible norms. The source instead studies settings where these geometries differ, including vector norms and their matrix counterparts. It asks for the optimal oracle complexity of minimizing such functions using black-box first-order information. The stated gaps concern how smoothness, domain geometry, dimension, and target accuracy interact. Matching algorithms and lower bounds would show whether sparse and low-rank optimization models permit faster convergence than methods designed around a single common norm suggest.

title: Deterministic near-linear-query approximation schemes for matroid intersection
importance_reason: A broad derandomization and oracle-efficiency question for a central combinatorial optimization primitive, covering all common ranks and arbitrary matroids.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that, given independence-oracle access to any two matroids on a common \(n\)-element ground set and any rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), finds a common independent set of size at least \((1-\varepsilon)r\) using at most \(Cn\log^a(n+2)\varepsilon^{-b}\) oracle queries, where \(r\) is the maximum size of a common independent set?
question_excerpt: Therefore, it remains an open question whether a deterministic \(\widetilde{O}\)\(\varepsilon  (n)\) independence-query \((1 -  \varepsilon )\)-approximation algorithm can be achieved for almost the entire range of […]
definitions: A matroid on \(V=[n]\) is a family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^V\) containing the empty set, closed under taking subsets, and satisfying augmentation: if \(X,Y\in\mathcal I\) and \(|X|<|Y|\), some \(e\in Y\setminus X\) has \(X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). The two unknown families \(\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2\) are supplied through separate exact independence oracles. A query specifies an index \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and a subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), and returns one bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I_j\). The total number of calls to both oracles is charged, including repeated calls. Queries may depend on all previous answers. The algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but need not be told \(r=\max\{|S|:S\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\), and receives no representation, rank oracle or additional promise. It must output the elements of a feasible common independent set, not merely estimate \(r\). The guarantee must hold for every pair of matroids and every attainable \(0\leq r\leq n\); loops, parallel elements, unequal matroid ranks and rank zero are allowed. Computation between queries is unrestricted but finite, and the algorithm is deterministic and uniform over \(n\) and the binary accuracy parameter. The target measures query complexity rather than arithmetic or bit running time. The constants and exponents in the displayed bound are independent of the matroids, \(n,r\) and \(\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the stated feasibility, approximation and query bounds, or prove that no such deterministic approximation scheme exists in this oracle model. A randomized scheme, a nearly linear scheme only when the common rank is a constant fraction of n, or a scheme that uses stronger rank queries does not decide the target.
context:
Terao’s 2025 paper explicitly asks whether deterministic near-linear-query approximation can approach one throughout the rank range. Its soft-O convention permits polynomial factors in inverse accuracy and logarithms of n; the displayed bound makes those factors explicit.

For two partition matroids representing the endpoints of a bipartite graph, common independent sets are matchings. General matroids can hide much more information behind each membership bit, so algorithms for explicitly represented graphs alone do not answer the oracle question.

A greedy maximal common independent set gives a one-half approximation with a linear number of independence queries. Terao improves the ratio to two thirds minus an accuracy term with O(n/ε+r log r) queries. This is a fixed approximation threshold, not an arbitrarily accurate scheme.

Blikstad and Tu achieve a near-linear-query randomized approximation scheme. Their work also provides a deterministic strictly linear-query guarantee in the large-common-rank regime for fixed accuracy. These results show why neither randomization nor the quantifier over all ranks can be omitted.

Terao’s 2026 algorithm for linear matroid intersection accesses two explicit matrices and exploits linear-algebraic structure. Its input-sparsity running time is a different resource guarantee and does not yield a deterministic near-linear membership-query algorithm for arbitrary matroids.

Taking ε very small eventually forces an exact answer because the output size is integral. This causes no contradiction with exact-intersection lower bounds: the allowed polynomial dependence on 1/ε may then be large. The interesting approximation regime fixes accuracy while n and the optimum rank vary.
why: The question asks whether random sampling is essential for information-efficient approximate intersection of arbitrary matroids. A positive answer would derandomize a central combinatorial optimization primitive at near-linear query cost; a negative answer would establish a separation in the power of adaptive deterministic and randomized oracle access.
status_note: Terao’s 2025 source explicitly leaves the deterministic near-linear independence-query approximation scheme open across general ranks. The checked 2026 result is for explicit linear matroid representations. No matching resolution for arbitrary independence oracles was located in the bounded September 2026 check.
progress: 2025: Blikstad and Tu obtain a randomized near-linear-query approximation scheme and deterministic results for large common rank. | 2025: Terao obtains a deterministic two-thirds-minus-ε approximation and poses the near-one question. | 2026: Terao improves approximation algorithms for explicitly represented linear matroids, a different input model.
working_summary: Two unknown matroids are accessed only by tests of whether a proposed subset is independent. The algorithm must output a large set independent in both matroids. The target is deterministic approximation arbitrarily close to optimum with near-linear query complexity. The guarantee must cover every common rank, without stronger rank queries or matrix representations. Randomized near-linear schemes and a deterministic two-thirds approximation are known.

title: Polynomial-time linear convergence for geodesically convex optimization
importance_reason: A broad extension of efficient convex optimization to curved geometry, requiring both high-accuracy query efficiency and computationally controlled geometric steps.
formal: In the geometric arithmetic model below, is there a deterministic first-order algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that minimize every Lipschitz geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex ball in a complete Riemannian manifold, using at most \(C(d+\zeta)^a\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)\rceil\) objective-oracle queries and at most \(C(d+\zeta)^b\) additional operations between consecutive queries? Here \(d\) is the manifold dimension, \(\zeta=r\sqrt K/\tanh(r\sqrt K)\), with value one at \(K=0\), and the required additive objective error is \(\varepsilon Lr\). The same polynomial overhead bound applies before the first query and after the last.
definitions: The input consists of a complete connected smooth \(d\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), \(d\geq1\), a reference point \(x_0\), a radius \(r>0\), a Lipschitz bound \(L>0\), a sectional-curvature bound \(K\geq0\), and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\). All sectional curvatures lie in \([-K,K]\). The distance \(\operatorname{dist}\) is the infimum of lengths of connecting curves in the given Riemannian metric. The closed ball \(D=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x)\leq r\}\) is promised strongly geodesically convex: every two points of \(D\) have a unique minimizing geodesic in \(\mathcal M\), and its whole segment lies in \(D\). If \(\gamma\) is such a segment parametrized on \([0,1]\) at constant speed, the unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))\), and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\). A function query at \(x\in D\) returns \(f(x)\) exactly and any tangent vector \(g\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for every \(y\in D\); correctness is required for every valid sequence of returned subgradients. Here \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) is the initial velocity at time zero of the unit-time minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). Only functions and subgradient oracles meeting these conditions are inputs. The output must be a point \(\widehat x\in D\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_D f\leq\varepsilon Lr\). Completeness makes the closed bounded ball compact, so this minimum exists. The algorithm has no access to a formula for \(f\). For computational access to geometry, points and tangent vectors are exact typed objects supplied by a geometric oracle; the input includes an orthonormal basis of \(T_{x_0}\mathcal M\). The available geometric operations are: distance between points; inner product of two vectors in one tangent space; linear combination of such vectors; \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\), the time-one point of the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\); \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) for \(x,y\in D\); and parallel transport of a tangent vector along the explicitly specified geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(tv)\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). Each such operation is charged \((d+1)^3\) units, irrespective of point or vector magnitude. Object storage and access cost one unit; objects cannot be inspected except by these operations. Exact real scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root on nonnegative arguments, exponential, logarithm on positive arguments, comparisons and integer indexing operations each cost one unit. There is no floor or extraction of bits from a real register. All computation, including geometric operations, is charged apart from the separately counted function queries. One uniform finite program must work for every admissible manifold, basis, oracle and parameter tuple. There is no randomization, integral oracle, convex-hull oracle or free optimization subroutine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the required uniform objective accuracy, logarithmic query dependence on inverse accuracy, and polynomial overhead independent of inverse accuracy, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated access model. A query bound with an uncomputable geometric step, a theorem only for a particular manifold, or an additional logarithmic factor in the query count does not meet the target. A negative result must allow the full list of geometric primitives provided here.
context:
This retains the manifold, curvature, ball and objective quantifiers of the source’s Open Question 1. The source leaves the computational representation of a general manifold implicit. The listed exact geometric primitives and their costs are an explicit editorial choice making its arithmetic-overhead requirement testable. A result in this model is not automatically a polynomial bit-complexity result for an arbitrary encoded metric.

The parameter \(\zeta\) is comparable within universal constants to \(1+r\sqrt K\). It allows dependence on the curvature scale and radius. The source explains that curvature dependence cannot generally be removed, even though logarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy remains the requested target.

The source distinguishes methods with good query complexity but expensive geometric work from subgradient methods with cheap steps but slower precision dependence. Thus proving either resource guarantee separately does not settle the joint question.

For constant-curvature spaces the source gives an ellipsoid-like method with \(O(\zeta d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and polynomial per-query work. This is a substantial partial result, but its extra logarithm and restricted geometry are both relevant to the full statement.

Positive definite matrices with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric are an important nonconstant-curvature example discussed by the source. Boumal’s textbook gives explicit distance, exponential and logarithmic maps for that geometry. These differ from the log-Euclidean metric, under which a coordinate logarithm makes convexity Euclidean.

Criscitiello and Kim’s 2025 work develops algorithms for horospherical convexity, a stronger geometric notion with additional structure. It does not by itself supply the required method for every geodesically convex objective in this question.
why: Euclidean cutting-plane methods show that high accuracy need not require a polynomial number of inverse-accuracy steps. Extending that efficiency to geodesic convexity would provide a general computational foundation for optimization on curved spaces, including matrix geometries used in scaling and statistical models.
status_note: The joint query-and-computation question is open in the 2023 source. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a resolution for the full geodesically convex class. The computational oracle convention is an explicit editorial specification, not a claim that all manifolds admit efficient finite-precision geometric implementations.
progress: 2023: Criscitiello, Martínez-Rubio and Boumal pose the full joint-resource question and prove a constant-curvature result with a squared logarithm in inverse accuracy. | 2025: Criscitiello and Kim develop a theory and algorithms for the more restrictive horospherically convex setting.
working_summary: Geodesically convex optimization replaces straight segments with shortest paths on a Riemannian manifold. The question asks for a deterministic first-order algorithm with query complexity polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in inverse accuracy. It also requires polynomial arithmetic work per query, so a powerful but computationally intractable geometric oracle would not suffice. The source develops an ellipsoid-like approach for constant-curvature spaces and identifies obstacles on more general manifolds. A solution would extend the efficient precision dependence of Euclidean convex optimization to curved spaces while respecting the cost of manipulating their geometry.

title: Gap-entropy conjecture
importance_reason: A central instance-sensitive sample-complexity conjecture in pure exploration, with a precise adaptation cost beyond the usual inverse-square gap sum; a fresh matching proof claim is explicitly flagged.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) such that, for every Gaussian best-arm instance \(I\) defined below and every \(0<\delta<1/10\), \[cH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)\leq L(I,\delta)\leq CH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)?\] Here \(L\) is the order-oblivious instance-wise optimum over globally correct sampling algorithms, not the performance of one algorithm required to attain the bound on every instance.
definitions: An instance has \(n\geq2\) independent arms with distributions \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,1)\), unknown means \(\mu_i\in[0,1]\), and a unique largest mean \(\mu_*\) at index \(*\). Each pull of arm \(i\) reveals a fresh independent sample from its distribution. An adaptive sampling algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\delta\), chooses pulls using earlier samples and independent internal randomness, and eventually outputs an arm index. It is \(\delta\)-correct if on every valid instance it stops almost surely and outputs its unique best arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Local computation is unrestricted; the resource is total number of pulls, and expectations include sampling noise and algorithmic randomness. Algorithms are measurable so that these probabilities and expectations are defined. Let \(T_A(I)\in[0,\infty]\) be the expected number of pulls. If \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of arm labels and \(\pi I\) is the corresponding relabeled instance, define \(L(I,\delta)=\inf_A (1/n!)\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T_A(\pi I)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms correct on every instance of the same Gaussian model. The infimum is taken separately for each \(I,\delta\): an algorithm selected for favorable performance at I must nevertheless remain correct on all other instances. It need not attain the infimum. For each suboptimal arm, set \(\Delta_i=\mu_*-\mu_i\in(0,1]\), and \(H(I)=\sum_{i\ne *}\Delta_i^{-2}\). For integers \(r\geq0\), set \(G_r=\{i\ne *:2^{-(r+1)}<\Delta_i\leq2^{-r}\}\), \(H_r=\sum_{i\in G_r}\Delta_i^{-2}\), and \(p_r=H_r/H(I)\). The gap entropy is \(\operatorname{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0}p_r\log(1/p_r)\), with natural logarithms. Only finitely many groups are nonempty. The constants in the conjecture are independent of n, all means, the number of gap scales and δ.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of both uniform constant-factor bounds, or prove that no such universal pair of constants exists. A result only as δ tends to zero with the instance fixed, only for dyadic gaps or monotone algorithms, or an algorithm with an extra closest-gap term does not by itself prove the displayed claim about L. The recent claimed proof must meet the same mathematical and Lean-checking requirement.
context:
This card selects Chen and Li’s Conjecture 3.5, which gives an explicit formula for the instance-wise optimum. Their separate Conjecture 3.2 asks for one algorithm attaining that optimum up to an additive two-arm adaptation term. The two statements are related but are not interchangeable.

Averaging over relabelings prevents an algorithm from gaining an artificial advantage because the best arm was placed at a preferred index. Taking an infimum over globally correct algorithms still permits a different favored sampling schedule for each target instance; it does not allow an algorithm to simply output a known best label without verifying correctness elsewhere.

Gap entropy weights a scale by its share of the inverse-square sampling burden, not by its fraction of arms. It vanishes when all gaps fall in one group and can grow when many scales carry comparable burden. The specified dyadic endpoint convention includes gaps equal to one; changing boundary conventions affects the full proposed complexity by at most constant factors.

Chen, Li and Qiao’s 2017 progress gives a nearly matching algorithmic bound and a lower bound for dyadic-gap instances under a monotonicity condition on algorithms. These restrictions and extra factors are relevant because the conjecture quantifies over all Gaussian instances and all correct algorithms.

A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 by Aronow, Kallus and Lopatto states the displayed two-sided result as Theorem 1.1. It also states a separate uniform-algorithm theorem with the closest-gap adaptation term. The present review matched their definitions and theorem statements, but has not independently certified the complete proof.

Asymptotic confidence-optimal algorithms study δ tending to zero for a fixed instance, when log(1/δ) eventually dominates its fixed entropy. Such a limit does not determine the uniform cost when gap scales and confidence vary together. This is why the nonasymptotic quantifiers matter.
why: The conjecture predicts the full instance-sensitive cost of identifying the best alternative, including the cost of learning which gap scales matter. Its entropy term would explain why instances with the same total inverse-square gap can have different exploration costs at fixed confidence.
status_note: A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 explicitly claims a positive resolution of this exact Gaussian instance-wise conjecture. Its Theorem 1.1 matches the target and its separate uniform-algorithm theorem addresses the related conjecture. This 13 September review has not independently checked the entire proof or located an established validation, so the status is uncertain, not source-open and not certified resolved.
progress: 2016: Chen and Li define the order-oblivious optimum and pose the gap-entropy characterization as Conjecture 3.5. | 2017: Chen, Li and Qiao obtain partial matching bounds with restrictions and additional terms. | 2026-09-09: Aronow, Kallus and Lopatto submit a preprint claiming the full gap-entropy formula and the related almost-instance-optimal algorithm.
working_summary: The arms have independent Gaussian rewards with unit variance and a unique best mean. The benchmark averages expected sample cost over arm relabelings and takes an infimum over globally correct algorithms. The conjecture predicts that cost from the total inverse-square gaps and the entropy of their scale distribution. It differs from asking one algorithm to attain the benchmark on all instances without an adaptation cost. A 9 September 2026 preprint claims the precise formula; its proof has not been independently certified in this review.

title: Second-order cone lift dimension of semialgebraic convex hulls
importance_reason: A broad structural question about exact conic formulations, connecting real algebraic geometry with the extra dimension needed to represent convex optimization models.
formal: Determine the function \(a(S)\) giving the minimum number of auxiliary real scalar variables in an exact second-order cone representation of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), for every semialgebraic set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every integer \(n\geq1\). Set \(a(S)=\infty\) when no finite such representation exists. For finite values, the benchmark accepts a real approximation within absolute error \(1/100\); infinite values require proof of nonrepresentability.
definitions: A semialgebraic set is one defined by a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict or non-strict polynomial inequalities with real coefficients. Its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of its points: \(\sum_{i=1}^t\lambda_i s_i\), where \(t\geq1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of the empty set is empty. No closure is taken, and neither compactness nor closedness is assumed. For \(d\geq2\), the Lorentz cone is \(\mathcal L_d=\{(t,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}:t\geq\|z\|_2\}\); also let \(\mathcal L_1=\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). An admissible representation with \(r\in\mathbb N_0\) auxiliary variables has the form \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^r,\ E(x,y)=e,\ F_j(x,y)\in\mathcal L_{d_j}\ (1\leq j\leq N)\},\] where \(N\geq0\), all cone dimensions \(d_j\geq1\) are finite, \(E\) is a real linear map with finitely many rows, \(e\) is a real vector, and each \(F_j\) is a real affine map into \(\mathbb R^{d_j}\). There is no bound on the number or dimensions of the cones, the number of affine equations or coefficient sizes. The number \(r\) counts only the scalar coordinates of \(y\), not the original coordinates of \(x\), the number of constraints or their output dimensions. Let \(a(S)\) be the least such \(r\), or infinity if the set of admissible integers is empty. In particular, zero auxiliary variables are allowed. The domain consists of mathematical sets with their ambient dimension, not particular defining formulas; equivalent descriptions of the same set must give the same answer. Coefficients of both the input descriptions and the lifts may be arbitrary real numbers. This is a characterization problem, not a claim that arbitrary real coefficients have finite machine encodings.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular mathematical description or certified rule for \(a\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof identifying its infinite-value domain and giving a real-valued function \(g\) with \(|g(S)-a(S)|\leq1/100\) whenever \(a(S)<\infty\). A proved interval of width at most \(1/50\) may specify a finite answer through its midpoint. The approximation need not be integer-valued. Upper-bound constructions without matching minimality information, isolated representable families, or merely repeating the defining optimization over lifts are insufficient.
context:
Section 5.1 of the 2018 Dagstuhl report asks both when a semialgebraic convex hull has a second-order cone representation and how many extra variables are necessary. The minimum-auxiliary-dimension function combines these into one target. The displayed model is an explicit editorial convention for “extra variables”; it permits all finite Lorentz-cone dimensions and real affine coefficients.

Allowing auxiliary variables can express convex sets that are not intersections of second-order cone constraints in their original coordinates. The number of auxiliary variables differs from conic extension complexity measured by the number of cones, their total dimension, or a semidefinite matrix block size. Those measures cannot silently replace a(S).

Fawzi proves that the cone of positive semidefinite real symmetric three-by-three matrices has no second-order cone representation. Thus even a semialgebraic convex set with a direct semidefinite description can have an infinite value here.

Scheiderer proves that every closed convex semialgebraic subset of the plane is second-order cone representable. This establishes finiteness for that class, but does not on its own give the minimum number of auxiliary variables for each member.

Scheiderer’s 2025 preprint proves representability for compact convex semialgebraic sets with Nash-smooth boundary of strictly positive curvature and for Nash-smooth hyperbolicity cones. These are substantial additional sufficient conditions, not a characterization of every set or its minimum auxiliary dimension.

Exact equality matters even for nonclosed hulls: linear projections of closed conic feasible sets need not be closed. Replacing a convex hull by its closure can therefore change the problem. Since this target leaves constraint counts unrestricted, a small auxiliary dimension alone is not a polynomial runtime guarantee.
why: Second-order cone lifts expose nonlinear convex structure through a class of conic constraints with effective optimization methods. Understanding both representability and the minimum added dimension would distinguish intrinsic geometric obstacles from the overhead of particular reformulations, while keeping those questions separate from numerical relaxation quality.
status_note: The general characterization and auxiliary-dimension questions are open directions in the 2018 source. The individual review on 13 September 2026 checked major obstruction and positive-family results through 2025 but found no complete determination of the selected function. No exhaustive present-day openness certification is claimed.
progress: 2018: The Dagstuhl report poses representability and minimum-extra-variable questions. | 2019: Fawzi’s published nonrepresentability result gives a basic obstruction even for a small positive semidefinite cone. | 2021: Scheiderer establishes second-order cone representability for all closed convex semialgebraic planar sets. | 2025: Scheiderer posts sufficient conditions using smoothness and curvature in higher dimensions.
working_summary: A semialgebraic set is described by polynomial equalities and inequalities, while its convex hull collects all convex combinations of its points. The source asks when that convex hull can be represented using second-order cone constraints and auxiliary variables. It also asks how many additional variables such a representation requires. Representability is stronger than having a useful numerical relaxation, because the projected feasible region must agree exactly with the desired hull. A structural answer would identify nonlinear models that can be converted into a tractable conic formulation and quantify the cost of that conversion.

title: Deterministic competitive ratio for matching with delays
importance_reason: A central deterministic-versus-randomized frontier for online decisions with delay, requiring a uniform guarantee over arbitrary metric geometry and unbounded request streams.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\rho(n)\) for online minimum-cost perfect matching with linear waiting costs on a known \(n\)-point metric. The ratio must depend only on \(n\), uniformly over the number and timing of requests and all distances in the metric.
definitions: A metric on \([n]\) is a symmetric map \(d:[n]^2\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) that vanishes exactly on equal points and satisfies the triangle inequality. The algorithm knows the whole metric before requests arrive. An input is any finite sequence of \(m\geq2\) distinctly identified requests, with \(m\) even, locations \(v_i\in[n]\), and arrival times \(0\leq a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_m<\infty\). Repeated locations and simultaneous arrivals are allowed; all requests at a given time are revealed before decisions made at that time. The algorithm does not know \(m\), future arrivals or an end-of-input time. It can irrevocably match two currently unmatched requests \(i,j\) at any real time \(t\geq\max(a_i,a_j)\), paying \(d(v_i,v_j)+(t-a_i)+(t-a_j)\). Every request must eventually be matched at a finite time on every finite even input. There are no colors, capacities or restrictions on the pairs. A deterministic online algorithm is a causal rule: its decisions through time \(t\) depend only on the known metric and requests revealed through \(t\). Computation and memory are unrestricted and uncharged, and decisions may be scheduled between arrivals. The total cost is the sum of all pair costs. The offline optimum, knowing the entire sequence, is \[\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)=\min_{\text{perfect matchings }P}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in P}\bigl(d(v_i,v_j)+|a_i-a_j|\bigr),\] since an offline pair can be matched when its later request arrives. Define \(r(d)=\inf\{C\geq1:\exists A\ \forall\sigma,\ \operatorname{cost}_A(d,\sigma)\leq C\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)\}\), with infinity if no finite ratio is possible, and \(\rho(n)=\sup_{d\text{ on }[n]}r(d)\), for \(n\geq2\). The algorithm in the infimum may depend on the entire metric. This is pure multiplicative competitiveness, with no additive constant; an input of optimum zero must incur zero cost. Infima over algorithms and suprema over metrics need not be attained. For deterministic rules, allowing an adaptive adversary does not change the requirement over all inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG(n)\leq\rho(n)\leq CG(n)\) for universal positive constants and all sufficiently large \(n\). Upper bounds must hold for every metric and all finite even request sequences; lower bounds must apply to every deterministic online algorithm in the specified model. Use approaching bounds if an extremum is not attained. A ratio depending on the request count, a randomized expected guarantee, or a theorem only for the line or uniform metrics does not determine this function.
context:
Azar’s 2020 problem statement asks to close the deterministic competitiveness gap, expressed either through the metric size or through the number of requests. This card explicitly selects the known finite metric and metric-size parameter. Its separately mentioned red-blue matching variant is not part of the target.

The source reports an \(O(n)\) deterministic upper bound and a lower bound of order \(\log n/\log\log n\), the latter holding even against randomized algorithms. It also reports an \(O(\log n)\) randomized upper bound. These are dated source bounds and should not be conflated with a deterministic logarithmic theorem.

Dufay and Wattenhofer’s SODA 2026 result gives a deterministic \(O(\log^5 m)\)-competitive algorithm even when the metric and request count are unknown. It substantially improves the source’s request-count comparison. However, \(m\) can be arbitrarily large at fixed \(n\), so that displayed bound alone gives no uniform polylogarithmic bound in \(n\).

Gan, Sun and Umboh’s September 2026 paper studies general size-dependent delay rates and nonlinear convex waiting costs. Its tight deterministic result for the broader size-dependent model is not a matching lower bound for this fixed linear-per-request delay objective. Its uniform-metric results also have a narrower geometric scope.

Waiting may expose a nearby future partner, but it also accumulates cost on every unmatched request. The metric can have arbitrary scale and aspect ratio, making the information available from future arrivals essential even when computation of a present-day best matching is free.
why: This question measures the unavoidable cost of making irrevocable pairings while deciding how long to wait for future demand. A sharp deterministic ratio would separate the value of randomization from the difficulty of balancing spatial matching cost and elapsed waiting time in general metric spaces.
status_note: The n-parameter deterministic gap is open in the 2020 source. Checks through 13 September 2026 found the major new polylogarithmic m-bound and results for other delay models, but no matching characterization of the stated n-only function. This bounded review does not exhaustively certify current openness.
progress: 2020: Azar records the gap for deterministic matching with delays and distinguishes the metric-size and request-count parameters. | 2026: Dufay and Wattenhofer publish a deterministic polylogarithmic ratio in the request count; the uniform metric-size target remains distinct. | 2026-09-09: Gan, Sun and Umboh publish bounds for size-dependent and convex delay models, with different objective or metric restrictions.
working_summary: Matching with delays pairs arriving requests while charging both the distance between partners and the time each request waits. The selected question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as a function of the number of points in a known metric. The guarantee must hold for any finite even request sequence, with no bound on its length or advance notice of its end. A SODA 2026 algorithm gives a polylogarithmic ratio in the number of requests, which does not alone determine the ratio uniformly in metric size. Matching bounds in the metric-size parameter would clarify the value of randomization in balancing spatial cost against waiting.

title: First-order convergence to local minimax optima
importance_reason: A quantitative or model-specific learning frontier; resolving it would sharpen a useful guarantee but has more limited scope than a general learnability characterization.
formal: Is There a First-Order Method that Only Converges to Local Minimax Optima?
context: The data and computation needed to predict. Hypothesis classes, noise, distributions, and error guarantees define the learning problem.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Minimax optimization models a player minimizing an objective against a second player who maximizes it. In nonconvex–nonconcave problems, stationary points need not represent the intended local minimax behavior. The selected question asks for a first-order method whose stable convergence targets are restricted to local minimax optima. Reversing the players' optimization order or merely driving both gradients toward zero can select inappropriate solutions. A method with the desired guarantee would clarify the dynamics needed for adversarial optimization, including the mathematical problems underlying some generative-model training procedures.

title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
importance_reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.
focus_reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every dimension \(n\ge 1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\), and every locally Lipschitz \(f:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \mathbb{R}\) with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho =e^{- V}\), where \(V:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}\) is convex and \(\int \rho =1\); allowing \(V=+\infty\) includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means \(\int x d\mu (x)=0\) and \(\int xx^{T} d\mu (x)=I_{n}\). Variance is \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int (f- \int f d\mu )^{2}d\mu\), and \(\nabla f\) is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )\) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is \(\sup _{n} \sup_{\mu}  C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )<\infty\), with \(\mu\) ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\). There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of \(n, \mu\), or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, \(\psi_{\mu}\) is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; \(\psi_{\mu} ^{2}\) is comparable to \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )\) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on \(\psi_{\mu}\) must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable \(\Vert X\Vert _{2}\). Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds \(E(\Vert X\Vert _{2}- \sqrt{n})^{2}\) by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )=O(\log  n)\). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives \(\psi_{\mu} =O((\log  n)^{1/4})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )=O(\sqrt{\log  n})\). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.
why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.
status_note: The full KLS conjecture is explicitly open in the primary sources, including Letwin’s July 2026 preprint. Research through 10 September 2026 found no dimension-free general-function resolution. The recent quadratic-form and thin-shell results are not treated as proofs of the full conjecture; the July bound is labeled as a preprint result.
progress: 1995: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies. | 2022: Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques. | 2023: Klartag proves \(\psi_{\mu} =O(\sqrt{\log  n})\), equivalently \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )=O(\log  n)\), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality. | 2025–2026: Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls \(E(\Vert X\Vert _{2}- \sqrt{n})^{2}\) uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality. | 27 July 2026: Letwin’s preprint reports \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{T}MX)\le 2E\Vert \nabla (X^{T}MX)\Vert _{2}^{2}\) for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives \(\psi _{n}=O((\log  n)^{1/4})\). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is \(C_{\mathrm{P}}=O(\sqrt{\log  n})\), not \(O((\log  n)^{1/4})\).
working_summary: The KLS conjecture concerns log-concave probability distributions normalized to have mean zero and identity covariance. It asks whether every sufficiently regular function has variance bounded by a universal constant times its average squared gradient. That constant must work in every dimension and for every such distribution. Geometrically, this would exclude narrow bottlenecks that covariance normalization fails to reveal. The question connects high-dimensional convex geometry with the mixing of sampling algorithms, and control of particular observables alone does not settle it.

title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
importance_reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
focus_reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant \(C_{H}\ge 1\) such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric \(d_{G}\) admits a map \(f:V(G)\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}\) into some finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space satisfying \(d_{G}(u,v)\le \Vert f(u)- f(v)\Vert _{1}\le C_{H} d_{G}(u,v)\) for all vertices u,v?
definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum path length. In \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}, \Vert x- y\Vert _{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m} |x_{j}- y_{j}|\). The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant \(C_{H}\) may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |\(V(G)|\), the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embeddings.

The target \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log (\gamma +1)})\). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed \(\gamma\) and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of \(K_{2},_{n}\) as \((3k- 2)/(2k- 1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\). The values approach \(3/2\). This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.
why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.
status_note: The planar constant-distortion case remains explicitly open in the checked May 2026 notes. Restricted-family and face-cover results, including February 2026 exact values for \(K_{2},_{n}\), do not settle arbitrary fixed-minor-free metrics. The inherited fixed-treewidth approximation theorem uses a stronger relaxation and expressly does not prove a flow–cut-gap bound. No general settlement found through 11 September 2026.

working_summary: The GNRS conjecture asks how faithfully shortest-path distances in graphs excluding a fixed minor can be represented in \(\ell\)\(_{1}\). The graph may have arbitrary positive edge lengths, and every pair of vertices must be preserved within a constant factor. This constant may depend on the excluded minor but cannot grow with the graph. Because \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) metrics decompose into weighted cuts, the question also governs multicommodity flow–cut gaps. Even the planar case tests whether a strong topological restriction is enough to remove all growing distortion.

title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
importance_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
focus_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in \(O((N+1)^{c})\) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into \(S^{3}\); the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of \(S^{3}\) starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has \(O(n \log (n+1))\) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

There is another strong certificate theorem. Lackenby proves that any n-crossing unknot diagram can be reduced to a crossing-free circle using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local diagram changes preserving the knot type. The result bounds the length of a successful route; it does not identify which route to choose efficiently. Enumerating a branching collection of polynomial-length routes can still take exponential time.

In 2021, Lackenby announced an algorithm with quasipolynomial running time. The SoCG 2025 source still describes this as an announcement, and the checked author webpage lists talks on it. I retain that attribution rather than presenting a fully checked published proof. Quasipolynomial time, of the form \(\exp ((\log  N)^{O(1)})\), can be much smaller than exponential time while remaining above a fixed polynomial bound.

Practical algorithms illustrate a different kind of progress. He, Sedgwick and Spreer’s SoCG 2025 paper builds knot factorisation machinery around edge-ideal triangulations and normal-surface crushing. Their introduction notes that Regina’s unknot-recognition implementation behaves polynomially in experiments but has an exponential worst-case bound. Strong performance on a census or on difficult examples is useful evidence for implementation design, without controlling every possible input diagram.

Lackenby’s July 2026 preprint gives a new algorithm through incompressible surfaces and hierarchies. For a nontrivial knot, the boundary of its exterior is incompressible; for the unknot it is compressible. This turns knot recognition into a question about surfaces in a 3-manifold. The paper’s Section 9 explicitly leaves key hierarchy-length and surface-complexity parameters unbounded in terms of the input, so it does not establish polynomial running time.

The central challenge is algorithmic control over global topology. A small diagram may hide the disk or decomposition that makes its type evident. Good certificates show that concise explanations exist; an efficient recognizer would show how to decide without searching an uncontrolled space of explanations. Any verified polynomial-time solution, including the new claimed one, would resolve a basic benchmark of computational topology and change how we understand this gap.
why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.
status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. Established certificates and earlier algorithmic results are distinguished from this new claim. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1997–1999: Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger prove NP membership using normal surfaces, with deterministic exponential-time algorithms; FOCS 1997, JACM 1999. | 2013–2015: Lackenby proves a polynomial bound on the number of Reidemeister moves needed to simplify an unknot, without a polynomial algorithm to find the sequence. | 2016–2021: Lackenby establishes unconditional NP certificates for knottedness, placing unknot recognition in coNP; journal publication 2021. | 2021: Lackenby announces quasipolynomial-time unknot recognition; retained as an announced result. | 2025: He–Sedgwick–Spreer present practical factorisation algorithms and explicitly distinguish empirical performance from worst-case polynomial unknot recognition. | 2026-07-25: Lackenby gives a new hierarchy-based recognition algorithm; its Section 9 does not establish polynomial input-size complexity. | 2026-09-06: Musick’s preprint claims polynomial-time recognition via locally minimal bridge presentations. This review has not independently validated the proof.
working_summary: Unknot recognition asks whether a closed loop represented by a finite crossing diagram can be deformed into a circle without cutting. A complicated drawing may still represent an unknot, so simplifying visible crossings is not a complete decision method. The target here is a deterministic algorithm whose bit complexity is polynomial in the diagram encoding. The saved card records a September 2026 preprint claiming such an algorithm, with its proof not independently validated. This description therefore preserves the uncertainty around that claim while explaining the computational target.

title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
importance_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
