focus_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
formal: Do universal constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most \(C(n+d)^{k}\)?
definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with \(R^{d}\), where \(d\ge 1\), and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph \(G(\mathrm{P})\) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and \(2^{d}\) vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An \(n^{d}\) upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper \(n- d\) bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as \(Cn^{2}\) or \(Cn^{10}\). The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave \(n^{2+\log _{2}d}\); Todd improved it in 2014 to \((n- d)^{\log _{2}d}\). For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form \((n- d)^{\log _{2}d- \log _{2}\log  d+O(1)}\). The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves \(\Pi _{2}^{p}\)-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron \(\{x\in R^{N}:Ax=b,x\ge 0\}\), with A having r rows, the stated bound is \(O(r^{2}\log  r)\), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.
why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.
status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.
progress: 1992: Kalai–Kleitman establish a quasipolynomial general edge-diameter bound; Todd’s paper records and sharpens the recurrence-based result. | 2010–2012: Santos disproves the original linear Hirsch conjecture with a 43-dimensional bounded polytope having 86 facets. | 2014: Todd proves the upper bound \((n- d)^{\log _{2}d}\). | 2018–2019: Sukegawa’s asymptotic improvement lowers the exponent by \(\log _{2}\log  d\) up to an additive constant, still quasipolynomial. | 2025: The ETH geometry notes retain the polynomial problem; Wulf establishes \(\Pi _{2}^{p}\)-hardness of computing diameters even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes. | 2026-02-10: Natura’s revised manuscript proves polynomial circuit diameter, including monotone circuit walks; ordinary edge diameter remains open.
working_summary: The vertex-edge graph of a convex polyhedron records which feasible vertices can be joined by a single edge move. Its diameter is the largest shortest-path distance between any two vertices. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture asks for one polynomial bound in the number of facets and dimension that works uniformly for every pointed polyhedron. Counterexamples to the original linear Hirsch bound do not refute this weaker polynomial target. Resolving it would constrain the combinatorial geometry of linear programs, although short undirected paths would still not supply an efficient improving simplex rule.

title: Planar k-set extremal function
importance_reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.
focus_reason: A defining two-parameter extremal problem underlying levels and geometric selection; its source-defined asymptotic function is admissible under the restored numerical/function policy.
formal: Let \(K_{2}(n,k)\) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets \(S\subseteq \mathrm{P}\) of size k strictly separable from \(P\setminus S\) by a line. Determine \(K_{2}(n,k)\) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with \((a,b)\ne (0,0), ax\)+by<c for every \((x,y)\in S\), and ax+by>c for every \((x,y)\in\)\(P\setminus S\). The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression \(F(n,k)\) and absolute constants \(0<c_{0}\le C_{0}<\infty\) such that \(c_{0}F(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le C_{0}F(n,k)\) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values \(n/2<k<n; k=0,n\) each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
answer_criterion: Determine a positive function \(F(n,k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(cF(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le CF(n,k)\) throughout \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Prove the universal upper bound and existence of matching point sets for every parameter pair in Lean. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required; a mere restatement of the defining extremum is insufficient. This asymptotic-complexity target uses constant-factor precision, not additive 0.01. A fixed-k result or the halving case alone does not determine the whole function.
context:
A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when \(k=1\) the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves \((n- 2)/2\) of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed \((k- 1)\)-edges gives \(K_{2}(n,n/2)\) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is \(O(n k^{1/3})\), whereas constructions give \(n \exp (\Omega (\sqrt{\log  k}))\) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same \(4/3\) exponent in the balanced case.
why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.
status_note: The June 2025 problem entry retains the gap. The 2024 halving-line improvement changes lower-order terms rather than the exponent. No matching asymptotic bound was located in the status search through 10 September 2026.
progress: 1997–1998: Dey proves \(K_{2}(n,k)=O(n k^{1/3})\) for \(1\le k\le n/2\) through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an \(O(n^{4/3})\) upper bound. | 2000–2001: Tóth constructs planar point sets with \(n \exp (\Omega (\sqrt{\log  k})) k\)-sets for \(n\ge 2k>0\), improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows. | 2008: Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) halving edges for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). | 2024-07: Alonso, López, and Rodrigo improve a linear subtractive term in the upper bound on the maximum number of halving lines for even n, and improve some finite-n bounds. The asymptotic upper exponent remains \(4/3\). | 2025-06: The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.
working_summary: A planar k-set is a k-element subset of a point set that one line strictly separates from all remaining points. The target is the maximum number of such subsets over n points with no three collinear. Determine its growth within universal constant factors jointly in n and k, for \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). The problem counts subsets rather than separating lines and asks for combinatorial complexity rather than an enumeration algorithm. Both a uniform bound for every point set and matching examples throughout the parameter range are required.

title: Lang–Plaut problem
importance_reason: A major metric-embedding characterization problem: whether doubling and Hilbert embeddability suffice for finite-dimensional Euclidean representation.
formal: For every integer \(K\geq2\), do there exist a finite integer \(N(K)\geq1\) and a finite real constant \(D(K)\geq1\) such that every \(K\)-doubling subset \(X\) of real Hilbert space admits a map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^{N(K)}\) satisfying \[\|x-y\|_2\leq\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\leq D(K)\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in X)?\]
definitions: It suffices to use the real Hilbert space \(\ell_2=\{(x_i)_{i\geq1}:\sum_i x_i^2<\infty\}\), with norm \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\). A doubling subset of any Hilbert space is separable and isometrically identifies with a subset of this space. Give \(X\subseteq\ell_2\) the restricted Hilbert distance. It is \(K\)-doubling if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), the closed ball \(B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|_2\leq r\}\) is covered by at most \(K\) closed balls \(B_X(z,r/2)\) with centers \(z\in X\). No boundedness, closedness, compactness or finiteness of \(X\) is assumed. Empty sets and singletons cause no difficulty. The codomain has its ordinary Euclidean norm. The displayed lower inequality makes the map injective and fixes its arbitrary scale; without that normalization, distortion is the product of the Lipschitz constants of a map and its inverse on its image. The functions \(N,D\) must be chosen before \(X\), and may depend only on \(K\), not on the number of points, diameter, aspect ratio or ambient Hilbert dimension. The embedding may be nonlinear and may be chosen separately for each \(X\). There is no algorithm, continuity beyond the displayed bounds, or prescribed polynomial dependence on \(K\) required. Distances themselves must be preserved within these factors; replacing them by a power smaller than one changes the target.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal statement in Lean, or give a complete Lean-checked refutation with a fixed doubling bound for which no uniform pair of finite dimension and distortion bounds works. Equivalently, the qualitative Lang–Plaut formulation can be settled by proving that every doubling Hilbert subset has some finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding, or by exhibiting one that has none; the source proves the equivalence with the quantitative formulation. A restriction to linear maps, snowflaked distances, or bounds growing with the number of points does not resolve the question.
context:
Naor and Neiman state the Lang–Plaut question in Section 1.1 and justify its quantitative form in Section 4. This card uses that form so the dependence of dimension and distortion is explicit. The original question is attributed there to Lang and Plaut’s Question 2.4.

Every subset of a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space is doubling, with a bound controlled by dimension, and is already a subset of Hilbert space. A positive answer would make these two necessary conditions sufficient for finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embeddability.

Naor and Neiman prove that for an arbitrary doubling metric \((X,d)\), every snowflake \((X,d^{1-\eta})\), \(0<\eta<1/2\), embeds into a Euclidean space whose dimension depends only on the doubling constant. The distortion still depends on \(\eta\). Letting \(\eta\) tend to zero therefore does not supply the uniformly controlled embedding asked for here.

Lafforgue and Naor construct, for every \(p>2\), a doubling subset of \(L_p\) that has no bi-Lipschitz embedding into any finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Their theorem explicitly leaves the Hilbert case \(p=2\) open, so replacing Hilbert space by a general Banach space changes the answer.

Usual finite-set dimension reduction allows dimension to grow with the logarithm of the number of points. Here arbitrarily large or infinite sets with the same doubling bound must share a finite target dimension and distortion bound. This is a geometric existence question rather than a request for a faster implementation of a known projection.
why: The problem asks whether intrinsic local metric dimension completely controls Euclidean dimensional reduction once Hilbert embeddability is available. Its resolution would clarify a central obstruction to finite-dimensional metric representation and the limits of geometry-based compression independent of dataset size.
status_note: Open in the checked Naor–Neiman and Lafforgue–Naor sources. A bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a resolution for the Hilbert case. Results for other Banach spaces or restricted families do not supply one; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2001: Lang and Plaut pose the finite-dimensional embeddability question. | 2012: Naor and Neiman obtain snowflake embeddings with dimension independent of the snowflake exponent and explain why the unsnowflaked Hilbert question remains. | 2013: Lafforgue and Naor give a negative answer for every Lp with p greater than two, while retaining the Hilbert case as open.
working_summary: A doubling metric has uniformly limited local branching: each ball can be covered by a bounded number of smaller balls. The Lang–Plaut problem considers such a metric when it already sits inside a Hilbert space. It asks whether the points can be represented in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space while changing all distances by only a bounded factor. Both dimension and distortion should depend only on the doubling constant. The issue is whether intrinsic metric simplicity suffices to eliminate an infinite-dimensional ambient representation.

title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
importance_reason: A longstanding and precisely isolated computational-topology problem connecting finite combinatorial input with fundamental four-dimensional topology.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine which, on every finite simplicial complex K promised to be a closed combinatorial 4-manifold, halts and decides whether K is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the boundary of a 5-simplex?
definitions: A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite family of finite vertex sets closed under taking subsets; its maximal sets are its facets. The input lists all facets with integer vertex labels in binary. K is pure of dimension 4 when all facets have five vertices. The link of a vertex v consists of the faces \(\sigma\) not containing v for which \(\sigma \cup \{v\}\) is a face of K. A closed combinatorial 4-manifold here is a nonempty pure 4-dimensional complex in which each vertex link is a PL 3-sphere; connectedness is not promised. The standard PL d-sphere is the boundary complex of a \((d+1)\)-simplex. Two complexes are PL homeomorphic when they admit finite simplicial subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic, equivalently when their geometric realizations admit a homeomorphism affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions. A simplicial subdivision triangulates the same realization by smaller simplices contained in the old simplices. Correctness and termination are required on every promised input; no behavior is required on other inputs. There is no time or space bound beyond termination.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A triangulation is finite data, but deciding the global space it describes may exceed the power of every algorithm. Sphere recognition is decidable in low dimensions and undecidable from dimension five onward; dimension four is the exceptional unresolved case in this PL formulation.

The category matters: a topological homeomorphism need not supply a PL equivalence. The practical study explicitly distinguishes a homology four-sphere, a topological four-sphere and the standard PL four-sphere. This card asks for recognition of the last object.

Successful recognition on large test collections does not establish termination on every promised manifold. The question is about the existence of a decision procedure, rather than the speed or reliability of a particular implementation.
why: Locate the remaining decidability boundary for recognizing spheres in the piecewise-linear category.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 presentation and 2022 research paper support the unresolved PL four-dimensional target; no later resolution was found.
progress: 2022: The computational study distinguishes recognizing the standard PL sphere from detecting a topological sphere and reports inconclusive four-dimensional instances. | 2025-07-15: The research presentation retains dimension four as the unresolved recognition boundary.
working_summary: The input is a finite triangulation promised to be a closed combinatorial four-dimensional manifold. The task is to recognize the standard piecewise-linear four-sphere. The question asks for a terminating decision algorithm, with no polynomial-time requirement. Recognizing a topological sphere or checking its homology would answer a different question. The problem marks the exceptional dimension between established decidability and undecidability results for sphere recognition.

title: Optimal size of weak \(\varepsilon\)-nets for convex ranges
importance_reason: A foundational extremal problem in discrete geometry, with nonmatching upper and lower bounds already in dimension two and consequences for geometric transversals.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), determine the asymptotic order of \(f_d(\varepsilon)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(d\). Here \(f_d(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest worst-case number of auxiliary points required to hit every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\).
definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(G_d(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that for each fixed \(d\geq2\) there are \(c_d,C_d,\varepsilon_d>0\) with \(c_dG_d(\varepsilon)\leq f_d(\varepsilon)\leq C_dG_d(\varepsilon)\) whenever \(0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_d\). Upper bounds must cover all finite configurations; lower bounds must establish configurations requiring the matching order. Constants may depend on dimension but not on accuracy or input size. The exponent alone, bounds missing logarithmic factors, or a solution only for the plane do not characterize the stated family.
context:
Rubin’s paper explicitly identifies the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension at least two as an outstanding problem. The cardinality function above is the source’s extremal target, with its counting, rounding and range conventions made explicit.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.
why: Weak nets quantify how many representatives can preserve every large convex part of an arbitrary finite configuration. Sharp bounds would settle a basic gap in discrete geometry and clarify the geometric cost underlying transversal, selection and approximation results.
status_note: The extremal asymptotic question is open in the checked sources, including the higher-dimensional revision of December 2023. The bounded later-work review on 13 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the stated family. Publication and revision dates are distinguished from the date of this status check.
progress: 2011: Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch establish superlinear lower bounds in every fixed dimension at least two. | 2018: Rubin obtains the first improvement of the longstanding general planar upper bound. | 2023-12: The revised higher-dimensional work supplies further upper-bound improvements; matching growth rates remain undetermined.
working_summary: A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net places auxiliary points so that every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a given point set contains an auxiliary point. The auxiliary points may lie anywhere in the ambient Euclidean space. For each fixed dimension, the task is to determine the smallest worst-case net size as \(\varepsilon\) decreases. The challenge comes from hitting all sufficiently populated convex regions simultaneously, regardless of the original configuration. Sharp bounds would quantify how economically a finite set can represent its large convex subsets.

title: Dürer’s conjecture
importance_reason: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.
formal: For every bounded three-dimensional convex polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with nonempty interior, is there a connected edge unfolding whose distinct face interiors do not overlap in the plane?
definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.
context:
A net lays out the actual faces of a solid in one plane without stretching them. A cube provides familiar examples: its six squares can remain connected along selected edges and spread out without their interiors covering one another. The conjecture asks for such a choice for every convex polytope, regardless of the number, shape or arrangement of its facets.

The connected gluing pattern matters independently of overlap. Keeping a tree of facet adjacencies attaches every face to one planar assembly. It does not guarantee that faces far apart in that tree avoid one another after flattening. The existence question concerns a suitable choice of the whole pattern, not whether every possible net succeeds.

Only original polytope edges are available for cuts. Triangulating a facet and then allowing cuts on the new diagonals, slicing through face interiors, or returning disconnected pieces changes the task. Nonconvex examples without suitable unfoldings likewise do not refute a statement restricted to convex input.

This card retains its explicitly chosen nonoverlap convention: relative interiors of distinct facets must be disjoint, while boundary contacts are allowed. A requirement that the entire unfolded boundary be a simple Jordan curve is an additional condition; no equivalence to that stricter condition is assumed. The distinction is explicit in the unfolding literature.

O’Rourke’s March 2026 preprint still identifies even the general prismatoid case as unresolved. A prismatoid is a convex polytope whose vertices lie in two parallel planes. Its nested special cases concern a restricted geometric arrangement, leaving arbitrary convex polytopes outside their guarantee.

The July 2026 overlap construction finds convex polyhedra with particular edge unfoldings of arbitrarily large overlap thickness. Showing that one choice of cuts overlaps is different from showing that every choice overlaps. The latter universal failure would be needed for a counterexample to the existence question.
why: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The March 2026 prismatoid paper retains the general existence question; the July overlap construction does not refute it. This card uses its explicit disjoint-facet-interior convention with boundary contacts permitted, without asserting equivalence to a stricter simple-boundary requirement. The bounded source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.
progress: 2001: The problem source records the general convex edge-unfolding question as open and distinguishes known nonconvex obstructions. | 2026-03-23: The revised prismatoid paper retains the general prismatoid and convex edge-unfolding questions while analyzing a restricted subclass. | 2026-07-10: A preprint constructs selected unfoldings with arbitrarily high overlap; it does not show that every unfolding of any convex polytope overlaps.
working_summary: The input is a convex three-dimensional polytope. Its faces may be separated only along original edges. The output sought is one connected planar net. Distinct face interiors must not overlap. Allowing cuts across faces or disconnected pieces gives a different problem.

title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
importance_reason: A central distance-preserving graph compression question, now settled for fixed-minor-free families but still demanding a topology-independent constant in general graphs.
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every finite connected undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge lengths and every terminal set \(K\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|K|\geq2\), there is a reweighted terminal-preserving minor \(H\) with vertex set exactly \(K\) satisfying \[d_G(s,t)\leq d_H(s,t)\leq C\,d_G(s,t)\qquad(s,t\in K)?\]
definitions: The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_G\) is the minimum path length between its endpoints. Zero-length edges are allowed, so distinct terminals can have distance zero; the displayed inequalities then require their distance in \(H\) to be zero too. To specify precisely the terminal-preserving minor condition, choose pairwise disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets \(B_t\subseteq V(G)\), one for each \(t\in K\), with \(B_t\cap K=\{t\}\). The graph \(H\) is a simple graph on the labeled set \(K\); an edge \(st\) of \(H\) is permitted only if some edge of \(G\) joins \(B_s\) to \(B_t\). Not all such permitted edges have to be kept, and vertices outside the branch sets may be deleted. Thus vertices can be deleted, edges deleted or contracted, and parallel edges or loops removed, but no two terminals are identified and no surviving vertex is a nonterminal. Each edge of \(H\) may receive an arbitrary new nonnegative real length, independent of the original length of an edge witnessing its adjacency. This is a topological minor relation with allowed reweighting, not a requirement that contraction preserve inherited edge lengths. Define \(d_H\) by shortest paths and as infinity for disconnected pairs; the guarantee forces finite terminal distances. Both inequalities must hold simultaneously for all pairs in one chosen minor. The same \(C\) must work independently of the numbers of vertices, edges and terminals, graph topology, edge-length magnitudes and aspect ratio. The target is existential and imposes no construction-time, input-encoding or randomness requirement on a proof of existence.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a universal constant and the required rooted minor for every input in Lean, or prove its negation: for every finite \(C\), some graph and terminal set admit no minor meeting all the inequalities. A family with unbounded necessary distortion is a valid negative answer; a single fixed lower bound on the constant is not. Expected distortion for each pair, additional surviving Steiner vertices, or a guarantee only in a restricted graph class does not settle the statement.
context:
The source describes Steiner point removal for general graphs before solving the version excluding a fixed graph minor. This card retains the general-graph question from the inherited record. The word minor includes terminal identities and permitted edge reweighting, which are made explicit in the branch-set definition.

Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\log k)\) for arbitrary graphs with \(k\) terminals. This bounds the loss in terms of the size of the surviving vertex set, but does not provide a constant independent of that size.

For trees, the source recounts an upper bound of eight and examples with necessary distortion approaching eight. Thus even on trees exact preservation is not generally possible, and a universal positive answer must allow nontrivial distortion.

Chang, Conroy, Le, Milenković, Solomon and Than prove constant distortion for every class excluding a fixed complete graph minor. More specifically, for \(K_r\)-minor-free graphs their Theorem 1.4 gives \(2^{O(r\log r)}\) distortion. This settles the planar case and much more, but the constant depends on the excluded minor and is not uniform over all graphs.

If the minor condition is dropped, the complete graph on the terminals with original shortest-path distances as edge lengths preserves every terminal distance exactly. The scientific constraint is preserving a graph-minor representation while removing every other vertex. Distances alone would give a much easier problem.

Choosing a distribution over minors with a small expected stretch for each pair need not produce a single minor that has small stretch on every pair. Likewise, allowing a few extra vertices changes the compression target. Neither relaxation is silently included here.
why: Steiner point removal asks how much of a network’s geometry and topology can survive when only designated terminals remain. A universal constant would establish a strong form of graph compression; an unbounded lower bound would show that the topology of general graphs forces a growing loss even when edge lengths may be redesigned.
status_note: The checked 2024 source settles fixed-minor-free graphs and records logarithmic distortion for general graphs. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a universal constant for all graphs or a refutation. The solved planar question is not presented as still open.
progress: 2001: Gupta establishes constant-distortion removal on trees, as recounted in the source’s historical overview. | 2018: Filtser gives logarithmic distortion in the terminal count for arbitrary graphs. | 2024: Chang and coauthors settle the fixed-minor-free case, including planar graphs; their constant depends on the excluded minor.
working_summary: Steiner point removal starts with a weighted graph and a designated set of terminals whose mutual distances matter. The goal is to delete the other vertices through graph-minor operations, leaving a graph on exactly those terminals. Its edges may be reweighted, but terminal distances should never shrink and should grow by at most a universal factor. The same guarantee must work regardless of how many terminals the input contains. This asks whether graph topology and useful terminal geometry can both survive an extreme reduction in representation size.

title: Klee’s measure problem
importance_reason: A basic measure-computation problem underlying geometric union and coverage algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge 3\), determine the optimal deterministic worst-case running time, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\), for computing the exact d-dimensional volume of the union of n axis-aligned boxes in the arithmetic real-RAM model below. The dimension may affect constants and the algorithm, but is not an input parameter in this running-time question.
definitions: An input is a list of \(n\ge 0\) closed boxes \(B_{i}=\prod _{j=1}^{d} [a_{i},j,b_{i},j]\), specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with \(a_{i},j\le b_{i},j\). Overlaps, coincident endpoints, duplicate boxes and zero side lengths are allowed. The output is the exact Lebesgue measure of ∪_\(i B_{i}\), returned as a real number; the empty union has volume zero. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. The requested precision is a \(\Theta\) bound: logarithmic factors count, and constants may depend on d. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied.
answer_criterion: For each fixed \(d\ge 3\), give a rate \(T_{d}(n)\), an exact algorithm with worst-case time \(O(T_{d}(n))\), and an unconditional lower bound \(\Omega (T_{d}(n))\) for every correct algorithm in the same model. If no single rate is attainable within constant factors, establishing that failure of asymptotic optimality also answers the stated optimal-time request. An improved upper bound alone, a conditional lower bound, a restriction to particular box shapes, or a result only for approximate or dynamic volume does not complete the classification.
context:
Two boxes may cover the same region, so adding their individual volumes overcounts their intersection. In three dimensions, \([0,2]^{3}\) and \([1,3]\times [0,2]^{2}\) each have volume 8, but their union has volume 12. The task requests this single total volume; it does not request a full description of the union boundary. In higher dimensions a box is simply a product of intervals.

Chan’s 2013 algorithm computes the union volume in \(O(n^{d/2})\) time for every fixed \(d\ge 3\). This gives \(n^{3/2}\) in dimension three and \(n^{2}\) in dimension four. The unresolved target is a matching classification of the fastest possible exact computation. The known relationship with clique problems supplies conditional evidence for the exponent, rather than a matching unconditional lower bound for all algorithms.

The real-RAM question counts an arithmetic operation on a coordinate as one step even when the coordinate would require many bits to encode. Chan also obtains logarithmic improvements for integer coordinates in a word-RAM setting. Those improvements do not automatically transfer to unrestricted real inputs, and the source explicitly discusses this distinction. The detailed primitive and worst-case conventions above make the inherited real-RAM target explicit.

The SoCG 2025 work speeds up approximation of union volume and proves a lower bound for algorithms restricted to certain object queries. A small relative error is permitted there. The ICALP 2026 work maintains exact volume under insertions and deletions and measures amortized update time. Both are significant results, but neither determines the unconditional optimal time of a single exact static computation in this card’s model.
why: A basic measure-computation problem underlying geometric union and coverage algorithms.
status_note: The general exact static bound remains \(O(n^{d/2})\) in the checked ICALP 2026 discussion; its optimality evidence is conditional. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching unconditional classification. Approximation, integer word-RAM and dynamic results have different guarantees.
progress: 2013: An exact \(O(n^{d/2})\) static algorithm is obtained for fixed \(d\ge 3\); separate word-RAM improvements use integer-coordinate assumptions. | 2025-06: Faster box-union approximation and a general object-query lower bound are published. | 2026: Exact dynamic data structures achieve near-optimal amortized update bounds under a stated combinatorial clique hypothesis, leaving the present unconditional static classification separate.
working_summary: Klee’s measure problem asks for the volume covered by a union of axis-aligned boxes. Overlapping regions count once, and only the exact total volume is required. For each fixed dimension at least three, the question seeks matching worst-case time bounds in a specified arithmetic real-RAM model. Chan’s general upper bound is \(O(n^{d/2})\), with no matching unconditional classification supplied by the checked later work. Recent approximation and dynamic advances answer different questions.

title: Polynomial-time recognition of the 3-sphere
importance_reason: Determine the complexity of a basic three-dimensional topological recognition problem.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether a finite simplicial complex promised to triangulate a closed connected PL 3-manifold is PL-homeomorphic to the standard 3-sphere?
definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. The complex is represented by its vertex set and list of maximal tetrahedra, with all faces implicit. The promise requires each point of its realization to have a neighborhood PL-homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R} ^{3}\) and requires compactness, connectedness and no boundary. The standard PL 3-sphere is the boundary of a 4-simplex. PL-homeomorphism means that after finite subdivisions there is a simplicial isomorphism. Correctness is required on promised inputs; the time bound holds on all encodings.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Sphere recognition is a canonical task in computational topology. Decidability is known, but a decision algorithm can still be far too expensive as a triangulation grows.

The source places 3-sphere recognition in NP, separating certificate length from the existence of an efficient search or decision algorithm. The target is polynomial time for arbitrary promised triangulations. Results about generic triangulations or short simplifications of small examples do not settle it.
why: Determine the complexity of a basic three-dimensional topological recognition problem.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2011: The source establishes NP membership, not deterministic polynomial-time recognition.

title: Simultaneous embedding with fixed edges for two graphs
importance_reason: A central simultaneous graph-drawing problem about making overlapping structures geometrically consistent.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given any two finite simple planar graphs \(G_{1}=(V,E_{1})\) and \(G_{2}=(V,E_{2})\) on the same labeled vertex set, decides in polynomial time whether they admit planar topological drawings that coincide on every shared vertex and every shared edge?
definitions: The input gives \(n\ge 0, V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), and two symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is \(H=(V,E_{1}\cap E_{2})\), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points \(p(v)\in \mathbb{R} ^{2}\) to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints \(p(u),p(v)\), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same \(p(v)\) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in \(E_{1}\cap E_{2}\). Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) with at most \(C(N+1)^{c}\) bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.
context:
Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

Take \(G_{1}\) to be \(K_{5}\) with one edge deleted and \(G_{2}\) to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. \(G_{1}\) is planar, and \(G_{2}\) can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to \(G_{1}\). This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph \(K_{5}\). Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

Three-graph SEFE is NP-complete, but the number two is essential here. The March 2026 work on two paths studies straight-line grid drawings and optimizes geometric quantities. Its hardness result for edge length does not imply hardness of deciding whether unrestricted curved-edge drawings exist.
why: A central simultaneous graph-drawing problem about making overlapping structures geometrically consistent.
status_note: The general two-graph problem is explicitly open in the checked ISAAC 2025 and JGAA 2025 sources. The March 2026 path result concerns geometric optimization. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this topological decision problem; proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2015: The updated survey separates SEFE from geometric and freely redrawn-edge variants. | 2025: Two current primary papers describe connected-common-graph SEFE as polynomially solvable and the unrestricted two-graph case as open. | 2026-03: Work on two paths addresses geometric grid optimization, a separate target.
working_summary: Two planar graphs share labeled vertices and possibly some edges. The question asks whether the existence of compatible planar drawings can be decided in polynomial time. Each shared vertex and edge must look identical in both drawings, while edges exclusive to different graphs may cross. The case with connected common graph is known to be efficiently solvable. The remaining target covers arbitrary common graphs and is distinct from straight-line or three-graph variants.

title: Euclidean minimum spanning tree complexity
importance_reason: A foundational geometric optimization problem with a linear-size answer but an implicit quadratic edge set, tied to bichromatic closest-pair complexity in higher fixed dimensions.
formal: For each fixed integer \(d\geq3\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic worst-case time for computing an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of \(n\geq2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\). The input is the array of coordinates of the points \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\); the output is a list of \(n-1\) pairs of indices forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) that minimizes \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\) over all spanning trees on these labels. Include logarithmic factors in the requested complexity, and use the real-arithmetic model below.
definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n)\) for every fixed \(d\geq3\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of matching uniform upper and lower bounds. For each \(d\), one correct deterministic program must have worst-case time at most \(C_dg_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Every correct program must have worst-case time at least \(c_{A,d}g_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(c_{A,d}>0\). The constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\) and, for the lower bound, on the program. An approximation scheme, an expected-time bound alone, or the polynomial exponent without matching logarithmic factors does not determine this target.
context:
The original entry asks whether exact Euclidean MST computation can approach the sorting-scale \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound. This card makes its resource question concrete by requesting optimal deterministic arithmetic complexity in every fixed dimension at least three. This is an editorial sharpening of the source’s informal word “close,” not an assertion that the source prescribed a particular logarithmic overhead.

An MST has only a linear number of edges. Nevertheless, applying a graph algorithm after explicitly creating the complete graph already processes quadratically many candidate edges. The unresolved issue is the cost of identifying the optimum from the much smaller coordinate description.

Agarwal, Edelsbrunner, Schwarzkopf and Welzl relate Euclidean MST computation to bichromatic closest pairs: given red and blue points, find a shortest pair with opposite colors. Their 1991 results include subquadratic expected-time algorithms in fixed dimensions. Those randomized guarantees are not silently assigned to the deterministic model used here.

The plane admits a sorting-scale exact MST algorithm, whereas higher fixed dimensions are the subject of the source question. Large-dimensional distance problems, approximate spanning trees and dynamic maintenance ask for different guarantees.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.
why: The problem asks how effectively fixed-dimensional geometry can accelerate one of the most basic graph optimization tasks. Sharp complexity bounds would clarify the algorithmic cost of exact geometric connectivity and its relation to proximity searching.
status_note: The original exact-complexity gap is source-backed. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the specified deterministic fixed-dimensional family. The 1991 randomized results are dated partial progress, not asserted to be current deterministic records.
progress: 1991: Primary work relates exact Euclidean MST to bichromatic proximity and gives fixed-dimensional randomized upper bounds. | 2002: The Open Problems Project records the gap between sorting-scale lower bounds and higher-dimensional geometric upper bounds. | 2026-01-13: New prediction-based results concern planar inputs with additional data.
working_summary: A Euclidean minimum spanning tree connects the input points with minimum total edge length. The input gives coordinates, while the complete graph of candidate edges is implicit. The card asks for the optimal deterministic arithmetic running time in every fixed dimension at least three. Exact computation must be distinguished from approximation and from algorithms with predictions or random-input promises. A resolution would determine how much low-dimensional geometry can reduce the cost of this basic connectivity problem.

title: Exact planar Euclidean matching
importance_reason: A longstanding gap for a fundamental geometric pairing problem, connecting exact weighted matching with the algorithmic value of low-dimensional coordinates.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors including logarithmic factors, the optimal deterministic worst-case running time for computing a minimum-length perfect matching of \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for all integers \(n\geq1\), in the exact real-arithmetic model below. The output is a list of \(n\) unordered pairs of input indices, every index occurring exactly once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\) among all perfect matchings. The input consists only of the point coordinates; the complete graph is implicit.
definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(g:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds in the stated model. The upper bound must give one uniform deterministic algorithm with worst-case time at most \(C g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The lower bound must show that every correct uniform algorithm has worst-case time at least \(c_A g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), where \(c_A>0\) and the threshold may depend on the algorithm. Constants are independent of the point configuration and \(n\). Approximate matchings, a bound only for bipartite matching, or a polynomial exponent with unresolved logarithmic factors do not meet this criterion.
context:
The Open Problems Project asks for the optimal complexity of exact Euclidean matching in the plane and mentions the bipartite problem separately. This card retains the unrestricted objective and makes the deterministic arithmetic and worst-case conventions explicit.

A matching contains only a linear number of edges, but the coordinate input describes quadratically many possible pairs. Its objective is the sum of their Euclidean lengths; replacing lengths by squared lengths can change the minimizing matching.

Varadarajan proves an \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) exact algorithm. The separator subroutine in the author manuscript has a deterministic implementation, so this is an upper bound for the deterministic target rather than merely an expected randomized bound.

Hougardy and Tammemaa’s April 2026 journal article still identifies Varadarajan’s bound as the fastest known exact algorithm. Their new results improve fast approximation guarantees and do not compute the exact optimum.

The same article recalls an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for deterministic geometric approximation algorithms with approximation ratio depending only on input size. Thus the exact task has a substantial known gap even before finer logarithmic factors are considered.

The arithmetic convention matters because the objective involves square roots and comparisons between sums of lengths. Counting each such arithmetic step is different from bounding the number of bit operations needed to certify every comparison for rationally encoded points. The requested output here is an optimal pairing, not a decimal expansion of its total length.
why: Exact Euclidean matching is a basic geometric optimization primitive. Its unresolved complexity tests how far geometric structure can reduce the cost of optimization over an implicit complete graph, beyond the easier approximation guarantees.
status_note: The exact complexity gap is explicitly present in the checked April 2026 article. The bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The real-arithmetic model is an explicit editorial specification of the geometric task; bit complexity and approximation are separate targets.
progress: 1998: Varadarajan obtains an exact \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) algorithm. | 2001: The Open Problems Project records optimal exact planar matching complexity as unresolved. | 2026-04-08: The new journal article improves deterministic approximation while continuing to identify the 1998 bound as the best exact upper bound.
working_summary: Given an even number of planar points, a perfect matching pairs every point with exactly one other point. The Euclidean objective minimizes the sum of the lengths of all chosen segments. The question is the optimal complexity of computing that minimum exactly, with bipartite matching as a related restricted variant. Approximation algorithms can exploit geometry differently and do not by themselves settle the exact problem. Sharper algorithms would improve a central geometric pairing primitive whose implicit complete graph contains quadratically many candidate edges.

title: NP certificates for homeomorphism of three-manifolds
importance_reason: A major unresolved verification bound for topological classification in dimension three, beyond decidability and the recognition of specific manifold classes.
formal: Does homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds, have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) of total encoded length \(N\), \[H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;V(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the NP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem below.
definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed existence of \(p,V\) with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer needs completeness for every homeomorphic promised pair and soundness against every candidate witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair, with polynomial worst-case verification time in \(N+|w|\). The verifier need not find the witness. A negative answer must exclude all polynomially bounded certificate systems in this model, not merely certificates made from a particular type of topological transformation. A result restricted to a fixed manifold, orientable closed manifolds, or one geometric class does not settle the full domain.
context:
Schleimer’s Question 3 asks whether Homeo(3) lies in NP. His standing domain is compact connected manifolds supplied by triangulations. The boundary, orientation and binary-verifier conventions above make that domain explicit.

Two very different tetrahedron lists can describe the same space. A positive certificate must establish equality of the represented topological types, rather than just exhibit a relabelling of the supplied pieces. Its form is unrestricted; the polynomial bound concerns the entire witness and its verification.

Kuperberg proves an elementary-recursive decision algorithm for closed oriented 3-manifolds: the running time has a fixed-height exponential-tower bound. This establishes a quantitative decidability result in that setting, not polynomial certificates for the broader domain.

Jackson proves NP recognition for compact orientable Seifert fibered spaces with nonempty boundary, together with NP and coNP certification for their naming problem. The paper explicitly asks about general homeomorphism, which its special-class results do not decide.

NP verification concerns yes instances. It does not imply a polynomial-time method for constructing a homeomorphism, nor provide short certificates when the manifolds differ. The latter is the separate coNP question.

The 2025 seminar report asks a related fixed-parameter tractability question measured by the treewidth of the input triangulations. A parameter-dependent algorithm with no global polynomial bound would not by itself resolve this certificate question.
why: Short certificates would separate the cost of discovering topological equivalence from the cost of checking it. An NP upper bound would place a fundamental classification problem within the standard theory of efficient verification.
status_note: The NP question is explicit in the 2024 report and Jackson’s 2024/2025 article. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no general certificate theorem. The stated target retains the source’s broad compact connected domain; closed-oriented and Seifert results are limited to their published hypotheses.
progress: 2019: Kuperberg establishes elementary-recursive decidability for the closed oriented setting. | 2024-02: Schleimer states the general NP question as Question 3. | 2024-06-20: Jackson’s first online publication proves NP recognition for Seifert fibered spaces with boundary; the journal volume is dated 2025.
working_summary: Two triangulations can describe the same three-dimensional manifold while looking combinatorially unrelated. This question asks whether every homeomorphic pair has a certificate whose size and verification time are polynomial in the input. Such a certificate need not be found efficiently by the verifier itself. The challenge is to encode the necessary topological equivalence without an excessively long sequence of transformations. An NP upper bound would distinguish the difficulty of discovering a homeomorphism from the difficulty of checking convincing evidence that one exists.

title: Minimum-weight triangulation in NP
importance_reason: Asks whether exact geometric optimization has short certificates despite the algebraic cost of verifying lengths.
formal: Does the following language belong to NP? An instance consists of a finite set \(S\subset \mathbb{Q} ^{2}\) of explicitly given points and a rational bound B; it is a yes instance exactly when S has a triangulation whose total Euclidean edge length, counting every edge once, is at most B.
definitions: The input lists \(n\ge 0\) distinct points \((x_{i},y_{i})\), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight \(\mathrm{W}(T)=\sum _{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\sqrt{(x_{i}- x_{j})^{2}+(y_{i}- y_{j})^{2}}\). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality \(\mathrm{W}(T)=B\) is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if \(V(x,y)\) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.
context:
A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points \((0,0), (1,0), (0,1)\) have a single triangular boundary of total length \(2+\sqrt{2}\). A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.
why: Asks whether exact geometric optimization has short certificates despite the algebraic cost of verifying lengths.
status_note: The original theorem establishes NP-hardness, not NP membership. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established membership or nonmembership resolution for this exact Euclidean decision problem. The checked 2025 source confirms the related radical-comparison gap but is not itself a triangulation-status theorem.
progress: 2008: Strong NP-hardness is proved, while NP membership for exact Euclidean costs remains explicitly unresolved. | 2018: Practical exact methods scale to very large tested point sets. | 2025: A later primary paper still records the unresolved NP placement of the related square-root-sum comparison problem.
working_summary: The input gives rational planar points and a rational limit on the total length of a triangulation. Every input point must be used, no extra points may be added, and Euclidean edge lengths are compared exactly. The question asks whether every feasible instance has a short certificate that can be checked in polynomial bit time. NP-hardness is known, but the sum of potentially irrational edge lengths prevents the usual edge-list argument from establishing NP membership. Practical exact solutions and rounded-cost variants do not settle the certificate question for arbitrary exact inputs.

title: Output-sensitive convex hull complexity
importance_reason: A fundamental input/output tradeoff in higher-dimensional geometry; it asks whether the work needed to find a hull can be matched to its actual facial complexity.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq4\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic output-sensitive running time for constructing the convex hull of \(n\geq d+1\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in general position, as a function of \(n\) and the actual number \(f\) of hull facets. The coordinate array is the input. Output the complete facial structure of the hull, as specified below. The required complexity must cover every realizable pair \((n,f)\), including small hulls, and retain logarithmic factors.
definitions: General position means every subset of at most \(d+1\) input points is affinely independent. The convex hull is \(H=\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). Its proper nonempty faces are intersections with supporting hyperplanes; a facet has dimension \(d-1\). The promise makes \(H\) full-dimensional and simplicial, with exactly \(d\) vertices per facet. Output each proper nonempty face by its set of input-vertex indices and list every containment incidence between faces of consecutive dimensions; also identify the facets. The total output size is \(O_d(f)\). Interior input points need not be output. Let \(\mathcal D_d\) be the pairs \((n,f)\) realized by a valid input, and let \(T_A(n,f)\) be the supremum of algorithm \(A\)’s steps over all such inputs with exactly these parameters.
