One finite deterministic program per fixed \(d\) must work for all \(n\); it is given neither \(f\) nor advice. The model has exact real registers with rational program constants and indexed memory; \(+,-,\times,/\), comparisons, copies and memory accesses cost one each. Integer indices and counters have \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits at time \(t\), with ordinary word arithmetic and comparisons charged. No floor, extraction of real digits, or free geometric query is available. Reading input and reporting faces are charged. Coordinates have no bounded-precision promise, and no randomization or input distribution is used.
answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n,f)\) on each domain \(\mathcal D_d\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds. For each fixed \(d\geq4\), give one uniform algorithm \(A_d\) with \(T_{A_d}(n,f)\leq C_dg_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). For every correct algorithm \(A\), prove \(T_A(n,f)\geq c_{A,d}g_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). Positive constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\), and in the lower bound on \(A\), but not on the feasible pair. A worst-case bound in \(n\) alone, listing only extreme vertices, or resolving only dimensions two and three is insufficient.
context:
The Open Problems Project asks for the best output-sensitive hull algorithm. The general-position convention used here is explicit in Chan’s cited primary paper. Without it, a facet can contain many vertices, and the number of facets alone need not measure the amount of output.

Output sensitivity accounts for what the particular input produces. Many points may lie inside a hull with few facets, so a bound based solely on the largest possible hull of an equally large point set can greatly exceed the size of the actual result.

Chan’s 1996 theorem gives \(O_d(n\log f+(nf)^{1-1/(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1)}\log^{O_d(1)}n)\) time. The paper contrasts this with the \(\Omega_d(n\log f+f)\) lower bound and explains the range of small outputs where its upper bound is optimal. These are dated results, not a claim that every intervening bound has been exhaustively surveyed.

The same paper distinguishes the hull’s full facial structure from the task of finding only its extreme points, and records optimal \(O(n\log f)\) algorithms in dimensions two and three. In dimension four there are also stronger specialized bounds than a literal use of the general-dimensional expression.

The ESA 2025 work on universal optimality concerns planar hulls and additionally reports certificates for interior points. It addresses a refined form of input sensitivity but does not settle the higher-dimensional two-parameter target here.

The fixed dimension is allowed to affect constants; the input size and output size are not. General position is a substantive source assumption, not a license to perturb a degenerate input while pretending its output size remains unchanged.
why: Sharp output-sensitive hull bounds would connect the work of discovering a geometric boundary to its actual combinatorial size. This matters for hull construction, polyhedral representations and geometric computations whose input contains many nonextreme points.
status_note: The complexity question is open in the primary source and problem entry. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no matching characterization for the stated higher-dimensional family. The displayed general-dimensional bound is attributed to 1996 rather than presented as a verified current record.
progress: 1996: Chan obtains output-sensitive upper bounds in every fixed dimension under general position. | 2001: The Open Problems Project records the unresolved optimal output-sensitive complexity. | 2025: The ESA paper establishes a refined planar universal-optimality result, for a different dimensional and output setting.
working_summary: An output-sensitive convex hull algorithm charges for both its input points and the facets it actually produces. The question asks for the best such running time for point sets in fixed-dimensional Euclidean space. Small hulls should be cheaper than the worst-case hull complexity would suggest. The difficult target is to reconcile reading the input, identifying extreme structure, and listing the output with nearly optimal overhead. Progress would improve geometric optimization whenever many input points contribute little to the final convex boundary.

title: Earth mover distance sketching complexity
importance_reason: A central compression problem for optimal transport, with a consequential unresolved constant-approximation/polylogarithmic-space regime and a full information-versus-accuracy tradeoff.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the minimum sketch length \(s(n,c)\) for approximating planar earth mover distance for every integer \(n\geq2\) and real approximation factor \(c\geq1\). Inputs are subsets \(A,B\subseteq[n]^2\) of equal cardinality, with unit mass at each occupied grid point, and \[\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)=\min_{\pi:A\to B\ \mathrm{bijection}}\sum_{a\in A}\|a-\pi(a)\|_1.\] Each set must be encoded independently using the same public randomness. From the two \(s\)-bit encodings the decoder must return \(\widehat d\) satisfying \(\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)\leq\widehat d\leq c\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every fixed pair.
definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_1=|x-u|+|y-v|\); grid spacing and point mass are both one. Empty sets are allowed and their distance is zero. There are no repeated points, arbitrary real weights or bounds on cardinality beyond \(|A|=|B|\leq n^2\). A length-\(s\) scheme for parameters \((n,c)\) is a probability space of public seeds \(R\), encoders \(L_R:2^{[n]^2}\to\{0,1\}^s\), and decoders \(D_R:\{0,1\}^s\times\{0,1\}^s\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\), with all relevant events measurable. The estimate is \(D_R(L_R(A),L_R(B))\). The seed is independent of the inputs and available to both encoders and the decoder. Seed length and local computation are unrestricted and not charged; this is information-theoretic sketch length in bits, not streaming update time or the dimension of a real vector. The decoder knows \(n,c,R\), but receives no input-dependent information beyond the two sketches; any stored cardinality is charged. The same encoder works for both inputs. Success is required for each fixed pair chosen independently of \(R\), not simultaneously for all pairs under one seed or against adaptive exposure of the seed. When \(A=B\), success requires estimate zero. Define \(s(n,c)\) as the least integer \(s\geq0\) admitting such a scheme; it is finite because the entire \(n^2\)-bit incidence vector can be stored. The displayed interval fixes the usual one-sided multiplicative convention explicitly; it is not an additive-error guarantee.
answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g(n,c)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \(a g(n,c)\leq s(n,c)\leq b g(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\) and every \(c\geq1\). The upper bound must supply schemes with the stated probability and bit length; the lower bound must cover all allowed, possibly nonlinear, public-coin schemes. Constants and \(n_0\) cannot depend on \(c\), so varying approximation regimes and logarithmic factors must be accounted for. A single upper bound, a linear-embedding lower bound alone, or the answer for only one fixed approximation factor does not determine the requested tradeoff.
context:
Indyk’s 2011 question asks for the sketch-length/approximation tradeoff and highlights the possibility of constant \(c\) with \(s=\operatorname{polylog}n\). The card retains that full tradeoff and specifies the grid, masses, randomness and approximation convention.

A sketch must be computed without seeing the other set. The decoder then estimates one transport cost from two compressed descriptions. A fast algorithm that reads both complete inputs can exploit information that the sketch decoder does not have.

Andoni, Do Ba, Indyk and Woodruff prove that, for any fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), a sketch of polynomially sublinear grid-size dependence can obtain approximation \(O(1/\varepsilon)\). Their Theorem 1.1 uses \(O(n^\varepsilon)\) integer coordinates of polynomial magnitude; for sets this converts to \(O(n^\varepsilon\log n)\) bits. Thus constant-factor approximation is possible with more than polylogarithmic space in the stated construction.

Andoni, Krauthgamer and Razenshteyn prove that the full planar transportation norm cannot have both constant approximation and constant-size distance-threshold sketches. That norm allows general signed real mass vectors; the theorem neither identifies this subset-only bit tradeoff nor rules out polylogarithmic sketches.

The published STOC 2026 lower bound of Gartland and Ostrovskii closes the planar \(L_1\)-distortion gap for transportation cost spaces at order \(\log n\). An embedding theorem is not a theorem about every arbitrary decoder of two finite sketches, so this result does not automatically resolve the present question.

The number of grid locations and the number of occupied points are different parameters. Here the grid side length is the parameter and every equal-size pair is covered. Likewise, replacing the one-unit point masses by arbitrary weighted distributions would enlarge the input family.
why: EMD sketching asks how much information must be retained to compare geometric mass distributions without keeping the original data. Sharp tradeoffs would clarify the limits of metric compression and the distinction between embeddings, sketches and full-input transport algorithms.
status_note: The full tradeoff and highlighted constant-approximation/polylogarithmic-size question are open in the 2011 source. The bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no matching characterization for this exact subset and public-coin model. Full transportation-norm and L₁-distortion results have been checked separately and do not by themselves certify a resolution.
progress: 2009: Theorem 1.1 provides sublinear-size sketches with constant approximation when its parameter is fixed. | 2011: Indyk records the tradeoff question and specifically asks for constant approximation with polylogarithmic bit length. | 2015–2017: Sketching/embedding equivalences imply nonconstant resources for the full transportation norm, with a different input domain and threshold task. | 2026-06-09: The planar L₁-distortion gap is closed in the STOC publication; this is not a general sketch-decoder lower bound.
working_summary: Each planar grid subset must be compressed independently before the other input is available. The decoder uses the two bit strings to estimate the minimum Manhattan-cost matching of equal-size sets. The target is the optimal tradeoff between sketch length and multiplicative approximation, with constant success probability for every fixed pair. Known embedding and full transportation-norm results do not automatically characterize arbitrary decoders for these subset sketches. Sharp bounds would establish how much information optimal-transport comparisons must retain.

title: Near-quadratic Voronoi complexity of lines in three dimensions
importance_reason: This is a central unresolved complexity gap for a fundamental three-dimensional proximity structure, closely connected to lower-envelope and arrangement bounds.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that every regular Euclidean Voronoi diagram of \(n\ge2\) distinct affine lines in \(\mathbb R^3\), under the exact stratum convention below, has total complexity at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\)?
definitions: A line is the set \(\ell_i=\{p_i+tv_i:t\in\mathbb R\}\), where \(p_i,v_i\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(v_i\ne0\). Distances are ordinary Euclidean point-to-line distances. For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(V_I\) to be the set of points whose set of nearest lines is exactly \(\{\ell_i:i\in I\}\). Regular means that \(V_I\) is empty for \(|I|>4\), and for \(1\le|I|\le4\) each nonempty \(V_I\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(4-|I|\). The cells counted are the connected components of every nonempty \(V_I\), including unbounded components and zero-dimensional components. Let \(b_0(V_I)\) be the number of such components, with \(b_0(\varnothing)=0\); total complexity is \(\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]}b_0(V_I)\). These semialgebraic sets have finitely many connected components. The statement is an extremal mathematical bound; no bit encoding or construction algorithm for real coordinates is required. The constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the lines or their coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated bound for every \(\varepsilon>0\) on all diagrams in the defined regular class, or prove its logical negation in Lean: some \(\varepsilon_0>0\) has unbounded total complexity divided by \(n^{2+\varepsilon_0}\) over that class. The count must include connected components in all four dimensions, including unbounded ones. A bound only for four sites, one ruled-surface family, vertices alone, or a different metric does not establish the full statement.
context:
At each point of space, the nearest-line set describes which sites compete to be closest. Regions with one nearest line, interfaces with two, curves with three, and isolated points with four form the strata counted here. A stratum can have several connected components, and unbounded components count as well. Counting just the input lines would omit this geometric arrangement.

The question concerns Euclidean distance to complete affine lines in three dimensions. The source records a quadratic lower bound and an upper bound of \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), leaving a full exponent gap. A nearest-point diagram, a planar diagram, or a polyhedral distance function is a different object.

The conjectured guarantee is \(n^{2+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), with a constant allowed to depend on that exponent slack. It does not require a single \(Cn^2\) bound. Conversely, a bound with one fixed exponent strictly above two does not meet the universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon\).

The source also distinguishes the full diagram from a fixed-distance level set, describable through a union of cylinders. Complexity controlled at one distance does not automatically count all strata of the nearest-site partition throughout space.

The March 2026 four-line classification describes a base case with zero through eight Voronoi vertices under general-position assumptions. The result clarifies local configurations, but fixes the number of sites and supplies no asymptotic bound for arbitrary input size.

The August 2026 regulus preprint claims quadratic total complexity when all lines lie in one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric: one of the two line families covering that surface. Its hypotheses strongly restrict the line configuration. It explicitly retains the broader quadratic-to-cubic gap for arbitrary Euclidean line sites. The present card spells out its own regular-stratum convention rather than leaving “general position” undefined.
why: This is a central unresolved complexity gap for a fundamental three-dimensional proximity structure, closely connected to lower-envelope and arrangement bounds.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The August 2026 regulus preprint still records the general quadratic-to-cubic gap; its quadratic theorem and the March four-line classification are restricted results. This benchmark retains the explicitly defined regular-stratum interpretation from the preceding individual development, without claiming that every source uses identical degeneracy conventions. No matching resolution was located; new proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2001: The problem source records the near-quadratic conjecture and the gap to the known general upper bound. | 2026-03-20: A preprint classifies general-position four-line diagrams; the cardinality is fixed. | 2026-08-27: A preprint claims quadratic complexity for one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric, while retaining the unrestricted gap.
working_summary: Each point in three-dimensional space has a set of nearest input lines. Connected regions with the same nearest-line set form the diagram’s cells. The question counts cells of all dimensions. The proposed bound is arbitrarily close to quadratic. The Euclidean metric and the specified nondegeneracy convention are essential parts of this formulation.

title: coNP certificates for three-manifold homeomorphism
importance_reason: A broad certificate question for distinguishing topological types, with a consequential implication for graph nonisomorphism via the known many-one reduction.
formal: Does nonhomeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Allow boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) with total input length \(N\), \[\neg H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;W(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the coNP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem.
definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(p,W\) exist, or that none exist. A positive answer needs a short accepted witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair and rejection of every candidate witness for every homeomorphic promised pair. Verification time must be polynomial in \(N+|w|\) on every binary input. A particular invariant that distinguishes only some pairs is insufficient. A negative answer must rule out all polynomial certificate systems, rather than showing the inadequacy of one invariant or representation. Conditional upper bounds qualify only if the additional hypothesis is also proved.
context:
Schleimer states this as Question 4, separately from NP membership and NP-hardness. Its quantifiers run over nonhomeomorphic pairs; changing the sign of the target changes which instances need certificates.

Different triangulations can share many familiar invariants without being homeomorphic. The card does not prescribe an invariant: an accepted certificate system may use any finite evidence, but it must be complete for every pair in the full domain.

Lackenby gives a polynomial-time many-one reduction from graph isomorphism to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Consequently a coNP certificate system for the domain here would also provide polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism. The implication runs from a manifold upper bound to a graph upper bound.

Jackson’s naming theorem provides both NP and coNP certificates within the compact orientable Seifert setting with nonempty boundary. These two-sided certificates apply to the specified naming problem, not arbitrary pairs of triangulated 3-manifolds.

A decidability theorem guarantees that a search eventually terminates. It does not bound the size of evidence for a negative answer by a polynomial. Similarly, an NP system for homeomorphic pairs supplies no general witness for the opposite answer.

If homeomorphism were both NP-hard under the valid-output reductions defined in the related hardness card and in coNP, then \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). This is a logical consequence of the two prospective results, not a proof that either is false.
why: The question asks whether topological difference always has efficiently checkable finite evidence. Its reduction from graph isomorphism ties the difficulty of distinguishing 3-manifolds to a central unresolved certificate problem in complexity theory.
status_note: The general coNP question is explicitly open in the 2024 report. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no general result meeting these unconditional quantifiers. Special Seifert naming certificates do not establish the full target.
progress: 2017: Lackenby proves the graph-isomorphism reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. | 2024-02: Schleimer poses the coNP question and discusses its connection to graph isomorphism. | 2024-06-20: Jackson proves two-sided certificates for a Seifert naming problem with boundary.
working_summary: The homeomorphism problem asks whether two triangulations represent the same three-dimensional space. This card asks for short certificates precisely when those spaces are not homeomorphic. Every nonhomeomorphic pair must have verifiable evidence, including pairs that agree on familiar invariants. A general positive result would imply polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism through a known reduction. It would clarify whether topological distinction has a uniformly efficient theory of verification.

title: Point location in three-dimensional subdivisions
importance_reason: A central static spatial-search problem asking whether linear representation size can coexist with logarithmic exact navigation in arbitrary three-dimensional subdivisions.
formal: Do there exist uniform deterministic preprocessing and query algorithms that, for every explicitly represented polyhedral subdivision of a three-dimensional box of total boundary complexity \(n\), store \(O(n)\) words and answer every point-location query in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time? A query gives an arbitrary point \(q\in\mathbb R^3\) and must return the label of a subdivision region whose closure contains \(q\), or the exterior label for points outside the box. Constants are universal, the guarantee is exact, and the subdivision may have nonconvex regions.
definitions: The input includes a bounded axis-aligned box \(B\) with nonempty interior, real coordinates of vertices, an embedded finite triangle mesh containing \(\partial B\), and the labels of the two incident regions of every triangle (one label is the exterior on \(\partial B\)). Nondegenerate closed triangles meet only in a common whole edge, a common vertex, or not at all. The input is promised to describe the boundaries of a partition: bounded regions are closures of the connected components of \(\operatorname{int}(B)\) minus the mesh, with disjoint interiors and no unrepresented boundary; the exterior region is \(\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(B)\). Arbitrary topology and collinear or coplanar incidences consistent with these conditions are allowed. Bounded regions have distinct labels \(1,\ldots,r\), with \(r\leq n\), and the exterior has label zero. All vertex coordinates, triangle vertex-index triples and incident labels are explicitly listed. Define \(n\) as their total number of real-coordinate and integer-index entries, including the box. Thus complicated polygon boundaries are charged through their triangulated representation. Any incident region is acceptable for a query on a shared face, edge or vertex, including the exterior on \(\partial B\). The algorithms are finite deterministic programs independent of the input, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each real \(+,-,\times,/\) operation on its domain, comparison, copy or memory access costs one step. Each stored word contains one real or one integer; query-stage integer words have \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged. Floor and digit extraction from reals, size-dependent advice and free geometric oracles are excluded. Storage includes the input retained for queries and temporary query workspace. Preprocessing must halt on every valid input but has no prescribed time or temporary-space bound; only the final stored structure and each query have the stated bounds.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such algorithms, or refute it, with a complete Lean-checked proof. Existence requires constants \(C_s,C_q\) and one pair of uniform algorithms such that every valid subdivision yields a structure of at most \(C_s n\) words and every query is answered correctly within \(C_q\log_2(n+2)\) steps. Refutation must exclude all such pairs in the defined model. Expected performance, a query-distribution promise, linear storage with slower queries, or logarithmic queries with superlinear storage do not establish the positive statement.
context:
The Open Problems Project asks for linear space and logarithmic point-location queries in a three-dimensional subdivision. Snoeyink’s 2017 handbook version states the question for a subdivision with a linear number of faces and vertices. This card makes the total boundary representation explicit; it does not count an arbitrarily complicated polygonal face as a constant-size input.

The source asks for a data structure: one preprocessing stage must support arbitrary later queries without knowing them in advance. Checking membership in every region can save storage but loses the logarithmic query requirement.

The 2017 handbook reports \(O(n\log n)\) space and \(O(\log^2 n)\) query time for general three-dimensional subdivisions, with \(O(n\log n)\) preprocessing. Its Section 38.6 then explicitly lists achieving both target bounds as open.

The same section distinguishes point membership in a single convex polyhedron and subdivisions into axis-aligned boxes, where stronger bounds are known. An algorithm restricted to those objects does not handle the arbitrary oblique subdivision boundaries in this card.

A boundary convention is necessary for exact inputs: a query may fall on a face shared by several regions. Returning any incident label avoids making the answer undefined while preserving the search task. No average over query positions or perturbation promise is used.

The target measures words and exact arithmetic operations. The finite representation and word operations prevent treating a real constant as a free oracle encoding answers to all queries; no claim about bounded coordinate bit lengths is implicit in the statement.
why: Point location is a basic spatial-search operation. Resolving the simultaneous storage and query bounds would establish whether arbitrary three-dimensional partitions admit the same asymptotic search economy as planar subdivisions.
status_note: The checked 2017 handbook explicitly retains the joint bound as open. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no resolution for the general subdivision model. The triangulated total-complexity representation and deterministic arithmetic conventions are explicit editorial specifications, rather than hidden assumptions about arbitrary face sizes.
progress: 2001: The Open Problems Project records the simultaneous linear-space/logarithmic-query target. | 2017-08-10: The third-edition handbook retains the problem and distinguishes known general bounds from convex and orthogonal special cases.
working_summary: A three-dimensional subdivision divides space into labelled polyhedral regions. After preprocessing the boundary representation, a query asks for the region containing an arbitrary supplied point. The target is simultaneous linear storage and logarithmic worst-case query time, measured in the total representation size. Queries on boundaries may return any incident region, and neither random queries nor convex cells are assumed. A resolution would determine whether arbitrary spatial partitions can support exact search as economically as planar ones.

title: NP-hardness of three-manifold homeomorphism
importance_reason: A major lower-bound question for topological equivalence, asking whether general NP computation can be encoded in valid pairs of 3-manifolds.
formal: Is homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Use the domain \(\mathcal D\) below, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Equivalently, is there one uniform polynomial-time Turing machine \(R\) which, on every binary string \(x\), outputs a valid pair \((T_x,U_x)\in\mathcal D\), such that \[x\in\mathrm{3SAT}\iff H(T_x,U_x)?\] Outputs must satisfy the manifold promise on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs.
definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning. The language \(\mathrm{3SAT}\) consists of encodings of satisfiable conjunctions of clauses containing at most three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variable indices and the entire clause list are explicitly encoded in binary; malformed strings are outside the language. A many-one reduction returns one pair, with its entire length and construction time bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\). It does not query a homeomorphism oracle or obtain a sequence of adaptive answers. The verifier machinery in the common domain description is not an extra NP-membership assumption on homeomorphism. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, the stated valid-output reduction gives a reduction from every NP language to this promised problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a valid-output reduction exists, or that no such deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists. A positive result must establish the polynomial resource bound, validity of every output manifold and both directions of the satisfiability/homeomorphism equivalence. A negative result must exclude all reductions of this kind. NP-hardness of a related knot, embedding or triangulation-optimization task is insufficient without a reduction to this exact equivalence question. No proof that homeomorphism belongs to NP is required for the positive answer.
context:
Schleimer’s Question 5, attributed there to Burton, asks for NP-hardness of Homeo(3). This card fixes polynomial-time many-one reductions and requires valid triangulated manifolds on every output.

NP-hardness is a lower-bound comparison: any polynomial-time algorithm for homeomorphism would then decide every NP language in polynomial time. It does not assert NP membership, and hence does not by itself assert NP-completeness.

Lackenby establishes hardness relative to graph isomorphism through a many-one reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Graph-isomorphism hardness alone is not the required NP-hardness theorem.

Kuperberg’s elementary-recursive algorithm concerns closed oriented manifolds and provides an upper bound on decision complexity. Such an upper bound is compatible with NP-hardness; decidability and NP-hardness are not mutually exclusive.

The yes/no orientation of the reduction matters. A transformation that sends satisfiable formulas to nonhomeomorphic pairs would instead compare SAT with the complement problem. Likewise, allowing invalid geometric outputs would evade the promised decision task.

A positive answer together with a general NP certificate theorem would make the promised homeomorphism problem NP-complete under valid-output reductions. Combined instead with a coNP certificate theorem, it would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). These consequences explain why the three questions are retained separately.
why: NP-hardness would locate a central topological classification task relative to general combinatorial search. It would supply a stronger complexity obstruction than the currently known reduction from graph isomorphism.
status_note: The NP-hardness question is open in the checked 2024 report, and the 2025 discussion retains graph-isomorphism hardness as the known comparison. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no valid-output NP-hardness resolution for the stated target.
progress: 2017: Lackenby gives a many-one reduction from graph isomorphism to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. | 2024-02: Schleimer records Burton’s NP-hardness question separately from the two certificate questions. | 2025: The later seminar discussion continues to describe graph-isomorphism hardness while asking a parameterized homeomorphism question.
working_summary: Deciding whether two triangulated three-manifolds are homeomorphic has algorithms, but decidability alone says little about feasible running time. This question seeks an NP-hardness lower bound for the general decision problem. A reduction would have to encode arbitrary instances of a known hard problem into pairs of manifolds. Hardness of related knot or triangulation optimization tasks does not immediately supply that encoding. Such a result would locate manifold equivalence more precisely among familiar computational problems and constrain expectations for general-purpose recognition algorithms.

title: Polygon visibility graph recognition
importance_reason: A longstanding graph-realization problem whose difficulty persists even with the polygon boundary order fixed; it tests the boundary between combinatorial recognition and real-coordinate geometry.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a cyclic order \(C=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of its vertices, decides whether some simple polygon with these labelled vertices in boundary order \(C\) has visibility graph exactly \(G\)? Here \(n\geq3\), the graph is given by its complete adjacency matrix and the cyclic order by an explicit list. Both visible and nonvisible pairs must be realized, and the polygon has no holes or additional vertices.
definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm P\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.
context:
The source problem supplies the boundary order as well as the graph. This removes the need to search for a Hamiltonian boundary cycle, but leaves the geometric realizability question. The statement above fixes simple closed polygons and closed-segment visibility explicitly.

Constructing the visibility graph of an already drawn polygon and recognizing a graph that could arise from some polygon are different tasks. Recognition has to account simultaneously for every edge and every absent edge without being given any coordinates.

The 2024 compendium by Schaefer, Cardinal and Miltzow explicitly retains polygon visibility recognition as open even when the boundary order is supplied. It defines visibility by containment of the complete joining segment in the polygon.

The same compendium distinguishes several related recognition problems with \(\exists\mathbb R\) hardness or completeness results, including polygons with holes and simultaneous interior/exterior visibility. Those results impose different objects or additional data and do not settle this simple-polygon problem. Here \(\exists\mathbb R\) denotes problems reducible in polynomial time to the existence of real solutions of finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Lin and Skiena study coordinate requirements for realizing visibility graphs. The fact that a realization is a finite list of real points does not by itself make it a polynomial-length certificate in the Turing model.

A polynomial algorithm would identify when a purely combinatorial collection of sight lines can come from one polygonal environment. The fixed boundary order is part of the scientific question; discarding it or requiring a convex polygon would change the class being recognized.
why: The problem is a central inverse question about geometric visibility: whether pairwise sight-line information and a boundary order can be tested for realizability efficiently. It connects graph recognition with geometric representation complexity.
status_note: The specified fixed-order recognition question remains explicitly open in the checked 2024 compendium. The bounded search through 13 September 2026 did not locate a later resolution. Closed visibility and permitted collinear labelled vertices are explicit formulation conventions; no unrestricted rational-witness assumption is used.
progress: 1995: Lin and Skiena investigate representation complexity and its bearing on short recognition certificates. | 2001: The Open Problems Project lists the fixed-boundary-order polynomial recognition question. | 2024-07-25: The compendium explicitly states that recognition remains open even with boundary order given.
working_summary: A polygon's visibility graph records which pairs of vertices can be joined by a segment lying inside the polygon. The source supplies both a candidate graph and a Hamiltonian cycle specifying the intended polygon boundary. It asks for an efficient decision procedure for whether a simple polygon realizes exactly that information. Choosing coordinates must satisfy visibility and obstruction requirements simultaneously. The problem tests whether a combinatorial record of sight lines contains enough accessible structure to reconstruct a genuine geometric environment.

title: Estimating Earth-Mover Distance
importance_reason: Estimating Earth Mover Distance concerns the efficient approximation of a widely used transportation metric.
formal: Estimating Earth-Mover Distance
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: A stream presents red and blue points on a planar grid, with equally many points of each color. Their Earth Mover Distance is the minimum total cost of matching each red point to a blue point. The source asks which approximation guarantees are possible when the stream can be retained only through a small memory state. A central target is constant-factor approximation with space polynomial in the logarithms of the input and grid sizes. Transportation structure must be captured without storing all points or the matching itself.

title: Linear-size universal point sets for planar graphs
importance_reason: This asks whether a linear geometric host can represent all planar combinatorial structures of a given size, rather than dedicating a separate layout to each graph.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some set \(U_n\subset\mathbb R^2\) of at most \(Cn\) distinct points supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices?
definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.
context:
A universal point set is chosen before the graph is known. Once a graph arrives, its vertices may be assigned to any suitable distinct points of that same set. The question is whether a constant number of available points per graph vertex always suffices for every planar graph of that size.

Location matters even for four vertices. The complete graph on four vertices is planar, but putting all four vertices on the corners of a convex quadrilateral forces its two diagonals to cross. A planar straight-line drawing can instead place one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three. Thus a large collection of points in convex position is not by itself universal for planar graphs.

Classical straight-line grid-drawing theorems give a universal \(O(n)\)-by-\(O(n)\) grid and therefore \(O(n^2)\) available points. Lower bounds exceeding \(n\) show that using exactly one point per vertex is too restrictive in general, but a constant-factor lower bound does not refute the existence of some larger universal linear constant.

The 2023 work gives linear-size sets for restricted classes of planar graphs. A host set for a class with additional structural constraints need not support all planar graphs. This is why the quantified graph family, as well as the number of points, is part of the target.

A preprint posted on 10 September 2026 claims universal sets of size \(n^{1+o(1)}\) for unrestricted planar graphs. This improves the stated general upper frontier if its proof is correct, but it does not assert \(Cn\) for a fixed constant. For example, \(n\log n\) also has the form \(n^{1+o(1)}\) while its ratio to \(n\) is unbounded. The preprint’s claim is recorded without an independent proof audit.

The input graph has no prescribed embedding or fixed correspondence between vertex labels and host points. Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers. Allowing a bend in each edge, prescribing the vertex-to-point assignment, or requiring a small integer grid would change the existence question.
why: This asks whether a linear geometric host can represent all planar combinatorial structures of a given size, rather than dedicating a separate layout to each graph.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Gordon’s new preprint claims n^{1+o(1)} universal point sets for general planar graphs, but does not state the fixed-constant linear bound requested here. The new proof has not been independently verified. No proof or refutation of the O(n) target was located in the bounded source search.
progress: 2023: Linear-size constructions for restricted planar graph classes do not establish a universal linear bound for all planar graphs. | 2026-09-10: Gordon’s preprint claims an unrestricted \(n^{1+o(1)}\) upper bound. This is not a constant-factor linear bound, and the proof has not been independently verified in this pass.
working_summary: One point set is selected for each graph size. Every planar graph of that size must have a straight-line drawing using some of those points. Vertex assignments may depend on the graph. The question asks whether only linearly many points suffice. Results for subclasses do not settle the universal requirement.

title: Polynomial flip-distance bounds for three-manifold triangulations
importance_reason: Polynomial bounds for triangulation transformations would give quantitative control over topological equivalence representations.
formal: Polynomial flip-distance bounds for three-manifold triangulations
context: Computing invariants and deciding topological properties. Dimension and the finite representation of a space are crucial.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Triangulations of the same compact three-manifold are connected by local bistellar flips. The question asks whether two triangulations can always be connected using polynomially many such moves in their input sizes. The polynomial is initially allowed to depend on the fixed manifold. A path may temporarily use different numbers of tetrahedra, so connectivity alone provides no useful quantitative bound. title: NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds
importance_reason: Short certificates for recognizing major three-manifold classes would refine the algorithmic structure of topological classification.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that, for every finite PL-triangulation T of a compact connected three-manifold M, M is closed and admits a hyperbolic metric if and only if there exists a binary certificate w with |\(w|\le p(|T|)\) and \(V(T,w)=1\)?
definitions: The input consists of t abstract tetrahedra and a finite list of affine face identifications, each encoded by two tetrahedron indices, face indices and a permutation of the face vertices. Unpaired faces are permitted. Identifying these faces produces the quotient space \(M=|T|\). The input is promised to be a PL-triangulation of a compact connected topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary; no orientability or irreducibility promise is imposed. Its encoding length |T| counts all bits in the explicit tetrahedron and face-pairing data, with binary indices. Closed means that M has empty boundary, since compactness is already promised. A hyperbolic metric means a Riemannian metric locally isometric to hyperbolic three-space \(H^{3}\); for example \(H^{3}\) is the upper half-space \(\{(x,y,z)\in \mathbb{R} ^{3}:z>0\}\) with metric \(ds^{2}=(dx^{2}+dy^{2}+dz^{2})/z^{2}\). Equivalently, the metric has constant sectional curvature −1. On closed M it is complete. The abstract tetrahedra in the input are topological data and are not supplied as geometric tetrahedra in that metric. V is one uniform deterministic Turing algorithm without advice or an oracle, and runs in time polynomial in |T|+|w| on all encoded inputs. Correctness is required on every promised manifold triangulation; no particular certificate format or method is prescribed. The polynomial certificate bound and verifier are fixed for the entire problem, not chosen separately for each manifold.
answer_criterion: Give a polynomial certificate bound and a uniform polynomial-time verifier that accepts some bounded-length certificate for every closed hyperbolic input and accepts none for every other promised manifold input. Alternatively, prove that no such bound and verifier exist. A terminating recognition algorithm alone, or certificates for non-hyperbolicity, do not establish this NP membership.
context:
The input says which faces of finitely many tetrahedra are glued together. It determines a topological space, but does not hand the verifier a hyperbolic metric. The question asks whether existence of that global geometric structure always has a short, efficiently checkable witness.

Two very different gluing descriptions can represent the same manifold. A successful verifier must accept every description of a closed hyperbolic manifold with some certificate polynomial in that description’s size. It cannot be limited to triangulations that visibly carry a convenient geometric structure.

Schleimer’s 2024 report records decidability of hyperbolic recognition and separately asks for NP membership. Decidability guarantees eventual termination; NP requires a polynomial bound on both the witness size and verification work.

Haraway and Hoffman study non-hyperbolicity certificates for orientable manifolds with torus boundary. Their results give coNP statements about hyperbolicity in that setting. The present question concerns positive certificates for closed hyperbolic manifolds, so it has both a different input class and a different answer direction.
why: Would show that a global constant-curvature geometry can always be certified using polynomially bounded discrete evidence from an arbitrary triangulation. It would sharpen the complexity of a central geometric recognition problem beyond mere decidability.
status_note: Original manifold and triangulation conventions recovered, and subsequent-work searches checked through 11 September 2026; no matching NP-resolution result located. Related cusped non-hyperbolicity results have different promises and answer direction. Proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2002: The 2024 report attributes decidability of hyperbolic recognition to Casson and Manning, while retaining the stronger NP question. | 2022-09: Haraway and Hoffman give non-hyperbolicity certificates in the cusped orientable setting; their Theorem 1 assumes \(S^{3}\) recognition lies in coNP, while their irreducible cusped case is unconditional. | 2024: Schleimer explicitly poses NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds as Question 12.

title: Half-snowflake embeddings into Wasserstein p-space
importance_reason: A structural universality conjecture about transport metrics that asks for a larger snowflake exponent with size-independent distortion. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed real \(p\in(2,\infty)\), does there exist a finite constant \(C_p\ge1\) such that every finite metric space \((X,d)\) admits a map \(F:X\to\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) and a scale \(s>0\) satisfying \(s\sqrt{d(x,y)}\le W_p(F(x),F(y))\le C_p s\sqrt{d(x,y)}\) for all \(x,y\in X\)? The constant may depend on p but must be independent of X, its number of points and its distances.
definitions:
A finite metric space consists of a finite set X and a symmetric function d:X×X→[0,∞) with d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its half-snowflake is the metric space with distance √d(x,y). The square root applies to the original distances, not to the Wasserstein distance or to the dimension. Distances in the base space R³ are the usual Euclidean distances.

The set \(\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) consists of Borel probability measures μ on R³ satisfying \(\int\|u\|_2^p\,d\mu(u)<\infty\). A coupling of μ and ν is a probability measure π on R³×R³ with these two marginals. Write Π(μ,ν) for all such couplings. The Wasserstein metric is \(W_p(\mu,\nu)=(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|u-v\|_2^p\,d\pi(u,v))^{1/p}\). Thus the transport cost uses the pth power of Euclidean distance and takes a pth root after minimizing. Images may be arbitrary measures of finite pth moment; no support-size, equal-mass, rational-coordinate or computability restriction is imposed.

The two-sided inequality means a bi-Lipschitz embedding of distortion at most C_p after a common rescaling s. It forces F to be injective when X has more than one point. Both F and s may depend on p and the entire finite metric. The quantifier order is ∀p>2 ∃C_p<∞ ∀(X,d) ∃F,s; there is no single bound required to work uniformly as p varies, and p=∞ is excluded. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic running-time target.

The source writes c_Y(X,√d)≤D_p, where c_Y is the infimum of the distortions of all embeddings. The infimum need not be attained. Existence of some finite uniform bound in that formulation is equivalent to the displayed formulation: increasing an available finite infimum bound, for example to twice its value, allows actual embeddings for each finite X. The source's stronger suggestion D_p=1 instead means distortion arbitrarily close to one for every finite metric. It must not be silently replaced by a demand for an attained isometric embedding, and neither strengthening is required here.

The already-proved theorem embeds the 1/p-snowflake, with distances d(x,y)^{1/p}, with distortion arbitrarily close to one. When p>2 its exponent is smaller than 1/2, so it does not answer this question. At p=2 it does give the half-snowflake result; that endpoint is background, outside the unresolved range.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform-in-X finite-distortion assertion for every fixed p>2, or refute it by finding a fixed p>2 for which half-snowflake distortions into this exact target space are unbounded across finite metrics. A single finite metric with distortion greater than one does not refute the claim. Results allowing the distortion or base-space dimension to grow with |X|, or using exponent 1/p instead of 1/2, do not settle it. No optimal numerical value of C_p is requested.

The source separately raises almost-isometric half-snowflake embeddings, embeddings of the entire Wasserstein-2 space into Wasserstein-p space, and sharp lower bounds above exponent 1/2. Those are not substituted for this finite-distortion conjecture.

title: Decidability of contractibility for finite two-dimensional complexes
importance_reason: A foundational low-dimensional decidability boundary linking computational topology and balanced group presentations. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, on every finite nonempty simplicial complex \(K\) of dimension at most two, halts and decides whether \(K\) is simple-homotopy equivalent to a point? Equivalently, can contractibility of all such \(K\) be decided?
question_excerpt: Hence, any pair of contractible 2-complexes can be connected by a simple-homotopy equivalence of dimension at most four – but determining whether we can always […]
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.

title: Linear-size sample compression
importance_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
focus_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class \(H\subseteq \{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge 1\) admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying \(k+b\le Cd\), in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept \(h\in H\) is a total function \(X\to \{0,1\}\). A finite set \(A\subseteq X\) is shattered if \(\{h|_{A}:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{A}; d\) is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times \{0,1\}\) agreeing with some \(h\in H\). A scheme consists of deterministic maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\), which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable \(S, \kappa (S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\) is an unordered labeled subset with |\(T|\le k\) and \(z\in \{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor \(\rho (T,z):X\to \{0,1\}\) agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size \(2^{O(d)}\), settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size \(O(t \log (t+1))\) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.
why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

The claimed breakthrough at arXiv:2603.23561 is withdrawn and is included only to document its status. working_summary: Sample compression represents a labeled training set by retaining only a few examples and a bounded amount of extra information. A fixed reconstruction rule must recover a hypothesis agreeing with every original training label whenever the sample is realizable. This project asks whether every binary class of VC dimension d admits a scheme whose total charged size is proportional to d. title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.
focus_reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.
formal: For every fixed rational noise rate \(\eta\) with \(0<\eta <1/2\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret \(s\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), recovers s with probability at least \(2/3\) from independent samples \((a,\langle a,s\rangle \oplus e)\), where a is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and e is independently \(Bernoulli(\eta )\)?
definitions: The inner product \(\langle a,s\rangle\) is \(\sum_{i} a_{i} s_{i}\) modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with \(\Pr [e=1]=\eta\). The learner knows n and the fixed rate \(\eta\), and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed \(\eta\) the algorithm and its polynomial bound \(p\eta\) may depend on \(\eta\), but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most \(p\eta (n)\) bit operations and requests at most \(p\eta (n)\) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational \(\eta\) does not demand a running-time bound uniform as \(\eta\) approaches \(1/2\) with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability \(1- \eta\). Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the \(2^{n}\) candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At \(\eta =1/4\), for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement \(3/4\), while every incorrect parity has expected agreement \(1/2\). A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a \(2^{O(n/\log  n)}\)-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) examples for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). The resulting running time is \(2^{O(n/\log  \log  n)}\). This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either \(\Omega (n^{2}/(1/2- \eta ))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed \(\eta\), the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by \(b\oplus \langle a,r\rangle\), learn the masked secret \(s\oplus r\) and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.
why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.
status_note: The primary literature checked through 11 September 2026 leaves classical polynomial-time learning at fixed constant noise open. The card asks for all fixed rational rates separately, allowing rate-dependent polynomial bounds. The September 2026 reduction is conditional; sparse, quantum-example and limited-memory models do not replace the specified problem.
