working_summary: A parity function returns the XOR of a hidden subset of input coordinates. Without label noise, random examples produce linear equations that reveal the hidden subset efficiently. This project asks whether a polynomial-time classical algorithm can still recover it when each label is independently flipped at a fixed rate below one half. Polynomially many samples contain enough information, but searching all candidate subsets takes exponential time. An efficient learner must avoid that search using only ordinary random examples, without chosen noiseless queries or restrictions that make the unknown subset sparse.

title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
importance_reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
focus_reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n, 2^{k}\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), with uniform-distribution error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: For integers \(0\le k\le n, a k\)-junta is a function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) for which there is an unknown set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}, |S|\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that \(f(x)=g\)(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer \(t\ge 3\), setting \(\varepsilon =1/t\). Each requested example consists of an independently uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) and its exact, noiseless label \(f(x)\). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least \(2/3\) over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that \(h(x)\ne f(x)\) is at most \(1/t\). One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most \((n+2^{k}+t)^{C}\) steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of \(2^{k}\) is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with \(2^{k}\) entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about \(n^{k}\) possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most \((k+1)n^{k}\cdot 2^{2^{k}}\) juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that \(O((2^{k}+k \log (n+1)+\log (k+1)+1)/\varepsilon )\) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most \(\varepsilon\), with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately \(n^{0.704k}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(n,2^{k})\) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and \(2^{k}\), through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, \(f(x)=x_{1} \mathrm{XOR} x_{2} \mathrm{XOR} x_{3}\) is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and \(2^{k}\) is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most \(2^{k}\). Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class \(F_{k}\) of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^{k},1/\varepsilon )\) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when \(k=O(\log  n); a\) learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. Conditional hardness allowed as an outcome in the source is also weaker than an unconditional negative answer here. The source record is consolidated as a related milestone, not asserted to be an equivalent formulation; The removed TCS-0023 keeps its reserved ID and deletion reason; its bibliography and weaker milestone are preserved here.
why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.
status_note: No general learner with the stated polynomial dependence, or impossibility theorem for unrestricted learners, was found through 11 September 2026. Current sources retain the uniform-example barrier. Efficient membership-query, monotone-junta and correlated-random-walk results do not meet this exact model.

working_summary: A Boolean junta depends on only k coordinates even though its input contains n possible features. The project asks whether it can be learned from uniformly random labeled examples in time polynomial in n, the size of its k-variable truth table, and the inverse error tolerance. The allowed exponential dependence on k accommodates an arbitrary function of the relevant coordinates. The difficult step is locating useful coordinates without enumerating all possible subsets of the n features. A learner with this guarantee would turn hidden low-dimensional structure into efficient prediction even when the number of relevant variables grows logarithmically with n.

title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
importance_reason: A defining computational learning problem originating with the PAC framework, explicitly highlighted in successive surveys and connected to representation-independent learning hardness, decision-tree learning and junta learning. Selected for the Learning theory focus prefix after correcting the mislabelled junta record; the score reflects breadth and foundational significance, not the date of this review.
focus_reason: A defining improper PAC-learning question for compact Boolean rules under arbitrary input distributions, with broad consequences for decision-tree and junta learning. The general target and its conditional-hardness evidence are now stated precisely.
formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every \(n,s\ge 1\), every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and all accuracy and confidence parameters \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n,s,1/\varepsilon\) and \(\log (1/\delta )\)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
definitions: A literal is a variable \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form \((\mathrm{DNF})\) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers \(t,b\ge 2\) and set \(\varepsilon =1/t\) and \(\delta =2^{- b}\). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(p(n,s,t,b)\) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair \((x,f(x))\) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least \(1- \delta\) over the examples and internal randomness, \(\Pr_{x\text{ drawn from }D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\). Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most \(3^{n}\) simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by \((3^{n}+1)^{s}\). The finite-class union bound therefore gives \(O((ns+\log (1/\delta ))/\varepsilon )\) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical \(n^{O(s)}\) algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound \(2^{\widetilde{O} (n^{1/3} \log  s)}\). For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most \(2^{k}\) terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.
why: Determine whether compact Boolean rules that need only polynomially many observations can also be learned with polynomial computation, without assumptions on the input distribution. A positive result would cover decision trees and uniform-example juntas; a negative result would identify a fundamental computational barrier in realizable learning even when the output representation is unrestricted.
status_note: No unconditional resolution was identified in the primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The 2025 survey retains the general computational gap; random-SAT and local-PRG lower bounds remain conditional, and the checked 2026 result changes the distribution and learning model.
progress: 2012: Feldman separates the general PAC question from Fourier-based learning under uniform or product distributions in the inherited source. | 2016: Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz prove improper-learning hardness under a random K-SAT refutation assumption. | 2021: Daniely–Vardi derive hardness for a growing number of DNF terms under a local-pseudorandom-generator assumption. | 2025-11-11: Servedio’s survey retains polynomial-time DNF learning as a longstanding goal and records the subexponential general upper bound. | 2026-05-17: Iterative Chow Filtering gives a quasipolynomial uniform-distribution result in a different learning model.
working_summary: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of Boolean literals, representing a union of rule-defined regions. The question asks whether an unknown DNF with at most s terms can be learned from independent labelled examples under every input distribution in time polynomial in n, s, inverse error and log inverse failure probability. The learner may output any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis but cannot request labels for inputs of its choice. Polynomially many samples suffice information-theoretically, while known hardness for unrestricted hypotheses relies on explicit complexity assumptions. A solution would settle a foundational computational-learning barrier and would also yield an efficient learner for uniform-example juntas.

title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
importance_reason: One of the simplest nonlinear concept classes whose efficient distribution-independent learnability remains unresolved.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified learner-existence statement or its negation in the specified arithmetic and sampling model. A positive answer includes the learner, its hypothesis representation, the polynomial training and evaluation bounds, and its distribution-independent accuracy guarantee. A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.
context:
A single separating hyperplane with a margin is a basic tractable classification model. Intersecting two such regions is already a substantial test of distribution-independent learning: allowing an arbitrary output hypothesis removes the requirement to recover two separating hyperplanes themselves.

Diakonikolas, Ma, Ren and Tzamos obtain an efficient learner when the distribution factors between the span of the two normal vectors and its orthogonal complement. Their general-model discussion on printed page 1473 leaves the distribution-free margin problem unresolved. The factorization promise is an additional assumption, not a consequence of a geometric margin.

A July 2026 revision by Alman, Patel and Servedio reports subexponential-time distribution-free learning for Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces. That running time does not meet the polynomial bound asked here.

A separate July 2026 revision by Patel and Vempala reports a margin-sensitive algorithm for intersections of a variable number of halfspaces. Its abstract does not establish a polynomial-time learner for two halfspaces; its discussion of matching lower bounds cannot be transferred to the fixed-two case without checking their parameter range.
why: This asks whether the simplest intersection of linear classification rules remains efficiently learnable from ordinary examples under arbitrary distributions. A positive answer would remove a distributional assumption from a central margin-learning model; a negative answer would establish a computational obstruction even when the learner may use any efficiently evaluable representation.
status_note: The 2025 source explicitly describes the general margin-learning question as open. On 13 September 2026, a targeted small-text search and the July revisions of two 2026 abstracts did not supply a resolution of the fixed-two polynomial-time target. The 2026 proofs and their complete lower-bound parameter regimes were not independently checked; status remains source_open.
progress: 2025: The published paper supplies the realizable two-margin-halfspace model and proves polynomial-time learning with an extra factorization assumption. | 2026-07-30: The revised preprint reports a subexponential algorithm for learning Boolean functions of a fixed number of unrestricted halfspaces; this does not yield the polynomial-time guarantee. | 2026-07-30: The revised margin-polyhedra preprint reports improved dependence on the margin and the number of halfspaces, with a dimension-dependent exponential term. Only the abstract was checked in this pass.
working_summary: The intersection of two halfspaces labels a point positively when both linear inequalities hold. This question asks whether such labels can be learned in polynomial time from independent examples under any distribution with a margin from both boundaries. The learner may output a different kind of hypothesis, provided that predictions remain efficient. The 2025 source proves efficient learning under an extra factorization assumption, while two 2026 preprints report broader bounds that do not by themselves meet this polynomial target. A resolution would determine whether two linear rules can be learned efficiently without favorable structure in the example distribution.

title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
importance_reason: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized learner which, for all \(n,s\ge 1\) and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), learns every size-at-most-s Boolean decision tree on n variables from uniform random labeled examples in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s,1/\varepsilon )\), with error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: A decision tree has internal nodes querying one input coordinate, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and leaves labeled zero or one. Size counts all nodes. Samples are independent uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) labeled by the unknown target f. The learner receives \(n,s,\varepsilon\) and may draw samples but cannot request labels at chosen inputs. It outputs a Boolean circuit h of polynomial size, with \(\Pr_{x\text{ uniform}}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) on at least two thirds of runs. All sampling, computation, circuit writing and evaluation costs use classical bit operations; the total worst-case learning time has one polynomial bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Decision trees are an elementary representation for Boolean classification. Uniform data removes distributional pathologies but still leaves open whether random examples suffice for fully polynomial learning.

Kalai and Teng contrast the unresolved uniform-distribution problem with their positive result for most perturbed product distributions. Chosen-input queries can provide information unavailable from examples alone. The existing proper-learning card allows membership queries and requires a tree output. This target permits improper output but removes that query access.

The backdoor-defense source also raises efficient learning of polynomial-size decision trees from uniform random labeled examples. The access is random examples; free membership queries at selected inputs would change the learning problem.
why: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2008: The source learns from most randomly perturbed product distributions, leaving the fixed uniform distribution unresolved.

title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
importance_reason: Determine whether combining two elementary classifiers already defeats efficient distribution-free learning.
formal: Is there a single randomized learner that, for every distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), every target \(f\) expressible as the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces of total description length at most a supplied bound \(B\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), uses only independent labeled examples from \(D\) to output a Boolean circuit \(H\) with \(\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time polynomial in \(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\)?
definitions: A halfspace is \(h(x)=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}\ge \theta\), with \(w_i,\theta\in\mathbb{Z}\) in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs \((x,f(x))\) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least \(n+1\) steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by \(P(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon))\). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit \(H:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) in the explicit \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis. The success condition is \(\Pr_{\mathrm{samples,coins}}[\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon]\ge2/3\), uniformly over \(n,B,\varepsilon ,D\) and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof constructing and bounding a learner under all the stated quantifiers, or a Lean proof that none exists. Proper-learning hardness and statistical-query lower bounds do not exclude all allowed learners. A margin promise, a restricted input distribution or membership queries would change the problem.
context:
A single halfspace is efficiently learnable, but combining only two thresholds introduces a longstanding computational obstacle. Allowing an arbitrary output representation avoids the known hardness of proper learning.

The existing TCS-6544 explicitly assumes a positive margin and polynomial dependence on its reciprocal. This candidate instead concerns unrestricted integer-weight thresholds on the Boolean cube. The distinction affects the running time and cannot be hidden behind their similar titles.
why: Determine whether combining two elementary classifiers already defeats efficient distribution-free learning.
status_note: The 2026 TheoretiCS source explicitly retains the fixed-two-halfspace polynomial-time question. A July 2026 subexponential-time preprint does not establish the requested polynomial bound. Checked through 13 September 2026 within a bounded literature review.
progress: 2009: The source distinguishes proper-learning hardness from the unresolved unrestricted-output learning question. | 2026-04-28: Tiegel’s published hardness result still describes polynomial-time learning of two halfspaces as open; its lattice-based bound concerns a growing number of halfspaces. | 2026-07-30: A later preprint gives subexponential-time learning for arbitrary Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces, without establishing polynomial time for the present two-halfspace target.
working_summary: One threshold is efficiently learnable from labeled examples, but the target here combines two thresholds. Examples follow any fixed distribution on the Boolean cube and no positive margin is promised. The learner receives a bound on target description length and may output any efficiently evaluable classifier. Hardness for proper learners or growing numbers of halfspaces does not settle this two-halfspace target. The question asks for a uniform polynomial-time guarantee across all distributions and permitted target descriptions.

title: Optimal multiclass regret versus Littlestone dimension
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: The minimax regret of every multiclass hypothesis family tests whether Littlestone dimension alone captures online prediction difficulty, even with infinitely many labels.
formal: Determine \(R(d,T)=\sup\){\(R_{T}(H): H\) is a nonempty multiclass hypothesis class with \(\mathrm{L}(H)\le d\)}, up to universal constant factors, for integers \(T\ge d\ge 1\). The supremum ranges over arbitrary instance and label sets, including infinite label sets. \(R_{T}(H)\) is the full-label online minimax regret defined below; learners have no computational-efficiency restriction.
definitions: Let X be an instance set, Y a label set and \(\varnothing \ne H\subseteq Y^{X} a\) known hypothesis class. On round t an adversary presents \(x_{t}\in X\), the learner chooses a probability distribution \(p_{t}\) on Y, and the adversary then reveals \(y_{t}\in Y\). The learner suffers loss \(1- p_{t}(y_{t})\), the probability of a wrong randomized prediction. It observes the actual label, not just whether its prediction was correct. Its regret is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}(1- p_{t}(y_{t}))- \min _{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^{T}1[h(x_{t})\ne y_{t}]\). Let \(R_{T}(H)\) be the infimum over learner strategies of the supremum of this regret over adversarial plays; the adversary may observe \(p_{t}\) before choosing \(y_{t}\). This distribution-valued convention already accounts for prediction randomness. There is no computational-efficiency restriction on a strategy, and it may know T. A depth-d Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance \(x\in X\) at each internal node and two distinct labels from Y on its two outgoing edges. It is shattered by H if every root-to-leaf path has some \(h\in H\) whose labels on the encountered instances equal all the path’s edge labels. The Littlestone dimension \(\mathrm{L}(H)\) is the greatest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. Define \(R(d,T)\) by the supremum in the statement; the bound sought is uniform across all choices of X,Y,H. If \(\mathrm{L}(H)=0\) all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The domain \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime in which regret is capped by T.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(d,T)\) and constants \(a,A>0\) independent of both parameters, all label sets and all hypothesis classes, and prove a \(g(d,T)\le R(d,T)\le A g(d,T)\) for every integer \(T\ge d\ge 1\). Lower bounds may use families of classes; a worst-case class need not attain the supremum. This is an asymptotic regret target with multiplicative constants, not additive 0.01 error.
context:
The labels need not be consistent with any \(h\in H\). The learner is charged only for its excess expected mistakes over the best one fixed hypothesis chosen after the whole sequence is known.

The 2023 paper proves sublinear regret for every finite-Littlestone-dimension multiclass class, even with infinitely many labels. The remaining question is the sharp rate, not whether such classes are learnable at all.

The source gives O(\(\surd\)(dT log(eT/d))) regret, compared with the known \(\Omega (\sqrt{dT})\) lower bound. Writing \(\Theta (dT)\) would lose the square root and describe a fundamentally different claim.

For finite Y the source also obtains \(O(\sqrt{dT \log |Y|})\). This yields the desired rate when |Y| is a fixed constant, but its hidden coefficient grows with the label count. The conjecture asks for a numerical constant independent of that count.

The original conjecture predicts \(R(d,T)=\Theta (\sqrt{dT})\); the source gives a universal lower bound at that scale and an upper bound with an extra square-root logarithm in T. Determining the full minimax function permits a different answer if the conjecture fails. No equivalence to the proposed sharp bound is asserted.
why: Would determine whether Littlestone dimension alone controls the exact minimax cost of multiclass sequential prediction, beyond the already known learnability characterization.
status_note: The original game, dimension, horizon range and both upper bounds were checked. Later-result searches, the source’s arXiv version record and the May 2026 oracle-efficiency paper were checked through 12 September 2026. The latter explicitly studies binary classification; no resolution of the universal multiclass constant was located.
progress: 2023: The source proves label-independent regret within a square-root logarithmic factor of the lower bound and asks to remove that factor. | 2023: For finite label spaces, the same paper removes the horizon logarithm at the cost of a log|Y| factor under the square root.
working_summary: An online learner predicts a label and then sees the correct label on each round. Regret compares its cumulative prediction loss with the best hypothesis in a known class. Littlestone dimension measures which labeled binary trees that class can realize. The target is the worst minimax regret among all classes of dimension at most d over T rounds, with no bound on the label-space size. Determining the full tradeoff would settle whether the familiar square-root dT scale needs an extra factor in the multiclass setting.

title: Memory–sample tradeoffs for noisy parity learning
importance_reason: The memory cost of noisy parity learning separates information retained from samples from computation time and exposes a basic resource cost of noise.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(c_{1},c_{2}>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\), every \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) and every one-pass learner recovering a uniformly random \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) from the noisy parity samples defined below, its worst-case memory S and maximum sample count T satisfy \(S\ge c_{1}n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2}\) or \(T\ge 2^{c_{2}n}\)? Constants are independent of \(n, \varepsilon\) and the learner, and \(\varepsilon\) may tend to zero with n. This states the bounded-error recovery interpretation of Conjecture 1; it does not additionally require a lower bound at exponentially small success probability.
definitions: Arithmetic in 𝔽\(_{2}=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two; \(\langle a,x\rangle =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}x_{i}\) mod 2. First choose x uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and hold it fixed. Independently for each t, choose \(a_{t}\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and a noise bit \(Z_{t}\) with \(\Pr [Z_{t}=1]=1/2- \varepsilon\); observe \((a_{t},b_{t})\) with \(b_{t}=\langle a_{t},x\rangle +Z_{t}\) mod 2. Noise bits, query vectors and internal learner coins are mutually independent. The learner outputs one estimate x̂; success means \(\hat\{x\}=x\), and its probability averages over x, all observations and internal coins. The learner sees each sample once in order, cannot choose \(a_{t}\) or revisit discarded observations, and has no computational-time restriction. Formally use a branching program with \(T+1\) layers and width at most \(2^{S}\), one start vertex and one outgoing edge for each possible sample at each nonterminal vertex, all going to the next layer. Leaves, possibly in earlier layers, are labelled by estimates in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). Randomized learners may use fresh coins to choose state updates; retained coins are part of the state. Equivalently, the lower bound may be checked on deterministic nonuniform programs, since a random tape can be fixed to achieve at least the average success under this fixed input distribution without increasing width or length. The program may depend on n and \(\varepsilon\); its transition description, current layer and input sample are not charged as stored data. Memory counts persistent state bits, \(S=\lceil \log _{2}(\operatorname{width})\rceil\), and T is the maximum number of consumed samples, not its expectation. No hypothesis is made about the hardness of LPN in unrestricted computation.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal bounded-error memory/sample tradeoff with constants uniform in \(\varepsilon\), or refute that asymptotic claim by showing that no such constants can work. A bound \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ), a\) result only for constant \(\varepsilon\), or a lower bound in a restricted statistical-query model does not settle the proposed dependence on noise.
context:
Without noise, every observation is a correct linear relation about the hidden vector. Here the relation is only slightly more likely to be right than wrong when \(\varepsilon\) is small. The question asks whether this forces a quadratic loss in the storage threshold as the bias tends to zero.

The source proves that a learner needs \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon )\) memory or exponentially many samples, and records an upper bound using \(O(n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\) memory and \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) samples. The conjecture asks whether the stronger memory dependence is necessary below an exponential sample budget.

The lower bound concerns retained information, not the time needed to process it. It must hold for arbitrary state-transition rules and therefore would be unconditional even though efficient learning of noisy parity is also used as a computational hardness assumption.

For \(\varepsilon\) fixed away from zero, the two memory bounds differ only by constants. The unresolved content is their uniform dependence on \(\varepsilon\), together with an exponential sample threshold whose exponent does not shrink with \(\varepsilon\).

The 2024 DIMACS project abstract identifies the same \(n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2}\)-versus-exponential tradeoff as its long-term goal and describes intermediate observations in a modified model. It is evidence of continued study, not a proved lower bound or a fresh claim that all later work has been exhausted.
why: Would quantify how observation noise increases the storage needed for a central learning problem, strengthening unconditional limits relevant to streaming learning and bounded-storage cryptography.
status_note: Checked the complete conference statement and branching-program model, the arXiv version record, a 2024 follow-up abstract and the author’s 2026 publication list. No resolution was found through 12 September 2026. The listed 2026 planted-structure work has a different stated scope; its abstract, not its full proofs, was inspected.
progress: 2021: The published lower bound has memory dependence \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon )\); Conjecture 1 proposes \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\) under a subexponential sample budget. | 2024: A subsequent research-project abstract reports partial investigations and keeps the full tradeoff as its goal.
working_summary: A hidden binary vector is observed through uniformly random parity equations with independent noise. Each equation is correct with probability one half plus \(\varepsilon\). The proposed lower bound requires either \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\) stored bits or exponentially many samples. The source proves the weaker \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon )\) memory threshold and gives a matching-to-the-conjecture space upper bound. The card fixes bounded-error exact recovery and requires constants uniform in \(\varepsilon\).

title: Proper decision-tree learning in polynomial time
importance_reason: A central proper-learning question, with a near-polynomial algorithm but no polynomial bound for the uniform membership-query setting; representation and access to labels both materially affect its complexity.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized membership-query algorithm that properly learns Boolean decision trees under the uniform distribution in polynomial time? For every \(n,s\geq1\), every integer \(m\geq2\), and every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a decision tree with at most \(s\) leaves, the learner is given \(n,s,m\) and oracle access to \(f\). It must output an explicitly represented decision tree \(h\), with probability at least \(2/3\), such that \[2^{-n}|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:h(x)\ne f(x)\}|\leq1/m.\] Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in \(n,s,m\).
question_excerpt: Design a \(\operatorname{poly}(n, s, 1/\varepsilon )\)-time membership query algorithm for properly learning size-s decision trees over n variables to error \(\varepsilon\) under the uniform distribution.
definitions: A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node queries one coordinate \(x_i\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and its two outgoing edges correspond to values zero and one. Leaves are labelled zero or one; following the input’s path defines the output bit. Size means the number of leaves. Repeated coordinate tests are allowed. The unknown target need only admit a tree with at most \(s\) leaves; that tree is not supplied. A membership query may be any chosen bit string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and returns the exact noiseless bit \(f(x)\). The learner is one finite probabilistic multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice, and no other oracle. Writing the \(n\)-bit query costs ordinary bit steps; reading its returned label costs one. All random-bit generation, computation and output are charged. Its time is bounded by \(K(n+s+m+1)^a\) on every target and every random execution, for constants \(K,a\) independent of parameters. Integers are supplied in binary. The accuracy convention \(\varepsilon=1/m\) specifies the usual inverse-accuracy parameter without an arbitrary real input encoding; existence for these accuracies is equivalent to existence for arbitrary requested positive accuracy by rounding to a smaller reciprocal accuracy. Properness is weak properness: the output must be a decision tree, but need not have at most \(s\) leaves. Its full explicit description, with variable indices, children and leaf bits, must fit the polynomial time bound. The success probability concerns the learner’s randomness; prediction error is measured over a fresh uniform point and the guarantee holds for every promised target.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that a learner satisfying all these quantifiers exists, or that no such learner exists. The positive direction requires polynomial bit time, a proper explicit tree output and the uniform-distribution error bound with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative result must rule out all randomized learners of this kind, including those allowed polynomial-size trees larger than the target. An improper hypothesis, a random-examples-only result, distribution-free hardness alone, or a conditional obstruction whose assumption is unproved does not settle the stated existence question.
context:
Open Problem 1 asks for polynomial time in the number of variables, target size and inverse accuracy. The source explicitly distinguishes strict properness, which preserves the target size bound, from weak properness, which merely returns a tree; its question is open even for the latter.

The representation constraint matters: an efficient predictor need not come with a comparably small tree representation. Membership queries also matter because they let the learner choose inputs instead of relying only on the examples that a distribution happens to provide.

The source’s Theorem 2 reports an almost-polynomial proper query learner, with time \(\widetilde O(n^2)(s/\varepsilon)^{O(\log((\log s)/\varepsilon))}\). In the usual polynomial-size, constant-error regime this yields \(n^{O(\log\log n)}\), which still exceeds a fixed polynomial.

Koch, Strassle and Tan prove NP-hardness for distribution-free proper learning with queries in FOCS 2023. Their paper explicitly contrasts that result with the easier uniform-distribution setting. A lower bound obtained from a specially chosen distribution does not rule out this card’s learner.

Their FOCS 2024 coding-theoretic work gives further hardness connections for decision-tree learning. Its discussion distinguishes the remaining uniform-distribution problem from the distributions used in its reductions.

An empirical tree-fitting procedure and its success on a finite collection of datasets are not the universal learning guarantee. The error bound must hold for every small-tree target, even when the target’s structure is unknown and the output tree has a different topology.
why: The question tests whether efficient prediction can be achieved while retaining a decision-tree representation in a basic, well-specified query model. Its resolution would clarify the computational cost of proper learning beyond sample complexity alone.
status_note: The exact uniform-distribution proper query question is explicit in the 2022 source. Checked later hardness results do not cover this distributional setting. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no polynomial-time learner or unconditional impossibility theorem for the stated model.
progress: 2022: The open-problem paper records an almost-polynomial proper learner and asks for a polynomial bound. | 2023: Distribution-free proper query learning is shown NP-hard; this does not settle the uniform case. | 2024: New connections to nearest-codeword approximation give further learning hardness under different distributional/access assumptions.
working_summary: Proper learning of decision trees requires the learner to output a decision tree, preserving the target representation's simple branching structure. The source asks for a polynomial-time algorithm under the uniform input distribution with membership queries available. Those queries let the learner choose inputs and observe their target labels, making this different from learning from random examples alone. Existing algorithms in the source are faster than earlier quasipolynomial approaches but still fall short of polynomial time. A solution would provide an efficient way to recover an interpretable tree hypothesis without abandoning the tree representation during learning.

title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
importance_reason: A major hardness question for unrestricted polynomial-size hypothesis representations, linking worst-case NP difficulty, agnostic learning and cryptographic assumptions; substantially broader than hardness of proper learning for one representation.
formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.
context:
An improper learner may return a larger circuit than any circuit in the comparator class. Showing hardness only for size-preserving output can therefore leave an efficient improper learner possible. The quantification over every fixed polynomial output-size bound makes this distinction explicit.

The source defines learning reductions by giving the oracle a sampling circuit for a distribution and receiving a sufficiently accurate hypothesis. This card retains that oracle interface. Sampling distributions are generated by the reduction; the task does not give a practical learner arbitrary target membership queries.

The polynomial target-size exponent is fixed before the allowed output exponent. For each allowed output exponent the reduction may be different. Adaptive randomized Turing reductions are allowed; the card does not impose the additional deterministic, nonadaptive, witness-mapping or honesty conditions used in some of the source’s cryptographic consequences.

The June 2026 paper proves conditional hardness for a related full-support learning problem. It assumes a strong indistinguishability obfuscator and a lower-bound hypothesis for propositional proof systems. These are substantive assumptions, so the result does not by itself give the unconditional reduction asked for here.
why: This asks whether learning general small circuits remains hard when the learner is free to use a different and polynomially larger representation. Establishing such hardness from SAT would connect worst-case NP difficulty with a central general learning task, while the known links to witness encryption expose consequences beyond learning itself.
status_note: Open in the CCC 2025 source. The subsequent ECCC TR26-091 checked on 2026-09-14 establishes related conditional hardness under cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions, not the unconditional claim here. The selected formal oracle-reduction variant and its quantifier order are explicit; this bounded check is not an exhaustive literature or proof verification.
progress: 2025: Goldberg and Kabanets relate restricted forms of learning hardness to witness encryption and explicitly leave general improper circuit-learning NP-hardness open. | 2026-06-04: Goldberg, Juvekar and Kabanets give randomized reduction results for full-support PAC learning under additional cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions. The checked statement does not eliminate those assumptions.
working_summary: The question asks whether SAT reduces to agnostic learning of general polynomial-size Boolean circuits. The learning oracle receives a circuit sampling labeled examples and returns an approximately optimal hypothesis. The returned hypothesis may use an arbitrarily larger fixed polynomial size than the comparator circuits. The reduction must work with every valid oracle reply and without additional cryptographic assumptions. A June 2026 follow-up gives related conditional hardness, leaving the unconditional target unresolved.

title: Proper unlabeled compression of ample classes
importance_reason: Optimal proper unlabeled compression of every ample class is a substantial structural case of the central sample-compression programme.
formal: Does every nonempty ample concept class \(C\subseteq \{0,1\}\)ᵁ on a finite domain U admit a proper unlabeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(d=\operatorname{VC}(C)\)? Precisely, do there exist maps \(\kappa :RS(C)\to \{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\) and \(\rho :\{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\to C\) such that, for every realizable labeled partial sample \(s, \kappa (s)\subseteq dom(s)\) and \(\rho (\kappa (s))\) agrees with every label in s? The stored object is only an unordered subset of the sample’s input points. The bound is d, not an unspecified multiple of d.
definitions: A concept \(c\in C\) is a function \(c:U\to \{0,1\}\). A set \(A\subseteq U\) is shattered by C if \(\{c|_{A}:c\in C\}=\{0,1\}^{A}\). It is strongly shattered if some \(b:U\setminus A\to \{0,1\}\) has the property that, for every \(a:A\to \{0,1\}\), the combined labeling \(a\cup b\) belongs to C. Thus strong shattering requires a full cube of concepts with identical labels outside A. The class is ample when every shattered set is strongly shattered; ample classes are also called lopsided or shattering-extremal. Its VC dimension d is the maximum size of a shattered set. A labeled partial sample is a function \(s:A\to \{0,1\}\) on some \(A\subseteq U\), equivalently a set of pairs \((x,s(x))\) with distinct x. It is realizable if \(s=c|_{A}\) for some \(c\in C; RS(C)\) contains every such sample, including the empty sample. The compressor \(\kappa\) sees the entire labeled sample and may use its labels to choose a subset \(\kappa (s)\) of its domain, of size at most d. It sends only that subset. The reconstructor \(\rho\) receives no labels, ordering, multiplicities, sample size, omitted sample points or auxiliary bits; \(U,C,\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are fixed and shared beforehand. It returns a total concept belonging to C, which must agree with the original entire sample, including omitted labels. This is the proper convention explicitly used in the full source. Requiring \(\rho\) on all subsets of size at most d is equivalent to defining it only on \(Im(\kappa )\), because C is nonempty and unused inputs can be assigned any fixed concept. The existence of \(\kappa ,\rho\) is quantified separately for each finite C; no running-time bound for constructing or evaluating them, distributional assumption or probability of error is part of the statement. For \(d=0 a\) nonempty class has a single concept and the empty compressed set suffices. A maximum class of dimension d has cardinality \(\sum_{j=0}^{d} binomial(|U|,j)\); every maximum class is ample, but the converse need not hold.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the two maps with the stated d-point bound for every finite nonempty ample class, or give an ample class with a proof that no such pair of maps exists. A scheme retaining labels, returning a hypothesis outside C, storing extra information, or exceeding d points does not meet the target. A scheme that handles only full concepts rather than every realizable partial sample is also insufficient. Failure of a proposed corner-peeling construction alone does not refute existence of a compression scheme.
context:
The source constructs proper unlabeled schemes of size d for maximum classes. Its open extension concerns all ample classes, a strictly larger family.

Size-d labeled compression is already known for ample classes. The new requirement is that the reconstructor recover a consistent concept from selected input points after all their labels have been removed.

The source exhibits a maximum class of VC dimension three without a corner, refuting earlier corner-peeling arguments. It nevertheless proves the compression theorem for maximum classes. The absence of corners therefore does not imply the desired maps do not exist.

The 2024 paper proves proper unlabeled schemes for oriented matroids and for complexes of oriented matroids admitting corner peelings. It explicitly states that the general ample-class question remains open.
why: Would extend sharp label-free sample compression from maximum classes to the larger class characterized by equality of shattering and strong shattering, clarifying how far the VC dimension controls lossless reconstruction of consistent samples.
status_note: Read the full proper-compression definition and the distinction between maximum and ample classes, then checked the 2024 oriented-matroid theorem and its explicit remaining-question paragraph. Also checked the revised labeled-compression work for complexes of oriented matroids, whose retained labels make its result different. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for every finite ample class; searches are not exhaustive.
progress: 2019: The source corrects earlier corner-peeling claims, proves size-d unlabeled compression for maximum classes and asks for an ample-class extension. | 2022: The journal treatment explicitly uses proper reconstruction and retains the ample extension as open. | 2024: Proper unlabeled compression is proved for additional oriented-matroid classes, while the general ample question is explicitly retained.
working_summary: An ample class strongly shatters every set of coordinates that it shatters. A compressor selects at most d input points from any realizable labeled sample, where d is the class’s VC dimension. A reconstructor must recover a concept in the original class consistent with all sample labels while receiving only the selected points. Maximum classes satisfy this exact bound, and labeled compression is known more generally. The 2024 oriented-matroid results still leave proper unlabeled size-d compression for all ample classes open.

title: Non-clashing teaching dimension versus VC dimension
importance_reason: The sharp universal relation between VC dimension and non-clashing teaching compares two basic notions of information needed to identify concepts.
formal: For every finite set X and every nonempty concept class \(C\subseteq 2^{x}\), is \(NCTD(C)\le \operatorname{VC}(C)\)? Equivalently, if C has VC dimension d, does there exist a teaching map assigning at most d correctly labeled examples to each concept such that no two distinct concepts are mutually consistent with one another’s assigned examples? Both positive and negative examples are allowed. The target constant is exactly one, not merely a bound \(O(d)\).
definitions: A concept \(C\in C\) is a subset of the finite instance set X, identified with its indicator function \(1_{C}:X\to \{0,1\}\). A labeled sample is an unordered subset of \(X\times \{0,1\}\). It is consistent with C if each \((x,y)\) in it has \(y=1_{C}(x)\). A teaching map T assigns a sample \(T(C)\) consistent with C to every concept C in the class. It is non-clashing if, for every distinct \(C,D\in C, T(C)\) is not consistent with D or \(T(D)\) is not consistent with C. Equivalently, some point appearing in either teaching set has different labels under C and D. The condition is pairwise: \(T(C)\) need not by itself distinguish C from every other concept. A positive example has label 1 and a negative example has label 0; both count as one example. The size of T is \(\max _{C\in C}|T(C)|\), and \(NCTD(C)\) is the minimum of that size over all non-clashing teaching maps. The minimum exists because X and C are finite and giving all labels is a valid map. No sample order, extra message or additional side information is part of this definition. A subset \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by C when \(\{C\cap S:C\in C\}=2\)ˢ. The VC dimension \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the maximum cardinality of a shattered set. For a singleton concept class it is zero, and the empty teaching set works. The statement quantifies over all finite X and nonempty C, including that case; it concerns existence of a map, without an efficiency or encoding-size requirement on constructing it. The positive-only parameter NCTD\(^{+}\) restricts \(T(C)\) to samples with label 1 and can be larger. It is not the parameter in this conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove the exact inequality for every finite concept class by establishing existence of a valid map of maximum size at most its VC dimension, or give a finite concept class and a proof that every non-clashing teaching map has larger maximum size. A quadratic bound or even a larger-constant linear bound is insufficient. A separation for positive-only maps, another teaching model, or an algorithmic hardness result for finding maps does not refute this existence statement.
context:
The source and journal article give a universal upper bound quadratic in VC dimension. Their conclusion asks for the sharper inequality with coefficient one, and reports no counterexample to that inequality.

If a class of VC dimension d on X attains Sauer’s size bound \(\sum_{i=0}^{d} binomial(|X|,i)\), the cited representation-map result supplies a non-clashing map of size d. Maximum classes are a special case, not all finite classes.

The COLT 2024 paper constructs small maps for balls in particular graph classes and explicitly repeats the general open question. A size-four upper bound together with a VC-dimension-three upper bound for another family does not prove NCTD exceeds VC there.

The journal article separately studies stronger restrictions on avoiding collusion. Their optimal teaching parameter need not equal NCTD. Likewise, a map for the concepts themselves is not automatically a sample-compression scheme that must reconstruct from arbitrary samples.
why: Would show that every finite concept class can be taught with at most its VC dimension many examples per concept in the non-clashing model, giving a sharp link between learning capacity and teaching complexity.
status_note: Read the finite-domain no-clash definition and conclusion, the expanded JMLR treatment, and the COLT 2024 special-case results. Later searches through 12 September 2026 also found work on computing positive graph-ball teaching maps, but no proof or counterexample to the universal signed NCTD\(\le\)VC inequality. Search is not exhaustive.
progress: 2019: The ALT paper defines NCTD, proves general and special-case bounds, and asks for the exact inequality NCTD\(\le\)VC. | 2023: The expanded JMLR article retains the universal question and distinguishes stronger teaching restrictions. | 2024: COLT results establish additional bounds for graph-ball classes and explicitly preserve the general conjecture.
working_summary: A teacher assigns correctly labeled examples to each concept in a finite class. No two different concepts may both fit each other’s assigned examples. The conjecture asks whether at most d examples per concept always suffice when the VC dimension is d. A quadratic general bound and exact bounds for certain special classes are known. The sharp signed-example inequality remains distinct from positive-only teaching, computational map-finding and sample-compression questions.

title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture
importance_reason: A fundamental proposed relationship between two established learning-complexity measures, with a general quadratic bound and an unresolved universal linear target.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(X\) and every finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\), \[\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)\leq K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)?\] Both dimensions are the combinatorial quantities defined below. The constant must be independent of the number of concepts, the domain size and the class itself.
definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.
context:
Simon’s 2023 Open Problem 3 asks for precisely this universal linear relationship. The earlier Simon–Zilles open-problem paper is retained as provenance from the already consolidated duplicate; there is a single active target.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Recursive teaching measures the hardest easiest-to-teach concept that remains after restricting the candidate class; it is not the maximum ordinary teaching dimension of the original class.

Hu, Wu, Li and Wang prove \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=O(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)^2)\). This bounds teaching complexity by VC dimension alone but leaves open whether the dependence can always be linear.

Simon’s 2025 paper verifies the conjecture for graph-induced star classes and graph-induced connected-set classes. These positive results cover rich families but not arbitrary Boolean classes.

Compton, Pabbaraju and Zhivotovskiy give lower bounds for particular greedy teaching-set constructions in 2025. They describe the universal conjecture as unresolved; limitations of those constructions are not counterexamples to the existence of small teaching sets.

The conjecture permits any universal constant, so examples separating the two dimensions by a fixed factor are compatible with it. Its failure would require ratios with no finite upper bound, while an affirmative result would uniformly connect two distinct notions of information needed for learning.
why: A universal linear bound would connect sample-based combinatorial complexity with the number of examples needed for structured teaching. It asks whether recursive teaching can always be controlled at the same scale as VC dimension.
status_note: The conjecture is explicitly open in the 2023 source and the checked 2025 work. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no general linear upper bound or unbounded-ratio counterexample. The new results address special classes and particular construction rules.
progress: 2015: Simon and Zilles pose the linear RTD-versus-VC question. | 2017: A general quadratic upper bound is proved. | 2023: Simon explicitly retains the universal linear bound as Open Problem 3. | 2025: New graph-class theorems confirm special cases, while greedy-construction lower bounds do not refute the conjecture.
working_summary: A finite concept class can be studied through both its VC dimension and its recursive teaching dimension. VC dimension measures the ability to realize label patterns, while recursive teaching measures how examples can identify concepts through successive elimination. The question asks whether one universal constant always bounds recursive teaching dimension by that constant times VC dimension. The same constant must work for every finite class. The project seeks a direct quantitative link between the complexity of learning from samples and the information needed for structured teaching.

title: Statistical-query complexity of sparse halfspaces
importance_reason: Sparse-halfspace statistical-query complexity locates an important computational learning barrier.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C\ge 2\) and \(a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}])\le C n^{b}\), where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function \(h:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,+1\}\) of the form \(h(x)=+1\) if \(\sum j w_{j}x_{j}\ge \theta\) and \(h(x)=- 1\) otherwise, where \(w\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) has at most r nonzero coordinates and \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and \(0<\gamma <1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,\gamma )\) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions \(h_{1},\ldots ,hd\) in Hn,r satisfying |\(\sum x D(x)h_{i}(x)h_{j}(x)|\le \gamma\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Then \(SQ-DIM(Hn,r,\gamma )\) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its \(O(1)\) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than \(Cn^{b}\) with pairwise absolute correlations at most \(1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}]\). The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.
context:
A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. For example, a rule depending only on \(x_{7}\) is one-sparse regardless of how many other features are supplied. Attribute efficiency asks whether learning can benefit from this sparsity without requiring labeled information proportional to every coordinate.

An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function \(\varphi (x,h(x))\in [- 1,1]\). A tolerance \(\tau\) allows any answer within \(\tau\) of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. The source relates inverse-polynomial tolerance in r log n to attribute-efficient use of labeled examples.

Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules \(2x_{1}- 1\) and \(2x_{2}- 1\) have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

The allowed correlation scale is inverse-polynomial in r log n, while the required bound on the number of nearly uncorrelated functions is polynomial in n. Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

The source gives bounds connecting this correlation parameter to weak SQ learning. Its discussion of converting weak learning to high accuracy additionally allows unlabeled samples. The exact Problem 3 dimension question keeps those access models distinct.
why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.
status_note: Source Problem 3 and its definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of this worst-distribution, inverse-\(\operatorname{poly}(r \log  n)\) parameter question was located. Results for noisy, Gaussian, smoothed or ordinary sample-access learning do not automatically settle it. No exhaustive literature or proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2014: Feldman states the precise sparse-halfspace correlation-dimension question and connects the parameter to attribute-efficient SQ learning.
working_summary: An r-sparse halfspace uses at most r of the n Boolean input coordinates. Statistical-query learning accesses approximate expectations instead of individual labeled examples.
