The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}\) with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof or refutation of the stated existence implication for this exact modulus ensemble and inverse-polynomial average-success convention. A refutation must establish the inverter premise together with failure of the factoring conclusion. Excluding only a chosen class of black-box reductions is insufficient; results for other exponents or worst-case oracles must first be related to the specified average-case problem.
context:
Factoring an RSA modulus gives the private exponent and hence breaks encryption, but the reverse reduction is a longstanding cryptographic question. It would identify whether RSA inversion rests on precisely the factoring assumption or on a potentially weaker computational task.

Boneh’s survey asks about factoring with an RSA inversion oracle. This card retains the imported fixed-exponent average-case specialization and explicitly compares inverse-polynomial average success on its balanced-prime ensemble. The implication permits arbitrary constructions; restricted-model separation results do not refute it.
why: Identify the computational assumption underlying one of the central public-key primitives.
status_note: The primary 1999 survey poses the broader RSA inversion-to-factoring question. The exact exponent-65537 average-case formulation is an editorial specialization. Rechecked its formulation on 13 September 2026; the saved bounded status search found no resolution, and no exhaustive current-open claim is made.
progress: 1999: The survey distinguishes factoring-to-inversion from the unresolved converse.
working_summary: Factoring an RSA modulus permits inversion of its encryption permutation. This card asks for a converse implication with exponent 65537 on a specified ensemble of balanced prime products. Both inversion and factoring are measured by inverse-polynomial average success of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The implication allows unrestricted use of an inverter’s code and is not confined to black-box reductions. The fixed-exponent average-case question is an explicit specialization of the broader oracle question in Boneh’s survey.

title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
importance_reason: Determine the intrinsic role of interaction in information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.
formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.

title: PZK versus SZK
importance_reason: A foundational comparison between two information-theoretic privacy notions, posed in a standard cryptography textbook, supported by a nontrivial oracle separation and explicitly retained in recent work on perfect zero knowledge.
formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that on \(x\in Y\) the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(1- \varepsilon (|x|)\), and on \(x\in N\) every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most \(\varepsilon (|x|)\). Negligible means smaller than |\(x|^{- d}\) for every fixed \(d>0\) at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside \(Y\cup N\). The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of \((\mathrm{P},V*)(x)\), for every \(x\in Y\). Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.
context:
Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.
why: Determine whether allowing any negligible statistical simulation error increases the expressive power of information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.
status_note: No unrelativized resolution was found through 11 September 2026. The 2024 paper explicitly retains the equality as open. Oracle separations and perfect-zero-knowledge results in PCP or multiprover models do not settle this target.
progress: 2001: Goldreich lists PZK versus SZK as open and distinguishes strict from expected-time simulation. | 2020: The journal paper proves an oracle separation of SZK from PZK, not an ordinary class separation. | 2024-03-18: The PCP paper explicitly retains the ordinary interactive-proof equality as unknown.

title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
importance_reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.
formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over \(F_{2}\) and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.
context:
LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.
why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-09-08: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.
working_summary: Learning parity with noise asks for information about hidden binary linear equations when some answers have been flipped. This project asks whether worst-case hardness of the binary nearest-codeword problem implies average-case hardness for a specified low-noise LPN distribution. The chosen regime uses quadratically many samples and a noise rate inversely proportional to the square root of the secret dimension. A reduction must produce that particular random-instance distribution rather than merely another hard coding problem or a different noise level. Such a connection would strengthen the theoretical foundation of low-noise LPN in the way worst-case reductions support lattice-based assumptions.

title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
importance_reason: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family?
definitions: The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function \(\nu (\lambda )\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \nu (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on \((1^{n},f(U_{n}))\) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform \(U_{n}\). A polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) family is generated from \(1^{n}\) in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). Those constructions establish plausible \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.
why: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists. The original personal-list citation studied attacks on Goldreich’s candidate; the foundational locality-construction reference is used here instead.

title: Exponentially hard weak versus strong one-way functions
importance_reason: A foundational hardness-amplification question separating ordinary cryptographic equivalences from security exponential in input length, with direct connections to average-case hardness and meta-complexity.
formal: Does the existence of an exponentially hard weak one-way function imply the existence of an exponentially hard strong one-way function, in the following nonuniform-adversary, negligible-success formulation? The premise is that there exist a uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(f\), a real \(a>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and \(n_0\), such that \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)\le1-n^{-k}\] for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every circuit \(C\) with \(n\) inputs, \(n\) outputs and at most \(2^{an}\) gates. The desired conclusion is that there exist another uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(g\) and a real \(b>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(n_d\) with \[\operatorname{Inv}_g(C,n)\le n^{-d}\] for every \(n\ge n_d\) and every such circuit with at most \(2^{bn}\) gates. The constants and function in the conclusion may depend on those witnessing the premise.
definitions:
A length-preserving function is a single map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(|f(x)|=|x|\), computed by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(A(n+1)^r\) steps on every input of length \(n\), for some fixed constants \(A,r\). The same convention applies to \(g\). There is no oracle or advice in forward evaluation.

For a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), define its inversion success by \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)=\Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n}\bigl[f(C(f(x)))=f(x)\bigr],\] where \(U_n\) is uniform on all length-\(n\) bit strings. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as success; the output need not equal the originally sampled \(x\). The challenge is sampled by applying \(f\) to a uniform input, not by choosing a uniform element of its image.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs of fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates and constants, with named inputs and outputs. Size counts noninput gates, including constants; no restriction is placed on fan-out. Real size limits mean their integer floors. Every circuit is allowed independently at each input length, including circuits with information built into their wiring and constants. No uniform procedure for generating the attack circuits is required. Deterministic circuits suffice for the displayed average-success bound: a randomized attack is a distribution over such circuits, and averaging cannot exceed their common bound.

Weakness means a fixed inverse-polynomial fraction of the sampled challenges defeats every allowed attacker. Strongness here means that the maximum success of any allowed attacker is negligible: smaller than every fixed inverse power for sufficiently large lengths. The exponent \(b\) is fixed before \(d\). This explicitly uses negligible success against exponential-size circuits; it does not add a separate exponentially small success requirement. Security is measured against the input length of each function itself, on all sufficiently large lengths. Both functions are length-preserving, following the source's stated convention; arbitrary padding is not assumed to preserve exponential hardness.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this implication, or a proof of its negation. A positive answer may use an arbitrary construction or existence argument and need not preserve the original security exponent. It must produce a single polynomial-time function with a positive linear exponential attack-size exponent and negligible inversion success. A negative answer must refute the existence implication itself; a barrier for black-box transformations or for a restricted amplification method is insufficient.
context:
The reverse implication is immediate: negligible inversion success also leaves an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs hard. The substantive question is the weak-to-strong direction. It does not ask to prove that one-way functions exist without assumptions.

The usual direct-product amplification evaluates the weak function on many independent blocks. Its enlarged input length can turn exponential security in a block length into only stretched-exponential security in the new length. The 2025 revision explicitly identifies this loss as the unresolved issue.

Security-preserving amplification is known under regularity assumptions: at a fixed input length, every value in the image of a regular function has the same number of preimages. The present premise includes arbitrary functions with unequal fiber sizes, so that special case does not establish the general implication.

The question is about existence of a suitable strong function. It does not demand a black-box reduction, restrict forward computation to constant depth, or require the new function to use the same input length as a single invocation of the old one. Its exponential guarantee is nevertheless measured in its own full input length.
why: Ordinary hardness amplification equates weak and strong one-wayness at polynomial security scales. Preserving hardness exponential in the actual input length would extend that equivalence to a much stronger regime and clarify how fine-grained average-case hardness supports cryptographic security.
status_note: The 2021 source and its 25 August 2025 revision explicitly leave exponential weak-to-strong amplification open. Checked on 2026-09-14, together with the regular-function amplification source and a bounded later-work search. The card states the nonuniform, length-preserving, negligible-success convention explicitly; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.
progress: 1990: Goldreich, Impagliazzo, Levin, Venkatesan and Zuckerman give security-preserving amplification for regular weak one-way functions. | 2021: Ren and Santhanam connect weak one-way-function hardness to meta-complexity and distinguish the open exponential weak-to-strong question from ordinary amplification. | 2025-08-25: Their second ECCC revision retains the unresolved exponential-hardness amplification question in Remark 5.4.
working_summary: The premise is a polynomial-time function that defeats exponential-size inversion circuits on an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs. The question asks whether this already guarantees a function whose inversion success is negligible for exponential-size circuits. An attacker succeeds by finding any preimage of a challenge sampled from a uniform input. Ordinary repetition enlarges the input and can lose hardness exponential in the new length. Security-preserving results for regular functions do not settle the general case, which remains open in a 2025 revision.

title: Subpolynomial-key perfectly secure three-server DPFs
importance_reason: A central server-count and exact-privacy boundary for an information-theoretic cryptographic primitive used in private retrieval and secure computation; the question asks for an asymptotic qualitative improvement rather than tuning one construction.
formal: Does there exist a fixed finite Abelian group \(G\), with \(|G|\ge2\), and a uniform three-server distributed point function with perfect correctness, perfect privacy against any one server, and worst-case key length \(\ell(N)=N^{o(1)}\)? For every integer \(N\ge2\), location \(\alpha\in[N]\), and value \(\beta\in G\), key generation must produce three binary keys \((k_0,k_1,k_2)\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^{2}\operatorname{Eval}_i(k_i,x)=\begin{cases}\beta&x=\alpha,\\0_G&x\ne\alpha\end{cases}\qquad\text{for every }x\in[N]\] with probability one. For each individual \(i\), the distribution of \(k_i\) must be identical for all pairs \((\alpha,\beta)\) with the same \(N\). Every generated key must have at most \(\ell(N)\) bits. The fixed output group may be chosen as part of a positive answer; requiring all output groups is the source's separate question.
definitions:
Write \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). A finite Abelian group is a finite set with an associative and commutative addition, identity \(0_G\), and additive inverses. Its elements have fixed binary names, and its addition table is fixed with the scheme. The point function is zero away from one specified input and takes the specified value there. The case \(\beta=0_G\) is included.

A scheme consists of one randomized Turing machine \(\operatorname{Gen}\) and three deterministic Turing machines \(\operatorname{Eval}_i\), all fixed independently of \(N,\alpha,\beta\). The generator receives the binary encodings of \(N,\alpha,\beta\) and produces three finite bit strings. It may use independent fair bits and must halt with probability one. This convention permits exact sampling from a fixed group of odd order by rejection sampling. Each evaluation machine halts on every valid key and domain input and returns one element of \(G\). The key determines \(N\); its encoding, all public corrections, and any parameter descriptions used in evaluation count toward key length. The machines and the fixed group table are public. There is no additional shared random tape, hidden setup, or uncounted data depending on the particular point function.

This card asks for the information-theoretic key-length bound: it imposes no running-time bound beyond these algorithmic termination conditions. Perfect correctness means that the displayed identities hold simultaneously for all domain inputs with probability one over key generation. Perfect privacy means equality of each single key's entire probability distribution, including its length. Consequently even unlimited computation and arbitrarily many evaluations of that key cannot reveal the location or value. Privacy against a coalition of two servers is not required.

The bound is uniform over locations, values, server indices, and all keys having positive probability. Subpolynomial length means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(N_\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\ell(N)\le N^{\varepsilon}\) for all integers \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same fixed group and algorithms must work for all \(N\). A security parameter is unnecessary because the privacy error is exactly zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a scheme exists, or a proof that no such scheme exists. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and prove correctness, equality of all required key distributions, termination, and the asymptotic key-length bound. A negative answer must cover every fixed nontrivial finite Abelian output group. Statistical privacy with arbitrarily small positive error, or a construction using four servers, does not meet this target.
context:

The requirement hides both the special location and its output value. The card makes the output-group scope explicit: existence for some fixed nontrivial group. It does not require a bound uniform over growing groups. The later paper extends the groups supported by efficient information-theoretic constructions, but the checked statements use different server counts or permit statistical security.

The 2026 survey continues to distinguish the known four-party perfectly secure construction from the three-party statistically secure one. Its stated literature snapshot is February 2026, even though the arXiv version was submitted in July.

Each server can evaluate its own share, and the three outputs must add to the requested point function. A single key must reveal exactly no information about either the location or the stored value. The target is a key length smaller than every positive power of the domain size over some fixed nontrivial finite Abelian group. Known subpolynomial constructions achieve perfect privacy with four servers or statistical privacy with three, a distinction retained in a 2026 survey.

title: Sublinear communication for perfectly secure two-party computation
importance_reason: Tests whether polynomial preprocessing can beat circuit-linear communication for general perfectly private computation; separates an information-theoretic barrier from progress using special circuit structure or computational assumptions.
formal: Is there a uniform two-party protocol in the trusted correlated-randomness model that perfectly computes every Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial setup and computation, and online communication \(O(n+g(s))\) for some function \(g(s)=o(s)\), where \(s\) is the circuit's supplied size? More precisely, seek fixed algorithms, constants \(K,q\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) with \(\lim_{s\to\infty}g(s)/s=0\), such that every circuit and every pair of inputs satisfy the correctness and privacy conditions below; dealer computation, total setup length and both parties' computation are at most \(K(n+s+1)^q\), while at most \(K(n+g(s))\) bits are exchanged online. The circuit is arbitrary, without a layering or depth restriction. The additive input-length term fixes the source's sublinearity question in a form that also covers circuits of linear size.
question_excerpt: It is still an open problem whether it is possible to make the communication complexity sublinear in the circuit size in the setting that the […]
definitions:
A circuit is an explicitly given finite directed acyclic graph with \(2n\) input vertices, Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Let \(s\) count all vertices, including inputs and constants; in particular \(s\ge2n\). Gates and predecessors are encoded in topological order with binary indices. Both parties and the dealer know this public description. The inputs \(x_0,x_1\in\{0,1\}^n\) are private to their respective parties. The size in the bound is that of the supplied circuit; the protocol may optimize its computation, but cannot charge an artificially padded circuit to increase its communication allowance.

Before the parties receive their inputs, a trusted randomized dealer, given only \(C\), samples finite correlated strings \((r_0,r_1)\) and privately sends \(r_b\) to party \(b\). These strings may depend on \(C\) but not on either input. The dealer then takes no further part. Dealer randomness consists of independent fair bits; its computation and output length obey the polynomial bound on every run. Independent local random tapes can be included in these strings. After this phase the parties are deterministic machines on their input, setup string and message history. Their descriptions are fixed across all circuits and lengths, and their complete online runtimes obey the same polynomial bound. There is no other setup, oracle or computational hardness assumption.

The parties exchange binary messages and output private bits \(y_0,y_1\). Perfect correctness means
\[\Pr[y_0\mathbin\oplus y_1=C(x_0,x_1)]=1\]
for every input pair, where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The task uses the source's shared-output convention: neither party is required to learn the reconstructed answer. Perfect privacy against one passive corruption means that, for each \(b\) and each fixed \(C,x_b\), the distribution of party \(b\)'s entire view is identical for every choice of the other party's input. Its view includes \(r_b\), all sent and received messages and its output. A passive adversary follows the protocol and may inspect that entire view with unlimited computation; the parties do not collude. Privacy and correctness have zero error.

Online cost is the worst-case number of bits sent in both directions, over inputs and all dealer outcomes of positive probability. Message boundaries, control information and input-dependent stopping must be encoded in this communication; timing and silence are not free channels. There is no separate round bound beyond polynomial runtime. The dealer's private deliveries are excluded from online communication but included in the setup-length bound. For every family whose circuit size is polynomial in \(n\), the stated \(\operatorname{poly}(n+s)\) resource bound is polynomial in the input length, as required by the source. A single choice of algorithms, \(K,q,g\) must work for all such families, not only a fixed function or depth.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence, including perfect privacy, correctness, polynomial setup/computation and a uniform sublinear \(g\), or prove that no such protocol and resource bounds exist. A protocol for layered circuits only, a computationally secure construction, or a truth-table protocol using setup exponential in \(n\) does not settle this target. A negative answer must rule out all sublinear savings allowed above, rather than only exactly optimal or one-round online communication.
context:
The input-independent setup is a resource, not a free truth table of the function. Beaver-style evaluation uses linear-size correlated randomness and linear online communication. A one-time truth table can make communication linear in the input length, but its exponential setup falls outside this question.

Couteau gives perfect passive-security protocols for layered circuits with communication \(O(n+s/\log\log s)\) for a fixed number of parties and a constant-size output, using polynomial storage. In a layered circuit every edge joins consecutive layers. Transforming a general circuit into this form can increase its size and therefore does not automatically give sublinear cost relative to the original circuit.

The 2023 source proves exponential setup lower bounds when each party sends exactly as much information as its input, including a stronger bound for a single online round. Its functions have a two-bit shared output and input domain size \(N\); the lower bounds are in \(N\), which is exponential in input bit length. These endpoint results do not rule out \(O(n+g(s))\) communication with additional interaction.

Computationally secure protocols may replace large correlations by short pseudorandom descriptions under hardness assumptions. Perfect privacy here requires exact equality of view distributions even for an unbounded observer, so those constructions answer a different question.
why: Standard perfectly private evaluation pays communication proportional to circuit size, even after preprocessing. A general sublinear protocol would show that polynomial preprocessing can reduce this online cost without relying on conjectured cryptographic hardness. A lower bound would expose a fundamental limit on what preprocessing can achieve, beyond the extreme regime of exactly optimal communication.
status_note: The 2023 source, Couteau’s 2019 theorem and open extension, and his 2024 research synthesis were checked on 2026-09-14. A bounded search of later work found no general perfectly private polynomial-setup protocol meeting the selected bound. Layered-circuit savings and computational-security results do not resolve this arbitrary-circuit target.

working_summary: Two parties want to compute a Boolean circuit while keeping each input perfectly private. A trusted dealer can distribute correlated randomness before either input is supplied. The question asks whether polynomial setup and computation can give online communication sublinear in the circuit size, apart from the input-length cost. Such savings are known for layered circuits, while completely optimal communication can require exponential setup. The unresolved target covers arbitrary circuits with perfect passive privacy and shared outputs.

title: Polynomial-time computationally sound verification of \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\)
importance_reason: Computationally sound verification for counting would extend the scope of succinct cryptographic verification.
formal: Do there exist deterministic uniform algorithms \(P,V\), integers \(C>c\ge1\), and a constant \(K\ge2\) giving the following plain-model argument system for exact \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\), without unproved hardness assumptions? On a Boolean formula \(\Phi\) encoded in \(N\) bits, \(P\) produces a proof of length at most \((N+1)^C\) in time \(T_P(N)=2^{K(N+1)^c}\). The verifier runs in time \(K(N+1)^C\) and outputs either the exact number of satisfying assignments or the rejection symbol \(\bot\). Completeness requires \(V(\Phi,P(\Phi))=\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) on every valid formula. Soundness requires that every uniform randomized adversary running in any fixed polynomial in \(T_P(N)\) has only negligible probability, as a function of \(T_P(N)\), of generating a length-\(N\) formula and a proof on which \(V\) outputs an incorrect number. This card fixes the unconditional version of the source question; conditional constructions are recorded below.
definitions:
Fix a polynomial-time parsable binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT. An instance lists its \(n\) variables explicitly, so \(n\le N\), and its formula is a finite tree with leaves among those variables and Boolean constants. The value \(\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) is the number of assignments in \(\{0,1\}^n\) on which the formula evaluates to one, including choices of any listed unused variables. The answer is written in binary and has at most \(n+1\) bits. Measuring resources in the full encoding length fixes the meaning of polynomial-size formulas and includes the cost of reading their descriptions.

The prover and verifier are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. The proof is one finite binary string; there is no interaction, oracle, common reference string, advice, secret setup or verifier randomness. The verifier rejects malformed instances and overlong proofs. It halts within its stated bound on every input, reading at most one symbol beyond the permitted proof length to detect excess input. Increasing the fixed constant \(K\) absorbs encoding and rejection overhead. The honest prover must construct its proof in the stated exponential time; mere existence of a proof with no bound on its production is insufficient.

More explicitly, for every uniform probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) whose worst-case runtime on \(1^N\) is at most \(T_P(N)^a\) for some fixed \(a\ge1\), and for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(N_{A,d}\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_{A,d}\),
\[\Pr_{(\Phi,\pi)\leftarrow A(1^N)}\bigl[\Phi\text{ is valid},\ |\Phi|=N,\ V(\Phi,\pi)\notin\{\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi),\bot\}\bigr]\le T_P(N)^{-d}.\]
Probability is over independent fair random bits used by \(A\). Any output that is not a valid formula/proof pair is a failed attack. The adversary chooses both the formula and its proof, knows \(P,V\), and has no nonuniform advice or auxiliary input. The polynomial exponent \(a\) may be arbitrarily large and is not fixed by the protocol. Negligibility is measured in the honest prover's time, rather than merely inverse polynomial in the formula length. The constants \(c,C,K\) and the two machines must be fixed before quantifying over adversaries and accuracy exponents.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a system exists, including all completeness, uniformity, running-time and soundness requirements, or prove that no such system exists. A positive answer must be unconditional. A construction assuming a conjectured hard function is progress but does not settle this selected version. Randomized verification, interaction, a setup string, soundness only against polynomial-in-input-length adversaries, or an unbounded honest prover changes the question.
context:
Computational soundness permits incorrect proofs to exist, provided no adversary with the specified resources can generate a false instance together with an accepted proof. Ordinary NP soundness forbids every false proof. Allowing nonuniform advice would let an adversary hardwire a false pair at each input length, removing this distinction.

The honest prover is allowed exponential time, and the adversary is allowed every polynomial in that time. Requiring a polynomial-time honest prover would instead give a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm by composing prover and verifier. Allowing an arbitrarily stronger honest prover than the attacker would also distort the model; the later paper explains why.

The 2023 source gives, under strong assumptions, verification in time \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with an honest prover and adversaries using \(2^{O(n)}\) time. Its next question asks for a polynomial-time verifier.

The 2025 paper proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{cs}\text{-}\mathrm{NP}\) under strong assumptions about functions that remain hard for small-space computation on efficiently samplable inputs. Its Definition 1.1 explicitly allows a polynomial-time verifier with an exponential-time honest prover. Applying its polynomial-space verification result to exact-count claims gives conditional progress on this card, since exact counting can be performed in polynomial space. The paper does not prove the required hardness assumptions.
why: Exact counting requires certifying that no satisfying assignments were missed, as well as that counted assignments exist. This question tests whether computational soundness can give deterministic short verification of such global information while retaining an honest prover with a specified running time. It connects the power of proof systems with derandomization and the distinction between uniform computational attacks and arbitrary false witnesses.
status_note: Open Problem 4.5 of the 2023 source was checked together with the 3 April 2025 revision of Chen–Rothblum–Tell on 2026-09-14. The latter gives conditional polynomial-time verification under strong hardness assumptions; this card explicitly selects unconditional existence with its honest-prover/adversary convention. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution.

This substantially advances the source question, while leaving unconditional existence unsettled.
working_summary: The task is to check the exact number of satisfying assignments to a Boolean formula in polynomial time. An exponential-time honest prover supplies a short proof to a fully deterministic verifier. Even adversaries running in any polynomial in the honest prover’s time must almost never find a false counting claim that the verifier accepts. A 2025 theorem gives such verification for polynomial-space claims under strong hardness assumptions. This card asks whether the specified counting-verification system exists without those unproved assumptions.

title: Unconditional zero knowledge for gap circuit complexity
importance_reason: A structural zero-knowledge question connecting circuit meta-complexity with the difference between worst-case hardness and cryptographic assumptions. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there a fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) for which \(\mathrm{Gap}_{\varepsilon}\mathrm{MCSP}\) admits a computational zero-knowledge interactive proof system without a computational hardness assumption? Given the length-\(N=2^n\) truth table of a Boolean function, the promise distinguishes circuit size at most \(N^\varepsilon\) from size greater than \(N^{1-\varepsilon}\). This card selects the MCSP branch of the original question and the gap family used by Hirahara and Nanashima; it does not claim equivalence with every MINKT or other gap variant.
question_excerpt: Does (some gap version of) MCSP or MINKT admit a computational zero knowledge proof system?
definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(C(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(C(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(C(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Negligible means smaller than \(N^{-c}\) for every fixed positive \(c\) at sufficiently large \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.
context:
Yes-instances have polynomially checkable small-circuit witnesses, so this is a promise problem in NP. Revealing the entire witness supplies an ordinary proof, but does not establish zero knowledge.

The standard one-way-function theorem supplies zero-knowledge proofs for NP. The original question asks for an unconditional result; the case where the problem is worst-case hard but suitable cryptographic hardness is unavailable is not covered by that theorem.

Ilango, Ren and Santhanam obtain infinitely-often average-case protocols, with locally samplable distributions in their MCSP statement. That does not give a protocol correct on every promised input at every length.

Hirahara and Nanashima characterize one-way functions using both membership of the gap problem in CZK and worst-case hardness of CZK. The theorem does not establish the gap problem’s unconditional CZK membership. Their 2024 full version also distinguishes errorless average-case schemes from error-prone ones.
why: Would provide a natural unconditional zero-knowledge protocol for a central problem about circuit descriptions. It probes the connection between worst-case complexity, average-case cryptographic hardness and verification that reveals no efficiently usable information beyond the claim.
status_note: Read Question 12 and the ECCC full source, STOC 2022 Theorem 2.7, and full ECCC 2024 Theorem 2.1 with Definitions 4.1–4.2; checked the January 2026 publisher abstract and dates. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no unconditional worst-case resolution. The MCSP branch and the later source’s fixed power-gap family are explicit editorial scope choices, not a claimed equivalence with all original alternatives. The 2026 full publisher proof was not read.
progress: 2022-03: The source asks for unconditional zero knowledge for some gap MCSP or time-bounded Kolmogorov problem. | 2022-06: STOC work gives infinitely-often average-case zero-knowledge protocols, with the stated distribution restrictions. | 2024-04: The full author paper states a worst-case characterization involving gap MCSP membership in CZK together with a separate hardness condition. | 2026-01-26: The journal version of the characterization is published; its abstract retains both conditions and does not announce unconditional gap MCSP membership.
working_summary: The input is a complete truth table promised to have either a small or a much larger minimum circuit. The selected question asks for some fixed gap admitting an unconditional computational zero-knowledge proof. The verifier is efficient, while soundness must hold even against an unbounded cheating prover. All promised inputs and all input lengths must satisfy the guarantees. Average-case protocols and the later one-way-function characterization do not establish this membership.

Removing those extra premises would connect the security guarantee more directly to foundational hard problems. The saved 2016 note does not name the precise extra assumptions or compactness conventions, so its current status and exact target require separate review rather than treating any lattice-based FHE scheme as a resolution.

working_summary: Cryptographic hardness must occur on instances that honest users can efficiently generate, rather than only on a difficult exceptional input. The cited question asks whether \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\), or a suitable average-case separation between distributional classes, already implies one-way functions. It also asks about the stronger possibility of trapdoor functions, where secret information enables inversion that remains hard publicly. These targets add progressively more structure to a bare claim that efficient algorithms cannot solve everything. Establishing the implications would connect cryptographic foundations to broad complexity assumptions instead of relying on individual number-theoretic or algebraic candidates.

title: Quantum PCP conjecture
importance_reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.
focus_reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.
formal: Do there exist integers \(k,d\ge 1\) and a rational constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of \(m\le (n+1)^{d} k\)-local Hermitian terms \(H_{i}\) on \(n\ge 1\) qubits and rational \(a<b\) in \([0,1]\), with \(0\preceq H_{i}\preceq I\) and \(b- a\ge \varepsilon\). For \(H=(1/m)\sum_{i} H_{i}\), distinguish \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)\le a\) from \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)\ge b\).
definitions: Here \(1\le m\); each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}\) is the smallest eigenvalue. \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N- M\) is positive semidefinite, equivalently \(z*(N- M)z\ge 0\) for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with \(a<\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)<b\) are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs \((Y,N_{0})\) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |\(0\rangle\). \(H=2^{- 1/2}((1,1),(1,- 1))\) is the Hadamard matrix, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For \(x\in Y\) some witness gives acceptance probability \(\ge 2/3\); for \(x\in N_{0}\) every witness gives probability \(\le 1/3\). A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and \(N_{0}\) into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants \(k,d,\varepsilon\) are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.
why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2013: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions. | 2026-08-19: Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.
working_summary: The quantum PCP conjecture asks whether even a coarse estimate of a quantum system's lowest energy can capture the difficulty of verifying quantum proofs. The system is specified by local interactions, each involving only a bounded number of qubits. The target is hardness for distinguishing two possible ground energies separated by a constant after normalizing the total interaction strength. Normalization prevents a small gap from becoming a constant merely by multiplying the Hamiltonian by a large number. The problem connects robust quantum verification with entanglement, quantum codes, and the limits of approximation algorithms.

title: BPP versus BQP
importance_reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.
focus_reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.
formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most \(1/3\) separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on \(1^{n}\) generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |\(x\rangle\), polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |\(0\rangle\), and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\) would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.
why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.
status_note: Wigderson’s Conjecture 11.4 explicitly asks for strict containment. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no unrelativized separation of these bounded-error decision classes was located. Oracle and shallow-circuit sampling advantages are recorded with their model restrictions.

Wigderson’s Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2 state the model and inclusion. | 1994 conference / 1995–1996 preprint: Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms. No unconditional classical polynomial-time lower bound for those tasks follows. | 2019 conference / 2022 journal: Raz and Tal prove an oracle separation \(\mathrm{BQP}\not\subset \mathrm{PH}\). This also separates BQP from BPP relative to that oracle, but not in ordinary unrelativized computation. | 2026-08: Bene Watts and Parham publish an unconditional shallow-circuit sampling separation. Its classical resource restrictions and sampling output differ from the unrestricted decision model fixed here.
working_summary: This problem asks whether efficient quantum computation can decide something that efficient randomized classical computation cannot. BPP and BQP both require a reliable yes-or-no answer on every input, with bounded probability of error. Quantum interference gives promising candidate advantages, including the algorithms underlying factoring, but those examples do not establish an unconditional classical lower bound. Separations using special oracles or restricted classical circuits concern narrower comparisons. Settling the ordinary class separation would identify whether quantum computers enlarge the set of efficiently decidable problems at its most basic level.

title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
importance_reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.
focus_reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.
formal: For every fixed local dimension \(q\ge 2\), interaction range \(r\ge 1\), interaction incidence bound \(g\ge 1\), norm bound \(J>0\), and spectral gap \(\Delta >0\), is there a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta )\) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), has unique ground state \(\psi\) satisfying \(S(\rho _{A})\le C|\partial A|\) for every \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\)?
definitions: Let \(\mathrm{L}\ge 1\) be an integer, \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}=\{1,\ldots ,\mathrm{L}\}^{2}\) with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of \(C^{q}\) over its sites. Write \(H=\sum_{a} h_{a}\), where each \(h_{a}\) is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support \(X_{a}\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every \(h_{a}\) is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector \(\psi\) and its next eigenvalue is at least \(\Delta\) above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), let \(A^{c}\) be its complement in \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(\rho _{A}=Tr_{A^{c}}(|\psi \rangle \langle \psi |)\) and \(S(\rho _{A})=- Tr(\rho _{A} \log _{2} \rho _{A})\), with \(0 \log _{2} 0=0\). The boundary \(\partial A\) is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy \(m \log _{2} q\). For a square block of side length \(\ell\), that is proportional to \(\ell\)\(^{2}\), whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times \(\ell\). The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension \(q^{\mathrm{L}}\), which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.
why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.

In arXiv version 3, the explicit bound is \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) at the end of §4. | 2026-02-05: Arad, Firanko, and Jain extend approximate-projector methods to mutual information of maximally mixed ground states; their theorem still requires a good approximate ground-space projector. | 2026-04-15: Garratt and Abanin derive entropy bounds from thermodynamic information and area laws for frustration-free systems with suitably bounded subsystem ground-space degeneracies.
working_summary: An area law says that entanglement between a region and its surroundings grows with the region's boundary rather than its volume. This problem asks for such a bound for the unique ground state of a general two-dimensional local Hamiltonian with a fixed positive spectral gap. Interaction strength, local dimension, and interaction range are held fixed as the lattice grows. Known routes involving frustration-free systems or additional conditions do not automatically establish the unrestricted statement recorded here. A solution would clarify how strongly locality and an energy gap constrain many-body quantum states, without by itself supplying an efficient algorithm to find them.

title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
importance_reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.
focus_reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.
formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol \((\mathrm{P},V)\) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let \(p(C)\) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have \(p(C)\ge 2/3\) and NO instances have \(p(C)\le 1/3\). V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]\(\ge 2/3\). On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]\(\le 1/3\). Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A user who can run only classical computations would like to check the answer returned by a quantum computer. Repeating the same claimed computation on the same untrusted device gives no independent reason to trust it. Interactive verification instead lets the user issue challenges whose answers constrain whether the reported result is correct. The survey by Gheorghiu, Kapourniotis and Kashefi organizes approaches according to what the verifier can do and which resources or assumptions establish trust. This card fixes the most restrictive physical verifier: entirely classical.

The usual inclusion \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}\) does not settle the question. Since quantum polynomial time is contained in polynomial space, Shamir’\(s \mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) theorem supplies a classical interactive proof with an unrestricted prover. However, a proof system whose honest prover must carry out much harder auxiliary computations cannot be implemented merely by running the quantum computation being certified. Requiring the honest prover to be quantum polynomial time is therefore substantive.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev show that a verifier with a small quantum register can verify arbitrary efficient quantum computations. Quantum authentication lets a weak client protect data while delegating its processing. This demonstrates that a very limited quantum capability can be enough, but its communication and trusted operations do not satisfy the all-classical interface specified here. Their 2017 paper supplies the completed journal treatment of work first reported in 2008.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani provide another route: a classical verifier interacts with separated quantum devices sharing entanglement. Correlations in nonlocal games can force the devices to implement the required states and measurements. Isolation is crucial because it prevents the devices from coordinating arbitrary answers during the test. Combining both devices into one freely communicating prover removes that constraint, so the multiprover result cannot simply be reused for this card.

Mahadev’s 2018 breakthrough gives classical verification with one efficient quantum prover under the hardness of Learning With Errors for quantum algorithms. Cryptographic structure conceals information needed to cheat in the measurement tests. Its soundness is computational: the theorem protects against efficiently implementable attacks under the assumption. The present question deliberately quantifies over unbounded cheating strategies, which may break the underlying cryptography.

Recent work continues to refine these neighboring models. Kalai, Khurana and Raizes’s February 2026 construction verifies computations using one reusable QMA witness without destroying it, with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE. This is useful when the input quantum state cannot be copied. It retains the computational soundness assumption and therefore does not supply an unconditional protocol for the simpler BQP target here.

Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier’s May 2026 journal article achieves information-theoretic verification without trusted state preparations or measurements. Its client still applies trusted quantum gates: one construction uses single-qubit Z rotations and bit flips. Removing two particular hardware requirements is meaningful progress, but a client performing these gates is not a purely classical verifier.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi explicitly retain the single-prover question in April 2026. They prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\subseteq MIP^{O}\) for every classical oracle O using an exponentially long classical proof queried in polynomially many locations. Their theorem concerns multiple classical provers and does not establish efficient honest provers. Relativization is proposed as a way to investigate the difficulty, rather than as an equivalence that resolves it.
why: This asks whether efficient quantum computation has an equally efficient, purely classical way to establish trust without computational hardness assumptions or isolated extra devices. A resolution would identify a basic boundary between producing quantum answers and certifying them.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves this single-prover, information-theoretic question open. The May 2026 trusted-gate result changes verifier resources, and the February 2026 witness-preserving protocol retains LWE. Neither meets this card’s classical-verifier and unbounded-cheater requirements.
