working_summary: A classical user would like to check a computation performed by a single quantum device using only classical messages. The honest device must be able to carry out the verification protocol in quantum polynomial time. The difficult requirement is soundness against any cheating device, including a computationally unbounded one. Existing approaches may instead give the user limited quantum capabilities, use separated devices, or assume that a cryptographic problem is hard. The question isolates whether an entirely classical client can obtain unconditional trust in efficient quantum computation under this single-device model.

title: NPT bound entanglement
importance_reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.
focus_reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.
formal: Do there exist finite integers \(a,b\ge 2\) and a bipartite density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{a}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{b}\) such that \(\rho\) has negative partial transpose, but \(\langle \psi |(\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}})^{\otimes k}|\psi \rangle \ge 0\) for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\) of Schmidt rank at most two across \((\mathbb{C} ^{a})^{\otimes k}:(\mathbb{C} ^{b})^{\otimes k}\)?
definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by \((\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}})_{ij,k\ell}=\rho _{i\ell ,kj}\). Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that \(\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}}\) has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is \(\psi\). Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs \((|00\rangle +|11\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(d,\alpha )=(I+\alpha F)/(d^{2}+\alpha d)\), where \(d\ge 3, - 1\le \alpha \le 1\) and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when \(\alpha <- 1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly when \(\alpha <- 1/2\). Consequently the interval −\(1/2\le \alpha <- 1/d\) consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for \(d\ge 3\). The endpoint \(\alpha =- 1/2\) is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. The distinction makes the remaining challenge concrete: control every admissible rank-two witness across the full collection of copies, rather than only witnesses with a convenient internal structure.
why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.
status_note: The all-copy NPT bound-entanglement question remains explicitly open in the July 2026 primary sources. New two-copy solutions and restricted three-copy progress do not settle this formulation. Reviewed through 11 September 2026.

working_summary: Entangled states can sometimes be converted into nearly perfect shared Bell pairs using many copies and local operations with classical communication. Bound entanglement means that this distillation remains impossible despite the presence of entanglement. The question asks whether such states can have a negative partial transpose, a spectral property associated with distillability in simpler settings. Failure of a protocol on one copy or any fixed number of copies does not establish the required obstruction for every number of copies. Resolving the question would sharpen the distinction between entanglement as a property and entanglement as a usable communication resource.

title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
importance_reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.
formal: Do there exist constants \(r,\delta ,s>0\) and integers \(w,b\ge 1\), and stabilizer codes Q on unbounded numbers n of qubits, such that Q encodes at least rn logical qubits, has distance at least \(\delta n\), every listed check has weight at most w, every qubit occurs in at most b checks, and the normalized check Hamiltonian satisfies \(H\succeq (s/n)D_{Q}\)?
definitions: Use the Hilbert space \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})\otimes n\). On a computational basis bit, X flips the bit and Z multiplies |\(1\rangle\) by −1 while fixing |\(0\rangle ; Y\)=iXZ. A Pauli operator is a tensor product of I,X,Y,Z, up to phase, and its weight is the number of nonidentity tensor factors. A listed check \(S_{j}\) is a nonidentity Hermitian Pauli operator with eigenvalues ±1. The \(m\ge 1\) checks commute, and the group they generate must not contain −I. Their joint +1 eigenspace Q has dimension \(2^{k}\), where k is the number of encoded logical qubits. Code distance d is the minimum weight of a Pauli operator that preserves Q but whose restriction to Q is not a scalar multiple of the identity. Checks may be redundant; both the weight bound and the per-qubit incidence bound refer to the listed checks. Define \(H=(1/m)\sum_{j=1}^{m}(I- S_{j})/2\). For \(0\le t\le n\), let \(Q_{t}\) be the linear span of \(E|\psi \rangle\) over all |\(\psi \rangle \in Q\) and Pauli errors E of weight at most t, and let \(\Pi _{t}\) be the orthogonal projector onto \(Q_{t}\). Define \(D_{Q}=\sum_{t=0}^{n- 1}(I- \Pi _{t})\). The operator inequality \(H\succeq (s/n)D_{Q}\) means that its difference is positive semidefinite, or equivalently that the corresponding expectation inequality holds for every quantum state. All five constants are fixed independently of n, and \(k\ge rn\) and \(d\ge \delta n\) must hold throughout an infinite family with \(n\to \infty\). This card uses the bounded-degree stabilizer version of qLTC existence. Checks need not be geometrically local, and no efficient construction algorithm is required.
answer_criterion: Construct or prove existence of an infinite family satisfying all the stated conditions with fixed constants, or prove that every family of stabilizer presentations fails at least one of them. The target requires maximum check weight and qubit incidence to be bounded, not merely their averages. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance does not qualify. Verifying soundness only for some low-weight errors is insufficient: the operator inequality must hold on the entire Hilbert space.
context:
A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

Distance from the code must account for quantum degeneracy. A large Pauli operator can be a stabilizer and leave every encoded state unchanged; another can implement a logical operation while still remaining inside the code space. Neither should be called far from the code merely because its written support is large. The spaces \(Q_{t}\) and the operator \(D_{Q}\) measure how many physical qubits are needed to leave the entire code space in each orthogonal error sector. The soundness condition also covers superpositions and mixed states.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has \(k=\Omega (n)\), distance \(\Omega (n/\log ^{3}n)\), soundness \(\Omega (1/\log ^{3}n)\), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.
why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No bounded-degree stabilizer family with constant rate, relative distance and normalized soundness was located. The corrected 2025 and July 2026 constructions retain inverse-polylogarithmic losses, while constant-soundness variants increase locality or sacrifice other parameters.
progress: 2021–2022: Panteleev–Kalachev construct good quantum LDPC codes and, separately, good classical LTCs. | 2022–2023: Anshu–Breuckmann–Nirkhe resolve NLTS using good quantum codes without constructing good constant-soundness qLTCs. | 2024-10-18: Cross and coauthors publish constant-soundness qLTCs with compromises in distance, rate or maximum locality. | 2024-11-20: Wills–Lin–Hsieh analyze soundness under general distance balancing. | 2025-09-04: The corrected Dinur–Lin–Vidick version achieves constant rate and locality with \(\log ^{3}n\) losses in relative distance and soundness. | 2026-06-08: Sun–Vidick apply qLTCs to quantum interactive oracle proofs with polylogarithmic query complexity. | 2026-07-02: Li–Li–Liu replace the invalid April argument and retain transversal-gate claims for almost-good codes.
working_summary: A locally testable quantum code should reveal a substantial error by checking only a few qubits. The desired family must also encode a linear amount of quantum information and tolerate errors on a linear number of physical qubits. Each check and each qubit's participation in checks must remain bounded as the code grows. These requirements strengthen ordinary good quantum LDPC codes by demanding a quantitative relation between distance from the code space and rejection probability. Such codes would connect robust quantum error detection with the complexity of low-energy states and the broader search for quantum PCP constructions.

title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions
importance_reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.
formal: Does there exist a family of three-dimensional, bounded-density local Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonians \(H_{n}\) and a fixed inverse temperature \(0<\beta <\infty\) for which the lifetime \(\tau _{n}(\beta )\) of one encoded qubit, under the thermal dynamics below and without intervention during storage, tends to infinity as \(n\to \infty\)?
definitions: The family may use an unbounded subsequence of qubit counts n. Place the qubits in \(\mathbb{R} ^{3}\), with at most B qubits in each unit ball. Let \(H_{n}=\sum_{j}(I- S_{j})/2\), where the \(S_{j}\) are commuting nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks, each supported in a ball of radius R, each qubit belongs to at most B checks, and their joint +1 eigenspace has dimension two. B and R are constants independent of n. A Pauli check is a signed tensor product of I,X,Y,Z; X flips |\(0\rangle\) and |\(1\rangle , Z\) changes the sign of |\(1\rangle\), and Y=iXZ. Use the following fixed Davies-type thermal generator, in units with ℏ=\(k_{B}=1\). If \(\Pi _{E}\) is the energy-E spectral projector of \(H_{n}\), define \(A_{i,\mathrm{P},\omega}=\sum_{E' - E=\omega}\Pi _{E'}\mathrm{P}_{i}\Pi _{E}\) for every qubit \(i, \mathrm{P}\in \{X,Y,Z\}\), and energy difference \(\omega\). Put \(g\beta (\omega )=\min \{1,\exp (- \beta \omega )\}\) and \(\mathrm{L}_{n},\beta (\rho )=- i[H_{n},\rho ]+\sum_{i,\mathrm{P},\omega}g\beta (\omega )[A\rho A\dagger - (A\dagger A\rho +\rho A\dagger A)/2]\), with \(A=A_{i,\mathrm{P},\omega}\) in each summand. Its evolution is \(\Phi _{n},\beta ,t=\exp (tL_{n},\beta )\). Every single-qubit Pauli error is coupled to the bath; energy-raising rates are positive, and attempt rates do not shrink with system size. Choose a completely positive trace-preserving encoding map Enc\(_{n},\beta\) from one-qubit states to n-qubit states, with a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse at \(t=0\). It may use a thermal auxiliary state and need not be efficiently preparable. For this fixed encoding, let \(\varepsilon _{n},\beta (t)=\inf _{D} \sup _{\rho} \Vert D\circ \Phi _{n},\beta ,t\circ\)Enc\(_{n},\beta (\rho )- \rho \Vert _{1}\), where \(\rho\) ranges over all one-qubit density matrices, D over recovery channels from n qubits to one, and \(\Vert A\Vert _{1}=Tr\sqrt{A\dagger A}\). Define \(\tau _{n}(\beta )=\inf \{t\ge 0:\varepsilon _{n},\beta (t)>1/10\}\), with infimum of the empty set equal to infinity. Encoding happens before storage and recovery only at the end. This card fixes a stabilizer and thermal-bath model for the broader physical existence question; it imposes neither translation invariance nor a symmetry restriction on allowed errors.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family, one fixed finite \(\beta\), and encodings with \(\tau _{n}(\beta )\to \infty\), or prove that no family in this stated model has that property. A bound \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) for a fixed \(\eta >0\) would be stronger than required. A lifetime improving only up to a temperature-dependent maximum system size does not suffice. Cooling the bath as n grows, increasing local interaction strengths, slowing error rates with n, enforcing an error-forbidding symmetry, or applying active correction during storage changes the target.
context:
This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some \(\eta >0\). Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.
why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.
status_note: Claimed affirmative resolution in arXiv:2605.10943, 11 May 2026, for passive storage with thermal encoding. Its assumptions and stated theorems were checked, but the full proof was not independently verified. This is not labelled confirmed open. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

working_summary: Passive quantum memory aims to preserve an encoded qubit through the natural dynamics of a material without repeated active correction. The question here fixes a nonzero temperature and asks whether lifetime can grow without bound in a three-dimensional local stabilizer system. Protecting a qubit requires retaining phase information as well as distinguishing its classical basis states. The saved card records a May 2026 claimed affirmative construction, while distinguishing its proof claim from an independently verified conclusion. This makes the record a useful guide to the precise thermal model and remaining verification questions rather than an unqualified assertion that the original existence problem is still open.

title: Quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
importance_reason: A benchmark capacity problem connecting quantum error correction, information-theoretic converses and the operational effect of entangled encodings.
formal: Determine \(Q(q)\), the unassisted asymptotic quantum capacity of \(D_{q}(\rho )=(1- q)\rho +(q/3)(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z)\), for every real \(q\in [0,1]\). Capacity is measured in reliably transmitted qubits per independent channel use, under the coding definition below.
definitions: \(\rho\) is a one-qubit density matrix. The Pauli operators satisfy \(X|0\rangle =|1\rangle , X|1\rangle =|0\rangle , Z|0\rangle =|0\rangle , Z|1\rangle =- |1\rangle\) and Y=iXZ. Thus q is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error, each type having probability \(q/3\). For block length n, choose an integer \(k_{n}\ge 0\) and completely positive trace-preserving maps \(E_{n}\) from \(k_{n}\) qubits to n qubits and \(R_{n}\) from n qubits to \(k_{n}\) qubits. Let |\(\Phi _{k}\rangle =2^{- k/2}\sum_{x\in \{0,1\}^{k}}|x\rangle _{A}|x\rangle _{B}\), and define \(F_{n}=\langle \Phi _{k_{n}}|[id_{A}\otimes (R_{n}\circ D_{q}^{\otimes n}\circ E_{n})](|\Phi _{k_{n}}\rangle \langle \Phi _{k_{n}}|)|\Phi _{k_{n}}\rangle\). A rate \(r\ge 0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with \(\liminf _{n} k_{n}/n\ge r\) and \(F_{n}\to 1\). \(Q(q)\) is the supremum of achievable rates. Sender and receiver have no initially shared entanglement, classical side channel, feedback, or auxiliary quantum channel. Encoding and recovery may be computationally unrestricted and jointly process an entire block. The same q is used independently on every channel use. This definition concerns transmission of quantum states, not merely classical bits through a quantum device.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(q\in [0,1]\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- Q(q)|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
context:
This channel is a basic model of unbiased qubit noise: a bit flip, a phase flip, or both occur with equal probabilities. Its one-parameter definition hides a hard coding problem. A quantum code must preserve superpositions and correlations with a reference system, which is why the fidelity test in the definition uses half of a maximally entangled state. Correctly transmitting only computational-basis strings would test a weaker, classical task.

Noise conventions differ substantially between papers. In this card q is the total Pauli error probability. A paper writing probabilities \((1- 3p,p,p,p)\) uses \(p=q/3\). A paper writing \((1- \lambda )\rho +\lambda I/2\) uses \(\lambda =4q/3\) on the usual mixture range \(q\le 3/4\). For example, \(q=3/4\) completely erases the input, even though the channel formula remains a valid quantum channel for all \(q\le 1\). The 2026 threshold values below have been converted to q once.

Quantum coding theorems give an exact but unbounded optimization: \(Q(q)=\sup _{n} \max _{\sigma} I_{c}(\sigma ,D_{q}^{\otimes n})/n\). Here \(I_{c}\) is the output entropy minus the entropy jointly held by the output and a purifying reference, with entropy \(S(\tau )=- Tr(\tau  \log _{2}\tau )\). This regularization permits inputs entangled across channel uses. It identifies the mathematical quantity, but does not by itself evaluate this particular function.

Using a maximally mixed one-qubit input gives the hashing lower bound \(\max \{0,1- h_{2}(q)- q \log _{2}3\}\), where \(h_{2}\) is binary entropy and \(0 \log _{2}0\) is interpreted as zero. The expression becomes zero near \(q=0.1893\). Degenerate quantum codes can surpass this benchmark because multiple physical errors can have the same effect on the encoded information. Consequently counting error types as if each required separate correction can underestimate achievable rates.

Agarwal and coauthors’ May 2026 paper searches rank-two input states inside the permutation-symmetric subspace, using representation theory to evaluate many-copy coherent information. It reports a 45-copy numerical positivity threshold \(p=0.064657\), or \(q=0.193971\) here, and explains how degeneracy suppresses the effective environment entropy. This is evidence for better codes and a lower bound on the true threshold, not an optimization over all possible block lengths and states.

Krohn-Grimberghe’s August revision provides an explicit 45-copy state with exact-arithmetic certificates for positive coherent information at \(q=48717/250000=0.194868\). The result extends positivity to smaller q by channel composition and data processing. The preprint distinguishes the threshold printed in the May paper from a stronger state in its authors’ public repository, and bounds both that state and the new witness using certified arithmetic. The certificates are supplied by the author; this review checked the stated bounds and conventions but did not independently rerun the verification artifact.

On the upper-bound side, \(Q(0)=1\) and \(Q(q)=0\) for every \(q\ge 1/4\). In the latter range the channel is antidegradable: the environment can simulate the receiver’s output. Reliable positive-rate transmission would then permit incompatible copies of unknown quantum information. Between the current positive-capacity lower bound and \(q=1/4\), even the location where capacity vanishes remains unsettled. Determining that location would still leave the positive-rate curve to be determined with the required accuracy.

There are also finer results away from the threshold. Leditzky, Leung and Smith control the gap between single-letter coherent information and capacity at low noise through approximate degradability. Zhu and coauthors optimize channel extensions to obtain tighter upper bounds, with their work presented at TQC 2026. These techniques reduce the gap without proving that a proposed family of codes is optimal at every noise value.

Kondra and coauthors’ August 2026 strong-converse result concerns fidelity decay above capacity for degradable and antidegradable channels. Such a theorem strengthens the operational meaning of an upper bound, but does not supply the unknown capacity curve of the depolarizing channel in its intermediate regime. A full resolution here must match the best achievable rates with upper bounds that apply to arbitrary encodings and arbitrary block lengths.
why: The unresolved communication limit of a canonical quantum-noise model. It tests whether quantum coding theory can turn regularized existence formulas into sharp quantitative limits despite degeneracy and multi-copy advantages.
status_note: Exact unassisted capacity remains open in the 2026 primary literature. The August certificate improves a positive-capacity lower bound, without claiming an exact threshold or capacity formula. All displayed thresholds use total Pauli error q. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

working_summary: A depolarizing channel models a qubit subjected to randomly chosen Pauli errors. Its quantum capacity measures how much unknown quantum information can be transmitted reliably per channel use when many uses are encoded together. The goal is the capacity curve throughout the noise range under the unassisted coding convention fixed in the card. Coding across several uses can behave differently from optimizing a single use, which complicates attempts to match achievable rates with impossibility bounds. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.

title: NP outside BQP
importance_reason: A foundational relation between quantum algorithms and NP-completeness; a noncontainment proof would also separate P from NP.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq \mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, is there no uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that decides satisfiability of every Boolean 3-CNF formula with error probability at most \(1/3\) on each input?
definitions: NP is the class of languages \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* for which there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) exactly when some binary string y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). BQP consists of languages decided by polynomial-size quantum circuit families \(\{C_{n}\}\) that a deterministic classical algorithm generates from \(1^{n}\) in polynomial time. The circuits use a fixed finite universal gate set, for example Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, polynomially many qubits initialized with the input x and zero ancillas, and a final measured output bit. Acceptance probability is at least \(2/3\) when \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) and at most \(1/3\) when \(x\notin \mathrm{L}\). The size bound counts all elementary gates, not only calls to a selected subroutine. There is no advice, postselection, oracle or supplied witness. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. The input length is the length of a conventional explicit binary encoding; malformed encodings are rejected. \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) asserts the existence of at least one language in NP outside BQP, rather than merely inequality of the two classes.
answer_criterion: Prove an unconditional separation \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq \mathrm{BQP}\), or refute it by establishing \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\). By NP-completeness and closure under classical polynomial-time reductions, the latter is equivalent to putting 3-SAT in BQP. An oracle separation, a lower bound only on unstructured search, an algorithm for a restricted family of formulas, or a conditional hardness statement does not settle the question. A separation from BQP must exclude every uniform polynomial-size circuit family, not just a particular quantum algorithm or architecture.
context:
An NP witness gives a short, classically checkable reason for a yes answer. For satisfiability, that witness is an assignment to the variables. The question is whether the existence of such a witness can always be decided efficiently using quantum computation, even when the witness itself is not supplied. Wigderson lists the noncontainment as Conjecture 11.5 in the inherited 2018 draft.

The distinction between verification and discovery is essential. A quantum computer can certainly evaluate a Boolean formula on a proposed assignment. It can also place assignments into superposition. But a measurement does not reveal a list of the values computed on every assignment. An efficient algorithm must arrange interference so that the eventual measurement supplies the desired decision with bounded error.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms show that quantum computation can exploit special mathematical structure to solve important problems in polynomial time. Their speed comes from extracting periodic information, not from a general procedure for every efficiently checkable witness relation. Factoring is not known to be NP-complete, so its quantum algorithm does not imply that 3-SAT or all of NP belongs to BQP.

Grover’s search algorithm gives a different kind of advantage: a quadratic improvement for an unstructured search space. Applied to N Boolean variables, the space has 2ᴺ assignments, so the generic search scale becomes \(2^{N/2}\), with additional polynomial work to evaluate the formula. This is a substantial speedup and remains exponential in N. The distinction is about asymptotic resources, even if that reduction could be valuable on concrete instances.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove a matching black-box obstruction and an oracle separation of NP from quantum polynomial time. Their result excludes a universal shortcut that treats the witness verifier only as an unknown function. An explicit formula reveals more than black-box evaluations: an algorithm can inspect shared variables, clauses and every feature of its encoding. Thus the oracle theorem does not establish the unrelativized separation asked for here.

There is a useful elementary implication. Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in \(\mathrm{BQP}, \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would put all of NP in BQP. Therefore a positive answer to this card would also prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The converse implication is unavailable: \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone does not rule out quantum polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems. This helps explain why proving an unrestricted quantum lower bound is such an ambitious target.

The decision version already captures efficient witness finding for SAT. If a bounded-error quantum SAT decider existed, one could repeatedly fix a variable, ask whether the remaining formula is satisfiable, and retain a satisfiable branch. Amplifying the decision success probability makes the probability of any mistake across the polynomially many calls small. Finally, the resulting assignment can be checked classically. This is a consequence of SAT’s self-reduction, not an assumption that a quantum algorithm hands over all possible witnesses at once.

The conjecture also supports hardness results for tasks whose inputs and outputs are intrinsically quantum. In June 2026, Cifuentes proves that an efficient quantum algorithm for detecting a large nonidentity Pauli coefficient of a circuit-prepared state would imply \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\). The reduction holds even for pure states and a constant threshold with a promised gap. It transfers the conjecture to a tomography-related task; it does not prove the conjecture itself.

Several nearby questions should remain distinct. BPP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation adds power beyond classical randomization. NP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation can solve every classically verifiable decision problem. Allowing a quantum witness changes the verifier class again, to QMA. Establishing a separation or a speedup involving one pair does not automatically establish the relation between the others.

A resolution would locate a fundamental boundary of quantum computation. If \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\), quantum algorithms would provide a universal efficient route to classical constraint satisfaction and its many reductions. If \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq \mathrm{BQP}\), some efficiently verifiable problems would resist even ideal fault-tolerant quantum computers. Neither answer is about today’s hardware capacity: the model already grants arbitrarily scalable, accurate quantum computation with polynomial resources.
why: Determine whether efficient classical verification always leads to efficient quantum solution, a central limit on what quantum computation can achieve.
status_note: No unconditional separation or general quantum polynomial-time SAT algorithm found through 11 September 2026. Black-box lower bounds do not establish the ordinary language-class separation. June 2026 work continues to use \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) explicitly as an unproved hardness hypothesis.

working_summary: This problem asks whether quantum computers still face an unavoidable efficient-computation barrier on some NP problems. An equivalent target is to rule out a bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithm for every instance of Boolean satisfiability. Fast quantum algorithms for structured tasks do not imply an algorithm for general NP-complete search or decision problems. title: QMA versus QCMA
importance_reason: Separates quantum from classical witnesses and therefore addresses a basic source of quantum computational power.
formal: Is $\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}$? Both classes have a polynomial-time quantum verifier and bounded error. QMA permits a polynomial-size quantum witness; QCMA permits only a polynomial-length classical string. The question concerns the standard classes without an oracle.
definitions: Use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification, completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\), with no shared advice or oracle. Classes here contain promise problems; the witness may depend on the whole input.
answer_criterion: Prove QMA is contained in QCMA, or prove the existence of a promise problem in QMA outside QCMA. A separation relative to an oracle does not settle these unrelativized classes.
context:
A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. A classical proof is still allowed to instruct the verifier to perform a sophisticated quantum computation, so this is not simply a comparison between classical and quantum algorithms.

To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. Observing that a particular state has a long classical description is not sufficient: a different classical argument might certify the same claim without describing that state.
why: This identifies what kind of information might be intrinsically necessary for efficient verification.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2025–2026: A separation relative to a classical oracle is known. The February 2026 paper gives a simpler construction. It leaves the unrelativized class question untouched.
working_summary: A quantum verifier may receive either a quantum state or a classical string as evidence that an input is a yes-instance. QMA permits the former kind of witness, while QCMA restricts the witness to classical information. The question asks whether this change in the form of the evidence changes what can be verified efficiently. Both models already allow quantum computation during verification, so the issue is the additional power of the witness itself. An answer would clarify whether quantum states can serve as fundamentally stronger proofs in the ordinary setting without an oracle.

title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
importance_reason: A foundational computability question about regularized information quantities, separating lack of efficient algorithms from the possible absence of any certified approximation algorithm.
formal: Does there exist a single classical Turing algorithm that, given any effectively described finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channel \(\Phi\) and a positive rational \(\varepsilon\), halts and outputs a rational r satisfying |\(r- Q(\Phi )|\le \varepsilon\), where Q is the unassisted quantum capacity in qubits per channel use?
definitions: The input includes positive integers \(d_{A},d_{B}\) and a program describing the unnormalized Choi matrix \(J(\Phi )=\sum_{ij} |i\rangle \langle j|\otimes \Phi (|i\rangle \langle j|), a\) matrix of order \(d_{A} d_{B}\). On input \(k\ge 1\), that program must halt and output a rational complex matrix whose real and imaginary entries approximate the corresponding entries of \(J(\Phi )\) within \(2^{- k}\). It is promised that the limiting matrix is positive semidefinite and \(Tr_{B} J(\Phi )=I_{A}\), so it defines a completely positive trace-preserving linear map from \(d_{A}\)-dimensional input states to \(d_{B}\)-dimensional output states. This explicitly specifies “effective description”; finite algebraic matrix descriptions are included. The requested algorithm need only meet its guarantees on inputs satisfying these promises. Memorylessness means n uses implement \(\Phi ^{\otimes n}\), allowing arbitrary joint encoding and decoding across those uses. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary channel is free. Operationally \(Q(\Phi )\) is the supremum of asymptotically achievable quantum transmission rates with error tending to zero. Equivalently, \(Q(\Phi )=\sup _{n\ge 1} n^{- 1} \max _{\rho} I_{c}(\rho ,\Phi ^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\); if \(\psi _{RA^{n}}\) is any purification and \(\omega =(id_{R}\otimes \Phi ^{\otimes n})(\psi )\), then \(I_{c}=S(\omega _{B^{n}})- S(\omega _{RB^{n}})\), with \(S(\tau )=- Tr(\tau  \log _{2}\tau )\) and \(0 \log _{2}0=0\). There is no running-time bound beyond eventual halting for every valid channel description and every \(\varepsilon >0\).
answer_criterion: A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm with a proved finite stopping rule and additive error guarantee for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such approximation algorithm exists in this specified representation. An asymptotic formula without an effective convergence bound, hardness only for polynomial-time computation, or undecidability of a different assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity is insufficient. Undecidability of testing the exact equality \(Q(\Phi )=0\) alone would also not disprove computable additive approximation.
context:
Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem expresses capacity through regularized coherent information: optimize over a block of n uses, divide by n, and take the supremum over every block length. Devetak’s coding theorem gives an operational justification for this expression. It is an exact mathematical characterization, but it involves infinitely many optimization problems. A numerical procedure needs an additional way to know when unexamined block lengths cannot improve the answer by more than \(\varepsilon\).

For each fixed block length, the input dimension is finite and the coherent-information objective can be approximated on the compact space of density matrices. Exhaustive computation can therefore produce successively better certified lower bounds on Q. This can be absurdly expensive and still count as computation here. The obstruction is that increasing lower bounds need not come with a computable certificate of how far they remain below their limit.

Cubitt, Elkouss, Matthews, Ozols, Pérez-García and Strelchuk show that no universal constant number of channel uses suffices even to expose positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there, but becomes positive at a larger block length. These are different channels as the chosen length changes. The theorem does not rule out an algorithm whose stopping time depends on the channel description and requested precision.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.
why: Determine whether the fundamental reliable quantum communication rate is algorithmically accessible even without efficiency constraints.
status_note: No uniform computability theorem or impossibility proof for this finite-dimensional memoryless unassisted capacity found through 11 September 2026. The corrected 2026 paper explicitly leaves the general question open: its quantum-capacity result is QMA-hardness, while its undecidability result concerns a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity.

working_summary: Quantum channel capacity describes the best asymptotic rate for transmitting quantum information through a noisy channel. This problem asks whether that number can always be approximated by an algorithm from an effective finite description of the channel. The algorithm may be slow, but it must halt and meet any requested rational accuracy. Optimizations involving arbitrarily many channel uses make the asymptotic definition harder to turn into a guaranteed finite computation. Establishing computability or an obstruction would separate the existence of an operational communication rate from our ability to calculate it even in principle.

title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
importance_reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.
formal: Does there exist one uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(N\ge 2\) and every oracle f hiding a subgroup H of \(D_{N}\), the algorithm outputs generators of H with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(C(\lceil \log _{2}N\rceil +\ell +2)^{c}\) total operations, where \(\ell\) is the bit length of an oracle value?
definitions: The dihedral group \(D_{N}\) has 2N elements represented as pairs \((x,b)\) with \(x\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\) and \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and multiplication \((x,b)(y,d)\)=(\(x+(- 1)^{b}y\) mod \(N,b+d\) mod 2). Its identity is \((0,0)\). The classical input is N in binary and the positive integer \(\ell\) specifying the output-register width. An arbitrary subgroup \(H\le D_{N}\) is hidden by \(f:D_{N}\to \{0,1\}^{\ell}\) when \(f(g)=f(g' )\) if and only if \(gH=g' H\), equivalently \(g^{- 1}g' \in H\). Thus distinct left cosets have distinct labels, whose bit patterns carry no promised structure. Quantum access is the reversible XOR oracle \(U_{f}|g,z\rangle =|g,z\oplus f(g)\rangle\), usable on superpositions; it acts as the identity on invalid group encodings. Each call costs one oracle operation. Count all other elementary quantum gates, measurements and classical bit operations as well, using a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T. Uniformity requires an effective polynomial-time classical controller, with no advice depending on N, H or f. There is no input truth table for f and no additional subset-sum, state-preparation or memory-access oracle. The output is a finite list of encoded group elements whose generated subgroup equals H; the empty list is allowed for \(H=\{1\}\). The success probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and measurements, for every legal hiding function separately. The displayed bound is a worst-case bound on total work, not merely query count or parallel depth. When \(\ell\) is polynomial in log N, as in the usual oracle model, the target is polynomial time in log N.
answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct a quantum algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial total-work guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A polynomial number of oracle queries with superpolynomial postprocessing, a speedup using uncounted parallel hardware, or an algorithm requiring an additional subset-sum oracle does not suffice. Failure of one family of measurements or sieves is not a negative solution for all quantum algorithms.
context:
Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has \(H=H_{s}=\{(0,0),(s,1)\}\), with an unknown \(s\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\). The hiding promise says \(f(x,0)=f(x+s,1)\), and each restriction to \(b=0\) or \(b=1\) is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

A coherent oracle query followed by discarding the function value yields a coset state. In the reflection case it has the form \((|0,x\rangle +|1,x+s\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) for an unknown random x. Fourier transformation of the cyclic coordinate produces a known random label k and a qubit with relative phase exp(\(2\pi\)iks/N). The phase contains information about s, but measuring that qubit does not simply reveal the modular product ks as a classical number.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\). It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length \(n\approx \log  N\): the target here is \(n^{O(1)}\), not \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\).

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving \(\sqrt{\log  N \log  \log  N}\). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores \(\exp (O(\sqrt{\log  N}))\) time while using only \(O(\log  N)\) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be \(N/2\), which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.
why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No verified polynomial-time solution is recorded. Simon’s August 2026 coset-algorithm claim is disputed: the September 1 Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response proves failure of the proposed template, and Guo–Yang identify an unsupported independence hypothesis. The review checked these primary statements without independently rerunning the Lean development. The 2022 Moore–Young claim was explicitly withdrawn.

working_summary: The dihedral hidden subgroup problem presents a function that is constant on cosets of an unknown subgroup of a dihedral group. The task is to recover generators for that subgroup using quantum access to the function. The target is a uniform algorithm whose total running time is polynomial in the length of the group description and oracle values. Counting only a small number of oracle queries is insufficient if processing the resulting quantum information is expensive. An efficient solution would extend the reach of hidden-subgroup methods beyond the abelian setting and illuminate connections with lattice-related algorithmic problems.

title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
importance_reason: A central quantum-algorithm target linking graph algorithms, permutation groups and the computational use of entangled states.
formal: Is \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform quantum algorithm decide, on every pair of finite simple graphs on n vertices given by their adjacency matrices, whether they are isomorphic, with error probability at most \(1/3\) and worst-case total running time \(n^{O(1)}\)?
definitions: A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and has no parallel edges. For equally sized vertex sets \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), an isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(\pi :[n]\to [n]\) satisfying \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\) if and only if \(\{\pi (u),\pi (v)\}\in E(H)\) for every \(u\ne v\). The input consists of the two explicitly written binary adjacency matrices; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately and empty graphs are handled trivially. There are no promises of rigidity, bounded degree, typicality, or a particular input distribution. BQP means a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits over a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T, acting on computational-basis encodings of the classical input and initialized ancillas, with a measured output bit. There must be fixed constants C,c such that all gates, measurements and classical control can be implemented within \(C(n+2)^{c}\) total elementary operations. The algorithm accepts each isomorphic pair with probability at least \(2/3\) and each nonisomorphic pair with probability at most \(1/3\). It receives no nonuniform advice, witness, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle or uncounted memory-preparation service. The target is the decision problem for an ordinary vertex permutation; it is not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory.
answer_criterion: Prove membership by giving a correct uniform quantum algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial total cost, or prove \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\). A classical polynomial-time algorithm would also answer yes. A separation for a specified Fourier-sampling or sieve model is not a negative answer for unrestricted BQP; an invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic pairs is not a complete positive answer.
context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |\(\pi \rangle |\pi G\rangle\) is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\) would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

A further naming distinction appears in the 2026 paper on the NPA hierarchy by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman. It studies a quantum isomorphism relation and its noncommutative semidefinite relaxations, with polynomial-time algorithms at each fixed level. Those statements concern a different relation on graphs and fixed relaxations; they do not establish a quantum algorithm deciding whether an ordinary vertex bijection exists.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.
why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm for ordinary graph isomorphism, or proof of \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\), was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 correlation tests, state-isomorphism classifications and NPA hierarchy results do not settle this question.
progress: 2005: Aaronson lists graph isomorphism as a target for new quantum algorithmic ideas. | 2005–2010: Coset-state lower bounds establish the need for highly joint measurements in the standard hidden-subgroup approach; the joint journal paper appears in 2010. | 2015–2017: Babai gives a classical quasipolynomial-time algorithm; his January 2017 update repairs the affected recursion and restores the bound. | 28 January 2026: Kar–Roberson–Seppelt–Zeman publish polynomial algorithms for fixed levels of a hierarchy for a different quantum isomorphism relation. | 12 May 2026: Gheorghiu and coauthors classify several group-action quantum state problems, with GI-hardness for the Clifford-group version. | 2 June 2026: Maxwell–van den Hoven–Renema revise their quantum-inspired necessary-condition algorithm; its sufficient full-order version is not efficient.
working_summary: Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabeling of vertices preserves every edge. This question asks whether a quantum algorithm can decide that equivalence in polynomial time for every pair of explicitly given graphs. The algorithm must include all processing costs and achieve bounded error, rather than merely extract a small amount of information from an oracle. Symmetry makes graph isomorphism a natural testing ground for quantum methods, but quantum access to related group structure is not itself a complete algorithm. A resolution would clarify whether quantum computation can efficiently handle this central classification problem.

title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
importance_reason: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.
formal: For every entangled finite-dimensional bipartite state \(\rho\), do finitely many copies \(\rho ^{\otimes}k\) and local filters suffice to produce correlations violating a Bell inequality, without an auxiliary entangled state?
definitions: A state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on \(H_{A}\otimes H_{B}\). It is entangled when it is not a convex combination of product states. Local filters are trace-nonincreasing completely positive maps \(F_{A},F_{B}\) applied to the respective k-fold systems before measurement questions are selected; the joint success probability must be positive. Normalize the successful filtered state. Each party then chooses a local measurement from a finite set of positive-operator-valued measurements. The resulting conditional distribution p(a,b|x,y) is Bell-nonlocal when it has no representation \(\sum_{\lambda} q_{\lambda} p_{A}(a|x,\lambda )p_{B}(b|y,\lambda )\), with nonnegative \(q_{\lambda}\) summing to one. Such a representation is precisely a local hidden-variable model for finite questions and answers. Local ancillary states and shared randomness are allowed, but no additional shared entangled state is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Entanglement and observable Bell nonlocality are related but distinct resources. This question asks whether repeated access to the same entanglement always reveals nonlocal behavior after local preprocessing.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove an activation result using a suitable auxiliary state. That resource is stronger than additional copies of the given state and is expressly excluded here. Direct one-copy Bell tests also do not settle the finite-copy filtered target.
why: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2012: The source establishes activation with an additional state while distinguishing the unresolved repeated-copy setting.

title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
importance_reason: Determines the strongest quantum query advantage when the function has no promise, a basic limit on quantum computation.
formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
