The 2026 paper proves a streaming Hamiltonian verification result. It discusses a possible game application with short questions but polynomial-size answers; that application is not a theorem in the checked passage, and even those parameters would not meet this card’s answer bound.
why: Would connect efficient verification of quantum witnesses to succinct classical interaction with entangled provers. The honest-prover requirement preserves the computational meaning of the witness, which unrestricted entangled proof-system containments do not ensure.
status_note: The full CCC 2026 question and the 2024 status note were checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching efficient-prover protocol or impossibility theorem was located. The stronger logarithmic-question/constant-answer conjecture is distinguished explicitly.
progress: 2024-03-19: The status note formalizes witness-assisted efficient provers and explains why the earlier claimed quantum games PCP construction does not establish the conjecture. | 2026: The CCC paper proves streaming gap amplification and explicitly leaves efficient-prover games with polylogarithmic questions and answers open.
working_summary: The question asks whether every quantum-verifiable problem has a short classical game with entangled provers. Both questions and answers must have polylogarithmic length, with a constant completeness–soundness gap. Honest provers must prepare their entanglement and answer in polynomial time given copies of a polynomial-size witness. Soundness must hold even against computationally unrestricted cheating provers. Existing unrestricted entangled proof systems and the source’s streaming Hamiltonian result do not establish this efficient-prover communication target.

title: Completeness and soundness amplification in StoqMA
importance_reason: A foundational robustness question for stoquastic proofs, equivalent to a central equality between quantum-inspired and classical verification classes. Existing score retained.
formal: For every pair of efficiently computable threshold functions \(a(n),b(n)\) with \(1/2\le b(n)<a(n)\le 1\) and \(a(n)- b(n)\ge 1/q(n)\) for some polynomial q, and every integer-valued polynomial \(\ell\)\((n)\ge 2\), is \(StoqMA(a,b)\) contained in \(StoqMA(1- 2^{- \ell (n)}, 1/2+2^{- \ell (n)})\)? Here n is the classical input length. The new verifier must remain in the same one-witness stoquastic circuit model, with polynomially many gates, witness qubits and ancillas.
definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in \(StoqMA(a,b)\) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit \(V_{x}\) on \(m(n)+r(n)+s(n)\) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |\(w\rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes r}\otimes |+\rangle ^{\otimes s}\), where |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the \(\{|+\rangle ,|- \rangle\}\) basis, with |−⟩=\((|0\rangle - |1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least \(a(n)\). If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most \(b(n)\). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within \(2^{- t}\) in time polynomial in \(n+t\). The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and \(\ell\). Soundness approaches \(1/2\) from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and \(\ell\), or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above \(1/2\) while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.
context:
The computation is classically reversible, but its ancillas and final measurement allow a nonnegative quantum witness to affect acceptance. This restricted verification model arises in the complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonians. Familiar error-reduction statements for unrestricted quantum verification do not automatically give the required stoquastic verifier.

The source’s Theorem 5 maps thresholds \((1/2+u/2,1/2+v/2)\) to \((1/2+u^{r}/2,1/2+v^{r}/2)\) for polynomial r. This improves excess soundness but can also lower completeness. Conjecture 6 asks for simultaneous amplification towards completeness one and soundness one half.

The 2025 published paper proves that negligible completeness error with a suitable inverse-polynomial gap is already contained in MA, the class of promise problems verified in polynomial time with a classical witness and random bits. Its Corollary 1.5 makes general StoqMA error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA.

The July 2026 preprint still explicitly calls general one-witness error reduction open. Its restricted repetition results do not supply the two threshold limits required here for arbitrary original completeness.

The May 2026 preprint claims that the number of stoquastic provers can be reduced while retaining an inverse-polynomial gap. It explicitly avoids assuming general amplification. This preprint claim is not recorded as a solution of the one-witness error-reduction question.
why: Would determine whether the stoquastic verification model has ordinary exponential error reduction and, through the published equivalence, whether its proof power collapses to classical Merlin–Arthur verification.
status_note: Read Conjecture 6, the verifier definition and soundness-only theorem, the 2025 published equivalence, and the relevant statements in the May and July 2026 preprints. No full one-witness amplification theorem was found through 12 September 2026. The July 2026 source explicitly still calls the general question open.
progress: 2021: Soundness-only error reduction is established, while Conjecture 6 states the simultaneous completeness/soundness target. | 2025-09-11: A published theorem establishes that general StoqMA error reduction is equivalent to StoqMA=MA. | 2026-07-12: A revised preprint on unentangled stoquastic proofs retains the general error-reduction problem as open and studies more restricted amplification guarantees.
working_summary: A StoqMA verifier uses classical reversible gates, special initial ancillas and one final measurement in the plus/minus basis. It accepts a suitable nonnegative quantum witness on yes instances and must reject arbitrary witnesses with the prescribed soundness bound on no instances. The question asks whether every inverse-polynomial gap can be amplified to completeness exponentially close to one and soundness exponentially close to one half. Soundness-only repetition is known, but it does not provide this simultaneous improvement. A published theorem makes full error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA, and July 2026 work still states the general problem as open.

title: Simulation or postselection universality for algebraic two-qubit interactions
importance_reason: A broad classification question for the computational power of restricted quantum interactions; an exact simulation convention is needed for a benchmark-ready dichotomy. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed Hermitian \(4\times4\) matrix \(H\) with complex algebraic entries, does at least one of the following hold: all of its basis-input, basis-output circuits admit polynomial-time classical sampling to arbitrary inverse-polynomial total-variation accuracy; or \(\mathrm{PP}\subseteq\operatorname{Post}(H)\), with the circuit, uniformity and postselection conventions below?
definitions: The matrix \(H=H^*\) is fixed, not part of a circuit input. Its entries are algebraic complex numbers, specified by finite integer-polynomial and isolating-region descriptions that may be hardcoded into an algorithm depending on \(H\). A circuit has \(N\ge1\) qubits initialized to an explicitly supplied computational-basis string \(b\in\{0,1\}^N\). Each gate chooses an ordered pair of distinct qubits and applies \(\exp(-itH)\) on that pair for a signed rational time \(t\); negative times give exact inverse evolution. There are no free single-qubit gates or intermediate measurements. At the end all qubits are measured in the computational basis, defining a probability distribution \(p_C\) on \(\{0,1\}^N\). The input explicitly lists the initial bits, gate sequence, ordered wire indices and rational numerators and positive denominators in binary. It also includes a unary integer \(B\ge1\) with \(|t|\le B\) for every gate. Let \(L\) be the full bit encoding length. This charges enough description length for polynomial physical evolution time, as required by the source model. The simulation branch requires a single uniform randomized Turing machine for this fixed \(H\), taking \(C\) and a binary rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), that halts on every random tape within a fixed polynomial in \(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\) and outputs a string with distribution \(s_C\) satisfying \(\tfrac12\sum_z|s_C(z)-p_C(z)|\le\varepsilon\). It uses independent fair coins and no oracle or advice. Define \(\operatorname{Post}(H)\) as follows. For a language \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a uniform deterministic polynomial-time compiler maps each input \(x\) to such a circuit \(C_x\), a designated output bit, and a disjoint list of postselection bits with prescribed values. There is a polynomial \(p\) such that the prescribed event has probability at least \(2^{-p(|x|)}\) on every input. title: Exponential repetition of two-player entangled games
importance_reason: A general soundness-amplification question central to the power of entanglement in nonlocal games and interactive proofs. Current status must account for a directly relevant new claimed proof. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every finite two-player, one-round game \(G\) with entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)<1\) admit a constant \(c_{G}>0\) such that \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq \exp(-c_{G}n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq1?\] The repetition uses the unchanged game and requires winning every coordinate. The 2016 paper proves convergence to zero at a polynomial rate; an August 2026 manuscript claims the exponential bound, with verification limits recorded below.
question_excerpt: The results of Bavarian, Vidick and Yuen show that, while we do not know if the Quantum Parallel Repetition Conjecture holds for all games \(G, [\ldots ]\)
definitions:
A game is specified by finite nonempty question sets \(X,Y\), finite nonempty answer sets \(A,B\), a probability distribution \(\mu\) on \(X\times Y\), and a winning predicate \(V:X\times Y\times A\times B\to\{0,1\}\). The referee samples \((x,y)\) from \(\mu\), sends \(x\) only to Alice and \(y\) only to Bob, and accepts their answers \(a,b\) exactly when \(V(x,y,a,b)=1\). The two questions may be correlated, and some pairs may have probability zero.

Before receiving their questions, the players may share any finite-dimensional bipartite quantum state \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal H_{A}\otimes\mathcal H_{B}\). On question \(x\), Alice applies a measurement \(\{E^{x}_{a}:a\in A\}\); on question \(y\), Bob applies \(\{F^{y}_{b}:b\in B\}\). Each measurement is a family of positive semidefinite operators summing to the identity. Their conditional answer probability is
\[\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho(E^{x}_{a}\otimes F^{y}_{b})\bigr).\]
They cannot communicate after receiving the questions. Shared randomness is permitted and can be incorporated into the shared state.

The entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)\) is the supremum of the winning probability over all such finite-dimensional states and local measurements. The dimensions have no fixed upper bound, and a strategy attaining the supremum need not exist. This is the finite-dimensional tensor-product model, not the possibly larger commuting-operator or general nonsignaling model. No efficiency restriction is placed on a strategy.

In \(G^{\otimes n}\), the referee samples \(n\) independent pairs from \(\mu\), sends the complete tuple of Alice's questions to Alice and the complete tuple of Bob's questions to Bob, and receives answer tuples in \(A^{n}\) and \(B^{n}\). Acceptance requires \(V(x_{i},y_{i},a_{i},b_{i})=1\) for every coordinate \(i\).

Each player may use one joint local measurement depending on their entire tuple. Their shared state and its dimension may depend on \(n\). Thus independent sampling by the referee does not force independent play. Product strategies give the lower bound \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\geq\omega^{*}(G)^{n}\); this is not the requested upper bound.

The constant \(c_{G}\) may depend on the entire fixed game, including its soundness gap \(1-\omega^{*}(G)\). It must be positive and independent of \(n\), the strategy and its dimension. No universal optimal exponent or algorithm for computing \(c_{G}\) is requested. A transformed game with added questions is a different game and cannot replace \(G\) in this statement.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal exponential upper bound in the stated strategy model, or exhibit one fixed finite game with value below one for which no positive \(c_{G}\) works. A sequence of different games with progressively slower exponential constants is not a counterexample. Polynomial decay, convergence to zero, exponential decay only for a special game family, or amplification after changing the game does not settle the conjecture.
context:
Yuen proves \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})=O_{G}(n^{-1/4}\log n)\) for \(n\geq2\). Hence the repeated value cannot stay bounded away from zero. The surrounding text explicitly leaves exponential decay as the full conjecture; the previous working summary conflated these two targets.

The source describes anchoring and fortification transformations that add auxiliary questions and give exponential decay for the resulting game while preserving quantum completeness. This supplies useful gap amplification but does not bound standard repetition of every original game.

Chapter 6, Theorem 1.1, claims a universal \(c>0\) with \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq\exp\!\left(-c\,\frac{\varepsilon^{13}}{\varepsilon+\ln(|A||B|)}\,n\right),\qquad\varepsilon=1-\omega^{*}(G)>0.\] Its definitions allow arbitrary finite-dimensional joint strategies and correlated question distributions for the unchanged game. If valid, this resolves the displayed conjecture; the exponent \(13\) is not claimed optimal.

This review checked the manuscript’s version date, theorem and model against the original conjecture. It did not independently verify the proof or establish an independently reviewed publication of this result. The card therefore records an uncertain claimed resolution rather than labeling the conjecture securely open or verified resolved.

title: Martin’s conjecture
importance_reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.
focus_reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.
formal: Assume \(ZF+DC+AD\). Do both assertions hold? \((I)\) Every Turing-invariant function \(f:2^{\omega}\to 2^{\omega}\) is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies \(x\le _{T} f(x)\) on a cone. \((II)\) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}(f)+1\) in this prewellorder.
definitions: A real \(x\in 2^{\omega}\) is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write \(x\le _{T} y\) if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and \(x\equiv _{T} y\) for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when \(x\equiv _{T} y\) implies \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\). A cone above a real a is \(\{x:a\le _{T} x\}\). Being constant on a cone means \(\exists a,b \forall x\ge _{T} a, f(x)\equiv _{T} b\); the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define \(f\le _{M} g\) by \(\exists a \forall x\ge _{T} a, f(x)\le _{T} g(x)\), and \(f\equiv _{M} g\) by mutual \(\le _{M}\). Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which \(id\le _{M} f\), where \(id(x)=x\). The prewellorder assertion says that \(\le _{M}\) is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding \([f]\). The jump of a real y is \(y'\)={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; \(f' (x)=f(x)'\). ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying \(f(x)\le _{T} x\) on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing \(x\equiv _{T} y\) into indices witnessing \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which \(f(x)\) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.

The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.
why: A central structural problem in computability theory: whether invariance alone, under determinacy, forces nontrivial operations on computational degrees into a well-ordered hierarchy. It connects relative computability, definability, descriptive set theory, and analogies with hierarchies of proof-theoretic strength.
status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.

working_summary: Turing-invariant functions act on sets of integers in a way that respects mutual computability. Under determinacy and dependent choice, Martin's full conjecture proposes a rigid cone-wise hierarchy for these functions. Its first part says a function is eventually constant in degree or eventually computes its input, and its second organizes the nonconstant behavior with the jump as the next rank. The conjecture would explain why natural operations on degrees appear in a remarkably ordered progression. The reviewed statement includes arbitrary invariant functions, so results requiring uniformity, order preservation, or special definability leave part of the challenge untouched.

title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
importance_reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.
focus_reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.
formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
definitions: Work in Cantor space \(2^{N}\), with coordinates numbered \(0,1,\ldots\) and fair-coin product measure \(\mu\). For a finite binary string \(\sigma\), the cylinder \([\sigma ]\)={\(X:\sigma\) is a prefix of X} has measure \(2^{- |\sigma |}\). A Martin-Löf test is a sequence \((U_{k})_{k\ge 1}\) of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs \((k,\sigma )\), with \(U_{k}\) equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and \(\mu (U_{k})\le 2^{- k}\). A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test \(X\notin \bigcap _{k} U_{k}\). A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier \(q\in [0,2]\), before seeing \(X(j)\). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After \(X(j)\) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by \(2- q\) if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. \(q=1\) allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most \(1/R\). Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.
why: A central equivalence problem for algorithmic randomness: determine whether adaptive computable prediction detects every failure of effective measure-theoretic randomness.
status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

working_summary: Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategies may adaptively inspect previously unseen bits in any order while making fair computable bets. The question asks whether every sequence defeating all such strategies is Martin-Löf random. Martin-Löf randomness instead requires avoidance of every effective sequence of small-measure exceptional sets. Equality would show that flexible computable betting captures the full statistical-test notion of algorithmic randomness. The reviewed model allows partial strategies and unbounded capital success, so limitations for fixed reading orders or weaker betting rules cannot settle the comparison.

title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
importance_reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.
formal: Is every order automorphism of the partial order \((D_{t},\le _{t})\) of all Turing degrees the identity? Equivalently, does every bijection \(\pi :D_{t}\to D_{t}\) satisfying \(a\le _{t}b\) if and only if \(\pi (a)\le _{t}\pi (b)\), for all \(a,b\in D_{t}\), also satisfy \(\pi (a)=a\) for every \(a\in D_{t}\)?
definitions: For sets \(A,B\subseteq \mathbb{N} , A\le _{t}B\) means that an oracle Turing machine with membership-query access to B halts on every natural-number input and decides membership in A. There is no time or space bound. \(A\equiv _{t}B\) means \(A\le _{t}B\) and \(B\le _{t}A\). The Turing degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of A under ≡\(_{t}\), and \(D_{t}\) is the quotient of all subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\) by this equivalence. The relation \([A]\le _{t}[B]\) is independent of the chosen representatives and is a partial order. An automorphism is any set-theoretic bijection of \(D_{t}\) preserving and reflecting this order. It is not assumed computable, definable, continuous, measure-preserving or induced by one operation on representatives. The domain includes all degrees, not only degrees of computably enumerable sets or degrees below a fixed bound. The question is interpreted for the actual degree structure in ordinary set theory, for example ZFC.
answer_criterion: Prove that every such bijection fixes every degree, or prove the existence of one order automorphism and one degree that it moves. An automorphism of a proper substructure, a non-surjective order embedding, or a permutation of subsets that fails to descend to degrees is not a counterexample. Rigidity of one cone or of a restricted class of induced automorphisms is only a partial positive result. An independence result should specify the axiomatic base and would settle provability relative to that base rather than assert either mathematical answer.
context:
Turing degrees classify decision problems by what can be computed from an oracle for them. Different encodings that compute one another become one point, and the order records comparative computational power. The rigidity question asks whether this order has any genuine symmetry: could all degrees be consistently relabeled, changing at least one degree while preserving every reducibility comparison? A positive answer would make the entire relative-computability structure intrinsically asymmetric.

Elementary examples illustrate what is already forced. The degree 0 of computable sets is the unique least element and therefore cannot move. The join of \([A]\) and \([B]\) is represented by \(A\oplus B\), which stores A on even positions and B on odd positions; because it is the least upper bound, every order automorphism preserves joins as well. These observations do not identify arbitrary degrees, whose patterns of predecessors and successors are far more complicated.

The Turing jump sends \([A]\) to the degree of the halting problem for machines equipped with oracle A. Shore and Slaman prove that this operation is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Consequently every automorphism commutes with the jump, and fixes \(0' , 0''\) and all finite iterates starting from 0. This is a major restriction, but commuting with an operation does not by itself force a map to fix every argument.

Slaman and Woodin prove that every automorphism fixes every degree above \(0''\). Their analysis also shows that the automorphism group is at most countable, despite the continuum-sized underlying degree structure. The unresolved region is the complement of that upper cone. It includes degrees incomparable with \(0''\), not just degrees strictly below it. Thus describing the remaining question as only the interval below \(0''\) would omit part of the problem.

One possible way to construct an automorphism would be to permute the natural-number coordinates of every oracle set. Kjos-Hanssen rules this out: if one permutation of \(\mathbb{N}\) induces an order automorphism on all Turing degrees, the induced automorphism is trivial, and the permutation itself must be computable. His result also treats homeomorphisms of Cantor space preserving all Bernoulli product measures. The full question imposes none of these representation or measure restrictions.

Rigidity must also be distinguished from defining every single degree by a first-order formula without parameters. There are only countably many such formulas but uncountably many degrees, so the latter is impossible. A rigid infinite structure can contain elements that are not individually definable: absence of global symmetries is weaker than having a separate finite logical description of each element.

The historical literature includes an announced nontrivial automorphism by Cooper in 1999. Slaman’s survey explicitly reports that its construction had not been independently verified and continues to treat rigidity as open. Kjos-Hanssen’s later journal article likewise states the general question as open. These cards follow the established partial-result literature; an old announcement alone is not treated as a resolution.

This is a foundational computability question rather than an efficient-algorithm problem. Its significance is whether relative computability already determines its own global structure, or whether the degree order admits hidden symmetries that are invisible to all reducibility comparisons.
why: A central structural question about relative computability: whether the ordering of computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. It tests how much mathematical information is recoverable from reducibility alone.
status_note: Literature search checked through 10 September 2026. The checked primary sources explicitly retain general rigidity as open; no later verified resolution was located. The last substantive result documented here is the 2018 journal article, not a claimed 2026 advance. The historical Cooper announcement is distinguished from an independently verified solution.

working_summary: Turing degrees identify sets of integers that compute one another and order them by relative computability. The rigidity question asks whether every order-preserving bijection of this entire partial order fixes every degree. A positive answer would mean that the order structure alone determines the identity of each degree. This is a basic structural question about how much information is encoded by the pattern of computational reducibility. The saved review permits arbitrary set-theoretic automorphisms, so excluding computable transformations or automorphisms induced by a special action on representatives is only a restricted result.

title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
importance_reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.
formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$ by specifying a machine $M_*\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape and proving that $T(M)\le T(M_*)$ for every $M\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape. Here $\mathcal{M}_6$ is the class of deterministic Turing machines with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape, as defined below, and $T(M)$ counts transitions up to and including the first entry into the separate halting state. The answer is then $BB(6)=T(M_*)$; the witness runtime is an exact description of the value.
definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in \(T(M)\). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$. For a halting machine \(M, T(M)\) is the least positive integer t at which the execution enters Z. The answer convention never applies T to a nonhalting machine: halting of the proposed witness is a required part of its certificate. Its explicitly specified transition table together with that certificate defines a terminating step-counting computation and hence a unique exact integer, even when evaluating that computation is impractical.
answer_criterion: Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular machine \(M_\ast\) in the stated class. Provide Lean-checked proofs that (1) \(M_\ast\) halts from the specified blank-tape initial configuration, and (2) every machine M in this class that halts from that initial configuration executes at most \(T(M_\ast)\) transitions. Together these certify \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_\ast)\) exactly. The runtime of this proved-halting concrete machine is an accepted finite description of the integer; a simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. Specifying a machine without proving its halting and universal maximality, restating the defining maximum over all machines, or giving only an approximate or one-sided bound does not meet this criterion.
context:
Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved \(S(5)=47,176,870\) with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. A concrete machine with proved halting and universal maximality specifies that integer through its runtime, without a simple closed form or decimal expansion. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.
why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
importance_reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.
formal: Over RCA\(_{0}\), does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA\(_{0}^{+}\)? Equivalently, does RCA\(_{0}+HT\) prove that every set X has an \(\omega -th\) Turing jump?
definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA\(_{0}\) has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, \(\Sigma ^{0}_{1}\) induction and \(\Delta ^{0}_{1}\) comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every coloring c of the positive integers into \(\{0,\ldots ,k- 1\}\), there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that \(c(\sum_{h\in F}h)=i\) for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump \(X'\) is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom says \(\forall X\exists Y\) [\(Y_{0}=X\) and \(\forall j(Y_{j+1}=Y_{j}' )\)], where \(Y_{j}=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle \in Y\}\) and \(\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle\) is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) is RCA\(_{0}\) plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
answer_criterion: Prove the \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom in RCA\(_{0}+HT\), or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA\(_{0}+HT\) in which some set has no coded \(\omega\)-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA\(_{0}\) alone, an upper bound of ACA\(_{0}^{+}\), or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}\); an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
context:
Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA\(_{0}\) allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The \(\omega\)-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) demands more set existence than ACA\(_{0}\). Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the \((\omega +1)-st\) jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an \(\omega\)-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA\(_{0}\); four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly \(n\ge 3\) terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no \(\Sigma ^{0}_{2}\) solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}^{+}\). A finite set F is exactly large when |\(F|=\min (F)+1\), so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low\(_{2}\) solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA\(_{0}\). The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the \(\omega\)-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.
why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the \(\omega -th\) Turing jump.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No proof or separation for RCA\(_{0}+HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) was found in the checked primary literature. The recent variable-word and Carlson–Simpson results have different formulations and do not establish this reversal.
progress: 1987: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) over RCA\(_{0}\), leaving the reversal in this card open. | 2012–2014: Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal. | 2017–2020: Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA\(_{0}\) lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020. | 2018: Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT. | 11 June–2 July 2026: Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength. | 30 July 2026: Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.
working_summary: Hindman's theorem finds an infinite set whose nonempty finite sums all receive the same color in any finite coloring. The question asks whether this principle proves the existence of every set's iterated omega-th Turing jump over RCA0. It measures the theorem's logical strength rather than asking whether the combinatorial statement is true in ordinary mathematics. A positive implication would show that unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity entails a strong closure principle for computability. The reviewed formulation allows sums of arbitrarily many distinct elements, so results for exactly two terms or other restricted variants do not answer it automatically.

title: Universality of Turing equivalence
importance_reason: A classical universality question with consequences for Martin’s conjecture and for the distinction between definable and uniform computational encodings.
formal: For every countable Borel equivalence relation E on a standard Borel space X, does there exist a Borel function \(f:X\to 2^{\mathbb{N}}\) such that x E y if and only if \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), for all \(x,y\in X\)?
definitions: The space \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\) consists of all infinite binary sequences, identified with subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\). For \(a,b\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}, a\le _{T} b\) means that some oracle Turing machine with oracle b computes every bit of a and halts on every input coordinate; \(a\equiv _{T} b\) means both \(a\le _{T} b\) and \(b\le _{T} a\). There is no time or space restriction on these computations. A standard Borel space is a set with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of some Polish topology. The relation E must be a Borel subset of \(X\times X\) and each equivalence class must be at most countable; X itself may be uncountable. The function f is Borel measurable: inverse images of Borel sets are Borel. It need not be computable, continuous, injective on points, or uniform on indices witnessing equivalence. It must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence on every input pair, not merely almost everywhere for a chosen measure. The quantifiers ask for a separate Borel reduction for each E, without requiring an algorithm that takes a code for E and outputs f. This is the ordinary ZFC formulation of Borel universality.
answer_criterion: Prove that Turing equivalence is universal by producing the requisite Borel reductions, or prove it is not by identifying one countable Borel relation that does not reduce to it. Equivalently, settle whether \(E_{\infty}\le _{B}\equiv _{T}\) for a fixed standard universal countable Borel relation \(E_{\infty}\). A negative theorem conditional on a form of Martin’s conjecture must be labeled conditional. Failure of reductions with an additional uniformity or computability requirement is not a negative solution to the unrestricted Borel question.
context:
Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of \(f(x)\) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

It suffices to study a single standard benchmark \(E_{\infty}\). One realization is the orbit relation for the shift action of the free group \(F_{2}\) on \(\{0,1\}^{F_{2}}\): two labelings x,y are equivalent when \(y(h)=x(g^{- 1}h)\) for some group element g and every \(h\in F_{2}\). This countable Borel relation is universal. A reduction of that one relation to Turing equivalence would therefore answer the full universally quantified question.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Finer and coarser relations do not give an automatic transfer here. A coding that keeps two outputs inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may still make them equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. Once that happens, the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction fails. Preserving the encoding under all additional computations is the missing task; simply reusing the polynomial-time result does not complete it.

There is also a structural obstruction to familiar coding approaches. With Turing equivalence generated in its usual way by oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Roughly, uniformity would require indices for computations between encoded outputs to be chosen solely from the indices witnessing the original equivalence, independently of the particular objects. Marks develops this distinction and shows why the choice of generating maps must be specified.

The present problem permits arbitrary Borel reductions, so that uniform obstruction is not the desired nonuniversality theorem. Whether ordinary universality must entail appropriate stronger uniformity properties is itself part of the surrounding theory. A proof that rules out one common coding pattern therefore reveals a methodological barrier without exhausting all Borel encodings.

Martin’s conjecture supplies a competing prediction. Its Borel form implies that Turing equivalence is not universal; in particular, it obstructs reducing two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. Conversely, a universality proof would contradict that prediction. The point is a genuine conditional connection between two major structural questions, not an unconditional settlement in either direction.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision investigates an older question about writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. A positive answer would imply nonuniform invariant functions and universality of ordinary many-one equivalence. Their consequences remain conditional on that decomposition question, and concern distinctions among degree relations that must not be collapsed into a proof of Turing universality.

Settling the card would tell us whether mutual computability provides a universal language for countable Borel classification, or has a structural limitation absent from some nearby degree notions. Either outcome would matter beyond computability: it would constrain the ways orbit equivalence relations, invariants and definable encodings can interact. The answer criterion is a precise existence theorem for reductions, with no algorithmic-efficiency requirement hidden inside the word “Borel.”
why: A central bridge between computability and descriptive set theory, asking whether equality of computational power can encode every countable Borel classification problem.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No proof or refutation of ordinary Borel universality of unrestricted Turing equivalence was found in the checked sources. Arithmetic and polynomial-time universality, nonuniformity obstructions and the conditional February 2026 consequences concern distinct statements.
progress: 1992: Kechris’s universality question is recorded in the historical sources surveyed by Caicedo–Löwe. | 2011–2016: Marks–Slaman–Steel publish the universality proof for arithmetic equivalence and explain the conflict between Turing universality and Martin’s conjecture. | 2016–2018: Marks proves universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence; online publication is 2016 and the journal issue is 2018. | 2017: Marks develops uniform universality and records the obstruction for Turing equivalence with its standard generating reductions. | 2024: Kechris’s book preprint retains Turing universality as Problem 12.5. | 16 February 2026: Day–Marks revise their paper connecting an unresolved decomposition question to nonuniform invariance and many-one universality.
working_summary: Turing equivalence groups infinite binary sequences according to mutual computability. The question asks whether every countable Borel equivalence relation can be reduced to this relation by a Borel map. Such universality would mean that relative computability realizes the full classification complexity available among countable Borel equivalence relations. The map must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence for every pair, rather than merely describe typical behavior. The saved statement does not require the map to be computable or uniform on witnesses, making results about more restrictive reductions or resource-bounded equivalence separate issues.

title: Mortality of \(2\times 2\) integer matrix semigroups
importance_reason: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite list \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\) of \(2\times 2\) integer matrices, halts and correctly decides whether there exist \(\ell\)\(\ge 1\) and indices \(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{\ell}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(A_{i_{1}} A_{i_{2}} \cdots  A_{i_{\ell}}=0_{2}\)?
definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.
context:
A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.
why: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.
status_note: The checked 2024 primary manuscript explicitly leaves unrestricted \(2\times 2\) integer mortality open. The 2020 determinant-restricted algorithm and April 2026 embedding results do not settle it. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established general resolution; proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2012: The two-dimensional integer mortality problem is shown NP-hard; lower-bound attribution checked in later primary papers. | 2020-07: The revised affine-reachability paper proves NP-completeness under the determinant promise {0,+1}. | 2024: The same authors explicitly retain general two-dimensional mortality as open while resolving membership complexity for \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\). | 2026-04: New results concern word representations and embeddings in complex matrix structures rather than unrestricted integer mortality.
working_summary: A finite list of two-by-two integer matrices generates all nonempty products with arbitrary order and repetition. The question asks whether a terminating algorithm can decide if any such product is the zero matrix. Matrix entries and the number of generators are unrestricted. NP-hardness is known, while decidability results for restricted determinants do not cover the general case. Resolving the question would locate a basic computability boundary for products of small matrices.

title: Scaling joint Kolmogorov-complexity profiles
importance_reason: Scaling complete algorithmic-information profiles asks whether shared information has a universal homogeneous geometry, across arbitrary tuples rather than one example.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\) and real \(\lambda >0\), does there exist a constant \(c>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every tuple of binary strings \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}\) of length at most n, there are finite binary strings \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{k}\) satisfying |\(C(b_{S})- \lambda  C(a_{S})|\le c \log _{2} n\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,k\}\)? The same tuple b must satisfy all \(2^{k}- 1\) inequalities simultaneously.
definitions: Fix one optimal plain Kolmogorov machine U: an optimal partial computable map from finite binary programs to finite binary strings. \(C(x)\) is the minimum program length with U(program)=x. For \(S=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{r}\}\), encode the tuple \(x_{S}\) as \(1^{r}0\) followed, in that order, by the strings \(1^{|x_{i}|}0x_{i}\), and let \(C(x_{S})\) mean the complexity of this encoding. This is a fixed computably decodable encoding. The strings \(b_{i}\) have no prescribed lengths and need not be computable from the \(a_{i}\) by a fixed transformation. Only joint unconditional complexities of all nonempty subtuples are required. The constants may depend on \(k, \lambda\) and U but not on n, the input strings or S. The additive slack is measured in bits. This uses the original length normalization \(O(\log  n)\); it does not silently replace it by the potentially smaller \(O(\log  C(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}))\).
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal statement, or its logical negation with the same quantifier order. Failure of one algorithm for producing b, or failure of obtaining the scaling by conditioning the original strings on an auxiliary string, is not a refutation. The logarithmic slack is part of the proposition, not a numerical-estimation tolerance.
context:
Scaling each component separately can destroy its shared-information pattern with other components. The target scales the entire joint profile, retaining those dependencies.

The original card asked for \(\lambda =1/2\). The retained question asks for every fixed positive \(\lambda\), as in Question 1 of the 2025 paper. It is a broader formulation; no equivalence to the single halving case is asserted.

The 2025 paper separates freely choosing a new tuple from conditioning the original tuple on one auxiliary string. Its negative conditioning result does not settle the new-tuple problem. Its discussion retains nonintegral scaling for general tuples as open.
why: Scaling complete algorithmic-information profiles asks whether shared information has a universal homogeneous geometry, across arbitrary tuples rather than one example.
status_note: The 2025 primary source retains the general scaling question; its conditioning obstruction is a different target.
progress: 2025: Question 1 retains arbitrary joint-profile scaling as a problem, while distinguishing the conditioning formulation addressed by the paper.
working_summary: Every tuple of strings has a profile of complexities of its nonempty subtuples. The question asks whether that whole profile can be multiplied by any fixed positive real factor. One new tuple must realize all the scaled quantities within logarithmic additive error. No fixed algorithm mapping the old tuple to the new one is required. The target concerns the homogeneous geometry of shared algorithmic information.

title: Equivalence of Shannon and algorithmic network coding
importance_reason: Equivalence of Shannon and algorithmic network coding would connect two general frameworks for distributed information.
formal: Equivalence of Shannon and algorithmic network coding
context: The limits of algorithmic solvability and description length. Oracles, uniformity, and representations can change the statement.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question compares the power of models or representations. Resolving it would identify whether their difference changes what can be computed, rather than only the implementation cost.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Shannon network coding studies transmission of random information through a network, while algorithmic network coding describes information using individual strings and program lengths. The question asks whether the two frameworks have equivalent capabilities in the source's sense. Such an equivalence would connect probabilistic entropy-based feasibility with finite-object descriptions lacking an underlying distribution. It could explain when network coding conclusions transfer between statistical and algorithmic information theories. The saved index does not preserve the network model, approximation terms, or asymptotic scaling, so the exact meaning of equivalence must be recovered before matching their achievable regions.

title: Strong extractors for infinite sequences
importance_reason: Relating randomness, extraction, computational bounds, and logical strength would clarify general principles in algorithmic information.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(F\) such that for every pair of infinite binary sequences \(x,y\) with
\[\dim(x)=\dim(y)=\tfrac12\]
and global algorithmic independence as defined below, all computations \(F^{x\oplus y}(i)\), \(i\ge0\), halt with a bit, and the resulting sequence \(z(i)=F^{x\oplus y}(i)\) satisfies
\[\dim^x(z)=\dim^y(z)=1?\]
Here \(\dim^a\) is effective Hausdorff dimension measured with the entire sequence \(a\) available as an oracle. The same machine must work for all promised pairs; it receives no description of their independence constants.

This card takes the explicit dimension-one-half instance in the 2012 question and uses “independent” in the global oracle sense of Calude–Zimand's Definition 2.1. The weaker finitary prefix-independence notion is distinguished below; it is not silently substituted for this premise.
definitions:
An infinite binary sequence is a function \(a:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), with positions starting at zero. Its length-\(n\) prefix is \(a{\upharpoonright}n=a(0)\cdots a(n-1)\). The join is the interleaving \((x\oplus y)(2i)=x(i)\), \((x\oplus y)(2i+1)=y(i)\).

Fix an optimal plain universal Turing machine and an optimal plain universal oracle Turing machine. For a finite binary string \(u\), let \(C(u)\) be the minimum number of program bits required by the first machine to halt with exactly \(u\) as output. Let \(C^a(u)\) be the corresponding minimum for the oracle machine with access to the entire sequence \(a\): a query at index \(i\) returns \(a(i)\). No time, space or oracle-use bound is imposed. Programs are finite binary strings and are not required to form a prefix-free set. Optimality means simulation of every fixed machine of the same type with an additive constant in program length, uniformly in the oracle for the oracle version. Changing the chosen optimal machines changes the complexities only by constants and does not change the dimensions or independence condition here.

Define
\[\dim(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\qquad
\dim^b(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C^b(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\]
where \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Both dimensions lie in \([0,1]\). The input requirement is equality to one half, not a uniform finite-prefix lower bound with a supplied deficiency. In particular the point at which a lower estimate begins to hold may depend on the sequence and on the estimate's accuracy.

Global algorithmic independence means that there exists a finite constant \(c\ge0\), depending on the pair but not on prefix length, such that for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[C^y(x{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2),\qquad
C^x(y{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(y{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2).\]
An additive constant can be absorbed into \(c\), so this fixes the logarithmic-loss convention also at small lengths. These are requirements about individual infinite sequences; there is no probability distribution from which inputs must be sampled.

For comparison only, finitary independence requires a constant \(d\ge0\) such that for every \(n,m\ge1\),
\[C((x{\upharpoonright}n)(y{\upharpoonright}m))\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)+C(y{\upharpoonright}m)-d\bigl(\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(m+2)\bigr).\]
Juxtaposition here is finite-string concatenation. Global independence implies this condition, but the converse fails; the finitary condition alone is not this card's input promise. The 2007 extraction paper uses “independent” for that weaker condition, whereas the 2010 paper explicitly distinguishes both.

The machine \(F\) has a finite program and input the binary representation of the output position \(i\). It may adaptively query either sequence through the join and use arbitrarily much finite time and space on each halting computation. Each output bit must halt for every promised pair. The machine may diverge on pairs outside the promise, and no computable uniform bound on oracle positions queried is required. There is no additional oracle, random seed or input-dependent advice.
