title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
importance_reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.
focus_reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.
formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
context:
Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.

A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) has some ordinary Frege proof \(\rho\) of the same formula with |\(\rho |\le C(|\pi |+2)^{k}\)? Fix formulas over negation \(
eg\) and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), and modus ponens: infer B from A and \(A	o B\). A proof is a finite sequence ending with \(\varphi\); earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair \(e	o 	heta\) and \(	heta 	o e\), where e is a new variable absent from \(\varphi , 	heta\) and all preceding lines. \(	heta\) may use variables of \(\varphi\) and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds \(ho\) from \(\pi\). In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The extension rule gives reusable names to intermediate computations. If a subformula is used many times, ordinary formula syntax writes out each occurrence; Extended Frege can define it once and refer to its name. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. That upper bound constrains possible lower bounds for the family, but it does not demonstrate a separation and does not rule out a polynomial Frege upper bound. Quasipolynomial and polynomial must remain distinct in this problem.

Krajíček’s June 2026 paper gives a circuit-rewriting description of EF reasoning. An EF proof of circuit equivalence yields a polynomially long chain of equivalence-preserving rewrites; each rewrite adds at most seven gates and may delete gates. This is a normal-form result about circuit reasoning. The intermediate objects still retain circuit sharing, so it does not turn an arbitrary EF proof into a polynomial-size formula-based Frege proof.

A September 2026 preprint by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay proves a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a partially commutative formula version of the Ideal Proof System over \(GF(2)\). Variables lie in two groups: they commute across groups but not within a group. The proof formalizes an identity-testing algorithm inside Frege. The restrictions on the algebraic certificates, and the quasipolynomial overhead, both matter; the theorem is not the full EF simulation asked for here.

A negative answer would establish a concrete benefit of reusable definitions for strong propositional reasoning. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. By contrast, proving that Frege has some hard tautologies, or assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), does not automatically separate it from EF: those same tautologies might require equally long EF proofs. The separate question of whether EF itself is polynomially bounded asks about a different comparison.
why: This asks whether reusable definitions fundamentally shorten mathematical proofs, beyond any polynomial factor. It is one of the central comparisons between strong propositional proof systems and captures the difficulty of reasoning with shared circuits versus explicit formulas.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.
progress: 1979: Cook–Reckhow’s framework establishes the robustness of standard Frege and Extended Frege presentations; EF contains ordinary Frege. | 1991: Buss characterizes the simulation by polynomial-size Frege proofs of partial EF consistency statements. | 2014: Buss’s mini-tutorial explicitly identifies Frege versus EF as a longstanding open simulation question. | 2015–2018: Aisenberg and coauthors obtain polynomial EF and quasipolynomial Frege upper bounds for Kneser–Lovász principles, without proving a lower-bound separation. | 2026-06-11: Krajíček gives an EF/circuit-equivalence rewriting characterization, retaining circuit intermediate representations. | 2026-09-05: ECCC TR26-166 extends quasipolynomial Frege simulation to two-group partially commutative formula IPS over \(GF(2)\).
working_summary: Extended Frege adds reusable formula definitions to ordinary Frege reasoning. The question asks whether every Extended Frege proof has an ordinary Frege proof of the same conclusion with only polynomially larger size. Expanding definitions directly can be exponentially expensive, but another Frege argument might avoid that expansion. The comparison tests whether sharing intermediate computations fundamentally increases propositional proof strength. The saved review asks only for existence of short translated proofs, carefully separating this size simulation from a polynomial-time procedure that actually finds them.

title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
importance_reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.
formal: For every fixed prime p, does there exist a family of propositional tautologies \((\tau _{p,n})_{n\ge 1}\), constructible in time polynomial in n, whose encoded lengths lie between n and \(n^{O}(1)\), such that each \(\tau _{p,n}\) is a DNF and, for every fixed proof-line depth d and every constant \(r>0\), infinitely many n have the following property: every depth-at-most-d Frege proof with \(MOD_{p}\) connectives of \(\tau _{p,n}\) has total encoded size greater than \(n^{r}\)? The proof system and depth convention are specified below; the family may depend on p but not on d or r.
definitions: A tautology evaluates to true on every Boolean assignment. A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. Fix a conventional sound, implicationally complete finite Frege calculus F over constants 0,1 and connectives NOT, AND, OR. A proof is a sequence of formulas, each a substitution instance of an axiom or obtained from earlier lines by a rule of F; earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily. Extend the language and rules as F(\(MOD_{p}\)) in Krajíček §\(5: MOD_{p,j}(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{t})\) is true precisely when the number of true arguments is j modulo p, for \(0\le j<p\). Besides F’s rules with formulas from this language, permit the empty-list axioms \(MOD_{p,0}\)() and \(\mathrm{NOT} MOD_{p,j}\)() for \(j\ne 0\), and all instances of \(MOD_{p,j}(\Gamma ,A) \leftrightarrow\) [(\(MOD_{p,j}(\Gamma ) \mathrm{AND} \mathrm{NOT} A\)) OR (\(MOD_{p,j- 1}(\Gamma ) \mathrm{AND} A\))], with \(j- 1\) taken modulo p and \(\Gamma\) any list of formulas. Constants and variables have depth zero; NOT and MOD increase depth by one, while consecutive ANDs, or consecutive ORs, are flattened and together count as one layer. Every line, including instantiated axioms, obeys the bound d. Proof size counts all symbols and encoded variable indices across all lines, together with rule annotations. Proofs are ordinary Frege proofs, without extension-variable definition axioms; they need not be tree-like or have bounded derivation-graph depth. Standard choices of F give equivalent systems up to polynomial overhead and a constant depth adjustment, immaterial when every fixed d is quantified.
answer_criterion: Exhibit the uniform tautology families and prove the stated superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds, or refute their existence. The tautology condition must itself be established: a formula that has no short proof because it is false is not a hard tautology. A lower bound only for bounded derivation depth, regular proofs, a restricted algebraic subsystem or Boolean circuits alone does not settle this question. A result for one prime is a major partial answer; this single card groups the full fixed-prime frontier rather than duplicating it for each modulus.
context:
Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when \(p=2\). Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth \(\Omega (w^{2}/\log  S)\) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as \(n^{10}\) and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.
why: A central frontier in propositional proof complexity: current methods can handle ordinary bounded-depth reasoning but still cannot establish explicit superpolynomial lower bounds once modular counting is available. The problem tests how circuit lower-bound ideas can constrain entire deductions.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary sources retain modular Frege lower bounds as open. ITCS 2026.99 does not prove that its hard-to-prove candidates are tautologies. ECCC TR26-018 restricts derivation depth or proves a polynomial size bound; TR26-070 treats a restricted algebraic certificate representation. None establishes the fully specified tautology families and unrestricted derivation size lower bounds requested here.

working_summary: \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege uses bounded-depth proof formulas that may include modular counting connectives for a fixed prime p. The saved target asks for explicit polynomial-size DNF tautologies requiring superpolynomial proofs at every fixed formula depth. Modular gates can retain counting information that ordinary restriction methods erase. A lower bound would extend the reach of proof complexity beyond the established bounded-depth systems without modular counting. The reviewed record distinguishes logical depth within proof lines from derivation depth and explains why circuit lower bounds do not automatically imply the requested proof lower bound.

title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
importance_reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.
formal: Is the Frege proof system not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every \(C>0\) and \(c\ge 1\), does some propositional tautology \(\varphi\) have shortest Frege proof size \(s_{F}(\varphi )>C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\)?
definitions:
Use explicitly written Boolean formulas over propositional variables, negation \(
eg\) and material implication →. Fix the axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), where A,B,C may be replaced uniformly within an instance by any formulas. A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each either an instance of one of these schemes or inferred from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\) by modus ponens. Its last line is \(\varphi\). There are no undischarged assumptions and no extension rule introducing abbreviations for other formulas. Previously derived lines may be reused arbitrarily. Intermediate formulas may have arbitrary depth and length; there is no independent cap on a line’s size. Variables not occurring in \(\varphi\) may occur in ordinary axiom instances and inference lines. A tautology is a formula true under every Boolean assignment. Fix a standard binary encoding with variable indices in binary and explicitly encoded connectives, delimiters and inference references. The input size |\(\varphi |\) and the proof size are their full bit lengths, including every repeated formula occurrence. The minimum over all such proofs is \(s_{F}(\varphi )\). Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so polynomial boundedness is independent of this choice of basis. The question concerns existence of proofs, without a uniform algorithm to generate either the hard tautologies or their shortest proofs.
answer_criterion: Prove that no one polynomial bounds the minimum Frege proof size of every tautology, or refute this by proving a universal bound \(s_{F}(\varphi )\le C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\) for fixed C,c. A fixed-degree lower bound, a lower bound for a restricted subsystem, or hardness of searching for proofs is not a complete affirmative answer. An explicit efficiently generated hard family would be a stronger form of a positive solution, but is not required by the quantified statement.
context:
Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |\(\varphi |\), and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Consequently, \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, \(Res(\log )\), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.
why: A defining lower-bound problem for formal reasoning. It asks whether an elementary, robust and powerful language of efficiently checkable proofs necessarily fails to certify some short tautologies with polynomial-size derivations.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for unrestricted Frege proof size was found in the checked primary sources. The April 2026 tree-like result has a line-size cap, the formalization result concerns bounded-depth proofs, and the June 2026 algebraic result does not translate into the required propositional lower bound.

working_summary: Frege systems formalize propositional deduction through finitely specified rules and reusable intermediate lemmas. The question asks whether tautologies sometimes require proofs exceeding every polynomial in their own encoded length. It concerns the shortest possible derivation, not the time spent by any particular proof-search strategy. A lower bound would establish a substantial limitation on a familiar model of mathematical reasoning. The saved review notes that powerful counting arguments give short Frege proofs where weaker systems struggle, and that separating Frege alone would not establish \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\).

title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
importance_reason: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?
definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}*\to\)TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(\mathrm{P}(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists \mathrm{P} \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |\(\pi |\).
answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.
context:
Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\).

Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.
why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
status_note: Primary definitions and the 1989 equivalence theorem were checked, together with February and ICALP 2026 primary sources. The latter retain the propositional optimality questions; their oracle results do not resolve this unrelativized target. A search through 11 September 2026 found no full resolution, and proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 1989: Theorem \(2.1(ii)\) relates polynomial simulation of all propositional proof systems to optimal tautology recognition and finite-consistency proof construction; \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) implies this existence. | 2026-02-02: Q1 explicitly retains (p-)optimality for TAUT as open. New oracle constructions show barriers for relativizing answers even with assumptions about the polynomial hierarchy. | 2026-07: ICALP work on recursive jump operators gives oracle barriers and results for other languages, while retaining the propositional optimality questions.
working_summary: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system? The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length. Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial. This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology. The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
importance_reason: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
formal: Do disjoint languages \(A,B\in \mathrm{NP}\) exist such that, for every disjoint pair \(C,D\in \mathrm{NP}\), there is a deterministic polynomial-time function f with \(f(C)\subseteq A\) and \(f(D)\subseteq B\)?
definitions: All four languages consist of finite binary strings. NP means membership has a polynomial-length certificate checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Disjoint means \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(C\cap D=\varnothing\). The total function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* may depend on \((C,D)\); its running-time polynomial need not be universal across pairs. No requirement is imposed on \(f(x)\) when \(x\notin C\cup D\). Completeness uses one function for both sides, not two unrelated reductions.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
A disjoint NP pair expresses two efficiently certifiable cases that cannot occur together. Complete pairs would provide a universal object for this kind of promise complexity.

Canonical disjoint pairs arise from propositional proof systems, tying the question to proof simulation and finite incompleteness. The existence of a p-optimal proof system would imply a complete pair, but the converse is not asserted. This card asks the pair-completeness question itself.
why: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2017: The paper organizes the complete-pair question and its connections to proof-complexity conjectures.

title: Effective polynomial simulation of Extended Frege by Resolution
importance_reason: Tests whether conventional proof-size separations remain meaningful when hard instances themselves must be found efficiently.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer \(s\ge 1, R\)(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
definitions:
A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation \(
eg\) and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent \(C\lor D\) of earlier clauses \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor 
eg x\). Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), or follow by modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\). One may also introduce an extension axiom \(z\leftrightarrow B\), where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here \(z\leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((z	o B)\land (B	o z)\). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.
context:
Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

From \(x\lor y\) and \(\neg x\), Resolution derives y. Together with the clause \(\neg y\), it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.
why: Determines whether allowing efficient preprocessing fundamentally changes the apparent gap between elementary clause reasoning and proof systems that can name arbitrary intermediate Boolean computations. This affects what proof-size separations say about algorithms for finding proofs.
status_note: Checked the original simulation definition and subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The checked 2024 simulation theorem concerns two Resolution systems and does not settle the EF target. No unconditional resolution of the stated question was located; paper proofs were not independently audited.

title: Frege lower bounds from circuit hardness
importance_reason: Would connect circuit hardness with the power of propositional proof systems, transferring progress between two difficult lower-bound areas.
formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{Frege is not polynomially bounded}.\]
Precisely, assuming that some NP language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuit family, must it be true that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every constant \(C\ge1\), there is a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\), in the fixed system below, has
\[|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+1)^k?\]
This asks for a conditional connection between two lower-bound statements. It does not separately require proving the circuit-hardness premise.
definitions:
A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary string \(y\), with \(|y|\le p(|x|)\), satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). A Boolean circuit has input bits, constants zero and one, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one output. Its size is its number of gates, and its depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The class P/poly consists of languages decided at each input length \(n\) by a circuit \(D_n\) of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for fixed \(C,k\). These circuits need not be produced by an algorithm: they may be chosen nonuniformly. Thus NP not contained in P/poly asserts that at least one NP language has no such circuit family.

Fix the following classical Hilbert presentation of Frege. Formulas are finite trees built from propositional variables \(p_0,p_1,\ldots\), negation \(\neg\), and implication \(\to\). Under a Boolean assignment, negation reverses the truth value and \(A\to B\) is false exactly when \(A\) is true and \(B\) false. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its finitely many variables. The axiom schemes, allowing arbitrary formulas \(A,B,D\), are
\[A\to(B\to A),\]
\[(A\to(B\to D))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to D)),\]
\[(\neg A\to\neg B)\to(B\to A).\]
The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each an instance of an axiom scheme or obtained by this rule; its last formula is the theorem proved. No extension axioms introducing a new variable as an abbreviation for a formula are allowed.

Choose a fixed uniquely parsable binary tree encoding with constant-length tags for connectives and binary, self-delimited variable indices. Let \(|\varphi|\) be its bit length. Encode a proof by its full sequence of formula strings, with line delimiters; let \(|\pi|\) be that total bit length. Identical subformulas are written out each time they occur, not stored as a shared circuit. Earlier proof lines may be reused in multiple inferences. Including explicit rule tags and premise indices changes these sizes by at most polynomial factors and does not affect polynomial boundedness. The source recalls that standard finite complete Frege presentations polynomially simulate one another, so fixing this presentation does not change its lower-bound question.

Frege is polynomially bounded if there exist \(C,k\) such that every tautology has at least one proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\). Its negation does not require a polynomial-time generator for the hard tautologies or a single explicit family: existence of arbitrarily hard tautologies with the displayed quantifiers suffices. Formula size, proof size and circuit-input length are different parameters and are not silently identified.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication or of its negation. A positive proof may use exactly the circuit-hardness premise, without assuming additional cryptographic hardness, a feasible-interpolation property of Frege, or a lower bound for another system. A proof of the negation must establish both NP not contained in P/poly and polynomial boundedness of the fixed Frege system. An oracle separation or an obstruction to one reduction technique is not itself a negation of the stated unrelativized implication.
context:
Feasible interpolation turns short proofs in some weaker systems into small circuits, permitting circuit lower bounds to imply proof lower bounds there. The source emphasizes that such interpolation is not available for general Frege under the same assumptions; granting it for free would change the question.

The source asks about ordinary Frege, with unrestricted formula depth. Lower bounds for bounded-depth Frege do not settle it. Extended Frege permits abbreviation variables and is a stronger system; the names should not be interchanged.

Pich and Santhanam study connections in the direction from proof lower bounds to circuit hardness, using additional witnessing or provability conditions. These results do not supply the source’s implication from the bare NP circuit-hardness premise to ordinary Frege lower bounds.

The September 2026 report extends simulations between Frege and algebraic proof systems with partially commutative formulas. Its identity-testing and algebraic-model restrictions do not yield the general Boolean-circuit implication asked here.
why: General Boolean circuit lower bounds and Frege proof lower bounds are two major barriers in complexity theory. A positive implication would make progress on the former sufficient for the latter, even without an explicit hard-tautology construction. It would clarify whether these difficulties are formally linked or whether proof complexity requires an additional source of hardness.

title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
importance_reason: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic would clarify the proof-theoretic strength of basic theories of feasible computation.
formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

For each integer \(r\ge1\), \(T_2^r\) has the displayed BASIC axioms and, for each \(\varphi(x,\vec a)\in\Sigma_r^b\), the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a).\]
Parameters are allowed and are not required to be numerals. There are no induction axioms for formulas outside the specified class unless they are consequences of these axioms. Since the formula classes are nested, \(T_2^j\subseteq T_2^i\) in deductive strength when \(j<i\). A positive answer therefore gives a strict inclusion. The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential separation. A positive answer must establish one pair of standard integers \(i>j\ge1\), a closed sentence provable in \(T_2^i\), and its nonprovability in \(T_2^j\); the latter can equivalently be proved by a model of \(T_2^j\) falsifying the sentence. A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). A difference between axiom lists, a lower bound on the shortest proof of a still-provable sentence, a relativized separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved complexity conjecture does not settle this target.
context:
Open Problem 5.5 asks to separate some two levels with positive indices. This is not a request to select one predetermined pair or to give proof-length lower bounds. The survey places it alongside the question of whether feasible arithmetic can prove that P equals NP.

The complete finite axiom list matters because the target concerns formal provability, not only the intended meaning of addition and binary length. The model above uses the book’s first-order language without its optional sequence-function extension.

The 2026 preprint extends conditional comparisons between theories with different induction and bounded collection principles. Its introduction recalls the implication from noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy to noncollapse of bounded arithmetic, and Section 1.3 expressly leaves unconditional separations open. This is progress on related conditional statements, not a claimed unconditional witness for this card.
why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

A bounded subsequent search found no matching unconditional separation or proof that all positive levels coincide. This records the checked sources and search limits, not exhaustive certification of present openness.

working_summary: The question asks whether two positive levels of Buss’s bounded-arithmetic hierarchy prove different sentences. Each level has the same basic arithmetic axioms but permits induction for a different class of bounded formulas. A solution may choose any two distinct positive levels and must prove an unconditional difference in their deductive strength. The full axiom list, formula grammar and induction scheme specify the theories without relying on an unstated standard model. Recent conditional separations do not provide the unconditional nonprovability witness required here.

title: Unprovability of polynomial circuit upper bounds in \(S_2^1\)
importance_reason: An unprovability result for circuit or proof bounds would expose the limits of formal theories used to reason about efficient computation.
formal:
Is the following unconditional unprovability statement true?
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists\eta\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\qquad S_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta].\]
Here \(\eta(x,y)\) must be a \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula for which \(S_2^1\) proves that every \(x\) has exactly one output \(y\). It therefore represents a polynomial-time function. The sentence \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\), defined below with explicit coding, asserts that the predicate “the output is nonzero” has exact Boolean circuits of description size at most \(c n^k\) on every positive input length \(n\).

For each fixed exponent, the same represented function must resist provability for every fixed coefficient. The question concerns what this formal theory can prove; it does not ask directly for a circuit lower bound in the standard natural numbers or for unprovability of all possible upper bounds for one fixed function.
definitions:

(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]

\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\

\end{gathered}\]

\[\begin{gathered}

a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\

a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

The theory \(S_2^1\) has BASIC and the universal closure over the parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(H(x),\vec a)\to\varphi(x,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a)\]
for every \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula \(\varphi\). This is polynomial induction, with halving in the hypothesis; it is not unrestricted successor induction for these formulas.

To specify the polynomial-time predicate without leaving its formal representation implicit, let \(\eta(x,y)\) range over \(\Sigma_1^b\) formulas whose only free variables are among \(x,y\) and for which
\[S_2^1\vdash\forall x\,\exists y\bigl(\eta(x,y)\land\forall z(\eta(x,z)\to z=y)\bigr).\]
Thus the theory proves that \(\eta\) defines one total number-valued function. The associated language consists of numbers whose unique output is nonzero. By the definability/witnessing characterization of \(S_2^1\), these provably total \(\Sigma_1^b\) graphs represent polynomial-time functions. This is a base-language presentation of the source's polynomial-time function symbols in a conservative definitional extension. The formula \(\eta\), rather than just its extension in the standard natural numbers, is part of the witness being quantified over.

Here is an explicit arithmetic encoding of the circuits used in the upper-bound sentence. An \(n\)-input circuit has constants at nodes zero and one, inputs at nodes \(2,\ldots,n+1\), and \(g\ge0\) computational nodes \(n+2,\ldots,n+g+1\) in evaluation order. Each computational node has a two-bit operation tag: zero is AND, one OR, two NOT of the first predecessor, and three a copy of the first predecessor. It also has two predecessor indices, both less than its own index; the second is ignored for the last two tags. The output is any node. Shared values and unrestricted depth are allowed, with exact correctness on all inputs. Copy gates are only a serialization convenience and can be removed; this is an ordinary bounded-fan-in Boolean model.

Let \(w=\ell(n+g+2)\), \(q=2+2w\), and \(d=gq+w\). The circuit number \(C\) has binary length \(d+1\); its highest bit is a delimiter. In the lower bits, counted from position zero at the least significant bit, gate \(i\in\{0,\ldots,g-1\}\) has its tag at positions \(iq,iq+1\), first predecessor in the next \(w\) bits, and second predecessor in the next \(w\) bits. The output index occupies the \(w\) bits starting at \(gq\). A valid encoding has both predecessors below \(n+2+i\) and output below \(n+g+2\). Denote these conditions by \(\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\). The description size charged in the sentence is \(\ell(C)+\ell(g)\); the input length is supplied separately. Thus the measure is a binary description length, not an unannounced change to an exact gate-count bound.

All bit and field operations in this description have the following fixed bounded-arithmetic expansion. For \(X\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{Field}(X,a,b,v)\) by the existence of \(z,t,u,r,s\), all at most \(X+(1\#X)+1\), such that
\[\begin{gathered}
z=1\#H(z),\quad \ell(z)=a+1,\quad t=1\#H(t),\quad \ell(t)=b+1,\\
X=uz+r,\quad r<z,\quad u=st+v,\quad v<t.
\end{gathered}\]
Here \(a\) is the starting position, \(b\ge1\) is field width, and \(u< v\) abbreviates \(u\le v\land u\ne v\). The equations select \(z=2^a\) and \(t=2^b\). Define \(\operatorname{Bit}(X,a,e)\), for \(e\in\{0,1\}\), as
\[(\ell(X)\le a\land e=0)\ \lor\ (a<\ell(X)\land\operatorname{Field}(X,a,1,e)).\]
This also defines the padded zero bits of \(X=0\). In \(\operatorname{Valid}\), each extracted tag or index is a bounded existential variable at most \(n+g+4\); gate checks are quantified over \(i<g\). These conventions expand validity into one definite arithmetic formula.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\) to assert that the encoded circuit outputs one on the \(n\)-bit, zero-padded representation of \(x\). Its arithmetic expansion is: validity holds and there exists an integer
\[V\le (N\#N)\cdot(C\#C)\]
whose bits at node indices give a correct evaluation, with output bit one. Bits zero and one of \(V\) equal zero and one respectively; for each \(r<n\), bit \(r+2\) of \(V\) equals bit \(r\) of \(x\); and for each \(i<g\), the bit at \(n+2+i\) is the Boolean operation indicated by the tag applied to the predecessor bits. All field and bit occurrences use the preceding formulas, with Boolean auxiliary variables bounded by one and extracted indices bounded by \(n+g+4\). The four Boolean operations are specified by their truth tables. The output index is extracted from its field and its \(V\)-bit must be one. The quantifiers over nodes and gates are bounded by \(n\) and \(g\). Since validity implies \(g\le\ell(C)\) and \(n=\ell(N)\ge1\), the displayed bound is ample for the finite evaluation vector. This description fixes the formula through bounded quantifiers and Boolean combinations, and introduces no extra axioms about an opaque evaluator.

For fixed positive integers \(c,k\), let \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) be the following closed \(L\)-sentence, with the defined predicates expanded:
\[\begin{split}
\forall N\ge1\ \exists g\ \exists C\ \bigl(&\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\land\ell(C)+\ell(g)\le c\,n^k\\
&\land\forall x\ \forall y\bigl((\ell(x)\le n\land\eta(x,y))\to
(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\leftrightarrow y\ne0)\bigr)\bigr),
\end{split}\]
where every \(n\) abbreviates \(\ell(N)\). The fixed numeral \(c\) and fixed power \(n^k\) are expanded using multiplication. formal: Does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time learner for arbitrary Boolean circuits under the uniform input distribution, with membership queries and the resource bounds below, imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\)?

definitions: Targets are Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) computed by finite acyclic fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT circuits with constants and one output. A single oracle Turing machine \(A\) receives \(1^n,1^s\) and binary rationals \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), and may query \(f(x)\) at any chosen \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Queries may be adaptive and cost the time to write the query plus one step for the answer. The learner has independent fair random coins and no advice, target description or additional oracle. title: Optimal proof systems outside NP
importance_reason: A basic existence boundary for optimal proof systems, connecting proof-length comparison to NP membership and known relativization barriers. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a nonempty language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) that has an optimal Cook–Reckhow proof system, where optimality compares proof lengths and does not require an efficient translation between systems?
question_excerpt: Hence, for most sets we do not know whether they have optimal proof systems and proving their existence would require to overcome at least the […]
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has certificates of length polynomial in the string length that a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check.

A Cook–Reckhow proof system for \(L\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad \operatorname{range}(f)=L.\]
The input \(\pi\) is a proof and \(f(\pi)\) is the statement it proves. Thus every output is in \(L\), and every member of \(L\) has some proof. The running time is polynomial in \(|\pi|\), including writing the output. No polynomial bound in the statement length is imposed on the shortest proof. The system is one uniform algorithm, with no nonuniform advice.

For two systems \(f,g\) for the same language, \(f\) simulates \(g\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[\forall \pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists \sigma\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad f(\sigma)=g(\pi),\quad |\sigma|\leq p(|\pi|).\]
The polynomial may depend on the two systems, but not on the individual proof. The system \(f\) is optimal if it simulates every total polynomial-time system \(g\) whose range is exactly \(L\).

Only the existence of these short translated proofs is required. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm that computes \(\sigma\) from \(\pi\) defines the stronger notion of \(p\)-optimality, which is not the target here. Optimality also does not say that all statements have polynomial-length proofs: the comparison is against competing proof systems, not directly against statement length.

This card selects the existential question explicitly stated on page 2 of the source, making its broad page-3 discussion concrete. It asks for at least one language outside \(\mathrm{NP}\), without requiring arbitrarily high complexity or choosing the tautology language in advance. Such a language is automatically computably enumerable, because it is the range of \(f\); decidability is not an additional requirement.
answer_criterion: Give an unconditional example of a language \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) and prove that it has an optimal system under the stated simulation relation, or prove that every language admitting such an optimal system belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). A conditional existence theorem, an oracle construction, or an example using advice or a weaker simulation relation does not by itself settle this question.

title: Weak automatability of Resolution
importance_reason: A central remaining distinction between proof search in Resolution and recognizing formulas with short refutations, directly relevant to the limits of SAT-solving proof systems. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(|F|+s\), that on input a CNF formula \(F\) and a unary proof budget \(1^{s}\) distinguishes the following two promised cases: \(F\) is satisfiable, or \(F\) has a Resolution refutation with at most \(s\) clauses?
question_excerpt: While it is now known and well understood that fully automating propositional Resolution as a proof system for propositional logic is NP-hard, it remains an […]
definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. A conditional obstruction must state its hypothesis explicitly. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.
context:
Atserias and Müller show that finding a Resolution refutation in time polynomial in the formula size and the shortest available refutation length would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Their proof-length gap distinguishes short refutations from very long or nonexistent ones. The latter side may include unsatisfiable formulas, so it does not give the SAT-versus-short-refutation promise required here.

Buss and Yolcu show that weak automatability of regular Resolution would imply weak automatability of general Resolution. Their definition allows the output proof to use another system. This relation between systems is not an algorithm or a hardness result for the full promise problem.

The May 2026 full version of The Proof Analysis Problem develops algorithms that analyze supplied proofs of Resolution lower bounds.
