title: Log-rank conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.
focus_reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
context:
Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.

Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis

importance_reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.
focus_reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.
formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, H(f)\le C I(f)\), where \(H(f)\) is the base-two Shannon entropy of its squared Fourier coefficients and \(I(f)\) is its total influence under the uniform distribution, as defined below?
definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq [n]\), let \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and let \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Put \(q_{S}=\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\); Parseval gives \(\sum _{S} q_{S}=1\). Define \(H(f)=\sum _{S} q_{S} \log _{2}(1/q_{S})\), with a zero summand when \(q_{S}=0\). If x is uniform and \(x^{\oplus i}\) differs only by flipping coordinate i, define \(I_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})]\) and \(I(f)=\sum _{i=1}^{n} I_{i}(f)=\sum _{S} |S|q_{S}\). All Boolean functions are quantified, without circuit-size, monotonicity, balance, or efficient-computability assumptions. The same C must work for all dimensions and all functions. Constant functions have \(H(f)=I(f)=0\) and satisfy the non-strict inequality.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The Fourier expansion expresses a Boolean rule as a linear combination of parity tests on subsets of its inputs. Squaring the coefficients produces a probability distribution on these subsets. Its entropy measures how dispersed that distribution is; total influence measures the expected size of a subset sampled from it. The conjecture says that the Boolean constraint forces the first quantity to be at most a constant times the second, even though there are exponentially many possible subsets.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

A useful consequence would be spectral concentration: for any \(0<\delta <1\), all but \(\delta\) of the Fourier mass could be captured by at most \(2^{C I(f)/\delta}\) coefficients. This follows by applying Markov’s inequality to the surprisal \(\log _{2}(1/q_{S})\) of a random spectral subset. It supplies a quantitative connection between stability under individual bit flips and approximation by a short linear combination of parities. The dependence on \(\delta\) is essential; the claim is not an accuracy-independent support bound.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou establish the conjecture for symmetric Boolean functions and for functions computed by read-once decision trees. Their paper also explains the connection to learning DNF formulas: the conjecture would imply polynomial Fourier concentration for a DNF with polynomially many terms, at each fixed approximation accuracy. This is a structural learning-theory consequence, rather than an assertion that arbitrary Boolean functions become efficiently learnable.

A general bound proved by Han is \(H(f)\le O(I(f)+\sum _{i} I_{i}(f) \log (1/I_{i}(f)))\). The extra term records how influence is distributed across coordinates. It can exceed a constant multiple of \(I(f)\), so this does not settle the conjecture. The December 2025 revision adds an acknowledgement of related earlier work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. Bounds on min-entropy concern the largest Fourier coefficient alone and must not be substituted for a Shannon-entropy bound.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s June 2026 revision verifies additional classes, including \(\delta\)-tribes and functions with specified separation properties. Their method splits on selected coordinates and stops at restrictions already satisfying FEI. It also demonstrates failure of a stronger sufficient inequality when the splitting coordinate is chosen badly. Those examples do satisfy FEI when handled with a suitable coordinate, so they expose a limitation of that inductive route rather than a counterexample to the conjecture.

Slote’s August 2026 preprint disproves a quantum analogue using Hermitian unitary operators with flat, very large Pauli expansions. For the constructed degree-d operators, the spectral entropy grows quadratically in d while the influence grows linearly. These are quantum Boolean functions, not scalar maps on the classical Boolean cube. The result makes the distinction between the two settings concrete and does not provide a classical counterexample.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.
why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 primary paper explicitly retains classical FEI as open and proves only specified classes. The August 2026 disproof is of the quantum extension. No classical resolution was found in the checked sources; the formulation uses Shannon entropy, uniform measure and scalar Boolean functions throughout.

working_summary: A Boolean function has a Fourier expansion whose squared coefficients form a probability distribution. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture bounds the entropy of that distribution by a universal constant times total influence. Intuitively, it asks whether small average sensitivity prevents Fourier weight from being spread across too many descriptions. The bound would connect the spectral complexity of a function with how often changing one input bit changes its value. The saved review distinguishes this classical conjecture from stronger coordinate-wise statements and quantum analogues, whose failures do not by themselves refute the stated Boolean inequality.

title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Connects a basic dimension-independent influence bound to almost-everywhere classical simulation of quantum queries, bringing Boolean analysis and quantum complexity together.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C\ge 1\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\) and every real multilinear polynomial f of degree at most d satisfying \(0\le f(x)\le 1\) for every \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\), some coordinate i satisfies \(Inf_{i}(f)\ge (\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\)?
definitions: All expectations use the uniform distribution on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\). Write \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq [n]} \hat\{f\}(S)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}\), with \(\hat\{f\}(S)=E_{x}[f(x)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}]\); degree at most d means \(\hat\{f\}(S)=0\) when |\(S|>d\). Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be x with just coordinate i negated. Define \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=E[(f- E f)^{2}]=\sum_{S\ne \varnothing}\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\) and \(Inf_{i}(f)=E[(f(x)- f(x^{\oplus i}))^{2}]/4=\Sigma\)_{S∋i}\(\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\). This is squared \(\mathrm{L}_{2}\) influence, with the factor \(1/4\) fixed explicitly. The pointwise range restriction holds on the entire cube, not merely with high probability. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers; no sparsity, coefficient-size, block structure, Boolean-valued-output or quantum-realizability promise is imposed. C must be independent of n,d,f and its variance. Constant polynomials satisfy the inequality trivially with both sides zero. The one-power notation is a normalized version of a polynomial lower bound in variance and inverse degree; because \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\le 1/4\), fixed positive prefactors can be absorbed by increasing C.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal exponent C works for every admissible polynomial, or show that for every proposed C there is an admissible polynomial of positive variance for which every coordinate has influence smaller than \((\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\). Refuting one particular exponent is insufficient to refute existence of some universal exponent. An exponential-in-degree influence bound, a theorem only after randomly fixing coordinates, or a result for a restricted subclass is partial progress.
context:
A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

Bhattacharya’s random-restriction theorem approaches the unrestricted class differently. Fix most coordinates independently to random signs and leave roughly a \(\log (d)/d\) fraction available. Under a lower bound on the original variance, a non-negligible fraction of restrictions have a polynomially influential remaining variable. The accompanying junta theorem approximates restricted functions using few coordinates. Neither assertion directly guarantees such a variable in the original, unrestricted function.

Two recent results clarify the frontier. Blanc and coauthors obtain the desired almost-everywhere classical simulation for a fixed number of quantum query rounds; their exponent depends on the number of rounds. This does not address arbitrary adaptivity or prove the full polynomial inequality. Escudero Gutiérrez, Saucedo and Palazuelos subsequently obtain an optimal root-influence inequality for completely bounded block-multilinear polynomials, improving simulation to allow nonadaptive classical queries for that setting.

The September inequality controls the sum of square roots of influences by the number of blocks times the completely bounded norm. Its extra norm hypothesis is precisely what prevents applying it to every polynomial in this card. The paper explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture. A historical general proof claim by Keller and Klein is withdrawn because of an error in a key lemma, and is recorded as a withdrawal rather than progress establishing the conjecture.
why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.
status_note: The 4 September 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture open. Recent restricted-model and bounded-round results do not prove it; the 2019 general claim remains withdrawn. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2009–2014: Aaronson–Ambainis formulate the influential-variable conjecture and prove its implication for almost-everywhere classical query simulation. | 2019-12-02: Keller–Klein withdraw their claimed general proof; the arXiv notice identifies failure of Lemma 5.3. | 2022: Bansal–Sinha–de Wolf establish the conjectured behavior for completely bounded block-multilinear forms. | 2025: Bhattacharya proves junta approximation after random restrictions and influential-variable guarantees for a non-negligible fraction of restrictions. | 2026-03-04: Revision 2 of the random-restriction preprint updates presentation and references while retaining its restriction and variance hypotheses. | 2026-08-19: Blanc–Docter–Strassle–Tan prove almost-everywhere simulation for bounded-round quantum algorithms, with a round-dependent polynomial exponent. | 2026-09-04: Escudero Gutiérrez–Saucedo–Palazuelos sharpen completely bounded block-multilinear root-influence bounds to the optimal constant and obtain nonadaptive simulation in that setting.

working_summary: A bounded low-degree polynomial on the Boolean cube describes a real-valued function with controlled algebraic complexity. The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture asks whether some variable has influence polynomially large in the variance and inverse degree. It predicts that meaningful variation cannot be distributed too evenly among all coordinates when the degree stays small. The question matters for understanding when quantum query behavior admits efficient classical simulation. The reviewed record stresses that results for random restrictions, bounded-round algorithms, or completely bounded norms impose additional structure and do not settle the unrestricted scalar-polynomial statement.

title: Mansour’s conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A defining conjecture in Boolean function analysis and learning theory, connecting representation size to approximate Fourier sparsity and agnostic learning.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), integer \(s\ge 2\), Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most s terms, and \(\varepsilon \in\)(\(0,1/2\)], some family \(F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) satisfies |\(F|\le \lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) and \(\sum_{S\notin F} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\le \varepsilon\)?
definitions: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of literals \(x_{i}=1\) or \(x_{i}=- 1; a\) satisfied formula has value +1 and an unsatisfied formula value −1. Term widths, overlaps, and the number of occurrences of a variable are unrestricted. On the uniform probability space \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}, \chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}, \chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Parseval gives \(\sum_{S} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}=1\). Thus \(\varepsilon\)-concentration on F means that the polynomial \(g=\sum_{S\in F}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\) has \(E[(f- g)^{2}]\le \varepsilon\). The coefficients are ordinary Walsh coefficients, not a basis adapted to a different distribution. The same C must work for all \(n,s,\varepsilon\) and f. This is an existence question about the spectrum; no efficient algorithm for finding F is part of the proposition.
answer_criterion: An affirmative resolution proves the stated bound with one universal C. A negative resolution must show that for every C some admissible \(s,n,\varepsilon\) and DNF require more than \(\lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) coefficients to leave squared Fourier mass at most \(\varepsilon\). A polynomial bound whose exponent has an unspecified dependence on \(\varepsilon\) would settle only the weaker fixed-accuracy form.
context:
A DNF describes a function as a short list of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier expansion describes the same function through parity correlations. Mansour’s question asks whether a short description in the first language forces an approximately short description in the second. The number n of available variables may greatly exceed the number s of terms, yet the proposed number of relevant correlations depends only on s and the permitted error.

The approximation is measured in squared error under uniformly random inputs. It does not require exact agreement everywhere, and the approximating polynomial need not have Boolean outputs. Keeping the largest squared coefficients is the best approximation with that many Walsh characters. Consequently the question is a statement about how rapidly the sorted Fourier mass decays, independent of an algorithm’s ability to identify the important characters.

Sparsity and degree are different resources. A parity involving every variable has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient but has degree n. Conversely, restricting a polynomial to degree d can leave a number of possible coefficients that grows like \(n^{d}\). A theorem saying that high-degree coefficients have little total mass therefore does not by itself give the requested bound, which must avoid such dependence on the ambient dimension.

Even one wide conjunction can have many nonzero coefficients exactly. This does not contradict the conjecture: if the conjunction fixes w distinct coordinates, its satisfying event has probability \(2^{- w}\). Approximating its ±1-valued function by the constant −1 incurs squared error \(4\cdot 2^{- w}\). Rare accepting terms can therefore produce an exactly dense spectrum while contributing very little approximation error. Combining many overlapping terms is where the simple observation stops being sufficient.

There are two common strengths of the named conjecture. The weaker one allows \(s^{K(\varepsilon )}\) coefficients for an arbitrary function K of the error. The stronger one in this saved record asks for \(K(\varepsilon )=O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))\). O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explicitly distinguish these statements. The card preserves the stronger target instead of treating all polynomial concentration claims as interchangeable.

The connection to Fourier entropy explains that distinction. If the Fourier entropy were \(O(\log  s)\), Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal \(\log (1/\hat\{f\}(S)^{2})\) would capture all but \(\varepsilon\) of the mass on at most \(s^{O(1/\varepsilon )}\) coefficients. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture, combined with the influence bound for DNF, would supply such an entropy estimate. This implication gives the weaker form, but its exponent does not establish the logarithmic dependence required here.

Mansour’s classical general bound gives \(s^{O(\log  \log  s)}\) coefficients at fixed accuracy. Klivans–Lee–Wan proved polynomial concentration for a specified random-DNF model and for every fixed read number. These are substantial structural results, but randomness in the formula cannot be assumed in a worst-case statement about every DNF. Their final May 2010 revision corrects an earlier issue in the read-number argument.

Lecomte–Tan sharpen the fixed-accuracy general estimate to \(s^{O(\log  \log  k)}\), where k bounds the number of terms containing a variable. Their stronger small-read theorem gives \((s/\varepsilon )^{O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))}\) concentration for read number up to a stated roughly doubly logarithmic range. The explicit \(s/\varepsilon\) base should be retained when comparing accuracy parameters. Their work also explains how control of term covers improves Fourier estimates beyond a single global norm bound.

The learning consequences depend on access to the target. Through the agnostic-learning reduction described by Klivans–Lee–Wan, suitable sparse Fourier approximation yields efficient agnostic learning under the uniform distribution with membership queries, for fixed approximation accuracy. Such queries allow selected input points; they are stronger access than an ordinary stream of independently sampled labeled examples. This conjecture should not be advertised as automatically solving every version of passive DNF learning.

Recent neighboring results retain these distinctions. Han’s 2025 entropy estimate contains an additional sum involving individual influences, rather than the full conjectured constant times total influence. González–MacManus–Pereyra’s June 2026 revision proves FEI for further classes under structural separation conditions. Neither is a universal theorem with the strong DNF accuracy bound in the question.

Heidari–Khardon’s June 2026 revision studies generalized Fourier representations associated with Bayesian networks. Its DNF learning theorem uses membership queries and a restricted distributional model; its agnostic result concerns decision trees. These changes in basis, distribution and target class are mathematically meaningful, but they do not establish concentration of every DNF in the ordinary uniform Walsh basis used here.
why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.
status_note: Open in the strong logarithmic-accuracy form stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Fixed-error polynomial concentration, restricted DNF models, and generalized-basis learning results do not by themselves settle this formulation.

The random model does not cover arbitrary formulas. | 2011: O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explain the weak and strong versions and the weaker accuracy bound implied by FEI. | 2021-10-15: Lecomte–Tan’s revision improves dependence on the read number and obtains polynomial concentration for a growing range of small read numbers. | 2025: Han proves a new Fourier entropy bound with additional individual-influence terms; this is partial progress on the broader FEI direction. | 2026-06-02: Heidari–Khardon revise generalized-Fourier learning results under Bayesian-network distributions; the setting differs from this uniform spectral conjecture. | 2026-06-09: González–MacManus–Pereyra extend FEI to further structured classes; no universal DNF concentration theorem is claimed.

working_summary: A short DNF describes a Boolean function as a small collection of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier representation describes the same function using correlations with parity functions. Mansour's conjecture asks whether almost all Fourier mass lies on a small set of coefficients whose size is controlled by the number of DNF terms and logarithmically scaled accuracy dependence in the exponent. This is a sparsity claim, so a bound on polynomial degree alone does not establish it. Proving the proposed concentration would connect two very different descriptions of Boolean functions and strengthen a central structural foundation for learning DNFs.

title: Maximum influence of polynomial threshold functions
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n, M(n,d)=\max\){\(I(f): f=\operatorname{sign}(p):\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, \deg (p)\le d\), and p has no zero on the Boolean cube}, using total influence as defined below.
definitions:
A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with \(p(x)
e 0\) at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing \(x_{i}^{2}\) to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), let \(x^{i}\) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define \(Inf_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)
e f(x^{i})]\), pointwise sensitivity \(s_{f}(x)=|\{i:f(x)
e f(x^{i})\}|\), and \(I(f)=\sum_{i} Inf_{i}(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). The constants in the requested matching asymptotic bounds must be independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing \(d=0\) adds only these trivial cases. The maximum exists because only finitely many Boolean functions occur on a fixed cube; realizing polynomials may have arbitrary real coefficients. The earlier asymptotic Gotsman–Linial question asks for \(M(n,d)=O(d\sqrt{n})\), while an exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture was disproved.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(h(n,d)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c h(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le C h(n,d)\) for all \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\), and prove both bounds in Lean. This must determine the joint parameter dependence, including saturation at large degree, within constant factors. No particular extremizing Boolean function is prescribed; merely refuting one candidate formula does not determine M.
context:
The quantitative target is the maximum influence as a function of dimension and degree. The following history concerns the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture and the separately disproved exact-extremizer claim.

A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2D/2^{n}\). The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of \(C d\sqrt{n}\) would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with \(\sqrt{n}\); once \(d\ge \sqrt{n}\), the elementary bound \(I(f)\le n\) already suffices with \(C=1\).

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other \(n- 1\) coordinates split evenly, giving I(\(MAJ_{n}\))=\(n\cdot \operatorname{binom}(n- 1,(n- 1)/2)/2^{n- 1}\), asymptotic to \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order \(d\sqrt{n}\). Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement discussed here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives \(O(d\sqrt{n})\). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot (\log  n)^{O(d \log  d)}\cdot 2^{O(d^{2} \log  d)}\) for \(d\ge 2\). For each fixed d, this is \(\sqrt{n}\) times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area \(BSA(f)=E[\sqrt{s_{f}}(x)]\). The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from \(I(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise \(s_{f}(x)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot \sqrt{s_{f}}(x)\) yields only \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot BSA(f)\). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.
why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The exact symmetric-maximizer conjecture is false, but the universal \(O(d\sqrt{n})\) influence bound remains open in the checked primary literature, including the April 2026 revisions on rational degree and Boolean surface area.
progress: 2012–2013: Kane establishes the correct \(\sqrt{n}\) exponent up to degree-dependent polylogarithmic factors. | 2017: Kim–Maldonado–Wellens establish influence estimates for structured quadratic coefficient graphs. | 2018: Chapman disproves the original exact extremizer conjecture while preserving the asymptotic open question. | 2022: Chapman’s MIT thesis again distinguishes the exact, asymptotic and weaker polylogarithmic formulations. | 8 April 2026: Kothari and coauthors’ revised rational-degree paper restates the conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue in §5.2. | 27 April 2026: Chang and coauthors’ second revision proves polylogarithmic Boolean surface area for fixed-degree PTFs, a different moment from total influence.
working_summary: A polynomial threshold function takes the sign of a real polynomial on the Boolean cube. Total influence is the expected number of coordinate flips that change its output. The target is the largest possible influence as a joint function of dimension n and degree bound d, within universal constant factors. The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture gives a proposed upper scale, whereas a stronger exact-extremizer claim was disproved. The statement permits arbitrary realizing polynomials and does not prescribe a particular extremal construction.

title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A basic lower-bound question about whether symmetry prevents any edge query from being avoided.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}; a\) graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |\(U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.
context:
Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.
why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The October 2025 revision of Elekes, Kátay and Kocsis explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. No later resolution matching the full graph-property model was located. The June 2026 topological counterexample announcement concerns a broader symmetry condition; only its abstract and an in-preparation listing were accessible, so no claim about its proof or graph specialization is made. Source/model review is not an independent proof audit.

The conjecture asks whether every nonconstant monotone property invariant under vertex relabeling has some input requiring all possible pairs to be queried. Queries may be adaptive and all computation between them is free. The example of looking for one edge illustrates how an easy positive instance can coexist with an empty graph that requires a complete scan. The exact claim is known for prime-power vertex counts, while results about quantum queries, infinite graphs and broader topological symmetry must be distinguished from the full finite deterministic question.

title: Real Grothendieck constant
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Determining this constant would settle a foundational quantitative barrier shared by functional analysis, semidefinite optimization and quantum correlations.
formal: Determine the real Grothendieck constant \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}\), defined as the least universal comparison factor between the vector and sign bilinear optima below.
definitions: For positive integers m,n and a real matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define \(S(A)=\max_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^{m},\,\delta\in\{-1,1\}^{n}}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\varepsilon_i\delta_j|\) and \(V(A)=\max_{u_1,\ldots,u_m,v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^{m+n},\,\|u_i\|_2=\|v_j\|_2=1}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|\). The inner product and norm are Euclidean. Define \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}=\sup_{m,n\ge1,\,A\ne0}V(A)/S(A)\). The denominator is positive for nonzero A. Grothendieck’s inequality makes the supremum finite. The vector dimension m+n permits every possible Gram matrix of these m+n vectors; this is the unrestricted real constant, with no fixed dimension, complex vectors, computational restriction, or asymptotic input model.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number a and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute difference from the defined constant is at most \(1/100\). A proved containing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. The constant is unconditional: a lower bound relying on an unproved complexity assumption settles only the corresponding conditional statement. Merely restating the defining infimum is not a determination.
context:
The two optima compare a discrete sign assignment with its vector relaxation. The universal loss quantifies a basic limitation of this relaxation across all real bilinear objectives.

The earlier strict improvement over Krivine’s bound disproved a proposed value without determining the constant. A 2026 preprint reports a lower bound of \(6\pi/11\) and a further quantitative upper bound; their separation still exceeds the benchmark tolerance.
why: Determining this constant would settle a foundational quantitative barrier shared by functional analysis, semidefinite optimization and quantum correlations.
status_note: The cited primary sources and a targeted later-work search were checked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of this precise target was located. This is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of openness or an independent verification of the cited proofs.
progress: 2011 / 2013: Braverman, Makarychev, Makarychev and Naor prove a strict improvement over Krivine’s upper bound. | 2026-08: A preprint reports \(6\pi/11\le K_G^{\mathbb R}\le\pi/(2\log(1+\sqrt2))-10^{-4}\); these claims do not determine the constant to absolute error 0.01.
working_summary: The real Grothendieck constant compares the best vector assignment with the best sign assignment for a bilinear objective. The supremum ranges over every finite real matrix, so fixed-dimensional constants are different targets. The 2011 breakthrough disproved the proposed optimality of Krivine’s bound. title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.
formal: For a total Boolean function $F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}$, let $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)$ be public-coin randomized communication complexity and $Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F)$ quantum communication complexity with unlimited shared entanglement. Is there a universal polynomial $p$ such that $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)\le p(Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F))$ for every total $F$?
definitions: X and Y are arbitrary finite sets. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits or qubits, and error at most \(1/3\) is required on every input pair. Public random bits and prior entanglement, respectively, are not charged as communication.
answer_criterion: Establish one polynomial bound valid for every finite total Boolean communication problem, or prove that no universal polynomial bound holds. Promise problems and restricted subclasses do not suffice.
context:
Partial functions can exhibit exponential quantum savings. Requiring correctness on every input pair may fundamentally restrict that advantage.

Alice receives x and Bob receives y. They need to compute a function of both inputs while exchanging as little information as possible. The classical protocol may use randomness, and the quantum protocol may begin with shared entanglement. The cost being compared is the communication, not the complexity of their local computation.

Totality means every pair of legal individual inputs must receive a correct answer, including pairs that a promise problem would exclude. A universal polynomial simulation would limit quantum communication savings across all such functions. A bound for a special composition, or one with an additional dependence on the input length, does not automatically supply that universal relation.
why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

working_summary: Two parties must evaluate a Boolean function when each holds one part of the input. The question asks whether randomized classical communication is polynomially bounded by quantum communication with shared entanglement for every total function. Both models allow bounded error on each input, and their costs count transmitted bits or qubits rather than local computation. A positive answer would limit quantum communication advantages whenever the function is defined on every input pair. The totality condition is central: results for promise problems cannot be substituted, and the polynomial must be universal across all finite domains.

title: Sharp low-degree Fourier weight of halfspaces

formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every linear threshold function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\), is \(\mathrm{W}^{\le 1}(f)=\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat\{f\}(\{i\})^{2}\ge 2/\pi\)?
definitions: A linear threshold function has \(f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i}- \theta )\) for some real weights \(w_{i}\) and threshold \(\theta\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(t)=1\) when \(t\ge 0\) and −1 otherwise. Constant functions are included. Under the uniform measure on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), define \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with empty product 1. Thus \(\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )\) is the mean and \(\hat\{f\}(\{i\})\) is the correlation with the i-th coordinate. The displayed squared coefficients are the Fourier weight in degrees zero and one. There is no bound on dimension, weights or bias, and no regularity assumption on the halfspace. The constant \(\pi\) is the usual circle constant.

title: Removing low-influence directions from convex sets
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Dimension-free stability of negligible Gaussian influence would give a general geometric meaning to an irrelevant direction in a convex set.
formal: Does there exist a function \(\tau :(0,1)\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}}\tau (\varepsilon )=0\) such that the following holds for every \(n\ge 1\), every centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(K\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), every unit vector v and every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\)? If \(Inf_{v}[K]\le \varepsilon\), then there exists a centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(C\subseteq v\perp\) such that \(\gamma _{n}(K \triangle  (C+\mathbb{R} v))\le \tau (\varepsilon )\). The same \(\tau\) must work in all dimensions and for all such sets and directions.
definitions: \(\gamma _{n}\) is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent \(N(0,1)\) coordinates. Central symmetry means \(K=- K\), with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means \(tx+(1- t)y\in K\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in [0,1]\). Write \(1_{K}\) for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is \(Inf_{v}[K]=(1/\sqrt{2}) E[1_{K}(X)(1- \langle v,X\rangle ^{2})]\). This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is \(v\perp =\{y:\langle v,y\rangle =0\}\), and \(C+\mathbb{R} v=\{y+tv:y\in C,t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection \(x- \langle v,x\rangle v\). The symmetric difference \(K\triangle \mathrm{L}\) consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on \(\gamma _{n}(K)\), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus \(\tau\) tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.
context:
The approximating set is unrestricted along v. Moving any distance parallel to v cannot change membership, although membership may depend arbitrarily on the orthogonal projection.

The definition compares membership with the squared coordinate in direction v. It differs from boundary surface area, resampling influence and the total influence summed over directions.

Proposition 11 says that zero influence is equivalent, up to Gaussian null sets, to membership being independent of the coordinate along v. The conjecture asks for a dimension-free robust form of that statement.

Conjecture 1 controls the number of relevant directions using total influence. This card is Conjecture 2: one specified direction has small influence, and only that direction must be removed.
why: Would make convex influence a robust measure of whether a Gaussian direction matters, strengthening the analogy between symmetric convex sets and Boolean functions with irrelevant variables.
status_note: The correct numbered conjecture, influence normalization and zero-influence statement were recovered. The author’s full-version link and arXiv revision history were checked, and subsequent-result searches through 12 September 2026 located no resolution of the dimension-free directional statement.
progress: 2022: The source proves the exact zero-influence characterization and states the dimension-free approximate version as Conjecture 2.
working_summary: The problem concerns symmetric convex sets under standard Gaussian measure. A specified direction has small convex influence, measured by a normalized second-moment statistic. The conjecture asks whether the set is close to a symmetric convex cylinder that ignores this direction. The approximation error must tend to zero with influence independently of dimension. The exact zero-influence case is known, while the robust dimension-free statement remains the source’s Conjecture 2.

title: Fourier rank versus sparsity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Asks for the exact qualitative relation between two fundamental Boolean Fourier complexity measures. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a sequence of integers \(n_{j}\ge 1\) and Boolean functions \(f_{j}:\{- 1,1\}^{n_{j}}\to \{- 1,1\}\) such that \(k(f_{j})\to \infty\) and \(r(f_{j})/\sqrt{k}(f_{j})\to \infty\) as \(j\to \infty\), where k is Fourier sparsity and r is Fourier rank over \(F_{2}\)? Equivalently, is the ratio \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\) unbounded over all finite-dimensional Boolean functions?
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\), put \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\). The Fourier coefficient is \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\), so \(f=\sum _{S\subseteq [n]}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\). The support is \(\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})=\{S:\hat\{f\}(S)\ne 0\}\), and \(k(f)=|\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})|\). It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in \(F_{2}^{n}\) and define \(r(f)=\dim _{F_{2}}\) span\(\{1_{S}:S\in \operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})\}\). The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit \(r(f_{j})=\omega (\sqrt{k}(f_{j}))\) means that for every real \(M>0\), the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on \(n_{j}\) in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that \(r(f)\le C\sqrt{k}(f)\) for every n and every such f. Since \(r(f)\le k(f)\), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.
context:
Fourier sparsity counts the nonzero parity coefficients. Rank counts how many independent parity directions are needed to contain their support. The question asks how far these two structural measures can diverge at the square-root scale.

title: Constant-factor randomized direct sums for total Boolean functions

formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty finite input sets \(X,Y\), every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), \[R_{1/3}(f^{\otimes k})\ge c\,k\,R_{1/3}(f),\] where communication is public-coin, worst-case and measured with one global error probability?
question_excerpt: A classic example is the case of direct sum in communication complexity: a near-perfect direct sum result holds in the non-deterministic case \([49, 38]\), but […]
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know \(f\) and the finite domains. A public-coin protocol selects a deterministic binary communication tree using a finite string of independent shared fair random bits, independent of the inputs. At a node, the designated player sends one bit determined by that player’s own input, the public string and the transcript so far. At termination Bob outputs a bit determined by his input, the public string and transcript. The worst-case cost is the maximum number of communicated bits over all inputs and public strings. Local computation and the public random string are free; its finite length may depend on the protocol. There is no message to reveal the public seed, no advice depending on private inputs and no restriction to one-way communication. The complexity \(R_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum cost of a protocol whose output equals \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair. It is finite because Alice can send an encoding of her input. Protocols may depend nonuniformly on the finite function; no uniform construction from its truth table is requested. For \(f^{\otimes k}:X^k\times Y^k\to\{0,1\}^k\), Alice and Bob receive their full tuples and Bob must output \((f(x_1,y_1),\ldots,f(x_k,y_k))\). Success probability at least \(2/3\) concerns the entire vector simultaneously on every tuple pair. The inputs need not be independent draws from a distribution: the cost and error guarantees are worst-case. The protocol may communicate across coordinates in any way. The constant \(c\) must work for all domains, functions and copy counts; a different constant for each fixed function is insufficient. Zero-communication functions impose the vacuous lower bound zero.

title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
importance_reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.
focus_reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
context:
Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.
why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.
status_note: The precise deterministic statement remains an unproved hypothesis in the checked sources. The July 2026 preprint improves a fixed-width randomized analysis and does not supply the quantified deterministic refutation. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; its imported inequalities and numerical certificates were not independently verified.
