working_summary: SETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rates for fixed-width satisfiability approach one as the allowed width grows. Every proposed constant saving from exhaustive search must fail at some fixed width. To refute it, one saving must work at every fixed width, although the algorithms and polynomial factors may vary with that width. Faster algorithms for width three, including recent randomized ones, do not meet that requirement. The hypothesis underlies many precise conditional lower bounds, including problems whose algorithms already run in polynomial time.

title: Truly subcubic APSP
importance_reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.
focus_reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.
formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least \(2/3\)? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs \(O(1)\), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on \(O(\log  n)\)-bit index words cost \(O(1)\). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.
why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is a fixed exponent saving for arbitrary real edge weights; the 2026 node-weighted triangle result does not supply it.
progress: 2010: Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish truly subcubic equivalences between APSP and several path, matrix, and weighted-triangle tasks. | 2013 / 2014: Williams gives a randomized real-RAM algorithm with time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$, demonstrating a substantial subpolynomial saving while leaving a fixed exponent improvement unresolved. | 2026-05: Akmal and Fischer solve the node-weighted zero-triangle problem in matrix-multiplication time; their introduction explicitly distinguishes it from the edge-weighted variant governed by the APSP hypothesis.
working_summary: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a weighted directed graph. The graph may contain negative edges but no negative cycle. The target is an algorithm with a fixed positive improvement over the cubic exponent in the specified comparison-addition model. Small subpolynomial savings do not meet that target. The question matters both as a basic graph optimization problem and as the organizing hypothesis behind many conditional running-time lower bounds.

title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
importance_reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.
formal: Is it true that for every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) there is a fixed integer \(c\ge 1\) for which no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm decides bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors on two lists of n vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), with \(d=\lceil c \log _{2} n\rceil\), in worst-case time \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on every input?
definitions: Here \(n\ge 2\) and the two input lists A and B each have length n; repeated vectors are allowed. The answer is YES exactly when some \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=1}^{d} a_{j} b_{j}=0\) as an integer sum, equivalently their supports are disjoint. This is not an inner product over the field with two elements. Inputs are explicitly supplied as packed binary vectors. Computation uses a uniform classical RAM with words of \(\Theta (\log (n+d))\) bits, ordinary constant-time word arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, memory access and generation of a random word. Each program uses a fixed word-length constant; arbitrary-precision unit-cost operations, nonuniform advice and free preprocessing tables are excluded. Reading, preprocessing and all subsequent computation count in the time bound. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) and c, hidden time constants and the program may depend on these parameters, but not on n. There is no promise on vector weights, overlap or input distribution. Randomness is internal to the algorithm; correctness must hold for every pair of lists.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower-bound proposition, or refute it by exhibiting one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) such that for every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\) an algorithm \(A_{c}\) meets the \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) time and error bounds. This quantifier order matters: the algorithms and constants may depend on c, but the exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every c. Giving a different positive saving \(\varepsilon _{c}\) that tends to zero with c, shaving logarithmic factors from quadratic time, or proving lower bounds only for restricted circuit models does not settle the proposition.
context:
Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on c is the main subtlety. There are already truly subquadratic algorithms for each fixed c, with a saving that can deteriorate as c increases. The polynomial-method algorithm of Abboud, Williams and Yu runs in time \(n^{2- 1/O(\log  c)}\) in the relevant large-c regime. This is consistent with the hypothesis: selecting a sufficiently large c can make that known saving smaller than any proposed universal \(\varepsilon\). The source is SODA 2015; some later bibliographies mistakenly label it 2014.

Very small dimension permits another strategy: enumerate possible coordinate patterns and aggregate the input instead of considering all pairs separately. The 2026 low-dimensional algorithms achieve a randomized bound of \(\widetilde{O}\)\((1.25^{d} n)\), with a further reported \(O(1.16^{d} n)\) bound obtained through computer-aided parameter evaluation. These improve the useful range of the pattern-based approach, but their exponential dependence on d becomes a power of n when \(d=c \log _{2} n\).

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The hypothesis is useful because disjointness can encode compatibility between partial solutions. In the standard split-and-list SAT reduction, each half-assignment produces a vector marking clauses it fails to satisfy. Two half-assignments extend to a satisfying assignment exactly when their vectors are disjoint. Sparsification controls the number of clause coordinates. For the randomized version stated here, the corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a conditional justification; a deterministic-only SAT assumption must not silently be used to exclude randomized solvers.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.
why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.
status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly states the unrestricted OV conjecture as open while proving restricted-model variants. Low-dimensional and average-case improvements do not negate its quantifier order. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2015: Abboud–Williams–Yu obtain dimension-dependent truly subquadratic algorithms via the polynomial method; the exponent saving decreases with the dimension constant. | 2019: Rohatgi develops OV-based conditional hardness for exact Earth Mover Distance, illustrating geometric consequences. | 2024-10-29: Alman–Andoni–Zhang improve average-case OV algorithms; the work appears at SOSA 2025. | 2026-07-01: Dürr–Kipouridis–Lampis–Węgrzycki present \(\widetilde{O}\)\((1.25^{d} n)\) randomized low-dimensional algorithms at ICALP, with a computer-aided \(O(1.16^{d} n)\) refinement. | 2026-07-26: Choudhury and coauthors establish the logarithmic-dimension monotone-circuit version for the negated predicate and strengthen other restricted-model lower bounds.
working_summary: Bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors asks whether two collections of binary vectors contain a pair with disjoint supports. The hypothesis excludes one fixed polynomial saving over quadratic time across all sufficiently large logarithmic dimension constants. Checking a pair is easy, but identifying a compatible pair among quadratically many possibilities is the bottleneck. Fine-grained reductions use this task to transfer precise barriers to geometric, string, and other algorithms. The saved review notes that subquadratic algorithms at each fixed small dimension are compatible with the hypothesis because their exponent savings can deteriorate as the dimension constant increases.

title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
importance_reason: A principal fine-grained benchmark connecting clique detection, matrix multiplication, dynamic data structures, and constraint optimization.
formal: Let \(\tau (k)\) be the infimum of worst-case time exponents of randomized algorithms deciding k-Clique, as specified below, and let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over C. Is \(\liminf _{k\to \infty} \tau (k)/k=\omega /3\)?
definitions: For each fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), the input is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph on \(n\ge k\) labeled vertices; accept iff some k distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. A uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, and its time bound must hold for every random tape. Set \(\tau (k)=\inf\){\(a\ge 0\): such an algorithm runs in \(O(n^{a})\) time as \(n\to \infty\)}. The program and hidden constants may depend on k, but not on n. Words have \(C_{k}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed constant \(C_{k}\); arithmetic modulo the word range, division with remainder, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect memory access cost one step, and a fresh random word costs one step. Initial memory apart from the input is zero; preprocessing counts; there is no nonuniform advice, giant-word operation or free oracle. For \(\omega\), let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary +,−,× gates in a circuit over C that computes all entries of the product of two formal \(N\times N\) matrices. Arbitrary complex constants and sharing are allowed, but division and branching are not. Define \(\omega =\inf \{a:M(N)=O(N^{a})\}\). This fixes the characteristic-zero arithmetic convention, separately from the bit-based graph algorithm. The question concerns the coefficient of k in the exponent; it does not fix k proportional to n or treat the latest published numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) as its exact value.
answer_criterion: The matrix-multiplication reduction gives the upper asymptotic benchmark \(\omega /3\). An affirmative answer therefore proves that, for every \(\delta >0\), there is K such that \(\tau (k)\ge (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for every fixed \(k\ge K\). A negative answer proves a strict saving in this coefficient, for example via algorithms with \(\tau (k)\le (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for arbitrarily large k and one \(\delta >0\). Saving logarithmic time factors or an additive \(o(k)\) in the exponent does not refute this leading-exponent formulation.
context:
For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For \(k=3r\), create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are \(O(n^{r})\) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent \(\omega k/3\).

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the \(n^{\omega k/3- o(k)}\) form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, \(\omega\) is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on \(\omega\) immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true \(\omega\). The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports \(\omega <2.371177\), improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is \(n^{k}(\log  n)^{- (k+1)}(\log  \log  n)^{k+3}\). Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by \(o(1)\) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below \(\omega /3\). Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.
why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.
status_note: Open in the stated unrestricted randomized leading-exponent form, following the inherited hypothesis and later primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The liminf and machine conventions make the asymptotic claim explicit. Logarithmic speedups, matrix-exponent improvements and conditional lower bounds do not settle it.

working_summary: For each fixed k, graph k-Clique asks whether k vertices are all pairwise adjacent. The reviewed hypothesis asks whether the leading coefficient of the optimal time exponent approaches the matrix-multiplication benchmark \(\omega /3\). Grouping a candidate clique into three parts connects detection to multiplication on auxiliary graphs. A lower exponent would change the foundation of many conditional optimality results for other computational tasks. The comparison uses the true matrix-multiplication exponent, so beating an old numerical upper bound or saving logarithmic factors does not by itself refute the hypothesis.

title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
importance_reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.
formal: For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge 3\) and \(k>h\) and every constant \(\varepsilon >0\), is there no classical randomized \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\)-time algorithm deciding whether an n-vertex h-uniform hypergraph contains a k-clique, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input?
definitions: The input hypergraph \(H=([n],E)\) is simple and unweighted, with E a subset of the h-element subsets of \([n]\). It is given by a dense table containing one Boolean membership entry for each h-element subset, in a fixed computable order. A k-clique is a set \(S\subseteq [n]\) of k distinct vertices such that every h-element subset of S belongs to E. The task outputs one yes/no bit and requires neither counting nor listing cliques. Fix the classical word-RAM with \(O(\log (n+2))\)-bit words, constant-time arithmetic, bitwise operations and random access on words; the word-length constant and runtime constants may depend on the fixed \(h,k,\varepsilon\). Random bits are allowed, but quantum operations, nonuniform advice and precomputed input-dependent tables are not. All processing of the input and construction of auxiliary data are charged. The excluded algorithm must run in \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\) steps on every execution and answer correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) for every input. The quantifiers concern each fixed pair h,k separately, not only a limit as k tends to infinity. The card explicitly uses the bounded-error randomized version of the classical hypothesis.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion of all such algorithms, or refute it by giving one fixed pair \(h\ge 3,k>h\), one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and a correct algorithm with the required worst-case time and per-input success probability. A conditional confirmation must name the stronger assumption. A logarithmic-factor speedup, an algorithm for a sparse or promised subclass, or a circuit-size bound in a restricted algebraic model is not a resolution of the full claim.
context:
A graph records pairwise compatibility. An h-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of h vertices at a time. For \(h=3\) and \(k=4, a\) positive instance contains four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Knowing that every pair participates in some hyperedge is insufficient: the compatible triples must be exactly those supported on the same four vertices. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed h and k, exhaustive search takes \(O(n^{k})\) time: enumerate all k-element vertex sets and check the fixed number of required hyperedges. The problem is therefore already polynomial-time for every individual card parameter pair. The conjecture asks whether that polynomial exponent can be reduced by a positive constant. Ordinary NP-hardness when k varies would not establish such a fine-grained statement.

The graph case \(h=2\) behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at \(h=3\), instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time \(n^{k}\) divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an \(O(n^{3.99})\) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding prevents an implicit promise about sparsity. Its size is \(\Theta (n^{h})\) table entries, which is below the exhaustive-search exponent because \(k>h\). Any refuting exponent saving can be reduced to a smaller positive saving so that reading this table still fits the claimed time. Thus routine conversions between explicit dense representations do not provide an artificial refutation.

The inherited paper works with k-partite hypergraphs. This is essentially equivalent for fixed k: make k copies of the vertex set and place an edge between copies in distinct parts whenever their distinct original vertices form an input hyperedge. Selecting one vertex from each part then tests the original clique condition. The vertex blowup depends only on k, preserving a positive polynomial exponent saving.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß go further in their ICALP 2025 regularization theorem. They transfer algorithms between general k-partite hypergraphs and a strongly regular class in which each transversal \((h- 1)\)-tuple has the same number of extensions to a hyperedge. Controlling these overlapping incidences without introducing false cliques is the substantive part of the construction. The result shows that this regularity promise does not remove the conjectured difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work gives another connection: a refutation for the 3-uniform, 4-clique case would yield a truly subquadratic algorithm for detecting four-term arithmetic progressions in an integer universe. Their paper studies verification of algebraic identities and uses this relationship for conditional lower bounds. It supplies a new consequence or conditional foundation, rather than establishing the hyperclique lower bound outright.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.
why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No classical bounded-error algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving for a covered h,k pair was found in the checked sources. The 2025 regularization and 2026 reductions use or relate the hypothesis; they do not prove it unconditionally.
progress: 2017–2018: Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams develop hyperclique hypotheses, their Max-h-SAT connections and conditional graph-algorithm lower bounds. | 2025: Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß prove regularization preserving fine-grained clique complexity and apply it to Boolean CSP optimization. | 30 March–June 2026: Dudek and coauthors relate the 3-uniform 4-hyperclique hypothesis to arithmetic-progression detection in their STOC 2026 study of algebraic identities. | July 2026: Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß analyze when sparsity helps for hypergraph independent sets and use hyperclique assumptions for matching lower bounds.
working_summary: A clique in an h-uniform hypergraph requires every h-element subset of its vertices to be a hyperedge. The hypothesis asserts that, for fixed h at least three and k greater than h, exhaustive k-tuple search admits no constant exponent saving. Higher-order compatibility cannot be verified merely by checking pairwise adjacency as in a graph. This conjectured barrier supports fine-grained lower bounds for optimization with higher-arity constraints. The saved review fixes randomized classical algorithms and dense inputs, while distinguishing genuine polynomial savings from logarithmic improvements or algorithms benefiting only from sparsity.

title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
importance_reason: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.
formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma =\{0,1\}\), do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], a constant \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair \(x,y\in \Sigma ^{n}, A\) outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(ED(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2- \varepsilon}\) operations?
definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.
context:
The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.
why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.
status_note: The checked primary literature gives conditional exact-distance lower bounds and a March 2026 approximation advance. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established deterministic truly subquadratic exact algorithm or unconditional exclusion in this model.
progress: 2015 / 2017: Backurs–Indyk prove a SETH-based obstruction to truly subquadratic exact edit distance; the 2017 full revision also records subsequent developments. | 2015-04: Bringmann–Künnemann establish the conditional lower bound already on binary strings. | 2026-03: A randomized approximation scheme obtains a quasi-polynomial speedup; it does not compute exact distances.
working_summary: Can exact edit distance between two length-n binary strings be computed in truly subquadratic time? Each insertion, deletion and substitution costs one, and the algorithm must always return the exact minimum. The requested deterministic worst-case bound has a fixed positive saving in the exponent of n. Known reductions rule out such an algorithm if SETH is true, but that hypothesis remains unproved. The 2026 approximation improvement has different accuracy and randomness guarantees.

title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
importance_reason: A widely reusable fine-grained hardness hypothesis underlying trade-offs for many dynamic problems; its consequences reach well beyond matrix-vector multiplication.
formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with a fixed positive polynomial saving in the total time, including preprocessing, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. A subpolynomial saving does not refute the OMv conjecture.
context:
If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.
why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The truly subcubic Boolean online problem remains open; structured-matrix and different-product results require separate assumptions.
progress: 2015: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity. | 2017: Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture. | 2025: Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

working_summary: Online Boolean matrix-vector multiplication starts with a fixed Boolean matrix and then receives vectors individually. Each Boolean product must be returned before the next vector becomes available. The conjecture excludes a fixed polynomial improvement over cubic total time for a full sequence of vectors, including preprocessing. Batching the vectors into another matrix would violate the online requirement. Its importance comes from reductions that turn matrix queries into graph updates and thereby connect the conjecture to limits on dynamic algorithms.

title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
importance_reason: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.
context:
Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.
why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The ICALP 2026 paper still states the unrestricted min-plus convolution hypothesis, records a subpolynomial unrestricted speedup, and proves faster results for monotone bounded-range inputs. No fixed-saving algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this explicit integer formulation was located. Source proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2014: Convolution algorithms exploit pair-sum structure without establishing a fixed exponent improvement for general min-plus convolution. | 2026: Deterministic faster algorithms handle the monotone structured variant; they do not settle arbitrary polynomially bounded arrays.
working_summary: Min-plus convolution returns the minimum sum of two array entries for each possible sum of their indices. The input arrays contain polynomially bounded integers and need not be monotone. The question asks for a fixed improvement in the quadratic running-time exponent. Bounded-error randomization is allowed and every output entry must be correct simultaneously. Faster algorithms for monotone instances do not settle this unrestricted fine-grained barrier.

title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
importance_reason: Truly subquadratic 3SUM is a central fine-grained hypothesis with consequences for a large family of geometric and combinatorial problems.
formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.
context:
Known algorithms beat \(n^2\) by logarithmic factors. Such bounds are \(o(n^2)\), but they do not give \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). The modern conjecture concerns this latter, truly subquadratic improvement.

The three-set input convention follows the source. The integer word-RAM and polynomial-universe choices distinguish this target from real-RAM variants and from decision trees that charge only selected comparisons. The lower-bound claim is not restricted to a comparison-only instruction set.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat formulate the modern conjecture even for expected running time and use Las Vegas complexities in their reductions. The zero-error convention here follows that formulation; it is made explicit rather than silently identifying different randomized models.

Recent work improves time–space tradeoffs after sets have been preprocessed. This is useful progress for data structures, but the present input arrives from scratch, so the entire preprocessing time must be included in its complexity.
why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.
status_note: The source problem list and Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat’s modern expected-time formulation were checked on 2026-09-14, together with 2026 preprocessed-3SUM work. A bounded later search found no from-scratch Las Vegas algorithm or general lower bound resolving the explicitly selected polynomial-universe variant.
progress: 2005: Subquadratic integer algorithms with logarithmic-factor savings are among the results reviewed by the source; they leave a fixed polynomial saving open. | 2016: Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat develop reductions from the modern expected-time 3SUM conjecture to set-intersection, graph and data-structure tasks. | 2026: ICALP work obtains improved subquadratic-space tradeoffs for preprocessed 3SUM; the model retains a preprocessing phase and does not establish a truly subquadratic from-scratch algorithm.
working_summary: 3SUM asks whether a value in one integer list is the sum of values from two other lists. The target is a fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic running time on a precisely specified word RAM. The selected variant allows every fixed polynomial integer universe and requires a common exponent saving. Randomization may change the running time but must never produce an incorrect answer. Known logarithmic savings and faster queries after preprocessing do not meet the from-scratch target.

title: Hitting Set conjecture
importance_reason: A standard hardness hypothesis behind fine-grained diameter and graph-distance barriers.
formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length \(w=\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

title: P versus BPP
importance_reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.
focus_reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.
formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
definitions: Input length is \(n=|x|\). A polynomial-time bound means \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.
why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
importance_reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.
focus_reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators \(G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), for all integers \(n,w\ge 2\) and \(p\ge 1\), with \(s\le C(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\), such that \(\left|\Pr_{u\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{s}}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{n}}[B(z)=1]\right|\le2^{-p}\) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_{i}\) using at most \(D(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\) work bits and time \((nw\cdot 2^{p})^{D}\).
definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers \(V_{0},\ldots ,V_{n}\), each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in \(V_{0}\), and an accepting subset of \(V_{n}\). For each layer \(i- 1\), each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to \(V_{i}\). On input z, the program follows the edge labeled \(z_{i}\) at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order \(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{n}\). Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this dyadic formulation gives the usual \(O(\log (nw/\varepsilon ))\) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The program processes a long stream while remembering only its current state. Width w corresponds to about \(\log _{2} w\) bits of memory; length n is the number of random bits it can inspect. A pseudorandom generator replaces that long random stream with the deterministic expansion of a much shorter genuinely random seed. The requirement is simultaneous: the same generated distribution must fool every permitted program, even though their transition tables may be entirely different.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to the seed-length target. After padding to w states, the number of programs is at most \(w\cdot 2^{w}\cdot w^{2nw}\). Choose a list of independent uniform n-bit strings and use a uniformly chosen list position as the seed. A concentration bound and union bound show that a list of \(O(\varepsilon ^{- 2}(nw \log  w+w))\) strings suffices to approximate every acceptance probability. Indexing that list takes \(O(\log  n+\log  w+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\) bits. The argument does not tell us how to generate its entries in the tiny workspace required here.

The computational payoff is direct. Fix an input to a bounded-error logarithmic-space randomized machine and view its evolution on random bits as a polynomial-length, polynomial-width branching program. A logarithmic seed permits enumeration of all seeds, regeneration of individual pseudorandom bits and counting accepting runs within logarithmic space. With constant error small enough to preserve the acceptance gap, this would prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\). The card asks for a uniform generator, which is a particular strong route to that complexity-class equality.

Nisan’s construction gives seed length \(O(\log  n\cdot \log (nw/\varepsilon ))\). For polynomial width and constant error this is \(O(\log ^{2}n)\), so reaching the target would remove an entire logarithmic factor. The difficulty is generating a universally useful sample space in little space, rather than merely showing that some sample space exists. Even considerable improvements for simpler transition structures need not survive arbitrary merging of states.

Weighted pseudorandom generators relax the distribution requirement. They approximate acceptance by a weighted sum of program evaluations, with weights that may be negative. Hoza’s RANDOM 2021 construction attains seed length \(O(\log ^{2}n+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\) for width-n, length-n programs, improving the dependence on small error. Such weighted estimates can support deterministic simulation, but negative mass cannot be sampled as an ordinary probability distribution over the generated strings.

Cheng and Wu’s SODA 2026 work improves weighted generators across width and error regimes. Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction and the dependence on the input alphabet. It still constructs a weighted object. Its discussion credits Cheng and Hoza’s earlier reduction showing that sufficiently good ordinary-generator dependence on alphabet size and error would break the log-squared barrier. That implication does not turn the newly constructed weighted generator into an ordinary one.

The role of hitting sets provides another useful distinction. A hitting set ensures that an accepting string is included when the accepting fraction is sufficiently large; it does not directly approximate that fraction. Cheng and Hoza prove that sufficiently strong logspace hitting sets nevertheless imply two-sided logspace derandomization through a more involved reduction. Their results explain why a derandomization theorem need not arrive packaged as the universal probability distribution requested here.

Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber’s July 2026 paper gives an ordinary generator for permutation programs with seed \(O((\log  w+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\log  n)\), by a new analysis of the INW generator. In this subclass each symbol acts bijectively on the states between layers. The result has optimal logarithmic dependence on length when width and error are fixed, but the permutation promise excludes the arbitrary state merging allowed in this card.
why: An optimal generator would remove randomness from logarithmic-space computation and identify how little entropy suffices to fool every small-memory streaming computation. The question joins explicit constructions, space complexity and the gap between real distributions and useful signed approximations.

title: L versus BPL
importance_reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. The class equality merits a full card even alongside a more specific generator-construction target.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, for every language \(S\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* decided with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by a uniform randomized Turing machine using \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space?
definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within \(K(n+2)^{c}\) steps and uses at most \(K \log _{2}(n+2)\) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least \(2/3\) if \(x\in S\) and at most \(1/3\) if \(x\notin S\). This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.
