A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using \(O(\log ^{3/2} n)\) space. Hoza improved the bound to \(O(\log ^{3/2} n / \sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.
why: Determine whether randomness increases decision power when only logarithmic work space is available.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026, including the latest displayed ECCC revision of the 2026 weighted-PRG paper. No deterministic logarithmic-space simulation of all BPL languages was found.
progress: 2021: Hoza improves the deterministic space bound to \(O(\log ^{3/2} n / \sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), without reaching \(O(\log  n)\). | 2026-05-04: Revision 3 of Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs improves parameter dependence for weighted generators; it does not prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\).
working_summary: BPL permits bounded-error randomized decisions using logarithmic work space and polynomial time. The question asks whether every such language has a deterministic logarithmic-space decider. Random bits are fresh independent coin outcomes, and remembering them consumes counted work space. Known deterministic simulations and recent weighted-generator improvements still use more space or establish different parameter guarantees. The completed card keeps this class-equality target separate from constructing a particular optimal pseudorandom generator.

title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
importance_reason: An optimal derandomization problem connecting compressed sensing, pseudorandomness, additive combinatorics and explicit geometric constructions.
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C,B,b>0\) and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers \(N\ge 2\) and \(2\le s\le N\), outputs in at most \(B N^{b}\) bit operations a rational \(m\times N\) matrix A, with \(m\le C s \ln (eN/s)\), such that \((2/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\le \Vert Ax\Vert _{2}^{2}\le (4/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\) for every real vector \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{N}\) with at most s nonzero coordinates?
definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most \(B N^{b}\). Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion \(\delta =1/3\). The condition must hold simultaneously for every support of size at most s and every real choice of coefficients on that support. No probability over supports or signals is permitted. The natural logarithm and the factor e ensure a nonzero expression when s is close to N. The omitted case \(s=1\) is trivial and can be handled by a single row of ones.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm satisfying all the uniform dimension, encoding, time and restricted-isometry requirements, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A negative result conditional on a complexity assumption must state it. An existence proof, a construction using random bits, success for most sparse signals, or a deterministic construction with a larger asymptotic row count does not settle the stated question.
context:
Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of \(A_{S}^{T}A_{S}\) must lie between \(2/3\) and \(4/3\). Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion \(1/3\), then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square \(t^{2}\) within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±\(1/t\). This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal \(s \log (eN/s)\) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with \(O(s \log (N/s) \log  s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\)-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.
why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polynomial-time deterministic construction with the required uniform optimal row bound was found in the checked sources. Optimal randomized row counts, restricted parameter regimes and coherence guarantees are recorded as partial progress.
progress: 2010–2011: Bourgain and coauthors give explicit RIP matrices beyond the coherence-based square-root bottleneck in a restricted parameter range. | 2013: Bandeira–Fickus–Mixon–Wong compare deterministic verification methods and formulate frame-based routes toward stronger constructions. | 2023–2025: Rao obtains optimal row counts with fewer random bits; the December 2024 revision appeared in Information Processing Letters 189 (2025), article 106553. | July–December 2025: Fickus–Lake’s revised and published frame results describe minimal dependencies in doubly transitive equiangular tight frames; their introduction still identifies optimal deterministic RIP construction as open.
working_summary: A restricted-isometry matrix approximately preserves the Euclidean length of every sparse vector. The reviewed question asks for deterministic polynomial-time construction with \(O(s \log (eN/s))\) rows and fixed distortion. Random matrices achieve this row order, but a usable deterministic construction must control every sparse support simultaneously. Optimal explicit matrices would provide guaranteed measurement designs for compressed sensing without random setup choices. The saved review identifies the limitations of pairwise coherence analyses and notes that reduced randomness or success on typical signals does not establish the requested all-signal guarantee.

title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
importance_reason: Reach the information-theoretic entropy threshold for a foundational seedless randomness primitive.
formal: Do a constant C and a deterministic algorithm running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time exist that compute \(E_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times \{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) with |\(\Pr [E_{n}(X,Y)=1]- 1/2|\le 0.01\) for every pair of independent sources X,Y of min-entropy at least \(\log _{2}n+C\)?
definitions: The algorithm receives n and the two n-bit strings, and defines one function for every \(n\ge 1\). A source is any probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\); its min-entropy is −\(\log _{2}(\max _{x} \Pr [X=x])\). Independence means the joint law is the product of the two marginal distributions. For n where the entropy threshold exceeds n there are no eligible sources. No auxiliary uniform seed, advice or distribution description is supplied. The constants and time polynomial are universal.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Two independent weak sources can contain much randomness while neither source by itself yields even one predictably unbiased bit. The target reaches the entropy threshold permitted by a random truth table with a polynomial-time evaluable function.

Xin Li’s construction achieves entropy \(O(\log  n)\), with an unspecified multiplicative constant. The requested \(\log _{2}n+C\) threshold is stronger than that asymptotic-order statement. This distinction also matters when converting extraction into explicit Ramsey graphs.
why: Reach the information-theoretic entropy threshold for a foundational seedless randomness primitive.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2023: Li obtains explicit two-source extractors for \(O(\log  n) \min\)-entropy; the coefficient-one plus additive-constant target is not asserted.

title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
importance_reason: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP would remove randomness in a broad regime without hardness assumptions.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.
context:
Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.

If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm P\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.
why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

The question asks whether all of them have exact deterministic simulations in the class SUBEXP. title: Linear-seed hardness-to-randomness sampling
importance_reason: Optimal hardness-to-randomness generators would strengthen a central bridge between lower bounds and deterministic algorithms.
formal:
Does there exist one explicit family of point samplers
\[H_{\ell,s}:\{0,1\}^{d(\ell,s)}\to(\{0,1\}^{\ell})^{m(\ell,s)}\]
and absolute constants \(C\ge1\) and rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) with the following property for every pair of integers \(\ell\ge1\), \(s\ge2\)? The lengths obey
\[d(\ell,s)\le C\ell,\qquad \max\{1,\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\}\le m(\ell,s)\le s.\]
For every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[\forall B\text{ of size at most }s,\quad\Pr_{x\sim U_{\ell}}[B(x)=f(x)]\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1s,\]
form the \(m\)-bit generator
\[G_f(z)=f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_1)\,f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_2)\cdots f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_m).\]
Must it then satisfy
\[\forall D\text{ of size at most }m,\quad\bigl|\Pr_{z\sim U_d}[D(G_f(z))=1]-\Pr_{u\sim U_m}[D(u)=1]\bigr|\le1/m?\]
The circuits, explicitness and probability spaces are defined below. The sampler is chosen independently of \(f\); each output bit of \(G_f\) is exactly one evaluation of \(f\) at the corresponding sampled point.
definitions:
\(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on \(t\)-bit strings. The probabilities in the premise and conclusion use fresh independent uniform strings of the indicated lengths. They are computational distinguishability guarantees, not statistical closeness against unbounded tests.

A Boolean circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input wires, free Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one output wire. Size counts computation gates, including NOT gates, but not input wires or constants. The circuits \(B\) and \(D\) are deterministic and completely nonuniform; \(B\) has \(\ell\) inputs and \(D\) has \(m\). Their choices may depend on all parameters and on \(f\). They have no oracle access to \(f\). Allowing additional independent random input wires does not change these guarantees, because fixing the random bits gives a deterministic circuit of no greater size and averaging preserves the displayed inequalities. The premise means that even the best size-\(s\) predictor has advantage at most \(1/s\) over a fair guess.

Explicitness is uniform deterministic polynomial-time computation of the sampler. There are fixed multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that the parameter machine on \((1^{\ell},s)\), with \(s\) binary, outputs integer lengths \(d,m\), and the evaluation machine on \((1^{\ell},s,z)\) writes the ordered list of all \(m\) sampled \(\ell\)-bit strings. Each runs in at most \(K(\ell+s+1)^q\) steps on valid inputs. Equivalently the time can be polynomial in \(\ell+m\), because of the polynomial relationship between \(s\) and \(m\). All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, hard-function description or hard-function truth table available to these machines.

The constants and the machines precede the parameters, and \(H_{\ell,s}\) precedes the universal quantifier over \(f\). The family must be computed even for parameter pairs at which no function satisfies the hardness premise; its implication is then vacuous. No algorithm recognizing hard functions is required. The function \(f\) need not itself be efficiently computable: this is a transformation guarantee conditional on its finite-length circuit hardness, not a claim that such hard functions have been constructed. When \(f\) is also computable within a suitable exponential-time bound, the transformation has the usual derandomization applications.

The normalization \(m\le s\) and the lower bound using \(\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\) express the source's polynomially many output bits. A larger qualifying output can be truncated, and fixed multiplicative factors in a polynomial lower bound can be absorbed by reducing \(\beta\) and handling finitely many small hardness parameters. The single-evaluation requirement excludes encoding or otherwise transforming the truth table of \(f\) before producing the output bits.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated sampler-family claim. A positive proof must supply the uniform sampler and constants and establish the implication for every promised \(f\), including the linear seed bound, polynomial output length and size-\(m\), error-\(1/m\) guarantee. A negative proof must rule out all such families, not merely one combinatorial-design construction or one kind of security reduction. A general hardness-to-randomness generator that encodes the hard function or combines several evaluations per output bit does not answer this sampling question.
context:
The Nisan–Wigderson construction evaluates the hard function at correlated points determined by a combinatorial design. The source obtains a seed bound of order \(\ell^2/\log s\) while keeping polynomially many output bits. This is linear in \(\ell\) when \(s\) is exponential in \(\ell\), but not throughout the lower-hardness range.

General hardness-to-randomness constructions already improve the seed dependence to linear in the relevant hard-function input length. Vadhan explains that their output bits can depend on an encoding of the entire hard function. Open Problem 7.25 asks for the more restrictive point-evaluation form written here, so those results do not directly settle it.

The 2022 Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman theorem refines quantitative derandomization under hardness for randomized single-valued nondeterministic circuits. It uses pseudoentropy and extraction and assumes a different, stronger type of circuit hardness. Its nearly optimal parameters are not a theorem for every ordinary average-case-hard function under the one-evaluation-per-bit requirement.

A lower bound for one construction or for a specified reconstructive proof technique would not refute the semantic existence statement. Conversely, merely assuming that a hard function exists is not the desired answer: the question requires one uniform sampler with the stated implication for every function meeting the premise.
why: This asks whether strong average-case hardness can be converted into many pseudorandom bits while using a seed only a constant factor longer than one input to the hard function, and preserving an especially simple evaluation form. Such a result would make the hardness-to-randomness connection more modular and usable across different computational classes. The restriction concerns the structure of the transformation, not merely the final existence of a short-seed generator.

title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
importance_reason: Optimal seeded extraction parameters concern one of the central universal tools for converting weak randomness into usable randomness.
formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
definitions:
All lengths \(n,k,d,m\) are integers measured in bits, with \(d,m\ge0\), and logarithms have base two. For a finite random variable \(X\),
\[H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x].\]
Thus the source promise is \(\Pr[X=x]\le2^{-k}\) for every \(n\)-bit string \(x\). The source may have arbitrary dependencies between its coordinates and need not be samplable by an efficient algorithm. The extractor receives a sample string, not a description of its distribution. \(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(t\)-bit strings, including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). For distributions \(P,Q\) on the same finite set,
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The condition is statistical and quantifies over every promised source, with no computational restriction on a test of the output.

A family is explicit if there are two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\): a parameter machine on \((1^n,k)\), with \(k\) in binary, outputs \(d(n,k),m(n,k)\) in binary; an evaluation machine on \((1^n,k,x,y)\) outputs the entire \(m(n,k)\)-bit string. Both halt within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps on all valid inputs. All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, randomized construction or length-dependent table supplied for free. The machines, \(C,\Delta,K,q\) are chosen before \(n,k\) and before the source distribution.

Total entropy loss means \(k+d-m\): it counts the source's guaranteed entropy together with all perfect seed bits consumed. This ordinary extractor requirement concerns the output distribution alone. It does not require that the output remain uniform when the seed is separately disclosed. A strong extractor, whose output is uniform jointly with a disclosed seed, may be converted to an ordinary one by including its seed in the total output, but those seed bits must then be counted in \(m\). The convention \(m\le k+d\) is harmless output truncation for this error level. Integer entropy thresholds suffice for the stated additive-constant target; rounding down a real threshold changes the loss by less than one bit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform construction claim. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and universal constants and prove the extraction guarantee, logarithmic seed bound, constant total loss and polynomial evaluation time throughout the parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform family. An existence proof without efficient evaluation, a loss growing with \(n\) or \(k\), or an output bound that ignores consumed seed entropy does not meet the criterion.
context:

In applications that enumerate seeds or pay exponentially for entropy loss, the additive loss determines a multiplicative cost. Resolving the question would distinguish information-theoretic feasibility from the achievable efficiency of explicit extraction.

title: Extraction with log n plus constant seed length
importance_reason: Optimal seeded extraction parameters concern one of the central universal tools for converting weak randomness into usable randomness.
formal:
Is there an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors with error at most \(1/100\), a rational constant \(\gamma\in(0,1]\) and an integer constant \(C\ge0\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)},\qquad d(n,k)\le\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+C,\qquad m(n,k)\ge\lfloor\gamma k\rfloor?\]
For every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings satisfying \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), and a uniform seed independent of \(X\), the required guarantee is
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100.\]
The family, \(C\), \(\gamma\) and its polynomial evaluation bound must be uniform across \(n,k\). This selects the main \(m=\Omega(k)\) target in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.42, retaining its weaker polynomial-output alternative as context.
definitions:
The parameters \(n,k,d,m\) are nonnegative integer bit lengths, with the domain restrictions in the statement and \(m\le n+d\). The latter is a harmless output-length normalization. All logarithms have base two. Min-entropy is \(H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x]\), so the source promise bounds every point mass by \(2^{-k}\). No efficient sampling assumption, independence between source coordinates or extra side-information promise is imposed. The extractor gets \(x,y\), not a source distribution or its support. The seed distribution \(U_d\) assigns equal probability to each \(d\)-bit string and is independent of the source. \(U_0\) is the point mass at the empty string. Statistical distance is \(\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\frac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\).

Explicitness means that two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines, using no advice or oracle, compute the parameters on \((1^n,k)\) and the full output on \((1^n,k,x,y)\), respectively. Here \(k\) is binary, \(|x|=n\), and \(|y|=d(n,k)\). There are fixed integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that each computation, including preprocessing and writing its output, halts within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps for every valid input. The parameters must be computed by the family; they cannot depend on the unknown source. Correctness is statistical for every promised distribution, even one with no efficient sampler.

The extractor is ordinary: the output alone must be close to uniform. Uniformity conditional on a separately disclosed seed is not an additional requirement. The seed may contribute bits to the ordinary output, which is why a nontrivial source-output condition is expressed uniformly over all \(k\). The fixed coefficient one in \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+C\) is essential: a bound \(A\log n\) with unspecified \(A>1\) need not qualify. Rounding changes the seed length and minimum output by at most one bit and does not alter the additive-constant and constant-fraction target.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of the specified uniform family. Existence requires algorithms and universal constants proving the seed bound with logarithmic coefficient one, output at least \(\lfloor\gamma k\rfloor\), statistical error at most \(1/100\) for every promised source, and polynomial evaluation time for all \(n,k\). A refutation must rule out every such choice. A construction for a restricted entropy range, a seed bound \((1+\delta)\log_2 n+O(1)\) with fixed \(\delta>0\), or merely \(k^{\beta}\) output for fixed \(\beta<1\), is insufficient for this selected main target.
context:
The source explicitly separates two improvements over constant-factor-optimal extraction: constant total entropy loss, and a seed of \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) bits. This card concerns the latter and does not require constant loss.

Open Problem 6.42 presents \(\Omega(k)\) output as its main target and also asks about the weaker possibility of \(k^{\Omega(1)}\) output. The card makes the constant-fraction target precise; it does not treat the two as equivalent.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman obtain short seeds in a substantial entropy regime. Their Theorem 1.7 gives seed length \((1+c\alpha)\log n+c\log(1/\varepsilon)\) and output of order \(n^{1-2\alpha}\) for entropy at least \(n^{1-\alpha}\), under the stated parameter conditions. This is a finer seed bound than unspecified \(O(\log n)\), but for fixed positive \(\alpha\) it does not meet coefficient one or constant-fraction output throughout the card’s domain.

The 2026 revised Doron–Ribeiro theorem improves the running time of constructions with \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) seed length and a constant fraction of the entropy as output, with entropy and preprocessing qualifications. Its asymptotic seed bound leaves the leading constant unspecified.
why: A logarithmic seed is often enumerated over all possibilities. Fixing its leading coefficient at one makes that enumeration linear in the source length up to a constant factor, instead of an unspecified polynomial. Achieving substantial output at that seed length for arbitrary min-entropy would sharpen a central resource bound in explicit randomness extraction.

title: Universal determinant evaluations for bipartite matching
importance_reason: Explicit simultaneous isolation for matchings would remove a fundamental use of randomness in graph algorithms.
formal:
Can one construct, in uniform deterministic NC, an integer table
\[\alpha^{(m)}=(\alpha_{i,j}^{(m)})_{i,j\in[m]}\in\{0,1,\ldots,m2^{m^2}\}^{m^2}\]
for each integer \(m\ge1\), such that the same table works for every simple bipartite graph \(G\) with labeled vertex classes \([m]\) and \([m]\)? Precisely, define the integer matrix
\[A_G(\alpha)_{i,j}=\begin{cases}\alpha_{i,j}&\text{if }(i,j)\in E(G),\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
The requirement is
\[\forall G,\qquad \det A_G(\alpha^{(m)})\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ has a perfect matching}.\]
The construction receives only \(1^m\), not \(G\). This card selects the NC construction explicitly proposed in Vadhan's Open Problem 3.7; its more permissive request for an efficient or even subexponential sequential construction is not an equivalent target.
definitions:
The notation \([m]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A simple bipartite graph in the statement is an arbitrary subset \(E\subseteq[m]\times[m]\), with no multiple edges. A perfect matching is a permutation \(\pi\) of \([m]\) for which \((i,\pi(i))\in E\) for all \(i\). The determinant is over the integers:
\[\det B=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)},\]
where \(S_m\) is the set of all permutations and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\) is their parity sign. Nonzero means exact integer nonzero, not a floating-point test or a residue modulo an unspecified prime.

Encode each entry of \(\alpha^{(m)}\) as a nonnegative binary integer padded to
\[L_m=\lceil\log_2(m2^{m^2}+1)\rceil\]
bits, and list entries in row-major order. The output contains exactly \(m^2L_m\) bits. Exponentially large entry values thus have polynomially many bits; their entire encoding is counted.

Uniform deterministic NC here means a logspace-uniform Boolean circuit family computing this full output from \(1^m\). There are fixed positive integers \(K,a,b\) such that the circuit for length \(m\) has at most \(K(m+1)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil^b\). Gates are fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and Boolean constants. A single deterministic Turing machine, on \(1^m\), writes the circuit and its output-wire list using \(O(\log(m+1))\) work space and polynomial time. Its output tape is write-only and is not free readable memory. No random bits, advice, oracle or table depending on \(m\) is supplied. The constants, circuit-generation machine and computation family precede the universal quantifiers over \(m,G\). Arbitrary unit-cost operations on integers are not part of this Boolean model.

The graph can be represented by its \(m^2\)-bit incidence table when stating correctness, but it is not an input to the constructor. An assignment chosen separately for each graph, or an algorithm deciding matching using another matrix, does not by itself provide a universal scalar table in the specified range.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of this NC construction claim. A positive proof must specify the uniform circuit construction, its polynomial-size and polylogarithmic-depth bounds, the entry range, and the determinant equivalence simultaneously for every graph. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform NC family. Nonconstructive existence of the tables, graph-dependent substitutions, or an NC matching algorithm without the required universal tables is insufficient.
context:
The determinant polynomial of the symbolic bipartite adjacency matrix is nonzero exactly when a perfect matching exists. Distinct perfect matchings contribute distinct monomials before evaluation; cancellation between their evaluated integer contributions is the obstacle the table must avoid.

The source proves that a suitable table exists for each \(m\). There are \(2^{m^2}\) graphs, and a uniformly chosen table from the specified range makes the determinant vanish incorrectly for any fixed matching-containing graph with probability at most \(m/(m2^{m^2}+1)\). The resulting simultaneous-existence bound does not supply an efficient uniform constructor.

The 2016 Fenner–Gurjar–Thierauf result gives uniform circuits of quasipolynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for bipartite perfect matching. Quasipolynomial size exceeds the polynomial-size NC requirement in this card.

The July 2026 Chatterjee–Ghosh–Gurjar–Raj–Thierauf preprint claims NC algorithms for bipartite matching, including weighted and search versions. Its decision algorithm tests the rank of a larger block matrix built from the input graph. The checked construction is a different algebraic test and does not supply one scalar substitution into the original adjacency matrix for all graphs. This card therefore retains the universal-table question, while recording that its historical algorithmic motivation has a separate new claimed resolution.
why: A universal evaluation table would give a reusable deterministic replacement for all random entries in the classical determinant test for bipartite matching. The same polynomial-size data would preserve every matching-existence test at a given graph size. The source uses NC construction as a particularly strong form of explicitness, connecting this algebraic derandomization object to efficient parallel computation.

title: Lossless condensers with constant output overhead
importance_reason: Improved condensers and extractors would strengthen general-purpose randomness-processing constructions.
formal:
Is there an explicit family of functions
\[\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
and absolute integer constants \(C,\Delta\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad k+d(n,k)\le m(n,k)\le k+d(n,k)+\Delta,\]
and for every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings with \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), there is a distribution \(Y_X\) on \(m(n,k)\)-bit strings satisfying
\[H_{\infty}(Y_X)\ge k+d(n,k),\qquad \operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),Y_X\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). The family must have one deterministic polynomial-time evaluator for all parameters. This is the lossless-condenser formulation of Vadhan's Open Problem 6.35, paired in the source with the expander question 5.36.
definitions:
All lengths are integers in bits and all logarithms have base two. The min-entropy of a finite distribution is \(H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x]\). The input promise therefore says that every point has probability at most \(2^{-k}\). Input distributions may be arbitrary; their coordinates need not be independent, and they need not have efficient samplers. The input to the condenser is a sample string and a seed, not a distribution description. \(U_t\) is uniform on all \(t\)-bit strings, with the single empty string when \(t=0\). Statistical distance is
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The comparison distribution \(Y_X\) may depend on the entire source distribution. Its existence is a mathematical guarantee; no algorithm for producing or sampling it is required.

Explicitness means that two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines compute the lengths from \((1^n,k)\) and the full output from \((1^n,k,x,y)\), respectively. The entropy parameter is binary, \(|x|=n\), and \(|y|=d(n,k)\). For some fixed positive integers \(K,q\), each computation uses at most \(K(n+1)^q\) transitions, including preprocessing and output writing. No advice, oracle, randomized choice of construction or free length-dependent table is allowed. The machines and constants are fixed before \(n,k,X\); the comparison distribution is quantified after \(X\).

Lossless means that the comparison distribution preserves all \(k+d\) guaranteed input-and-seed entropy bits. The bounded quantity \(m-(k+d)\) is the output entropy gap, or output overhead, not lost entropy. The condenser is not required to output an almost-uniform string: it only has to be close to a distribution with the specified min-entropy. Uniformity conditional on a separately disclosed seed is not imposed.

There is an equivalent graph view for these parameters. Let \(N=2^n\), \(D=2^d\), \(M=2^m\), and \(K_0=2^k\). Treat the condenser as a neighbor function \([N]\times[D]\to[M]\), identifying integers with fixed-length binary strings. It defines a left-regular bipartite multigraph; seeds label edges, and repeated neighbors are permitted. The lossless condition is equivalent to requiring at least \((99/100)DK_0\) distinct neighbors for every set of exactly \(K_0\) left vertices. The size bounds become \(D\le(2n)^C\) and \(DK_0\le M\le2^{\Delta}DK_0\). Only this source-equivalent one-sided expansion is required; neither right-regularity nor right-to-left expansion is an additional condition.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform condenser-family claim. A construction must specify its algorithms and constants and establish all length, time, distance and entropy requirements over the entire domain. An equivalent graph construction qualifies with a proved translation to these guarantees. A negative answer must rule out every such family. A constant fraction of output entropy gap, a superlogarithmic seed, or a construction only for a restricted entropy regime does not meet the target.
context:
Open Problem 5.36 asks for degree polynomial in \(\log N\), expansion \(0.99D\), and only \(O(K_0D)\) right vertices. Proposition 6.33 translates the powers-of-two case into lossless condensation. The card fixes the binary representation and the exact fixed-error condenser formulation of Open Problem 6.35.

The 2022 Kalev–Ta-Shma construction gives a different lossless condenser with logarithmic seed length. Its Theorem 2 allows an output entropy gap proportional to the source entropy, with parameter restrictions; it does not establish an absolute constant gap. The paper explicitly distinguishes entropy loss from entropy gap and describes small-gap extraction as an outstanding challenge.

The September 2026 paper proves that the Kalev–Ta-Shma graph also expands losslessly in the reverse direction and characterizes its expansion. No joint polynomial dependence on \(k\) is required. The displayed error is an input fraction at every sufficiently large length, not a probability over simulation coins. P/poly consists of languages whose length-\(n\) characteristic functions have polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no uniformity between lengths. Boolean circuits are finite acyclic networks of fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and constants, with one output. Circuit size is the length of an explicit binary gate-and-wire encoding. title: Pseudodeterministic construction of primes at every length
importance_reason: A foundational explicit-construction challenge and concrete test of pseudodeterministic search, with a major infinitely-often theorem leaving a consequential uniform length-coverage gap. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a constant \(c\), and a sequence of primes \((p_{n})_{n\geq2}\), with \(2^{n-1}\leq p_{n}<2^{n}\), such that \(A\) runs in time \(O(n^{c})\) on input \(1^{n}\) and \[\Pr[A(1^{n})=p_{n}]\geq 2/3\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq2?\]
question_excerpt: In the context of polynomial time pseudo-determinism, there are many fundamental problems with polynomial time randomized algorithms where the existence of pseudodeterministic polynomial time algorithms […]
definitions:
The input \(1^{n}\) is unary: a string of \(n\) copies of the symbol 1. The output is the ordinary binary representation of an integer. An \(n\)-bit prime is an integer \(p\) in \([2^{n-1},2^{n})\) whose only positive divisors are 1 and \(p\). The domain begins at \(n=2\), since there is no one-bit prime.

The machine is a single classical probabilistic Turing machine, with independent unbiased random bits and a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every random tape. There is no advice depending on \(n\), precomputed table of primes, oracle, or free preprocessing. All computation, including any primality tests, counts toward its time bound.

Pseudodeterminism means that for each fixed length there is one fixed prime \(p_{n}\) returned with the stated probability across independent executions. The prime may depend on the algorithm and on \(n\), but not on the execution’s random bits. It need not be the smallest \(n\)-bit prime or a prime prescribed in advance. The remaining probability mass may produce a failure symbol, another prime, or an invalid output.

The guarantee is required at every length. Success on infinitely many unbounded lengths alone does not suffice. A guarantee for all sufficiently large lengths would suffice, since finitely many shorter lengths can be handled by a fixed finite part of the algorithm.

The constant success probability is the usual bounded-error convention for pseudodeterminism. Independent repetitions followed by a majority output can amplify concentration on the same canonical prime with polynomial overhead. Merely finding some prime with high probability, while different runs usually return different primes, does not meet the requirement.

The source lists several distinct search tasks. This card explicitly selects prime generation as its main target; it does not assert that solving it is equivalent to making every randomized search problem pseudodeterministic.

definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.
why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.
status_note: The textbook and Bottesch explicitly state the unresolved separation, and the later approximation papers retain it as an assumption. The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review does not independently reprove the cited results.
progress: 2015: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH. | 2018-08-27: Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation. | 2021-02-09: Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1]. | 2024–2025: Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication. | 2024–2026: Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.
working_summary: A k-clique is a set of k graph vertices joined by every possible edge. The question asks for one exact deterministic algorithm whose input-size exponent is constant while a computable multiplier absorbs all dependence on k. Polynomial time separately for each fixed k does not establish that uniform bound. Clique completeness makes the question equivalent to FPT equalling W[1]. Conditional lower bounds and recent fixed-k or approximation results explain the conjecture’s significance without deciding it.

title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
importance_reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.
focus_reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.
formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
context:
NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.
why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.
status_note: The original sources and the July 2026 ICALP paper continue to use ETH as an unproved hypothesis. The optimal-rate definition and cited algorithmic upper bound were checked against the full relevant source passages. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; bounded searches do not independently verify the cited proofs or exhaust all later literature.
progress: 2001-01-21: Impagliazzo and Paturi define the exponential rates of bounded-width satisfiability and relate positive rate at width three to positive rates at other fixed widths. These are structural results about the hypothesis, not a proof of it. | 2013: The authors’ IPEC survey explicitly defines ETH by a positive infimum and distinguishes the number of variables from the complete input length. | 2015: The parameterized-algorithms textbook retains the positive-infimum definition, explains its distinction from ruling out a single subexponential algorithm, and gives consequences for parameterized complexity. | 2018–2020: Liu gives a deterministic \(1.32793^n\) upper bound for 3-SAT up to polynomial factors, recorded in the checked March 2020 revision of the ICALP 2018 work. This leaves the positivity of the optimal rate unresolved. | 2026-07-01: Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia and Zhang derive new lattice approximation hardness under ETH or randomized ETH, with different assumptions for their closest-vector and shortest-vector results. The paper still treats these as assumptions and distinguishes Gap-ETH.

working_summary: ETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rate for 3-SAT is strictly positive. The exponential parameter is the number of distinct variables, while polynomial factors account for the complete encoded input. One positive rate must obstruct every algorithm, and refutation permits different algorithms for arbitrarily small positive rates. Known exponential-time algorithms provide upper bounds but no positive lower bound on the optimum. The hypothesis supports quantitative lower bounds throughout exact and parameterized algorithms without being established by those conditional consequences.

title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
importance_reason: A central exact-algorithm question with a sixty-year base-two barrier and a modern improvement that carefully distinguishes prefactor from exponent. It is separate from metric TSP approximation and from Hamiltonian-cycle detection.
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), c\ge 1\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on \(n\ge 3\) labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((2- \varepsilon )^{n}(n+\mathrm{L})^{c})\)?
definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with \(w=B\lceil n+\log _{2}(\mathrm{L}+2)\rceil\) bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in \(n+\mathrm{L}\). The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants \(\varepsilon ,c,B\) and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) time by a factor \(2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\). Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield \(O*((2- \varepsilon )^{n})\) for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.
why: Locate the fundamental exponential-time cost of exact weighted routing beyond the long-standing subset barrier.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No fixed classical exponential-base improvement for general binary-weighted TSP was found; polynomial-factor improvements and quantum algorithms are different guarantees.
progress: 1962: The Bellman and Held–Karp subset formulation gives the classical \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) bound, recalled by the 2024 primary paper. | 2024-05-27: Stoian v2 states deterministic time \(2^{n} n^{2}/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\), retaining base two.

title: Set Cover conjecture
importance_reason: One of the few central exact-algorithm barriers not simply interchangeable with SAT hypotheses.
formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.
context:
A subset dynamic program solves the problem in \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\) time. The target asks whether the base two can be reduced by a constant independent of the maximum allowed set size. Polynomial factors are explicitly permitted and may grow with that fixed size bound.

The family is given explicitly and each set has at most d elements. This is distinct from requiring exactly d elements, requiring a partition into disjoint sets, or bounding how many sets contain each element. The 2024 source studies reductions between such variants, but the card fixes the at-most-d covering version.

Cygan and coauthors use the Set Cover assumption for tight conditional bounds on several exact algorithms. Their work does not prove that the ordinary Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this Set Cover conjecture.

Björklund and Kaski prove that Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture would yield a randomized sub-two-base algorithm and hence refute SCC. Pratt strengthens the conditional algorithm. These are incompatibility and conditional-algorithm theorems, not unconditional resolutions of either conjecture.
why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.
status_note: The 2024 SCC formulation and both STOC 2024 asymptotic-rank connections were checked on 2026-09-14, together with a bounded later-work search. The rank-based algorithms are conditional; no unconditional proof or refutation of the selected randomized SCC was identified.
