working_summary: Set Cover asks whether a few supplied sets can cover a given universe. The conjecture concerns exact algorithms when each available set has a fixed maximum size. It says that no constant improvement over exponential base two works across all such size bounds. The target allows bounded-error randomization and polynomial factors that depend on the fixed bound. Recent results show that a major conjecture about tensor rank would refute SCC, but neither side is settled unconditionally.

title: FPT approximation of twin-width
importance_reason: A central algorithmic access problem for a major graph-width parameter, with consequences for the applicability of logical algorithms on bounded twin-width classes.
formal: Do there exist total computable functions \(f,g:N\to N\) and a constant \(c\ge 1\), and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer \(k\ge 0, A\) halts within \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations and either correctly reports \(tww(G)>k\) or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most \(g(k)\)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
definitions: The input gives n, the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of \(V(G)\), starting with the singleton partition and ending with \(\{V(G)\}\), each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair \(x\in X,y\in Y\) and a nonadjacent pair \(x' \in X,y' \in Y\) in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width \(tww(G)\) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the \(n- 1\) merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If \(tww(G)\le k\), rejection is forbidden. If \(tww(G)>k\), either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Twin-width measures how many mixed adjacency relations arise while vertices are progressively grouped. A graph may possess a low-width sequence even when finding that sequence from its ordinary representation is difficult.

The research-project question asks for fixed-parameter approximation with arbitrary computable width loss. It is therefore more basic than obtaining a particular approximation ratio: even a very large output-width function depending only on k would answer it.

Recognition and structural descriptions at twin-width one are established special cases. Approximation procedures for ordered structures receive additional information that this input does not contain. Neither result supplies the requested general algorithm.
why: Determine whether the structural certificates behind twin-width algorithms can be found efficiently from an unordered graph.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Bonnet lists the FPT approximation question, and the 2025 recognition paper explicitly leaves even general XP approximation open. No general resolution was found in the same-day review.
progress: 2025: The twin-width-one recognition paper still describes general XP approximation, and therefore FPT approximation, as open.
working_summary: Twin-width measures mixed adjacency during repeated merges of vertex groups. The question asks for an algorithm that finds a bounded-width merge sequence whenever the graph has twin-width at most k. Its running time may depend arbitrarily on k but only polynomially on graph size, with an exponent independent of k. The algorithm receives the graph alone, without a useful vertex order or decomposition. A positive answer would make twin-width-based algorithmic methods accessible from ordinary graph input.

title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
importance_reason: A central graph-cut kernelization problem: whether arbitrarily large instances can be compressed to size polynomial in the edge-deletion budget.
formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.
context:
The source contrasts polynomial kernels for each fixed terminal count with the open case of arbitrary terminal sets. For a bound \(|T|\le s\), the earlier kernel has a size exponent depending on \(s\); that dependence is exactly what the present question must avoid.

Wahlström proves a randomized quasipolynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut in the revised 2021 manuscript, with size \(k^{O(\log^3 k)}\) in the displayed bounds. The same work distinguishes a smaller nonconstructive mimicking-network bound from the network size achievable by randomized polynomial-time preprocessing.

The source’s mimicking networks preserve a richer family of terminal cut values. The benchmark asks only for an equivalent Edge Multiway Cut decision instance, so a solution does not need to construct such a stronger universal network.

The 2025 MFCS paper obtains deterministic kernels using quasipolynomial-time preprocessing for several problems whose randomized polynomial kernels were already known. It explicitly treats Multiway Cut with deletable terminals and separately mentions quasipolynomial-size Edge Multiway Cut kernels. Neither changing the deletion model nor allowing more preprocessing time resolves this card.
why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

The question asks whether polynomial-time preprocessing can reduce any instance to an equivalent instance of size polynomial in the deletion budget alone. The number of terminals is unrestricted, and the size exponent must not depend on it. Randomized preprocessing is allowed with a per-instance equivalence guarantee of at least two thirds. title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
importance_reason: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(L\) is the total binary input length?
definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.
context:
Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.
why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The SODA 2026 paper retains the worst-case classical exponential question; the August 2026 preprint improves a quantum bound instead. No classical fixed-saving worst-case algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this model was located. The new quantum proof was not independently verified.
progress: 2018: The source explicitly records the classical worst-case half-exponent barrier separately from its quantum results. | 2026: The worst-case exponential question remains in the introduction; the new theorem concerns pseudopolynomial computation. | 2026-08-07: A preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) bound; the classical worst-case target remains outside that result.
working_summary: Subset Sum asks whether some subcollection of given positive integers adds to a target. The classical worst-case benchmark comes from the meet-in-the-middle exponent. The question asks for a fixed positive saving in that exponent with polynomial dependence on binary input length. Bounded-error classical randomization is allowed, with no random-instance promise. Quantum, pseudopolynomial and polynomial-factor improvements do not establish this fixed exponent saving.

title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
importance_reason: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A_{k}\) and constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\ge 1\) such that \(A_{k}\) decides whether \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.
context:
Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound \(N^{k+2}\) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime \(f(k)N^{c}\) and c independent of k.

Polynomial-time recognition is known through \(k=3\), with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain \(k=4\) as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

A procedure that returns an expression with \(f(k)>k\) labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.
why: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.
status_note: The fixed-threshold question is explicitly open in the checked 2009 primary paper and 2012 recognition abstract. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. The checked July 2026 algorithmic result assumes an input expression and is not a current-status theorem about recognition. No independent proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2009: The variable-threshold recognition problem is proved NP-complete; the paper explicitly leaves recognition at each fixed threshold open. | 2012: The full polynomial-time recognition algorithm for clique-width at most three is published. | 2026-07: New graph algorithms exploit a supplied clique expression; they do not determine whether such an expression exists at an exact threshold.
working_summary: Clique-width measures how many reusable vertex labels are needed to build a graph with four specified operations. Even a complete graph of arbitrary size needs only two labels. The question asks whether graphs of width at most k can be recognized in polynomial time for every fixed k. The polynomial exponent may depend on k, so known NP-completeness when k is input does not settle it. Small thresholds are understood, while approximate or supplied decompositions do not give exact recognition at every threshold.

title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
importance_reason: A general algorithm-versus-representation question connecting graph structure, dynamic programming and automatization beyond one decomposition family.
formal: Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every finite simple graph G on \(n\ge 1\) vertices and nonnegative integer weight vector w, A outputs the maximum independent-set weight within \(C(\tau (G)+n+\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) bit operations, where L is the total binary encoding length of w and \(\tau (G)\) is the minimum size of a tropical MWIS circuit defined below? Only G and w are supplied; neither \(\tau (G)\) nor a circuit is part of the input.
definitions: G is given by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix. The n nonnegative weights are binary integers with delimiters, all counted in L. A vertex set I is independent when no edge has both endpoints in I. \(MWIS(G,w)=\max\)_{I independent}\(\sum_{v\in I}w_{v}\), allowing \(I=\varnothing\) with weight zero. A tropical circuit for G is a finite acyclic circuit with one designated output, arbitrary fan-out, input gates labeled \(x_{v}\) or the constant 0, and binary internal gates labeled max or + with their ordinary real-number meanings. No other constants or operations are allowed. Size counts every gate, including input and constant gates. An MWIS circuit must output \(MWIS(G,x)\) for every vector \(x\in R_{\ge}0^{n}\), so its topology depends only on G. Define \(\tau (G)\) as the minimum size of such a circuit. This minimum exists because finitely many independent sets can each be summed and their maximum computed. The output algorithm may use general deterministic computation, not only tropical operations. Constants C,c are uniform over all graphs and weight vectors.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A small tropical circuit describes a compact computation of the optimum for every assignment of weights to a fixed graph. Knowing that this description exists does not immediately provide an algorithm for discovering or exploiting it.

The source paper fixes binary max and addition gates and the constant zero. It proves restricted-class automatization results; arbitrary graphs are the issue here. Correctness for all nonnegative weights and for all real weights give polynomially equivalent size parameters, as discussed in Section 2.2.

This card selects the polynomial target from the author’s polynomial-or-quasipolynomial question and measures actual bit cost. It asks to compute the optimum, rather than requiring the algorithm to output a circuit.
why: Determine whether small nonuniform dynamic programs can always be exploited by a uniform exact algorithm without being supplied as certificates.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The current author list retains general automatization as open; the 2021 positive results are restricted to bounded-degree or fixed-minor-free classes.
progress: 2021: Korhonen proves tropical-circuit lower bounds and polynomial-overhead circuit construction on bounded-degree and fixed-minor-free graph classes. | 2026-09-11: The current list asks for polynomial or quasipolynomial runtime relative to optimal circuit size on arbitrary weighted graphs.
working_summary: A tropical circuit combines vertex weights using only maximum and addition. For each graph, \(\tau\) measures the smallest circuit that computes maximum independent-set weight for every nonnegative weight assignment. The question asks for a uniform algorithm whose runtime is polynomial in \(\tau\) and the input size. The algorithm receives no circuit or decomposition and may use unrestricted deterministic computation. A positive answer would turn the existence of a compact dynamic program into an effective algorithmic guarantee.

title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
importance_reason: Resolve a major parameterized isomorphism boundary for a broad graph-decomposition measure.
formal: Do a computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), an absolute constant c and a deterministic algorithm exist which decide isomorphism of graphs G,H in time \(f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^{c}\), where \(k=\max (\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H))\)?
definitions: Graphs are finite simple undirected graphs given by adjacency matrices. Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. For a graph G and \(X\subseteq V(G)\), the cut-rank is the rank over the two-element field of the adjacency submatrix with rows X and columns \(V(G)\setminus X\). A rank decomposition is a tree of maximum degree three whose leaves are bijectively labeled by \(V(G)\). Every tree edge partitions the leaves and hence defines a cut-rank; the decomposition width is the maximum of those ranks. Rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width, with \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\) for at most one vertex. No decomposition or parameter value is supplied to the algorithm. The exponent c is independent of the rank-width.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Rank-width measures graph complexity through low-rank adjacency cuts and supports many structural algorithms. Graph isomorphism on bounded rank-width is tractable at each fixed width, but that does not by itself yield one exponent independent of the parameter.

Neuen’s 2026 survey identifies the remaining parameterized isomorphism frontiers. An \(n^{g(k)}\) algorithm or a quasipolynomial dependence involving n does not establish fixed-parameter tractability. The target concerns testing isomorphism, without additionally demanding canonization.
why: Resolve a major parameterized isomorphism boundary for a broad graph-decomposition measure.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2026: The survey distinguishes known parameter-dependent-exponent algorithms from the remaining FPT target.

title: Polynomial exact metric sparsifiers with a crossing-edge budget
importance_reason: One small edge set preserving every metric-labeling query is a broad graph-compression principle, with substantially more content than a bound for one cut objective.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that the following holds? For every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) of size r, and integer \(p\ge 0\), there is a set \(Z\subseteq E\) with |\(Z|\le C(1+p+r)^{c}\) having this universal property: for every finite nonempty label set D, every metric \(\mu :D\times D\to R_{\ge 0}\), and every terminal labeling \(\tau :T\to D\), if there exists a labeling \(\lambda :V\to D\) extending \(\tau\) with at most p crossing edges, then some labeling \(\lambda\)* of minimum \(\mu\)-cost among all such budget-feasible extensions has all its crossing edges in Z. The same Z must work simultaneously for every \(D,\mu ,\tau\) and depends only on G,T,p. This is the polynomial-size version of the contraction-based metric-sparsifier property in the source’s Theorem 22; that theorem’s earlier quasipolynomial upper-bound claim was later retracted.
definitions: A crossing edge of \(\lambda\) is an edge uv with \(\lambda (u)\ne \lambda (v)\). Write \(X(\lambda )=\{uv\in E:\lambda (u)\ne \lambda (v)\}\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mu}(\lambda )=\sum_{uv\in E}\mu (\lambda (u),\lambda (v))\). A metric has \(\mu (a,b)=\mu (b,a), \mu (a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and \(\mu (a,c)\le \mu (a,b)+\mu (b,c)\). The admissible labelings for a query are \(B(G,T,p,D,\tau )\)={\(\lambda :V\to D:\lambda |_{T}=\tau\) and |\(X(\lambda )|\le p\)}. If B is nonempty, the finite set \(D^{V}\) ensures that \(\min _{\lambda \in B}\operatorname{cost}_{\mu}(\lambda )\) is attained. The universal requirement is that this minimum equals the minimum with the additional constraint \(X(\lambda )\subseteq Z\); in particular the latter feasible set must be nonempty. The number p bounds crossings, not the real-valued metric cost. Labeling \(\tau\) need not be injective or surjective, and |D| is unbounded independently of \(p+r\). The constants C,c may not depend on the graph, budget, label set, metric or terminal labeling. Using \(1+p+r\) only handles zero parameters and is asymptotically equivalent to polynomial size in \(p+r\). Restricting all edges outside Z to have equal endpoint labels is exactly the labeling constraint imposed by contracting those edges; Z measures the original retained edges. The question is existence of this universal set, not the running time to find it, so it neither assumes rational metric entries nor a numerical oracle for them. Exact equality of optimum values is required; no multiplicative or additive error is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal polynomial bound, or refute it by showing that no fixed constants C,c can bound the required retained edges over all G,T,p. A negative result must respect the quantifier order: every candidate small Z must fail for some label set, metric and terminal labeling with a feasible budgeted extension. Hardness of finding a small Z does not disprove its existence. Bounds for one fixed metric, a fixed number of labels, ordinary terminal cut values, or approximate values do not settle this target.
context:
A 0-Extension instance extends fixed labels on terminals to the rest of a graph while minimizing metric distances across edges. The desired sparsifier is chosen before either the metric or the terminal labels, and must retain an optimal extension whenever the crossing-edge budget is feasible.

Theorem 22 uses \(p+r\), with p counting disagreeing endpoints and r counting terminals. This differs from the total terminal degree used for ordinary multicut-mimicking networks elsewhere in the paper. An unrestricted terminal-count lower bound is therefore not automatically a lower bound for this question.

The corrected March 2021 version explicitly reports an incorrect proof for the preliminary 0-Extension claims and retracts the claimed quasipolynomial metric sparsifiers. It retains the underlying existence question. The retraction also appears in the accepted journal manuscript; the paper’s ordinary multicut results and the earlier Reidl–Wahlström results are stated to be unaffected.

Anand, Lee, Li and Saranurak’s 2024 work obtains randomized polynomial-time ordinary multicut-mimicking networks with \(k^{O(\log ^{2} k)}\) size, where k is total terminal degree. Their preserved quantities are minimum multiway-cut cardinalities for terminal partitions. This does not reestablish the retracted all-metrics, crossing-budget property.
why: Would determine whether a graph can be compressed once for every metric-labeling objective under a bounded number of label changes, a stronger form of reusable exact information than preserving ordinary terminal cut values.
status_note: Recovered the exact universal-set property from conference Theorem 22 and read the corrected full version’s explicit retraction and retained question. Checked the journal metadata and indexed author-manuscript retraction, the 2024 multicut theorem and later sparsifier searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution of this exact metric/budget property was found; the retracted theorem is not treated as established progress.
progress: 2020: The conference paper posed the polynomial-size question alongside a claimed quasipolynomial theorem for metric sparsifiers. | 2021-03-05: The corrected full version retracts the metric-sparsifier theorem because its proof is incorrect and was not repaired; the metric-sparsifier question remains. | 2024: Constructive size bounds improve for ordinary multicut-mimicking networks, with a different preserved objective family and parameter.
working_summary: A graph with terminals is queried by choosing labels for the terminals and a metric on the labels. The goal is a small retained edge set that supports an optimal extension for every such query. Only labelings with at most p crossing edges are compared, and the retained set must have size polynomial in p plus the number of terminals. The original claimed quasipolynomial metric-sparsifier result was explicitly retracted in the corrected paper. Ordinary multicut sparsifiers preserve a different collection of values and do not settle this universal metric question.

title: Slice-wise Polynomial Space Conjecture
importance_reason: A class-wide hypothesis about simultaneous memory and time, with consequences for many parameterized graph algorithms. Existing score retained.
formal: Is it true that no XNLP-hard parameterized decision problem has a single deterministic algorithm with both worst-case time \((n+2)^{f(k)}\) and working space \(f(k)(n+2)^{c}\), for any total computable function \(f:N\to N\) and any absolute constant c? Here k is the parameter, n is the bit length of the ordinary input, and both resource bounds must hold on the same execution. Hardness uses parameterized logspace many-one reductions defined below.
definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of \(\{0,1\}*\times N\), with input \((x,k), n=|x|\) and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time \(g(k)(n+2)^{a}\) and working space \(g(k)\log _{2}(n+2)\) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction \(Q_{1}\le Q_{2}\) is a deterministic halting transducer mapping \((x,k)\) to \((y,k' )\), preserving the yes/no answer, with \(k' \le h(k)\) for a total computable h and space \(h(k)+C \log _{2}(n+2)\) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by \(n+2\) only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.
context:
Parameterized dynamic programs often store tables of size \(n^{O(k)}\) and run in a comparable amount of time. Allowing a larger exponent in time does not automatically show whether the memory exponent can be made independent of k.

Its machines use only a parameter-dependent multiple of log n working space while running in fixed-parameter polynomial time. Many problems on graphs with linear decompositions are complete for this class.

The target would prohibit all deterministic algorithms with a fixed polynomial space exponent while retaining polynomial time on each fixed-parameter slice. It is a simultaneous tradeoff conjecture, not a claim that the problems cannot be solved in polynomial space with unrestricted time.

The Algorithmica paper establishes XNLP-completeness for several familiar graph problems and explicitly retains this time-space assertion as Conjecture 1. Such classifications transfer the conjectured obstruction; they do not prove it.
why: Would explain a broad barrier to reducing the memory of parameterized dynamic programming while keeping polynomial time for each fixed parameter, connecting practical table-size tradeoffs with a uniform complexity-class obstruction.
status_note: Read the source’s resource/reduction definitions and the retained Algorithmica conjecture. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026, including 2026 XALP and scheduling classifications, found no resolution of the stated obstruction.
progress: 2022: Conjecture 14 states the simultaneous time-space obstruction and relates it to earlier work of Pilipczuk and Wrochna. | 2025: The journal study of linear graph structure retains the statement as Conjecture 1 while proving new XNLP-completeness results.
working_summary: XNLP describes parameterized problems with short nondeterministic working memory and fixed-parameter polynomial running time. The conjecture forbids deterministic algorithms for XNLP-hard problems with both slice-wise polynomial time and a fixed polynomial space exponent. One algorithm must meet both guarantees on every input. The parameter may affect the time exponent and the space multiplier, but not the space exponent. Later completeness results retain this as a conjecture that would explain memory barriers in dynamic programming.

title: Disjoint-union closure of tractable forbidden patterns
importance_reason: Would organize the parameterized complexity dichotomy for forbidden induced subgraphs by showing that disconnected obstructions introduce no new tractability barrier beyond their components. Existing score retained.
formal: For every pair of fixed nonempty finite simple graphs \(H_{1},H_{2}\), is the following implication true? If Independent Set parameterized by the requested set size k is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{1}\)-free graphs and is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{2}\)-free graphs, then it is fixed-parameter tractable on \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free graphs. Here exclusion is as an induced subgraph, ⊔ is disjoint union of the forbidden patterns, and fixed-parameter tractability has the deterministic meaning defined below. The two forbidden graphs may themselves be disconnected and may be isomorphic.
definitions: For a fixed graph H, an input to Independent Set on H-free graphs is a finite simple undirected graph G on n labeled vertices, encoded by its adjacency matrix, and a binary integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), under the promise that no subset of \(V(G)\) induces a graph isomorphic to H. The answer is YES exactly when there is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|\ge k\) and no edge between distinct members of S. Only k is the parameter; H is fixed in the definition of the restricted problem and is not supplied as a variable-size input. Call H tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{H}, a\) total computable function \(f_{H}:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) and a constant \(c_{H}\ge 0\) such that \(A_{H}\) correctly decides every promised input in at most \(f_{H}(k)(n+1)^{c_{H}}\) bit operations. The algorithm is uniform over n,k and its guarantees are worst-case and exact. Behavior outside the H-free promise is unrestricted. Constants, algorithms and computable functions may depend on H, while \(c_{H}\) cannot depend on k or n. For \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) take disjoint copies of their vertex sets, preserve the edges within each copy, and put no edges between copies. Thus a graph contains an induced \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) precisely when it has disjoint induced copies of \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\) with no cross-edge between them. Excluding this one disconnected pattern is weaker than simultaneously excluding both \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\). The conjecture says that the set of tractable forbidden patterns is closed under ⊔. Its quantifier is over existence of algorithms for each fixed pair; it does not additionally demand one effective transformation that constructs an algorithm from descriptions of \(H_{1},H_{2}\) or from the two assumed algorithms. Input graphs G are not promised to be disconnected. Weighted Independent Set and randomized fixed-parameter algorithms define different variants; this card uses the source’s unqualified deterministic FPT convention.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \(H_{1},H_{2}\) satisfying the two tractability premises there exist an algorithm A, a computable f and a constant c, all allowed to depend on that pair, deciding the \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free problem in \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) time; or refute this universal implication. A refutation must establish both premises and failure of the conclusion for its pair. A \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof for the conclusion is only a conditional refutation unless the relevant FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) separation is assumed explicitly. A result for the intersection of the two graph classes or for disjoint input components does not settle this statement.
context:
Every \(H_{1}\)-free or \(H_{2}\)-free input is automatically \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free, but the latter class can also contain both patterns. The conjecture asks whether this enlargement preserves parameterized tractability. It is not the elementary decomposition of Independent Set across disconnected input components.

When the forbidden graph is a disjoint union of cliques, the paper gives an FPT algorithm. The concluding conjecture asks whether the same closure principle holds for all tractable forbidden patterns, not only clique components.

The author-hosted Algorithmica manuscript repeats the disjoint-union implication in its conclusion. It also distinguishes this question from another proposed closure operation, adding false twins, which the paper shows does not preserve the hoped-for tractability classification under the usual complexity separation.

The ISAAC 2019 follow-up provides additional tractable forbidden patterns and randomized FPT algorithms for dart- and cricket-free graphs. These results concern individual patterns and do not prove the general disjoint-union implication. In particular, a randomized result is not silently substituted for the deterministic premises here.
why: A closure theorem would reduce the classification of parameterized Independent Set with one forbidden induced pattern to its connected components. It would organize many currently separate tractability results through one general structural principle.
status_note: Read the original conjecture, induced-exclusion definition and parameter convention, the expanded journal manuscript’s conclusion, and the later ISAAC paper’s individual-pattern results and randomness qualification. Searched subsequent work without finding a resolution of the full closure implication. This is a source-grounded open status, not an exhaustive absence proof. No independent proof verification.
progress: 2018: Work presented at IPEC 2018 proves the disjoint-clique special case and states the general disjoint-union conjecture; proceedings appeared 5 February 2019. | 2019-11-28: ISAAC follow-up obtains more individual-pattern algorithms, including randomized dart- and cricket-free cases. | 2020-06-17: Journal version published; the expanded author manuscript retains the general closure conjecture.
working_summary: Independent Set asks whether a graph contains k pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Suppose the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when either one of two fixed induced patterns is forbidden. The conjecture asks whether tractability persists when only their disjoint union is forbidden. This is already known when the forbidden components are cliques, and the 2020 journal manuscript retains the general conjecture. The problem concerns the forbidden pattern, not whether the input graph itself is disconnected.

title: Expected FPT delay from small-witness decision
importance_reason: A general relationship between parameterized decision and enumeration complexity, with a substantive gap between total work and responsiveness. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every self-contained \(k\)-witness problem whose decision version is fixed-parameter tractable admit an always-correct randomized enumeration algorithm with expected delay \(f(k)L^{O(1)}\), where \(L\) is the encoded input length and \(f\) is a computable function? The algorithm must output every distinct witness exactly once and terminate, with the same expected bound before the first output and after the last. This selects the expected-delay branch of the source question; deterministic delay and the weaker incremental bounds are distinct companion questions.
definitions:
A problem instance I has an explicitly represented finite universe U and a parameter k≥1. Its witnesses form a family W(I,k) of k-element subsets of U, not a family of ordered tuples or of certificates attached to the same subset. For example, when a witness is a k-vertex set supporting a path, several paths on that same vertex set do not create several witnesses. Each output is one subset, represented by its sorted list of element indices. The output order among subsets is unrestricted. Let N=|W(I,k)|; the algorithm is not given N. Instances with k>|U| have no witnesses.

“Self-contained” means that restricting the instance to X⊆U preserves exactly the witnesses contained in X: W(I|X,k)={W∈W(I,k):W⊆X}. The restriction examines only the retained elements and their relationships, is computable in polynomial time, and has encoded length polynomial in the original length L. A decision procedure on I|X therefore answers whether X contains a witness of the original instance. This is the inclusion query INC(I,X,k). Witnesses whose validity depends on their relationships to deleted elements, such as a vertex cover of the original graph, do not automatically satisfy this property.

The premise is a deterministic algorithm deciding whether W(I,k) is nonempty in time g(k)L^a, for some computable g and constant a independent of k and I. It thus also implements inclusion queries with an FPT bound. The desired enumerator may depend on the fixed witness problem, as may f and its constant polynomial exponent, but all of them must be uniform over its instances and parameter values. This is an implication between algorithmic existence statements; it does not additionally require an effective compiler from arbitrary decision-program code, or restrict the enumerator to a black-box oracle.

For a fixed input, let τ_i be the time when the ith distinct witness has finished being written, τ₀=0, and τ_{N+1} the termination time. Expected FPT delay requires E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤f(k)(L+1)^b for every i=0,…,N, with a constant b independent of k,I,i,N. When N=0 it bounds the whole time to termination. Expectation is over the internal randomness on this fixed input, without conditioning on a particular random execution history. The algorithm never outputs a false or duplicate witness and finishes the complete list with probability one. Its bound charges all work, including any preprocessing, inclusion-query execution, duplicate handling and writing outputs. The question imposes no additional polynomial-space requirement.

An expected-incremental-FPT bound instead allows E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤h(k)(L+i+1)^c, which grows with the number already output. An expected-output-FPT bound controls only the final expected time by h(k)(L+N+1)^c. Such a total bound may conceal a long wait before the next output. Dropping “expected” requires the corresponding deterministic bound. These notions are not identified with each other here. An extension query additionally asks whether some witness W satisfies Y⊆W⊆X for a prescribed Y; the premise provides no such forced-inclusion operation.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated implication for all self-contained k-witness problems, or exhibit a problem satisfying its decision premise and prove that no enumerator with the stated expected-delay guarantee exists, with any complexity assumption made explicit. A bound only on final expected running time, a delay allowed to grow polynomially with the number already output, a randomized list that can omit witnesses, or a result assuming an efficient extension oracle does not settle this selected branch. The source’s deterministic and incremental companion questions require separate conclusions.
context:
A decision algorithm applied to restricted universes provides an inclusion test. The question asks what control that information gives over the pauses while listing all distinct witness subsets.

The journal Theorem 1.1 gives an always-correct randomized enumerator with expected work e^{k+o(k)}g(k)|U|^{O(1)}N when N is positive and inclusion queries take g(k)|U|^{O(1)} time. One initial inclusion test handles N=0. This is an expected-output guarantee, and the conclusion still asks about delay and incremental guarantees.

The source supplies examples where efficient inclusion queries do not yield FPT extension queries unless FPT=W[1]. That obstruction to one standard route does not itself prove a lower bound against every possible enumerator.

The later version formulates its broader question in terms of an FPT inclusion algorithm. For the self-contained problems retained on this card, ordinary decision supplies that operation by restriction. The paper’s approximate-enumeration results with fallible oracles have a different correctness guarantee.
why: Tests how far an efficient existence test can be converted into a reliably responsive generator of all small solutions. The distinction between total work and delays matters when a solution set is large and users need successive answers before enumeration finishes.
status_note: Read the IPEC definitions and complete conclusion, the January 2018 author-final v4, and the publisher’s corresponding definitions and conclusion. Targeted later-work searches through 12 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the expected-delay implication. This card explicitly selects that branch from the source’s several alternatives; it does not claim that solving it negatively settles the weaker incremental branch.

An FPT decision algorithm can therefore test whether a chosen subset contains a witness. title: Polynomial kernels for forbidden-minor vertex deletion
importance_reason: A major generic preprocessing question for graph-minor deletion, with vertex planarization among its unresolved instances. Existing score retained.
formal: Does vertex deletion to exclude any fixed finite family of graph minors admit a polynomial kernel, parameterized by the number of vertices allowed to be deleted? Precisely, for every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\), is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation of \((G,k)\) into an equivalent instance \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same \(\mathcal F\)-deletion problem whose total encoding length and parameter are bounded by \((k+1)^{O_{\mathcal F}(1)}\)?
definitions:
The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before inputs are supplied; it is not part of the parameterized input. Its members are finite nonempty undirected graphs and may be disconnected. The original source allows parallel edges, as in its two-vertex examples. Use finite undirected loopless multigraphs with all edge copies explicitly listed for the general convention here; simple graphs are included.

A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained from a subgraph by contracting edges. Contraction identifies their endpoints, removes resulting loops and retains parallel edges. It is not induced-subgraph containment or topological-minor containment.

The input consists of \(G\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It is a yes-instance if there is \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) contains no member of \(\mathcal F\) as a minor. All vertices have unit deletion cost. There is no planarity, degree, connectivity or sparsity promise on \(G\). The empty forbidden family is trivial and may be omitted. Since every forbidden graph is nonempty, \(k\geq |V(G)|\) is immediately a yes-instance.

A polynomial kernel is a deterministic algorithm that runs in a polynomial in the total binary input length and outputs a single pair \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) for the same fixed family. It must preserve the yes/no answer exactly on every input. There must be constants \(C_{\mathcal F},c_{\mathcal F}\) such that the total bit length of the output and the numerical value \(k'\) are at most \(C_{\mathcal F}(k+1)^{c_{\mathcal F}}\). Vertex labels can be renumbered. Counting only vertices while leaving arbitrarily many explicit parallel edges or a large encoded parameter would not suffice.

The algorithm, its polynomial running-time degree and the output exponent may depend on \(\mathcal F\). The question does not require one exponent that works for all families, nor an effective procedure constructing the kernel algorithm from an arbitrary family description. Such uniformity requirements would strengthen the target.

The parameter is the solution budget \(k\). It is not the size of a supplied vertex cover, a set whose removal leaves bounded treedepth, or another structural parameter. A kernel supplies one smaller equivalent instance, unlike an algorithm querying many small instances. Approximate kernels that lose a constant factor in deletion cost do not satisfy the exact equivalence requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family in this solution-budget model, allowing family-dependent exponents, or establish that some fixed family does not admit one. A conventional lower bound of the form “a polynomial kernel would imply NP is contained in coNP/poly” must retain that complexity assumption and is a conditional obstruction, not an unconditional separation. Special-family algorithms and approximate or structural-parameter kernels alone do not establish the universal claim.
context:
The source observes that every fixed-family problem is fixed-parameter tractable. This guarantees preprocessing to a size depending only on the solution budget, but does not guarantee polynomial dependence.

The FOCS 2012 work obtains polynomial kernels when the forbidden family contains a planar graph. The 2026 introduction explains how a later deterministic approximation removes the randomized ingredient from that kernel construction.

For \(\mathcal F=\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}\), the output after deletion must be planar. Both obstructions are nonplanar, so the preceding theorem does not apply. The later constant-factor approximate kernel does not preserve the exact decision threshold.

Theorem 1 transfers an existing solution-size kernel to a different parameterization for connected forbidden families. It does not supply the missing kernel for every family, and its introduction explicitly retains the general and planarization questions.
why: Would give a general guarantee that graphs close to a minor-closed class can be reduced efficiently to a polynomial amount of relevant information. It unifies preprocessing questions for vertex cover, feedback vertex set, bounded-width deletion and planarization.

title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
importance_reason: A central long-standing kernelization problem separating fixed-parameter solvability from polynomial-size preprocessing for directed cycle deletion. Existing score retained.
formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.
question_excerpt: Directed Feedback Vertex Set has a kernel of exponential size \(k O(k)\) , as the problem was shown fixed-parameter tractable by Chen et al. \([4], [\ldots ]\)
definitions:
A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has a finite explicitly listed vertex set and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc have no effect and need not be represented. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{0},\ldots,v_{r-1}\), with \(r\ge1\), having arcs from each vertex to the next, including from \(v_{r-1}\) to \(v_{0}\). Thus a self-loop is a cycle and two opposite arcs form a cycle.

A directed feedback vertex set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that the induced digraph \(D[V\setminus S]\) has no directed cycle. The decision instance is YES exactly when some such set has \(|S|\le k\). The remaining graph may be any directed acyclic graph, including a disconnected one.

Encode vertices by integers \(1,\ldots,n\), list all vertices and arcs, and encode \(k\) in binary using a fixed ordinary self-delimiting binary encoding. Measure preprocessing time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine in the total input length \(L\). The output uses the same encoding, with newly numbered vertices and a nonnegative binary integer \(k^{\prime}\). Bounding only the number of output vertices while permitting arbitrarily much auxiliary information would not meet the stated size requirement.

A kernel preserves the YES/NO answer, not necessarily the optimum value, the original vertex labels, or every solution. The output budget may differ from the input budget. The requirement is a single small instance of this same unweighted decision problem; a list of oracle queries or a compression into a different language is a different notion.

The preprocessing time must be polynomial in \(L\), uniformly for all \(k\). A procedure taking \(f(k)L^{d}\) time for an unrestricted computable function \(f\) is not by itself a polynomial-time kernelization. The case \(k=0\) is covered by the bound \(C(k+1)^{c}\). Allowing loops makes the model explicit and does not change the question: each loop forces its vertex into any deletion set, while repeated arcs can be removed.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of an algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial preprocessing, exact answer equivalence, and polynomial output bit bound depending only on the original deletion budget, or refute that existence. A conditional lower bound must state its complexity assumption explicitly; it is not an unconditional refutation. A kernel using a larger structural parameter does not settle this target.
context:
The 2016 source recalls a \(k^{O(k)}\)-size kernel following from fixed-parameter tractability, while explicitly leaving a polynomial-size kernel open. The missing improvement concerns how small a polynomial-time preprocessing can make every instance, rather than whether exponential dependence on the solution budget is possible.

The source proves polynomial kernels when deletion must leave an out-tree, an out-forest, or a directed pumpkin. These are stronger conditions than merely destroying directed cycles, so the results do not constitute a kernel for general Directed Feedback Vertex Set.

The WADS 2019 result, subsequently published in the 2025 journal article, gives a polynomial kernel with parameter \(k+\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the size of a supplied vertex set whose removal leaves an underlying undirected graph of fixed bounded treewidth. Here treewidth at most \(\eta\) means that there are vertex bags indexed by a tree, each of size at most \(\eta+1\), covering all vertices and both endpoints of every edge, with the bags containing each vertex forming a connected subtree. The constant \(\eta\) is fixed. The extra \(\ell\) need not be bounded by a polynomial in \(k\); the general question therefore remains distinct.

The same work distinguishes the combined parameter \(k+\ell\) from parameterization by \(\ell\) alone. Its conditional obstruction for the latter does not rule out a polynomial kernel in the solution budget \(k\).
why: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central test of how much efficient preprocessing can compress a fixed-parameter tractable cycle-hitting problem. A polynomial kernel would reduce every large instance with a small deletion budget to a polynomial amount of relevant information. A rigorous obstruction would distinguish directed cycle constraints from many successful kernelization settings.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.
focus_reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.
formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every integer \(1\le k\le |V|, A(G,k)\) outputs a set \(S\subseteq V\) with |\(S|=k\) and |\(E(G[S])|\ge \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)/C\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max _{T\subseteq V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|\)?
definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. \(G[S]\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with \(n=|V|\) or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree \(2|E(G[S])|/k\), or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The task asks for a fixed-size collection of vertices containing as many internal interactions as possible. The cardinality restriction is what turns an otherwise tractable density objective into a central approximation problem. Without a prescribed size, maximizing edges per vertex can be solved in polynomial time. Allowing at least k vertices also changes which solutions compete: a large moderately dense region may be a valid answer even when no comparably useful k-vertex portion can be extracted.

Exact optimization contains CLIQUE: a graph has a k-clique precisely when \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=k(k- 1)/2\). This observation alone gives almost no multiplicative approximation gap. A k-set missing only one possible edge is nearly optimal as k grows, even though it is not a clique. To rule out a constant-factor algorithm, a reduction must create a substantial separation between the best densities of its YES and NO instances, not merely a one-edge difference.

Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige and Vijayaraghavan achieve \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O}(1/\varepsilon )\) time for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Their method uses small tree patterns and a hierarchy of conditioned information to identify a dense region. The \(O(n^{1/4})\) phrase in the paper’s title needs care: attaining that endpoint in their analysis takes quasipolynomial \(n^{O}(\log  n)\) time. Neither rate is a constant approximation.

There is substantial evidence against the target. Manurangsi proves that ETH rules out even approximation within \(n^{1/(\log  \log  n)^{a}}\), for a universal constant \(a>0\). ETH asserts that 3SAT has no \(2^{o}(N)\)-time algorithm on N variables. This is a stronger assumption than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); the result therefore already excludes every fixed constant under ETH, while leaving the weaker-assumption hardness problem unresolved. Its YES instances can contain a k-clique, a property called perfect completeness.

Semidefinite-programming lower bounds supply a different kind of evidence. Bhaskara, Charikar, Guruswami, Vijayaraghavan and Zhou construct polynomial integrality gaps for strong hierarchies of relaxations. A relaxation can assign a large fractional or vector-valued objective even when no genuine k-set has comparable density. Such a gap limits approximation guarantees obtained from that relaxation, but it is not a theorem excluding every polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within \(2^{(\log  n)^{\varepsilon}}\) for some \(\varepsilon >0\). Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a \((3/2- \varepsilon )\) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.
why: Densest k-Subgraph is a basic test of how well algorithms can identify a concentrated combinatorial structure. Its unresolved approximation landscape influences many reductions and separates strong evidence of difficulty from the hardness consequences currently obtainable from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

The target is a polynomial-time algorithm whose edge count stays within one universal constant of optimum. Fixing the number of vertices prevents using a larger, moderately dense region as a substitute. Such a guarantee would clarify a central gap in approximation theory and influence several related network problems. The saved review describes strong conditional hardness under ETH, while distinguishing this evidence from hardness based only on \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

title: Unique Games Conjecture
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.
focus_reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.
formal: For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon ,\delta >0\) with \(\varepsilon +\delta <1\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge 2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). An edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries an explicitly given permutation \(\pi _{e}:[q]\to [q]\) and is satisfied exactly when \(\pi _{e}(\ell (u))=\ell (v)\). Thus \(\operatorname{val}(G)=\max _{\ell} |\){e satisfied by \(\ell\)}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the \(\ge 1- \varepsilon\) case and every unsatisfiable formula into the \(\le \delta\) case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on \(\varepsilon ,\delta\). Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a \(1/q\) fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below \(1/q\) is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.
why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.
status_note: The 2025 journal account distinguishes the proved 2-to-2 theorem from full UGC. No resolution of the quantified near-one-completeness statement was located in the primary-source search through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2002: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters. | 2008: Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). | 2010: Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute \(\alpha >0\), an \(\exp (q n^{\varepsilon ^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm finding a \((1- \varepsilon ^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling in a \((1- \varepsilon )\)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-\(\varepsilon\) regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial. | 2018–2020: The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness \(1/2\) and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved. | 2025-11: The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.
