title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.
formal: Do there exist constants \(a\ge 1\) and \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most \(a(\log _{2}(k+2))^{C}\) times optimum with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E), a\) root \(r\in V, a\) nonempty terminal set \(T\subseteq V\setminus \{r\}\) with \(k=|T|\), and nonnegative rational arc costs \(c_{e}\) given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset \(F\subseteq E\) such that \((V,F)\) contains a directed path from r to every \(t\in T\). Its cost is \(\sum_{e\in F}c_{e}\), counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least \(2/3\) over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of \(n=|V|, k\) and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\)-approximation for every separately fixed \(\varepsilon >0, a\) polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
context:
The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting \(\varepsilon\) to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an \(O(\log ^{2} k/\log  \log  k)\)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an \(O(\log  k)\) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.
why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.
status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly leaves this general-graph question open. The inherited 2024 claim was withdrawn, and its October 2025 replacement is restricted to a special supplied fractional solution; that claim is not counted as an established general result. Planar and quasipolynomial algorithms do not satisfy this card. Checked through 11 September 2026.

The question asks for randomized polynomial-time approximation within a fixed power of the logarithm of the terminal count. Sharing arcs between routes can save substantially, but directionality complicates selecting useful branching structures. A positive result would close a major gap between polynomial-time algorithms and stronger guarantees obtainable in quasipolynomial time. title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.
formal: For every rational constant \(\eta \in (0,1/2)\), is there a rational constant \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with \(\delta n\) an integer, distinguish YES: some \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\le \eta\), from NO: every \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\ge 1- \eta\).
definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin \mathrm{L}\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.
context:
Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.
why: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.
status_note: No proof or refutation located through 11 September 2026. The original exact-size regular-graph promise was checked separately from later weighted, volume and randomized variants. The August 2026 least-squares result is conditional on such a variant.
progress: 2010: Raghavendra–Steurer introduce the exact-size expansion promise and relate its hardness to Unique Games. | 2010 / 2012: Raghavendra–Steurer–Tulsiani establish reductions and conditional hardness for Balanced Separator and Minimum Linear Arrangement. | 2026-08: A sparse least-squares lower bound is obtained assuming a randomized weighted exact-volume SSE variant.
working_summary: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size? The target set occupies a fixed fraction \(\delta\) of the graph, with \(\delta\) chosen after the gap parameter \(\eta\). Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set. A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size. Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

title: Subtour-LP integrality gap for metric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.
formal: Determine \(\Gamma =\sup _{n\ge 3,c} \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(c)/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\), where c ranges over every metric on n labeled points and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is the symmetric subtour relaxation defined below.
definitions: For \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(E=\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\}, a\) metric has \(c_{uu}=0, c_{uv}=c_{vu}>0\) for \(u\ne v\), and \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\). Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta (S)\) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(x(F)=\sum_{e\in F}x_{e}\). Define \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min  \sum_{e} c_{e} x_{e}\) subject to \(x(\delta (\{v\}))=2\) for every \(v, x(\delta (S))\ge 2\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\), and \(0\le x_{e}\le 1\) for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma |\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
context:
The target is the value of the universal integrality gap. The classical \(4/3\) conjecture proposes \(\Gamma =4/3; a\) larger determined value is also an answer to this quantitative question.

The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor \(4/3\) says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical \(3/2\) guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost\(\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) does not establish \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\), since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below \(3/2\), extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound \(\Gamma \le 3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}\). The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to \(3/2\).

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the \(4/3\) bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are \(1/2\) or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a \(10/7\) guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since \(10/7\) exceeds \(4/3\), it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of \(11/8\) on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the \(4/3\) bound when an optimal solution has at most \(n+6\) nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most \(n+6\) vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through \(n=16\) and for half-integral extreme points through \(n=18\). It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, \(\varepsilon\)★>\(2.05522\cdot 10^{- 30}\), through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\). The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the conjectured ratio \(4/3\).
why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.
status_note: The general \(4/3\) equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is \(3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}; a\) September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

working_summary: The metric traveling-salesperson problem asks for a cheapest tour through every point. Its subtour linear program permits fractional edges while preserving degree and cut constraints. This card asks for the supremum ratio of the integral tour optimum to that relaxation over all finite metrics. The classical \(4/3\) conjecture identifies a proposed value of this ratio. Benchmark acceptance requires a Lean-certified numerical value within absolute error 0.01, without assuming the supremum is attained.

title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric k-Median
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.
formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm always opens at most k facilities and has cost at most \(r\cdot\)OPT with probability at least \(2/3\) on every metric k-Median instance}, in the model below.
definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets \(C,F\subseteq V\) of clients and allowable facilities with \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le |F|\). The table is promised to satisfy \(d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0\) exactly when \(u=v\), and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) define \(\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min _{s\in S}d(c,s)\), and OPT=\(\min \{\operatorname{cost}(S):S\subseteq F,1\le |S|\le k\}\). L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed guarantee r in the infimum, require one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{r}\), with constants \(K_{r},d_{r}\) such that every execution takes at most \(K_{r} \mathrm{L}^{d_{r}}\) bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) with |\(S|\le k\), and on each input \(\Pr [\operatorname{cost}(S)\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}]\ge 2/3\). Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The algorithm and constants may depend on r but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0. The infimum need not be attained by one algorithm. An exact value \(\rho\) means that feasible guarantees approach \(\rho\) from above and no algorithm in the stated class guarantees a factor smaller than \(\rho\).
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{med}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any additional complexity assumption must be explicit; a conditional hardness theorem proves only the corresponding conditional value or bound.
context:
The target is the optimal approximation ratio itself, with the exact facility budget and randomized polynomial-time model fixed. The previously selected \(1+2/e\) threshold is a candidate value motivated by the hardness evidence described below.

Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold \(1+2/e\); the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is \(2+\varepsilon\). The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost \((3- 2p)\) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most \(1- 1/e+\eta\), for any fixed \(\eta >0\). Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least \(1+2/e- 2\eta\) per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{RP}\) for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above \(1+2/e\).

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a \(2+\varepsilon\) cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline \(2+\varepsilon\) theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings \(y_{s}\), assignments \(x_{c,s}\le y_{s}\), unit total assignment for each client, and \(\sum_{s} y_{s}\le k\). For a star with \(q\ge 3\) leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and \(k=q- 1\), every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to \(1/(q- 1)\), each leaf opening to \((q- 2)/(q- 1)\), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs \(q/(q- 1)\), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Determining the optimal ratio would locate the computational price of general metric clustering. A value at the coverage threshold would match the known obstruction, whereas a larger value would require a different limiting obstruction. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.
why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains \(2+\varepsilon\) with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is \(1+2/e\). The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
progress: 1998: Feige proves the \(1- 1/e\) hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the \(1+2/e\) metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction. | 2002: Jain–Mahdian–Saberi give the classical k-Median lower bound via Set Cover approximation; Theorem 10 states the historical reduction. | 2019: Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li reach \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in fixed-parameter time with respect to k, not unrestricted polynomial time. | 2025–19 May 2026: Cohen-Addad–Grandoni–Lee–Schwiegelshohn–Svensson obtain a randomized polynomial-time \(2+\varepsilon\) approximation with at most k facilities; the May 2026 full-version revision retains the theorem. | 10 March 2026: Improved approximation-scheme runtimes apply to low-dimensional Euclidean clustering, a restricted metric setting. | 16 July 2026: Spectral dual fitting improves k-Means approximation; squared-distance clustering is a different objective.
working_summary: Metric k-Median selects at most k allowed facilities to minimize total client distance. The card asks for the infimum universal approximation ratio of randomized polynomial-time algorithms. The same algorithm must work for all input sizes at each fixed guarantee, with success probability at least two thirds. The familiar \(1+2/e\) target and the saved algorithmic bounds locate competing possibilities for this infimum. Lean acceptance requires absolute error at most 0.01, with any complexity assumptions stated explicitly.

title: Vertex Cover approximation below factor two
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Resolve a basic approximation threshold for a widely used covering primitive.
formal: Do a constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G, output a vertex cover of size at most \((2- \varepsilon )\tau (G)\)?
definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A vertex cover is a subset S of the vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge; \(\tau (G)\) is the minimum size of such a set. The graph is represented by its adjacency matrix. The same \(\varepsilon\) and algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no promise on degree, coloring or graph class. An edgeless input requires the empty cover. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm or unconditional refutation of its existence.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Vertex Cover is one of the canonical NP-hard covering problems and has a simple factor-two approximation. The absence of a fixed improvement despite extensive work makes the factor a central approximation barrier.

Unique Games implies hardness below two, while unconditional NP-hardness leaves a gap. A restricted graph-class algorithm does not answer the universal target. The source seminar situates the question in the development of approximation algorithms and primal-dual methods.
why: Resolve a basic approximation threshold for a widely used covering primitive.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.

context:
This card determines the universal subtour-LP integrality gap. The factor-two conjecture is a proposed exact answer; refuting that factor alone would not determine a larger gap.

A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. The NP-hardness claim means that for each fixed k there is a deterministic algorithm \(R_{k}\) and constants \(c_{k},C_{k}\) such that, on a 3-CNF formula F of bit length \(N, R_{k}\) outputs a digraph in time at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c}_{k}\), with satisfiable F mapped to the accepting side and unsatisfiable F mapped to the rejecting side. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated NP-hardness for every fixed \(k\ge 4\), or refute that universal hardness assertion. A polynomial-time k-coloring algorithm for some fixed k would contradict the claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Hardness for \(k=3\), bounds for a growing number of colors, or hardness without the two-colorability completeness promise do not suffice.
context:
In a directed path \(u\to v\to w\), all three vertices may receive the same color because there is no directed cycle. In a directed triangle \(u\to v\to w\to u\) they may not all receive the same color. This differs from ordinary graph coloring, which forbids any monochromatic edge.

The promise guarantees that two acyclic color classes exist. The algorithm is allowed more colors to make the search easier. If the two-coloring itself were supplied, the task would already be solved; it is deliberately absent from the input.

The paper asks about every constant k greater than three and then suggests that the problem may be NP-hard for every such k, as in a related hypergraph setting. This card adopts that explicit conjectural gap-hardness formulation, making the intended yes/no proposition reviewable.

The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm using at most \(2\sqrt{n}\) colors for a 2-dicolorable n-vertex digraph. It also records three-color hardness, even on tournaments. Neither result answers whether any larger fixed palette changes the complexity on general digraphs.

title: Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis from \(\mathrm{FPT} \ne  \mathrm{W}[1]\)
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A general bridge from exact parameterized hardness to constant-gap approximation hardness. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\), is there an absolute constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) such that no deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm can distinguish a satisfiable binary constraint satisfaction instance on k variables from an instance in which every assignment violates at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the constraints, with k as the parameter?
definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )=1\) or \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\le 1- \varepsilon\); no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.
context:
Exact unsatisfiability only says every assignment fails somewhere. PIH asks for a constant fraction of failures on every assignment. If an instance has many constraints, the existence of just one unavoidable violation need not give any fixed gap.

The alphabet is allowed to grow with the input. Exhaustive search takes \(n^{k}\) time, whose exponent depends on k; that is not fixed-parameter tractable. A running time such as \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) would qualify despite its very large dependence on k.

Baby PIH distinguishes satisfiable instances from instances for which even a constant-size list of values at each variable cannot satisfy every constraint. This is a different guarantee from saying that every ordinary assignment violates a constant fraction of constraints.

The Guruswami–Lin–Ren–Sun–Wu theorem derives PIH from the Exponential Time Hypothesis. ETH imposes a quantitative subexponential-time obstruction for 3SAT and is a stronger assumption than the parameterized separation sought here. The February 2026 survey still separates these targets.
why: Would supply a parameterized analogue of the PCP theorem from the standard exact-hardness assumption, giving a common basis for constant-gap inapproximability across many parameterized optimization problems.
status_note: Source definitions, the ETH theorem and the February 2026 survey checked with later-result searches through 12 September 2026. No proof under only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) was located.
progress: 2024: Baby PIH is established under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\); the full PIH implication is left open. | 2025: The journal version of PIH under ETH records the stronger-assumption theorem, whose preprint already appeared in 2023. | 2026-02: The survey explicitly retains the distinction between PIH under ETH and PIH under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
working_summary: The hypothesis \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) says exact parameterized problems such as k-Clique do not admit fixed-parameter algorithms. The question asks whether it also rules out distinguishing satisfiable binary constraint systems from systems that force a constant fraction of violations. The parameter is the number of variables, while the alphabet may grow with the input. PIH is already known under the stronger ETH assumption, and Baby PIH is known under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\). A proof of the full implication would provide a broad foundation for parameterized inapproximability.

title: Almost 3-colorable graphs versus graphs with no large independent set
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A graph-coloring hardness strengthening with a concrete consequence for the Vertex Cover approximation threshold. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every fixed pair of constants \(0<\eta <1\) and \(0<\varepsilon <(1- \eta )/3\), is it NP-hard to distinguish graphs G on N vertices in which an induced subgraph on at least \((1- \eta )N\) vertices is properly 3-colorable from graphs G with independence number \(\alpha (G)<\varepsilon N\)? This is the nonoverlapping promise range of the source’s Conjecture 23, whose intended demand is hardness for arbitrarily small positive \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\).
definitions: G is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph, represented by its adjacency matrix or edge list. An independent set is a set of vertices containing no edge; \(\alpha (G)\) is its maximum size. The subgraph induced by \(U\subseteq V(G)\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in U. It is properly 3-colorable if a map \(U\to \{1,2,3\}\) gives adjacent vertices different labels. Define iCol\(_{3}(G)=N^{- 1}\max\){|\(U|:G[U]\) is 3-colorable}. The yes case is iCol\(_{3}(G)\ge 1- \eta\), and the no case is \(\alpha (G)/N<\varepsilon\). Fractions refer to vertices, not edges or color classes of a fixed coloring. The parameters \(\varepsilon ,\eta\) are fixed before the reduction and are not part of the graph input. In the usual deterministic NP-hardness formulation, for each pair there must be a deterministic polynomial-time map from Boolean satisfiability instances to graphs that sends satisfiable inputs into the yes case and unsatisfiable inputs into the no case. The polynomial may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\). An algorithm for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on graphs in neither case. Since a 3-colorable set has an independent subset of at least one third its size, the displayed parameter restriction ensures disjoint cases. The paper’s already proved weaker theorem allows randomized reductions; that distinction must be retained when assessing a claimed resolution.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated gap NP-hardness for every fixed admissible \(\varepsilon ,\eta\), with a reduction and its completeness and soundness guarantees, or refute the universal hardness assertion. If a claimed hardness result uses randomized reductions, state that convention explicitly and distinguish it from deterministic NP-hardness. A polynomial-time algorithm would contradict the deterministic hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); without a complexity separation, it alone is not a logical refutation of NP-hardness.
context:
Deleting at most an \(\eta\) fraction of vertices must leave a properly 3-colorable graph. The input need not be exactly 3-colorable.

Every independent set must occupy less than an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the entire graph. Merely proving that no almost-spanning subgraph can be colored with a fixed number of colors does not give this guarantee.

For every fixed k, the paper obtains a positive \(\delta\) such that it is hard, under randomized reductions, to distinguish almost 3-colorability from failure to k-color all but a \(\delta\) fraction of vertices. Conjecture 23 asks for the substantially stronger independent-set soundness condition.

The complement of an independent set is a vertex cover. The requested gap would imply hardness of approximating minimum Vertex Cover within \(3/2- \zeta\) for every fixed \(\zeta >0\), as the source explains. This consequence is motivation, not an additional target.
why: Would strengthen almost-coloring hardness enough to improve a central Vertex Cover approximation barrier, linking graph coloring promises with independent-set soundness.
status_note: The full conjecture, its definition of induced coloring and the weaker proved theorem were checked. Subsequent-result searches through 12 September 2026, including the publisher abstract of the related MFCS 2025 matrix-completion paper, did not locate this stronger independent-set gap. That later abstract is not evidence of a resolution.
progress: 2023: Theorem 1 establishes the almost-coloring gap under randomized reductions; Conjecture 23 asks for no independent set of any prescribed small positive fractional size.
working_summary: The yes instances become 3-colorable after deleting an arbitrarily small fixed fraction of vertices. The no instances have no independent set occupying a prescribed small fixed fraction of all vertices. The conjecture asks for NP-hardness of distinguishing these two cases. The source proves a weaker almost-coloring gap with randomized reductions. The stronger independent-set gap would improve hardness of approximating Vertex Cover toward a factor of three halves.

title: Subquadratic factor-three edit-distance approximation
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A consequential accuracy-versus-runtime boundary for a fundamental sequence problem, contrasting strong approximation with fixed polynomial improvements over quadratic computation. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a classical randomized algorithm and constants \(\eta>0\) and \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of explicitly given strings \(X,Y\) of total length \(n\), the algorithm runs in at most \(C(n+2)^{2-\eta}\) time and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs an estimate \(\widehat d\) satisfying \[\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\leq\widehat d\leq3\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)?\]
question_excerpt: Recent developments in designing fast approximation algorithms \([2, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 25]\) culminated in an \(O(1)\)-approximation in near-linear time [3], but the existence […]
definitions:
The unit-cost Levenshtein edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(X\) into \(Y\). Each operation costs one, including substitution. There are no transpositions, moves of blocks, or cheaper substitution costs. The two strings can have different lengths or be empty.

The input consists of both strings in full, with their lengths. Let \(n=|X|+|Y|\). Characters can be encoded by integer labels in \(\{1,\ldots,\max\{1,n\}\}\); only equality of labels matters. This allows arbitrary alphabets occurring in the input, rather than a binary-alphabet promise. Renaming polynomially bounded integer symbols takes only a near-linear preprocessing cost, which is included.

Use the usual sequential random-access model with \(O(\log(n+2))\)-bit words: a word read or write, comparison, Boolean operation, shift, or arithmetic operation on a constant number of words costs one step. Memory is initially empty except for the input; reading the input, all preprocessing and writing the output are charged. The algorithm has independent fair random bits, but no advice or uncharged preprocessed strings, distance oracle, parallel processors or quantum operations.

One uniform algorithm and fixed constants must work at every input length, for every input pair and every distance regime. Its running-time bound holds for every random tape. The probability of meeting the approximation guarantee is over its internal randomness alone; the inputs need not be random or generated by a mutation model.

The estimate may be an integer: rounding a valid nonnegative rational estimate down preserves the inequalities because the true distance is an integer. No edit script or alignment has to be returned. When the strings are identical, a successful estimate must be exactly zero.

Truly subquadratic means a fixed positive exponent saving \(\eta\), independent of \(n\). A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log n\), or a stated improvement of the form \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{c}}\) with fixed \(0<c<1\), does not supply such a saving. A polylogarithmic overhead on an already fixed-power saving can be absorbed by decreasing \(\eta\).

The approximation factor is at most three, uniformly over the input size. A guarantee of \(3+\varepsilon\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), or \(3+o(1)\), does not itself establish this endpoint. The main question is existence of some positive runtime saving, not its optimal value.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm meeting the factor-three guarantee and some fixed positive exponent saving for all inputs in the stated model, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. State any hypothesis of a conditional negative result explicitly. An arbitrary constant approximation, a factor exceeding three, an average-case result, or a subpolynomial rather than fixed-power runtime saving is insufficient.
context:
Andoni and Nosatzki obtain \(O(n^{1+\gamma})\) time for every fixed \(\gamma>0\), with an approximation constant depending on \(\gamma\). Their theorem does not bound that constant by three. This is the known result preceding the source’s truncated question.

Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Its approximation factor approaches three from above and therefore does not certify the exact factor-three guarantee.

Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

The original paper also studies edit distance with cheaper substitutions and bicriteria guarantees involving substitution and insertion/deletion budgets. Those positive results concern a different cost model or additional parameters. The selected introductory question uses ordinary unit-cost distance on unrestricted inputs.
why: Tests how much accuracy can be retained while obtaining a fixed polynomial speedup for a basic sequence-comparison problem. It separates the power of approximation from the quadratic barrier for exact computation, with relevance to algorithms for aligning and comparing strings.

Verified the STOC 2026 publisher date. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no fixed-power-time factor-three resolution. The sequential model and constant success probability make explicit the randomized algorithmic target; no near-linear-time requirement is imposed.
progress: 2020: Near-linear time becomes possible with an arbitrary parameter-dependent constant factor, while another result reaches factor 3+o(1) in truly subquadratic time. | 2023: The source explicitly retains a truly subquadratic factor-three approximation as open. | 2026-06-09: The STOC approximation-scheme result achieves factors arbitrarily close to one, with a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time.
working_summary: The task compares two arbitrary explicit strings using unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions. The estimate must lie between the true edit distance and three times that distance. The algorithm must save a fixed positive power over quadratic time on every input. Known truly subquadratic algorithms approach factor three from above. The 2026 approximation scheme achieves better accuracy, but its proved time saving is smaller than a fixed power of the input length.

title: Constant-factor approximation of graph crossing number
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central approximability gap for a classical graph-layout objective, with a large separation between known general guarantees and constant-factor hardness. Existing score retained.
formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\geq1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite undirected graph \(G\), outputs a drawing \(D\) in the plane satisfying \[\operatorname{cr}(D)\leq C\,\operatorname{cr}(G)\] with probability at least \(2/3\)?
question_excerpt: There exists a \(c > 1\) such that \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) cannot be approximated within a factor c in polynomial time [4], but we do not know […]
definitions:
The input explicitly lists the vertices and edges of an unweighted graph. Parallel edges are permitted and counted separately, as in the source. Self-loops can be omitted because they can be drawn locally without crossings. There is no bound on degree, genus or crossing number, and no planar subgraph or embedding is provided. Running time is polynomial in the full input length on every random tape.

A drawing places vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple polygonal curve joining its endpoints, without passing through any other vertex. The objective \(\operatorname{cr}(D)\) is the total number of pairwise edge crossings, summed over the entire drawing. The crossing number \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) is its minimum over all drawings. One may restrict to good drawings: adjacent edges do not cross, two edges cross at most once, and no three edges cross at one point.

The output must specify a drawing, rather than only an unsupported estimate of its value. A finite combinatorial representation suffices: list crossings in order along each original edge and give a planar embedding of the graph obtained by replacing crossings with degree-four vertices. At each such vertex, the two segments of each original edge must be opposite in the cyclic order. This records the original curves and their crossings without requiring real-number coordinates.

Randomization with bounded error is explicitly allowed, in keeping with the later approximation literature; a deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The success probability is over internal coins for each fixed graph. The constant \(C\) and the polynomial time bound are independent of the graph. In particular, a factor depending on its maximum degree does not meet the target. When \(\operatorname{cr}(G)=0\), the approximation guarantee requires a drawing with no crossings.

This is ordinary topological crossing number. Edges need not be straight, there is no prescribed rotation system, and the objective is not the maximum number of crossings on any one edge. The source’s Multiple Edge Insertion problem additionally keeps a specified subgraph planar; that constraint is absent here.
answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm and prove its running time and universal constant-factor guarantee, or prove that none exists. A conditional impossibility result must state its complexity assumption and cover randomized algorithms in the stated model. Hardness for a particular small approximation factor alone does not exclude all constant factors.
context:
Cabello proves that there is a constant \(c_{0}>1\) for which deterministic polynomial-time \(c_{0}\)-approximation is impossible unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), even on cubic graphs. This does not rule out an algorithm with some larger fixed factor. A randomized algorithm is not excluded merely by assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Chuzhoy and Tan give a randomized approximation factor \(2^{O((\log n)^{7/8}\log\log n)}\operatorname{poly}(\Delta)\) for simple graphs with \(n\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). For bounded degree this is subpolynomial in \(n\), but still does not supply a universal constant.

Solé-Pi’s Theorem 1.2 constructs drawings with \(\operatorname{cr}(G)+O(n^{4}/(\log\log n)^{\delta})\) crossings, for an absolute \(\delta>0\), in randomized polynomial time. This yields asymptotic factor \(1+o(1)\) for dense simple graphs, but the additive error does not yield a constant multiplicative guarantee on arbitrary graphs with small crossing number.

The 2023 paper studies maximizing the number of retained edges subject to a crossing budget. Its conditional hardness for Maximum Bounded-Crossing Subgraph should not be read as hardness of every constant approximation for the minimum total crossings of the entire input graph.
why: Crossing minimization is a basic graph-layout optimization problem with applications to drawing networks and circuit layouts. A constant approximation would establish a general algorithmic guarantee across sparse and dense inputs, beyond the degree-dependent and additive-error bounds currently available.
status_note: Checked the original full question and drawing model, the 2022 full approximation theorem, the distinct 2023 hardness variant, and the 2025/2026 dense-graph theorem. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no universal constant-factor approximation or impossibility covering all constants. The randomized convention is explicit; the historical P ≠ NP hardness is stated only for deterministic algorithms.
progress: 2013: A fixed-factor inapproximability result establishes an obstruction to arbitrarily accurate polynomial-time approximation. | 2022: A subpolynomial approximation factor is obtained for bounded-degree graphs. | 2025-10-21: An additive-error approximation and drawing theorem yields asymptotically optimal approximation for dense graphs.
working_summary: Draw every graph in the plane using at most a fixed constant times its minimum possible number of crossings. The constant must be independent of the graph size and maximum degree. The algorithm must construct a drawing in polynomial time; bounded-error randomization is allowed. Existing low-degree and dense-graph results do not provide this guarantee for all graphs. Hardness for one fixed ratio above one leaves open the possibility of a larger universal constant.

All variables, indices, delimiters and table entries count in the input bit length \(L\); there is no succinct predicate circuit or implicit list. The value of an assignment is the number of satisfied constraints, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the maximum value. For fixed \((k,d)\), an admissible algorithm is a uniform fair-coin Turing machine that outputs an assignment and halts within \(C_{k,d}(L+1)^{a_{k,d}}\) steps on every input and random tape, including output time. Its code and constants may depend on the fixed parameters, but not on the instance. Define \(\rho(k,d)\) as the supremum of \(r\in[0,1]\) for which some admissible algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}(A(I))]\ge r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) on every instance; zero-optimum instances impose no additional ratio condition. The supremum is not presumed attained. Logarithms in \(q\) are natural. A constant-factor answer consists of a positive function \(g(k,d)\) and one \(C\ge1\) such that \(C^{-1}g(k,d)\le\rho(k,d)\le Cg(k,d)\) for all \(k,d\ge2\). No hidden constant may depend on either parameter. Here the Unique Games Conjecture means: for every rational \(0<\eta,\gamma<1/2\), there is a fixed label count \(R\ge2\) for which it is NP-hard to distinguish unique-game instances of optimum satisfied fraction at least \(1-\eta\) from those of optimum at most \(\gamma\). A unique-game instance is an explicitly listed finite bipartite multigraph with at least one edge, a label in \([R]\) at each vertex, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[R]\to[R]\) at each oriented edge; an edge is satisfied when its endpoint labels obey that permutation. The objective is the fraction of satisfied edges, counting multiplicity. NP-hardness of this promise problem means that every language with polynomial-time verifiable polynomial-length witnesses has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction mapping members to the first promise and nonmembers to the second. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized polynomial-time machine with error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The additional assumption \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) makes the NP-hardness premise exclude bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decision procedures. Both assumptions and the fixed-parameter algorithm convention are explicit editorial choices.

title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.
focus_reason: A foundational quantitative question about the price of future uncertainty on arbitrary metrics, with a persistent gap between general upper and lower bounds despite many settled special cases.
formal: For each integer \(k\ge 1\), determine \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\){\(r\ge 1\): for every metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points and every initial placement \(C_{0}\), there are a deterministic online rule A and a finite \(\beta \ge 0\) such that \(\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma ;C_{0})\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma ;C_{0})+\beta\) for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)}. Use the serving model below.
definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request \(r_{t}\) must be served before \(r_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server is already at \(r_{t}\), no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to \(r_{t}\), paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from \(C_{0}\) with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive \(\beta\) must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied. The ratio r depends only on k. The rule and additive constant may depend on the entire metric, \(k, C_{0}\) and r, but not on future requests or sequence length. The classical universal finite upper bounds make the infimum finite. It need not be achieved by one rule at its endpoint.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all integers \(k\ge 1\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
context:
The target is the function giving the best deterministic competitive ratio as the number of servers varies. The k-server conjecture predicts \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) together with a strategy attaining that ratio; the infimum formulation by itself does not demand endpoint attainment.

The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is \((2k- 1)\)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. That stronger statement would identify \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) using the known lower bound, while the quantitative target also permits other values. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega (\log ^{2}k)\). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and \(\log ^{2}k\) is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the \((2k- 1)\) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.

title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
importance_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
focus_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every unrelated-machine scheduling instance}, in the input and output model below.
definitions: An instance consists of \(m\ge 1\) machines, \(n\ge 0\) independent jobs, and an explicitly given \(m\times n\) matrix of processing times \(p_{ij}\) in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function \(\sigma :\{1,\ldots ,n\}\to \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(p_{\sigma (j),j}<\infty\). Its makespan is \(Cmax(\sigma )=\max _{i} \sum_{j:\sigma (j)=i} p_{ij}\), and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output \(\sigma\), not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. For each fixed achieved ratio r, the algorithm and its time polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{unrel}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.
context:
The target is the infimum polynomial-time approximation ratio. The factor-two algorithmic question discussed in the saved history selects one threshold in this larger numerical target.

Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with \(p_{ij}>T\) are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below \(3/2\). This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to \(2- 1/m\). That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. Beating the universal infimum two requires one fixed improvement independent of machine count; a \(2- 1/m\) guarantee alone does not give that.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time \(p_{j}\) on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time \((1.75+\delta )\)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives \(2- 1/n\)ᵟ for fixed \(\delta >0\), whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A \((2- 1/\alpha )\)-approximation for makespan, for constant \(\alpha \ge 2\), would yield an \((\alpha +\delta )\)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed \(\delta >0\). Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.
