title: Optimal approximation ratio for precedence-constrained makespan
importance_reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.
formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every identical-machine precedence-constrained scheduling instance}, in the input and output model below.
definitions: An input specifies \(n\ge 1\) jobs, a positive integer processing time \(p_{j}\) for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine \(a_{j}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_{j}\) for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [\(s_{j},s_{j}+p_{j}\)), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge \(i\to j\), require \(s_{j}\ge s_{i}+p_{i}\). Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=\(\max _{j}(s_{j}+p_{j})\); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in \(\sum_{j} p_{j}\). Each fixed achieved ratio r must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{prec}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.
context:
The target is the infimum polynomial-time approximation ratio. The factor-two algorithmic question discussed in the saved history selects one threshold in this larger numerical target.

Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work \(\mathrm{W}=\sum_{j} p_{j}\) needs at least \(\mathrm{W}/m\) time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax\(\le \mathrm{W}/m+(1- 1/m)\mathrm{L}\), and hence Cmax\(\le (2- 1/m)\)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not establish a fixed improvement of the universal infimum below two.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take \(m(m- 1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for \(m- 1\) time, and the final job finishes at \(2m- 1\). An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other \(m- 1\) machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound \((1+n/m)^{O(\sqrt{nm})}\) is subexponential when \(m=o(n)\), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.
why: Determine whether arbitrary precedence constraints allow a constant improvement over the classical factor-two makespan guarantee on identical machines.
status_note: No polynomial-time fixed \((2- \varepsilon )\) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

The target is the infimum universal approximation ratio of deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in the stated model. A schedule must balance total work against long dependency chains that cannot execute in parallel. Progress would sharpen a foundational approximation boundary for dependent parallel computation. The numerical benchmark requires a Lean-certified value within absolute error 0.01, and conditional lower bounds retain their assumptions.

title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
importance_reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.
formal: Do a universal integer \(C\ge 0\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The input is a list of \(n\ge 1\) rational item sizes \(s_{1},\ldots ,s_{n}\in\)(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map \(b:[n]\to [k]\) with \(\sum_{i:b(i)=j}s_{i}\le 1\) for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most \(KL^{d}\) bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least \(2/3\) over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+\(O(1)\) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance \(C=1, a\) valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) on the order of 1/OPT makes \(\varepsilon \cdot\)OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as \(\varepsilon\) shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\) is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with \(O(\log ^{2} \operatorname{OPT})\) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log  \operatorname{OPT}_{f})\), and hence OPT+\(O(\log  \operatorname{OPT})\). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\) would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring \(\Omega (\log  n)\). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.
why: A basic boundary between asymptotic approximation and almost exact combinatorial optimization: can efficient packing lose only a fixed number of bins on every instance?
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. The logarithmic-additive guarantee and recent high-multiplicity/support results do not settle this explicitly listed, randomized formulation.
progress: 1982: Karmarkar–Karp obtain polynomial-time bin packing with \(O(\log ^{2} \operatorname{OPT})\) additive loss. | 2011–2012: Permutation-discrepancy connections and lower bounds for specified item-rounding methods identify barriers to several approaches. | 2011: Newman–Nikolov construct three permutations requiring \(\Omega (\log  n)\) discrepancy, refuting Beck’s conjecture. | 2014: Bansal’s invited survey explicitly lists OPT+\(O(1)\), and even OPT+1, as open algorithmic targets. | 2015–2017: Hoberg–Rothvoss give an \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log  \operatorname{OPT}_{f})\) packing algorithm; preprint 2015, SODA 2017. | 2025: Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas prove exponential configuration support in the number of item types. | 2026: Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton establish a tight ETH-based lower bound for high-multiplicity exact bin packing in the stated parameter regime, without resolving constant additive approximation.
working_summary: One-dimensional bin packing places indivisible numerical items into unit-capacity bins using as few bins as possible. The reviewed question asks for randomized polynomial time with at most a universal constant of extra bins above optimum. This is an additive guarantee, so the allowed excess does not grow with the size of the instance. It would strengthen approximation schemes whose small proportional errors can still yield many extra bins. The saved review notes that ordinary exact-optimization hardness and a multiplicative scheme do not automatically resolve this stronger additive target.

title: Optimal competitive ratio for convex body chasing
importance_reason: A canonical geometric model of online optimization with movement costs.
formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors as a function of \(d\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\mathcal C(d)\) for general convex body chasing in Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^d\). The domain is every integer \(d\ge1\).

An online strategy starts at \(x_0=0\), sees a nonempty compact convex set \(K_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), and must immediately choose \(x_t\in K_t\) using only \(K_1,\ldots,K_t\). Its cost on a finite request sequence is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|_2\). Let
\[\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)=\min_{y_t\in K_t,\ y_0=0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|y_t-y_{t-1}\|_2\]
and define
\[\mathcal C(d)=\inf\left\{c\ge1:\ \exists A\ \forall T\ge1\ \forall K_1,\ldots,K_T,\quad\operatorname{cost}_A(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\right\}.\]
The strategy may depend on \(d\), but must serve all horizons and request sequences in that dimension. The target is the asymptotic order of this dimension-dependent ratio, resolving the source's gap between order \(\sqrt d\) and order \(d\).
definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_j^2)^{1/2}\). A request set is nonempty, compact and convex: it is closed and bounded, and contains \((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v\) whenever \(u,v\) lie in it and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). Lower-dimensional sets, including points and faces of polytopes, are allowed. There is no common diameter bound, containment relation or promise that consecutive requests intersect. In particular, the sequence need not be nested.

A deterministic online strategy is a sequence of maps \(A_t\), one for every positive integer \(t\), taking every length-\(t\) request history to a point in its final set. These maps jointly specify one causal strategy: two request sequences with the same prefix have the same choices on that prefix, irrespective of their eventual lengths or later requests. Its own previous locations are determined by that history. The full current set is available before choosing the current point; no future set, horizon, forecast, advice or random choice is supplied.

This is the information-theoretic model of competitive analysis used in the sources. Strategies are mathematical maps on convex sets, with unrestricted computation; a finite input encoding, polynomial-time evaluator or bounded number of membership queries is not an extra requirement. An answer must specify its strategy well enough to prove feasibility and cost, but the benchmark measures movement, not computational time.

The offline comparator starts at the same origin, knows the whole finite sequence, and may choose a different feasible point at every round. Compactness makes its displayed minimum attainable. There is no required return to the origin and no additional service cost or cost for reading a request. Competitiveness is a purely multiplicative guarantee on every finite sequence, with no additive constant. If OPT is zero, the online strategy must also incur zero cost; the definition uses an inequality to avoid division by zero. Requests may be selected adversarially after previous moves, since the guarantee covers every finite request history for a deterministic strategy.

The infimum is over all qualifying ratios and strategies in each dimension; it need not be attained. Its value is finite by the known dimension-dependent upper bound. Determination up to universal factors means providing a noncircular positive function \(h\) on the positive integers and constants \(a,b>0\), independent of dimension, such that \(a h(d)\le\mathcal C(d)\le b h(d)\) for every \(d\ge1\). Equivalent eventually valid asymptotic bounds may be extended over the finitely many smaller dimensions by adjusting constants. The question does not require an exact ratio or an additive \(1/100\) estimate of that ratio.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked determination of the asymptotic growth of \(\mathcal C(d)\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to universal constant factors. The upper bound must cover arbitrary finite, possibly non-nested request sequences with one horizon-independent deterministic strategy in each dimension. The lower bound must apply to every permitted strategy. A nonattained infimum may be handled by arbitrarily approaching bounds. Merely renaming the optimization defining \(\mathcal C\), proving a bound for nested requests, allowing the ratio to grow with the horizon, or establishing a lower bound in another norm does not meet the criterion.
context:
The 2025 source lists an \(O(d)\) upper bound for general convex body chasing and an \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bound in Euclidean space. It separately lists the stronger upper bound for nested requests; the saved card concerns the unrestricted sequence problem.

Sellke proves a competitive ratio of \(d\) for convex body chasing in an arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional normed space. That dependence is tight for the maximum-coordinate norm, but the corresponding general Euclidean lower bound is only of order \(\sqrt d\). A worst-case norm cannot be substituted for the fixed Euclidean norm here.

For Euclidean requests of horizon \(T\), Sellke also proves an \(O(\sqrt{d\log T})\) guarantee. Combining it with the dimension-only bound helps at shorter horizons, but it does not yield a sublinear-in-d bound uniformly over arbitrary \(T\).

The nested problem adds \(K_{t+1}\subseteq K_t\). Its \(O(\sqrt{d\log d})\) Euclidean upper bound is nearly the square-root lower bound, but that extra containment hypothesis is not available in this card. Recent applications to shrinking feasible regions therefore do not by themselves close the general chasing gap.
why: Convex body chasing isolates the movement cost of maintaining feasibility when constraints arrive without advance notice. The optimal dependence on dimension measures how much geometric complexity alone can penalize online decisions, independently of computational efficiency. Matching bounds would resolve a central quantitative gap between what convexity permits offline and what an online strategy can guarantee.
status_note: The 2025 source slides and the full November 2021 Sellke revision were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded search through 2026 found work on nested feasible regions and related chasing variants but no matching dimension-only upper and lower bounds for general Euclidean requests. The card records the established bounds and source-open gap without claiming an exhaustive current-status review.
progress: 1993: Friedman and Linial introduce convex body chasing; the later sources describe its finite-competitiveness conjecture and the square-root Euclidean obstruction. | 2020: The SODA results give linear dimension dependence for general requests, and a nearly square-root Euclidean bound for the nested variant. Sellke’s revised full manuscript separately states the horizon-dependent Euclidean improvement. | 2025: Gupta’s Winter School slides continue to distinguish the linear general bound, the nearly square-root nested bound, and the square-root Euclidean lower bound.
working_summary: Convex body chasing requires an online player to move into each newly revealed convex set. The player pays Euclidean movement while an offline comparator knows all future requests. This question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as dimension grows, up to universal constant factors. The strategy must work for arbitrary finite request sequences without knowing the horizon. The checked sources leave a gap between square-root and linear dimension dependence for general requests, with stronger results only in restricted settings.

title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
importance_reason: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly in dimension d and horizon T, the information-theoretic minimax expected regret \(R*(d,T)\) for one-point adversarial bandit convex optimization with losses in \([0,1]\). Use the oblivious-adversary, exact-feedback model and worst-case normalized convex body defined below; logarithmic dependence is part of the requested rate.
definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function \(g(d,T)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) with a \(g(d,T)\le R*(d,T)\le b g(d,T)\) for all \(d,T\ge 1\). Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate \(g(d,T)\) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.
context:
On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.
why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
status_note: The March 2026 primary book explicitly lists the minimax dimension dependence as open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching rate for the specified unrestricted one-point model. Recent smooth-loss and two-point results do not settle it.
progress: 2020: A general information-theoretic upper bound \(O(d^{2.5} \sqrt{T} \log (T \operatorname{diam}(K)))\) is proved for the oblivious exact-feedback model. | 2026-03: The book’s Outlook retains the gap between dimension-linear lower bounds and higher-degree general upper bounds. | 2026-06: Budgeted-perturbation results concern smooth underlying losses, including in the unperturbed case. | 2026-07: The revised two-point strongly convex result has a different feedback and comparator model.
working_summary: What is the optimal expected regret for adversarial convex losses when only one value is observed per round? The learner competes with the best fixed point in hindsight over a known convex body. The losses lie in \([0,1]\) and are chosen before the learner’s random actions, with no smoothness assumption. General upper and lower bounds still have different polynomial dependence on dimension. Two-point, strongly convex, smooth-loss and computational-efficiency results address different guarantees.

title: Matroid secretary conjecture
importance_reason: The main unresolved competitive-ratio question for online selection under general matroid constraints.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) such that every finite matroid M admits a randomized online selection strategy which, for every assignment of nonnegative weights to its elements, returns an independent set of expected weight at least \(\operatorname{OPT}(M,w)/C\) when the elements arrive in a uniformly random order?
definitions: A matroid is a finite set E and a nonempty family \(I\subseteq 2^{E}\) closed under subsets and satisfying augmentation: if \(A,B\in I\) and |\(A|<|B|\), some \(b\in B\setminus A\) has \(A\cup \{b\}\in I\). The strategy knows E and I in advance, but not the weights. A fixed adversary assigns \(w:E\to \mathbb{R} _{\ge 0}\) before the order and strategy coins are sampled. Upon each arrival its identity and weight are revealed. The strategy must accept or reject it irrevocably before the next arrival, keeping the accepted set in I. \(\operatorname{OPT}(M,w)=\max _{S\in I}\sum _{e\in S}w(e)\). Expectation includes a uniformly random permutation of E and the strategy’s independent random coins. There is no computation or oracle-query bound; this is the competitive-existence conjecture for the full-information matroid model.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The general matroid secretary problem asks whether random arrival order is enough to recover a constant fraction of a best feasible weighted set without seeing future weights. It unifies classical secretary selection with broad independence constraints.

The random-assignment model also randomizes where weights are placed, and admits stronger results. Those results do not settle the adversarial-assignment, random-arrival model used here.
why: The main unresolved competitive-ratio question for online selection under general matroid constraints.
status_note: Open target supported by the dated sources. Literature was checked on 11 September 2026, with the limits recorded here; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. No polynomial-time restriction has been silently appended. Earlier exclusions TCS-2570 and TCS-5552 address narrower algorithm/model questions.
progress: 2025: The source treats the general constant-competitive conjecture as open while resolving the more symmetric random-assignment setting.

title: Randomized competitiveness of k-server
importance_reason: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(k\to \infty , R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\){\(r\ge 1\): for every finite metric \((X,d)\) with |\(X|\ge k+1\) and every initial placement, some randomized online strategy and finite \(\beta \ge 0\) satisfy \(E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+\beta\) for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the strategy’s coins}, for integers \(k\ge 2\).
definitions: There are k movable servers at points of X; repeated server locations are allowed. Each request names a point of X. Before the next request, at least one server must occupy that point. Moving a server from u to v costs \(d(u,v)\). The full finite metric and initial placement are known. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum total movement of a strategy knowing the entire sequence and starting at the same placement. The adversary is oblivious: it fixes \(\sigma\) independently of the online strategy’s random coins. The strategy uses only the prefix revealed so far. No running-time bound is imposed. The competitive factor r is uniform over metric spaces and initial placements for each fixed k. The strategy and additive \(\beta\) may depend on the metric, initial placement, k and r, but not on the future sequence or its length. The infimum is finite by deterministic competitive strategies, and need not be attained.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f(k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c f(k)\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le C f(k)\) for all \(k\ge 2\), adjusting constants for finitely many small k if needed, and prove both inequalities in Lean. Upper bounds must hold for every finite metric and oblivious sequence in the stated model; lower bounds must apply to every eligible randomized strategy on suitable metrics. The asymptotic precision is constant-factor matching, not additive 0.01.
context:
This quantitative target asks for the growth of the optimal competitive ratio. The earlier polylogarithmic question asks only whether that growth is bounded by some fixed power of log k.

Randomized k-server is a central test of whether an online algorithm can manage a large changing state at a cost depending mildly on the number of servers. The number of metric points must not occur in the competitive ratio.

The old \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture is false: a superlogarithmic lower bound is known. Polylogarithmic dependence on k remains a different open target. Bounds containing log|X| do not settle it.
why: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
status_note: Open target supported by the dated sources. Literature was checked on 11 September 2026, with the limits recorded here; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. This is explicitly the polylogarithmic k-only question, not the false \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture or the resolved worst-case metrical-task-system ratio.
progress: 2026: The 2026 work gives \(O(\log ^{2} k)\) on hierarchical tree metrics and an \(O(\log |X| \log ^{2} k)\) consequence on general metrics; it does not remove dependence on |X|. | 2023: An \(\Omega (\log ^{2} k)\) lower bound refutes the original logarithmic conjecture; it is consistent with a polylogarithmic upper bound.
working_summary: In randomized k-server, an online strategy moves k servers to serve sequential metric requests. The request sequence is fixed independently of the strategy’s random choices. The target is the infimum competitive ratio as a function of k over all finite metrics, within universal constant factors. The metric and initial placement are known and may affect the strategy and fixed additive cost. The earlier polylogarithmic question is a qualitative consequence of determining this growth, and dependence on the number of metric points cannot be hidden in the ratio.

title: Minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
importance_reason: A fundamental quantitative problem in sequential prediction, with consequences for calibrated learning and decision making.
formal: Determine \(C(T)=\inf _{A} \sup _{B} E[\sum _{p\in \mathrm{P}_{A}}|\sum _{t:p_{t}=p}(y_{t}- p)|]\) up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer horizon T tends to infinity, in the finite-forecast sequential game below. The requested rate includes logarithmic factors.
definitions: Before play, forecaster A selects a finite set \(\mathrm{P}_{A}\subseteq [0,1]\), which may depend on T. Both players know this set and T. At each time t, A selects \(p_{t}\in \mathrm{P}_{A}\) and adversary B selects \(y_{t}\in \{0,1\}\) simultaneously; neither sees the other’s current selection. Each may randomize using independent coins and the full history \((p_{s},y_{s})_{s<t}\), and after the round both selections become public. The infimum is over every such finite set and randomized forecaster, and the supremum is over all randomized adaptive adversaries. There is no computational restriction. The displayed sum measures unnormalized \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) calibration error and is finite; groups are defined by exact equality of predictions. Expectation is over both players’ coins.
answer_criterion: Determine the stated minimax quantity up to universal multiplicative constants, including all logarithmic factors, with matching upper and lower bounds. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Calibration asks whether forecasts agree with empirical frequencies on the rounds when each probability was announced. The minimax rate measures the unavoidable error in this requirement against an adaptive sequence of binary events.

The long-standing \(T^{2/3}\) upper bound has already been improved by a constant in the exponent. A lower bound strictly above \(\sqrt{T}\) is also known. definitions: For \(k\ge 1\) an instance environment consists of a finite set X with |\(X|\ge k+1\), uniform distance \(d(x,y)=1\) if \(x\ne y\) and 0 otherwise, positive real weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\), and an initial location \(c_{i}\in X\) for each labeled server i. title: One forecaster with the optimal regret rate for every proper loss
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: A general adaptation question for online forecasting across unknown downstream proper losses. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For each fixed number \(K\ge 2\) of outcomes, does there exist one randomized online forecaster A, not given the loss function, such that for every bounded proper loss \(\ell\) its worst-case expected regret satisfies \(R_{A},\ell (T)\le C_{\ell},K\cdot (1+R*_{\ell},K(T))\cdot (\log (T+2))^{c_{\ell},K}\) for all \(T\ge 1\), for some constants \(C_{\ell},K>0\) and \(c_{\ell},K\ge 0\) independent of T? Here \(R*_{\ell},K\) is the minimax regret achievable by a forecaster tailored to that particular loss. This spells out the source’s “optimal up to constant or logarithmic factors in T” target; the additive one covers losses with zero or bounded optimal regret.
definitions: The prediction space is the simplex \(\Delta _{K}=\{p\in \mathbb{R} ^{K}:p_{i}\ge 0,\sum p_{i}=1\}\). At round t, A chooses a possibly random \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\in \Delta _{K}\) from earlier revealed outcomes, then observes \(y_{t}\in \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\), where \(e_{i}\) is the ith unit vector. The adversary fixes \(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{T}\) in advance, knowing A but not its random bits. For a measurable loss \(\ell\):\(\Delta _{K}\times \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\to [- 1,1]\), propriety means \(E_{Y\sim p}\ell (p,Y)\le E_{Y\sim p}\ell (q,Y)\) for every \(p,q\in \Delta _{K}\); the minimizer need not be unique. Define \(Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)=E_{A}[\sum _{t=1}^{T} \ell (\mathrm{P}_{t},y_{t})]- \inf _{p\in \Delta _{K}}\sum _{t=1}^{T}\ell (p,y_{t})\). The expectation is over forecasting randomness, while the comparator is the best single fixed probability prediction in hindsight. Propriety makes the empirical outcome distribution a minimizing comparator. Set \(R_{A},\ell (T)=\sup _{y_{1}:T}Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)\), and \(R*_{\ell},K(T)=\inf _{B} R_{B},\ell (T)\), where B ranges over randomized online prediction strategies allowed to know \(\ell ,K\) and T. The desired A may know K and the horizon T, but its predictions are independent of which downstream loss is evaluated. Constants and logarithmic exponents may depend on the fixed loss and K; the asymptotic comparison is in T. This is an expected-regret comparison for each loss, not one simultaneous high-probability event over all losses. The question does not impose a particular polynomial running-time bound or a finite-precision implementation model; the target is the attainable online regret rate.
answer_criterion: Construct a loss-independent forecaster and prove the comparison for every bounded proper loss, or show that every such forecaster has some bounded proper loss for which its worst-case expected regret exceeds every allowed logarithmic-factor comparison with that loss’s minimax rate. Achieving \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{T})\) for all losses alone does not settle the question, because some individual losses admit logarithmic or smaller regret.
context:
A probability forecast can be used by many downstream decision makers. Proper losses reward reporting the true probability distribution in expectation, but different losses penalize mistakes differently. The forecaster must issue the same \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\) before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

For squared loss, logarithmic regret is attainable. A general guarantee of order \(\sqrt{T}\) can therefore be much worse than a user could obtain with a loss-specific forecaster. The target adapts to each loss’s own difficulty, rather than just the hardest loss in the class.

The paper gives one efficient algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((K^{5/4}\sqrt{T})\) regret for every bounded proper loss and \(O(\beta  \log  T+\beta \sqrt{K} \log  K)\) for bounded \(\beta\)-smooth proper losses. It also extends logarithmic guarantees to a broader relative-smoothness class. These are substantial simultaneous guarantees, but do not characterize every individual proper loss.

The hindsight benchmark is one fixed probability vector p, chosen after all outcomes are known. Competing with a different optimal \(p_{t}\) on every round would be a much stronger and generally impossible target under arbitrary outcome sequences.

For each fixed loss, average regret over A’s own randomization must have the required rate against every fixed outcome sequence. The statement does not claim that a single realized random trajectory satisfies all loss bounds with high probability.
why: Would establish whether a general-purpose probability forecaster can match every downstream user’s best possible learning rate without knowing that user’s loss. It refines universal sublinear regret into adaptation to the intrinsic difficulty of each scoring rule.

title: Additive-one approximation for bin packing
importance_reason: A major additive-approximation question for a foundational packing problem: whether efficient algorithms can remain within one bin of the integer optimum on every instance. Existing score retained.
formal:
Is there a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for one-dimensional offline bin packing that uses at most one more bin than optimum? Explicitly allowing randomization, the target is one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every finite input list \(I=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n})\) of rational sizes \(0<s_{i}\le1\), \(A\) runs within \(p(L)\) steps for every coin sequence, always outputs a feasible packing, and satisfies
\[
\Pr\bigl[B(A(I))\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+1\bigr]\ge\tfrac23.
\]
Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, \(B\) is the number of bins used, and probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits for each fixed input. A deterministic algorithm with the same bound on every input also qualifies.
definitions:
All items and their sizes are given before computation starts. Each item is listed separately, including repetitions. Write \(s_{i}=a_{i}/b_{i}\), where \(a_{i},b_{i}\) are positive binary integers and \(a_{i}\le b_{i}\). Input length includes the item list, numerators, denominators and separators; arithmetic precision is not free.

A packing partitions the item indices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into nonempty bins \(B_{1},\ldots,B_{q}\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in B_{j}}s_{i}\le1\quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Items are indivisible and must each appear in exactly one bin. The output explicitly assigns every item to a bin. The integer \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum feasible number \(q\); the empty input has optimum zero and can be packed in zero bins. Zero-size items, if allowed by an alternative convention, can be handled separately without changing the existence question.

Running time is worst-case bit complexity on a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine. There is no input advice, supplied optimal packing or promise on the size distribution, number of distinct sizes or optimum. The input is an explicit list, not binary multiplicities representing exponentially many separate output items.

The additive allowance is exactly one bin with capacity exactly 1. It does not grow with the instance, and it is not a multiplicative factor \(1+\varepsilon\). Neither larger bin capacities nor discarding an item is permitted. The target concerns the integer optimum of the packing problem, not the optimum of a fractional relaxation.

The probability convention makes explicit an algorithmic interpretation that includes randomized approximation algorithms, as in the later logarithmic-additive result. Its theorem gives expected polynomial runtime with its quality guarantee; that is a separately reported form of the known result. For the target here, the output must always be feasible and only the one-extra-bin guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\).
answer_criterion: Give one algorithm and a proof of all stated time, feasibility and probability guarantees, or refute the existence of such an algorithm. A conditional impossibility result must expose its assumption, including any assumption needed to exclude randomized algorithms. An \(\operatorname{OPT}+C\) bound with unspecified constant \(C>1\), an asymptotic approximation scheme, or a nonconstructive fractional-integrality-gap bound alone does not meet the target.
context:
Problem 3 asks whether bin packing can join problems that admit polynomial-time solutions within one unit of their integer optimum. The book separately highlights a constant number of extra bins as significant progress. This card keeps the one-bin endpoint as its main target.

The book recalls the Karmarkar–Karp additive \(O((\log n)^{2})\) guarantee. Hoberg and Rothvoss later give a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial runtime and at most \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+2))\) bins, where \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\le\operatorname{OPT}\) is the fractional packing optimum. In particular this gives \(\operatorname{OPT}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}+2))\) bins, without establishing a constant additive bound.

The Gilmore–Gomory relaxation permits a nonnegative fractional number of copies of each feasible bin pattern and requires enough total coverage of each item type. Its objective is the total fractional number of bins. Statements comparing its optimum to integer packings concern an integrality gap; an existence bound for that gap does not by itself specify the efficient algorithm required here.

Bounds of the form \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}+C_{\varepsilon}\) can approach multiplicative ratio 1 while retaining an unbounded or larger additive loss. They therefore do not imply the requested one-extra-bin guarantee on every instance.
why: A one-extra-bin algorithm would show that a strongly NP-hard packing problem can nevertheless be solved to a uniformly tiny additive error. The question tests a much sharper notion of approximation than a ratio tending to one and is a long-standing benchmark for understanding the structure of feasible packings.

title: Planted clique conjecture
importance_reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.
focus_reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.
formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed \(\varepsilon \in (0,1/2)\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm A whose success probability in the experiment below is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large n, with \(k=\lfloor n^{1/2- \varepsilon}\rfloor\).
definitions: Set \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_{n}\) draws a simple undirected labeled graph by including each unordered pair independently with probability \(1/2\). The planted distribution \(\mathrm{P}_{n,k}\) first chooses S uniformly among all k-element subsets of \([n]\), includes all edges inside S, and includes every other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). Draw b uniformly from \(\{0,1\}\); draw G from \(N_{n}\) if \(b=0\) and \(\mathrm{P}_{n,k}\) if \(b=1\). Give A the binary integers n,k and the full adjacency matrix of G, but neither b nor S. It outputs a bit b̂. Success means \(\Pr [\hat\{b\}=b]\), averaged over b, the graph, S when present, and A’s independent random bits. Equivalently success is \((\Pr _{N}[A=0]+\Pr _{\mathrm{P}}[A=1])/2\). Polynomial time means at most \(C(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations for every input and random tape, with fixed C,c; they and A may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\). The forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N \forall n\ge N\), success\(\ge 2/3\). This is a one-graph detection problem; A may generate its own random graphs at its own computational cost. The size of S is exactly k, not an independent per-vertex planting probability. No advice, quantum computation, oracle, side information, or algorithm-family restriction is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size \(r=\lceil 3 \log _{2} n\rceil\) with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most \(n^{r}\cdot 2^{- r(r- 1)/2}\), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time \(n^{O}(\log  n)\). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt{n}\), with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as \(n^{- \varepsilon}\) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near \(\sqrt{n}\), despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt{n}\). Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.
why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis and a central test case for statistical–computational gaps. It asks for a clean separation between the presence of information and efficient extraction of that information; reductions transfer related assumptions to sparse estimation and latent-structure learning. Proving this formulation would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), since a polynomial algorithm for maximum clique would distinguish the distributions.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026; no unrestricted polynomial-time solution below \(n^{1/2- \varepsilon}\) or unconditional hardness proof was identified. The exact formulation fixes constant-success detection and exactly k planted vertices. Low-degree and sum-of-squares bounds remain scoped to their models; the optimal-advantage result is conditional.
progress: 1998: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery for \(k\ge c\sqrt{n}\) for any fixed \(c>0\), using spectral methods and boosting. | 2016–2019: Barak, Hopkins, Kelner, Kothari, Moitra, and Potechin prove a nearly tight sum-of-squares integrality gap: degree \(d=o(\log  n)\) assigns random graphs clique value \(n^{1/2- o(1)}\). This is a restricted-model lower bound. | 2023–2025: Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu show that an appropriate discrete gradient descent and low-temperature local chain recover at the \(\sqrt{n}\) scale from the full-graph initialization; the final preprint version is dated 15 May 2025. | 2025-07-19: Nagda and Raghavendra derive optimal efficient distinguishing advantages conditional on a planted-clique hypothesis, in the independent-vertex planting model. | 2026: Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller give robust sum-of-squares algorithms for multiple overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs when clique size is much larger than \(\sqrt{n \log  n}\). This is progress in a related model, not below the threshold fixed here.
working_summary: Planted clique detection distinguishes a random graph from one with a uniformly chosen clique inserted into it. The conjecture rules out polynomial-time classical randomized detection when the planted size is \(n^{1/2- \varepsilon}\) for fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). The graph statistically contains a signal, but the challenge is finding a computationally accessible feature that reveals it below the square-root scale. This makes the problem a central candidate for a gap between information and computation. The reviewed model fixes clique size exactly and asks only for detection, so recovery algorithms, different planting distributions, or lower bounds for restricted relaxations do not automatically settle it.

title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
importance_reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.
focus_reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.
definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given \(1^{n}\), halts within \(q(n)\) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution \(D_{n}\) is over finite binary strings \(x; |x|\le q(n)\), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives \((1^{n},x)\), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write \(T_{A}(1^{n},x)\) for its running time. The pair \((\mathrm{L},D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an \(A, \varepsilon >0, C>0\), and integer \(k\ge 1\) with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every \(n\ge 1\). The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |\(x|^{2}- 1\) further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.
why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone.
status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.
progress: 1986–1990: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory. | 2003: Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication. | 2018 / revised survey 2021: Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) implies average-case NP hardness. | 2026-01: Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

working_summary: Worst-case NP hardness means that some efficiently verifiable problem resists polynomial-time solution on all inputs. The question asks whether P unequal to NP forces such a problem to remain hard on average under an efficiently samplable distribution. The hard instances must occur often enough in a distribution that can itself be generated feasibly. A positive implication would connect worst-case complexity with the distributional hardness needed in many algorithmic and cryptographic settings. The reviewed target uses deterministic exact decisions and Levin's moment-based average-time definition, which differs from allowing errors on rare inputs or requiring only a polynomial first moment.

title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
importance_reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <(k- 2)/4\), and rational \(c\in (0,1)\), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of \(Y=n^{k/4- \varepsilon}v^{\otimes k}+Z\) specified below, achieves |\(\langle u,v\rangle |\ge c\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in \(R^{n}\) and the \(n^{k}\) ordered entries of Z are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables.
definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple \((i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k})\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}^{k}\), the signal entry is \(n^{k/4- \varepsilon}v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}\). Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for \(n\ge 2\) set \(b=\lceil 10k \log _{2}n\rceil\) and \(Q_{b}(x)=2^{- b}\lfloor 2^{b} \max (- 2^{b},\min (x,2^{b}))\rfloor\). The input consists of n and all entries \(Q_{b}(Y_{i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k}})\), represented as signed dyadic rationals with \(O(\log  n)\) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants \(k, \varepsilon\) and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector \(u=w/\Vert w\Vert _{2}\); zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |\(\langle w,v\rangle |\ge c\Vert w\Vert _{2}\). The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \((k,\varepsilon ,c)\) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at \(n^{k/4}\) does not supply the fixed power saving \(n^{\varepsilon}\) requested here.
context:
Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.
why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.
status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below \(n^{k/4}\). No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.
