working_summary: Dense tensor PCA observes a hidden rank-one tensor corrupted by independent Gaussian noise. The conjecture says that below a specified signal scale, no polynomial-time algorithm can recover a vector with constant correlation to the hidden direction. It asks about unrestricted computation rather than the performance of a particular spectral, gradient, or low-degree method. Resolving the threshold would clarify a prominent proposed gap between statistical recoverability and computational feasibility. The saved formulation fixes finite precision, unit-sphere normalization, one observation, and independent ordered noise entries, so results using different normalizations or extra samples require careful conversion.

title: Computational Kesten–Stigum threshold
importance_reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.
formal: Do there exist a fixed integer \(q\ge 5\), fixed rational constants \(a>b>0\) satisfying \((a- b)^{2}<q(a+(q- 1)b), a\) constant \(\delta >0\), and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model \(SBM(n,q,a,b)\), with expected overlap at least \(1/q+\delta\)?
definitions: Generate the hidden labels \(\sigma _{1},\ldots ,\sigma _{n}\) independently and uniformly from \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability \(a/n\) if its labels agree and \(b/n\) otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take \(n\ge a\). Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal \(n/q\). The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector \(\hat\{\sigma\}\in [q]^{n}\). Define \(overlap(\hat\{\sigma\},\sigma )=\max\) over permutations \(\pi\) of \([q]\) of \(n^{- 1}\sum_{i} 1\{\hat\{\sigma\}_{i}=\pi (\sigma _{i})\}\). The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline \(1/q\). Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put \(d=(a+(q- 1)b)/q\) and \(\theta =(a- b)/(a+(q- 1)b)\). The strict inequality is \(d\theta ^{2}<1\), below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm at every fixed parameter choice in the formulation. Recovery with unlimited computation does not answer the question. An algorithm with q growing with n, a result only above the threshold, or a lower bound conditional on an unproved computational hypothesis is partial progress. The question does not impose an extra promise of information-theoretic recoverability: any positive algorithmic example automatically has that property.
context:
Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity \(d\theta ^{2}\) compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and \(\theta\) describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case \(a>b\).

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above \(\sqrt{n}\). This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below \(\sqrt{n}\), so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.
why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.
status_note: Efficient recovery above the threshold and information-theoretic recovery below it in suitable fixed-q assortative regimes are proved. The checked fixed-community computational lower bound remains conditional on an unproved low-degree conjecture. Growing-community algorithms in the August 2026 revision concern a different quantifier regime. No unconditional settlement of this precise fixed-q question found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2015–2018: Abbe–Sandon prove efficient recovery above the Kesten–Stigum threshold for all fixed community counts; preprint 2015, revised 2016, journal publication 2018. | 2016: Banks–Moore–Neeman–Netrapalli prove information-theoretic recovery below the threshold in suitable assortative regimes with \(q\ge 11\), using a potentially exponential algorithm. | 2025-04-28: Ding–Hua–Slot–Steurer’s revised paper derives recovery lower bounds under its explicitly restricted low-degree conjecture; Theorem A.1 allows a fixed gap below the threshold. | 2026-08-23: Chin–Mossel–Sohn–Wein revise their many-community analysis, correcting the proof of Theorem 1.2. Their below-threshold algorithms require a growing community count and do not settle the fixed-q question.
working_summary: The symmetric stochastic block model generates a sparse graph with higher edge probability within hidden communities than between them. The question asks whether some fixed parameters below the Kesten–Stigum threshold permit polynomial-time weak recovery. Weak recovery means a constant improvement over chance after relabeling the output communities optimally. A positive example would cross a proposed computational threshold in a setting where information can persist beyond simple spectral methods. The reviewed model keeps the number of communities and edge parameters fixed, so results with growing community counts or only restricted-algorithm lower bounds do not settle it.

title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
importance_reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge 6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and \(\Pr [A(F)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]\to 1\) as \(n\to \infty\) for F drawn from \(R_{3}(n,Cn)\)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
definitions: For \(n\ge 3, R_{3}(n,m)\) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and independently negates each of its three variables with probability \(1/2\). Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every \(\eta >0\) there is n0 such that the probability is at least \(1- \eta\) for all \(n\ge n0\). There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers \(C\ge 6\) loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.
why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No sound polynomial-time refuter meeting the stated constant-density success guarantee was found. The exact-satisfiability variant must be distinguished from the stronger near-satisfiability formulations in the cited Feige-hypothesis literature.
progress: 2012: Barak records a gap formulation of Feige’s hypothesis, requiring soundness on nearly satisfiable instances. | 2015: Allen–O’Donnell–Witmer give general random-CSP refutation algorithms and distinguish weak and strong refutation. | 2026-04-30: Chan–d’Orsi–Xu extend random-CSP refutation tradeoffs to predicates without uniformly random literals; the constant-density 3-SAT target is not established.

title: Infinitely-often one-way functions from average-case NP hardness
importance_reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.
formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant \(c>0\), infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
definitions: DistNP consists of pairs \((\mathrm{L},D)\) with L in NP and \(D_{n} a\) polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from \(D_{n}\) have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.
context:
Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.
why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-06-23: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.
working_summary: Average-case NP hardness says that some efficiently sampled verification problem defeats the specified randomized heuristic schemes. The question asks whether this implies a polynomial-time function that is hard to invert at infinitely many input lengths. Such a result would connect distributional decision hardness with a basic cryptographic form of computational asymmetry. The security target quantifies separately over every polynomial-time inverter and every inverse-polynomial success threshold. The saved formulation deliberately uses infinitely-often security, so a claim of hardness at all sufficiently large lengths would be stronger than the implication being asked about.

title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
importance_reason: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every \(\varphi \ge 1/2\) and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on \([- 1,1]\) with probability densities bounded by \(\varphi\), the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most \(C(n+1)^{a}(1+\varphi )^{b}\)?
definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(\mathrm{W}_{w}(S)=\Sigma\)_{\(uv\in E\): exactly one of u,v lies in S} \(w_{uv}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(\mathrm{L}(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(\mathrm{L}=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(\mathrm{L}\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[\mathrm{L}(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.
context:
The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut \(\{1,2\}\) has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut \(\{1,3\}\) has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by \(\varphi\) prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most \(\varphi h\). Larger \(\varphi\) permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with \(\varphi\).

The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\) for fixed \(\delta >0\); arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.
why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. The general high-probability upper bound and the smoothed 3-FLIP lower bound were separated from the required guarantee. Proofs have not been independently audited.
progress: 2019 / 2020: Theorem 1.1 gives the general upper bound \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) with high probability, controlling every directed path in the improvement graph. | 2024-09-23: The sparse-graph theorem gives polynomial expected and high-probability bounds for arboricity \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\), with any fixed \(\delta \in\)(0,1]. The paper retains arbitrary graphs as an open case. | 2024-09-26: The author manuscript gives a smoothed superpolynomial lower bound for 3-FLIP and unperturbed exponential single-FLIP examples; both have a different scope from this target.
working_summary: Does FLIP for Max-Cut have polynomial expected path length on every graph under independent bounded-density edge weights? Each step moves just one vertex and must strictly increase the cut weight. The expectation controls the longest path after the weights are sampled, including all starting cuts and improving choices. Polynomial bounds for sparse graph families and a general high-probability bound do not finish this target. The known smoothed superpolynomial example permits three-vertex moves, while its single-vertex analogue is unperturbed.

title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
importance_reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational threshold question for a canonical random constraint model, connected to discrepancy algorithms, solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness; its scope concerns all efficient algorithms rather than a single construction.
formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.
question_excerpt: As \(\kappa  \to  0\), the algorithmic threshold for the 2 ). SBP is at \(\Theta\)(\(\kappa\) In particular, we conjecture that up to factors that are […]
definitions:
The dimension \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Margin \(\kappa\) and density \(\alpha\) are positive rational constants held fixed while \(n\) tends to infinity; write \(M=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\). The \(Mn\) entries of \(G\in\mathbb R^{M\times n}\) are mutually independent with probability density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). A feasible output is a full vector of \(n\) signs satisfying every displayed two-sided constraint. When \(M=0\), every sign vector is feasible. A failure symbol, a malformed vector or an infeasible vector counts as failure. No conditioning on satisfiability or planting of a hidden solution is performed.

The normalization is by \(\sqrt n\), the square root of the number of variables, and the density is constraints divided by variables. The symbol \(\kappa\) denotes the allowed absolute margin. All constraints are symmetric around zero; there is no one-sided inequality in place of the absolute value. This is the Gaussian version, not a matrix of independently uniform signs. For a nonzero row count the maximum is the usual infinity norm; the empty maximum is taken to be zero.

A permitted algorithm has a finite program with rational numerical constants and finite discrete control, real registers with exact arithmetic, and integer registers for array addresses and loop counters. It can read the supplied matrix, copy values, apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and branch on equality or order comparisons. Integer-address arithmetic is addition, subtraction and comparison; addresses used must be valid nonnegative integers. Each such instruction, register access, input access, output instruction and branch costs one operation. There is no floor, bit-extraction operation on a real register, arbitrary function oracle or infinite program-specific real constant. Division by zero must be handled by an explicit branch, not a source of extra computational power.

For internal randomness, the program may request independent fair bits or independent standard Gaussian real samples, each in one operation. These samples are independent of the input matrix and of all prior samples. The algorithm can be deterministic by making no random requests. There must be constants \(D>0\), \(d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that it halts after at most \(D(n+1)^d\) operations on every real input matrix of the required dimensions and every sequence of random choices, returning either a sign vector or failure. Space and all input inspection count through these operations. The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed rational pair \((\alpha,\kappa)\), but not on \(n\) or on the sampled matrix. No advice string depending on \(n\) is provided. Exact real arithmetic is a declared computational convention; operation count is not a bound on finite-precision bit complexity.

Let \(\mathcal D_\kappa\subseteq\mathbb Q_{>0}\) be the set of densities \(\alpha\) for which such an algorithm \(A\) exists with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{G,R}\bigl[A(G;R)\text{ returns a feasible sign vector}\bigr]=1.\]
Here the probability is over both the independent Gaussian entries and the algorithm's permitted internal randomness. The convergence need not have a supplied rate. The algorithm must be one uniform program for the full sequence of dimensions at the fixed parameter pair, rather than a different program at every dimension. Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\sup\bigl(\mathcal D_\kappa\cup\{0\}\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\]
The supremum need not be attained; this definition does not assume an algorithm at the threshold or an all-input guarantee. The main conjecture includes a finite upper bound for sufficiently small margins. Showing algorithms whose densities approach a claimed lower endpoint can establish a lower bound on the supremum even if no endpoint algorithm exists.

In the displayed asymptotic claim, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and \(\kappa\) approaches zero through positive rationals. The constants \(C,a,\kappa_0\) are chosen once before all those margins. The limit in \(n\) defining the threshold is taken first, separately for each fixed pair. No polynomial dependence of the running-time coefficient or exponent on \(1/\kappa\) is imposed. A statement for a shrinking margin \(\kappa(n)\), or for one fixed value such as \(\kappa=1\), is a different quantifier regime.

The two sides have different meanings: the lower side concerns the existence of successful algorithms at enough densities; the upper side bounds the success densities of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm. A geometric obstruction proved only for algorithms satisfying an additional stability property is not an upper bound for this unrestricted class. Failure to achieve success tending to one does not require success to tend to zero; there may be nonvanishing success or different subsequential behavior.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed two-sided polylogarithmic envelope for the defined threshold. A positive answer must establish both inequalities with one set of fixed constants in the declared computational, input-distribution and order-of-limits conventions. A refutation must exclude every permitted choice of those constants, rather than only a selected logarithmic exponent or the stronger claim with no logarithmic loss. Bounds restricted to stable algorithms, experiments, existence of solutions without efficient search, or a result conditional on an unproved lattice hardness assumption do not alone settle the statement. The benchmark target is the asymptotic conjecture, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its logarithmic-factor precision.
context:
The source conjectures a \(\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\) scale. The logarithmic allowance is part of that conjecture, while the separate question of removing a logarithmic factor and the sharper overlap-threshold prediction are not added to this card’s acceptance criterion.

The full source gives the \(\Theta(\kappa^2)\) algorithmic benchmark via Bansal–Spencer for Rademacher entries and expressly describes transfer of the same guarantee to Gaussian entries as expected. This distribution qualification is preserved; the card does not cite that corollary as a proved Gaussian lower bound.

The source’s geometric obstruction rules out classes of stable algorithms. A bound for a specified stable class is evidence for the conjecture, while a proof of the upper inequality must cover every program allowed here.

Vafa and Vaikuntanathan give worst-case lattice reductions for a margin specified as a function of the inverse aspect ratio. Their stronger logarithmic-scale hardness conclusion uses a stronger lattice assumption. These are conditional results with their own algorithm and parameter conventions; they do not by themselves prove this unconditional fixed-margin real-arithmetic threshold statement.

The January 2026 preprint proposes parametric threshold predictions and reports practical performance of an algorithm. Its abstract does not state a universal lower bound excluding every polynomial-time search algorithm in the model above.
why: The symmetric binary perceptron is a basic random constraint model in which many solutions can exist while known algorithms reach much smaller densities. Locating the small-margin search scale tests whether the observed computational obstruction captures all efficient algorithms or only particular algorithm families. Its links to discrepancy, random solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness make the threshold a substantial average-case complexity question.

Read the full 2022 Gaussian model, tilde-scale conjecture and Rademacher qualification; checked the July 2025 lattice paper’s Theorem 3, Corollary 2, Remark 1 and reduction conventions, and the January 2026 prediction preprint’s abstract. The explicit real-arithmetic convention resolves a specification omitted in the source; no equivalence with every finite-precision formulation is asserted. title: Algorithmic threshold for random k-SAT
importance_reason: A central statistical-versus-computational gap in random constraint satisfaction, with rigorous algorithms and restricted barriers but no general matching lower bound. Existing score retained.
formal: Does the randomized polynomial-time satisfying-assignment threshold for random \(k\)-SAT satisfy \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)}{2^{k}\ln(k)/k}=1?\] For each fixed \(k\), \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) is the supremum of constant clause densities at which some polynomial-time algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with probability tending to one as the number \(n\) of variables tends to infinity. The distribution and quantifiers are specified below.
question_excerpt: Given the existence of satisfying assignments for \(\alpha  = Ok (2k ), a\) natural algorithmic question arises: can we find such an assignment efficiently?
definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\geq3\) and a real constant density \(\alpha\geq0\). On Boolean variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\), generate \(m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) ordered clauses. Each clause has \(k\) literal positions, each independently uniform among \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{1},\ldots,\neg x_{n}\). The formula is the AND of these OR clauses. Sampling is with replacement: repeated literals, tautological clauses and repeated clauses are allowed.

The algorithm receives the entire explicit formula, with variable indices in binary, together with \(n\). It must output one full assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfying every clause. It may report failure otherwise. The input is sampled without conditioning on satisfiability and without planting or revealing any assignment.

A density \(\alpha\) is algorithmically attainable at width \(k\) if there is a classical randomized algorithm \(A\), with no advice depending on \(n\), such that its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the explicit input length and \(n\) on every input and random tape, and
\[\Pr_{\Phi,A}[A(\Phi)\text{ outputs a satisfying assignment of }\Phi]\longrightarrow1
\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]
The probability includes both the random formula and the algorithm's internal randomness. One fixed algorithm must work for all \(n\) at the chosen \(k,\alpha\). Its code, polynomial degree and constants may depend on those fixed parameters. They are not allowed to depend separately on each input length.

Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) be the supremum of all such densities. Attainment at the supremum is not required. First take \(n\to\infty\) at fixed \(k,\alpha\); only then consider the asymptotic behavior as \(k\to\infty\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This is a leading-order asymptotic question, not a request for an exact critical density at a particular small \(k\).

The target ranges over all randomized polynomial-time assignment-finding algorithms. It imposes no locality, stability, low-degree representation or restriction to a named heuristic. Deciding satisfiability without producing an assignment, satisfying only most clauses, or proving a barrier for a restricted algorithm family is a different guarantee.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed asymptotic equality, or refute it. The known algorithm gives the lower bound \(1-o_{k}(1)\) on the ratio, so the missing positive direction is the matching upper bound for all polynomial-time algorithms. A refutation must change the limiting leading-order behavior along arbitrarily large widths; an improvement confined to one fixed small width or a lower-order term does not suffice.
context:
For sufficiently large fixed \(k\), the satisfiability threshold is known and is asymptotic to \(2^{k}\ln 2\). This is about existence of an assignment; it does not provide an efficient way to find one throughout that range.

Coja-Oghlan’s Fix algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with high probability below \((1-\varepsilon_{k})2^{k}\ln(k)/k\), where \(\varepsilon_{k}\to0\). Thus the conjecture asks whether its leading asymptotic scale is optimal among all polynomial-time algorithms.

Bresler and Huang prove a low-degree obstruction above a constant multiple of this scale; their main stated constant is about \(4.911\), and their appendix discusses improvements. Theorem 2.6 concerns a specified normalized polynomial representation and requires a quantitatively small failure probability, stronger than an arbitrary \(o(1)\) failure rate. Their local-algorithm theorem rules out much smaller success probabilities within a narrower class. Neither theorem covers all polynomial-time algorithms.

The 2025 source explicitly retains the algorithmic conjecture. Its sharp geometric results for random SAT use growing clause width in the relevant exact-solution regime. They do not establish the fixed-width, all-algorithm upper bound asked here.
why: Pinpoints a possible computational barrier inside a regime where satisfying assignments typically exist. A resolution would clarify whether the geometry of random constraint problems predicts the power of arbitrary efficient algorithms, beyond individual heuristics and restricted computational models.
status_note: Read the conference source and full July 2025 version, the Fix publisher abstract and author introduction, and the full low-degree definitions and principal theorem statements. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for arbitrary polynomial-time assignment finding. The supremum definition spells out the source’s asymptotic algorithmic-threshold question. The source’s damaged saved density and its separate incidental logarithm typo are not used as mathematical definitions.

working_summary: The input is a random conjunction of fixed-width clauses, with all literal positions sampled independently. The algorithm must find an assignment satisfying every clause with probability tending to one. The conjectured leading threshold is two to the clause width times its natural logarithm, divided by the width. Known algorithms reach this scale, while satisfying assignments exist at substantially higher densities. Existing overlap-gap and low-degree barriers do not establish optimality against every polynomial-time algorithm.

title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.
focus_reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.
formal: Do absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree \(\Delta\) and every integer \(q\ge \Delta +2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^{c}\)?
definitions: Let \(n\ge 1\) and \(\Omega\)={\(\sigma :V(G)\to [q] : \sigma (u)\ne \sigma (v)\) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from \(V(G)\), then choose a colour uniformly from \([q]\)\\(\{\sigma (u):u\in N(v)\}\) and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega\). Define \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min \{t\in Z_{\ge 0}: \max _{\sigma \in \Omega} (1/2)\sum_{\tau \in \Omega}|\mathrm{P}^{t}(\sigma ,\tau )- \pi (\tau )|\le 1/4\}\). This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of \(n, \Delta , q\) and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold \(\Delta +2\) has a concrete role. On a clique with \(\Delta +1\) vertices and exactly \(\Delta +1\) colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least \(\Delta +2\) colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and \(q/(q- \Delta )\). That factor is at most \(1+\Delta /2\) in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’\(s q>2\Delta\) regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly \(11\Delta /6\). The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the \(11/6\) threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains \(\Delta +2\) as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes \(\Delta \ge 125\) and \(q\ge 1.809\Delta\) and proves \(O(n \log  n)\) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal \(O(n \log  n)\) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on \(\Delta\) and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves \(n^{O(\operatorname{tw}(G)^{3})}\) mixing with \(q\ge \Delta +2\), so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses \(q\ge (1+\varepsilon )(\Delta +1)\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting \(\varepsilon\) that shrinks with \(\Delta\), does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) mixing for the Metropolis chain when \(q\ge (1+\delta )\Delta , \Delta\) is sufficiently large in terms of fixed \(\delta >0\), and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap \(\Omega _{\delta}(1/n)\) and mixing time \(O_{\delta}(n^{2} \log  q+n \log (1/\varepsilon ))\); the sharper \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of \(\delta\). Both the girth restriction and the dependence on \(\delta\) matter. Taking \(\delta =2/\Delta\) is not justified by a theorem that first fixes \(\delta\) and then requires sufficiently large \(\Delta\).

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained \(\Delta +2\) conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.
why: A central boundary question for Markov-chain sampling: does the simplest local recolouring process mix efficiently whenever the universal ergodicity threshold is met?
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general-graph \(\Delta +2\) conjecture remains open in the checked sources. August 2026 results improve restricted-girth regimes with fixed relative slack; they do not establish the universal additive-two bound.

The reviewed question asks for polynomial-time convergence to the uniform distribution whenever the palette has at least two more colors than the maximum degree. That amount of slack makes the state space connected, but connectivity alone does not exclude bottlenecks that trap a random walk. A universal mixing bound would show that the simplest local sampler works throughout this universally convergent range. The saved progress covers restricted graph classes or larger relative color slack, whose parameter dependence does not establish the additive two-color target for every graph.

title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A central obstruction to a general theory of uniform sampling with fixed combinatorial marginals.
focus_reason: A central obstruction to a general theory of uniform sampling with fixed combinatorial marginals.
formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.
context:
Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.
why: A general guarantee for a basic sampler that preserves individual degrees, with applications to network and fixed-margin statistical models. The reported solution would close the gap between eventual convergence and a uniform polynomial sampling bound.

Each attempted move chooses a two-by-two rectangle and may exchange its two checkerboard patterns. The target is polynomial convergence to the uniform distribution for every feasible choice of margins and every starting matrix. Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 preprint states an explicit bound meeting this target and supplies a Lean formalization. The card records that claimed resolution with uncertain status because its proof and formalization were not independently verified here.

title: Polynomial mixing of critical three-dimensional Ising dynamics
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A fundamental question about efficient sampling at a phase transition in the standard three-dimensional Ising model.
formal:
For the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the three-dimensional box \(V_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^{3}\) with free boundary conditions, at the infinite-lattice critical inverse temperature \(\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) defined below, is the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time of random-site heat-bath dynamics polynomial in \(L\)? Precisely, do there exist constants \(C,a>0\) such that
\[\forall L\in\mathbb N,\ L\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)\le C(L+1)^a?\]
Time is counted in individual site-update attempts. The critical parameter is fixed independently of \(L\), and the target is the exact critical point, not a subcritical parameter approaching it at an unspecified rate.
definitions:
Let \(E_L\) contain each unordered pair of vertices of \(V_L\) at lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{3}|u_i-v_i|=1\), once. A configuration is \(\sigma\in\Omega_L=\{-1,+1\}^{V_L}\). At inverse temperature \(\beta\ge0\), the Gibbs probability is
\[\pi_{L,\beta}(\sigma)=Z_{L,\beta}^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\]
where \(Z_{L,\beta}\) is the sum of the displayed weight over all configurations. Each interaction strength is one, there is no external magnetic field, and free boundary means there are no interactions with vertices outside \(V_L\). Boundary vertices inside the box are updated just like other vertices.

To specify the critical inverse temperature without a numerical approximation, let \(B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^{3}\subset\mathbb Z^3\), for integers \(R\ge1\). Define \(\mu^+_{R,\beta}\) on spins in \(B_R\) by fixing all neighboring exterior spins to \(+1\): its weight is proportional to
\[\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\subset B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in B_R,\ v\notin B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right).\]
Internal unordered edges and crossing edges are each counted once. Set
\[m_+(\beta)=\inf_{R\ge1}\mathbb E_{\mu^+_{R,\beta}}[\sigma_0],\qquad\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m_+(\beta)>0\}.\]
The monotone limit of finite-volume plus-boundary magnetizations gives this standard infinite-lattice critical value, which is finite and positive. Plus boundaries are used only in defining the infinite-volume threshold; the finite chain being tested has free boundaries.

In one discrete step, choose a vertex \(v\) uniformly from the \(L^3\) sites, independently of previous choices. With \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\), redraw its spin as \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\]
and as \(-1\) otherwise, leaving all other spins unchanged. Choosing its existing value still counts as one step. Set \(\beta=\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) and denote the resulting transition matrix by \(P_L\). This finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has stationary measure \(\pi_L=\pi_{L,\beta_c}\).

For distributions on \(\Omega_L\), \(\operatorname{TV}(\nu,\pi)=\frac12\sum_{\sigma\in\Omega_L}|\nu(\sigma)-\pi(\sigma)|\). Define
\[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega_L}\operatorname{TV}(P_L^t(\sigma,\cdot),\pi_L)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes every deterministic initial spin configuration. The question concerns this exact mathematical Markov chain; approximating its transition probabilities on finite-precision hardware is not an additional task. Rates in a continuous-time convention with one rate-one clock per site have an extra factor of the volume relative to individual updates; that normalization does not affect polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the polynomial mixing bound or its negation for this exact model. A positive proof must establish finite constants independent of \(L\), with the critical parameter, free boundaries, update rule, worst initial state and distance threshold specified here. A negative proof must show that no fixed polynomial bounds this sequence of mixing times. Results at a tree threshold, in another lattice dimension, below criticality, with different boundaries or from a restricted initialization do not meet the criterion.
context:
Bauerschmidt and Dagallier relate functional inequalities for Ising dynamics to susceptibility bounds. Their critical finite-volume application uses mean-field susceptibility behavior and yields polynomial control on free-boundary lattice boxes in dimensions at least five. The checked result does not establish the needed hypothesis or conclusion in dimension three.

The source also distinguishes the earlier two-dimensional critical theorem from the higher-dimensional argument. Having polynomial mixing in dimension two and in dimensions at least five leaves the three-dimensional target separate; interpolation between dimensions is not a stated theorem.

The 2024 Prodromidis–Sly note proves polynomial mixing at the uniqueness threshold of the infinite regular tree for bounded-degree graphs. At degree six its parameter is \(\operatorname{arctanh}(1/5)\). The word critical in that title refers to the tree threshold, not to the infinite cubic lattice threshold defined in this card.

Boundary conditions materially affect low-temperature dynamics. The source contrasts slow mixing with free boundaries and a different conjecture under all-plus boundaries. Keeping the free-boundary convention is necessary to preserve this card’s specific critical-lattice question.
why: This is a basic question about whether a standard local sampling dynamics remains efficient at a phase transition in three dimensions. The equilibrium system has correlations on many scales, so high-temperature mixing guarantees do not directly apply. A polynomial bound or a superpolynomial obstruction would clarify the computational cost of critical fluctuations in one of the central lattice models.

The parameter in their theorem is distinguished from the cubic-lattice critical point.
working_summary: This question concerns local heat-bath sampling of the Ising model at the critical point of the infinite cubic lattice. The finite system is a three-dimensional box with free boundaries and zero external field. It asks whether every initial spin configuration becomes close to equilibrium after polynomially many individual updates. The critical inverse temperature is specified by the infinite-volume magnetization threshold, without relying on a numerical estimate. Known critical results in other dimensions and at the regular-tree threshold do not settle this three-dimensional lattice problem.

title: Polynomial mixing of planar Ising dynamics with plus boundaries
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A long-standing model question about whether boundary phase selection makes local sampling efficient throughout the planar Ising model’s low-temperature regime. It connects geometric interface relaxation with worst-state Markov-chain mixing and remains explicitly open in 2026 primary work.
formal:
For every fixed finite inverse temperature \(\beta\in[0,\infty)\), does random-site heat-bath Glauber dynamics for the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}\), with all exterior boundary spins fixed to \(+1\), mix in time polynomial in \(n\)? Precisely, is it true that
\[\forall\beta\in[0,\infty)\ \exists C_\beta,a_\beta>0\ \forall n\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}^+(n,\beta,1/4)\le C_\beta(n+1)^{a_\beta}?\]
The mixing time is worst-case over every initial configuration inside the box and counts individual site-update attempts. The constants may depend on the fixed temperature, but not on \(n\). The finite-temperature convention and the update rule are specified below.
definitions:
Vertices are adjacent when their lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=|u_1-v_1|+|u_2-v_2|\) is one. Let \(E_n\) consist of the unordered adjacent pairs inside \(V_n\), and let \(\partial V_n\) be the vertices outside \(V_n\) adjacent to it. A state is \(\sigma\in\Omega_n=\{-1,+1\}^{V_n}\). Extend it to \(\widetilde\sigma\) by assigning \(+1\) to every vertex of \(\partial V_n\). The Gibbs measure is
\[\pi_{n,\beta}^+(\sigma)=\frac1{Z_{n,\beta}^+}\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_n}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in V_n,\ v\in\partial V_n\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right),\]
where the normalizing constant is the sum of this weight over \(\Omega_n\). Internal and crossing edges are each counted once and all interaction strengths are one. There is no external field beyond the effect of the fixed boundary spins. A corner vertex has two crossing edges; each contributes to its local field.

At each discrete step choose \(v\in V_n\) uniformly and independently, and replace \(\sigma_v\) by \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\qquad h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\|u-v\|_1=1}\widetilde\sigma_u,\]
and by \(-1\) otherwise. The other interior spins are unchanged and exterior spins are never updated. An update that retains the old value counts as a step. For every finite \(\beta\), the chain has strictly positive conditional probabilities, is irreducible and aperiodic, and has stationary measure \(\pi_{n,\beta}^+\). Denote its transition matrix by \(P_{n,\beta}^+\).

Total-variation distance between distributions \(\nu,\pi\) on the finite state space is \(\operatorname{TV}(\nu,\pi)=\frac12\sum_{\sigma\in\Omega_n}|\nu(\sigma)-\pi(\sigma)|\). Define
\[t_{\mathrm{mix}}^+(n,\beta,1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega_n}\operatorname{TV}((P_{n,\beta}^+)^t(\sigma,\cdot),\pi_{n,\beta}^+)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes the all-minus interior configuration; it is not restricted to typical or mostly-plus starts. The boundary is plus throughout, regardless of the interior initial state.

Inverse temperature is measured in units with interaction strength and Boltzmann constant equal to one. The domain includes \(\beta=0\), the independent-spin infinite-temperature limit, and every positive physical temperature, but not the separate zero-temperature limit \(\beta=\infty\). The quantified statement is pointwise in fixed \(\beta\); it does not demand common constants for temperatures varying with \(n\). In the continuous-time convention with one rate-one clock per interior site, the typical update count per unit time is \(n^2\). This polynomial factor preserves the question of a polynomial mixing bound, but matters when comparing exact exponents. This card studies the exact mathematical chain, not finite-precision implementation of its probabilities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed all-finite-temperatures polynomial bound or its negation. A positive answer must cover every fixed finite \(\beta\) and every interior initial state with all-plus boundaries. A negative answer must establish at least one fixed finite inverse temperature for which no polynomial in box side length bounds the specified mixing time. Bounds only from biased initializations, only in the zero-temperature limit, or of quasipolynomial size do not meet the target.
context:
Question 1 of the source is explicitly two-dimensional: an n by n grid with all-plus boundaries. Its remarks about higher dimensions are related context, not an enlargement of this card’s quantifiers.

The published Lubetzky–Martinelli–Sly–Toninelli bound is \(n^{c(\beta)\log n}\) in the low-temperature regime. It is a substantial improvement over earlier subexponential bounds, but its exponent grows with \(n\), so it is not polynomial.

The May 2026 Gheissari–Sly preprint still identifies polynomial plus-boundary mixing as a long-standing open problem. Its Theorem 4 strengthens control of the temperature dependence in a quasipolynomial bound. Its rapid phase-ordering theorem uses biased initial configurations and a different convergence target, rather than providing the worst-state polynomial mixing bound here.

Zero-temperature interface dynamics and finite-temperature mixing are distinct statements. The new preprint discusses the known zero-temperature polynomial bounds as supporting evidence, while retaining the finite-temperature question. The card fixes finite inverse temperature to avoid treating a non-irreducible limiting chain as the same ergodic model.
why: This question asks whether fixing a coherent boundary phase is enough to make local sampling efficient at every positive temperature. At low temperature, convergence from an opposing interior phase is controlled by the disappearance of large interfaces. A polynomial bound would quantify how boundary information removes the slow phase switching that occurs under other boundary conditions.

title: Cutoff for bounded-degree transitive expanders
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A central cutoff conjecture connecting expansion, spatial symmetry and abrupt equilibration. It asks for a general principle on sparse graphs used throughout theoretical computer science, rather than another estimate for one random-walk family.
formal:
Does every sequence of bounded-degree vertex-transitive expander graphs exhibit total-variation cutoff for lazy simple random walk? More precisely, consider any sequence \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) of finite connected undirected simple graphs, with \(N_k=|V(G_k)|\to\infty\). Assume each \(G_k\) is vertex-transitive, that there is a fixed integer \(D\ge3\) with \(3\le d_k\le D\) for its vertex degree \(d_k\), and that the lazy-walk spectral gaps satisfy \(\gamma_k\ge\delta\) for some constant \(\delta>0\) independent of \(k\). Must
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{t_k(\varepsilon)}{t_k(1-\varepsilon)}=1?\]
The transition rule and worst-start mixing times \(t_k\) are defined below. The constants \(D\) and \(\delta\) may depend on the sequence. No quantitative cutoff window or common leading constant for different sequences is demanded.
definitions:
A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. Vertex-transitive means that for any vertices \(x,y\) there is a bijection of the vertex set preserving adjacency in both directions and mapping \(x\) to \(y\). Consequently all its vertices have the same degree \(d_k\). The graph sequence is deterministic and need not come from a particular construction or a random-graph model.

One lazy-walk step stays at the current vertex with probability \(1/2\), and otherwise chooses a neighbor uniformly and moves there. Its transition matrix is
\[P_k(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/2&y=x,\\1/(2d_k)&\{x,y\}\in E(G_k),\\0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
The stationary probability is \(\pi_k(y)=1/N_k\). List the real eigenvalues in decreasing order as \(1=\lambda_{1,k}>\lambda_{2,k}\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_{N_k,k}\ge0\), and set \(\gamma_k=1-\lambda_{2,k}\). A uniformly positive lower bound on \(\gamma_k\), together with bounded degree, is the expander assumption used here. Laziness includes bipartite graphs without periodicity problems.

At an integer time \(t\ge0\), let
\[d_k(t)=\max_{x\in V(G_k)}\frac12\sum_{y\in V(G_k)}\left|P_k^t(x,y)-\frac1{N_k}\right|,\qquad t_k(\eta)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_k(t)\le\eta\}\quad(0<\eta<1).\]
The maximum is over every starting vertex. Times count discrete lazy steps, including steps that stay put. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), the denominator \(t_k(1-\varepsilon)\) is positive for all sufficiently large \(k\); the limit uses this eventual tail. The displayed ratio condition defines total-variation cutoff. It asks that the transition between distance near one and distance near zero occupy a vanishing fraction of the mixing time.

The source first states the question with one fixed degree. Allowing degree to vary in a fixed finite range is equivalent at the level of this universal conjecture: each degree occurring infinitely often gives a fixed-degree subsequence. Neither degrees growing without bound nor expansion constants tending to zero are admitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every sequence satisfying the hypotheses has the displayed cutoff property, or a Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must establish a sequence satisfying every hypothesis for which the ratio limit fails for at least one fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\). A single finite graph cannot refute an asymptotic cutoff statement. Logarithmic mixing-time bounds alone, cutoff in a different distance, or a result only for a special class of expanders do not meet the criterion.
context:
The textbook asks this question for a fixed degree and explicitly chooses lazy random walk. The card retains that walk and the total-variation meaning of cutoff, while making the graph-sequence and uniform-gap quantifiers explicit.

Salez’s 2025 notes state the vertex-transitive expander conjecture as Problem 2.3. The notes explain that expansion already gives mixing time of logarithmic order in the graph size; cutoff asks for substantially finer asymptotic information.

Lubetzky and Peres prove cutoff for simple random walk on non-bipartite \(d\)-regular Ramanujan graphs, where all adjacency eigenvalues other than \(d\) have absolute value at most \(2\sqrt{d-1}\). This is a much stronger spectral condition than an arbitrary fixed positive gap. Their result supplies a major special case, not a proof for every transitive expander.
why: Expanders combine sparse connectivity with fast random-walk mixing and are central objects in algorithms and pseudorandomness. This conjecture asks whether spatial symmetry forces their approach to equilibrium to be abrupt. A resolution would separate the role of expansion in the speed of mixing from the role of symmetry in the shape of convergence.

This question asks whether vertex symmetry forces a sharp transition to equilibrium in every bounded-degree expander sequence. The model uses a lazy walk, a uniformly positive spectral gap and graph sizes tending to infinity. Cutoff requires the mixing times at any two fixed total-variation accuracy levels to become asymptotically equal.
