title: Weakly negatively regressive sampling of matroid bases
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A general matroid rounding question connecting prescribed marginals, negative dependence and submodular optimization; its scope covers all matroids and its consequences extend beyond a particular objective or sampling construction.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every finite matroid \(M\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) given by an independence oracle and every rational point \(p\) of its base polytope, samples a basis \(B\) with exact marginals
\[\Pr[i\in B]=p_i\quad(i\in[n])\]
and a weakly negatively regressive output distribution, in expected time polynomial in \(n\) and the binary encoding length of \(p\)?

Here weak negative regression (WNR) requires, simultaneously for every \(i\in[n]\) and every increasing function \(f:2^{[n]\setminus\{i\}}\to\mathbb R\),
\[\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{i\in B\}} f(B\setminus\{i\})]\le p_i\,\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})].\]
The algorithm receives no objective function \(f\). One output law must satisfy all these inequalities.

This card selects WNR, the weakest of the three alternative dependence requirements in the source question. Negative association or negative regression would also suffice by implying WNR. The independence-oracle, rational-input and exact expected-time sampling conventions below make the source's efficiency question precise; they are explicit editorial conventions.
definitions:
A matroid \(M=([n],\mathcal I)\), with \(n\ge1\), consists of a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) of independent sets. If \(A\in\mathcal I\) and \(A'\subseteq A\), then \(A'\in\mathcal I\). If \(A,D\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|D|\), some \(e\in D\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). A basis is an inclusion-maximal member of \(\mathcal I\); all bases have the same cardinality. Let \(\mathcal B(M)\) be their family, including the singleton family containing the empty set for a rank-zero matroid.

The base polytope is
\[P_B(M)=\left\{\sum_{B\in\mathcal B(M)}\lambda_B\mathbf 1_B:\lambda_B\ge0,\ \sum_B\lambda_B=1\right\},\]
where \(\mathbf 1_B\in\{0,1\}^n\) is the incidence vector. This is the convex hull of bases, as specified by the source's maximal-independent-set convention. It is distinct from the convex hull of all independent sets.

An oracle query supplies an \(n\)-bit incidence vector for a set \(A\) and receives the exact bit indicating whether \(A\in\mathcal I\). The oracle is fixed throughout a run and is promised to describe a matroid. The input gives \(n\) in binary and \(p_i=a_i/b_i\), with binary integers \(0\le a_i\le b_i\) and \(b_i\ge1\). Let \(L\) be their total encoding length. The promise is \(p\in P_B(M)\); membership testing is not an additional required output. A convex decomposition of \(p\), an explicit list of bases and a sampling oracle are not supplied.

Use a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with this independence oracle and independent fair random bits. All ordinary bit operations, random-bit generation, oracle-query preparation and output writing count toward time; obtaining the answer to a completed oracle query costs one additional step. There must be fixed constants \(C,d\) such that expected total work is at most \(C(n+L+1)^d\) on every promised input and every matroid oracle. These constants and the machine are independent of the instance. No arbitrary real-arithmetic operations or nonuniform advice are available.

The machine must halt with probability one, and every terminating run must output the incidence vector of a basis. Its probability law over outputs must have the exact stated marginals and satisfy WNR without an additive tolerance. There is no failure output or exceptional probability on which feasibility or the distributional guarantees may fail. Expected time permits exact sampling with rational probabilities whose denominators are not powers of two. Independent invocations use fresh random bits; a joint coupling across different inputs is not required.

Increasing means \(f(A)\le f(D)\) whenever \(A\subseteq D\). The domain is finite, so each real-valued \(f\) has finite expectation. For \(0<p_i<1\), the displayed WNR inequality is equivalent to
\[\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\in B]\le\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\notin B].\]
For \(p_i=0\) or \(p_i=1\), the unconditional inequality is automatically an equality and does not invoke undefined conditional probabilities. WNR concerns all increasing functions of the remaining coordinates, not just pairwise covariances or linear functions.

For context, a set function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular when \(F(A)+F(D)\ge F(A\cup D)+F(A\cap D)\) for all sets \(A,D\). Submodular dominance at marginals \(p\) means \(\mathbb E[F(B)]\ge\mathbb E[F(R_p)]\) for every such \(F\), where \(R_p\) includes each element independently with probability \(p_i\). This consequence of WNR is not a substitute for the stronger specified distributional target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement in the declared oracle and bit-computation model. A positive answer must establish one uniform sampler, exact feasibility and marginals, all WNR inequalities, almost-sure termination and the expected polynomial resource bound for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such sampler exists; it need not show that a WNR law is nonexistent for any individual input. A theorem that only supplies a distribution nonconstructively, approximate marginals, pairwise negative correlation, submodular dominance, or a sampler for a restricted class of matroids does not by itself meet the full criterion.
context:
The 2022 question asks about sampling for arbitrary matroid marginals with WNR, negative association or negative regression. The latter two properties each imply WNR. This card adopts the first listed branch and retains arbitrary matroids; it does not impose one particular rounding procedure.

WNR implies submodular dominance: every submodular objective has expectation at least that under independent inclusion with the same marginals. Matching marginals alone fixes linear objectives, but does not establish this nonlinear guarantee.

The source reports a gap in an earlier claimed negative-association sampler for general matroids. It also observes that maximum-entropy matroid distributions need not have the required negative dependence, because even uniform distributions can have positively correlated coordinates.

The 2026 journal paper proves dimension-free submodular lower-tail bounds under one-negative association, equivalent to WNR for binary variables. Its introduction continues to flag the gap in the earlier general-matroid sampling claim and leaves the dependence properties of standard matroid rounding procedures open. These are conditional consequences of the dependence property, not a construction for every matroid.

The 2026 correlated-sampling paper gives cardinality-constrained rounding with preserved marginals and submodular dominance. Its discussion of negative association includes a known hypersimplex sampling law, and the introduction mentions a partition-matroid extension. Cardinality and partition constraints are special cases of matroids; the paper does not establish the arbitrary-matroid target here.
why: Randomized rounding must reconcile combinatorial feasibility with the dependence created by exact marginal requirements. This question asks whether every matroid base point has an efficiently accessible law controlling all monotone effects of conditioning on one coordinate. Such a general sampling theorem would support objective-independent rounding and strong guarantees for nonlinear submodular objectives, beyond the linear expectations fixed by marginals alone.

title: Monotonicity of Ising spectral gaps
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A general comparison principle for the relaxation of ferromagnetic sampling, combining temperature and graph modifications. Its significance lies in a universal relation between interactions and dynamics, beyond bounds for one lattice or one parameter regime.
formal:
Does strengthening any collection of ferromagnetic interactions always weakly decrease the spectral gap of zero-field random-site heat-bath Ising dynamics on a fixed finite vertex set? For every integer \(n\ge1\), put \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Let \(J=(J_{uv})_{u<v}\) and \(J'=(J'_{uv})_{u<v}\) be finite nonnegative real interaction strengths on the unordered vertex pairs. Is the following statement true?
\[\bigl[\forall u<v,\ 0\le J_{uv}\le J'_{uv}\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\gamma(J')\le\gamma(J).\]
Here \(\gamma\) is the spectral gap per individual uniformly chosen site update, defined below. There is no external magnetic field or fixed boundary spin. This is the common interaction-strength generalization explicitly asked in Question 2 of the source.
definitions:
The state space is \(\Omega=\{-1,+1\}^{V}\). Use the symmetric convention \(J_{vu}=J_{uv}\) and \(J_{vv}=0\). The Gibbs probability of a configuration is
\[\pi_J(\sigma)=Z_J^{-1}\exp\!\left(\sum_{u<v}J_{uv}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\qquad Z_J=\sum_{\tau\in\Omega}\exp\!\left(\sum_{u<v}J_{uv}\tau_u\tau_v\right).\]
Each unordered pair is counted once. A zero interaction means the corresponding edge is absent, so arbitrary finite graphs, isolated vertices and edge additions are included. Inverse temperature is absorbed into the interactions. All couplings are finite; the infinite-coupling limit is not a separate input.

At each step choose \(v\in V\) uniformly, independently of previous choices. Set \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u\ne v}J_{uv}\sigma_u\). Replace the spin at \(v\) by \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-h_v(\sigma))},\]
and by \(-1\) otherwise; all other spins stay fixed. Retaining the current spin counts as one update. Write \(P_J(\sigma,\tau)\) for this transition probability. The chain is finite, irreducible and reversible with stationary distribution \(\pi_J\).

For \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\), set \(\overline f_J=\sum_\sigma\pi_J(\sigma)f(\sigma)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_J}(f)=\sum_\sigma\pi_J(\sigma)(f(\sigma)-\overline f_J)^2\). Define
\[\gamma(J)=\inf_{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_J}(f)>0}\frac{\frac12\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Omega}\pi_J(\sigma)P_J(\sigma,\tau)(f(\sigma)-f(\tau))^2}{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_J}(f)}.\]
Equivalently, this is \(1-\lambda_2(P_J)\), with eigenvalues ordered decreasingly and the stationary eigenvalue \(1\) first. The heat-bath matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues because it averages conditional-expectation projections. Thus the spectral and absolute spectral gap agree for this update rule. The relaxation time is \(1/\gamma(J)\).

Both compared chains have exactly the same \(n\) sites and site-selection probabilities. Adding an edge does not add a vertex or rescale the clock. The assertion uses a non-strict inequality and does not assume differentiability of eigenvalues. The question is about exact real transition matrices; numerical simulation or a choice of finite-precision implementation does not define the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal implication, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may specify a finite vertex set and two allowed interaction arrays \(J\le J'\) and prove \(\gamma(J')>\gamma(J)\). A positive answer must cover arbitrary graph structure and independent changes in edge strengths, including edges of initial strength zero. A theorem only for common rescaling of all interactions, or for a restricted family of graphs, does not establish the universal claim. Approximate eigenvalue calculations require rigorous bounds certifying the claimed strict reversal.
context:
For fixed nonnegative physical edge weights \(K\), changing inverse temperature replaces \(J\) by \(\beta K\). The proposed interaction-wise inequality therefore implies that the spectral gap increases with physical temperature. Allowing zero strengths also includes the edge-addition question. The source separately asks about monotonicity of total-variation distances at fixed times; that stronger question is not part of this card’s answer criterion.

Nacu proves monotonicity in each individual coupling on a cycle. The argument also permits zero strengths by a limiting convention, including the path obtained by removing a cycle edge. This remains a graph-family result.

Kargin proves temperature monotonicity for the complete graph when all interaction strengths are equal and varied together. The theorem allows a uniform fixed external field, and hence includes zero field. Its one-parameter comparison does not establish independent edge-wise monotonicity on general graphs.

Salez’s 2023 theorem identifies the spectral gap of an order-preserving Markov chain with its optimal curvature. In that work, monotone means preservation of increasing functions of the state. It is distinct from the proposed comparison between chains with different interaction arrays.
why: The conjecture asks whether stronger attractive interactions universally slow the relaxation of local sampling. A positive answer would give a comparison principle across both temperature and graph structure, while a counterexample would expose a limit of that basic physical intuition. The difficulty is a global dynamical property, even though each update uses only the neighboring spins.

title: Mixing of the self-avoiding-walk pivot chain
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A substantial gap between a widely used polymer-sampling method and rigorous control of equilibration from arbitrary starts. The target connects geometric constraints, nonlocal Monte Carlo moves and worst-state mixing, beyond implementation tuning.
formal:
Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\) of the following pivot chain on rooted \(n\)-step self-avoiding walks in the square lattice. The target is an asymptotic order \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) for which there exist constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge1\) such that
\[c\,h(n)\le t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\le C\,h(n)\qquad\text{for every }n\ge n_0.\]
A step is one attempted pivot, including a rejected proposal. The exact proposal distribution and the distance threshold \(1/4\) are fixed below. This is an explicitly selected asymptotic mixing-time formulation of the source’s broader request to analyze convergence.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), the finite state space \(\Omega_n\) consists of sequences \(\omega=(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\) such that \(\omega_0=(0,0)\), \(\|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1\) for \(0\le i<n\), and \(\omega_i\ne\omega_j\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Here \(\|(x,y)\|_1=|x|+|y|\). Walks are ordered, rooted at the origin and not identified under rotation, reflection or reversal. There is no confining box or additional energy weight. Let \(\pi_n\) give equal probability \(1/|\Omega_n|\) to each walk.

In one step independently choose \(k\) uniformly from \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S\) uniformly from these five maps:
\[(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y).\]
These are the three nontrivial quarter-turn rotations and the two coordinate-axis reflections in Example B.5. Propose
\[\omega'_i=\begin{cases}\omega_i&i\le k,\\\omega_k+S(\omega_i-\omega_k)&i>k.\end{cases}\]
If the proposal belongs to \(\Omega_n\), accept it; otherwise keep \(\omega\). In either case the time increases by one. Fresh choices are independent at subsequent steps. In particular \(k=n\) always leaves the walk unchanged. Denote this transition matrix by \(P_n\).

The proposal maps occur with the same probabilities as their inverses, so the chain is reversible for \(\pi_n\). The irreducibility established in the source, together with the positive holding probability, gives a unique stationary law and convergence to it. Define
\[d_n(t)=\max_{\omega\in\Omega_n}\frac12\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_n}\left|P_n^t(\omega,\eta)-\pi_n(\eta)\right|,\qquad t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_n(t)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes every valid walk, not just a straight walk, an equilibrium start, or a numerically typical configuration.

The clock counts proposals rather than CPU operations or accepted pivots. Testing whether a proposed walk intersects itself is part of implementing a transition, but its computational cost is not multiplied into this mathematical mixing time. The textbook’s instruction to repeat after rejection is interpreted as proceeding to the next proposal with the old state retained, as explicitly specified in Clisby’s standard pivot dynamics. Discarding all rejected attempts from the clock would define a different chain and is not the convention here.
answer_criterion: Supply a non-circular asymptotic description \(h(n)\) and complete mathematically correct Lean-checked upper and lower bounds establishing the displayed inequalities for the specified chain. The constants must be independent of \(n\). A function defined merely by renaming the unknown mixing time is not a determination. A polynomial upper bound alone is a partial result unless it comes with a matching-order lower bound. Average cost per update, autocorrelation estimates for selected observables, empirical equilibration tests and a different sampling algorithm do not establish worst-state total-variation mixing of this chain.
context:
Example B.5 fixes the square lattice and five allowed symmetries, proves irreducibility, and leaves convergence behavior open. The card preserves that geometry and proposal set. It makes asymptotic worst-state mixing the concrete target rather than requiring an unspecified convergence analysis.

Clisby explicitly retains the old walk on a rejected pivot and identifies detailed balance with the uniform law. The card uses that standard rejection convention to specify exactly what a Markov-chain step means.

Clisby’s work substantially improves the computational implementation of individual pivots. Its introduction and autocorrelation study distinguish heuristic and numerical performance evidence from a rigorous worst-state bound on total-variation mixing. A fast transition implementation by itself does not establish the mixing-time order requested here.

The source also mentions the Randall–Sinclair approximate sampler, which uses a different underlying Markov chain. Existence of another sampler does not determine the convergence rate of the fixed pivot chain.
why: The pivot algorithm is a major sampling method for self-avoiding walks, a basic model of polymers with excluded volume. Its practical efficiency makes the absence of a matching rigorous convergence analysis especially consequential. Determining its mixing order would quantify when samples have forgotten an arbitrary initial shape, beyond the behavior of a few measured observables.

title: Deterministic approximation scheme for graph cover times
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A persistent deterministic-versus-randomized approximation question for a fundamental global exploration statistic. Arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on all graphs asks for more than the known universal constant-factor comparison or special-family algorithms.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the expected cover time of simple random walk from a specified starting vertex of an arbitrary finite connected undirected simple graph? Specifically, does there exist one deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every integer \(q\ge2\), there are constants \(C_q,a_q>0\) for which every allowed \(n\)-vertex input \((G,v,q)\) is processed within \(C_q(n+1)^{a_q}\) bit operations and the output rational number \(\widehat C\ge0\) satisfies
\[\left|\widehat C-C(G,v)\right|\le\frac{C(G,v)}q?\]
Here \(C(G,v)\) is defined below. The runtime is polynomial in graph size for every fixed accuracy \(1/q\); its exponent may depend on \(q\). This restores the relative-approximation question actually stated by Aldous and Fill, rather than the unsupported exact-output wording in the imported draft.
definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. It is promised connected. Its encoding consists of \(n\) in unary followed by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix, a binary starting label \(v\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the integer accuracy parameter \(q\ge2\) in binary, with standard self-delimiting integer fields. All graph families and degrees are allowed; in particular there is no bounded-degree or rapid-mixing promise.

For \(n\ge2\), let \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the discrete-time walk with \(X_0=v\). At each step it independently chooses a uniformly random neighbor of its current vertex. It has no added holding probability. Define
\[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=V(G)\},\qquad C(G,v)=\mathbb E_v[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}].\]
The initial vertex is already visited at time zero, and time counts edge traversals. There is no requirement to return to \(v\) after the last new vertex is visited. For \(n=1\), put \(C(G,v)=0\). Connectedness guarantees finite expectation. The quantity \(\max_v C(G,v)\), often called the graph’s cover time, is related but is not substituted for the supplied-start expectation.

The algorithm is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no random bits, advice or sampling oracle. Input processing, rational arithmetic and output writing count toward the runtime. Its output is a pair of binary integers representing a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. The required inequality holds for every input, not merely with high probability. When \(n=1\), it requires output zero.

The integer \(q\) represents reciprocal relative accuracy. This discretization covers any fixed requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). The constants \(C_q,a_q\) are independent of the graph and the starting vertex. No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is demanded; that would be the stronger fully polynomial scheme. Nor is an exact numerator and denominator for the unknown expectation demanded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that an algorithm with the displayed correctness and runtime guarantees exists, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must work at arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on every allowed graph and starting vertex. A constant-factor estimate, a randomized approximation, a theorem restricted to trees or a promise on hitting times, and a procedure that computes only the worst-start maximum do not establish the stated scheme. An exponential-time exact formula by itself does not establish the polynomial-time guarantee.
context:
Section 6.8.3 explicitly introduces numerical evaluation of the supplied-start expectation up to a fixed factor \(1\pm\varepsilon\), then asks for deterministic polynomial time. The older imported title “exact cover time” omitted this convention. This review restores the original accuracy and starting-vertex scope; exact computation remains a stronger possible route to a positive answer, not a requirement.

The 2017 textbook notes describe exponential-size exact computation and then cite Aldous–Fill’s question in compressed form. They also record the later constant-factor approximation. Reading the original accuracy convention avoids treating those sentences as a new explicitly exact-output conjecture.

Ding, Lee and Peres give a deterministic constant-factor approximation for the maximum expected cover time over starting vertices. Their theorem resolves that weaker approximation question; neither the precision nor the starting-vertex guarantee is the full target of this card.

Feige and Zeitouni obtain a fully polynomial approximation for trees. Their main theorem concerns cover and return, and Section 3.2 extends the method to ordinary cover time from a specified vertex. The tree restriction is essential to the scope of the cited result.

Meka’s 2015 Gaussian-process approximation theorem has a cover-time application on bounded-degree graph sequences satisfying \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}=o(t_{\mathrm{cov}})\), as specified in Section 1.1. Here \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}\) is the maximum expected time to hit one vertex from another and \(t_{\mathrm{cov}}=\max_v C(G,v)\). The application is qualified by that assumption and does not assert this card’s all-graph, supplied-start guarantee.
why: Cover time is a global measure of how efficiently a random walk explores a network. It is readily estimated by randomized simulation, while deterministic evaluation must account for the distribution of entire exploration histories. A scheme for arbitrary graphs would resolve a concrete derandomization question about an important graph parameter, with accuracy beyond universal constant-factor estimates.

title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
importance_reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.
focus_reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.
formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number \(Z(G)\) of perfect matchings in every finite undirected simple graph G? More precisely, is there one randomized algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every explicitly encoded graph G and rational \(0<\varepsilon <1, A\) halts within \(p(\mathrm{L},\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil )\) bit operations and outputs a nonnegative rational Ẑ satisfying \(\Pr [(1- \varepsilon )Z(G)\le \hat\{Z\}\le (1+\varepsilon )Z(G)]\ge 3/4\), where L is the total binary input length?
definitions: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. It is perfect if every vertex is incident to exactly one selected edge. \(Z(G)\) is the number of distinct such edge sets; edges and vertices are unweighted. The graph is specified by a labeled vertex set and its full edge list, without bipartiteness, density, degree, expansion or planarity promises. For an odd number of vertices \(Z(G)=0\); for the empty graph \(Z(G)=1\). The random bits are independent fair bits, all computational and output costs are counted, and the time bound holds for every random tape. When \(Z(G)=0\), require output zero with probability one; this causes no loss of generality because existence of a perfect matching can be decided deterministically in polynomial time before approximation begins. The fixed success probability \(3/4\) can be amplified to \(1- \delta\) by independent repetitions and a median, with an \(O(\log (1/\delta ))\) multiplicative overhead. The same polynomial p must work for all graphs and all requested accuracies. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Finding a perfect matching and estimating how many exist are different tasks. Edmonds’ algorithm handles existence and maximum cardinality in general graphs, whereas exact counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs. Approximation avoids asking for every digit of a potentially exponential count, but still requires a reliable multiplicative estimate. The 2018 paper of Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes places this gap at the center of general matching-counting research.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda resolve the bipartite case through an FPRAS for the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. A square bipartite adjacency matrix records allowed pairs between two fixed vertex classes; a permutation chooses one partner for every vertex. The algorithm combines a Markov chain on perfect and near-perfect matchings with simulated annealing and weights that balance different pairs of unmatched vertices.

Applying that theorem to the ordinary adjacency matrix of a nonbipartite graph does not count its perfect matchings. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine: the latter also counts directed cycle-cover patterns. The corresponding general-graph quantity is a hafnian, a sum over partitions of the vertex set into unordered pairs. The distinction is combinatorial, not a matter of merely changing the matrix dimensions.

Counting all matchings is another solved neighboring problem: Jerrum and Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function. The desired perfect matchings may form a very small fraction of that distribution. A disjoint union of k edges already has \(2^{k}\) matchings and just one perfect matching. Thus approximate uniform sampling from all matchings, followed by waiting for a perfect one, need not run in polynomial time. This example concerns that proposed reduction, not hardness of counting on the example graph.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes show that the straightforward extension of the JSV chain encounters exponential mixing bottlenecks on general graphs; changing weights based only on the unmatched-vertex pattern does not give a universal remedy. They also use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to obtain algorithms for structurally restricted graphs. A factor-critical component is one whose deletion of any one vertex leaves a perfect matching. Their parameter concerns the number of ears in such a component’s ear decomposition, not simply its vertex count.

The problem matters beyond matching counts themselves. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s 2025 journal paper classifies approximation of several two-state spin-system partition functions. Some parameter settings are linked by approximation-preserving reductions to perfect-matching counting in general graphs, and the paper explicitly retains that task as a central open question. A resolution would therefore determine tractability for related counting models as well.

On 27 August 2026, Chen, Vigoda and Yang post an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(r\times r\) zero–one matrix their stated bound is \(O(r^{6} \varepsilon ^{- 2} \log ^{5} r \log (2/\delta ))\), improving the previous leading dependence at fixed accuracy and success probability. Their analysis controls mixing of observables describing unmatched-vertex patterns through a restricted Poincaré inequality and coupled flows. The state space remains bipartite; the new theorem does not remove the general-graph obstruction.

The central issue is whether the extra structure available in bipartite graphs is essential for efficient approximate counting. A positive result would extend one of the landmark successes of randomized counting to all graphs. A negative result would establish a striking boundary: even though perfect matching existence remains efficiently decidable on both sides, relative counting would become computationally harder once arbitrary odd-cycle structure is permitted.
why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general-graph question remains open in the checked primary literature. The August 2026 improvement is a permanent algorithm for bipartite graphs. Slow mixing of the particular general-graph Markov chains does not establish impossibility of all FPRAS approaches.

working_summary: A perfect matching pairs every vertex of a graph with exactly one neighbor. The question asks for a randomized relative approximation to the number of perfect matchings in every graph, in time polynomial in input size and inverse accuracy. Existence is efficiently decidable, but counting requires estimating the total number of complete pairings. The saved review distinguishes this task from the solved bipartite permanent problem and from counting all matchings. Known bottlenecks obstruct particular general-graph sampling chains, while leaving open whether another algorithm can overcome the odd-cycle structure.

title: FPRAS for #BIS
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.
focus_reason: #BIS is the canonical intermediate approximate-counting problem: an FPRAS would resolve a central boundary shared by many spin-system and combinatorial counting tasks.
formal: Does there exist one probabilistic Turing algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every finite simple bipartite graph G and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), A(G,\varepsilon )\) halts within \(p(\mathrm{L},\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil )\) steps on every random tape and returns a nonnegative rational Ẑ with \(\Pr [(1- \varepsilon )Z(G)\le \hat\{Z\}\le (1+\varepsilon )Z(G)]\ge 3/4\)? L is the full input bit length, including \(\varepsilon ; Z(G)\) is the number of independent sets.
definitions: The input lists the vertices, their bipartition U,V and all edges, with no loops or repeated edges; \(\varepsilon\) is supplied as a positive binary numerator and denominator. An independent set \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) contains no edge’s two endpoints. \(Z(G)\) counts all such subsets, including \(\varnothing\), so \(Z(G)\ge 1\) and the empty graph has \(Z=1\). The output is a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator representing \(\hat\{Z\}\ge 0\). A uses independent fair coin bits, with no advice or oracle. All input reading, computation, random-bit access and output writing count toward the bound. The success probability is separately required on every input and is over A’s coins. The same program and polynomial work for all bipartitions, degrees, graph sizes and accuracies.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
#BIS asks for the number of independent sets in an arbitrary bipartite graph. Exact counting is already difficult, while approximate counting places the problem in a widely studied intermediate regime: it is a canonical complete problem for the class #\(RH\Pi _{1}\) under approximation-preserving reductions, and many spin-system and combinatorial counting problems are equivalent to it. The main unresolved issue is whether this intermediate status hides a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme.

The relative-error requirement matters when the graph has few independent sets as well as when it has exponentially many. The algorithm must work for every explicitly encoded graph and every requested accuracy, with no structural promise that would make local sampling mix rapidly. A polynomial bound in |V| alone, an additive approximation, or an algorithm whose polynomial degree depends on the graph family would be a different statement.

Several restricted classes do admit efficient approximation schemes. For example, results for almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph and for dense regular bipartite graphs exploit expansion or spectral structure. These theorems demonstrate that the target is achievable on substantial subclasses, but they do not provide a worst-case FPRAS for arbitrary bipartite inputs.

The conjectured difficulty is deliberately weaker than #P-hardness of approximation. #BIS is believed not to have an FPRAS, yet it is also believed not to be NP-hard under the usual approximation-preserving reductions. Resolving the card would therefore locate a central intermediate point between problems with known FPRASes and problems with robust hardness barriers.

The earlier catalogue pointer TCS-6225 came from a paper on independent sets in random regular bipartite graphs and preserved only a truncated source excerpt. This card states the general #BIS question explicitly and keeps the restricted-family results as progress rather than treating them as a solution.
why: Determines whether the canonical intermediate approximate-counting problem can be solved with a uniform polynomial-time randomized relative-error algorithm, with consequences for many equivalent counting and statistical-mechanics problems.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No FPRAS for #BIS on arbitrary bipartite graphs, and no unconditional impossibility theorem, was found in the cited literature; the positive results listed here impose structural restrictions.
progress: 2019: Dell, Husfeldt and Nederlof describe #BIS as the canonical approximate-counting problem of intermediate complexity and record the belief that it has no efficient approximation algorithm without being NP-hard. | 2019: Liao, Lin, Lu and Mao give an FPTAS for independent sets on almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph, a restricted result that leaves arbitrary worst-case graphs open. | 2023–2024: Container and spectral methods give FPRAS or FPTAS results for additional dense, regular, or expanding subclasses, without resolving general #BIS.

title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
importance_reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given nonnegative rational \(n\times n\) matrix A and every rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), outputs a rational Z satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\operatorname{per}(A)\le Z\le (1+\varepsilon )\operatorname{per}(A)\) in time polynomial in the input bit length and \(1/\varepsilon\)?
definitions: For \(n\ge 1, \operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} A_{i,\pi (i)}\), where \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \([n]\). Each entry is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Let L be the total binary description length of A and \(\varepsilon\). There must be one fixed polynomial P such that the algorithm uses at most \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L},1/\varepsilon )\) bit operations on every input. Ordinary deterministic Turing computation is intended, with output bits and arithmetic costs counted; there are no random bits, nonuniform advice, counting oracles or exact-real unit-cost operations. No density, expansion, lower-bound-on-positive-entries, bounded-degree or matrix-scaling promise is imposed. Zero entries are allowed. If \(\operatorname{per}(A)=0\), the algorithm must return \(Z=0\) exactly. This zero case is decidable in polynomial time by checking whether the bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. FPTAS means fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: the running-time exponent must be independent of \(\varepsilon\), and the error is relative to \(\operatorname{per}(A)\), not additive relative to n!, a matrix norm, or another normalization.
answer_criterion: Construct such a deterministic approximation scheme or prove that none exists. A randomized FPRAS does not settle the deterministic question. An approximation within a factor depending superconstantly on n, or a scheme with running time \(n^{g(1/\varepsilon )}\), does not meet the stated guarantee. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a refutation, since using exponentially small \(\varepsilon\) is allowed to take exponential time under the FPTAS bound.
context:
For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to \(O(n^{6} \log ^{5} n)\) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor \(2^{n/2}\). This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor \(c^{n}\) for some absolute \(c<\sqrt{2}\). This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))=\exp (o(n))\). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than \(1+\varepsilon\).

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(A)^{r}\). If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within \(\exp (O(N^{1- \gamma}))\) for one fixed \(\gamma >0\), applying it at \(N=rn\) and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to \(O(n^{1- \gamma}/r^{\gamma})\). Polynomially many copies in n and \(1/\varepsilon\) would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase \(\log (rn)\) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.
why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.
status_note: The 9 September 2026 primary preprint explicitly leaves a deterministic FPTAS open. Its new general subexponential-factor guarantee improves the late-August exponential-base results without yielding arbitrary relative accuracy. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2001–2004: Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda establish an FPRAS for arbitrary nonnegative permanents. | 2018–2019: Anari–Rezaei obtain the tight \(2^{n/2}\) guarantee for the Bethe approximation; the result appears at FOCS 2019. | 2026-08-27: Chen–Vigoda–Yang improve the randomized permanent approximation running time; random sampling remains part of the algorithm. | 2026-08-28: Anari obtains a deterministic \(c^{n}\) approximation for an absolute \(c<\sqrt{2}\); the version checked is revised on 1 September. | 2026-08-31: Narang–Perkins independently obtain an exponential-base improvement through structural corrections near weighted two-by-two blocks. | 2026-09-09: Kudria–Luo–Majid give a deterministic polynomial-time \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))\) approximation and explicitly retain the FPTAS question.
working_summary: The nonnegative permanent sums the weights of all perfect matchings in a bipartite graph. The question asks for a deterministic approximation within any requested relative error, with fully polynomial running time. Randomized approximation already achieves this guarantee, so the missing resource is derandomization without sacrificing accuracy. The saved September review describes deterministic subexponential-factor progress but explains why that factor is still far from one plus epsilon. Zero entries and arbitrary rational weights are allowed, making bit complexity and reliable handling of very small positive values part of the full target.

title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
importance_reason: A canonical open problem of enumeration complexity connecting polyhedral computation and optimization. The bounded versus unbounded distinction and long-running algorithmic work give it a separate scientific role from counting or approximate optimization.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with \(\mathrm{P}=\{x\in R^{d}:Mx\le b\}\) bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within \(p(\mathrm{L}+S)\) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
definitions: The input specifies integers \(m,d\ge 1, M\in Q^{m\times d}\), and \(b\in Q^{m}\). Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: \(v\in \mathrm{P}\) such that \(v=(x+y)/2\) with \(x,y\in \mathrm{P}\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.
why: Determine whether an implicit linear description can always be converted into its exact extremal-point representation with polynomial output overhead.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. The cited bounded-polytope question remains unresolved in the inspected sources. Later searches, including the arrangement-enumeration result, found no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive proof of openness.
progress: 2016-07-09: The revised Reimers–Stougie paper gives total-polynomial enumeration for bounded branch-width while retaining the general bounded-polytope question. | 2024-01-30: The arrangement-enumeration preprint gives output-sensitive bounds for the vertices of the entire hyperplane arrangement, a different output.

title: FPRAS for counting undirected Euler tours
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved approximate-counting problem for natural graph traversals, distinct from the tractable approximation of Eulerian orientations.
formal:
Does the number of Euler tours of an arbitrary connected Eulerian undirected graph admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Using the labelled-edge, fixed-first-traversal normalization below, let \(Z(G)\) be the tour count. The question is whether there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,a>0\) such that, for every allowed graph \(G\) and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) in at most \(C(N+q+1)^a\) bit operations on every random tape and
\[\Pr\!\left[\left|\widehat Z-Z(G)\right|\le\frac{Z(G)}q\right]\ge\frac34.\]
Here \(N\) is the input encoding length and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits. The constants are independent of the graph and accuracy. There is no degree bound, planarity promise or prescribed sampling chain.
definitions:
A graph has labelled vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge1\), and labelled edges \(E=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct endpoints. Parallel edges are permitted and remain distinct by their labels; there are no loops. The graph is promised connected, and every vertex has even degree, counting parallel edges with their multiplicities. The input explicitly lists every edge, rather than encoding a multiplicity by a large binary number. One encoding uses unary \(n\), self-delimiting binary \(m\), the endpoint pair of each edge in label order, and self-delimiting binary \(q\). Graphs are unweighted.

If \(m>0\), write the endpoints of edge 1 as \(a_1<b_1\). Define \(Z(G)\) to be the number of sequences
\[v_0,e_1,v_1,e_2,v_2,\ldots,e_m,v_m\]
such that \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) is a permutation of all edge labels, \(e_1=1\), \(v_0=a_1\), \(v_1=b_1\), \(v_m=v_0\), and edge \(e_i\) joins \(v_{i-1}\) to \(v_i\) for every \(i\). Vertices may be revisited; edges may not. This fixes the starting point and traversal direction by the first labelled edge. It counts one representative of each closed tour modulo cyclic rotation and reversal, while retaining vertex and edge labels. No quotient by graph automorphisms is taken. For the single-vertex graph with no edges, put \(Z(G)=1\), counting the empty tour.

The allowed nonempty graphs have Euler tours. Allowing explicit parallel edges is compatible with the usual simple-graph formulation: replacing each labelled edge by a path through its own new degree-two vertex preserves the tour count under the corresponding first-edge convention and increases the input size only polynomially. Thus this representation choice does not demand a different approximation complexity.

The output is a pair of binary integers specifying a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. Its writing and all arithmetic are charged in the standard multitape Turing model; neither large integers nor rational operations have unit cost. All choices of random bits terminate within the stated bound. A bad random tape may give an inaccurate estimate, but the displayed success probability holds separately for every graph and accuracy input.

The accuracy \(1/q\) is relative to the count. It covers arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). Runtime is polynomial in \(q\), not merely polynomial in graph size for each fixed accuracy. The fixed success threshold \(3/4\) is the convention inherited from the card. No particular estimator, Markov chain or proof technique is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm meeting all displayed guarantees, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must approximate the normalized tour count on every allowed Eulerian graph in fully polynomial time. An exact-counting hardness theorem alone does not refute an FPRAS. Counting balanced orientations, solving a fixed-degree or fixed-grid-width subcase, or proving convergence of a sampler without a fully polynomial approximation guarantee is insufficient.
context:
Cryan’s 2024 abstract says that an FPRAS remains unknown even for undirected 4-regular graphs. It discusses rapid mixing for a particular two-row toroidal-grid chain, a restricted graph family. The full card asks for an algorithm on arbitrary Eulerian graphs.

Ge and Štefankovič explicitly state the general-graph FPRAS question. Their exact-counting results include hardness on planar 4-regular graphs, but exact hardness is not an approximation lower bound. Their introduction carefully separates exact reductions from approximation-preserving reductions.

The same paper gives an approximation-preserving reduction to counting A-trails in 4-regular maps. Such a map supplies a cyclic order of incident edges, and an A-trail requires consecutive traversed edges to be adjacent in that order. That additional model is distinct from ordinary tours on a 4-regular graph and is not silently substituted into this question.

An Eulerian orientation assigns one direction to each edge so that indegree equals outdegree at every vertex. The cited sampling notes prove an FPRAS for these orientations. An orientation records edge directions but not their traversal order, so its count is a different target from the number of tours.
why: Euler tours are elementary graph traversals whose existence is easy to decide, yet approximate enumeration remains a major counting question. A solution would clarify how much harder it is to impose one globally connected traversal than to satisfy local balance constraints on edge directions. This is a test case for the reach of randomized approximate counting beyond problems with tractable orientation or matching formulations.
status_note: The SCM 2024 abstract and event dates, Ge–Štefankovič’s full published text, and Theorem 3.3.8 with its proof in the CMU sampling notes were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-work search found no FPRAS or matching impossibility result for general undirected Euler tours. Orientation and hypergraph results were not treated as solutions. Source-open status is limited to these checked sources and searches.
progress: 2012: Ge and Štefankovič publish exact-counting hardness for planar 4-regular graphs and explicitly retain the general Euler-tour FPRAS question. | 2024-05: Cryan’s Scottish Combinatorics Meeting abstract again identifies the FPRAS question as open and reports work on the Kotzig chain for two-row toroidal grids.
working_summary: An Euler tour traverses every edge of an undirected graph exactly once and returns to its start. This question asks whether the number of such tours can be approximated by a randomized algorithm in fully polynomial time. The count uses labelled edges and a fixed first traversal to remove rotation and reversal ambiguity. The accuracy is multiplicative, and the success probability must be at least three quarters on every input. Known orientation-counting algorithms and restricted graph results do not resolve the general tour-counting question.

title: Output-polynomial hypergraph transversal enumeration
importance_reason: A central longstanding enumeration problem and a reference point for the complexity of many other complete-output tasks.
formal: Do a deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every explicitly given finite hypergraph \(H\), \(A\) outputs every inclusion-minimal transversal exactly once and terminates within \(C(L(H)+L_{\mathrm{out}}(H)+1)^c\) bit steps?
definitions: \(H=([n],E), n\ge 0\), is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges \(e\subseteq [n]\), each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. \(\mathrm{L}(H)\) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq [n]\) intersecting every \(e\in E\); it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for \(T=\varnothing\). If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is \(\varnothing\). If E contains \(\varnothing\), there is no transversal and \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{out}}=0\). Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a single algorithm meeting the total output-polynomial bound, including completeness, uniqueness and termination on every finite hypergraph, or a Lean proof that none exists. The target imposes no polynomial-delay or polynomial-space bound. A lower bound for one enumeration algorithm does not establish nonexistence of all algorithms.
context:
Minimal transversals are the irredundant ways to hit every edge of a hypergraph. Their number may be exponential in the input size, so the target charges time against the complete output as well as the input.

The August 2026 MMCS lower bound concerns one particular enumeration algorithm. The same paper explicitly retains the existence of some output-polynomial algorithm as open.
why: This central enumeration question governs the complexity of converting a hypergraph into the family of all its minimal hitting sets and underlies many enumeration reductions.
status_note: Explicitly open in the August 2026 primary preprint. Its negative result applies to MMCS, not to all algorithms. The original formulation and later abstract were checked on 13 September 2026; no exhaustive literature claim is made.
progress: 2021: Strozecki’s habilitation records membership in OutputP as unresolved. | 2026-08-03: Hörmann and Schirneck show that Minimal-to-Maximal Conversion Search is not output-polynomial, while their abstract explicitly leaves the general existence question open.

working_summary: A transversal meets every edge of a hypergraph and is minimal if removing any selected vertex destroys that property. The required algorithm lists all such sets exactly once and detects when enumeration is finished. Its total time must be polynomial in the combined input and complete output length. The output may be exponentially large, and no separate bound on delay is requested. A 2026 lower bound excludes a particular practical algorithm while leaving the existence of a general output-polynomial algorithm open.

title: Fully polynomial randomized approximation of mixed discriminants
importance_reason: Extend efficient relative-error counting beyond nonnegative permanents to a foundational matrix quantity underlying constrained determinantal distributions and convex geometry.
formal: Does an FPRAS exist for the mixed discriminant of arbitrary rational positive semidefinite matrices?
definitions: The input is an integer \(n\ge1\), symmetric matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) satisfying \(z^{\mathsf T}A_i z\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), and a rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Define \(D(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) to be the coefficient of \(t_1\cdots t_n\) in \(\det(\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_iA_i)\). This fixes the normalization: for n identical identity matrices, D=n!. This D is nonnegative. An FPRAS is one uniform randomized Turing machine returning a nonnegative rational Z with \(\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)D\le Z\le(1+\varepsilon)D]\ge3/4\) on every promised input, and worst-case time polynomial in the full binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\). Probability is over independent fair random bits. All entries and epsilon are encoded as integer numerators and positive integer denominators. Singular matrices and D=0 are included, in which case the event requires Z=0. No rank bound, commutativity, or lower bound on positive eigenvalues is promised.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with a complete Lean-checked proof covering the specified model and all quantifiers. A restricted model, additional unproved assumption, or partial parameter range does not settle the target.
context:
For diagonal positive semidefinite inputs this coefficient is a nonnegative permanent. The general case therefore extends a central approximate-counting success to matrices without a common diagonal structure.

The mixed discriminant also controls constrained determinantal sampling. The cited works distinguish exponential multiplicative approximation from an FPRAS; the latter requires arbitrarily small relative error in polynomial time.
why: Extend efficient relative-error counting beyond nonnegative permanents to a foundational matrix quantity underlying constrained determinantal distributions and convex geometry.
status_note: The cited primary sources and a targeted later-work search were checked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of this precise target was located. This is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of openness or an independent verification of the cited proofs.
progress: 2007: Gurvits explicitly identifies the FPRAS question as a main open problem. | 2017: The constrained-DPP paper records the missing FPRAS and explains its relationship to constrained determinantal sums.
working_summary: The mixed discriminant is a specified coefficient of the determinant of a linear matrix pencil. Positive semidefinite inputs make this coefficient nonnegative. An FPRAS must approximate it to arbitrary relative accuracy in time polynomial in the input size and inverse accuracy. Nonnegative permanent approximation addresses a special diagonal case but does not settle the general matrix target. A resolution would decide a central frontier connecting approximate counting and constrained determinantal sampling.

title: #BIS-easiness of Boolean log-supermodular counting CSPs
importance_reason: A broad missing piece in the classification of approximate counting and weighted constraint satisfaction.
formal: For every fixed finite family F of functions \(f:\{0,1\}^{r_{f}}\to \mathbb{Q} _{\ge 0}\) satisfying \(f(x\lor y)f(x\land y)\ge f(x)f(y)\) for all x,y, is #\(\mathrm{CSP}(F)\) approximation-preserving reducible to #BIS?
definitions: Arity \(r_{f}\) is a nonnegative integer fixed with \(f; \lor\) and ∧ act coordinatewise. A #\(\mathrm{CSP}(F)\) instance consists of finitely many Boolean variables and a list of constraints, each naming a function in F and an ordered tuple of variables of its arity; repeats in a tuple are permitted. Its value Z is the sum over all Boolean assignments of the product of all constraint values. Function tables are fixed nonnegative rationals, not part of the instance. #BIS counts all independent vertex sets of a finite simple bipartite graph. An approximation-preserving reduction is a randomized oracle algorithm which, on an instance I and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), returns a relative \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) estimate of Z with probability at least \(3/4\) using time polynomial in |I| and \(1/\varepsilon\). Its oracle calls request relative approximations to #BIS with inverse tolerances polynomially bounded in |I| and \(1/\varepsilon\). Oracle failure probabilities may be reduced to an inverse polynomial by independent repetitions; the reduction’s overall correctness guarantee includes them. If \(Z=0, a\) valid relative estimate is exactly zero. Reduction polynomials may depend on the fixed family F. The oracle is an approximation oracle, not exact counting.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
