title: Parity subgraph-counting dichotomy
importance_reason: A general structural dichotomy would complete a central classification of parameterized parity counting across all computable graph-pattern families, extending the established hereditary and tree classifications.
formal:
Is the following statement true? For every computable class \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple graphs whose matching-split number is unbounded, the parameterized problem \(\oplus\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal H)\) is complete for parity-\(\mathrm W[1]\) under deterministic fixed-parameter Turing reductions:
\[\oplus\mathrm{Clique}\ \leq^{\mathrm{fpt}}_T\ \oplus\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal H)\ \leq^{\mathrm{fpt}}_T\ \oplus\mathrm{Clique}.\]
The input to \(\oplus\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal H)\) is a pattern \(H\in\mathcal H\) and an arbitrary host graph \(G\); its output is the parity of the number of subgraphs of \(G\) isomorphic to \(H\), and its parameter is \(|V(H)|\). No closure property beyond invariance under isomorphism is imposed on \(\mathcal H\). This is the parity clause of the source conjecture, using the reduction convention made explicit in the later classification paper.
definitions:
All graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and simple, given explicitly by their vertex counts and adjacency matrices. Empty graphs and isolated vertices are permitted. A graph class is computable if one deterministic algorithm halts on every finite graph and decides membership. It is invariant under isomorphism: relabelling vertices does not change membership. The class is fixed when defining its counting problem, rather than supplied as part of an instance.

For a graph \(H\), define
\[s(H)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq V(H),\ \Delta(H[V(H)\setminus S])\leq1\}.\]
Here \(H[U]\) is the induced graph on \(U\), and \(\Delta\) is maximum degree, with value zero for the empty graph. Thus deleting a splitting set leaves disjoint edges and isolated vertices. Unbounded matching-split number means
\[\forall B\in\mathbb N\ \exists H\in\mathcal H:\ s(H)>B.\]
The corresponding bounded condition is existence of one constant \(B\) working for all patterns in the class; it is not a bound that may grow with the input pattern.

Let \(\mathrm{Sub}(H,G)\) consist of pairs \((U,F)\) with \(U\subseteq V(G)\) and \(F\subseteq E(G[U])\) for which the graph \((U,F)\) is isomorphic to \(H\). Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving both adjacency and nonadjacency between those two graphs. The output is \(|\mathrm{Sub}(H,G)|\bmod2\), in \(\{0,1\}\). Each pair is counted once, regardless of the number of isomorphisms to it. Copies need not be induced in \(G\), and no labels or colors constrain embeddings. In particular, counting injective maps instead of copies would change this parity problem. Inputs are promised to have \(H\in\mathcal H\); algorithms and reduction oracle calls need only meet this promise, so no runtime charge for deciding membership in the fixed class is imposed.

The reference problem \(\oplus\mathrm{Clique}\) takes a graph \(G\) and a positive integer \(k\), outputs the parity of the number of \(k\)-element vertex subsets with all pairs adjacent, and has parameter \(k\). A deterministic FPT Turing reduction from a parameterized problem \((P,\kappa)\) to \((Q,\lambda)\) is one deterministic oracle Turing algorithm that computes the exact output of \(P(x)\) in time \(f(\kappa(x))(|x|+1)^c\). Here \(f\) is a total computable function and \(c\) is a constant. Every query \(y\) to \(Q\) satisfies its input promise and \(\lambda(y)\leq g(\kappa(x))\) for a total computable \(g\). The reduction may make adaptive queries and combine their returned bits; writing query strings and all other work are charged to the runtime. Oracle answers themselves have unit cost.

Completeness in this card means the displayed two reductions. For each fixed class \(\mathcal H\), the reduction algorithms, computable bounds and constant exponents may depend on \(\mathcal H\). No single procedure taking a membership-decider code and synthesizing these reductions is required. The explicit Turing convention follows Sections 2.3–2.3.1 of Goldberg–Roth. A single-instance parsimonious reduction, which would preserve the output without multiple oracle calls, is not an additional requirement. Fixed-parameter tractability means an exact deterministic algorithm of time \(f(k)(N+1)^c\) for total input length \(N\), a total computable \(f\), and a constant \(c\) independent of \(k\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universally quantified completeness statement with these counting and reduction conventions. A positive proof must cover every computable pattern class with unbounded matching-split number, including classes that are neither hereditary nor classes of trees. A negative proof must establish failure of the statement for a qualifying computable class; one tractable class would refute it only together with whatever class-separation fact is needed to rule out the required reduction. No unproved separation between FPT and parity-\(\mathrm W[1]\), or exponential-time hypothesis, is an assumption of the requested completeness theorem. Showing hardness of exact counting, counting embeddings, or induced-subgraph counting alone does not settle this target.
context:
The 2021 paper proves tractability for bounded matching-split number and asks for hardness throughout the complementary region. Its modular-counting conjecture has a separate clause for moduli with odd factors; that separate target is not included here.

Goldberg and Roth establish the completeness conclusion for every hereditary pattern class of unbounded matching-split number and for every recursively enumerable class of trees with that property. A hereditary class is closed under taking induced subgraphs. Their full journal paper includes the tree classification, which is absent from the shorter ICALP 2023 extended abstract.

These completeness results are unconditional reductions. The consequence that the hard problems are not FPT requires a complexity assumption; the paper uses the randomized Exponential Time Hypothesis, which rules out bounded-error randomized \(2^{o(n)}\)-time algorithms for \(n\)-variable 3-SAT. That conditional consequence is distinct from the requested completeness statement.

The full journal paper’s conclusion explicitly retains the general conjecture after proving the hereditary and tree cases. This card follows its deterministic Turing-reduction convention, avoiding an unstated demand that all hardness proofs preserve parity through just one output instance.
why: A classification by a single structural parameter would identify exactly which graph-pattern families avoid the difficulty of parity counting, subject to the usual separation between fixed-parameter tractability and parity clique. This is a broad boundary theorem for counting complexity: taking counts modulo two can make families tractable even when exact counting remains hard. The unresolved scope is all computable pattern classes, beyond the substantial hereditary and tree cases.
status_note: The 2021 source’s definitions, Theorem 2 and Conjecture 14, together with the full 2024 Algorithmica paper’s Theorems 4–5, reduction definitions and conclusion, were read on 2026-09-14. The later paper expressly retains the full conjecture after its hereditary and tree classifications. A bounded later-work search through this review date found no matching resolution for every computable pattern class. Status remains source-open within these verification limits.
progress: 2021: Curticapean, Dell and Husfeldt establish the bounded matching-split algorithm and formulate the general parity-hardness conjecture. | 2024: The full Algorithmica paper proves the hereditary and tree classifications and explicitly leaves the unrestricted pattern-class conjecture open.
working_summary: The problem asks which graph-pattern families make counting copies modulo two parameterized-hard. The proposed boundary is whether deleting a bounded number of pattern vertices always leaves only edges and isolated vertices. Every computable class on the unbounded side is conjectured equivalent to parity clique under deterministic fixed-parameter Turing reductions. Copies are ordinary unlabelled subgraphs, and the input pattern size is the parameter. The classification is known for hereditary classes and classes of trees, while the general class-wide assertion remains the target.

title: Deterministic relative counting for DNF
importance_reason: Deterministic relative counting for DNF would remove randomness from a canonical approximate-counting problem.
formal:
Is there a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the number of satisfying assignments of an arbitrary explicitly given DNF formula? In the precise reciprocal-integer accuracy convention used here, do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and positive integers \(C,a\) such that for every DNF formula \(\varphi\) of encoding length \(N\) over its declared \(n\) variables, and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational number \(\widehat Z\) with
\[|\widehat Z-Z(\varphi)|\le Z(\varphi)/q,\qquad Z(\varphi)=|\{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\varphi(x)=1\}|,\]
and halts within \(C(N+q+1)^a\) steps? The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness, advice or an oracle. There is no bound on term width or on the number of occurrences of a variable other than the explicit input length.
definitions:
A literal is a declared variable \(x_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), or its negation. A term is a finite conjunction of literals; a DNF formula is a finite disjunction of terms. All literal occurrences and all terms are listed explicitly. Empty conjunctions evaluate to true and the empty disjunction evaluates to false. Repeated literals or terms are allowed, and a term containing both signs of one variable is false. A variable assignment specifies every declared variable, including unused ones; every satisfying assignment is counted once regardless of how many terms it satisfies.

Use an explicit encoding consisting of \(1^n\), a self-delimiting binary term count, and for each term its self-delimiting literal count followed by variable indices in binary and one sign bit per literal. Thus the declared variable set is part of the input, \(n\le N\), and arbitrary circuits or compressed representations of an exponentially larger DNF are excluded. Valid formulas with \(n=0\) are included and are evaluated on the unique empty assignment. Malformed encodings may be rejected in polynomial time and are not counted as instances of the formula problem.

The accuracy parameter \(q\) is given in binary. Computation uses a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine; one transition costs one step, and writing the output is counted. Represent \(\widehat Z\) by a binary nonnegative numerator and positive denominator. They need not be in lowest terms. The constants in the running-time bound are independent of the formula, its width, its variable occurrence counts and \(q\). All preprocessing is included.

The target is relative error \(1/q\). This is the usual fully polynomial accuracy convention: an arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) can be met by taking \(q=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\), with the time to read that request also counted. The runtime is polynomial in the reciprocal accuracy, not merely its bit length. If \(Z=0\), the output must equal zero exactly. If \(Z>0\), it must lie between \((1-1/q)Z\) and \((1+1/q)Z\). Additive error \(2^n/q\) is a different and potentially much weaker guarantee when satisfying assignments are rare. The algorithm is allowed to output a rational estimate; exact integer counting is not required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of this deterministic approximation scheme. A positive answer must specify the algorithm and prove its relative-error and fully polynomial-time guarantees for all formulas and all \(q\ge2\), including zero counts. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform deterministic scheme. Randomized high-probability estimates, an additive-error approximation alone, quasipolynomial runtime, or polynomial algorithms restricted to bounded-width or bounded-occurrence formulas do not settle the full target.
context:
The source’s randomized Algorithm 2.35 gives a relative approximation in time polynomial in formula size and reciprocal accuracy. Open Problems 2.36 and 7.32 ask for deterministic polynomial time, with the latter discussion supplying a quasipolynomial-time derandomization baseline.

Overlaps between terms are essential: adding the numbers of assignments satisfying the individual terms can count the same assignment many times. The problem counts the size of their union, with all declared variables included.

Trevisan gives deterministic multiplicative approximation in time linear in formula length and polynomial in reciprocal accuracy when term width is a fixed constant. Its dependence on that width does not provide a uniform polynomial bound for arbitrary DNF inputs.

Servedio and Tan study formulas in which each variable occurs at most k times, a restriction different from term width. Their relative-error algorithms have explicit dependence on k and accuracy; their results do not furnish the all-occurrence fully polynomial bound required here.
why: DNF counting is a canonical approximate-counting problem for which randomization gives an efficient relative approximation even when direct random assignment sampling rarely finds a solution. A deterministic scheme would remove randomness from this basic union-counting task across all formula widths and occurrence patterns. It would strengthen the explicit derandomization tools available for both complexity theory and probabilistic data processing.

The bounded later search through 2026 found restricted and randomized approximate-counting results but no deterministic fully polynomial relative-counting scheme for arbitrary DNF. Trevisan’s constant-width result and the full Servedio–Tan read-k manuscript were checked for the relevant distinction. No exhaustive current-openness certification is claimed.

title: Treewidth classification of approximate counting CSP
importance_reason: A general structural tractability classification for approximate counting of constraint solutions. Existing score retained.
formal: Assume that parameterized Clique has no randomized fixed-parameter algorithm with bounded error. For every fixed recursively enumerable class C of finite relational structures with a uniform bound on relation arity, are the following equivalent: (1) counting homomorphisms \(A\to B\) for \(A\in C\) and arbitrary compatible B is exactly solvable in polynomial time; (2) this problem admits a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme; (3) it admits a fixed-parameter randomized approximation scheme with parameter \(\Vert A\Vert\); and (4) the Gaifman graphs of structures in C have bounded treewidth? The missing implication is \((3)\Rightarrow (4)\). No fan-grid containment, minor closure or other closure property is assumed for C. This is the source’s Theorem 3 with its fan-class hypothesis removed.
definitions: A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite collection of relation symbols, each with a specified nonnegative integer arity. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A consists of a finite universe \(V(A)\) and, for every r-ary \(R\in \tau , a\) set \(R^{A}\subseteq V(A)\)ʳ. Input structures A and B share \(\tau\), but \(\tau\) may vary between instances. Every arity is at most a constant \(r_{C}\) fixed for the class C. Universes, symbols, arities and relation tuples are explicitly listed in a standard binary encoding; \(\Vert A\Vert\) denotes its length, and similarly for B. Nullary relations, if present, are either empty or contain the empty tuple and are checked in the same way as other relations. A homomorphism is any function \(h:V(A)\to V(B)\) such that for each relation tuple \((a_{1},\ldots ,a_{r})\in R^{A}\), the tuple \((h(a_{1}),\ldots ,h(a_{r}))\) belongs to \(R^{B}\). It need not be injective or surjective. Count all such functions, including zero when none exists. C is fixed before the input and can be enumerated by a Turing machine; a promised input has \(A\in C\), and an algorithm need not decide membership in C. The Gaifman graph \(G(A)\) has universe \(V(A)\) as vertices and joins distinct elements occurring together in some relation tuple. A tree decomposition assigns vertex bags to a tree so that every vertex is in a bag, every edge has both ends in a bag, and bags containing a given vertex form a connected subtree. Its width is the largest bag size minus one; treewidth is the minimum width, with empty graph assigned width zero here. Bounded treewidth of C means one constant w works for every \(A\in C\). It refers to A itself, not to a homomorphically equivalent core. An approximation scheme receives A,B and a rational \(0<\varepsilon <1\) and outputs an integer random variable X satisfying \(\Pr [|X- H|\le \varepsilon H]\ge 3/4\), where H is the homomorphism count. In particular it must output zero with that probability when \(H=0\). Probability is over internal fair random bits. An FPRAS uses time polynomial in \(\Vert A\Vert +\Vert B\Vert +\varepsilon ^{- 1}\); an FPTRAS uses \(f(\Vert A\Vert )\cdot (\Vert A\Vert +\Vert B\Vert +\varepsilon ^{- 1})^{a}\) for a computable f and constant a. Reading the rational accuracy encoding is included. These are worst-case time bounds, and a,f and the algorithm may depend on fixed C but not on individual input structures. The hypothesis means that no uniform randomized algorithm decides whether an N-vertex graph has a k-clique in \(g(k)N^{b}\) time for computable g and constant b, with error at most \(1/4\) on every instance. This states explicitly the randomized parameterized separation used in the source.
answer_criterion: Under the stated parameterized complexity hypothesis, prove the equivalence for every eligible class C, or refute it by a recursively enumerable bounded-arity class of unbounded Gaifman treewidth with an FPTRAS for its homomorphism-counting problem. The other implications are already known. An exact-counting hardness result, a theorem only for minor-closed or fan classes, or a classification with the right-hand structure fixed does not establish the missing unrestricted implication.
context:
Bounded treewidth gives exact polynomial-time counting, which yields an FPRAS and then an FPTRAS. The source proves the converse under its additional fan-class hypothesis; its conclusion asks whether that hypothesis can be removed.

The journal discusses the exact-counting classification by treewidth of the structures themselves. Decision can instead depend on treewidth modulo homomorphic equivalence. Replacing raw treewidth by core treewidth would change this approximation question.

Theorem 3.2 keeps the fan-class condition, including the minor-closed cases, and Section 5 repeats the question for all bounded-arity classes. The indexing change from conference Theorem 3 does not signal a broader theorem.

The 2024 list-homomorphism article gives exact running-time bases for each fixed target graph H, using treewidth of the source graph as a parameter. Here C restricts the source structures and the entire target structure B is unrestricted input.
why: Would determine whether approximation enlarges the tractable classes of structurally restricted counting CSPs, and whether treewidth remains the complete structural criterion.

Searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate an unrestricted extension or a counterexample. The later fixed-target exact-counting result has a different input restriction and resource parameter. Search is not exhaustive.

working_summary: The input asks how many homomorphisms map a source structure A from a fixed class C into an arbitrary target structure B. The conjecture says a fixed-parameter randomized approximation scheme exists exactly when C has bounded Gaifman treewidth. Relation arity is uniformly bounded, C is recursively enumerable, and the parameter is the size of A. The source proves this under a further fan-class condition and asks to remove it. The 2020 journal version retains that restriction, so exact-counting and fixed-target classifications do not settle the missing approximation direction.

title: Decision versus approximate counting for fixed-width SAT
importance_reason: A fundamental decision-versus-counting comparison in fine-grained satisfiability, isolating the cost of multiplicative estimation at fixed clause width. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed clause width \(k\geq3\), do randomized decision \(k\)-SAT and randomized multiplicative approximation of \(\#k\)-SAT have the same optimal exponential running-time rate in the number of variables? With \(d_k\) and \(a_k\) defined below, the target is \(a_k=d_k\) for every fixed \(k\geq3\). This makes “close the gap” precise at the exponential-rate level, as in the later source’s fixed-width question.
definitions:
An input is a Boolean CNF formula \(F\) on an explicitly declared set of \(n\) variables, with at most \(k\) literals in each clause. A literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(N(F)\) be the number of assignments to all declared variables satisfying every clause. Variables absent from clauses still contribute their two possible values. There is no promise of satisfiability or sparsity.

Decision asks whether \(N(F)>0\). Approximate counting receives a rational accuracy parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and must output a nonnegative binary-encoded rational \(Z\) such that
\[
(1-\varepsilon)N(F)\leq Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)N(F)
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. When \(N(F)=0\), a successful output is exactly zero. Probability is over algorithmic randomness. Decision also has success probability at least \(2/3\), allowing two-sided error.

Use ordinary classical randomized algorithms and worst-case bit-operation running time, over both inputs and random tapes. Let \(L\) be total input bit length, including the formula and, for approximate counting, the rational accuracy. Define \(d_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which decision has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}L^C)\) for some fixed \(C\). Define \(a_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which an approximation scheme has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}(L+\varepsilon^{-1})^C)\) for some fixed \(C\), for every admissible accuracy. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and hidden constants may depend on the fixed \(k\) and \(\alpha\), but not on the input or accuracy.

The infima need not be attained. Equality asks that every exponential decision rate can be matched for approximation with any arbitrarily small positive addition to that rate and polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy. It does not demand a single optimal algorithm at an unattained infimum, identical polynomial factors, or an effective compiler transforming all decision programs.

Already \(d_k\leq a_k\): a constant-relative-error estimate distinguishes zero from a positive count. The unresolved direction compares approximation with decision at the same fixed clause width. Taking a supremum or a limit over all widths is a different statement. A reduction whose decision queries add parity constraints or increase clause width must account for their cost before it can establish this comparison. The source uses an \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplicative convention; changing to the displayed relative-error convention only rescales accuracy by constant factors in this range.
answer_criterion: Prove equality of the two defined infimum rates for every fixed integer width at least three, or prove a strict separation for at least one such width. A reduction preserving the width and adding arbitrarily small exponential overhead would suffice for equality. Improved individual upper bounds, a result only as width tends to infinity, or hardness for exact counting alone does not settle this comparison.
context:
Thurley obtains a randomized approximation scheme substantially faster than the exact counting bounds cited in 2012. Schmitt and Wanka later improve the three-literal upper bound to \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}1.51426^n)\). These are historical upper bounds, not claims about the optimal rates or the latest decision record.

Dell and Lapinskas show that a common exponential saving for decision at every constant width transfers to approximate counting with arbitrarily small loss. Their Theorem 8 therefore matches the all-width saving, but its hypothesis is stronger than having a fast algorithm at one selected width.

The full journal version explicitly leaves the fixed-width exponential comparison open. Its main SAT reduction uses a decision problem with sparse parity constraints; encoding those constraints into CNF may require larger width. It also relates subexponential decision and approximation, without settling each fixed positive exponential rate.
why: Tests whether estimating the number of satisfying assignments intrinsically requires more exponential work than finding out whether any exist. Equality would transfer the leading exponential savings in fixed-width SAT to a broader counting task.
status_note: Read the original approximation convention and question, the 2013 authors’ reported improvement, and the full November 2020 author version of the 2021 journal paper, especially its explicit fixed-width question and Theorem 13. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The chosen target is equality of infimum exponential rates with polynomial accuracy cost, not a requirement of polynomial-overhead reduction or identical lower-order running time.
progress: 2012: The source asks whether the exponential gap between approximate counting and decision can be closed. | 2013: An improved approximation scheme lowers the known counting upper bounds without matching the decision bounds. | 2021: The journal reduction preserves common all-width savings and states that the fixed-width comparison remains open.
working_summary: A fixed-width CNF formula has a finite number of satisfying assignments. Decision tests whether that number is positive; approximation estimates it to relative error. The question asks whether the optimal exponential rates in the variable count coincide for each fixed width. Polynomial accuracy costs and arbitrarily small losses in the exponential rate are allowed. Later all-width and subexponential equivalences do not settle this fixed-width comparison.

working_summary: The hypothesis \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would make existence of efficiently verifiable witnesses decidable in polynomial time. This question asks whether that hypothesis also forces exact polynomial-time computation of every #P counting function. title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.
focus_reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.
formal: For every integer \(t\ge 1\) and every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G, does \(\chi (G)\ge t\) imply that G contains \(K_{t}\) as a graph minor? Equivalently, is every \(K_{t}\)-minor-free graph \((t- 1)\)-colorable?
definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A proper coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors; \(\chi (G)\) is the minimum number of colors. \(K_{t}\) is the complete graph on t vertices. A \(K_{t}\) minor is witnessed by t pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_{1},\ldots ,B_{t}\) such that each induced subgraph \(G[B_{i}]\) is connected and every pair \(B_{i},B_{j}\) has at least one edge between it. These branch sets can be contracted and all unwanted vertices or edges deleted. They may have arbitrary sizes; the minor need not be induced and no parity condition is imposed. Equivalently, the Hadwiger number \(h(G)\), the largest t for which G has a \(K_{t}\) minor, must satisfy \(h(G)\ge \chi (G)\). The statement concerns existence, with no running-time requirement on finding the coloring or branch sets.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A graph can have very few large complete subgraphs and still need many colors. Hadwiger asks whether contracting connected pieces always reveals a complete graph as large as the number of colors originally needed. This would make a global obstruction to coloring visible through a precise structural certificate: disjoint connected regions linked in every pair. The complete graph \(K_{t- 1}\) shows that the proposed upper bound for \(K_{t}\)-minor-free graphs cannot be reduced.

The conjecture encompasses the Four-Color Theorem because planar graphs exclude \(K_{5}\) minors. Wagner’s structure theorem makes the \(t=5\) case equivalent to four-colorability of planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas extended this equivalence to \(t=6\) by proving that a minimal counterexample in that case would be apex: deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. Thus the known exact cases extend through \(K_{6}\) minors; the first unresolved case is \(t=7\).

The earlier general approach forced clique minors from high average degree. The resulting \(O(t\sqrt{\log  t})\) degeneracy bound gives a coloring bound of the same order by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse. That density threshold is sharp, so simply improving its numerical constant cannot yield Hadwiger’s linear target. The chromatic-number question requires using structure beyond this degree argument.

Delcourt and Postle obtain \(O(t \log  \log  t)\) colors through a reduction to coloring much smaller minor-free subgraphs, on roughly t times a polylogarithmic number of vertices. Their reduction also shows that proving a linear bound on these small graphs would imply a linear bound without a size restriction. It narrows where a genuinely new coloring argument is needed, without imposing the small-size hypothesis on the conjecture itself.

Liu and Luo’s September 2026 preprint builds on that reduction and claims \(O(t \log  \log  \log  t)\). Its proof combines contractions that reduce degeneracy with fractional colorings, which distribute weight across independent sets. Even this extra logarithm removed leaves both the \(O(t)\) weakening and the sharp coefficient in the original conjecture unresolved. The result is recorded as a new preprint claim, not as an independently verified proof.

An odd clique minor imposes additional compatibility conditions on two-colorings inside its branch trees. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson construct graphs with no odd \(K_{t}\) minor and chromatic number approximately 1.5t, disproving the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Their graphs are not counterexamples to the ordinary-minor assertion asked here: forbidding odd minors permits more graphs than forbidding all clique minors.
why: A flagship structural graph problem connecting coloring, contractions, and excluded-minor classes. A resolution would identify the exact universal coloring obstruction in every minor-closed setting; improvements also develop structural tools relevant to graph algorithms and approximation.
status_note: Ordinary Hadwiger remains explicitly open in the 9 September 2026 preprint; checked through 10 September 2026. The new triple-logarithmic upper bound is a preprint claim. The December 2025 disproof concerns the stronger odd-minor conjecture.
progress: 1943: Hadwiger proposes the relation between chromatic number and complete graph minors; the current preprint restates the original assertion. | 1982–1984: Kostochka and Thomason establish the asymptotically sharp average-degree threshold yielding \(O(t\sqrt{\log  t})\) colors; sharpness of this density method does not give a matching chromatic lower bound. | 1993: Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas prove the \(K_{6}\)-minor case using the Four-Color Theorem. | 2021–2025: Delcourt and Postle prove \(O(t \log  \log  t)\) coloring and their reduction to small graphs. The preprint began in 2021 and the journal version appeared in 2025. | 2025-12-23: Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson disprove the stronger odd-minor version, leaving ordinary Hadwiger open. | 2026-09-09: Version 2 of Liu and Luo’s preprint claims an absolute-C upper bound \(\chi (G)\le Ct \log  \log  \log  t\) for every \(K_{t}\)-minor-free graph and \(t\ge 16\) (Theorem 1.1). This does not reach \(\chi (G)\le t- 1\).
working_summary: Hadwiger's conjecture says that every graph requiring t colors contains a complete graph on t vertices as a minor. A minor may contract connected regions, so the required clique need not appear as an ordinary subgraph. The claim links coloring difficulty with a global obstruction built from pairwise adjacent connected branch sets. It is a central structural principle behind the relationship between graph decomposition and coloring. The saved review distinguishes ordinary minors from odd-minor variants, whose counterexamples do not refute the conjecture stated here, and does not require an efficient construction algorithm.

title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.
focus_reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.
formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered \(1,\ldots ,n\) and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of \(n- 1\) edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when \(\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\) is smallest among all spanning trees. For \(n=1\) the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use \(O(\log (m+n+2))\)-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right \(n- 1\) edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) time, where \(\alpha\) is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most \(3n/2\) edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.
why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.
status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.
progress: 1994: Fredman–Willard obtain deterministic linear time in a stronger integer-word model. | 1995: Karger–Klein–Tarjan obtain randomized linear time for arbitrary comparison weights. | 2000: Chazelle achieves deterministic \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) comparison-based time. | 2002: Pettie–Ramachandran match the optimal decision-tree complexity with a uniform deterministic algorithm, without determining that complexity. | 2008: Pettie–Ramachandran develop alternative randomized MST algorithms using far fewer random bits; complete deterministic linear time remains unresolved.
working_summary: A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex while minimizing the total weight of its edges. This project asks whether arbitrary real comparison weights admit a deterministic algorithm whose worst-case time is linear in the graph size. Randomized linear expected time and nearly linear deterministic bounds provide contrasting benchmarks. Integer operations on weight representations answer a different model-specific question. A resolution would explain whether the remaining cost comes from essential deterministic comparison work or from limitations of existing graph filtering methods.

title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.
formal: For every finite undirected simple graph H with at least two vertices, does there exist a real constant \(c(H)>0\) such that every n-vertex undirected simple graph G with \(n\ge 1\) and no induced copy of H satisfies \(\max \{\alpha (G),\omega (G)\}\ge n^{c(H)}\)?
definitions: An induced copy of H is an injective map \(f:V(H)\to V(G)\) such that distinct u,v are adjacent in H if and only if \(f(u),f(v)\) are adjacent in G. Thus both edges and nonedges must match. \(\alpha (G)\) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and \(\omega (G)\) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise adjacent vertices. The constant \(c(H)\) may depend arbitrarily on the entire fixed graph H, but not on G or n. No density, degree, dimension or algorithmic promise is imposed on G. The claim concerns existence of a clique or independent set, without requiring a polynomial-time construction. A hereditary graph class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs; the class of H-free graphs is hereditary.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least \(n/t\) vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least \(\sqrt{n}\). This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound \(\exp (c_{H}\sqrt{\log  n})\). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to \(\exp (c_{H}\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})\) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed \(\delta >0\) as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size \(2^{(\log  n)^{1- o(1)}}\). This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert \(n^{c}\) for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set \(\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}\) and edge set \(\{ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df\}\). It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least \((Cd)^{- d}\) for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.
why: A foundational prediction that forbidding any fixed induced pattern forces polynomial-size order inside a graph. Its links to hereditary classes, neighborhood complexity and sparse/dense decompositions make it a central structural question with connections to algorithmic graph theory.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary literature explicitly retains the full conjecture as open. Sági’s historical revised claim is recorded separately and is not treated as a verified solution; the withdrawal of its earlier version does not itself refute the revision. New six-vertex and bounded-VC-dimension results have restricted scope.

working_summary: Forbidding one fixed induced graph excludes both its edge pattern and its nonedge pattern. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture predicts that every graph with this restriction has a clique or independent set of polynomial size. The exponent may depend on the forbidden graph but must stay positive as the host graph grows. This would show that every proper hereditary restriction forces much stronger homogeneous structure than arbitrary graphs guarantee. The saved review records special-case advances and unvalidated full-solution claims separately, and a near-polynomial bound with a vanishing exponent does not establish the required fixed exponent.

title: Reed’s conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.
formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph G satisfy \(\chi (G)\le \lceil (\Delta (G)+1+\omega (G))/2\rceil\)?
definitions: A graph is simple when it has neither loops nor parallel edges. A proper k-colouring is a map from \(V(G)\) to \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) assigning different colours to endpoints of every edge; \(\chi (G)\) is the minimum such k. The degree of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and \(\Delta (G)\) is the maximum degree. A clique is a vertex set whose distinct vertices are all adjacent, and \(\omega (G)\) is its largest possible size. The ceiling \(\lceil x\rceil\) is the least integer at least x. The statement concerns all such graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices. For an edgeless nonempty graph, \(\chi =\omega =1\) and \(\Delta =0\). The empty graph can be included with \(\chi =\omega =\Delta =0\), without changing the question. There are no restrictions on graph size, maximum degree, forbidden subgraphs or the method used to obtain a colouring.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated inequality for every finite simple graph, or give a finite graph and a proof that its chromatic number exceeds the displayed ceiling. The target is an existence theorem, so a polynomial-time colouring algorithm is not required. An asymptotic bound with an additive error, a convex combination with clique coefficient less than \(1/2\), or a theorem restricted to sufficiently large maximum degree is partial progress unless the remaining cases are also covered.
context:
Two elementary bounds frame graph colouring. A clique needs a distinct colour for every vertex, so \(\chi \ge \omega\). On the other hand, greedily colouring vertices in any order uses at most \(\Delta +1\) colours: at most \(\Delta\) colours are forbidden by already coloured neighbours. Reed asks whether an upper bound halfway between these two numbers always suffices, after rounding up. This would sharply connect a local obstruction, the size of a clique, to the global task of partitioning all vertices into independent sets.

The rounding is essential even for a five-cycle. It has maximum degree two and clique number two, but it needs three colours because an odd cycle is not bipartite. The unrounded average is \(5/2\). Complete graphs also meet the proposed upper bound exactly. These examples show that the question is about a precise universal inequality, rather than merely reducing the leading constant in a loose estimate.

There is also a useful family explaining the coefficient \(1/2\). Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size t, joining every vertex of two replacement cliques whenever their cycle vertices were adjacent. The resulting graph has 5t vertices, maximum degree \(3t- 1\) and clique number 2t. An independent set contains at most two vertices, so at least \(\lceil 5t/2\rceil\) colours are necessary. A universal bound \(\lceil (1- \varepsilon )(\Delta +1)+\varepsilon \omega \rceil\) with \(\varepsilon >1/2\) would give fewer colours for large t. Thus the conjectured interpolation coefficient cannot be increased.

Reed established a weaker universal interpolation with some fixed positive coefficient \(\varepsilon\) in place of \(1/2\). This already gives a saving proportional to the gap between maximum degree and clique number. Proving such a saving is difficult because high degree need not mean that a neighbourhood resembles a clique, and local savings must coexist across many overlapping neighbourhoods.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang report \(\varepsilon =0.119\) for sufficiently large maximum degree, using a refined random colouring procedure and local sparsity estimates. Their published paper explicitly records a dependency: the 0.119 calculation uses a then-unreviewed result of Delcourt and Postle. Remark 3.1 gives \(\varepsilon =0.113\) using an alternative published ingredient. The September 2026 digraph paper continues to cite the 0.119 bound. Both constants remain far below the conjectured \(1/2\).

A different advance handles graphs with much smaller cliques. Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle bound the chromatic number by \(O(\Delta \sqrt{\log  \omega /\log  \Delta})\), with related list and correspondence colouring results. For suitable relations between \(\omega\) and \(\Delta\) this is much stronger than a small fixed improvement on the greedy bound. It does not prove the desired average bound across the full range of clique sizes.

Recent related work also changes the task. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether proper colourings can be connected by Kempe changes: swap two colours on a connected component induced by those colours. Its general conjectured interpolation coefficient is \(1/3\) because reconfiguration has obstructions beyond the existence of one colouring. Its positive results on odd-hole-free graphs therefore need to be read in that separate model.

Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta extend the framework to directed graphs, where each colour class must induce an acyclic digraph. Their SODA 2025 work, revised in September 2026, proves a positive-\(\varepsilon\) interpolation and proposes the exact half-average analogue. Replacing each undirected edge by arcs in both directions recovers ordinary colouring, so the proposed directed statement would imply Reed’s conjecture. The directed partial theorem does not supply the missing coefficient.
why: A central structural colouring problem with an exact, best-possible target. It asks how much the absence of a large clique must reduce the number of colours, and guides probabilistic, structural and algorithmic approaches to colouring.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The September 8 primary revision explicitly retains the exact undirected inequality as open. Small-clique estimates, sufficiently-large-degree interpolation bounds, and the recolouring and directed variants do not settle the full statement. The published 0.119 bound’s stated dependency is preserved in the context.
progress: 1998: Reed proposes the half-average bound and proves an interpolation with some universal \(\varepsilon >0\). | 2018–2022: Bonamy–Kelly–Nelson–Postle give stronger bounds in regimes with comparatively small clique number. | 2020–2022: Hurley–de Joannis de Verclos–Kang report \(\varepsilon =0.119\) for large \(\Delta\); Remark 3.1 records the dependency and an \(\varepsilon =0.113\) alternative. | 2025-02-14: De Meyer and coauthors develop a distinct Kempe-recolouring analogue with additional reconfiguration obstructions. | 2026-09-08: The revised digraph analogue retains the undirected exact inequality as Conjecture 1.1 and proves only a positive-\(\varepsilon\) generalization.
working_summary: Reed's conjecture bounds chromatic number by the rounded average of maximum degree plus one and clique number. It combines a local upper-bound scale from degree with the unavoidable coloring demand imposed by a largest clique. The question asks whether every finite simple graph admits a coloring at this intermediate threshold. A positive answer would give a unified quantitative relationship among three fundamental graph parameters. The saved formulation concerns ordinary vertex coloring on unrestricted graphs, so fractional, list, directed, or recoloring variants require separate interpretation and do not automatically settle the inequality.

title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. P is the class of all binary languages decided under these uniform deterministic polynomial-time conventions. Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm P\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
context:
The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.
why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.
status_note: Neuen’s survey, published online 5 February 2026, explicitly retains the unrestricted polynomial-time problem as open. The author correction and both consolidated primary-source passages were checked. Targeted subsequent searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified general polynomial-time result; this bounded search and formulation audit do not independently verify every cited proof.
progress: 2015–2016: Babai announces the general quasipolynomial-time isomorphism algorithm and presents the result at STOC 2016. The available arXiv versions predate the later correction. | 2017-01-09: Babai reports a replacement for the recursive call whose analysis had invalidated the original runtime claim, restoring quasipolynomial time. The January 14 addition supplies the corrected recursive step. | 2018: Babai’s ICM survey records the corrected general frontier and the unresolved possibility of polynomial time. | 2026-02-05: Neuen’s published survey explicitly describes general graph isomorphism as neither known to be polynomial-time solvable nor known to be NP-complete. Its newer upper bounds concern specified graph parameters.
working_summary: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite simple graphs agree after a bijective relabeling of their vertices. The target is a single deterministic algorithm that answers correctly on every explicitly encoded pair in polynomial time. A proposed relabeling is easy to verify, while ruling out all relabelings can require substantially more structure. The checked general upper bound is quasipolynomial, and efficient algorithms for restricted graph classes do not establish the unrestricted polynomial bound. A resolution would settle a central structural comparison problem whose position between P and NP-completeness remains unresolved.

title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A defining flow-existence conjecture with consequences for graph decompositions, orientations and directed-cut packing.
formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph G admit an orientation of every edge and an assignment \(f:E(G)\to \{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at each vertex, the sum of f on incoming edges equals the sum on outgoing edges as integers?
definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph consists of a finite vertex set and a finite set of distinct edge identities, each with two different endpoints. Several edges may have the same endpoint pair. An edge is a bridge if deleting that edge increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means there are no such edges; disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses a tail and head for each edge independently. At vertex v, integer flow conservation is \(\Sigma\)_{\(e:head(e)=v\)}\(f(e)=\Sigma\)_{\(e:tail(e)=v\)}\(f(e)\), with empty sums zero. A nowhere-zero k-flow is such an orientation and assignment with values \(1,\ldots ,k- 1\). The statement is an existence assertion, not a bound on construction time, and does not impose an embedding or a vertex-degree bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A nowhere-zero flow circulates a nonzero amount through every edge without accumulating anything at a vertex. Bridges prevent such circulation, so bridgelessness is a necessary condition.

The established 6-flow theorem proves that five positive integer values suffice. Tutte asks whether the palette can always be reduced to four. The orientation is part of the witness, so negative values in a fixed orientation are represented by reversing edges.

The 2025 work exhibits a quantitative connection between flow existence and disjoint sets meeting directed cuts. This gives the conjecture an algorithmic and optimization role beyond the existence of an edge labeling.
why: Determine whether four nonzero integral flow values suffice for every graph with the necessary bridgelessness condition.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 paper explicitly states the general 5-flow conjecture; the same-day search found no resolution. The known 6-flow theorem does not settle the target.
progress: 1981: Seymour’s 6-flow theorem gives the corresponding universal result with values 1 through 5, as recalled in the cited paper. | 2025: Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi state the 5-flow conjecture and connect nowhere-zero flow bounds to approximate dijoin packing.
working_summary: Tutte’s conjecture asks for a nowhere-zero 5-flow in every bridgeless graph. Each edge receives a direction and an integer from one to four. At every vertex the incoming and outgoing totals must agree. Parallel edges are allowed and are treated as distinct edges. The claim would sharpen the universal 6-flow theorem and strengthen a central graph-decomposition principle.

title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.
formal: Is there one randomized sequential algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with n vertices and m edges, outputs an exact maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\) and has expected running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\) in the word-RAM model below?
definitions: A matching \(M\subseteq E(G)\) is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is |M|, and \(\nu (G)=\max\){|M|:M is a matching in G}. The algorithm must output valid edge identifiers forming a matching on every terminating execution, and |\(M|=\nu (G)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input. It must terminate with probability one. Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots ,n\) and the input is an adjacency-list or edge-list representation of size \(O(n+m)\); isolated vertices are included in n. Put \(N=n+m+2\). Use a random-access machine with \(\Theta (\log  N)\)-bit words, supporting constant-cost reads, writes, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on words, and fresh uniform random words. Intermediate larger integers require multiple words and their processing is charged. Preprocessing and output writing are included. The program is uniform, with no advice or free precomputed tables. The time statement means that this same algorithm satisfies: for every real \(\varepsilon >0\) there are constants \(C\varepsilon\) and \(N\varepsilon\) such that for every input with \(N\ge N\varepsilon\), its expected number of operations is at most \(C\varepsilon  N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The expectation is over its own random choices, not a distribution on graph inputs. No edge weights, degree restriction, bipartiteness promise, approximation slack or auxiliary communication model is assumed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Alternating paths explain how a nonmaximum matching can improve. Such a path alternates edges outside and inside the matching and starts and ends at unmatched vertices. Flipping its edge membership increases the matching size by one. In general graphs, odd cycles complicate the search for shortest augmenting paths; contracted structures called blossoms keep track of these possibilities. Micali and Vazirani’s classical algorithm achieves \(O(m\sqrt{n})\) time, with later work developing its proof and presentation.

Bipartite graphs have a particularly effective flow formulation. Direct each edge from the left side to the right, join a source to left vertices and right vertices to a sink, and give every edge capacity one. Integral maximum flow gives a maximum matching. Almost-linear exact flow algorithms therefore solve bipartite matching within the desired time scale. There is no supplied bipartition in the present question, and the same construction does not automatically encode odd-cycle constraints.

A triangle illustrates the polyhedral obstacle without requiring a large example. If a fractional variable of one half is placed on each edge, every vertex has total incident value one, but the total value is \(3/2\) while an integral matching has size at most one. For any odd vertex set S, an integral matching uses at most \((|S|- 1)/2\) edges entirely inside S. Handling these additional odd-set restrictions efficiently is part of what distinguishes general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Algebraic algorithms offer another route. Mucha and Sankowski use Gaussian elimination to construct maximum matchings in randomized time governed by matrix multiplication, conventionally written \(O(n^{\omega})\) for an available exponent \(\omega >2\). This is a major improvement over combinatorial bounds on dense graphs. It still does not yield input-size almost-linear time on all sparse graphs, where a dense n-by-n matrix representation can itself exceed the input size by a large factor.

Approximation also behaves differently. Duan, Pettie and Su obtain a \((1- \delta )\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta ^{- 1} \log  \delta ^{- 1})\) time, hence linear time for fixed \(\delta\); unit weights cover cardinality. To force exact cardinality purely by rounding this guarantee, one would need \(\delta\) small enough that the possible loss is below one edge. When the optimum is \(\Theta (n)\), that requires \(\delta =O(1/n)\), so substituting it into the approximation running time loses the desired almost-linear bound.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.
why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.
status_note: No almost-linear exact general-graph algorithm was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Bipartite flow algorithms, approximation schemes and the 2026 catalytic-space result do not meet the stated target. This card explicitly permits bounded-error randomization and expected running time.
progress: 1980: Micali–Vazirani obtain the classical \(O(m\sqrt{n})\) algorithm; later correctness work refines its alternating-path theory. | 2004: Mucha–Sankowski construct maximum matchings using fast algebraic operations. | 2011: Duan–Pettie–Su obtain linear-time approximation for each fixed accuracy parameter in general weighted graphs. | 2022: Chen and coauthors achieve almost-linear exact flow algorithms, giving the corresponding bipartite matching consequence. | 2024-09-23: Ansaripour–Danaei–Mehlhorn publish a detailed implementation and experimental study of Gabow’s general matching algorithm. | 2026-06-01: The catalytic-logspace revision constructs general maximum matchings with a polynomial-time bound, a different resource guarantee.
working_summary: Maximum matching chooses as many mutually vertex-disjoint edges as possible in an undirected graph. The target is an exact randomized algorithm with expected running time almost linear in the explicit input size. General graphs introduce odd cycles and the blossom structures needed to manage them. A fast maximal matching or an approximation does not guarantee the same answer. Progress would clarify whether finding the globally best pairing can approach the cost of simply reading all vertices and edges.

title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.
formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer \(r\ge 1\), does there exist a finite integer \(B(T,r)\) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most \(B(T,r)\)?
definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number \(\omega (G)\) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number \(\chi (G)\) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the induced graph \(G[S]\) retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map \(\varphi :V(T)\to V(G)\) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if \(\varphi (x)\varphi (y)\) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is \(\forall T \forall r \exists B \forall G\): the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |\(V(G)|\), maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function \(f_{T}:N\to N\) with \(\chi (G)\le f_{T}(\omega (G))\) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for \(f_{T}\), or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs \(G_{k}\) satisfying \(\omega (G_{k})\le r\) and \(\chi (G_{k})\to \infty\). A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |\(V(G)|\), or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
context:
A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known.
