Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size \(n^{1- o(1)}\), and consequently a chromatic bound \(n^{o(1)}\), where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power \(n^{\varepsilon}\) eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also \(n^{o(1)}\) and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant \(B(T,r)\) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.
why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.
status_note: The 2025 near-linear-stable-set paper and April 2026 bounded-boxicity paper explicitly retain the general conjecture. The former yields \(n^{o(1)}\) rather than a size-independent bound; the latter restricts the host class. September 2026 results on tournament analogues concern directed parameters. No resolution of this ordinary undirected statement found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1994: Kierstead–Penrice establish \(\chi\)-boundedness when the excluded tree has radius at most two. | 2022–2023: Scott–Seymour strengthen radius-two results under complete multipartite subgraph exclusions; checked preprint revised 10 January 2023. | 2023–2024: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour force path-induced rooted copies of arbitrary trees, while permitting extra edges between branches. | 2024–2025: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour prove near-linear independent sets and subpolynomial chromatic bounds for every fixed forest and clique bound; journal publication 25 September 2025. | 2026-04-02: Davies–Yuditsky’s journal publication proves polynomial \(\chi\)-boundedness under the additional promise of boxicity bounded by a fixed dimension.
working_summary: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture considers graphs excluding a fixed tree as an induced subgraph. It asks whether bounding clique number then also bounds chromatic number, independently of graph size. The proposed principle says that high coloring complexity with no large clique must eventually force every prescribed induced tree. This would organize a large collection of hereditary coloring classes through one structural mechanism. The saved review distinguishes genuinely induced trees from weaker path-induced copies and ordinary coloring from fractional results, while allowing an arbitrary bound rather than demanding polynomial growth.

title: Optimal bounds in the Excluded Grid Theorem
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central quantitative problem in graph minor theory with direct implications for structural decompositions, routing, packing and parameterized algorithms.
formal: For each integer \(r\ge 2\), let \(f(r)\) be the least nonnegative integer t such that every finite simple undirected graph of treewidth at least t contains the \(r\times r\) square grid as a minor. Determine the asymptotic order of \(f(r)\) up to universal constant factors, including the correct logarithmic dependence.
definitions: The \(r\times r\) grid has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,r\}^{2}\), with an edge between \((i,j)\) and \((i' ,j' )\) exactly when |\(i- i' |+|j- j' |=1\). It has \(r^{2}\) vertices; r denotes side length. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges, after removing loops and merging parallel edges. Equivalently, a model of H consists of one nonempty connected vertex set in G for each vertex of H, all pairwise disjoint, with an edge of G joining the corresponding sets for every edge of H. Additional edges are permitted. A tree decomposition of G is a tree T with bags \(B_{t}\subseteq V(G)\), such that every vertex belongs to some bag, the endpoints of every edge belong together to some bag, and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is \(\max _{t} |B_{t}|- 1\); treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum such width. Robertson–Seymour’s Grid-Minor Theorem guarantees that \(f(r)\) is finite. The quantifier over G includes graphs of arbitrary size, degree and genus. This is an extremal existence threshold; no efficiency requirement for finding the grid model is imposed. Polylogarithmic factors mean \((\log  r)^{c}\) for a fixed constant c, and matching bounds here must resolve such factors rather than suppress them.
answer_criterion: Identify an explicit asymptotic function \(h(r)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) such that a \(h(r)\le f(r)\le b h(r)\) for all sufficiently large r. The upper bound must force a grid minor in every graph above the stated threshold; the lower bound must give graphs of comparable treewidth that exclude it. In particular, this determines whether \(f(r)=O(r^{2}(\log  r)^{c})\) for some fixed c. Merely improving a nonmatching polynomial exponent, solving the planar-host case, or replacing minors by a different containment relation is progress rather than a complete answer.
context:
Treewidth measures how large the interacting pieces of a graph must be when organized along a tree. Many algorithms work by dynamic programming across the bags of a tree decomposition, with a strong dependence on bag size. A grid provides a canonical obstruction to small treewidth: its rows and columns create many overlapping connections that cannot be separated into very small bags. The Excluded Grid Theorem states that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains such an obstruction as a minor.

The unknown quantity is how much treewidth must be spent to force a grid of a given side length. The qualitative theorem only says that some finite threshold exists. A sharp quantitative bound would explain how efficiently general tangled connectivity can be organized into a planar grid. This is not a statement that the graph itself is planar, or that a grid must appear as an induced subgraph.

A vertex-count example already rules out a linear threshold. The complete graph on \(r^{2}- 1\) vertices has treewidth \(r^{2}- 2\), but cannot contain an \(r\times r\) grid minor because taking a minor cannot increase the number of vertices. Thus \(f(r)\ge r^{2}- 1\). Its many edges cannot replace the need for \(r^{2}\) disjoint nonempty branch sets in a minor model. This is why the fact that the \(r\times r\) grid itself has treewidth r does not imply a linear bound for arbitrary host graphs.

The known lower bound is stronger: \(f(r)=\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\). Robertson, Seymour and Thomas obtain it using bounded-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs have treewidth proportional to their number of vertices, while every cycle is long. A large grid contains quadratically many vertex-disjoint small cycles; lifting those cycles through a minor model requires quadratically many disjoint long cycles in the host. This consumes a logarithmic factor of additional vertices.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial upper bound, replacing an enormous quantitative gap by a polynomial relationship between treewidth and grid size. Their proof is constructive: a randomized polynomial-time algorithm finds a grid model at the scale established by their theorem. This makes the result useful both as a structural guarantee and as a subroutine, although this card asks only for the optimal existence threshold.

Chuzhoy and Tan improve the general upper bound to \(O(r^{9}(\log  r)^{c})\) for an absolute constant c. Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the \(r^{2} \log  r\) lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even \(r^{2}\) times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold \(f(r)\) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the \(r\times r\) grid has treewidth \(O(gr+t^{2304})\), hence \(O(t^{2}r+t^{2304})\). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.
why: Determine the exact asymptotic loss when converting large treewidth into a square-grid minor, a foundational link between graph structure and algorithms.
status_note: The checked general bounds remain \(\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\) and \(O(r^{9} \operatorname{polylog} r)\). The November 2025 product-structure result and SODA 2026 fixed-minor result refine different aspects and do not determine the all-graphs threshold. No matching asymptotic bounds found through 11 September 2026. The problem does not assume that either the near-quadratic or cubic conjecture is correct.
progress: 1986: Robertson–Seymour prove that sufficiently large treewidth forces any fixed planar graph, including every square grid, as a minor. | 1994: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas strengthen quantitative bounds; logarithmic-girth expanders give the \(\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\) obstruction. | 2013–2016: Chekuri–Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial relationship, with a randomized algorithm finding a grid model; STOC 2014 and JACM 2016. | 2019–2021: Chuzhoy–Tan prove the general \(O(r^{9} \operatorname{polylog} r)\) upper bound; SODA 2019, Journal of Combinatorial Theory B 2021. | 2025-11-07: The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited gives a qualitative product-structure strengthening, with an unspecified blow-up factor depending on the excluded planar graph. | 2026-01: Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs gives bounds linear in grid side length and polynomial in |\(V(H)|\) under additional exclusion of H; SODA 2026.
working_summary: The Excluded Grid Theorem guarantees a large grid minor when a graph has sufficiently large treewidth. The question asks for the optimal treewidth threshold forcing an r-by-r grid, including the correct logarithmic factors. Treewidth measures how difficult the graph is to decompose into small overlapping bags, while a grid supplies a concrete witness of large-scale complexity. Sharp bounds would quantify this foundational connection used throughout structural and algorithmic graph theory. The reviewed target concerns all graphs and grid side length, so bounds for an additional excluded-minor promise or suppressed polylogarithmic factors do not finish it.

title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central directed-graph conjecture expressing a simple, general degree-versus-girth principle.
formal: For every pair of integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n- 1\), does every simple loopless digraph D on n vertices with minimum outdegree at least r contain a directed cycle of length at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\)?
definitions: A simple loopless digraph has a finite vertex set V and an arc set \(A\subseteq \{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}\); each ordered pair occurs at most once. Both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) are allowed. The outdegree \(d^{+}(v)\) is |\(\{u:(v,u)\in A\}|\) and minimum outdegree is \(\min _{v\in V}d^{+}(v)\). A directed cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 2\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) with \((v_{i},v_{i+1})\in A\) for every i and \(v_{\ell +1}=v_{1}\). Thus an opposite pair of arcs is a directed 2-cycle. \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\) is the least integer not smaller than \(n/r\). There is no planarity, regularity, connectivity or algorithmic assumption.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Positive outdegree ensures that some directed cycle exists, but it gives no immediate sharp estimate of its length. The conjecture proposes the threshold \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\) when every vertex has at least r outgoing neighbors.

Allowing opposite arcs makes the graph model a general simple digraph rather than an orientation of a simple graph. The ceiling and minimum-degree quantifiers must be preserved when comparing formulations.

Recent rainbow-cycle research continues to use this directed-girth assertion as an unresolved reference point. A theorem about several colored edge sets does not by itself supply the cycle in every digraph specified here.
why: Determine the sharp universal relationship between a local directed-degree condition and the existence of a short directed cycle.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Guo’s 2026 journal article retains the general conjecture; no resolution was located in the same-day review.
progress: 2025–2026: Guo’s preprint and journal article state the general conjecture while proving related rainbow-cycle statements.
working_summary: The conjecture links minimum outdegree with the length of a directed cycle. An n-vertex digraph of minimum outdegree r should contain a cycle of length at most the ceiling of n divided by r. Opposite arcs are allowed, but loops and parallel copies of an arc are forbidden. The assertion covers all graphs and all positive degree thresholds in the stated range. It is a sharp general principle connecting local expansion with global directed cycles.

title: Almost-linear triangle detection
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least \(2/3\) and worst-case running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\)?
definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges \(\{u,v\},\{v,w\},\{w,u\}\) are present. The input gives labelled vertices \(1,\ldots ,n\) and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of \(w=\lceil 4 \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The \(o(1)\) is a function tending to zero as \(n+m\) tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon >0\) the same algorithm eventually uses at most \((n+m+2)^{1+\varepsilon}\) operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic \(O(n+m)\) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an \(O(n^{2})\) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.
context:
Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) input edges and \(\Theta (n^{3})\) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in \(O(m\cdot a(G))\) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity \(a(G)\) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order \(\sqrt{m}\), so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent \(\tau\), the resulting standard bound is \(O(n+m^{2\tau /(\tau +1)})\), roughly \(O(n+m^{1.407})\) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent \(4/3\) in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is \(\{0,3,6\}\), consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims \(O(n^{2})\) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.
why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.
status_note: No established almost-linear algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem found through 11 September 2026. The 2024 combinatorial proposal is withdrawn. The stated parent-edge rule in the August 2025 linear proposal has the explicit counterexample described above. The separate September \(2026 O(n^{2})\) claim does not meet the all-density target and is not treated as an established bound.
progress: 1985: Chiba–Nishizeki give \(O(m\cdot a(G))\) triangle listing, yielding linear time for bounded-arboricity families. | 1997: Alon–Yuster–Zwick combine degree splitting with fast matrix multiplication to improve sparse triangle detection. | 2014: Abboud–Vassilevska Williams formulate the no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and derive conditional dynamic lower bounds. | 2024-03-05: Dumitrescu withdraws the claimed faster combinatorial algorithm because its case analysis is invalid. | 2026-07: Kumabe–Uezato use triangle hardness to exclude almost-linear matching for a restricted two-use backreference class, conditionally. | 2026-09-08: A separate Aegypti revision claims \(O(n^{2})\), which is not an almost-linear guarantee for all graph densities; correctness not adjudicated here.
working_summary: Triangle detection asks whether an undirected graph contains three pairwise adjacent vertices. The proposed randomized algorithm must decide this in almost linear time on every explicitly supplied graph. Only existence is requested, so graphs with many triangles do not impose a large-output obstacle. Sparse special classes offer useful successes without covering arbitrary inputs. The challenge is to avoid examining too many combinations of neighbors while still giving a reliable negative answer when no triangle exists anywhere.

title: Seese’s conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.
formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
definitions: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), membership \(x\in X\) in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class \(C, Sat_{MSO_{1}}(C)\) consists of all finite encoded MSO\(_{1}\) sentences \(\varphi\) for which some \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory \(Th_{MSO_{1}}(C)\)={\(\varphi\): every \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\)}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in \([k]\), disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The conclusion is \(\exists k\forall G\in C \operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\), with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
context:
An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO\(_{1}\) conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether \(n\in S\) if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO\(_{1}\) with the predicate \(Even(X)\), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO\(_{1}\) sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO\(_{1}\) formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO\(_{1}\) decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.
why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO\(_{1}\) decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.
progress: 1991: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO\(_{1}\) boundary. | 2007: Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO\(_{1}\) with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width. | 2020–2025: Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025. | 2025: Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s. | 12–26 July 2026: Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability.
working_summary: MSO1 permits quantification over vertices and vertex sets in a graph. Seese's conjecture asks whether decidability of this logic over a graph class forces bounded clique-width. The proposed implication connects an algorithmic property of the class's whole logical theory with a finite construction complexity for its graphs. A proof would identify a strong structural obstruction to decidable graph reasoning. The saved formulation imposes no hereditary assumption and excludes edge-set and counting extensions, so results for narrower classes or stronger logics cannot be substituted for the stated general MSO1 question.

title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central static graph optimization primitive with broad algorithmic consequences. The precise remaining overhead separates the established almost-linear breakthrough from the longstanding nearly linear target; this is a general problem rather than a refinement of one fixed algorithm.
formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 1\), do there exist a constant \(k\ge 0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{a}\) that, on every directed graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{a}\}\), outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((m+n)(\log (n+2))^{k})\)?
definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer \(f_{e}\) to each arc, with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length \(B_{a}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(B_{a}\) large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. \(A_{a}, k, B_{a}\) and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The \(m+n\) convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is \(O(m \operatorname{polylog} n)\).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.
why: Identify whether exact flow optimization with polynomially bounded capacities admits genuinely polylogarithmic overhead over graph input size.
status_note: Primary-source check through 11 September 2026 found almost-linear bounds, not the fixed-polylogarithmic overhead required here. New preprint proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2022: Exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow achieve almost-linear time for polynomially bounded integral data. | 2026-08-18: Li–Wice state an \(m^{1+o(1)}\) maximum-flow algorithm, leaving the polylogarithmic-overhead target unestablished.

title: Cereceda’s conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: The principal structural diameter conjecture in graph-colouring reconfiguration.
formal: For every fixed d, does the reconfiguration graph of proper \((d+2)\)-colourings of every n-vertex d-degenerate graph have diameter \(O_{d}(n^{2})\), where one step recolours one vertex?
context:
No matching Cereceda or general quadratic degenerate-recolouring question was found.

This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: The principal structural diameter conjecture in graph-colouring reconfiguration.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.
working_summary: A recoloring step changes one vertex's color while keeping the graph properly colored. The saved Cereceda question asks whether every pair of proper \((d+2)\)-colorings of an n-vertex d-degenerate graph can be connected in \(O_{d}(n^{2})\) steps. Degeneracy ensures that every subgraph contains a vertex of degree at most d, providing a natural elimination structure. The challenge is using that structure without forcing an excessively long cascade of recolorings. A quadratic bound would make the reconfiguration space quantitatively navigable, while the saved proposal still requires a fuller source and progress review before becoming a completed card.

title: Vertex reconstruction conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Tests whether a whole combinatorial structure is determined by all of its one-vertex views, with a direct graph-isomorphism connection.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\) and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality \(D(G)=D(H)\) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.
context:
Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If \(n\ge 3\), every original edge appears in exactly \(n- 2\) members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by \(n- 2\). Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.
why: The conjecture asks whether all overlapping one-vertex views determine an entire graph. It tests how much structural information survives deletion and loss of labels, and connects graph structure to reconstruction and isomorphism problems.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026: Dufresne and coauthors (April 2026) and Heinrich and coauthors (May 2026 revision) still treat the general conjecture as open. O’Shea and Wilkins’s 2024 publisher abstract claims a general proof, but its full text was inaccessible and the argument was not assessed here. This conflicting claim is recorded with uncertain status rather than accepted as a resolution. The checked 2026 interval-graph and structured bipartite incidence-deletion results do not establish the full conjecture.
progress: 2022-01-02: McKay’s version 4 reports exhaustive verification for all graphs on 3 through 13 vertices, including stronger reduced-deck checks in their applicable range. The computations were not rerun here. | 2024: O’Shea and Wilkins publish a claimed general proof. Only the publisher-indexed abstract and highlights were accessible in this review; no correctness conclusion is drawn from the claim. | 2026-04-17: Dufresne and coauthors state the full graph reconstruction conjecture as open and explain its invariant-theoretic formulation. | 2026-05-12: Heinrich and coauthors’ revised preprint proves every interval graph of order at least three reconstructible, with a polynomial-time reconstruction consequence. | 2026-06-08: The revised AI-driven proof-search paper states a restricted bipartite incidence-deletion theorem with additional structural hypotheses. It does not claim the general vertex-deletion theorem.
working_summary: The vertex reconstruction conjecture asks whether every finite simple graph with at least three vertices is determined by all its one-vertex-deleted views. The views forget vertex labels but retain the multiplicity of repeated isomorphism classes. Even the edge count and degree multiset can be recovered, while the full arrangement of edges is the unresolved target in current specialist sources. Finite computational checks and a theorem for interval graphs provide partial results. An earlier general proof claim is recorded without validation, and recent structured bipartite results are kept distinct from this full question.

title: Berge–Fulkerson conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A classical exact decomposition conjecture at the intersection of matching theory and global graph structure.
formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless cubic multigraph G have an ordered list \((M_{1},\ldots ,M_{6})\) of perfect matchings such that for every edge \(e\in E(G), |\{i\in \{1,\ldots ,6\}:e\in M_{i}\}|=2\)?
definitions: Edges of a multigraph have distinct identities and may share their unordered pair of endpoints; loops are forbidden. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, counting incident edge identities with multiplicity. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and bridgeless graphs have none. Disconnected graphs are allowed. A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share an endpoint. It is perfect if every vertex is incident with exactly one of its edges. The six matchings may repeat; membership counts positions in the list, not just distinct subsets. The conclusion requires every edge to occur exactly twice, with no omitted edge and no extra coverage. No algorithmic bound is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A single perfect matching chooses one incident edge at each vertex. Six such choices would give six incidences at every vertex; the conjecture asks for those incidences to be distributed evenly across its three edges.

The requirement is stronger than merely covering the edges with some collection of perfect matchings. Both the number six and exact multiplicity two belong to the target, and repeated matchings must be permitted.

The 2026 paper distinguishes the finite conjecture and its weaker matching-cover assertions while studying infinite graphs. A statement about a different cover object, such as a cycle double cover, does not establish this exact perfect-matching decomposition.
why: Ask whether every bridgeless cubic graph has a uniform six-term integral realization of its fractional perfect-matching structure.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 primary preprint explicitly states that the finite conjecture remains open. No subsequent resolution was located; proofs in the cited preprint were not independently checked.
progress: 2026-07-31: Magalhães Júnior and Silva explicitly retain the finite conjecture as open while investigating its infinite analogues and their equivalences.
working_summary: Every bridgeless cubic multigraph is asked to admit six perfect matchings. Each edge must occur in exactly two positions of that six-matching list. The matchings may repeat, and parallel edges remain distinct. The target is an exact integral decomposition rather than an approximate or fractional cover. It captures a longstanding structural question about how perfect matchings fit together globally.

title: Barnette’s conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A canonical and longstanding Hamiltonicity boundary with direct links between planar structure, graph traversal and drawing.
formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. A Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{n}\) of all vertices, each appearing exactly once, such that \(\{v_{i},v_{i+1}\}\) is an edge for every i, with \(v_{n+1}=v_{1}\). The cycle must use only edges already present in the graph. No algorithmic running-time guarantee is requested.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Hamiltonicity is a global demand: one cycle must visit every vertex. Barnette’s conjecture proposes that planarity, bipartiteness, cubic degree and vertex connectivity together always guarantee this traversal.

The recent approximation result uses a subhamiltonian ordering whose consecutive pairs need not all be original edges. Its \(5n/6\) guarantee is substantial progress in a relaxed setting, but the missing adjacencies distinguish it from the requested cycle.

The planar dual connects the conjecture with partitions of Eulerian triangulations into induced forests. The 2026 partition paper makes those links precise while continuing to distinguish the unresolved Hamiltonicity assertion.
why: Determine whether four basic structural conditions force a spanning cycle in every graph satisfying them.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The GD 2025 and February 2026 papers explicitly retain the conjecture; no general resolution was found.
progress: 2025: Bekos, Kaufmann and Pfister improve a relaxed subhamiltonian-cycle guarantee to at least \(5n/6\) original edges; this is not a Hamiltonian cycle in the original graph. | 2026-02-13: Cambie and coauthors restate Barnette’s conjecture as open and study related planar partition problems.
working_summary: Barnette’s conjecture concerns 3-connected cubic bipartite planar graphs. It predicts that every such graph contains a cycle through all vertices exactly once. Every consecutive pair on the cycle must be an existing graph edge. Relaxed book-embedding results may add missing adjacencies and therefore do not settle the conjecture. The question isolates a classical boundary between local structural restrictions and a global spanning traversal.

title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture is a classical universal expansion principle for arbitrary oriented graphs, with broad extremal significance.
formal: Does every finite nonempty oriented graph D contain a vertex v for which |\(N^{++}(v)|\ge |N^{+}(v)|\), where \(N^{+}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance one from v and \(N^{++}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two?
definitions: An oriented graph is a finite vertex set V and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\) with no loops and with at most one of \((u,v),(v,u)\) present for each distinct pair. Arc multiplicities are not allowed. \(N^{+}(v)=\{u:(v,u)\in A\}\). \(N^{++}(v)\)={\(w\in V\setminus (N^{+}(v)\cup \{v\})\): there exists u with \((v,u)\in A\) and \((u,w)\in A\)}. Thus a vertex already in the first neighborhood is not counted in the second, even if it is also reachable by a length-two walk. Cardinalities count vertices rather than paths or arcs. A sink has both sets empty and satisfies the inequality. No lower bound on outdegree, connectivity or planarity is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
The first out-neighborhood measures one-step reach. The second counts genuinely new vertices obtainable in two steps. The conjecture asserts that at least one starting point has no decrease in this particular count.

Excluding opposite arcs matters: a two-vertex directed 2-cycle would have a nonempty first neighborhood and an empty second neighborhood at both vertices. The oriented-graph hypothesis rules out this immediate obstruction.

The July 2026 specialist paper retains the general conjecture while treating a strengthening. A separate May 2026 manuscript claims a full solution. This conflict is recorded explicitly; the card does not certify a proof or dismiss the claim without analysis.
why: Ask whether every oriented graph has a vertex whose new two-step reach is at least its immediate reach.
status_note: Claim conflict recorded on 11 September 2026. Glover’s 30 May 2026 version claims a complete proof, whereas Bai–Li–Park’s 24 July 2026 paper explicitly treats the general conjecture as open. Neither acceptance nor correctness of the full-proof claim was established here; the status is therefore uncertain, not certified open or resolved.
progress: 2026-05-30: Glover’s revised manuscript claims a complete proof. This review has not verified that claim or established community acceptance. | 2026-07-24: Bai, Li and Park still explicitly state the general conjecture as open and prove special cases of a stronger matching property.
working_summary: Seymour’s conjecture concerns oriented graphs with no loops or opposite pair of arcs. It asks for a vertex with at least as many vertices at distance exactly two as at distance one. Second neighbors exclude first neighbors and count vertices rather than paths. The statement is a general local expansion principle without degree or planarity promises. A complete-proof claim conflicts with a later specialist paper still treating the conjecture as open, and that status uncertainty is preserved.

title: Strongly polynomial near-linear negative-weight shortest paths
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Removing numerical scaling dependence in a nearly input-linear bound would settle a central gap in exact shortest-path computation over arbitrary real data.
formal: Do there exist a uniform randomized comparison-addition algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\) that compute all exact distances from one specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary real arc lengths and no negative directed cycle, using at most \(C(m+n)(\log(n+2))^{k}\) operations and succeeding with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Arc lengths may be positive, zero or negative. A path length is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, or an infinity marker if unreachable. The promise excludes negative cycles anywhere in the graph. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The operation bound is independent of all magnitudes and numerical encoding lengths. On rational inputs, intermediate values must have bit length polynomial in the total binary input length; this is the usual additional encoding condition for strong polynomiality.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Negative lengths allow shortest paths to express costs, credits and difference constraints. They make the numerical model essential: a graph-size bound uniform over real weights is stronger than a bound depending on the number of bits in integer weights.

Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen obtained near-linear integer-weight shortest paths with a \(\log W\) dependence. Bringmann, Cassis and Fischer improve the logarithmic factors and explicitly ask whether strong polynomiality can remove that dependence.

The February 2026 preprint by Li, Li and Zhang gives \(n^{2+o(1)}\) time for real weights. This is almost linear for dense graphs, but it neither has polylogarithmic overhead nor gives the requested sparse-graph bound.

Mareš supplies the shortest-path background; the endpoint and status distinctions here come from the later research papers.
why: Removing numerical scaling dependence in a nearly input-linear bound would settle a central gap in exact shortest-path computation over arbitrary real data.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The approved real-weight formulation of the strong-polynomial endpoint fixes bounded error and worst-case operation cost. It is not the solved near-linear integer-weight question.
progress: 2022: Near-linear algorithms become available for integer weights with a numerical scaling factor. | 2026: The integer-weight near-linear bound is derandomized; the weight dependence remains. | 2026-02-18: A preprint states an \(n^{2+o(1)}\) real-weight algorithm, leaving the general near-linear target open.
working_summary: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary real edge lengths and no negative cycle. The task is to compute all distances from one source exactly. The question asks for near-linear comparison-addition time independent of weight magnitudes. Near-linear integer-weight algorithms and almost-quadratic real-weight algorithms leave this general target unanswered. A resolution would close a central gap between numerical scaling and strongly polynomial graph computation.

title: Strongly polynomial maximum flow below the \(mn\) barrier
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A polynomial improvement over the general strongly polynomial maximum-flow barrier would separate a central combinatorial optimization primitive from its longstanding arithmetic complexity bound.
formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform randomized strongly polynomial algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in every directed network with arbitrary nonnegative rational capacities, \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\ge n-1\) arcs, in \(O((mn)^{1-\varepsilon})\) worst-case arithmetic-RAM operations with success probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Capacities and output values are finite rationals. Use exact rational cells with unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational and comparison. Integer control and addresses use \(O(\log(n+m+2))\)-bit words with unit-cost arithmetic, Boolean operations and shifts; they cannot inspect rational encodings or apply floor to rationals. Fixed rational constants and a fixed finite program are allowed, with no advice or free tables. Charge all arithmetic, control, memory access, random-word generation and output operations, treating each rational input or output as one cell. The count is independent of capacity magnitudes and binary lengths. For input bit length \(L\), every intermediate numerator and denominator and the total used bit space must be polynomially bounded in \(L\), including on unsuccessful executions. Independent fair random words are allowed. The bound holds on every execution; the entire flow must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Constants and the polynomial bit-space bound are uniform over all instances.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Strongly polynomial flow bounds count arithmetic operations without making large numerical capacities a source of extra iterations. This distinguishes combinatorial network size from the bit complexity of the capacities.

Dadush, Orlin, Sidford and Végh explicitly ask for an \(O((mn)^{1-\varepsilon})\) strongly polynomial algorithm. Their SODA 2026 work improves structured networks while identifying \(O(mn)\) as the general bound.

Almost-linear algorithms for polynomially bounded integral capacities answer a different numerical-complexity question. Here one fixed exponent saving must hold for arbitrary rational capacities and every edge density.
why: A polynomial improvement over the general strongly polynomial maximum-flow barrier would separate a central combinatorial optimization primitive from its longstanding arithmetic complexity bound.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The explicitly sourced exponent-saving question is made precise for finite rational capacities, with bounded-error randomization and worst-case operation cost. The rational encoding condition is separate from the arithmetic count.
progress: 2026: The paper gives faster strongly polynomial algorithms for structured networks and retains the general \(O(mn)\) barrier.
working_summary: Maximum flow asks for the greatest feasible transfer between a specified source and sink under arc capacities. Here capacities are arbitrary nonnegative rationals. The question asks for a fixed polynomial improvement over the general strongly polynomial arithmetic bound. The operation count must be independent of capacity encodings while intermediate bit space remains polynomial. Fast algorithms for bounded integral capacities and special graph classes do not establish this target.

title: Erdős girth conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Connects extremal graph density with the optimal size of sparse distance-preserving structures; consequences extend across graph theory and algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.
answer_criterion: Prove the required graph families exist for every fixed k, or refute the universal claim for at least one fixed k. Proving the \(k=4\) case alone would resolve the first unknown case but not the whole conjecture.
context:
High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.
why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The general conjecture remains unresolved; several individual values of k are settled.
progress: 1993: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size. | 2026: Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.
