working_summary: The Erdős girth conjecture seeks graphs with many edges despite the absence of short cycles. For every fixed k, the target is arbitrarily large graphs with order \(n^{1+1/k}\) edges and girth greater than 2k. Such graphs would match the classical density upper bound up to a constant depending on k. They also force every stretch-\((2k- 1)\) spanner to retain all edges, connecting the extremal construction to sharp sparsification limits. The saved review notes that progress for special parameters or fault-tolerant spanner models does not supply the missing high-girth families in general.

title: List edge-coloring conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Asks whether arbitrary local restrictions on allowed edge colors impose any additional global cost.
formal: For every finite loopless multigraph G and every assignment L of finite sets of colors to its edges with |\(\mathrm{L}(e)|\ge \chi ' (G)\) for every edge e, does there exist a proper edge coloring c with \(c(e)\in \mathrm{L}(e)\) for every e? Equivalently, is \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)\) for every such G?
definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map \(\partial\) assigning to each edge \(e\in E a\) two-element subset \(\partial e\subseteq V\). Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer \(k\ge 0\) let \([k]=\{1,\ldots ,k\}\), with [0] empty; \(\chi ' (G)\), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map \(E\to [k]\). A list assignment is a function \(e\mapsto \mathrm{L}(e)\) where each \(\mathrm{L}(e)\) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is the least \(k\ge 0\) such that every assignment with |\(\mathrm{L}(e)|\ge k\) admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree \(\Delta\) counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.
context:
Think of an edge as a job requiring its two endpoint resources at the same time, and a color as a time slot. Jobs sharing a resource must use different slots. Ordinary edge coloring offers every job the same collection of slots. List edge coloring lets each job have its own availability restrictions and asks for a compatible schedule.

For two edges sharing one endpoint, ordinary edge coloring needs two colors. Lists {red,blue} and {blue,green} still each have size two, although their union has size three; choosing red for the first edge and blue for the second is valid. The conjecture compares the number of choices available to each edge, not the total number of distinct color names used across all lists.

Identical lists are permitted, so \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is always at least \(\chi ' (G)\). The question is whether arbitrary overlaps among different lists can ever create an additional obstruction. An ordinary coloring alone does not answer this, since a color assigned to an edge may be absent from that edge’s list.

The reference quantity is the chromatic index, rather than just maximum degree. A triangle has maximum degree two but needs three edge colors. If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every \(\varepsilon >0\), all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\le (1+\varepsilon )\chi ' (G)\). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}\) whenever p is an odd prime; \(K_{r}\) denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are \(p- 2\) and \(2p- 1\). These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.
why: The conjecture asks whether local restrictions on available edge colors ever increase the number of choices each edge must receive beyond the optimum with a shared palette. It tests whether ordinary scheduling feasibility is robust to arbitrary per-job availability, across all finite loopless multigraphs.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. Jafari’s 24 August 2026 preprint still leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open and claims results only for two prime-parameter families. No later resolution of the full multigraph conjecture was located. Galvin’s bipartite theorem and Kahn’s asymptotic theorem have narrower conclusions than the target. Recent claims and seminar announcements were not independently proof-audited.
progress: 1995: Galvin proves \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)=\Delta (G)\) for bipartite multigraphs; publisher abstract and Kahn’s discussion checked. | 2000: Kahn, Theorem 1.1, proves asymptotic equality of list and fractional chromatic indices for multigraphs; because the ordinary index lies between them, list and ordinary indices also have ratio tending to one. | 2024-05-21: Molloy’s seminar abstract announces the simple-graph bound \(\Delta +\Delta ^{2/5} \operatorname{poly}(\log  \Delta )\). This still allows an additive gap; only the abstract was checked. | 2026-08-24: Jafari’s version 1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, claims the conjectured exact values for \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}, p\) an odd prime. These partial claims do not cover all complete graphs or all multigraphs.
working_summary: A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to edges that share an endpoint. In list edge coloring, each edge must choose its color from its own finite set of allowed colors. The conjecture asks whether giving every edge as many choices as the ordinary chromatic index always suffices, even with arbitrary list overlaps and parallel edges. It holds for bipartite multigraphs, and a general asymptotic theorem leaves only a vanishing relative gap. Exact equality for every finite loopless multigraph would show that local availability restrictions never impose an additional per-edge palette requirement.

title: Triangle covering-to-packing ratio
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A fundamental integral packing-versus-covering problem tied to two canonical graph optimization tasks.
formal: Determine \(\Gamma _{\triangle}=\sup\){\(\tau _{\triangle}(G)/\nu _{\triangle}(G): G\) is a finite simple undirected graph with at least one triangle}, where \(\tau _{\triangle}\) and \(\nu _{\triangle}\) are defined below.
definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices together with all three edges between them. An edge set F meets every triangle if each triangle contains at least one edge of F; equivalently, deleting F makes G triangle-free. Define \(\tau _{\triangle}\) as the minimum cardinality of such \(F\subseteq E(G)\). A packing is a family of triangles whose three-edge sets are pairwise disjoint; triangles in a packing may share vertices. Define \(\nu _{\triangle}\) as the maximum cardinality of a packing. Both values are zero when G has no triangles, including the empty graph. The inequality concerns integral edge sets and integral packings, with no fractional weights and no running-time requirement. Restricting the ratio to graphs containing a triangle avoids a zero denominator; triangle-free graphs already satisfy every nonnegative-factor comparison. The supremum is finite: deleting every edge of a maximal triangle packing gives \(\tau _{\triangle}\le 3\nu _{\triangle}\). Attainment of the supremum is not required.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma _{\triangle}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
context:
The target is the best universal covering-to-packing factor. Tuza’s conjecture gives the candidate \(\Gamma _{\triangle}=2\), but the quantitative question also asks for the value if that conjecture fails.

A triangle packing exhibits many separate obstructions to triangle-freeness. An edge cover removes all such obstructions. Every cover must meet each member of a packing, while taking all edges of a maximal packing gives the elementary factor-three comparison.

Tuza asks whether the covering cost always stays within twice the maximum packing size. Edge-disjointness is essential: the triangles may meet at vertices. The four-vertex complete graph has packing number one and covering number two, so a smaller universal factor is impossible.

Results for dense or bounded-degree graphs and fractional relaxations do not establish the integral inequality for arbitrary graphs. The August 2026 degree-seven manuscript is recorded as a preprint claim rather than an independently verified proof.
why: Establish the proposed sharp factor-two relation between destroying all triangles and packing disjoint triangles.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 dense-graph paper and 2026 bounded-degree work do not settle the unrestricted conjecture. The new degree-seven result is a preprint claim; its proof was not independently checked. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
progress: 2025: The dense-graph paper proves special cases while retaining the unrestricted conjecture. | 2026-08-06: A preprint claims the conjecture for graphs of maximum degree at most seven, a restricted input family.
working_summary: Triangle covering deletes edges to eliminate every triangle, while triangle packing selects edge-disjoint triangles. The target is the supremum ratio of these two integral optima over finite simple graphs with a triangle. Packed triangles may share vertices but cannot share edges. Tuza’s conjecture predicts that the universal ratio equals two. The numerical benchmark requires a Lean-certified value within absolute error 0.01.

title: Deterministic Exact Matching
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: General Exact Matching is a clean test of removing randomness from algebraic graph algorithms beyond the bipartite setting.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.
answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
context:
Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.
why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 revision of the randomized algorithm and the April 2026 bipartite claim. The revised randomized-algorithm paper explicitly states that deterministic polynomial time remains open. This question allows nonbipartite graphs.
progress: 1987: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms. | 2023: El Maalouly surveys algorithms and related problems while retaining general deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open. | 2026-04: Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution. | 2026-08-10: Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using \(O(n^{\omega})\) finite-field operations, where \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.
working_summary: Exact Matching adds a prescribed red-edge count to the ordinary perfect matching problem. Given red and blue edges, an algorithm must decide whether some perfect matching contains exactly the requested number of red edges. The target is deterministic polynomial time on general graphs. Knowing the smallest and largest achievable counts is insufficient because intermediate counts can be absent. The problem isolates how to enforce an exact combinatorial constraint while avoiding the random algebraic choices used by existing approaches.

title: Neumann–Lara conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central directed planar-coloring conjecture linking planarity and decomposition into acyclic subgraphs.
formal: For every finite oriented graph D whose underlying undirected graph is planar, is there a coloring \(c:V(D)\to \{0,1\}\) such that neither color class induces a directed cycle?
definitions: An oriented graph has no loops or parallel arcs and contains at most one of \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) for each unordered pair of distinct vertices. Its underlying simple undirected graph joins u,v exactly when one of these arcs is present. Planarity means that graph admits a drawing in the plane with edges intersecting only at common endpoints. For a vertex set X, the induced subdigraph \(D[X]\) retains every arc of D whose two endpoints lie in X. A directed cycle is a cyclic sequence of distinct vertices with all successive arcs oriented forward. A digraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Color classes may be empty. This is not proper coloring: an arc may have endpoints of the same color provided no monochromatic directed cycle results. The assertion asks only for existence, without an algorithmic running-time bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Acyclic vertex coloring permits edges within each class but forbids a cyclic chain of directed dependencies. It is therefore different from ordinary proper coloring of the underlying planar graph.

Li and Mohar settle the case without directed triangles. The unrestricted target includes directed triangles and asks whether the entire graph can still be split into only two acyclic induced parts.

The 2026 partition paper connects this conjecture to planar Hamiltonicity and induced-forest questions. Its formulation on planar triangulations has the same general coloring target, because additional oriented edges can only impose more restrictions and every oriented planar graph extends to an oriented planar triangulation after harmless small cases.
why: Determine whether two acyclic classes always suffice to organize the vertices of an oriented planar graph.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The February 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the general conjecture. The related 2026 list-coloring result for the Erdős–Neumann–Lara conjecture concerns a different assertion.
progress: 2016: Li and Mohar prove two-colorability when the planar digraph has digirth at least four. | 2026-02-13: Cambie and coauthors explicitly state the general Neumann–Lara conjecture as open in Conjecture 3.
working_summary: The conjecture asks whether every oriented planar graph has a two-coloring with no monochromatic directed cycle. Arcs within a color class are allowed, so the coloring need not be proper. Loops and opposite pairs of arcs are excluded. The case without directed triangles is known, but directed triangles are allowed in the general target. The question is a directed analogue of central planar graph-decomposition principles.

title: Graph canonization versus graph isomorphism
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Distinguishes recognizing structural equivalence from efficiently choosing a unique representative of each equivalence class.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic oracle Turing machine A and a constant \(c\ge 1\) such that A, given any finite simple undirected graph G, computes a canonical form \(F(G)\) in at most \(O((N+1)^{c})\) steps using the graph-isomorphism decision oracle, where N is the input encoding length and F satisfies the conventions below?
definitions: A graph G on \(n\ge 0\) vertices is given by n and the symmetric zero-diagonal binary adjacency matrix on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Two such graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if a bijection between their vertex sets preserves both adjacency and nonadjacency. The oracle takes two graphs in this encoding and returns YES exactly when they are isomorphic. Each oracle answer costs one step; writing the query and all other computation count toward the polynomial bound, so query lengths and number of calls are polynomial in N. Adaptive queries are allowed. The output \(F(G)\) is an adjacency matrix of a graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), with \(F(G)\cong G\). For every pair of input graphs, \(G\cong H\) must imply \(F(G)=F(H)\) as labeled matrices; the reverse implication then follows automatically. Thus one algorithm chooses a single representative for every isomorphism class. No particular representative, lexicographic minimum or vertex permutation is prescribed. The same deterministic machine and polynomial bound apply to all graphs; it has no other oracle or nonuniform advice. The empty graph has the empty matrix as its canonical form.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives such an oracle algorithm and proves its worst-case polynomial running time, isomorphism preservation and identical outputs on every isomorphic pair. A negative answer rules out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with this decision oracle that computes any canonical-form function satisfying these conditions. A reduction that only finds an isomorphism between two supplied graphs does not suffice.
context:
Isomorphism asks whether two presentations describe the same graph after renaming vertices. Canonization takes just one presentation and returns a fixed presentation of that graph’s shape. For example, every relabeling of a three-vertex path must produce exactly the same three-by-three output matrix. It is insufficient to return a different isomorphic matrix depending on the input names. This consistency makes canonical forms useful for indexing and comparing stored structures.

The oracle can compare any two explicitly constructed graphs, but returns only YES or NO. The question grants this ability at unit cost and asks whether polynomially much additional work can select consistent representatives. Finding a vertex matching for one given isomorphic pair has a different output requirement: its choices need not agree across every possible presentation of the same graph.

Babai’s 2019 result gives general graph canonization in quasipolynomial time, meaning \(\exp (O((\log  n)^{d}))\) for a fixed constant d. It adapts the structure of an isomorphism algorithm and includes additional work to make choices canonical. Having quasipolynomial algorithms for both tasks does not establish a polynomial-time reduction that uses only decision answers.

The ICALP 2026 paper obtains efficient canonical labelling for random regular graphs with high probability and recalls general quasipolynomial bounds. A guarantee for almost all graphs in a random model leaves exceptional and arbitrary input graphs uncovered. The present target is a deterministic worst-case reduction for every finite graph, and remains separate from the unrestricted question whether graph isomorphism itself lies in polynomial time.
why: Distinguishes recognizing structural equivalence from efficiently choosing a unique representative of each equivalence class.
status_note: The reverse relation is open in the checked 2019 primary discussion. The reviewed ICALP 2026 result concerns random regular graphs and does not settle the general reduction. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution; this is not an independent audit of all later work.
progress: 2019: Babai gives a quasipolynomial canonical-form algorithm; the introduction leaves the general converse from efficient isomorphism testing unknown. | 2026: ICALP work gives canonical labelling guarantees for random regular graphs, without a general polynomial reduction to the decision oracle.
working_summary: Graph isomorphism recognizes when two labeled graphs have the same structure. Canonization assigns every presentation of that structure an identical representative. The question asks whether a polynomial-time algorithm can compute such representatives using only a graph-isomorphism decision oracle. General quasipolynomial canonization and efficient results for random graph families do not supply this reduction. A solution must handle every finite graph and keep its choices consistent across all relabelings.

title: Steiner Shortcut Conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: This is a central structural question about compressing directed reachability, with consequences for understanding the obstacles to efficient parallel graph algorithms.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C>0\) and integers \(a,b\ge0\) such that every finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge2\), \(m=|E|\ge1\) and no isolated vertices, has an augmentation \(G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})\) with \(|E_{+}|\le Cm(\log(n+2))^{a}\), preserving reachability between every ordered pair of original vertices exactly, in which every reachable original pair is joined by a directed path of at most \(C(\log(n+2))^{b}\) arcs?
definitions: Graphs are unweighted, finite and simple as directed graphs; opposite arcs are allowed. An isolated vertex is incident to no arc. The finite set \(V_{+}\) is disjoint from \(V\), and added arcs may have endpoints in either set. Reachability allows the empty path. Preservation means that for every \(u,v\in V\), a path from \(u\) to \(v\) exists in \(G_{+}\) if and only if it exists in \(G\). The path-length bound counts arcs and applies only to pairs in \(V\times V\). No thickness bound is imposed on consecutive Steiner vertices. Constants precede the quantifier over graphs. This is an existence statement with no construction-time requirement; unused isolated Steiner vertices may be omitted.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
A long directed path represents a long chain of dependencies. Shortcuts ask how compactly the same reachability relation can be represented with short paths.

The original conjecture allowed extra arcs only between old vertices and was refuted. Conjecture 2 of the cited paper permits additional Steiner vertices; the known old-vertex lower bounds do not settle this statement.

The representation may preserve a large reachability relation without listing every reachable pair. Existence would settle a structural compression question, while efficient parallel construction is a separate algorithmic demand.
why: This is a central structural question about compressing directed reachability, with consequences for understanding the obstacles to efficient parallel graph algorithms.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. Faithful existence version of Conjecture 2. Isolated original vertices can be added or removed without affecting its bounds. No efficient construction or bounded-thickness condition has been added.
progress: 2025-10-30: Conjecture 2 explicitly leaves unrestricted Steiner shortcuts open; the paper gives lower bounds when consecutive Steiner vertices are restricted.
working_summary: A Steiner shortcut augments a directed graph with new vertices and arcs. Reachability between all original vertices must remain exactly the same. The conjecture asks for near-linear many added arcs and polylogarithmic paths between reachable original pairs. The earlier conjecture forbidding new vertices was refuted, while this version remains a distinct structural question. The target concerns existence and does not impose a fast construction algorithm.

title: Deterministic almost-linear vertex connectivity
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Closing the deterministic gap for a basic network robustness measure would establish the computational role of randomness in a major exact graph primitive.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm computing the exact vertex connectivity and a minimum vertex separator of every simple unweighted undirected graph in \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time on a word RAM?
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph with labelled vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) edges; isolated vertices are included. For \(S\subseteq V\), delete its vertices and incident edges. The vertex connectivity \(\kappa(G)\) is the minimum \(|S|\) for which the remaining graph is disconnected or has at most one vertex. For a disconnected input it is zero, and \(\kappa(K_{n})=n-1\). Output both \(\kappa(G)\) and an attaining set \(S\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. All hidden constants are independent of the graph. No randomness is allowed, and the bound must hold for all connectivity values, including those growing with the graph size.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Vertex connectivity measures how many vertex failures a network can withstand. Its global nature requires the weakest separation to be found without specifying the separated vertices.

Li, Nanongkai, Panigrahi, Saranurak and Yingchareonthawornchai give a randomized reduction to a polylogarithmic number of maximum-flow computations. Together with modern exact flow algorithms this yields randomized almost-linear time.

The 2025 deterministic bound is \(m\kappa\,n^{o(1)}\), with \(\kappa\) the connectivity. It resolves important smaller-connectivity regimes but retains a polynomial overhead when connectivity is large.

Both lines build on the earlier vertex-connectivity algorithms of Henzinger, Rao and Gabow. The remaining demand is a uniform deterministic bound over all graphs.
why: Closing the deterministic gap for a basic network robustness measure would establish the computational role of randomness in a major exact graph primitive.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The endpoint fixes deterministic worst-case time, explicit isolated vertices and complete-graph conventions. Randomized almost-linear time and fixed-connectivity algorithms are distinguished.
progress: 2021: The randomized reduction transfers sufficiently fast maximum-flow bounds to vertex connectivity. | 2022: Almost-linear exact flow supplies an almost-linear randomized vertex-connectivity bound through the reduction. | 2025: Deterministic time becomes \(m\kappa\,n^{o(1)}\).
working_summary: Vertex connectivity is the smallest number of vertices whose removal disconnects a graph or leaves at most one vertex. The task is to find this number and an attaining separator in an unweighted undirected graph. The question asks for deterministic almost-linear worst-case time. Randomized almost-linear algorithms are known, while the reviewed deterministic bound still depends on the connectivity. The target tests the role of randomness in exact network robustness computation.

title: Constant-factor treewidth preservation by subcubic subgraphs
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A structural sparsification principle for a central graph parameter; the gap concerns universal preservation rather than a particular construction.
formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C\ge 1\) such that every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G contains a nonempty subgraph H with maximum degree at most 3 and \(\operatorname{tw}(H)\ge \operatorname{tw}(G)/C\)?
definitions: A subgraph \(H=(V_{H},E_{H})\) satisfies \(V_{H}\subseteq V(G)\) and \(E_{H}\subseteq E(G)\cap \{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V_{H},u\ne v\}\). Edges and vertices may be deleted, but no edge is contracted and no new vertex or edge is introduced. H need not be induced, connected or spanning. Its maximum degree is \(\max _{v\in V_{H}}|\{u:\{u,v\}\in E_{H}\}|\). A tree decomposition of a nonempty graph F consists of a finite tree T with vertex bags \(B_{t}\subseteq V(F)\), such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of each edge lie in a common bag, and the nodes whose bags contain a fixed vertex induce a nonempty connected subtree. Its width is \(\max _{t}|B_{t}|- 1\). Treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(F)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions; nonempty edgeless graphs have treewidth zero. C is independent of G and its treewidth. No bound on the number of vertices of H and no construction-time requirement is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Treewidth measures how far a graph is from having a tree-like organization. This question asks whether its full scale can always be retained after reducing every vertex degree to at most three.

The known degree-three sparsifier guarantee loses a polylogarithmic factor in treewidth. A universal constant would give a stronger structural witness regardless of the original graph’s density or degree distribution.

The target does not ask for an induced subgraph, a small number of vertices, or a grid minor. These additional output restrictions define different problems; arbitrary subcubic graphs need not have grid structure.
why: Determine whether large treewidth always has a bounded-degree witness with only constant loss.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 paper and current question list retain the gap between polylogarithmic and constant loss; no general constant-factor theorem was found.
progress: 2015: Chekuri and Chuzhoy establish degree-three subgraphs retaining treewidth up to a polylogarithmic factor. | 2025: Bonnet’s work on induced sparse subgraphs still cites polylogarithmic-loss treewidth sparsifiers as the available general degree-three guarantee.
working_summary: Every graph is asked to contain a subgraph of maximum degree three with comparable treewidth. Comparable means losing only a universal constant factor. The subgraph can delete edges and vertices but cannot contract edges or introduce new ones. Known general degree-three sparsifiers lose a polylogarithmic factor in treewidth. A constant-factor theorem would make bounded-degree structure a universal witness of large treewidth.

title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with nonnegative real weights
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Settle whether directed weighted reachability has the same input-linear cost as its basic unweighted counterpart in the integer model.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic comparison-addition algorithm computing all exact distances from a specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary nonnegative real arc lengths in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Each arc length belongs to \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). The length of a path is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, with an infinity marker for unreachable vertices. Zero-length arcs and cycles are permitted. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input without randomness, with a universal time constant.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Reading a graph and writing its source distances already requires linear time. The question asks whether arbitrary nonnegative real lengths and direction can be handled within that exact input-and-output budget.

Duan and coauthors broke the sorting barrier in 2025. The 2026 improvement gives \(O(m\sqrt{\log n}+\sqrt{mn\log n\log\log n})\) time, still with superlinear overhead.

Exact reals can be added and compared, while their bit representations cannot be inspected. This makes the model substantive: integer bit operations do not supply a real-weight algorithm.

Mareš develops the shortest-path background. The present endpoint follows the newer directed real-weight results rather than treating historical textbook bounds as current.
why: An optimal linear algorithm would determine whether directed shortest paths with general nonnegative numerical lengths can be computed at the cost of reading the graph.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. User-approved G7 is consolidated into TCS-7263. The former positive-integer word-RAM target is replaced by the real-weight comparison-addition target; these are not asserted equivalent. The change avoids duplicate near-identical catalogue endpoints and is recorded in the import report.
progress: 2025: A deterministic \(O(m\log^{2/3}n)\) real-weight algorithm breaks the sorting barrier. | 2026: The bound improves to \(O(m\sqrt{\log n}+\sqrt{mn\log n\log\log n})\).
working_summary: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary nonnegative real arc lengths and a specified source. The task is to output every exact source distance. The question asks for deterministic linear worst-case time using real addition and comparison. Recent algorithms break the sorting barrier while retaining superlinear overhead. A linear algorithm would match the cost of reading the graph and writing the distances.

title: Single-exponential exact cut mimicking networks
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Resolving the exponential-versus-doubly-exponential gap would determine how compactly an arbitrary network can represent all exact terminal separation costs.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that every finite undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge weights and a specified terminal set \(T\) of size \(k\ge2\) has an undirected nonnegatively real-weighted graph \(H\) containing the same labelled terminals, with \(|V(H)|\le2^{Ck}\), that preserves every minimum terminal bipartition cut value exactly?
definitions: Graphs are finite and simple, with finite edge weights. For every nonempty proper subset \(A\subset T\), define \(\lambda_{G}(A)=\min\{\sum_{e\in\delta_{G}(S)}w_{e}:S\subseteq V(G),\ S\cap T=A\}\), where \(\delta_{G}(S)\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). Define \(\lambda_{H}\) in the same way, using the weights of \(H\). Preservation means \(\lambda_{H}(A)=\lambda_{G}(A)\) simultaneously for every such \(A\). New nonterminal vertices and arbitrary nonnegative real weights are allowed; \(H\) need not be a subgraph, minor or contraction of \(G\). Its vertex bound includes the terminals. The constant is independent of \(G\), its weights and \(k\). No algorithm or construction-time bound is requested.

Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
A terminal cut function records how expensive it is to separate any chosen group of terminals from all the others. An exact mimicking network stores this whole function as a smaller graph.

For general graphs, the reviewed size gap is \(2^{\Omega(k)}\) versus \(2^{2^{O(k)}}\). Chen and Tan review this gap and improve bounds for special graph classes.

Requiring a contraction would change the answer: doubly exponential lower bounds are known in that restricted representation. The question permits an arbitrary replacement graph.

A Gomory–Hu tree preserves pairwise minimum cuts. A terminal bipartition constrains many vertices to each side simultaneously, so pairwise cut preservation does not establish this stronger representation property.

The question asks whether every weighted undirected graph has such a representation with singly exponential size in the number of terminals. Arbitrary new nonterminal vertices are permitted, with no restriction to contractions. The general gap between exponential lower bounds and doubly exponential upper bounds remains the target.

title: Edge reconstruction conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A longstanding reconstruction principle that tests how much global graph structure survives individual edge losses.
formal: For every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H with at least four edges, does equality of their edge decks \(D_{E}(G)=D_{E}(H)\) imply \(G\cong H\)?
definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and parallel edges are excluded. Isolated vertices and disconnected graphs are allowed. For \(e\in E\), let \(G- e=(V,E\setminus \{e\})\): deleting an edge retains every vertex, including vertices that become isolated. Two graphs are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. Write \([G- e]\) for the isomorphism class with vertex labels forgotten. The edge deck is the multiset \(D_{E}(G)=\{[G- e]:e\in E\}\); each edge contributes one entry, so repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. Deck equality requires each isomorphism class to occur equally often. Entries have no common vertex labeling and do not identify the deleted edge. The question concerns uniqueness from a deck known to arise from a graph, with no efficiency requirement on reconstruction.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all finite simple graphs with at least four edges, or give two nonisomorphic such graphs and prove that their complete edge decks agree with multiplicities. A result for a bounded number of vertices, a promised graph class or decks pooled from multiple graphs does not settle the universal claim.
context:
Think of making one copy of a network for each connection and deleting a different connection from each copy. The copies are shuffled and their vertex names erased. The conjecture says their shapes and repetition counts still identify the original network. For a four-cycle, the deck consists of four copies of the path on four vertices.

The threshold excludes a real ambiguity. A triangle together with one isolated vertex and the three-leaf star are nonisomorphic four-vertex graphs with three edges. Deleting any edge from either leaves a three-vertex path together with an isolated vertex. Their edge decks therefore agree, each containing three copies of the same graph.

An edge-deleted graph has the original number of vertices. A vertex-deleted graph loses a vertex and all edges incident to it. The imported McKay reference primarily studies the latter and its set-deck variant. Calle and Gould give the precise edge-deck formulation used here; retaining multiplicities and isolated vertices is part of that model.

The 2025 K-theory paper reformulates the ordinary conjecture and disproves a stronger statement about recovering several graphs from their pooled decks; it explicitly does not settle the single-graph conjecture. A September 2026 preprint instead studies how few selected entries suffice when the original graph is promised to be maximal planar. Such additional information changes the reconstruction task.
why: A longstanding reconstruction principle that tests how much global graph structure survives individual edge losses.
status_note: The checked 2025 paper explicitly leaves the ordinary edge reconstruction conjecture open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established general resolution; the recent maximal-planar result has a graph-class promise. McKay’s original linked paper is primarily about vertex reconstruction.
progress: 1964: Harary poses the edge reconstruction conjecture, as recounted by Calle and Gould. | 2025: An algebraic reformulation preserves the open ordinary conjecture while a pooled-deck generalization is disproved. | 2026-09: A preprint addresses selected-card reconstruction within the known class of maximal planar graphs.
working_summary: Delete each edge of a graph in turn, erase vertex labels and collect the resulting graphs with repetitions. The edge reconstruction conjecture asks whether this multiset determines every finite simple graph with at least four edges. All vertices survive deletion, and repeated copies of the same graph remain significant. A triangle plus an isolated vertex and a three-leaf star show why a three-edge version fails. Recent algebraic reformulations and results for promised graph classes leave the general uniqueness question open.

title: Lovász conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Resolve a canonical connection between graph symmetry and global spanning structure.
formal: Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path?
definitions: A graph is vertex-transitive if for every u,v there is a bijection of its vertex set preserving adjacency and sending u to v. A Hamiltonian path is an ordering of all vertices without repetition in which consecutive vertices are adjacent; the one-vertex graph is allowed. The target asks for existence, with no requirement to compute the path efficiently. It asks for a path rather than a cycle, and is not restricted to Cayley graphs.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Vertex transitivity expresses complete local symmetry, but does not give an obvious global route visiting each vertex once. The Hamiltonian-path conjecture is a classical structural question connecting graph symmetry with spanning paths.

It lies within the atlas’s accepted graph-structure and path scope. Positive results for particular group actions or graph families do not settle the universal statement. The cycle variant has exceptional behavior and is not substituted for the path question.
why: Resolve a canonical connection between graph symmetry and global spanning structure.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.

title: Almost-linear exact directed global minimum cut
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Exact global directed connectivity is a fundamental graph optimization problem whose unknown optimal terminals remain a major obstacle beyond fast single-pair flow.
formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), is there a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every directed graph with positive integer arc weights at most \(n^{a}\), outputs a nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\) minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E(S,V\setminus S)}u_{e}\), and its exact value, in \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Here \(E(S,V\setminus S)\) consists of arcs directed from \(S\) to its complement, and the objective counts each such arc once. There are no prescribed terminals. Zero optimum is allowed, including when the graph is not strongly connected. Weights are explicitly given integers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^{a}\}\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. All hidden constants are independent of the graph. The program, word-size constant, overhead function and time constant may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph or its weights.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
A directed global cut identifies the cheapest partition across which communication in one direction can be removed. The terminal pair is unknown, unlike a single source–sink flow problem.

Quanrud and independently Mosenzon obtain almost-linear approximation schemes. Their bounds depend inversely on the relative error parameter, so exact recovery of a large integer optimum need not retain almost-linear time.

The target asks for the optimal cut itself and its exact value over all partitions. It isolates the global directed-cut bottleneck after the major progress on exact single-pair flow.
why: Exact global directed connectivity is a fundamental graph optimization problem whose unknown optimal terminals remain a major obstacle beyond fast single-pair flow.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. Editorial exact almost-linear endpoint. The statement fixes positive polynomial integer weights, bounded error and global outgoing-cut semantics; approximation results do not settle it.
progress: 2025: An approximation scheme uses polylogarithmically many single-commodity flows multiplied by an inverse-precision factor. | 2026-07-20: The revised independent paper states \(O(m^{1+o(1)}/\varepsilon)\) time for polynomially bounded weights.
working_summary: A directed global cut removes every arc leaving a chosen nonempty proper vertex set. The task is to minimize its total weight without being given source and sink terminals. The question asks for exact almost-linear computation with bounded-error randomization and polynomially bounded integer weights. Known almost-linear approximation schemes retain a precision cost that matters for exact recovery. A resolution would address the global directed-cut bottleneck beyond single-pair maximum flow.

title: Almost-linear directed vertex connectivity
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A uniform almost-linear algorithm would settle the remaining general exact running-time gap for directed vertex robustness, a classical network problem.
formal: Is there a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computing the exact vertex connectivity and an attaining vertex separator of every simple unweighted directed graph in \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. For \(S\subseteq V\), remove \(S\) and all incident arcs. Define \(\kappa(G)\) as the smallest \(|S|\) for which the remainder is not strongly connected or contains at most one vertex. Strong connectivity means reachability for every ordered pair of remaining vertices. Thus an input that is not strongly connected has value zero, and a complete bidirected graph has value \(n-1\). Output the value and an attaining \(S\). Whenever at least two vertices remain, failure of strong connectivity is equivalent to a partition \((L,S,R)\) with nonempty \(L,R\) and no arc from \(L\) to \(R\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. All hidden constants are independent of the graph.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.
context:
Directed vertex connectivity measures resilience to vertex failures when communication is asymmetric. A single removed vertex can affect many arcs simultaneously.

Chuzhoy, Mosenzon and Trabelsi give randomized unweighted time \(\min\{m^{1+o(1)}\kappa,n^{2+o(1)}\}\). Their weighted result also improves the longstanding Henzinger–Rao–Gabow bound.

These bounds cover important sparse-connectivity and dense-graph regimes. The question requires an almost-linear bound for every density and connectivity, while allowing randomization.

Almost-linear relative approximation schemes are known, but their precision cost does not establish the general exact endpoint.
why: A uniform almost-linear algorithm would settle the remaining general exact running-time gap for directed vertex robustness, a classical network problem.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. Editorial exact endpoint with randomization allowed. The at-most-one-vertex convention completes the separator definition on complete bidirected graphs; it does not affect the unresolved general regime.
progress: 2026: The unweighted bound becomes \(\min\{m^{1+o(1)}\kappa,n^{2+o(1)}\}\), leaving intermediate regimes above almost-linear time.
working_summary: Directed vertex connectivity measures the smallest vertex failure set destroying strong connectivity or leaving at most one vertex. The task is to output its exact value and a minimum separator in an unweighted digraph. The question asks for a bounded-error randomized algorithm with almost-linear worst-case time. The reviewed algorithms cover important density and connectivity regimes but leave a general gap. The target demands one bound valid for every directed input graph.

title: Boolean dimension of posets with planar cover graphs
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A constant-size Boolean description of every order with a planar cover graph would explain how planar local structure controls global order information.
formal: Does there exist an integer \(d\ge 1\) such that every finite poset \(\mathrm{P}=(V,<)\) with a planar undirected cover graph admits strict total orders \(\mathrm{L}_{1},\ldots ,\mathrm{L}_{d}\) on V and a Boolean function \(\varphi :\{0,1\}^{d}\to \{0,1\}\) satisfying, for all distinct \(x,y\in V, x<y\) if and only if \(\varphi (1[x<_{\mathrm{L}_{1}}y],\ldots ,1[x<_{\mathrm{L}_{d}}y])=1\)?
definitions: A finite poset is specified by an irreflexive transitive relation < on a finite set V. The undirected cover graph has vertex set V and an edge \(\{x,y\}\) when \(x<y\) with no z satisfying \(x<z<y\), or the reverse relation. Planarity means that this undirected graph has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect; an upward planar drawing of the order is not required. A strict total order compares every distinct pair in exactly one direction and is transitive. The orders \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\) need not extend the partial order. Each indicator \(1[x<_{\mathrm{L}_{i}}y]\) is a bit. Both the d orders and \(\varphi\) may depend on P, but the bound d is universal and independent of |V| and the height of P. The least possible number of orders is Boolean dimension. The claim is purely existential, with no algorithmic requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A family of total orders supplies a short comparison signature for each ordered pair. Boolean dimension asks whether a single Boolean rule can reconstruct the partial-order relation from that signature. The orders are auxiliary encodings and need not respect every comparability.

Blake, Micek and Trotter connect this representation with reachability labeling and prove a constant bound under an additional unique-minimum assumption. That hypothesis is absent from the general question.

The underlying cover graph, rather than an upward planar drawing of the poset, is the specified planar object. Replacing one condition with the other would change the family of inputs.
why: Determine whether planar cover structure permits a constant-size comparison description of an arbitrary partial order.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The unique-minimum theorem and related clique-width results do not resolve arbitrary planar cover graphs; no general resolution was found.
progress: 2022: Blake, Micek and Trotter prove Boolean dimension at most 13 when the planar-cover-graph poset has a unique minimum. | 2026: The clique-width/dimension paper supplies related boundedness results but does not establish the target for all planar cover graphs.
working_summary: The cover graph records immediate comparabilities of a finite partial order. The question asks whether its planarity guarantees a constant number of total orders encoding every comparability. One Boolean rule interprets the pairwise comparison bits from those orders. The orders and rule may vary with the poset, but their number must have a universal bound. The target links sparse graph structure to concise representations of reachability.

title: Strongly explicit Ramanujan families for every degree
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Combine extremal spectral quality with efficient local access for arbitrary constant-degree expanders.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge 3\), is there one deterministic algorithm that computes the port rotation map of connected d-regular Ramanujan graphs for an unbounded set of vertex counts n in time polynomial in log n, with the effective family and graph conventions below?
definitions: The graphs are undirected multigraphs on \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); parallel edges and loops are permitted, as in the source’s graph convention. Each vertex has ports \([d]\). A rotation map \(Rot_{n}:[n]\times [d]\to [n]\times [d]\) is an involution: if \(Rot_{n}(v,i)=(w,j)\), then \(Rot_{n}(w,j)=(v,i)\). Paired ports encode an undirected edge; a fixed port encodes a loop. Define the symmetric integer adjacency matrix A by \(A_{vw}=|\{i\in[d]:\operatorname{first}(\operatorname{Rot}_n(v,i))=w\}|\), so every row sum is d and a fixed-port loop contributes one to the diagonal and degree. Connectivity means the underlying undirected graph is connected. List the real eigenvalues with multiplicity in decreasing order \(d=\lambda _{1}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{n}\). Require \(|\lambda_i|\le2\sqrt{d-1}\) for \(i\ge 2\), except that the single eigenvalue −d is permitted when the graph is bipartite. For each fixed d the answer supplies a decidable infinite set \(N_{d}\) of positive integers, a single total deterministic bit algorithm \(R_{d}\), and constants \(C_{d},a_{d}\). On input \((n,v,i)\) in binary, \(R_{d}\) runs in at most \(C_d(1+\log_2 n)^{a_d}\) steps for valid \(v\in [n],i\in [d]\). For every \(n\in N_{d}\) its outputs constitute the rotation map of such a graph. No graph-dependent advice, preprocessing or tables are supplied to \(R_{d}\); its fixed program may depend on d. The family’s size-membership decider must halt on all binary n but has no prescribed running-time bound. No bound on gaps between successive \(n\in N_{d}\) is required. Outputs at n outside \(N_{d}\) carry no graph promise. This retains the imported infinite-family target, which is weaker than requiring every admissible size; it does not impose simple-graph or non-bipartite restrictions.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the quantified family construction, including a size-membership decider, the uniform local rotation algorithm, infinitely many sizes, connectivity and the exact spectral bound for every fixed degree. Alternatively provide a Lean refutation for some degree. Spectral slack, graph-specific advice or polynomial time in the vertex count does not satisfy strong explicitness.
context:
Ramanujan families attain the limiting optimal spectral bound for their fixed degree. Strong explicitness requires computing local connections in time polynomial in the vertex-label length.

The source distinguishes exact Ramanujan families for certain degrees from constructions with spectral slack for general degrees. This question retains an unbounded effective family for each fixed degree, without requiring every admissible graph size.
why: Combine extremal spectral quality with efficient local access for arbitrary constant-degree expanders.
status_note: The primary source distinguishes available exact special-degree families from arbitrary-degree constructions with slack. The statement and a bounded later-work search were reviewed on 13 September 2026 without finding a general exact strongly explicit construction. This is not a claim of an exhaustive status audit.
progress: 2020: The source constructs explicit or strongly explicit near-Ramanujan graphs with stated slack, not the general exact strongly explicit target.
working_summary: A regular Ramanujan graph meets the optimal asymptotic bound on nontrivial adjacency eigenvalues. The question asks for an infinite family at every fixed degree at least three. One algorithm must compute each local port connection in time polynomial in the vertex-label length. The family may use only a decidable unbounded set of sizes and permits the stated multigraph conventions. Constructions with positive spectral slack or slower global access do not meet the exact strong-explicitness target.

title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Exact Matching is a central derandomization test even on bipartite graphs. Its importance remains high while the recent claimed solution is assessed.
formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.
answer_criterion: Establish a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for every bipartite instance, or prove that none exists. The April 2026 claimed algorithm would establish the positive answer if its proof is valid; this catalogue has not independently verified it.
context:
An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.
why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
status_note: Claimed resolution, verification pending. Reviewed 10 September 2026 using version 3. The preprint and its eight formalization hypotheses have not been independently proved or audited here.
progress: 2023: El Maalouly’s survey develops algorithms and reductions around Exact Matching while describing deterministic polynomial time as unresolved. | 2026-04-02: Du’s first preprint version claims a deterministic $O(n^6)$ algorithm for all bipartite graphs and describes its proof as formally verified. | 2026-04-09: Version 3 states $O(n^6)$ arithmetic complexity and qualifies the Lean result: the main theorem is reduced to eight explicit hypotheses. The claimed mathematical resolution and the formalization scope must be assessed separately.
working_summary: Bipartite Exact Matching asks for a perfect matching containing exactly a specified number of red edges. Even a small complete bipartite graph can have attainable red counts separated by gaps. This makes the equality constraint stronger than minimizing or maximizing the count. The saved card records an April 2026 preprint claiming deterministic polynomial time, together with limits on its verification. The project is therefore to explain and assess that claimed resolution of the historical question, while keeping the bipartite restriction explicit.

title: 3-colorability of diameter-two graphs
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph G of diameter at most 2, decides whether there is a map \(c:V(G)\to \{1,2,3\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge uv?
definitions: The input is the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph. Distance counts edges in a shortest path, and diameter is the maximum distance between any two vertices. The graph has no loops or parallel edges. For a singleton the diameter is 0. The algorithm must correctly decide existence of a coloring, including on graphs that are not 3-colorable; it is not supplied with a coloring or a promise of 3-colorability. The color set has fixed size three and there are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, degree bounds, or forbidden-subgraph assumptions. A polynomial-time algorithm has worst-case running time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) for constants C,k independent of G. One may equivalently define a total language that rejects disconnected or diameter-greater-than-two graphs, since the diameter promise can be checked in polynomial time. Restricting to diameter exactly two gives the same polynomial-time question: diameter-zero and diameter-one connected graphs are complete and their colorability is immediate.
answer_criterion: Prove that such an algorithm exists, or that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-completeness proof would establish the conventional hardness classification and imply a negative answer under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). A subexponential algorithm or an algorithm requiring an additional graph restriction does not settle this question.
context:
The 2019 source discusses several diameter-restricted coloring problems. This card selects its central explicit question, with three colors and diameter two. The same section also asks about triangle-free inputs and about coloring claw-free graphs with an input-dependent number of colors; these are distinct extensions, not additional requirements hidden in this question.

Bounding diameter means every pair of vertices is close, but it does not bound the amount of global information encoded by the graph. Diameter-one graphs are complete and trivial to color. Mertzios and Spirakis show that 3-colorability is already NP-complete at diameter three, even for triangle-free graphs. Diameter two is the remaining boundary between these neighboring cases.

A tempting hardness reduction adds a universal vertex to an arbitrary graph. This makes the diameter at most two, but the new vertex consumes a color that none of the old vertices can use. It transfers general 3-colorability to 4-colorability, so it does not prove hardness of the fixed three-color target. Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.

The best general upper bound identified in the July 2026 source is subexponential: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski give time 2 raised to \(O(n^{1/3} \log ^{2} n)\). Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.
why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.
status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 version of Murakami’s primary paper. Checked through 10 September 2026; no later general resolution located. Recent algorithms with an additional four-cycle exclusion do not settle this card.
