working_summary: Three-colorability asks whether vertices can receive three colors with adjacent vertices always different. Here every pair of vertices is promised to have distance at most two. The question is whether this strong proximity condition permits deterministic polynomial-time recognition of three-colorable graphs. Adding a universal vertex cannot directly transfer general three-color hardness because it consumes an additional color. The problem therefore probes a precise structural boundary where very short graph distances may or may not simplify coloring.

title: Polylogarithmic treewidth with forbidden induced minors
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A structural tractability threshold for Hamiltonicity or treewidth would support algorithms for entire graph families.
formal: For every integer \(t\ge 2\), does there exist an integer \(c_{t}\ge 1\) such that every n-vertex graph G with \(n\ge 2\), no clique of size t and neither Kt,t nor Wt as an induced minor satisfies \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le c_{t}(\log _{2} n)^{c_{t}}\)?
definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Write \(n=|V(G)|\) and take logarithms in base two. An induced subgraph \(G[S]\) retains precisely all edges of G whose endpoints are in S. Kt is the complete graph on t vertices; Kt,t is the complete bipartite graph with two independent sets of t vertices and every edge between the sets. A tree decomposition consists of a finite tree T and bags \(Bx\subseteq V(G)\), one per node x of T, such that every vertex occurs in a bag, both endpoints of every edge occur together in some bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is maxx |\(Bx|- 1\). Treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width of such a decomposition. For a concrete wall convention, construct Wt from vertices \((i,j), 0\le i\le t\) and \(0\le j\le 2t+1\): include all horizontal edges \((i,j)(i,j+1)\), and vertical edges \((i,j)(i+1,j)\) exactly when \(i+j\) is even, then repeatedly delete vertices of degree at most one until none remain. This is a fixed elementary hexagonal-wall family. Standard wall-size conventions differ by a fixed reindexing; since the source statement quantifies over every fixed t and allows its constants to depend arbitrarily on t, this indexing does not change the family-level claim. An induced minor is obtained by deleting vertices and contracting edges, with loops discarded and parallel edges merged, but without arbitrary edge deletions. Equivalently, its vertices can be represented by pairwise disjoint nonempty connected branch sets in G, with an edge between two branch sets exactly when their corresponding vertices are adjacent in the induced minor. The clique exclusion is an ordinary clique/induced-subgraph condition; the exclusions of Kt,t and Wt are induced-minor conditions. There is no bound on maximum degree. The constant \(c_{t}\) and the exponent \(c_{t}\) may depend on t, but not on n or G. Allowing separate constants for the multiplier and exponent is equivalent by increasing \(c_{t}\), since \(\log _{2} n\ge 1\). The statement is structural existence of tree decompositions and requests no algorithm for finding them. Restricting to \(t,n\ge 2\) removes only trivial small or undefined-log cases.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed bound for every t with constants depending only on t, or refute it by finding one fixed t for which, for every integer \(c\ge 1\), there is an admitted graph G with \(\operatorname{tw}(G)>c(\log _{2} |V(G)|)^{c}\). A subpolynomial upper bound or a bound on independence number inside bags does not establish the requested polylogarithmic bound on bag size.
context:
A tree decomposition organizes overlapping vertex sets along a tree. Vertices may appear in several bags, but their occurrences must remain connected. A path has treewidth one, whereas a complete graph on n vertices has treewidth \(n- 1\). Small bags allow many graph problems to be processed through their interactions along the decomposition.

The question removes large cliques and two specific induced-minor patterns: a complete bipartite graph and a hexagonal wall. Induced minors permit edge contractions but preserve the presence of edges between surviving branch sets. This makes their exclusion different from forbidding an ordinary graph minor, where arbitrary edges may also be deleted.

For each fixed t, the requested bound is a constant times a fixed power of log n. The power can grow with t. The statement does not ask for a constant treewidth bound and does not impose the maximum-degree restriction of the separate logarithmic-degree question.

The March 2026 version of Chudnovsky and coauthors’ preprint states \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le 2^{a_{t}(\log _{2} n)^{1- \varepsilon _{t}}}\) for constants \(a_{t}\) and \(\varepsilon _{t}>0\) under these same exclusions. It states the polylogarithmic bound separately as Conjecture 1.1. The reported upper bound is subpolynomial in n, but does not establish that conjecture.

The May 2026 coarse-decomposition preprint bounds how many vertices in a bag can be far apart in the original graph. A bag can contain many nearby vertices while that number remains small. Such bounds are not bounds on the number of vertices in the bag, which is what treewidth counts.
why: Would yield a substantially stronger structural bound for graphs excluding two induced-minor patterns and large cliques. Polylogarithmic treewidth supports quasipolynomial algorithms for many problems whose dependence on treewidth is exponential, making the quantitative improvement algorithmically significant.
status_note: Original question and the unambiguous March 2026 formulation checked, with searches through 11 September 2026. The subpolynomial and coarse-decomposition results do not resolve the stated polylogarithmic treewidth target. Preprint theorem statements were matched to the model; proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2025: Chudnovsky poses the polylogarithmic bound in the Dagstuhl report; a later source supplies an unambiguous statement of its graph exclusions. | 2026-03-19: Chudnovsky, Codsi, Fischer and Lokshtanov state a subpolynomial treewidth upper bound and retain the polylogarithmic target as Conjecture 1.1. | 2026-05-06: A related preprint obtains coarse tree-decomposition bounds on distance-based independence numbers, a different bag measure.
working_summary: Treewidth measures the largest bag needed to organize a graph in a tree decomposition. The question concerns graphs with no large clique and with neither a fixed complete bipartite graph nor a fixed wall as an induced minor. It asks whether their treewidth is bounded by a fixed power of the logarithm of their number of vertices. A March 2026 preprint proves a subpolynomial bound but still states the polylogarithmic target as a conjecture. The stronger bound would improve the structural and algorithmic understanding of these induced-minor-free graph classes.

title: Optimal exact-distance label length for planar graphs
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Closing this polynomial gap would identify the information needed to distribute an entire planar graph metric into independent vertex labels.
formal: Determine the asymptotic growth of \(\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\) up to universal constant factors, where \(\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\) is the least integer \(b\ge0\) permitting labels of \(b\) bits that determine every pairwise distance in every connected unweighted simple planar graph on \(n\ge2\) vertices using only the two labels.
definitions: For fixed \(n,b\), a permitted decoder is a function \(D:\{0,1\}^b\times\{0,1\}^b\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). The same \(D\) must work for every connected unweighted simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\): there must be a label assignment \(\lambda_G:[n]\to\{0,1\}^b\) such that \(D(\lambda_G(u),\lambda_G(v))=\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) for all vertices, where distance counts edges on a shortest path. The decoder may depend on \(n\) and \(b\), but not on \(G\), and receives no shared graph data, vertex identifiers or additional input. Both the decoder domain and graph class are finite for fixed \(n,b\); no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing labels or decoding. The target measures label information alone, with arbitrary values on label pairs never used by an assignment. Known efficient schemes provide upper bounds in this unrestricted model as well. Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); simple means no loops or parallel edges, and planar means admitting a drawing by nonintersecting arcs except at shared endpoints. Labels have the common fixed length \(b\); the target is the largest per-vertex bit length, not the sum over vertices. A finite admissible \(b\) always exists: each label can contain the whole finite graph description together with its vertex index, and a common decoder can recover graph distances from that description. Thus the least integer in the definition is well-defined.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified asymptotic rate \(f(n)>0\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\), \(n_0\), such that \(cf(n)\le\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\le Cf(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). Both bounds must use the same unrestricted exact-decoder model. Merely renaming the defining optimum, a one-sided improvement, or conditional hardness without its assumption proved does not meet this target. The accuracy requirement is constant-factor asymptotic matching, not an additive 0.01 error on big-O notation.
context:
A label is the information a vertex carries when the graph itself is unavailable. To answer a distance query, the decoder sees exactly the two endpoint labels. Its rule is common to the whole graph family, so it cannot have a different hidden graph stored for every labeling assignment.

Even the diagonal query constrains labels: a vertex is at distance zero from itself, while two distinct vertices in a connected unweighted graph are at positive distance. Two different vertices therefore cannot share a label. This simple observation only forces \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits, far below the known polynomial lower bound.

The reviewed upper bound is \(O(\sqrt n)\) bits per vertex, while the general lower bound is \(\Omega(n^{1/3})\). The gap is polynomial in \(n\), not just a missing logarithmic factor. An exact constant-factor answer must identify a rate that is both attainable and necessary for the same two-label model.

Decoding speed is a separate resource. The 2023 paper also gives a variant with polylogarithmic decoding time and \(O(\sqrt{n\log n})\)-bit labels. This card permits an arbitrary finite decoder for each \(n,b\), so a lower bound that applies only to fast decoders would not establish its information-theoretic optimum.

A shared distance oracle can distribute information between vertex identifiers and one common data structure; that common structure is absent here. Approximate distances, weighted graphs, and distances after a failure similarly change the information a pair of labels must provide. This target fixes connected, simple, unweighted planar graphs and exact edge counts.

The graph can determine its entire label assignment, but it cannot determine the decoder. The order of these choices permits graph-dependent labels while preventing the graph from being supplied for free through a query routine. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the labels or evaluating the decoder.
why: Closing this polynomial gap would identify the information needed to distribute an entire planar graph metric into independent vertex labels.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The reviewed author and journal sources give the square-root upper bound and cube-root lower bound for exact unweighted planar distance labels. The faster-decoding variant uses larger labels. No constant-factor matching resolution of the unrestricted decoder model was located in the bounded later-work check; proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2021 / 2023: The improved scheme removes a logarithmic factor from the previous upper bound, leaving the exponent gap between \(n^{1/3}\) and \(n^{1/2}\).
working_summary: Each vertex receives a short binary label. The exact distance between two vertices must follow from their labels alone. The same decoder serves every graph of the chosen size. The target is the optimal asymptotic number of label bits. Current lower and upper bounds differ by a polynomial factor.

title: Erdős girth conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A general extremal obstruction underlying sharp routing and distance-sparsification tradeoffs. Existing score retained rather than raised by this formulation review.
formal: For every integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(c_{k}>0\) and \(N_{k}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N_{k}\), some simple undirected graph G on exactly n vertices has at least \(c_{k} n^{1+1/k}\) edges and contains no cycle of length less than \(2k+2\)? Equivalently, is \(M_{2k+2}(n)=\Omega _{k}(n^{1+1/k})\) for every fixed k, where \(M_{s}(n)\) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no cycle shorter than s?
definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 3\) has \(\ell\) distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least \(2k+2\)” forbids every cycle of lengths \(3,\ldots ,2k+1\), including non-induced cycles. \(M_{s}(n)\) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists c_{k},N_{k} \forall n\ge N_{k} \exists G\). Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely \(n^{1+1/k- o(1)}\), nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive \(c_{k}\) and threshold \(N_{k}\) work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.
context:
Known extremal upper bounds give \(M_{2k+2}(n)=O_{k}(n^{1+1/k})\). The conjecture asks whether forbidding all these short cycles still permits that many edges up to a constant factor.

Using threshold \(2k+1\) instead of \(2k+2\) gives an equivalent asymptotic conjecture: a graph has a bipartite subgraph with at least half its edges, and that subgraph has no odd cycles. This equivalence changes neither the exponent nor the fixed-k target.

The cases \(k=1,2,3,5\) are known. The July 2026 spanner paper still lists exactly those cases; the next missing parameter \(k=4\) asks for \(\Omega (n^{5/4})\) edges with girth at least 10.

The source uses these graphs to establish conditional lower bounds on the memory needed by routing schemes with small stretch. More generally, the conjecture controls sharpness of size-versus-stretch bounds for graph spanners.

The 2026 preprint removes this assumption for a particular model of spanners tolerating edge failures of bounded degree. It explicitly distinguishes that result from constructing graphs of the girth and density required here.

This additional occurrence comes from the same compact-routing paper. The retained formal statement fixes its own girth threshold and graph-size quantifiers; a differently quantified girth conjecture is not automatically identified with it.
why: A central extremal graph question with direct consequences for compact routing and graph sparsification: it asks whether the standard density obstruction from short cycles is asymptotically tight at every fixed scale.

working_summary: A quasi-order is well-quasi-ordered when every infinite sequence contains an earlier object comparable below a later one. The source asks whether graphs have this property under pivot-minors. A positive answer would rule out infinite antichains and provide a strong finiteness principle for obstruction-based classifications. The challenge is that pivot operations preserve and transform structure differently from ordinary edge contractions. The saved survey question must retain its precise graph universe and pivot convention, and this draft does not infer the answer from the separate well-quasi-ordering theorem for ordinary graph minors.

title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
importance_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
focus_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})/(\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n)\) for all n, all initial trees \(T_{0}\) and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.
why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
status_note: The July 2026 primary preprint gives a growing competitive factor and still distinguishes its theorem from constant dynamic optimality. The primary text and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026; no complete resolution was found in that check. This review does not independently verify the new proof.
progress: 1985 / background: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree. | 2007: Tango trees give an online BST with an \(O(\log\log n)\) competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying. | 2026-07-20: The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.
working_summary: Splay trees reorganize a binary search tree after each access using local rotations. The question asks whether this simple rule is always within a constant factor of the best tree strategy that knows the entire request sequence. An additive linear allowance pays for the initial tree. Frequency and locality guarantees cover useful patterns but do not establish this universal comparison. Understanding this gap would show whether local adaptation can exploit every advantage available to an offline search tree.

title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
importance_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
focus_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.
why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.
status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

working_summary: A static data structure preprocesses a database and later answers queries by reading stored memory cells. This question seeks an explicitly computable Boolean query problem forcing more than logarithmically many reads despite unrestricted preprocessing. The saved formulation fixes short queries, logarithmic word size, near-linear space, and deterministic adaptive access. Free computation between reads makes this an information-access lower bound. Such an example would expose a fundamental limit on making useful information locally accessible through clever storage alone.

title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
importance_reason: A foundational derandomization question for exact lookup: linear construction, linear storage and constant worst-case queries would give many algorithms an optimal deterministic dictionary primitive. The 2024 and 2026 string-indexing applications show concrete dependencies on dictionary construction costs.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
definitions: The universe is \(U_{w}\)={\(0,\ldots ,2\)ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.
context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.
why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.

working_summary: A static dictionary stores distinct integer keys together with associated values and supports exact membership queries. The question asks for deterministic linear-time construction, linear space, and constant worst-case query time on the stated word RAM. All preprocessing work must be included in the construction bound. Random hashing motivates the desired efficiency but does not itself provide a deterministic construction. A solution would give other algorithms a dependable dictionary primitive without making their preprocessing randomized or increasing their asymptotic running time.

title: Constant-time deterministic dynamic dictionaries
importance_reason: This is a basic possible separation between the power of randomization and determinism in a general-purpose data-structure primitive.
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), does there exist a uniform deterministic word-RAM dictionary with capacity \(N\), word size \(w=\lceil c\log_2(N+2)\rceil\), \(O(N)\) words of space, \(O(1)\) worst-case lookup time and \(O(1)\) amortized insertion and deletion time? The guarantees must hold for every valid online sequence on \(w\)-bit keys and values, starting empty, after \(O(N)\) initialization.
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The program receives \(N\ge2\) and \(w\). Insert supplies a new key and a value, Delete names a present key, and Lookup returns its value or an absent marker. At most \(N\) keys are simultaneously stored. No random instruction is allowed in this deterministic target. For each fixed \(c\), constants may depend on \(c\) but not on \(N\), input keys or sequence length. The joint amortized bound is total cost \(O(N+q+u)\) for \(q\) queries and \(u\) updates, while every query individually costs \(O(1)\). All retained input information, including any direct-address table, counts toward the \(O(N)\) space bound. This logarithmic-word, fixed-capacity formulation asks already for constant amortized updates; it does not demand constant worst-case updates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
Randomized hashing provides constant lookup and expected amortized update guarantees in linear space. Pătrașcu identifies superconstant deterministic dictionary lower bounds as a research direction pursued with Thorup.

The dynamic target differs from constructing a static dictionary once: rebuilding, deletion and repeated adversarial changes must all fit the same operation budget. The related static construction card is retained separately.

title: Multiphase conjecture
importance_reason: The multiphase conjecture is a central candidate for proving polynomial operation lower bounds for dynamic data structures.
formal: Do there exist constants \(\gamma>1\) and \(\delta>0\) such that every always-correct Las Vegas word-RAM solution of the following three-phase problem has overhead \(\tau(n)=\Omega(n^\delta)\) for \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\)? Phase I preprocesses \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\subseteq[n]\) in expected \(O(kn\tau(n))\) time; Phase II receives \(T\subseteq[n]\) and takes expected \(O(n\tau(n))\) time; Phase III receives \(i\in[k]\) and decides whether \(S_i\cap T=\varnothing\) in expected \(O(\tau(n))\) time.
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. A candidate program chooses a fixed integer \(a\ge2\) and uses words of \(w=\lceil a\log_2(n+k+2)\rceil\) bits. All its addresses must fit in one word, so the available address space is polynomial; the lower-bound claim quantifies over every such fixed \(a\). Sets may be given as incidence vectors, so their input lengths are \(kn\) and \(n\) bits. One uniform finite program for each phase must work for all \(n\) in the selected \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\) regime. The program may retain its computed memory between phases; all computation, initialization and copying are charged to the phase performing them. Phase I does not know \(T\) or \(i\), Phase II does not know \(i\), and Phase III receives only the index plus the retained state. Inputs are fixed independently of the random bits. Answers are always correct and each phase terminates almost surely; expected bounds hold for every fixed complete input. Define overhead as the maximum of 1 and the three worst-input expected phase costs divided respectively by \(kn,n,1\). A constant-factor asymptotic lower bound is required for all sufficiently large \(n\); a conditional hardness proof is not an unconditional resolution.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
Pătrașcu introduces this staged set-disjointness task and shows how its hardness would transfer to dynamic problems. The issue is a polynomial overhead, not merely a logarithmic lower bound.

Ko and Weinstein obtain strong lower bounds under a restriction on query adaptivity. Their result does not cover unrestricted adaptive queries.

title: Randomized complexity of online labeling
importance_reason: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal amortized expected number of relabelings per insertion or deletion for randomized online list labeling with at most \(n\) live items and labels in \([2n]\), against an oblivious adversary. The target is one asymptotic rate \(f(n)\) with a matching upper bound and lower bound in the model below.
definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. An upper rate \(f\ge1\) means a uniform online algorithm and a constant \(C\) satisfy expected total cost at most \(C(n+M f(n))\) for every capacity and every finite valid sequence of \(M\) updates. For tightness, every algorithm and every rate \(g\) permitting such a bound must have \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\). Constants are independent of the sequence and capacity. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update. Here \(f(n)\) and competing rates \(g(n)\) concern integer capacities \(n\ge2\), and the asymptotic lower comparison is as \(n\to\infty\).
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously defined rate \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) and complete Lean-checked upper and matching lower bounds up to constant factors in the stated expected amortized movement model. The upper bound must provide one uniform online algorithm with expected total cost \(O(n+Mf(n))\) for every capacity and oblivious valid sequence. The lower bound must establish the stated \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\) requirement for every competing permitted algorithm and achievable rate. An unbounded polylogarithmic factor or a lower bound only for a restricted algorithm family does not meet the target.
context:
List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The original seminar question concerned randomized online labeling broadly. The retained benchmark selects constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary, matching the subsequently specified researcher-linked variant. The answer requires a tight asymptotic rate, rather than just the analysis of one named algorithm.

The cost counts how many existing items receive a different label. Randomization achieves nearly logarithmic expected amortized cost in the cited result. The remaining task is to determine the optimal asymptotic rate for constant slack.

title: Amortized decrease-key complexity of standard pairing heaps
importance_reason: A tight analysis would resolve the central complexity uncertainty for one of the simplest and most widely studied self-adjusting priority queues.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the amortized decrease-key bound \(d(N)\) of the standard two-pass pairing heap, while insert, meld and find-min are charged \(O(1)\) and delete-min is charged \(O(\log(2+N))\). The bound is required for every finite sequence starting from empty heaps with at most \(N\) live items in all heaps combined.
definitions: A heap is a rooted heap-ordered tree. Link compares two roots and makes the larger root the new leftmost child of the smaller. Insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the two roots. Decrease-key receives a handle, reduces its key and, if it is not a root, cuts its whole subtree and links it to the root. Delete-min removes the root, links consecutive children from left to right in disjoint pairs, leaving an unpaired last child unchanged, then combines the resulting roots from right to left by successive links. Find-min reads the root. Keys are opaque ordered values; ties follow a fixed identity order. Constant-size nodes have enough sibling and parent pointers for a cut in constant time. Charge comparisons, links, cuts and pointer work. An admissible upper bound is a function \(d\ge1\) for which a universal \(C\) bounds total cost by \(C(a+b\log(2+N)+c d(N))\), where \(a\) counts the constant-cost operations, \(b\) delete-min operations and \(c\) decreases. A tight answer must also prove that every admissible charge function dominates the supplied rate within a universal constant for sufficiently large \(N\); the constants cannot depend on the sequence. Variants changing either pass, rank metadata or the linking discipline are different algorithms.
answer_criterion: Supply a growth rate with a complete Lean-checked upper analysis and matching lower bound under the charge convention defined here. An improved upper bound without tightness, or a tight bound for another heap variant, is insufficient.
context:
A logarithmic-logarithmic lower bound rules out the original constant-amortized decrease-key expectation under the other standard charges. Related self-adjusting heaps attaining that bound do not automatically analyze the original two-pass algorithm.

The July 2026 paper proves a smaller gap for pure pairing heaps and announces an improved bound for standard pairing heaps in a forthcoming companion paper. Its conclusion explicitly retains the remaining gap. The announcement is recorded separately from a checked proof for the standard algorithm.

The conclusion announces \(O((\log\log N)^2\log\log\log N)\) for standard pairing heaps in forthcoming work; no independent verification of that announced proof was performed.
working_summary: The standard pairing heap uses a fixed two-pass consolidation during delete-min. Its pointer operations are simple, but decreases can affect the cost of future consolidations. The target is a tight amortized charge for decrease-key with the conventional costs for other operations. A logarithmic-logarithmic lower bound is known. Results for pure, multipass, smooth or rank-pairing heaps concern different algorithms.

title: Space-query exponent curve of 3SUM indexing
importance_reason: The curve asks how much information about a quadratic family of sums must be stored to support reusable membership queries, a general representation barrier underlying several string indexes.
formal: Determine \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) for every real \(s\in[1,2]\), where \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) is the infimum of real \(t\ge0\) for which, for every rational \(\eta>0\), a uniform randomized 3SUM index uses \(O(n^{s+\eta})\) words and answers queries in \(O(n^{t+\eta})\) worst-case time.
definitions: The input is two sets \(A,B\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n^4-1\}\), each of size \(n\ge2\), supplied explicitly. A query \(z\in\{0,\ldots,2n^4-2\}\) asks whether \(z=a+b\) for some \(a\in A,b\in B\), using ordinary addition. Set \(L=n\) and fix \(d=10\) in the word-RAM model below. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing may take arbitrary time but must terminate almost surely; this preserves the preexisting card’s space-hardness convention. Every retained input, table and random seed is counted. Each fixed input/query is answered correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) over preprocessing and query randomness, and space and query time bounds hold on every random outcome. Queries cannot communicate input-dependent state for free. For each chosen \(s,t,\eta\), one finite program pair and constants handle every \(n\); there is no per-size choice of advice. Parameters select programs and are not real-number computational inputs. The infimum need not be attained. The quantity is a dimensionless query exponent, and it ignores subpolynomial factors only through the displayed quantifiers.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire stated domain and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(|g(x)-\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(x)|\le 1/100\) at every point. Uniform certified upper and lower bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify via their midpoint. Exact equality also qualifies. A plot, finitely many sample points, one-sided improvement, or a renamed copy of the defining infimum is insufficient. This numerical acceptance tolerance does not establish a separate exact threshold conjecture.
context:
An index is built once for all future sum-membership queries. Storing every potential sum and scanning one input set occupy very different points of the space-query frontier.

The original framework separates different 3SUM-indexing hardness hypotheses; its strongest old tradeoff should not be treated as a theorem.

The revised 2026 paper improves intermediate space regimes without determining the entire frontier.

The previous card asked specifically for genuinely subquadratic space with polylogarithmic queries. The present curve broadens the target; a query exponent of zero or a numerical approximation to it does not by itself establish a polylogarithmic bound.
why: The curve asks how much information about a quadratic family of sums must be stored to support reusable membership queries, a general representation barrier underlying several string indexes.

The target is the best query exponent at each allowed storage exponent. All retained information is charged even though preprocessing time is unrestricted. The numerical curve target is broader than the saved polylogarithmic-query existence question.

title: Strong SetDisjointness conjecture
importance_reason: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.
formal: Is it true that every static word-RAM data structure for SetDisjointness with space \(S(N)\) and worst-case query time \(T(N)\) satisfies \(S(N)T(N)^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\)? The input is a list of nonempty sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq[N]\) with total size \(N=\sum_i|S_i|\), and a query \((i,j)\) asks whether \(S_i\cap S_j\) is empty.
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The sets are supplied as lists without repeated elements within a set, with \(m\le N\) and \(N\ge2\). Word size is \(w=\lceil10\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Restrict attention to \(N\le S(N)\le N^2\), rounding up and padding unused cells if needed. Preprocessing may use arbitrary finite time; all input-dependent information retained afterwards counts toward \(S(N)\). A query reads this static representation and begins without input-dependent private state. Randomized preprocessing and query algorithms are allowed; the answer to each fixed input/query must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Space and query time bounds hold for every random outcome. The notation means that, for each admissible data structure, there are constants \(c>0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(N_0\) such that \(S(N)T(N)^2\ge cN^2/(\log(2+N))^b\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). All sizes are measured in words and time in word-RAM steps. Uniform programs and exact empty/nonempty semantics are required; reporting the intersection is another problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal space-query lower bound or its logical negation, with the same model and quantifiers. Assuming the conjecture to derive another lower bound is not a proof of the conjecture.
context:
The source proposes \(S=\widetilde\Omega(N^2/T^2)\) and describes a matching upper tradeoff. Preprocessing time and representation size are distinct resources here.

The conjecture concerns intersections of two already stored sets. The related multiphase problem instead receives an additional set after preprocessing.

title: Data Structure Lower Bound in the Cell Probe Model
importance_reason: Stronger cell-probe lower bounds would advance a general technique for proving data-access limitations.
formal: Data Structure Lower Bound in the Cell Probe Model
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns the cost of a limited computational or informational resource. A sharp bound would separate a limitation of current algorithms from a limitation every algorithm in the model must face.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: A data structure preprocesses an n-by-n Boolean matrix and then answers matrix-vector products over AND and OR. The cell-probe model counts memory accesses while allowing free computation on the information read. The source asks for a superlinear-in-n query lower bound when the representation stores the matrix with only a small amount of extra space. Existing upper bounds show that this succinct model can outperform straightforward word-RAM expectations. A lower bound must therefore identify information that genuinely has to be fetched, rather than charge for the arithmetic or logical work of computing the answer.

title: Unified bound for binary search trees
importance_reason: The unified bound asks one search tree to exploit temporal and rank locality together, beyond proving separate working-set and dynamic-finger guarantees.
formal: Does a deterministic online BST algorithm exist with total access cost \(O(n\log(2+n)+U(X))\) for every sequence \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in[n]^m\), where \[U(X)=\sum_{t=1}^{m}\log_2\!\left(2+\min\left\{n,\min_{1\le s<t}(t-s+|x_t-x_s|)\right\}\right)?\] The minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\); the initialization term is independent of \(m\).
definitions: The keys are the fixed ranks \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A BST has one node per key in symmetric order. Each access begins with a pointer at the root; primitive costs are moving it to a parent or child, performing a rotation incident to the pointer, and visiting the requested key. Other input-dependent state must be kept in the tree with constant-size fields per node. The algorithm sees requests only as they arrive; it may restructure the tree but may not use arbitrary jumps, an auxiliary search structure or advance knowledge. Begin with a balanced tree, constructed within the initialization allowance. There are no insertions or deletions. The target uses the elapsed-access definition of the unified bound in the 2024 paper; the cap by \(n\) and the additive constants cover first accesses. A uniform algorithm and universal multiplicative constant must work for all \(n,m,X\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
Iacono introduced comparison-based structures satisfying the unified bound. Achieving it within a single BST remains the source question.

Skip-splay and the group-access construction obtain \(O(U(X)+m\log\log n)\), apart from initialization. The 2024 paper explicitly notes that an older cache-tree claim was questioned and retains the exact BST target as open.
why: The unified bound asks one search tree to exploit temporal and rank locality together, beyond proving separate working-set and dynamic-finger guarantees.

progress: 2024: The source matches the unified bound with an additive logarithmic-logarithmic charge per access and explicitly retains its removal as open.
working_summary: A search should be cheap when its key is close in rank to a recently requested key. The unified bound combines this spatial locality with temporal locality. The target requires a single online binary search tree. Known BST bounds include an extra logarithmic-logarithmic term per access. The cited source distinguishes an earlier disputed claim from an established solution.

title: Superconstant word-RAM time for prefix-\(U_1\)
importance_reason: A minimal dynamic set primitive whose superconstant word-RAM lower bound would establish a basic computational barrier and settle conditional constant-time classifications for regular word and tree languages.
formal:
Is it impossible to maintain a length-\(n\) bit sequence under substitutions and answer prefix-AND queries using a deterministic uniform word-RAM data structure with \(O(n)\) preprocessing and \(O(1)\) worst-case time for each update and each query?

An update \(\operatorname{set}(i,b)\) replaces the bit at position \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) by \(b\in\{0,1\}\). A query at \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) must return
\[\operatorname{prefix}(k)=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}b_i,\qquad\operatorname{prefix}(0)=1.\]
The word length is \(w=\lceil c\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer constant \(c\ge1\). The impossibility is to hold for every such fixed constant and every correct data structure in the model below.

This retains the source's worst-case time convention. The target is absence of any constant bound, not a prescribed logarithmic lower-bound rate or the stronger exclusion of amortized constant time.
question_excerpt: There is no structure for prefix-U1 with complexity \(O(1)\).
definitions:
The sequence length \(n\ge1\) remains fixed for the lifetime of the structure. Its initial bits are supplied explicitly, one per input cell. Preprocessing receives \(n\) and that sequence and must run in at most \(K(n+1)\) word operations for one fixed constant \(K\). It builds the state from which all subsequent operations are served. The two-element monoid \(U_1=\{0,1\}\) has multiplication Boolean AND, with identity one and absorbing element zero. Hence a nonempty prefix has product zero exactly when it contains a zero.

Equivalently, the zero positions form a changing subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Substitution adds or removes a supplied position, and the complemented prefix answer says whether \(S\cap\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is nonempty. Repeating a substitution with the present value is allowed and must also meet the cost bound. Queries do not ask for the minimum element itself or a predecessor of the query position. No insertion or deletion of sequence positions, change of \(n\), or restriction on which positions may change is included.

Use a finite-program unit-cost random-access machine whose cells and addresses are unsigned \(w\)-bit words. One operation can read or write one addressed cell, copy a word, compare two words or branch, apply word addition, subtraction or multiplication, apply unsigned integer division or remainder by a nonzero word, apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT, or shift a word left or right by a supplied integer amount. Arithmetic results are reduced modulo \(2^w\), except that division and remainder have their usual unsigned integer meanings; left shifts discard overflowing bits, right shifts insert zeros, and shifts by at least \(w\) give zero. Division by zero must be avoided or handled as an error, not an extra operation. Constant literals are fixed by the finite program. The program can use \(n\) and \(w\); both are supplied at initialization. Each listed operation has unit cost. No other arbitrary word function or input-dependent instruction is provided.

There are at most \(2^w\) addressable cells, all initially zero except the supplied input. Every read, write and table construction counts; no nonuniform precomputed table or advice depending on \(n\) is supplied free of charge. There is no additional linear-space requirement: the machine may use its polynomially many addressable cells, even if many were populated by previous updates. The fixed program, positive integer \(c\) and preprocessing constant \(K\) may depend on the data structure, but never on the input length, initial bits or future history. These explicit word operations instantiate the source's unit-cost arithmetic RAM convention, with only logarithmically many bits per word.

Updates and queries arrive one at a time. The answer to each query must be exactly correct for the state after all earlier updates, before a later operation is revealed. Every finite operation history is allowed, including histories selected using earlier answers and histories much longer than \(n\). All operation invocations must terminate. The structure is deterministic, with no error probability and no random or expected-time convention.

A constant-time structure would have one constant \(T\) bounding the work of every individual update and query, for every initial sequence, every length and every history. The work done by one operation cannot be charged to earlier or later operations. Allowing an onset \(n_0\) rather than all lengths gives the same existence question, since the finitely many smaller lengths can be handled separately. Consequently a positive impossibility result can be expressed as follows: for every correct linear-preprocessing structure, every proposed bound \(B\) and every onset \(N\), there is a length \(n\ge N\), an initial sequence and a finite operation history in which an individual operation takes more than \(B\) steps. No particular function tending to infinity is prescribed in advance.

The cell-probe model, mentioned in the context, charges only memory accesses and allows arbitrary computation on values already read at no cost. It is more permissive than the word-operation model just defined; a counting argument that ignores all such computation cannot automatically establish the requested word-RAM barrier.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the claimed nonexistence. A proof must exclude every correct deterministic uniform structure with linear preprocessing and fixed logarithmic word-length constant from having a common constant worst-case bound for both operations. It may give a quantitative lower bound, but must justify that it excludes all constants in this model. A refutation must give a single finite-program structure, some fixed word-length constant, linear preprocessing and exact constant worst-case bounds for both updates and queries on every history. An amortized or expected constant upper bound alone does not refute the specified worst-case conjecture. A lower bound for a stronger query task, larger monoid, smaller instruction set or stricter space limit does not alone prove it.
context:
Section 2 explicitly uses worst-case operation cost and linear preprocessing. The question concerns the two-element AND monoid. The separately discussed three-element monoid has a stronger predecessor-type task and a different known lower bound.

The source records an \(O(\log\log n)\) deterministic upper bound and a better expected bound when randomness is allowed. It emphasizes that this does not provide the superconstant lower bound and distinguishes the word-RAM problem from unrestricted local computation in the cell-probe model.

The 2022 string-data-structure paper formulates a stronger amortized constant-time hardness conjecture. Its conditional consequences are evidence of the primitive’s relevance, but this card retains the original worst-case question rather than silently changing the cost convention.

The 2025 tree-language paper still states prefix-U-one hardness as a conjectural premise. Under that premise it classifies constant-time maintainability for its specified class of regular tree languages with a neutral letter; it does not prove the premise.
why: This small dynamic problem isolates whether maintaining even threshold information about a changing minimum requires more than a constant number of actual word operations. Its hardness would complete conditional classifications of dynamic regular-language membership, and newer work extends that connection to tree languages. The challenge concerns computation inside the machine as well as memory access, making it a foundational word-RAM question.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: ICALP 2021 Section 2 and Conjecture 2.3, the 2022 amortized variant, and MFCS 2025 Section 6. The latter continues to use the original hardness premise conditionally. A bounded later-work search found no matching worst-case constant-time structure or proof of its nonexistence in the declared logarithmic-word model. The source-open label records these search and model limits, not exhaustive verification of current openness.
