working_summary: The prefix-U-one problem maintains a fixed-length bit sequence under substitutions and returns the AND of any requested prefix. The conjecture rules out a deterministic data structure with linear preprocessing and constant worst-case time for both operations. Its machine has logarithmic-size words and explicitly charged arithmetic, bit operations and memory accesses. Amortized constant time, expected constant time and stronger predecessor queries are separate questions. A resolution would settle a basic dynamic set barrier underlying conditional classifications for regular word and tree languages.

title: Logarithmic fully retroactive priority queues
importance_reason: This asks whether complete access to a changeable operation history can cost only as much asymptotically as an ordinary priority queue.
formal: Does a deterministic fully retroactive priority queue exist with \(O(m+1)\) space and \(O(\log(2+m))\) amortized time per operation, where \(m\) is the number of operations in its represented history? It must support adding or removing a historical insertion or extract-min and asking for the minimum immediately after any supplied historical time.
definitions: The comparison pointer machine stores constant-size records with a fixed number of pointer and data fields, accessed through a constant number of pointer registers. A step can follow or change a pointer, allocate a record, compare two keys or perform a constant-size control operation. Keys are opaque members of a totally ordered set; pointer arithmetic, array indexing by computed integers and unit-cost unbounded counters are unavailable. All work, including rebuilding, is charged. A history consists of insertion records \((t,x)\) and extract-min records \(t\), with pairwise distinct timestamps in an opaque totally ordered time domain. Replay records by timestamp from an empty queue. Inserted items have distinct identities and ordered priorities; ties are resolved by identity. Histories supplied after each edit are promised valid: extract-min never acts on an empty queue. An edit adds a record at an unused time or removes a named existing record. A query at \(t\) returns the minimum surviving item after replay through \(t\), or an empty marker. Removing a past operation changes the interpretation of all subsequent records. There is no monotonicity promise on inserted or extracted priorities. Space includes every retained historical record and index. For each finite edit/query sequence, the sum of \(1+\log(2+m)\) over operations bounds total computation within one universal constant; initialization is constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
Demaine, Iacono and Langerman introduced the retroactive model, which edits the past rather than merely preserving snapshots.

The April 2026 revision reports \(O(\log^2m\log\log m)\) time and \(O(m\log m)\) space for the general case. It attains logarithmic time and linear space for monotonic priority queues, leaving the unrestricted target open.
why: This asks whether complete access to a changeable operation history can cost only as much asymptotically as an ordinary priority queue.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2007: The retroactive framework formalizes edits to operation histories. | 2026-04-14: The monotonic restriction reaches logarithmic time and linear space; the abstract explicitly retains the general problem.
working_summary: Retroactivity permits inserting and deleting operations in the past. Each edit changes the queue state at later historical times. Queries must return the minimum at any chosen time. The target is logarithmic amortized operation time and linear history storage. A recent optimal result covers monotonic histories but not unrestricted priority queues.

title: Optimal randomized memory-reallocation overhead
importance_reason: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.
formal: Determine, up to absolute constant factors as \(\varepsilon\to0\), the optimal worst-case expected reallocation overhead \(F(\varepsilon)\) for online allocators with load at most \(1-\varepsilon\). The allocator stores objects in contiguous intervals of a fixed array and may relocate live objects after each insertion or deletion.
definitions: For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\) and integer array length \(M\ge1\), a request inserts a fresh object of positive integer size \(s\), or deletes a named live object. Valid finite sequences start empty and have total live size at most \((1-\varepsilon)M\) after every request. At each operation boundary, every live object occupies one contiguous interval of its size in \(\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\), and these intervals are disjoint. On an update involving an object \(x\), cost is \(1+\sum_y s(y)/s(x)\), where the sum is over objects live both before and after the update whose starting addresses change. This counts allocation changes at operation boundaries; local computation and allocation metadata are uncharged. The online rule may know \(M,\varepsilon\) but no future requests, and may use private randomness. A sequence is fixed independently of that randomness; allocations must always be valid. For a family of rules covering all \(M\), its overhead is the supremum, over all capacities, valid finite request sequences and individual update indices, of expected update cost. \(F(\varepsilon)\) is the infimum of those overheads over all such families. No history-independence or resizability constraint is imposed. The target measures each update’s expectation, rather than expected amortized cost or a high-probability bound.
answer_criterion: Supply an explicit function \(f(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(c f(\varepsilon)\le F(\varepsilon)\le C f(\varepsilon)\) for absolute positive constants \(c,C\) and all sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\). Bounds only for resizable or history-independent allocators, or only for amortized expectation, do not establish the required matching result.
context:
The 2024 work studies low-overhead memory reallocation and its relationship with stronger resizability and history-independence guarantees. Those extra guarantees are not required for the target here.

Jin’s February 2026 paper gives an upper bound \(O((\log(1/\varepsilon))^4(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^2)\) and a lower bound \(\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for general allocators. The new general lower bound improves the scope of earlier bounds restricted to resizable allocators.
why: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2026-02-17: Polylogarithmic overhead is achieved, and a logarithmic lower bound is proved for general allocators.
working_summary: Objects of different sizes share one nearly full memory array. Every object must occupy a contiguous interval. An insertion or deletion may require moving other live objects. Cost compares the total moved volume with the size of the updated object. The remaining problem is the tight expected overhead as the unused fraction tends to zero.

title: Deque conjecture
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete stress test for splay-tree adaptivity, already on the elementary deque interface; less sweeping than dynamic optimality.
formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing \(n\) ordered keys, and perform \(m\) legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always \(O(n+m)\), with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.
answer_criterion: Prove a universal \(O(n+m)\) total bound for the specified splay implementation, or prove that the ratio between total cost and \(n+m\) is unbounded over legal initial trees and operation sequences.
context:
A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.
why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.
progress: 2007 / 2008: Pettie proves \(O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))\) total cost, where \(\alpha^*\) counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant. | 2019: Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself. | 2026-07: The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.
working_summary: A deque permits insertions and deletions at either end of an ordered collection. This question studies the implementation that inserts extreme keys and splays an extreme key before deleting it. It asks whether every operation sequence costs linear total time, including an allowance for the initial tree. Alternating ends and inserting new keys creates behavior beyond a single sorted scan. The conjecture would show that self-adjusting search trees automatically attain the efficiency expected from this restricted interface.

title: Constant-update working-set heaps on pointer machines
importance_reason: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most \(C(M+\sum_{x\ \mathrm{extracted}}\log \Gamma(x))\)? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define \(\Gamma(x)=1+\) the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.
definitions: Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target. The required total-cost inequality must cover every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue; trading growing insertion time for constant decrease-key does not satisfy it.
context:
The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.
why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2025: Iacono states the pointer-model working-set/decrease-key problem at the Adaptive and Scalable Data Structures seminar. | 2026-07-02: The revised pointer-machine construction achieves O(1) amortized insertion, O(alpha(n)) amortized decrease-key, and O(1 + log Gamma(x)) worst-case extraction. Its introduction explicitly leaves removal of the inverse-Ackermann overhead open. | 2026-07-27: Haeupler, Hladík, Rozhoň, and Tarjan obtain constant amortized decrease-key and stack-like extraction, with insertion bounded by any fixed iteration of log-star. This is not a constant insertion bound.
working_summary: A priority queue supports insertions, priority decreases and minimum extraction. The extraction charge depends on the number of items inserted since the extracted item arrived. The target combines this adaptive charge with constant amortized insertion and decrease-key. Only pointer-machine operations and key comparisons are available. The latest cited constructions retain a slowly growing factor in at least one update operation.

title: Buffered fully persistent search trees
importance_reason: Efficient historical branching together with buffered writes would combine two major capabilities of storage indexes without sacrificing their I/O savings.
formal: For every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), can deterministic fully persistent comparison search trees in external memory support amortized update cost \(O(B^{\varepsilon-1}L_v)\), amortized successor queries \(O(L_v)\), sorted range reporting \(O(L_v+K/B)\), and cloning an arbitrary historical version in \(O(1)\) I/Os, with linear total space? Here \(L_v=1+\log_B(2+N_v)\), \(N_v\) is the size of the accessed version and \(K\) is the output size.
definitions: The I/O model has block size \(B\ge2\), internal memory \(M\ge2B\) and unlimited external memory; only transfers of blocks between them are charged. Keys and version handles occupy constant space, and keys support comparisons only. Begin with an empty version. A branch may be extended by inserting or deleting a key, preserving every preceding version; cloning an arbitrary version creates a new independently extendible branch with the same set. All historical versions remain queryable. Search returns the least key at least the supplied key, or an empty marker; Range returns keys in a closed supplied interval. Require correctness for every online sequence. For \(U\) updates and \(C\) clones, linear total space means \(O(1+(U+C)/B)\) external blocks, including version metadata. All bounds may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on sizes, block parameters or the operation sequence. Amortized bounds must hold jointly over every finite history; buffering cannot postpone a query answer past its operation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
The 2025 result obtains the buffered bounds with partial persistence: every historical version can be queried, but only the newest can be extended.

The paper separately describes constant-I/O cloning for unbuffered fully persistent trees and leaves efficient cloning with buffered full persistence open. This card fixes the simultaneous target rather than treating persistence and buffering separately.
why: Efficient historical branching together with buffered writes would combine two major capabilities of storage indexes without sacrificing their I/O savings.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2025: Optimal partial persistence is achieved; the conclusion leaves buffered full persistence with efficient cloning open.
working_summary: A search tree keeps all previous versions of its ordered set. A user may start a new branch from any past version. Buffered updates save external-memory transfers by processing writes together. The goal combines these savings with fast historical queries and constant-I/O cloning. The latest cited result supplies this update efficiency only for partial persistence.

title: Combined depth and size bounds for confluently persistent tries
importance_reason: The question concerns whether persistent hierarchical data can exploit shallow or local changes while also protecting users against arbitrarily deep versions.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), does there exist a deterministic uniform functional trie representation and a constant \(C_k>0\) that supports the version, finger-navigation and subtree-copy interface below, with worst-case navigation time \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\), no new permanent records from navigation, and both worst-case modification time and newly permanent record count at most \(C_k[1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}]\) for every valid operation sequence?
definitions:
A logical trie is a finite rooted tree, including its root, with distinct totally ordered labels on the outgoing edges of each node and one constant-size data atom per node. Logical occurrences are counted separately even when their physical representations share records. For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), every stored version has \(k\) finger positions, possibly coincident. Selecting a version restores those positions in at most \(C_k\) operations; navigation changes a working copy of them. Reading a node’s data also costs at most \(C_k\) operations. These calls do not permit uncharged preprocessing. It can reset a finger to the root, move it to its parent, follow a child with a supplied label, or read the data at a finger. A failed parent or child move reports failure and leaves the finger unchanged. A modification creates a new stored version and leaves every previous version usable. It can change data at a finger, add a new leaf with an unused child label, remove the non-root subtree at a finger, or copy the subtree at a finger of any source version as a child with an unused label at a destination finger. The source and destination versions may coincide. The copy is a logical duplicate, so later changes to either occurrence do not change the other. Surviving destination fingers keep their logical positions; fingers in a removed subtree reset to the root. A copy may replace any specified subset of the resulting finger slots by counterparts of source fingers inside the copied subtree. Thus at most \(k\) fingers are stored in the resulting version. All parameters are supplied through version handles, finger indices and constant-size atoms; arbitrary logical nodes cannot be addressed directly.

Use a deterministic uniform pointer program with a fixed number of fields per record. A field holds a pointer, an opaque label or data atom, or an integer counter. Reading a field, comparing or copying atoms or pointers, comparing labels, and adding, subtracting or comparing counters cost one operation. New records may be initialized, but a previously initialized record is never overwritten. There is no pointer arithmetic, address-indexed array lookup, arithmetic on labels, random choice, oracle or nonuniform table. Counters have magnitude polynomial in the largest logical version size and operation count so far; costs count record operations, not their bit implementation. The program and field count are independent of all versions and operation sequences; constants may depend on the fixed finger bound \(k\). The initial version is a single root and costs \(O(k)\) operations and records.

For a modification, let \(N\) be the sum of the logical node counts of its participating input versions and its output version, counting a shared input only once. Let \(\Delta\ge2\) be the maximum of two and all node outdegrees in those versions. Let \(D=1+\sum_f\operatorname{depth}(f)\), summing the depths of the \(k\) stored or working fingers in each participating input version; root depth is zero. Define \(B=1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}\). For navigation, \(\Delta\) is instead the maximum of two and the outdegrees in the selected logical version. Navigation must cost at most \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\) operations, and a modification at most \(C_kB\) operations, in the worst case for every individual call in every finite valid sequence.

A record is permanent when reachable from any stored version handle, including that version’s stored finger representation. All stored versions remain available. Navigation may allocate temporary records but must leave the set of permanent records unchanged. A modification is charged every record newly made permanent by its result, including records allocated during earlier navigation; this count must be at most \(C_kB\). Existing permanent records shared by the new version are not charged again. Temporary allocation time is always charged to the call performing it; the permanent-space guarantee is not a bound on peak temporary storage. All logarithms and bounds use logical version sizes, not the number of previously allocated physical records.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that representations and constants with every stated interface, persistence, worst-case time and permanent-space property exist for all fixed \(k\ge2\), or prove the logical negation in Lean. A positive proof must charge navigation records subsequently retained by an update and preserve all prior versions. Separate representations attaining the two bounds, an amortized guarantee, or a theorem only for point changes without subtree copies does not meet the combined specification.
context:
Version control must preserve old directory trees while allowing a whole directory to be copied between branches. A logical subtree copy can contain very many nodes, yet a representation can initially share their unchanged contents. Confluent persistence requires both source versions and all older versions to remain usable after this operation.

The source gives two functional representations. One exploits locality of finger operations with \(O(\log\Delta)\) time and allocation per call; navigation records can later become permanent. The other uses \(O(\log n)\) time and permanent space per modification, with \(O(\log\Delta)\) navigation time and no permanent navigation space. These are different guarantees because navigation may be followed by either another query or a modification.

An arbitrarily long path illustrates the size/depth distinction. A change near its root has small root depth even when the version is enormous, whereas a change near the bottom has large depth. The requested minimum would retain a shallow-update bound and also cap deep-update costs logarithmically in logical size. The question concerns one representation with simultaneous guarantees, not choosing a separate representation after seeing the next operation.

Charging only the records allocated inside the final update would conceal part of the first representation’s cost. Records produced by earlier finger moves count against the update if the new stored version retains them. Conversely, a navigation-only sequence produces no new stored versions, so discarded temporary work does not count as permanent history.

Editorial specification: Section 6 states the combined depth/size goal but leaves the multi-finger parameters implicit. This benchmark uses the sum of participating finger depths, a maximum degree over participating versions, and the sum of input/output logical sizes. With a fixed number of fingers these specify a single bound for copies and deletions; a one-finger point modification retains the root-depth scale \(1+d\). They are explicit conventions for the combined variant, not definitions quoted verbatim from the authors.

The source’s constant-time comparison of labels and functional pointer-record model are retained. This is not a claim about the cost of comparing arbitrary file-name strings, storing file contents, or implementing large counters in a bit machine. The documented temporary/permanent distinction is part of the target, rather than an unrecorded memory exemption.
why: The question concerns whether persistent hierarchical data can exploit shallow or local changes while also protecting users against arbitrarily deep versions.
status_note: The combined goal is explicitly open in the source’s Section 6. A bounded 13 September 2026 search did not locate a later resolution. The complete benchmark makes its multi-finger parameters and space accounting explicit editorial conventions; it does not claim that the source spelled out this entire interface or that absence of a later result was exhaustively established.
progress: 2010: The conclusion asks to combine the two functional bounds in one representation.
working_summary: Confluent persistence lets a subtree be copied between historical trie versions while retaining all old versions. The question asks for one functional representation combining a shallow-update bound with a logarithmic bound in logical version size. Navigation has its own worst-case time bound and may not extend permanent version history. An update must pay for any earlier navigation records that its new stored version retains. The model and parameters explicitly cover multiple fingers, logical sharing, subtree copies and temporary versus permanent memory.

title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
importance_reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
focus_reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
formal: Does there exist a single deterministic data structure and fixed constants \(C,c,d>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), an initially empty undirected simple graph on vertex set \([n]\) can be maintained under any online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, using at most \(C n^{d}\) words of memory and at most \(C(\log _{2} n)^{c}\) time for each individual operation? Initialization may take at most \(C n^{d}\) time and depends only on n. All connectivity answers must be exact in the word-RAM model specified below.
definitions: An insertion \(insert(u,v)\) adds a previously absent unordered edge \(\{u,v\}\), where \(u\ne v; a\) deletion \(delete(u,v)\) removes an existing edge. A query \(connected(u,v)\) returns whether the current graph contains a path from u to v, with \(connected(u,u)\)=true. Updates are valid, arrive one at a time and must finish before the next operation is revealed. No future operations or advance description of the sequence is supplied. The data structure must work for every finite sequence, including sequences chosen in response to its previous behavior. The word RAM has word size \(w=\lceil a \log _{2} n\rceil\) for a fixed constant a large enough to address its polynomial space. Unit-cost instructions are indirect reads/writes, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient/remainder, comparisons, Boolean bit operations and shifts; arithmetic results stored in one word are reduced modulo 2ʷ where appropriate. Arbitrary-precision computation costs its constituent word operations. All maintenance, rebuilding and query work is charged to the operation performing it. The exponent c is independent of n and of the length or contents of the operation sequence. The graph is unrestricted apart from being undirected and simple; no planarity, bounded-degree or expansion promise is given.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The difficulty is deleting an edge that belongs to a maintained spanning forest. Removing it splits one tree into two parts, but the graph might still connect those parts through an edge outside the forest. The data structure must find such a replacement quickly or correctly certify that none exists. A single deletion can expose a large cut, so simply scanning all candidate edges gives no small bound on the time of that update.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give deterministic \(O(\log ^{2} n)\) amortized operation bounds for connectivity, using a hierarchy of forests and edge levels. Their result establishes that long update sequences can be processed efficiently. The accounting permits an individual deletion to spend work paid for by other operations. Guaranteeing low latency after every deletion requires more than redistributing the same amortized accounting on paper.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case update time with randomization and a small error probability. Their cutset sampling technique tries to isolate a remaining edge across a cut, which can then be recovered from a compact sketch. Failure to recover an edge may mean either that the cut is empty or that the random samples missed it. Eliminating this uncertainty while keeping every update fast is part of the deterministic challenge.

Chuzhoy and coauthors use deterministic balanced-cut machinery to achieve \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time, removing the earlier polynomial barrier. This is a major improvement but still leaves the present target open. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) is smaller than every fixed positive power of n and larger than every fixed power of log n. Thus a subpolynomial theorem does not imply the polylogarithmic bound merely by choosing a small exponent.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 algorithm is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest and achieves polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time, even against an adaptive adversary with access to its state. It alternates vertex and edge sparsification in a hierarchy. Each graph update changes the output forest by at most two edges, so maintaining the explicit answer itself does not cause large update costs. The expectation remains a distinction from the deterministic target.

The same paper gives a concrete sufficient condition for derandomization. If a deterministic algorithm constructs a near-linear-edge subgraph together with paths routing the original edges through it in \(m\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(m)\) time, with congestion at most \((m/n)\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(m)\), the framework yields deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity. Congestion counts how many routed paths use the busiest retained edge. Finding any spanning forest is insufficient: its tree edges may carry far too many such paths.

A companion SODA 2026 result by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak controls both the time and the number of vertices removed when pruning an expander after one edge deletion. This avoids a large burst of changes propagating through a hierarchy. It is an ingredient in the recent randomized progress; it does not by itself supply the deterministic sparsifier construction needed for the full conclusion.

Known lower bounds do not rule out the target. Pătraşcu and Demaine prove logarithmic amortized cell-probe lower bounds, including for connectivity on disjoint paths. Those results show that dynamic connectivity already has a real information-transfer cost in very simple graphs, but a logarithmic barrier is compatible with polylogarithmic upper bounds. The open issue is whether exact connectivity, deterministic computation and a bound on every operation can be achieved simultaneously.
why: A basic unresolved guarantee for dynamic graph data structures. Connectivity is both a natural maintenance problem and a source of techniques used throughout graph algorithms; combining determinism, exactness and fast individual updates would close a longstanding gap.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The SODA 2026 connectivity paper explicitly retains deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case updates as open. Its unconditional new bound is randomized and expected; its deterministic polylogarithmic conclusion depends on the stated static low-congestion sparsifier construction. Deterministic subpolynomial worst-case bounds and polylogarithmic amortized bounds are already known.
progress: 1998–2001: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic polylogarithmic amortized connectivity; the journal version gives \(O(\log ^{2} n)\). | 2004–2006: Pătraşcu–Demaine establish logarithmic cell-probe lower bounds, including on disjoint paths; they do not exclude a polylogarithmic worst-case algorithm. | 2013: Kapron–King–Mountjoy give a Monte Carlo structure with polylogarithmic worst-case operation time and high-probability correctness. | 2019–2020: Chuzhoy–Gao–Li–Nanongkai–Peng–Saranurak obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case dynamic connectivity, published at FOCS 2020. | 2026-01-07: SODA publishes Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s Las Vegas expected polylogarithmic worst-case algorithm and conditional deterministic reduction, first posted 9 October 2025. | 2026-01-07: SODA also publishes expander pruning with worst-case recourse and update bounds, an ingredient in the connectivity framework.
working_summary: Dynamic connectivity maintains whether pairs of vertices remain connected as graph edges are inserted and deleted. The reviewed question asks for deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case time for every operation, with exact answers. Deleting a spanning-forest edge requires quickly finding a replacement across the exposed cut or certifying that none exists. This would combine deterministic reliability with consistently low latency on arbitrary update sequences. The saved review distinguishes amortized guarantees, randomized cutset recovery, and subpolynomial worst-case time from the stronger polylogarithmic bound required here.

title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
importance_reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.
focus_reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |\(M|\ge \nu (G)/(1+\varepsilon )\) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set \([n], n\ge 2; \nu (G)\) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) and constant \(a\ge 1\), require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon ,a}\) such that every sequence of \(T\le n^{a}\) updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most \(K[n+T(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}]\). Words have \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\), after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes \(O(1)\) time; enumerating all matching edges costs \(O(n)\) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to \(\nu (G)\) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a \(2- \sqrt{2}- \eta\) fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed \(\eta >0\). The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly \(n^{o(1)}\) times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: \(n^{o(1)}\) can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time \(n/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) times a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-\(\varepsilon\) question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.
why: The principal update-time frontier for maintaining actual near-optimal matchings under arbitrary edge insertions and deletions, beyond maximality and matching-size estimation.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.
progress: 2023–2024: Polylogarithmic-update algorithms beat factor two for matching-size estimation; SODA 2024 extends the \(2- \sqrt{2}- \eta\) fraction to general graphs. | 2024-03-05: Liu obtains \(n/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) update time for near-optimal bipartite matching, with polynomial accuracy dependence and connections to online matrix-vector problems. | 2024–2025: Behnezhad–Ghafari introduce the ordered-RS route; Assadi–Khanna–Kiss improve its update bound to roughly \(n^{o(1)}\) times the relevant ORS count. | 2025–2026: Pratt connects polynomial-density ordered and ordinary RS graphs; the result appears at SOSA 2026. | 2026-05-01: Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song post a deterministic \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-update maximal-matching algorithm, presented at STOC 2026. This is a weaker approximation target.
working_summary: A matching selects graph edges without shared endpoints. The reviewed question asks to maintain an explicit matching within a factor of one plus \(\varepsilon\) of maximum using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time. Although the optimum changes little after one update, repairing a particular matching may involve a long alternating path. A solution would combine nearly optimal allocation quality with efficient response to both insertions and deletions. The saved record requires actual partner information and distinguishes this task from estimating matching size or maintaining the weaker guarantee of maximality.

title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
importance_reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.
formal: Can an exact minimum spanning forest of a fully dynamic n-vertex graph with polynomially bounded integer weights be maintained with polylogarithmic worst-case time per edge update, polynomial preprocessing and space, and high-probability correctness against an oblivious adversary?
definitions: The graph is simple and undirected on the fixed labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), and starts empty. An update inserts one currently absent edge with integer weight in \(\{1,\ldots ,n^{4}\}\), or deletes one present edge. Edge weights remain fixed until deletion. A minimum spanning forest consists of one minimum-total-weight spanning tree for each connected component. Break equal-weight ties by the fixed lexicographic order (weight, smaller endpoint, larger endpoint), so the target is the unique forest selected by Kruskal’s algorithm in that order. After each update the data structure must report the edges removed from and added to the maintained forest; on a correct execution at most one edge of each kind changes. These reports specify the entire current forest starting from the empty one. Use a uniform randomized classical word RAM with \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words, standard word operations and random-word generation; all input processing and memory accesses count. For every fixed pair of integers \(a,b\ge 1\), the target permits a separately tuned uniform data structure and constants \(K,C\ge 1\) whose preprocessing and space are \(n^{O(1)}\), and for which every update takes at most \(K(\log _{2}(n+2))^{C}\) steps on every execution. For every valid update sequence of length at most \(n^{a}\) fixed before its random choices, all reported forests must be correct simultaneously with probability at least \(1- n^{- b}\). Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on a,b, but not on n or the sequence. This is a Monte Carlo worst-case-time formulation; an always-correct deterministic solution would also suffice. The integer range \(n^{4}\) is an explicit specialization, and weights occupy \(O(1)\) words. There is no advance access to future updates.
answer_criterion: Construct data structures satisfying the stated bounds for every fixed a,b, or prove the proposition false. Amortized polylogarithmic updates, merely subpolynomial worst-case updates, or maintaining an approximate minimum forest are insufficient. A lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone does not rule out the allowed randomization. A data structure that only stores the graph and postpones finding the forest to an expensive query does not meet the required per-update reporting guarantee.
context:
One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all \(n- 1\) tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of \(n^{o(1)}\) update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to \(\log (U)/\varepsilon\) for weights in \([1,U]\). The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking \(\varepsilon\) smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed \(1/\varepsilon\) overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.
why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.
status_note: Current sources distinguish exact subpolynomial worst-case MSF maintenance from polylogarithmic amortized maintenance and the 2026 approximate weighted extension of connectivity algorithms. The inherited ICALP 2021 link was a mismatched matching citation and is identified as such. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1998–2001: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized minimum-spanning-forest updates. | 2014–2015: Holm–Rotenberg–Wulff-Nilsen improve amortized bounds; the \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) option uses randomized priority queues in the stated RAM model. | 2017: Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. | 2020: Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition. | 2026-01-07: Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate with inverse-\(\varepsilon\) overhead.
working_summary: A minimum spanning forest connects each graph component as cheaply as possible under the current edge weights. The question asks for polylogarithmic worst-case update time in a fully dynamic graph. Randomization is allowed, with high-probability correctness against an update sequence independent of the random choices. The hard step is finding the cheapest replacement edge after deletion splits a tree. The saved review separates this exact maintenance target from amortized bounds and notes that reporting only actual forest changes avoids an artificial cost for repeatedly printing every tree edge.

title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
importance_reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.
formal: Can a fully dynamic simple, unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph maintain its exact global minimum-cut value with expected \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) amortized update time, worst-case \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) query time and polynomial space, with high probability over every polynomial-length oblivious operation sequence?
definitions: Fix vertices \([n], n\ge 2\). Start from the empty graph. A legal update inserts one absent unordered edge or deletes one present edge; there are no loops, parallel edges, weights or vertex updates. A query returns the integer \(\lambda (G)=\min \{|\{uv\in E:u\in S,v\notin S\}| : \varnothing \ne S\subsetneq [n]\}\). In particular \(\lambda (G)=0\) for a disconnected graph; no distinguished terminals are supplied. Only the value is required, not a list of vertices or edges realizing the cut. Use a uniform randomized word-RAM with \(\Theta (\log (n+2))\)-bit words, ordinary arithmetic, bit operations and random access, and count all maintenance and query work. Precisely, ask for fixed exponents b,c and an algorithm accepting any fixed constant \(a\ge 1\) as a confidence parameter. For every legal sequence with U updates and Q queries, \(U+Q\le n^{a}\), fixed independently of its random bits, it uses \(O_{a}(n^{b})\) words on every execution; expected total initialization and update work is \(O_{a}(n^{b}+U \log ^{c}(n+2))\); each query takes \(O_{a}(\log ^{c}(n+2))\) worst-case time; and all query answers are simultaneously correct with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\). Initial preprocessing may take \(O_{a}(n^{b})\) time, accounting for the additive term. Each operation must finish before the next is revealed. The exponents are independent of \(\lambda (G), n\) and a. This fixes an expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention explicitly; it does not demand correctness against updates chosen from the random internal state.
answer_criterion: Construct a data structure satisfying the complete specification for unrestricted cut values, or prove that no such data structure exists in the stated model. Conditional lower bounds must state their assumptions. Algorithms for insertion-only sequences, approximate cut values, bounded connectivity or subpolynomial but superpolylogarithmic update time are partial progress. Hardness for weighted cuts or fixed-terminal s–t cuts alone is not a negative resolution.
context:
The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. This simple stability is useful, but it does not tell an algorithm whether the answer actually changed. Certifying that no alternative cut is smaller is the difficult global part of an update.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

The update model is also decisive. Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup obtained deterministic polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. In that setting edges are only inserted. Deletions can invalidate the compressed structural information retained during a monotone growth process, so this theorem does not settle fully dynamic maintenance.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors obtained exact fully dynamic algorithms with roughly linear-in-n randomized worst-case update time and sublinear-in-m deterministic amortized update time. Their 2024 revision corrects a runtime in the expander-decomposition analysis. This establishes substantial reuse across updates without reaching a polylogarithmic bound.

De Vos and Christiansen improve the deterministic amortized bound to \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m^{11/12})\); their final 2026 theorem gives the more detailed minimum of \(m^{11/12}, m^{11/13}n^{1/13}\), and \(n^{3/2}\), up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses greedy tree packings: either a packed tree crosses a minimum cut only once, or a suitable contraction exposes a minimum cut around one vertex. Both structural outcomes help reduce the candidate cuts that must be maintained.

The inherited SODA 2026 paper of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li reaches \(n^{o(1)}\) deterministic amortized update time for exact cuts of size up to \(2^{\Theta ((\log  n)^{3/4- \eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta <3/4\) in the stated parameter regime. This greatly expands the previous small-cut range. It still restricts the minimum-cut value, and \(n^{o(1)}\) does not itself mean a fixed power of log n.

The same paper explains the accuracy barrier behind this restriction. Its recursive procedure controls a very small multiplicative approximation error, allowing exact recovery while the integral cut value stays below the inverse error. Making that error much smaller increases the work propagated between recursive levels. Thus simply substituting a large cut value into the theorem does not preserve its running time.

Approximation has progressed separately. El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. For an integer optimum \(\lambda\), rounding a multiplicative estimate to an exact answer generally needs additive error below one, hence relative error on the order of \(1/\lambda\). A fixed approximation guarantee cannot supply this for arbitrary connectivity.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.
why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No exact fully dynamic algorithm meeting the polylogarithmic bounds at unrestricted connectivity was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 exact \(n^{o(1)}\) result has a cut-size restriction, and the unrestricted 2026 tree-packing bound remains polynomial rather than polylogarithmic.
