working_summary: The global minimum cut is the smallest number of edges separating a graph into two nonempty parts. The reviewed question asks to maintain its exact value under insertions and deletions with expected polylogarithmic amortized updates. Queries must also be polylogarithmic, and randomized correctness is required over oblivious operation sequences. Even though one update changes the value by at most one, identifying whether another cut has become optimal requires global information. The target returns only the numerical value and uses zero for disconnected graphs, avoiding output-size and convention ambiguities.

title: Logarithmic Las Vegas dynamic connectivity
importance_reason: Closing the remaining iterated-logarithm gap would pin down a central dynamic graph primitive near its information-theoretic lower bounds.
formal: Does an always-correct Las Vegas word-RAM data structure maintain connectivity of an initially empty undirected simple graph on \([n]\) with \(O(\log(2+n))\) amortized expected time per edge update and \(O(\log(2+n))\) worst-case time per query, using \(O((n+m)\log^c(2+n))\) words for some fixed \(c\), where \(m\) is the current number of edges?
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. Here \(w=\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed constant \(a\) sufficient to address the allowed space. Insert adds a missing edge; Delete removes a present edge; Connected(u,v) returns whether a path joins the two supplied vertices. Valid operations form any finite sequence fixed independently of the random bits. The expected total cost is \(O(n\log^c(2+n)+(u+q)\log(2+n))\) for \(u\) updates and \(q\) queries; the first term includes initialization from the empty graph. Every individual query must meet its worst-case bound. Every answer is correct, and all operations terminate almost surely. This asks for amortized expected updates against an oblivious adversary, not deterministic or worst-case update guarantees. The algorithm has no advance access to future updates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
The 2023 Las Vegas structure has \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^2)\) amortized expected update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log\log n)\) worst-case queries.

Polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity is a separate research direction: a larger polylogarithm per operation does not provide logarithmic amortized update time.
why: Closing the remaining iterated-logarithm gap would pin down a central dynamic graph primitive near its information-theoretic lower bounds.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2023: The Las Vegas amortized bound comes within a squared logarithmic-logarithmic factor of logarithmic updates. | 2026: The expected worst-case polylogarithmic result concerns a different quantitative guarantee.
working_summary: An undirected graph changes one edge at a time. A query asks whether two vertices remain connected. The target is logarithmic amortized expected update time with always-correct answers. Known Las Vegas bounds retain an iterated-logarithm overhead. The related deterministic worst-case problem asks for different guarantees.

title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
importance_reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.
formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants \(a,d \ge  1\) such that the following holds for all \(n \ge  2\) and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in \(\{1,\ldots ,n^{c}\}\), under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for \(s=t\), and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with \(Theta(\log  n)\)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
context:
Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves \(O(n^{2} \log ^{3} n)\) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the \(n^{5/2}\) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.
why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.
status_note: The edge-sensitive target is open in the 2021 source. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate an exact algorithm with the stated sparse update and query bounds. This is a deterministic bounded-integer-weight specialization; approximate and worst-case vertex-update results are recorded with their different guarantees.
progress: 2004: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic \(O(n^{2} \log ^{3} n)\) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs. | 2021: Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise. | 2024-08-27: Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-\(O(n^{5/2})\) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee. | 2025: Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.
working_summary: Dynamic all-pairs shortest paths must answer exact distances while directed weighted edges change. The reviewed target combines polylogarithmic worst-case queries with amortized update time nearly linear in the edge bound m. It allows polynomial preprocessing and space while requiring deterministic answers. The principal gap is sparse graphs, where updates should cost much less than rebuilding a full distance table. The saved review explains that many distances changing simultaneously is not an impossibility argument, because the oracle may represent those changes implicitly and expose only one queried pair.

title: Worst-case logarithmic dynamic planar convex hulls
importance_reason: This asks whether optimal dynamic geometric query performance can be guaranteed for individual updates rather than only averaged over a sequence.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic data structure maintaining a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\) under point insertion and deletion, using \(O(1+|P|)\) space, with \(O(\log(2+n))\) worst-case time for every update and every extreme-point query? Here \(n\) is the larger set size immediately before and after the operation. An extreme-point query supplies \(u\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\) and returns a point maximizing \(\langle u,p\rangle\) over \(p\in P\), or an empty marker.
definitions: The set is initially empty. Insertions supply distinct points; deletions name a present point by a stable handle returned at insertion. Ties may be resolved by any fixed deterministic rule. Use an algebraic real RAM: exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value and comparisons each cost one step, as do constant-size record and pointer operations; no floor, bit extraction from reals or arbitrary-precision encoding operation is supplied. A point, pointer or scalar occupies one cell. One finite program must handle every finite valid online sequence, without advance knowledge, with universal constants in the bounds. Only a maximizing point is returned, not an explicit list of all hull vertices.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
Brodal and Jacob achieve logarithmic amortized insertion and deletion with logarithmic worst-case extreme-point queries in linear space. Their concluding questions explicitly include worst-case logarithmic updates.

A single update may change many hull vertices. The maintained query representation avoids requiring the entire polygon to be output after each change.
why: This asks whether optimal dynamic geometric query performance can be guaranteed for individual updates rather than only averaged over a sequence.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2019: The full analysis gives logarithmic amortized updates and explicitly retains worst-case logarithmic updates as open.
working_summary: A planar point set changes by insertion and deletion. A query asks for a point farthest in a supplied direction. The target is linear storage and logarithmic time for each individual operation. The known optimal update guarantee is amortized over a sequence. The question isolates whether geometric maintenance must sometimes cause expensive update spikes.

title: Near-linear incremental topological ordering
importance_reason: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.
formal: Does a uniform Las Vegas randomized algorithm maintain a topological ordering of an initially empty directed graph on \(n\) named vertices during edge insertions in expected total time \((n+m)^{1+o(1)}\), with \(O(1)\) worst-case order-comparison queries and \(O((n+m)(\log(2+n))^C)\) words of space for some constant \(C\)? Here \(m\) is the number of edges inserted so far, and every graph in the sequence is promised acyclic.
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. For each \(n\ge2\), vertices are \([n]\), no parallel edges or loops are inserted, and the complete finite insertion/query sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Word length is \(\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed algorithm-chosen constant \(a\) large enough for its storage addresses. After every insertion there must be a total order of all vertices with every edge directed forward. A query on \((u,v)\) returns whether \(u\) precedes \(v\) in that maintained order, with all queries between insertions referring to the same order. It is not a reachability query, and printing a fresh list of all vertices after every insertion is not required. Answers are always correct, and operations terminate almost surely. The update bound means that for every constant \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(C_\eta\) such that expected initialization plus update time is at most \(C_\eta(n+m)^{1+\eta}\) for every prefix; \(q\) order queries add \(O(q)\) time. No predictions, special graph family or advance edge information are supplied. The target allows the full stated RAM, without an undefined restriction to combinatorial algorithms.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
The 2025 report distinguishes maintaining a topological order from cycle detection, which already has almost-linear total update time. It records the dense-graph work of Bender and coauthors and sparse-graph bounds with a polynomial overhead.

The report also poses a more specific combinatorial improvement. This card instead formalizes the broader almost-linear ordering target discussed in the researcher list. Prediction-dependent graph maintenance does not establish this guarantee for arbitrary insertion sequences.
why: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2025: The report explicitly separates almost-linear cycle detection from the still-slower maintenance of a topological order. | 2026: Prediction-based incremental graph results concern additional input assistance and leave the stated unassisted target unchanged.
working_summary: Directed edges arrive one at a time without creating a cycle. The algorithm maintains a total vertex order consistent with every edge. Queries compare two vertices in the maintained order. The target is almost-linear total update time over the whole insertion sequence. Fast cycle detection by itself does not maintain the order required here.

title: Polylogarithmic dynamic maximal matching against adaptive updates
importance_reason: Dynamic maximal matching is a fundamental update-time benchmark and a building block for other dynamic graph algorithms.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that explicitly maintains a maximal matching in a fully dynamic \(n\)-vertex simple graph against an adaptive adversary, with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time? More precisely, are there an algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every horizon \(T\ge1\), and every valid adaptive update strategy, the algorithm is always correct and its expected total update work is at most
\[C T(\log_2(n+2))^c,\]
after initialization in at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^c\) expected time? The graph starts empty and each update inserts or deletes one edge. The model and adversary are defined below. A deterministic algorithm is permitted as a special case.

This card selects the polylogarithmic question expressly included in the 2022 source. Its earlier sublinear-time question has since received positive answers; that weaker threshold is retained as dated progress rather than presented as open.
definitions:
The fixed vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is undirected, loopless and simple, with no sparsity, degree or bipartiteness promise. An insertion gives two distinct vertex labels whose edge is currently absent; a deletion specifies a currently present edge. Both kinds may occur in any order, and the next update is unavailable until the current one is finished.

A matching \(M\subseteq E\) has no two edges sharing an endpoint. It is maximal if no edge of \(E\setminus M\) can be added while preserving this condition; equivalently, every edge of the graph has at least one endpoint incident to \(M\). The requirement is inclusion-wise maximality after every update. No maximum-cardinality optimality requirement is imposed.

Explicit maintenance means retaining an array \(\mathrm{mate}[1..n]\) with value zero for an unmatched vertex and value \(v\) at \(u\) when \(\{u,v\}\in M\). Array changes are charged to update time; reading one mate entry takes constant time. The whole matching need not be printed after each update.

Use a word-RAM with words of \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(c_w\) chosen with the algorithm, polynomially many addressable words of persistent memory, and unit-cost word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Each independent uniform random word also costs one operation. All preprocessing, memory management and changes to the maintained matching are charged. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\), with no graph-dependent advice or uncharged table depending on the input. Its memory bound and word-size constant are fixed independently of the update horizon.

Before selecting update \(t+1\), the adversary may inspect the complete current matching, all previous updates and all observed update runtimes. It has unbounded computation and may use its own independent randomness. It does not see hidden algorithm state, past unexposed random choices or future random bits. Correctness and expected cost must hold for every such adaptive strategy, with the horizon \(T\) fixed before the experiment. The expectation includes randomness of both parties. Allowing the adversary to inspect the matching is an observation convention, not a requirement to print the array at every step.

Always correct means that every completed update returns a valid maximal matching, and every finite valid adaptive experiment terminates with probability one. Randomness may affect running time and which maximal matching is chosen, but may never permit an incorrect answer. This is a Las Vegas guarantee. The total-time inequality is amortized: a single update may cost more than a polylogarithm, provided every finite prefix obeys the stated expected total bound. All constants are independent of \(n,T\), the graph and the adversary.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of an algorithm with these guarantees. A positive answer must maintain an explicit maximal matching for all valid adaptive insertion/deletion sequences, with the stated uniformity, always-correct behavior and expected prefix-total bounds. A bound only against an oblivious adversary, a maintained estimate of maximum matching size, or a matching that is approximately maximum but not maximal is insufficient. A merely sublinear polynomial update bound does not reach the polylogarithmic target. A negative answer must rule out randomized algorithms in this model, not just one deterministic implementation.
context:
The original problem paragraph asks several related questions. This review takes its explicit polylogarithmic target and fixes the permissive expected-amortized, always-correct randomized setting against an adversary observing the matching. It does not combine the separate lower-bound question into the answer criterion.

The 2026 paper reports earlier oblivious-adversary algorithms with constant amortized update time and polylogarithmic worst-case update time. Those guarantees assume that the update sequence cannot adapt to the maintained matching.

Bernstein, Bhattacharya, Kiss and Saranurak’s STOC 2025 results, summarized in the 2026 introduction, achieve \(\widetilde O(n^{3/4})\) randomized adaptive update time and \(\widetilde O(n^{8/9})\) deterministic update time, both amortized. Thus the source’s basic sublinear threshold is no longer the open target.

Chuzhoy, Khanna and Song’s Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic fully dynamic algorithm with amortized update time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\). This also tolerates adaptive updates, but its guarantee does not supply polylogarithmic update time. Here \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors, and \(o(1)\) in the exponent tends to zero as \(n\) grows.
why: Maximal matching is a basic dynamic graph primitive whose current answer can influence the next change to the graph. This problem asks whether the cost of responding to that feedback can be reduced to a polylogarithm. It would clarify a major difference between algorithms that assume an independently chosen update sequence and algorithms whose guarantees survive interaction.
status_note: The original Section 4.6 and Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song arXiv:2605.00797v1, including its introduction and Theorem 1.1, were read on 2026-09-14. The 2025 results resolve the source’s sublinear threshold, and the 2026 theorem improves the deterministic exponent. The selected polylogarithmic target is expressly asked in the source and is not established by these results. A bounded later-work search found no matching general adaptive polylogarithmic algorithm or impossibility theorem. The 2026 reference records the checked manuscript and its stated STOC venue rather than claiming a separately checked proceedings version.
progress: 2022-11: The workshop asks for sublinear and then polylogarithmic update time in the deterministic or adaptive-adversary setting. | 2025: The first sublinear adaptive and deterministic amortized bounds are obtained by Bernstein, Bhattacharya, Kiss and Saranurak, as recorded in the checked 2026 introduction. | 2026-05-01: The Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song manuscript states a deterministic \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) amortized bound in Theorem 1.1.
working_summary: A graph changes through edge insertions and deletions while an explicit maximal matching must remain available. The next change may depend on the matching the algorithm has just produced. The question asks for an always-correct algorithm with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against this adaptive feedback. Deterministic algorithms now achieve a square-root-scale amortized bound, resolving the older sublinear threshold. The much stronger polylogarithmic target remains distinct from constant-time results for update sequences fixed independently of the algorithm.

title: Dynamic spanning trees with polylogarithmic average stretch
importance_reason: Dynamically maintaining low-stretch spanning trees would provide a reusable primitive for graph optimization and numerical methods.
formal:
Is there a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains a spanning forest \(F_t\) of an unweighted simple graph \(G_t\) with polylogarithmic expected average stretch and sublinear expected amortized update time? Precisely, do there exist such an algorithm, constants \(C,a,c>0\), and a function \(u:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{u(n)}n=0,\]
such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every finite oblivious sequence of \(T\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty \(n\)-vertex graph,
\[\mathbb E[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)]\le C(\log_2(n+2))^c\quad(0\le t\le T),\]
and the expected total work for the updates is at most \(T u(n)\), after at most \(C n^a\) expected initialization work? The maintained object must always be an actual spanning forest using current graph edges.

For a connected graph, a spanning forest is a spanning tree. The componentwise convention below makes the target meaningful when a deletion disconnects the graph, as in the original dynamic low-stretch algorithm. This card chooses the first question in the workshop source, with the expectation and amortization conventions of that prior work; it does not also require resistance to adaptive updates.
definitions:
The graph \(G_t=([n],E_t)\) is finite, undirected, loopless and simple, with unit edge lengths. Its vertex set remains fixed. An insertion specifies an absent edge between two distinct labels, and a deletion specifies a present edge. No maximum-degree or sparsity promise is imposed, and components may split or merge. A valid spanning forest \(F_t=([n],E_t^F)\) has \(E_t^F\subseteq E_t\), is acyclic, and connects every pair of vertices that lie in the same connected component of \(G_t\). Thus it contains one spanning tree for each nontrivial component and all isolated vertices.

For \(\{v,w\}\in E_t\), let \(d_{F_t}(v,w)\) be the number of edges on the unique path between its endpoints in \(F_t\). Put
\[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)=\begin{cases}|E_t|^{-1}\displaystyle\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E_t}d_{F_t}(v,w),&|E_t|>0,\\0,&|E_t|=0.\end{cases}\]
All current edges participate in the average, including forest edges, whose distance is one. The target bounds this absolute stretch quantity, not its ratio to the best possible forest. The expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness at each fixed time, after averaging over the graph edges; a bound for every individual edge is not required.

The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is revealed one operation at a time. The algorithm is not given future updates. Its guarantee covers every finite sequence length, and hence every finite prefix of any fixed infinite valid sequence. The same constants and function \(u\) work for all graphs, edge counts, times and sequences.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed constant \(c_w\) large enough to address the algorithm's polynomially many persistent words. Unit-cost operations are word reads/writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, and independent uniform random words. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\); no input-dependent advice or uncharged precomputed table is allowed. Initialization starts with no graph edges and is charged separately as specified.

The forest is maintained explicitly as its edge set: a linked list or equivalent enumerable collection of its current edge records is stored, and each current graph edge record indicates whether it belongs to the forest. Given an existing edge-record handle, this flag is readable in constant time, and all forest edges can be enumerated in time proportional to their number plus one. Finding graph-edge records from endpoint labels, changing forest membership, random choices, rebuilds and memory management are included in update work. No full forest printout or rooted-parent array is required after every update.

Every completed update must produce a valid spanning forest, and each finite execution must terminate with probability one. Only the quality and runtime guarantees are in expectation. Amortized expected time bounds the sum of update costs; it imposes no worst-case per-update bound. The source's word 'sublinear' is made precise as \(o(n)\), without additionally requiring a fixed polynomial saving \(n^{1-\delta}\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence under the stated model. A positive result must simultaneously achieve the expected polylogarithmic average-stretch bound and an expected amortized update bound \(u(n)=o(n)\) on all valid fully dynamic graph sequences. A spanning forest with only \(n^{o(1)}\) stretch, a decremental-only algorithm, or a bound on an unrelated tree metric does not meet the target. The maintained forest must consist of graph edges; introducing auxiliary weighted tree edges or Steiner vertices is not allowed. A negative answer must apply to the stated randomized expected guarantees, not only to deterministic or worst-case variants.
context:
The workshop source records static spanning trees of average stretch \(O(\log n\log\log n)\), and dynamic algorithms with subpolynomial stretch and update time. Its first open question asks to improve the stretch guarantee to a polylogarithm while keeping updates sublinear.

Forster and Goranci formulate the dynamic object as a spanning forest and analyze expected average stretch against an oblivious adversary. Their Corollary 1.2 gives \(n^{o(1)}\) expected average stretch and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) expected amortized update time.

The workshop reports Chechik–Zhang’s SODA 2020 improvement to \(n^{o(1)}\) expected amortized update time while retaining subpolynomial average stretch.

A subpolynomial function grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of its argument, but need not be bounded by a fixed power of its logarithm. Consequently, the recorded subpolynomial-stretch algorithms do not automatically meet the polylogarithmic quality target.

Forster, Goranci and Henzinger obtain dynamic probabilistic metric-tree embeddings with polylogarithmic expected stretch at suitable update-time tradeoffs. Such an embedding may use a tree that is not a subgraph of the changing graph. Their introduction explicitly distinguishes this result from maintaining low-average-stretch spanning trees.

The source separately asks for algorithms tolerating adaptive adversaries. That requirement is not combined with the first question here: the requested improvement already concerns sequences chosen independently of the random choices.
why: Low-stretch spanning trees replace a graph by a particularly simple subgraph while controlling average detours. They underpin graph optimization and linear-system algorithms. The question asks whether a polylogarithmic quality guarantee can survive repeated edge changes without spending a linear amount of work per update; it isolates the cost of requiring the approximation to remain a genuine subgraph.
status_note: The November 2022 Section 4.3, Forster–Goranci’s full author manuscript (Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2), and Forster–Goranci–Henzinger arXiv:2004.10319v2 introduction were read on 2026-09-14. The Chechik–Zhang 2020 bound is recorded through the checked workshop report rather than a claimed full reading of that paper. A bounded later-work search through this review date found no matching all-graph fully dynamic spanning-forest result with the selected quality and update bounds. Related probabilistic tree embeddings and dynamic spanners do not meet the subgraph-forest requirement. Status remains source-open with these limits.
progress: 2019: Forster and Goranci establish fully dynamic spanning forests with subpolynomial expected average stretch and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) expected amortized update time. | 2020: Chechik and Zhang improve the update time to \(n^{o(1)}\) while retaining subpolynomial stretch, as reported in the checked workshop source. | 2021: Dynamic probabilistic tree embeddings achieve additional quality/time tradeoffs for a different maintained object. | 2022-11: The workshop explicitly asks for polylogarithmic average stretch with sublinear fully dynamic updates.
working_summary: A changing unweighted graph must retain a spanning tree in each connected component. The quality measure is the average tree-path length between the endpoints of graph edges. The question asks for polylogarithmic expected quality with sublinear expected amortized work per edge insertion or deletion. The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s randomness, and disconnected intermediate graphs are covered. Existing subpolynomial-stretch forests and polylogarithmic-stretch metric embeddings leave different parts of this target unresolved.

title: Dynamic edge coloring with sublinear additive slack
importance_reason: Dynamic edge or vertex coloring tests how efficiently structural graph guarantees can survive updates.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic edge-coloring algorithm and fixed constants \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(C\ge1\), and \(a,b\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge2\), every fixed degree bound \(1\le\Delta\le n-1\), and every valid oblivious sequence of edge insertions and deletions, it explicitly maintains a proper coloring with at most
\[K(n,\Delta)=\Delta+\left\lceil C\Delta^{1-\gamma}(\log_2(n+2))^a\right\rceil\]
colors in expected amortized update time at most \(C(\log_2(n+2))^b\)? The algorithm must always return a valid coloring. The bound must hold uniformly in both \(n\) and \(\Delta\), with the same constants, not only at each fixed \(\Delta\).

This is the update-time question in the workshop report, with the polylogarithmic factors and probability/cost convention made explicit. The author's separate, weaker recourse-only question is context rather than the main target.
definitions:
The graph is undirected, simple and unweighted, on a fixed vertex set \([n]\), and starts without edges. Every insertion adds a currently absent edge between distinct vertices, and every deletion removes a currently present edge. The sequence may contain both operations in arbitrary order, always respecting maximum degree at most the input bound \(\Delta\). This is a fixed upper bound for the whole sequence, rather than the current degree recomputed after each update. Disconnected graphs are allowed; no sparsity or bipartiteness promise is imposed.

A proper edge coloring is a map \(\chi:E\to[K(n,\Delta)]\) in which distinct incident edges have distinct colors. The palette consists of fixed integer labels throughout the execution. Explicit maintenance requires storing the current integer color with every existing edge; each change to such a stored label is charged. Given a handle to an existing edge record, its color is available in constant time. Updates use endpoint labels, and locating or creating the record is part of their cost. The algorithm need not print all edge colors after each update.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed algorithm-dependent constant \(c_w\), large enough for its polynomial space addresses and color labels. Charge one step for a word read/write, comparison, branch, Boolean operation, shift, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, or independent uniform random word. Only polynomially many persistent words are allowed, with one fixed exponent independent of the update horizon. The algorithm has a single finite program for all \(n,\Delta\); there is no uncharged input-dependent advice or table.

Initialization on the empty graph takes at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^b\) expected time. For every finite valid update sequence of length \(T\), the expected sum of all update work must be at most \(C T(\log_2(n+2))^b\). This includes writing colors, recolorings, lookup, memory management and any rebuilds. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is not revealed in advance. It may be arbitrarily long. Expectations are over the internal randomness; the constants are independent of \(n,\Delta,T\) and the sequence. Larger constants may absorb finite exceptional small instances.

Always-correct randomized behavior means that every completed update gives a proper coloring in the stated palette, and every finite valid execution terminates with probability one. No failure probability for an invalid coloring is allowed. Amortization permits expensive individual updates subject to every-prefix expected total bounds. Deterministic algorithms also qualify. The recourse is the number of existing edges whose colors change while processing an update; it is a lower bound on explicit update work, but bounding recourse does not bound the computation needed to select those changes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of such an algorithm and fixed constants. Any fixed positive \(\gamma<1\) suffices for a positive answer; an exponent that tends to zero with \(n\) does not. The time bound must be independent of polynomial factors in \(\Delta\), and every permitted graph and degree scale must be covered. A guarantee only on the number of recolorings, only on forests or bounded-arboricity graphs, or only for constant maximum degree is insufficient. A lower bound for repairing one adversarially prescribed starting coloring alone is insufficient to rule out an algorithm that controls the colorings it maintains.
context:
The workshop report asks for a power saving in the additive number of colors together with polylogarithmic update time. The constants in the displayed target spell out its two suppressed polylogarithmic factors.

Costa’s expanded note explicitly separates recoloring cost from computation and says that even its recourse-only version is open against an oblivious adversary with amortization. This card retains the report’s stronger total-update-work target while choosing that permissive adversary and amortization setting.

Known algorithms use \((1+\varepsilon)\Delta\) colors with update bounds polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), up to polylogarithmic factors. Substituting an inverse-polynomial-in-degree relative slack can therefore introduce a polynomial degree dependence in time, which the target forbids.

The May 2026 Sadeh–Kaplan revision gives recourse improvements for large palettes and for graphs of low arboricity, where arboricity is the minimum number of forests covering all edges. Those restrictions and the distinction between recourse and running time remain essential; they do not establish the all-graph update-time target.

The SODA 2026 deterministic algorithm uses a relative-error palette and achieves subpolynomial update time in its stated accuracy range. Subpolynomial time is a larger class of bounds than polylogarithmic time, so this result does not itself provide the required guarantee.
why: The question asks whether a changing graph can stay close to the optimal edge-color bound while each update costs only a polylogarithm. Its central issue is the joint dependence on graph size and degree: bounds that are fast for fixed relative error can become slow when the allowed extra colors shrink by a power of the degree. A resolution would sharpen the resource tradeoff for dynamic conflict-free scheduling represented by edge coloring.
status_note: The November 2024 report, Costa’s undated expanded primary note, Sadeh–Kaplan arXiv:2602.09497v2 (Theorems 2.5 and 2.8 and Section 3), and the publisher abstract for Christiansen’s SODA 2026 paper were checked on 2026-09-14. The recourse results retain restrictions on the palette or arboricity, and the deterministic result has a subpolynomial update bound rather than the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. A bounded search through the review date located no matching all-graph resolution. Source-open status records these verification limits, not an independent proof check of every cited result.
progress: 2024-11: Costa poses the additive-slack, polylogarithmic-update-time question at the workshop. | 2026: Christiansen’s SODA paper gives deterministic relative-approximation coloring in subpolynomial update time in its stated accuracy range. | 2026-05-10: Sadeh and Kaplan revise their recourse results for large palettes and low-arboricity graphs; total update time remains a separate issue.
working_summary: A changing graph must keep a proper integer color on every edge. The target allows only a power-sublinear additive number of colors above the maximum-degree bound, up to logarithmic factors. One uniform algorithm should maintain that coloring in polylogarithmic expected amortized time over all degree scales. The question remains meaningful even when updates are chosen independently of the algorithm’s randomness. Small recoloring counts and recent restricted-graph or subpolynomial-time results do not by themselves meet the stated total-work guarantee.

title: Low-loss deterministic reduction from weighted to unweighted dynamic matching
importance_reason: A general weighted-to-unweighted matching reduction could transfer dynamic improvements across broad matching variants.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic black-box transformation that converts every explicit fully dynamic \(\alpha\)-approximate maximum-cardinality matching algorithm into a fully dynamic \(\alpha(1-1/q)\)-approximate maximum-weight matching algorithm on general graphs, for every fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and integer \(q\ge2\), with only an accuracy-dependent polylogarithmic overhead in update time and with preservation of worst-case as well as amortized bounds?

The precise overhead and interfaces are specified below. The transformation must work at the original approximation ratio \(\alpha\); it may not demand a stronger unweighted algorithm with approximation approaching one as \(q\) grows. This card selects the deterministic, fully dynamic version of the source’s broader feature-preserving conversion question. Randomized and partially dynamic extensions are not part of this chosen statement.
definitions:
All graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and simple. A matching is a set of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints. For an unweighted graph \(H\), let \(\nu(H)\) be the maximum number of edges in a matching. An \(\alpha\)-approximation returns a matching \(M\) with \(|M|\ge\alpha\nu(H)\). For a positively weighted graph \(G\), let \(\operatorname{OPT}_w(G)=\max_M\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). The weighted output must satisfy
\[\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\ge\alpha(1-1/q)\operatorname{OPT}_w(G).\]
The empty graph has optimum zero.

Both problems start with an empty graph on a fixed labelled vertex set. Updates insert an absent edge or delete a present edge, in any order. Weighted insertions additionally specify an integer weight in \([W]\), for a supplied integer \(W\ge1\). A weight change can be expressed as deletion followed by insertion. No bipartiteness or sparsity promise is imposed. Updates are revealed sequentially and may depend on earlier outputs, since the chosen algorithms are deterministic. Weights, vertex labels, \(W\) and \(q\) are represented in binary.

The input subroutine \(A\) has a uniform finite program, initializes an empty unweighted graph, and supports edge insertion and deletion. It stores an explicit current matching: a mate lookup is constant-time and its edge list can be enumerated in time proportional to its length plus one. Each update supplies the list of matching edges inserted or removed during that update, and the cost of producing that list is included in \(A\)'s update time. Thus changes of output are charged, as required by the recourse condition in the 2021 source. The transformation can create independent instances of \(A\), call their operations and inspect their reported matchings; it cannot inspect their implementation or hidden state. Only their \(\alpha\)-approximation promise may be used, so the guarantee must survive every valid choice of approximate matching by the subroutine. The transformed algorithm also maintains its weighted matching explicitly and charges every output change.

Here is the required overhead. There must be one transformation, one total computable function \(F:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and one fixed exponent \(b\ge0\), independent of \(\alpha\) and \(A\). For a weighted sequence on \(n\ge2\) vertices with at most \(m\) edges present at any time, put
\[N=\lceil F(q)n\rceil,\quad D=\min\{\binom{N}{2},\lceil F(q)(m+n)\rceil\},\quad L=F(q)(1+\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(W+1))^b.\]
Let \(I_A(N)\ge N\) be any nondecreasing upper bound on empty-graph initialization time of \(A\). Let \(U_A(N,D)\ge1\) be any upper bound, nondecreasing in both arguments, on its update time for sequences with at most \(N\) vertices and \(D\) edges. The weighted algorithm must initialize within \(L(I_A(N)+n)\) operations and have update bound
\[L\bigl(U_A(N,D)+1\bigr).\]
If \(U_A\) is a worst-case per-update bound, this must be a worst-case weighted bound. If it is only an amortized bound, every weighted prefix of \(T\) updates must cost at most \(TL(U_A(N,D)+1)\), excluding the separately charged initialization. These are implications for each applicable bound, not a requirement to turn an amortized input guarantee into a worst-case output guarantee. Multiplicative constants may be absorbed into \(F\). No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is required: it is an accuracy parameter, and the source’s bipartite blueprint already allows a larger dependence.

Use a word-RAM with \(\Theta(\log_2(nWF(q)+2))\)-bit words, with a fixed sufficiently large constant multiplier. Word memory accesses, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication and quotient/remainder by a nonzero word have unit cost. Both subroutine calls and all surrounding work are charged; the subroutine is evaluated in the same word model. The transformation may use at most \(\lceil L\rceil\) simultaneous instances, each on at most \(N\) vertices and \(D\) edges, and auxiliary memory bounded by \(F(q)(n+\log_2(W+1)+2)^d\) words for one fixed exponent \(d\). Its state has no uncharged graph-dependent advice. The bound is uniform over every finite update sequence and over the given \(W\); using unit-weight graphs as oracle instances does not give their answers for free.

The explicit overhead formalizes an accuracy-dependent enlargement of the auxiliary graph and a polylogarithmic factor in size and weight range. Allowing \(m+n\) in the edge bound accommodates auxiliary vertices and edges; it does not promise exact preservation of sparse graph size. These bookkeeping choices and the deterministic restriction are editorial specifications of the source’s requested type of transformation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this uniform transformation and overhead parameters. A positive proof must cover every admissible approximation factor and subroutine, preserve its deterministic correctness, and establish the stated transfer of both kinds of time guarantee when applicable. A result requiring \(\alpha\) to approach one with \(q\), a constant multiplicative loss bounded away from one, or a conversion only for bipartite weighted graphs is insufficient. A weighted algorithm unrelated to the supplied subroutine does not establish the black-box theorem merely because it is polynomial-time. Failure of one particular transformation is not a refutation of the existence claim.
context:
The source asks for a general-graph analogue of the bipartite reduction, with little loss in approximation and update complexity. Its broader discussion also includes randomized and partially dynamic settings. This card isolates the deterministic fully dynamic feature-preserving statement and records its explicit interface and overhead.

Theorem 3.1 of Bernstein–Dudeja–Langley gives the desired \(\alpha\mapsto(1-\varepsilon)\alpha\) conversion on bipartite graphs, with accuracy-dependent graph enlargement and logarithmic weight-range dependence. Remark 3.2 explains why explicit matching output provides the recourse bound required by the conversion.

Bernstein and Chen’s SODA 2026 result gives a low-loss conversion for general weighted graphs when the unweighted algorithm already has approximation \(1-\varepsilon_0\), where \(\varepsilon_0\) must be polynomially smaller than the desired error. Theorem 6.5 is randomized and amortized.

The later paper’s limitations discussion explicitly says that its result cannot transfer arbitrary fixed approximation ratios with small loss, and retains that more general conversion as the desired goal. Thus its title and near-optimal result do not resolve the all-ratio deterministic statement selected here.
why: A low-loss conversion would transfer a broad range of dynamic matching improvements from counting matched edges to optimizing their weights. The central unresolved scope includes algorithms with fixed approximation ratios such as one half or two thirds, not only near-optimal algorithms. Preserving determinism and time guarantees would make the conversion useful across existing algorithmic tradeoffs without redesigning each algorithm.

An input algorithm with approximation ratio alpha should yield one with ratio alpha times one minus the chosen accuracy. The selected variant preserves determinism and transfers both worst-case and amortized update guarantees when the input algorithm provides them. The overhead may depend on accuracy but should be only polylogarithmic in graph size and weight range, apart from the stated auxiliary graph enlargement. A recent general-graph conversion works for near-optimal input algorithms, leaving the arbitrary-ratio target unresolved.

title: Logarithmic fully dynamic planar nearest neighbors
importance_reason: A logarithmic fully dynamic structure would establish the natural two-dimensional counterpart of a basic ordered-search interface.
formal: Does a uniform Las Vegas data structure maintain a finite set of planar points under insertions and deletions, answer exact Euclidean nearest-neighbor queries in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time, and support updates in expected amortized \(O(\log(n+2))\) time, using \(O((n+1)\log^c(n+2))\) space for some fixed constant \(c\)?
definitions: The structure initializes the empty set in constant time and space. An insertion supplies a real point not currently present and returns a stable handle. A deletion supplies the handle of a present point. A query supplies \(q\in\mathbb R^2\) and returns any present \(p\) minimizing \((p_x-q_x)^2+(p_y-q_y)^2\), or an empty marker. Ties may be resolved arbitrarily but correctly. At any instant \(n\) is the number of stored points. Use an algebraic real RAM with exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparisons, each at unit cost. A point coordinate, scalar, pointer or fixed-size record field occupies one cell. Reading, writing and following pointers cost one step; no floor, bit extraction from reals, or packing unbounded discrete information into a real is an available operation. The program is uniform and finite; there is no advice or free table construction. Each independently generated fair random bit costs one operation; sampling an arbitrary exact real number is not a primitive. All answers are exact on every terminating execution and the structure terminates almost surely. For every fixed finite legal operation sequence chosen independently of its random bits, with \(u\) updates and maximum set size \(M\), the expected total update time is \(O(u\log(M+2))\); each query separately has worst-case \(O(\log(n+2))\) time on every execution. Space holds on every execution, including retained points and temporary work. All constants are universal. This states the amortization convention using the maximum size of the sequence, without an adaptive-adversary guarantee. The space exponent \(c\) may be any fixed nonnegative integer. All logarithms are base two. The sequence and its real coordinates may depend on the program but are fixed before its random bits are sampled; the bounds impose no adaptive-adversary guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single uniform Las Vegas representation and constants satisfying all stated guarantees: exact answers, worst-case logarithmic query time, expected total update time \(O(u\log(M+2))\) for every oblivious finite sequence, and \(O((n+1)\log^c(n+2))\) space on every execution. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such representation and constants exist in the specified model. An insertion-only structure, approximate answers or a time bound retaining an unbounded extra logarithmic factor does not meet the full target.
context:
A nearest-neighbor query asks for an actual stored point minimizing Euclidean distance to the query. On a line, ordered search can inspect the predecessor and successor. In the plane, closeness depends on two coordinates together, and a nearby point in one coordinate can be far away in the other.

Deletion is a substantive operation. Removing the previously closest point can expose a different answer at many query locations, while the data structure must still answer whichever query arrives next. The target retains every allowed insertion and deletion sequence instead of assuming that the stored point set only grows.

The 2025 incremental result achieves \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertion time for fixed positive \(\eta\). Its query bound meets this target, but its insertion bound still has a growing factor over logarithmic time and the incremental interface does not include arbitrary deletions.

Randomness is permitted to affect work, not geometric correctness: every returned point must really minimize the squared distance, with any exact minimizer acceptable in a tie. Updates are bounded in expected total time over each fixed sequence, whereas a query must meet its time bound on every execution. These are separate promises.

The original source asks for logarithmic costs in the fully dynamic planar problem. The retained benchmark states an explicit Las Vegas variant with expected amortized updates, worst-case queries and near-linear space. Its real-arithmetic cost model does not claim a logarithmic bit complexity for arbitrary real coordinates.

Approximate-neighbor libraries, empirical query throughput and high-dimensional vector indexes address related applications but do not imply this exact two-dimensional worst-case interface. The space guarantee also counts temporary work and must hold for the current number of points.
why: A logarithmic fully dynamic structure would establish the natural two-dimensional counterpart of a basic ordered-search interface.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2025 incremental theorem has optimal logarithmic queries but a growing insertion overhead and no general deletion interface. A bounded later-work search did not locate a result meeting this explicit fully dynamic Las Vegas variant. Approximate high-dimensional indexing results do not meet its exact planar model; source proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2025-04-10: Iacono–Nekrich give \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertions for fixed \(\eta>0\) in an incremental structure.
working_summary: The structure maintains points in the Euclidean plane. Queries ask for an exact nearest stored point. Points can both enter and leave the set. Queries must be worst-case logarithmic and updates logarithmic in expected amortized cost. The recent incremental result does not meet the full dynamic target.

title: DynFO maintenance of red-predecessor parity
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A small canonical obstruction to understanding the dynamic expressive power of first-order logic with counting. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a DynFO program that maintains the Boolean query |\(\{y\in D:\exists x\in D (R(x)\land E(x,y))\}|\equiv 1\) mod 2 under arbitrary single-tuple insertions and deletions in a directed edge relation \(E\subseteq D^{2}\) and a red-vertex relation \(R\subseteq D\)? Use one fixed finite auxiliary relational vocabulary and fixed first-order update formulas for every finite domain D. All input and auxiliary relations are empty initially, and there are no built-in order or arithmetic relations. The program must be correct after every finite sequence of updates, with no bound on the length of that sequence.
definitions: The domain D is a fixed finite set throughout a run; updates do not create or delete vertices. An element y is covered when at least one red predecessor x has an arc \(x\to y\). A covered vertex is counted once, regardless of how many red predecessors it has, and it need not itself be red. E is a binary relation, so loops are allowed; R is unary. The four update types are \(ins_{E}(u,v), del_{E}(u,v), ins_{R}(u)\), and \(del_{R}(u)\). Insertions of present tuples and deletions of absent tuples leave the input relation unchanged and are also allowed. A program chooses finitely many auxiliary relation symbols S, each of a fixed finite arity, including a distinguished zero-ary answer bit Ans. For each S and update type \(\delta\) it supplies a first-order formula \(\varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{p\};\bar\{z\})\), where p̄ are the changed tuple’s parameters and z̄ has the arity of S. The formula may use equality, the current input and auxiliary relations, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual domain elements. It has no parity/counting quantifier, quantification over sets, function symbol or built-in numeric relation. After update \(\delta (\bar\{a\})\), each auxiliary relation becomes \(\{\bar\{b\}:(I,A)\models \varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{a\};\bar\{b\})\}\), evaluated on the old input I and old auxiliary state A. All auxiliary updates occur simultaneously, alongside the specified input change. Empty initialization makes Ans false, correctly answering the empty covered set. The program’s formulas and arities are independent of |D| and of the update history. The number and arities of auxiliary relations are unrestricted finite constants chosen by the program; thus it may use polynomially many auxiliary bits, with its own fixed polynomial exponent. DynFO measures expressibility of these updates, rather than sequential constant-time execution of a formula on a Turing machine.
answer_criterion: A positive answer is a finite collection of first-order update formulas and a proof of correctness from empty initialization for every finite domain and every finite update sequence. A negative answer must show that every such program, allowing arbitrary fixed auxiliary arities, fails on some domain and sequence. A lower bound only for quantifier-free formulas or a fixed arity, a program requiring unrestricted initial advice, or an algorithm for a bounded-degree variant does not settle the stated DynFO question.
context:
Parity of a directly stored unary set can be maintained by tracking individual membership changes. Here a red-vertex update can change the coverage of many successors, while overlapping red neighborhoods mean that not every incident successor actually changes status. The queried parity concerns covered vertices, not the number of red vertices or red incident edges.

The paper proves that ParityExists cannot be maintained with quantifier-free first-order update rules, even with stronger initialization allowances. Its open question permits full first-order quantification and auxiliary relations of any fixed finite arity, so that lower bound is insufficient.

The source studies the variant counting only covered vertices whose indegree is at most a threshold. It proves DynFO results when the threshold grows logarithmically, with the stated built-in order/BIT conventions and an active-domain version without them. This is a filtered counting query, not a solution of unrestricted ParityExists.

The query has the form of a parity quantifier outside an existential quantifier. Understanding it is a basic obstacle to classifying which queries from first-order logic with parity can be maintained by ordinary first-order updates. Solving this one query alone is not asserted to settle that broader inclusion.
why: Would clarify whether first-order dynamic maintenance can express a basic combination of existential coverage and parity counting, beyond the already understood parity of a directly stored set.
status_note: Checked the complete conference model and query orientation, the 2021 journal definitions and conclusion, and subsequent searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution was identified. The card states the standard empty-initialization model, keeping arbitrary-initialization lower bounds and built-in-relation variants separate.
progress: 2020: The conference paper proves a quantifier-free lower bound and degree-filtered upper bounds, leaving the full DynFO question open. | 2021-11-16: The expanded journal version retains the exact DynFO question in its conclusion and elaborates the initialization and degree-filtered results.
working_summary: A vertex is covered if some red vertex has a directed edge into it. After each edge or color insertion or deletion, the program must report whether the number of covered vertices is odd. The question permits fixed first-order update formulas and polynomially many auxiliary bits, starting with empty relations. Quantifier-free updates are insufficient, while degree-filtered versions have positive first-order results. The unrestricted query remains open in the expanded source and tests the ability of dynamic first-order logic to handle counting beyond direct-set parity.

title: Subquadratic exact fully dynamic weighted single-source distances
importance_reason: A fundamental reuse-of-computation question for changing networks, whose precise remaining significance depends on accuracy, weights, density and query guarantees. Existing score retained.
formal: Do a constant \(\delta>0\) and a deterministic data structure exist that maintain exact distances from one fixed source in every fully dynamic undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with positive integer edge weights at most \(n^3\), using polynomial preprocessing and space, \(O(n^{2-\delta})\) worst-case update time and \(O(1)\) worst-case time per distance query in the word-RAM model below?
question_excerpt: That is, we do not know how to do better than reconstructing from scratch after every edge update.
definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\), with \(n\ge2\), and the source \(s\in[n]\) is fixed at initialization. Graphs are simple and undirected. Every present edge has an integer weight in \(\{1,\ldots,n^3\}\). An update inserts an absent edge with its weight, deletes a present edge, or changes the weight of a present edge. A query supplies \(v\in[n]\) and must return exactly the minimum sum of edge weights along an \(s\)-to-\(v\) path in the current graph, or a special infinity symbol if no path exists; the distance to \(s\) is zero. Each operation must finish before the next is supplied. The sequence may be arbitrarily long and chosen using all previous outputs; the data structure receives no future operations. It must work at every density. The subquadratic bound is in the vertex count, so it expresses a saving over rebuilding for dense graphs, not a promised saving relative to the edge count of every sparse graph. The uniform machine is a word-RAM with word length \(w=c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for one fixed integer \(c\ge5\) chosen with the algorithm. Unit-cost instructions are indirect read/write of an addressed word, comparison, branching, unsigned addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), bitwise Boolean operations, shifts by fewer than \(w\) places, and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple words and charged operations. Initial input is an explicit adjacency/weight table. For fixed constants \(K,C\), initialization takes at most \(Cn^K\) operations and at most \(Cn^K\) words are stored at any time, with addresses fitting the word length. Each individual update takes at most \(Cn^{2-\delta}\) operations and each query at most \(C\), after enlarging constants for small \(n\). The program, constants and \(\delta\) are independent of \(n\), weights and the operation sequence. The machine has no randomization, nonuniform advice or unit-cost unbounded-precision arithmetic. A path certificate is not required.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof constructing the specified exact data structure with all worst-case bounds, or a Lean proof that none exists. A conditional lower bound is relevant context but does not establish unconditional nonexistence. Approximate distances, an unweighted-only result, amortized updates or nonconstant single-distance queries would change the selected target.
context:
The 2017 introduction asks about fully dynamic single-source distances beyond rebuilding, without choosing one complete resource and accuracy profile.

The authorized variant selects exact polynomially bounded integer weights, deterministic worst-case updates and constant-time distance queries. Later approximate and unweighted improvements are retained as progress rather than repeated as unresolved tasks.

The 2023 paper distinguishes its unweighted algorithm from the weighted setting, where it cites a conditional barrier to subquadratic updates. This card asks the unconditional existence question in its explicitly fixed model.
why: Dynamic shortest paths asks how much computation can be reused as a network changes. Separating update cost, query cost, approximation and graph density is essential to deciding whether a data structure meaningfully improves on a static computation.
status_note: The 2017 blanket rebuilding remark is obsolete for several variants. This user-authorized exact weighted variant was specified on 13 September 2026; the checked later sources separate it from approximate and unweighted results. Their conditional barriers are not an unconditional resolution, and no exact new theorem for the selected model was identified in the bounded search.
progress: 2017: The original introduction gives rebuilding as the general fully dynamic baseline. | 2019: The later approximate-distance result beats that baseline in weighted dense settings, but does not maintain the exact distances selected here. | 2023: The later paper gives an exact unweighted fully dynamic result and explicitly distinguishes polynomially weighted graphs and their conditional hardness.
working_summary: The data structure maintains exact distances from a fixed source while weighted edges are inserted, removed or changed. Every individual distance query must take constant time. The selected target is a fixed polynomial saving below quadratic worst-case update time in the vertex count. Weights are positive integers of explicitly bounded size and all computation is charged on a specified word-RAM. Known approximate and unweighted improvements do not settle this exact weighted variant.

title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
importance_reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.
focus_reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.
formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta \in (0,1)\), determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty , N_{\delta}(n)\): the least number of independent deletion traces that permit exact reconstruction of every unknown n-bit string with success probability at least \(2/3\), with no processing-time bound.
definitions: For \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}, a\) deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability \(1- \delta\) and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let \(\mu _{x,\delta}\) be its probability distribution on ⋃_\(\{k=0\}^{n}\{0,1\}^{k}\). Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given \(n, \delta\) and m independent samples from \(\mu _{x,\delta}\); it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and \(\delta\) must succeed for every x with probability at least \(2/3\) over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let \(N_{\delta}(n)\) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The requested asymptotic constants may depend on \(\delta\), but not on n or x. The value is finite because a trace of length n reveals the entire string, and this event has positive probability \((1- \delta )^{n}\). The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f_{\delta}(n)\) and, for every fixed \(\delta \in (0,1)\), constants \(0<c_{\delta}\le C_{\delta}<\infty\) such that \(c_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\le N_{\delta}(n)\le C_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\) for all \(n\ge 2\), allowing finitely many small n to be absorbed into the constants. Prove both the reconstruction guarantee and the worst-case information-theoretic lower bound in Lean. The dependence on n must be determined within constant factors; deciding only whether a polynomial number of traces suffices does not necessarily determine it.
context:
The target is the sample-complexity function, including its growth if it is polynomial. The older polynomial-sample question is one qualitative consequence of a determination, rather than the entire target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability \((1- \delta )^{n} a\) trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of \(\Omega (n^{3/2}/\log ^{7} n)\) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by \(\exp (p^{- 7/3}(\log _{2} n)^{c})\) for an absolute constant c, where \(p=1- \delta\). The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since this card imposes no processing-time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.
why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?
status_note: The July 2026 quasipolynomial sample theorem supersedes the saved 2025 general upper frontier but does not give polynomially many traces. The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.
