title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
importance_reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.
focus_reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.
formal: Do absolute constants \(C\ge 1, K>0\) and \(d\ge 0\) and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying \(ED(x,y)\le D\le C\cdot ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) in at most \(Kn(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}\) time?
definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of \(n\ge 1\) and two explicitly stored arrays \(x,y\in \{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}^{n}\). This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in \(O(\log  n)\) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When \(x=y\), success requires \(D=0\). When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as \(n^{0.9}\) can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor \(2^{\widetilde{O} (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive \(n^{1- \zeta}\) term in the general guarantee. The exponent \(\zeta\) and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), an \(O(n^{1+\varepsilon})\)-time randomized algorithm with approximation \(f(1/\varepsilon )\). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed \(\varepsilon =0.01\) gives a fixed approximation factor, but \(n^{0.01}\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter \(\eta >0\), it gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)}n}\) time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) permits a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) time for some fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’\(s O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.
why: Determines whether a universal constant loss in accuracy makes the basic string-alignment metric computable with only polylogarithmic overhead beyond input reading.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\)-time, fixed-constant approximation for all input pairs was found in the checked primary sources. The August 2026 journal publication gives \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) time, and the STOC 2026 approximation scheme targets a different runtime–accuracy regime.

working_summary: Edit distance counts the cheapest sequence of insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one string into another. The reviewed question asks for a randomized universal constant-factor approximation in near-linear time. Insertions can shift many positions, making direct coordinate comparisons misleading even when edit distance is tiny. The target would estimate global alignment cost without constructing the full quadratic dynamic-programming table. The guarantee is purely multiplicative, so identical strings must yield zero and nearby strings cannot be hidden behind a large additive error.

title: Almost-linear-time \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
importance_reason: A central accuracy–runtime frontier for sequence comparison, with recent work on each side of the tradeoff. It is a genuinely stronger near-exact runtime target than TCS-7220, retained under the user’s explicit acceptance of related edit-distance questions.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length \(n\ge 2\), outputs an integer D with \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using worst-case time \(n^{1+o(1)}\)?
definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with \(w=B_{\varepsilon}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer \(B_{\varepsilon}\); unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) there is one algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\), and for every rational \(\eta >0\) there are constants \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta},N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) such that every execution on every pair of total length \(n\ge N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) uses at most \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta} n^{1+\eta}\) operations. \(A_{\varepsilon}\) halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\); the algorithm may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but not on \(\eta\). All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) or effective procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) from \(\varepsilon\) is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its \(n^{1+o(1)}\) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy \(\varepsilon\), one algorithm must meet \(n^{1+\eta}\) bounds for every fixed \(\eta >0\) once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each \(\eta\), with uncontrolled dependence on \(\eta\), is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for each fixed \(\eta\). Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.
why: Determine whether worst-case sequence alignment can simultaneously achieve arbitrarily small fixed relative error and a time exponent approaching one.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No algorithm meeting the combined arbitrary fixed relative accuracy and \(n^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time target was found. Neither the 2026 scheme nor a family with fixed runtime slack is silently upgraded to that target.
progress: 2020–2022: Andoni–Nosatzki establish constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for every fixed \(\eta >0\). | 2026-03-31: Mao–Rubinstein give approximation schemes in quasi-strongly subquadratic time; this is not a near-linear bound.

title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
importance_reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), do there exist constants \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\in (0,1), K_{\varepsilon}>0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair of length-n strings \(x,y, A_{\varepsilon}\) runs in at most \(K_{\varepsilon}(n+2)^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time and outputs an integer D satisfying \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\)? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy \(O(\log  n)\) bits. Use a word RAM with word length \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common positive saving for all \(\varepsilon\), or efficient procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) is required. Rational \(\varepsilon\) suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in \(O(n^{2- \delta})\) time for any fixed \(\delta >0\). A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.
context:
Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing \(\varepsilon =0.01\) fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\) must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as \(n^{2}/\log ^{i} n\), for fixed i, is \(n^{2- o(1)}\) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as \(\varepsilon\) approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation for each constant \(\varepsilon\) in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)} n}\) time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed \(\eta >0, a\) constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time. The approximation constant depends on \(\eta\) and is not guaranteed to be \(1+\varepsilon\) for an arbitrarily prescribed \(\varepsilon\). Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before the input length grows; choosing \(\varepsilon\) below \(1/n\) to force exactness is outside any fixed-\(\varepsilon\) runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When \(ED=0 a\) successful estimate must be zero, and when \(ED=1\) and \(\varepsilon <1\) an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.
why: Determine whether arbitrarily accurate fixed-factor approximation can break the quadratic exponent for a central sequence-alignment problem. This tests a different computational boundary from constant-factor estimation with nearly linear overhead.
status_note: No resolution with a fixed positive exponent saving for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) was found in the primary-source check through 11 September 2026. The 2026 scheme improves quadratic time by a quasipolynomial factor and does not establish the target \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) bound.

working_summary: Unit-cost edit distance counts the fewest single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another. The question asks whether every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) permits a randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) time for some fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\) on every input pair. Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 approximation scheme gives a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time without establishing that fixed exponent saving. The numerical estimate must have purely multiplicative error even for strings with very small distance, and all preprocessing is included in the runtime. This accuracy target remains separate from TCS-6624, which allows a fixed constant factor but requires \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time.

title: Breaking two for sum-of-pairs multiple sequence alignment
importance_reason: This is a principal approximation barrier for a basic bioinformatics optimization problem, requiring an improvement that survives as the number of sequences grows.
formal: Does there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that returns a \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for minimum sum-of-pairs alignment of any number of strings under an input metric substitution-and-gap cost?
definitions: An instance gives \(k\ge2\) explicit strings over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a table \(d:(\Sigma\cup\{-\})^2\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) encoded by binary numerators and denominators. The distinguished gap symbol \(-\) is not an input-string symbol. Promise \(d(a,b)=d(b,a)\), \(d(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and the triangle inequality for all alphabet and gap symbols. An alignment is a \(k\)-row array of equal-length strings over \(\Sigma\cup\{-\}\) such that erasing gaps from each row returns its input string, and no column consists entirely of gaps. The cost is \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}\sum_c d(A_{i,c},A_{j,c})\). The minimum is over all such alignments. Empty input strings are allowed, and the all-empty instance has the empty alignment and zero optimum. The output is an explicit feasible alignment with cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\) times optimum. Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine in the total bit length of the explicit strings and metric table. The constant, finite program and polynomial are independent of \(k\), the alphabet, lengths and costs. The metric promise is part of the input domain; the algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial on all input strings, with output correctness required on well-formed promised instances. Ordinary length-delimited encodings list all alphabet symbols, all strings, and all metric-table entries; empty strings still have explicit list entries. If \(N\) is the total number of input symbols, every feasible alignment has at most \(N\) columns because each column contains at least one non-gap symbol. Hence the feasible set is finite and nonempty, and the stated minimum is attained. A zero optimum requires a zero-cost output. Gap costs are charged separately per column and pair; no additional gap-opening or run-length penalty is present.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), one uniform deterministic algorithm and one polynomial bit-time bound that always return a feasible alignment of cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for every promised instance, including zero-optimum cases. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The improvement and polynomial must be independent of the number of strings, alphabet, lengths and rational metric entries; a fixed-number-of-strings guarantee or a conditional lower bound alone does not decide the full proposition.
context:
An alignment adds gaps to put all strings into common columns while preserving the order of the original symbols. The sum-of-pairs objective charges every unordered pair of rows in every column. For example, a column containing a, a and a gap contributes twice the cost of comparing a with a gap, rather than one consensus-column penalty.

Pairwise comparison and multiple alignment are different optimization tasks. Pairwise alignments chosen independently need not be realizable simultaneously in one common table of columns. The target optimizes over globally feasible tables for all supplied strings, with the number of rows part of the input.

The classical metric guarantee is \(2-2/k\) for \(k\) strings. It is below two for every fixed \(k\), but the improvement \(2/k\) tends to zero as the number of strings grows. The conjectured algorithm must improve the factor by one fixed positive amount independent of \(k\).

The supplied survey also records extensions whose improvement depends on a fixed auxiliary parameter divided by the number of strings. Such guarantees do not by themselves supply one uniform polynomial-time constant improvement for arbitrary row counts. The source distinguishes the sum-of-pairs objective from evolutionary-tree alignment.

The metric includes the gap symbol and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality. Nonmetric scores, negative rewards, affine gap penalties, structural-contact objectives and maximization of a similarity score can have different algorithms and hardness results. They are not substituted for this minimum-cost metric problem.

Exact optimization is already difficult, but NP-hardness of exact optimization alone does not rule out a constant-factor approximation. A negative answer to the present question needs the quantified impossibility of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm; an approximation-hardness theorem conditional on a complexity assumption must retain that assumption.
why: This is a principal approximation barrier for a basic bioinformatics optimization problem, requiring an improvement that survives as the number of sequences grows.

Its objective sums costs over every pair of rows and every column. The question asks for a polynomial-time approximation below two by a fixed constant. An improvement shrinking with the number of sequences does not meet the target.

title: Almost-linear constant-factor approximation of LCS
importance_reason: A constant approximation in almost-linear time would make a central similarity measure usable at input scale while avoiding degradation on large alphabets.
formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every pair of explicit strings of total length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..n^2)\), returns a common subsequence of length at least \(\operatorname{LCS}(A,B)/C\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
definitions: A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more symbols without changing the remaining order; \(\operatorname{LCS}(A,B)\) is the maximum possible length common to both strings. Empty strings are permitted. The algorithm outputs the subsequence explicitly and must always output a valid common subsequence; only the approximation guarantee may fail. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The same finite algorithm and approximation constant work for every input size. The runtime convention means that for every real \(\eta>0\) there exist \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) such that every random execution takes at most \(K_\eta n^{1+\eta}\) steps for every \(n\ge n_\eta\). The probability is over internal randomness on each fixed input. The alphabet grows with input length; a guarantee depending on alphabet size is not a universal constant approximation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:

The 2026 comparison of LCS and LCStr describes a remaining approximation gap on growing alphabets.

Recent deterministic near-linear algorithms give input-dependent approximation factors rather than the universal constant requested here.

A constant-alphabet guarantee does not decide the general-alphabet target. Almost-linear time here belongs to one algorithm, not a different algorithm for each fixed polynomial runtime slack.

title: Text-to-pattern Hamming distances below the square-root barrier
importance_reason: A polynomial improvement would cross a central exponent barrier for exact approximate-matching computations and their arithmetic counting counterparts.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform Las Vegas algorithm that computes the exact Hamming distance at every alignment of an explicit pattern of length \(m\) in an explicit text of length \(n\), for all \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le m\le n\), in \(O(nm^{1/2-\varepsilon})\) expected time?
definitions: The alphabet is \([0..n^2)\), and the required output is the list \(h_i=|\{j\in[0..m):P[j]\ne T[i+j]\}|\) for \(i=0,\ldots,n-m\), in increasing alignment order. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The algorithm must terminate almost surely and return the entire list correctly on every terminating random execution. The expectation is over its internal randomness for each fixed input, with universal constants. There is no text preprocessing supplied for free, and time includes every output entry. The target is a fixed positive saving in the power of \(m\), uniformly over both lengths.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:
Computing the mismatch count at every position is the basic all-alignments comparison task. It asks for exact counts rather than threshold decisions or relative approximations.

The FOCS 2023 result gives \(O(n\sqrt m)\) Las Vegas time and a fine-grained equivalence with a range-restricted counting version of 3SUM.

The equivalence does not provide an unconditional matching lower bound, and the counting problem must not be replaced by ordinary decision 3SUM.
why: A polynomial improvement would cross a central exponent barrier for exact approximate-matching computations and their arithmetic counting counterparts.
status_note: Primary sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The fixed exponent saving is the explicit editorial threshold approved in the proposal; randomization is Las Vegas rather than bounded-error approximation.

working_summary: The task compares one pattern against every possible text alignment. Every mismatch count must be returned exactly. All preprocessing and output costs are charged. The target saves a fixed power of pattern length over the square-root bound. The known counting-3SUM equivalence does not itself prove the target impossible.

title: Linear-space k-mismatch text indexing
importance_reason: This is a core approximate-search interface whose space overhead can determine whether a large collection remains indexable.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), does a uniform deterministic static index of every text of length \(n\ge2\) exist using \(O(n)\) words, polynomial preprocessing time, and \(O(m+(\log(n+2))^{c(k)}+\mathrm{occ})\) worst-case query time for some function \(c:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\)?
definitions: The explicit text \(T\) and explicit query pattern \(P\) use alphabet \([0..n)\). A query has length \(1\le m\le n\) and reports every position \(i\in[0..n-m]\) with \(|\{j\in[0..m):T[i+j]\ne P[j]\}|\le k\), without duplicates and in any order. \(\mathrm{occ}\) is the number of these positions. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. A program may depend on fixed \(k\), but cannot depend on \(n,T,P\). Space, time and preprocessing constants may depend on \(k\). The text and all retained auxiliary information count toward linear word space, as does query workspace excluding the explicit query and streamed output. All queries are exact, and the pattern is not available during preprocessing.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:
Approximate indexing supports repeated searches allowing a bounded number of substitutions. Large output size is accounted for separately.

Kociumaka and Radoszewski improve the general-alphabet space bound to \(O(n\log^{k-1}n)\) and explicitly ask for further space and query improvements.

The linear-space question fixes each error budget independently and allows a polynomial in the logarithm for query overhead. Insertions and deletions are outside the model.
why: This is a core approximate-search interface whose space overhead can determine whether a large collection remains indexable.
status_note: Primary sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. working_summary: A text is indexed before query patterns arrive. A query reports all positions with at most a fixed number of substitutions. The proposed structure uses only linear word space. Its cost is pattern length, polylogarithmic overhead and output size. The recent general improvement still uses additional logarithmic factors in space.

title: Space-query exponent curve of gapped string indexing
importance_reason: A tight curve would reveal how reusable space substitutes for work in a general paired-pattern search primitive important in text analysis and biological motif queries.
formal: Determine \(s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)\) for every real \(\delta\in[0,1]\), where \(s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)\) is the infimum of \(s\ge1\) for which gapped string reporting admits static indexes with space \(O(n^{s+\eta})\) words and query time \(O(m_1+m_2+n^{\delta+\eta}(1+\mathrm{occ}))\) for every fixed rational \(\eta>0\).
definitions: The explicit text \(T\) has length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..n)\). A query gives two explicit nonempty patterns \(P_1,P_2\) of lengths \(m_1,m_2\le n\), and integers \(0\le a\le b<n\). Report without duplicates all ordered pairs \((i,j)\) of valid starts for these patterns with \(a\le j-i\le b\); overlaps and \(i=j\) are allowed when consistent. The output may have any order and its true size is \(\mathrm{occ}\). For each chosen \(\delta,s,\eta\), one uniform finite randomized preprocessing/query pair and its constants handle every text size and query. Preprocessing must run in polynomial time; its degree may depend on the chosen parameters. Space and query time hold for every random outcome; every fixed input/query has correct complete output with probability at least \(2/3\), over preprocessing and query randomness. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Stored inputs, random seeds and tables count. Query workspace is included in the space bound, apart from the query and streamed output. The infimum need not be attained. Parameters indexing the curve select uniform programs; they are not real-number advice supplied to a computation. The target is a dimensionless exponent function, not the memory size for one finite input.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire stated domain and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(|g(x)-s_{\mathrm{gap}}(x)|\le 1/100\) at every point. Uniform certified upper and lower bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify via their midpoint. Exact equality also qualifies. A plot, finitely many sample points, one-sided improvement, or a renamed copy of the defining infimum is insufficient. This numerical acceptance tolerance does not establish a separate exact threshold conjecture.
context:
Two sequence motifs can be meaningful together only when their occurrences lie within a requested distance range. The gap bounds here arrive with the query.

The STACS 2024 paper obtains simultaneous subquadratic space and sublinear query overhead, with explicit output-sensitive tradeoffs.

The 2026 3SUM-indexing improvements also affect string-indexing tradeoffs.

The curve fixes one reporting-time convention over its whole domain. It does not conflate start-position distance with the number of intervening characters, or existence queries with reporting.
why: A tight curve would reveal how reusable space substitutes for work in a general paired-pattern search primitive important in text analysis and biological motif queries.

working_summary: Queries supply two patterns and an interval of allowed separation. Every matching pair of positions must be reported. The separation is measured between starting positions. The target is the optimal storage exponent as a function of query-overhead exponent. The benchmark requires certified accuracy throughout that function’s domain.

title: Almost-quadratic unweighted tree edit distance
importance_reason: This would locate the cost of exact hierarchical sequence comparison relative to ordinary string edit distance and a broad family of structured dynamic programs.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm computing the exact unit-cost edit distance between two rooted ordered labeled trees with a total of \(n\ge2\) vertices in \(n^{2+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
definitions: Trees are supplied by explicit ordered child lists and vertex labels in \([0..n^2)\). A fixed unlabelled super-root is attached above each input root; it may not be deleted or relabelled and is not counted in \(n\). Intermediate objects may be ordered forests below this super-root. Deleting a vertex replaces it in its parent’s ordered child list by its own ordered children. Inserting a vertex is the inverse operation, grouping a consecutive block of children, possibly empty, under one new vertex. Relabelling changes one ordinary vertex label. Each of these three operations costs one. The distance is the minimum total cost of a sequence transforming the first ordered labeled object into the second. The output is this single integer, not an edit script. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The same algorithm works for all inputs. The time condition means that for every \(\eta>0\), some constants \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) bound its time by \(K_\eta n^{2+\eta}\) whenever \(n\ge n_\eta\). All preprocessing is charged, and no randomness is permitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:
Tree edit distance compares hierarchical structures while respecting the order of siblings. Paths give the string case, but branching adds structural interactions.

The 2026 monotone-product paper records and derandomizes an upper bound \(n^{(3+\omega)/2+o(1)}\), already below cubic.

The ITCS 2026 dynamic-hardness paper distinguishes the still-unresolved static relative difficulty of strings and unweighted trees.

The target asks for almost-quadratic exact computation. It replaces the old first-truly-subcubic question, rather than continuing to mark that resolved threshold as open.
why: This would locate the cost of exact hierarchical sequence comparison relative to ordinary string edit distance and a broad family of structured dynamic programs.
status_note: Primary sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the precise target was located; this is a bounded literature review, not exhaustive certification of current openness. The near-quadratic endpoint is the user-approved replacement direction for TCS-5851. Weighted and dynamic variants have different barriers.
progress: 2026: Current bounds already beat cubic time; this card asks for the substantially stronger almost-quadratic target.
working_summary: The inputs are rooted ordered trees with symbol labels. Insertion, deletion and relabelling each have unit cost. The task computes the exact minimum edit cost. The proposed bound is almost quadratic in the total number of vertices. The earlier question of obtaining any truly subcubic algorithm has already been surpassed.

title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
importance_reason: Asks whether a basic measure of reusable string structure can be approximated within a constant, linking compression and approximation complexity.
formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
context:
A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\), but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.
why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 using the primary approximation and fixed-alphabet papers, with a search for later results. No general constant-factor algorithm was located. Recent assembly-index work uses additional size conventions and is not treated as resolving this proposition.
progress: 2005: Charikar and coauthors give an \(O(1+\log (|s|/g*(s)))\) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below \(8569/8568\) unless \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\). | 2020-11 / 2021: Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.
working_summary: A grammar can compress a string by naming repeated pieces and assembling them through acyclic production rules. The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time approximation within a universal constant of the smallest such grammar. The size measure counts all symbols on right-hand sides, including references to other rules. Choosing repeated pieces is difficult because useful substrings can overlap and interact across scales. The saved review separates this constant-factor target from known logarithmic guarantees and emphasizes that alternative grammar-size conventions describe different optimization problems.

title: Optimal \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distortion of edit distance
importance_reason: Resolve a central metric-embedding barrier for sequence comparison.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(n\to \infty , D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\inf \{D\ge 1: \exists m\ge 1, f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}, a>0, \forall x,y, a\cdot ED(x,y)\le \Vert f(x)- f(y)\Vert _{1}\le D a\cdot ED(x,y)\}\), for integers \(n\ge 2\).
definitions: ED is Levenshtein distance with unit-cost insertion, deletion and substitution; intermediate strings may have other lengths. The \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) norm is the sum of absolute coordinate values. The dimension m is any finite positive integer and the map has arbitrary real coordinates. Neither dimension nor construction/evaluation time is bounded. The scale a and map may depend on n. The infimum is over all such embeddings and common scales, with the inequalities holding simultaneously for every pair. Every finite metric admits a finite-distortion embedding, so \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\) is finite. The target concerns metric existence, not running time of string comparison.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(h(n)\) and absolute constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) such that \(c h(n)\le D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\le C h(n)\) for all \(n\ge 2\), and prove the matching embedding and obstruction bounds in Lean. The bounds must concern unrestricted finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embeddings in the stated edit convention. Establishing only a polylogarithmic upper bound need not determine the requested asymptotic order.
context:
The quantitative target is the growth of the best distortion. The previous question asked only whether that growth can be bounded by a fixed power of log n.

An embedding compares a difficult sequence metric with the additive geometry of \(\ell\)\(_{1}\). Polylogarithmic distortion would sharply improve the known structural representation of edit distance.

The Ostrovsky–Rabani construction gives subpolynomial distortion that is larger than polylogarithmic. The existence target is distinct from fast approximation algorithms: a nonconstructive embedding need not be efficiently evaluable. The convention includes substitutions explicitly.
why: Resolve a central metric-embedding barrier for sequence comparison.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2005: The source constructs an embedding with subpolynomial distortion, leaving the polylogarithmic endpoint open.
working_summary: Edit distance counts unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions between binary strings. An \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embedding represents those distances by sums of coordinate differences, up to a common multiplicative distortion. The target is the smallest distortion as a function of string length, within constant factors. Embedding dimension and construction time are unrestricted. The earlier polylogarithmic-distortion question selects one possible growth regime of this extremal function.

title: Optimal top-k document retrieval in compact space
importance_reason: This joins ranked retrieval with compact text indexing, a basic requirement for searchable document and genome collections whose auxiliary indexes should not dominate their input.
formal: Does a uniform deterministic static index exist for every collection \(D_1,\ldots,D_d\) of nonempty strings of total length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..\sigma)\), where \(2\le\sigma\le n\), using \(O(n\log\sigma)\) bits and answering top-\(k\) queries in \(O(1+m/\log_\sigma n+k)\) worst-case time?
definitions: A query gives \(1\le k\le d\) and a nonempty packed pattern \(P\) of length \(m\le n\). The frequency of \(P\) in a document is its number of starting positions, counting overlapping occurrences. Return the identifiers of the \(\min(k,h)\) highest-frequency documents among the \(h\) documents containing \(P\), in decreasing frequency, breaking ties by increasing identifier. No occurrence crosses a document boundary. Documents are identified by their input order. The alphabet symbols occupy \(\lceil\log_2\sigma\rceil\) bits each in the packed query. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing takes polynomial time in \(n\). Space includes document boundaries, identifiers, retained text and every persistent auxiliary structure. Query working memory, excluding the supplied pattern and streamed output, also fits the stated bit bound. All constants are uniform in \(n,d,\sigma,m,k\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:
A collection-level search query often needs the most relevant documents rather than every individual occurrence of a pattern.

Navarro and Nekrich explicitly ask for optimal retrieval in space close to the packed text size. Their SODA 2025 structure uses a compressed suffix array plus an additional \(O(n\log\log n)\) bits.

On small alphabets that additional storage is asymptotically larger than the text. Sorting results by frequency and counting all stored boundaries are part of the target.

The desired index occupies only a constant multiple of packed text size. The query cost must match reading the packed pattern and writing the requested identifiers. title: General-alphabet Hamming oracles with optimal preprocessing
importance_reason: This isolates the cost of reusable exact similarity queries and tests whether large alphabets create an inherent preprocessing penalty.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic data structure which, for every pair of strings of lengths \(n,m\ge1\) and every integer \(1\le x\le\min(n,m)\), uses \(\widetilde O(nm/x)\) preprocessing time and stored words and answers exact substring Hamming-distance queries in \(O(x)\) worst-case time?
definitions: The strings \(A\) and \(B\) are supplied explicitly over \([0..(n+m)^2)\). A query \((i,j,\ell)\) satisfies \(0\le i\le n\), \(0\le j\le m\), and \(0\le\ell\le\min(n-i,m-j)\). It returns \(|\{t:0\le t<\ell,\ A[i+t]\ne B[j+t]\}|\). Positions are zero-based; a length-zero query returns zero. Set \(L=n+m\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The soft-O means multiplication by \((\log(L+2))^c\) for one fixed constant \(c\), independent of \(x,n,m\). One fixed algorithm receives \(x\) during preprocessing and handles all admissible parameters. The stored space includes both strings, if retained, and all auxiliary information. Query space is included; no offline knowledge of future queries is supplied.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:
The same pair of strings can participate in many comparisons between internal intervals. An oracle pays once for a reusable representation.

The CPM 2026 source gives \(\widetilde O(nm/x)\) preprocessing for constant alphabets but \(\widetilde O(nm/\sqrt{x})\) for general alphabets, both with \(O(x)\) queries.

The question transfers the smaller preprocessing regime to general integer alphabets. Exact answers, preprocessing time and query time are separate requirements.

title: Optimal approximation ratio for shortest common superstring
importance_reason: A long-standing approximation threshold for a basic string-assembly problem with direct algorithmic genomics and compression motivation.
formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{SCS}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every shortest common superstring instance}, in the input and output model below.
definitions: Symbols are integers from \(\{1,\ldots ,\sigma\}\), encoded in binary; \(\sigma\) and all strings are input. Running time is measured on a deterministic Turing machine in the total bit length of this explicit representation. String length counts symbols. Repeated and empty input strings are allowed. For an empty collection, OPT is zero. The output is an explicit string over the input alphabet, and containment means ordinary forward contiguous occurrence without reversal, reverse complementation or cyclic wraparound. All preprocessing is charged. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{SCS}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.

title: Polyloglogarithmic suffix-array access in compact space
importance_reason: This asks whether a representation close to the information content of a text can support powerful navigation with only an iterated-logarithmic time cost.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic static index that represents every binary string \(T\) of length \(n\ge2\) in \(O(n)\) bits and answers every suffix-array query \(\operatorname{SA}_T[i]\), for \(0\le i<n\), in \(O((1+\log\log(n+2))^c)\) worst-case time for one universal constant \(c\ge1\)?
definitions: \(\operatorname{SA}_T\) lists the starting positions of the nonempty suffixes of \(T\) in lexicographic order, with \(0<1\) and a proper prefix preceding the longer string. Positions and ranks are zero-based. Set \(L=n\) in the following model. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing is deterministic and polynomial in \(n\); its polynomial and all constants are fixed with the index. The bit-space bound includes all retained copies of the text, samples, pointers and tables. Temporary query storage is included in the same bound. The externally supplied query and returned answer each occupy one word.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.
context:

The proposed bound keeps the entire representation proportional to the binary text, rather than allowing one full pointer per suffix.

title: Preprocessing exponent of binary jumbled indexing
importance_reason: A sharp construction exponent would identify the true cost of a basic order-insensitive text-search primitive and clarify its relation to structured convolution.
formal: Determine \(\alpha_{\mathrm{BJ}}\), the infimum of real \(a\ge1\) for which, for every rational \(\eta>0\), a uniform deterministic index for binary strings of length \(n\) has \(O(n^{a+\eta})\) worst-case preprocessing time, \(O(n)\) words of stored space and \(O(1)\) worst-case query time.
definitions: The input is an explicit string \(T\in\{0,1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\). A query is a pair of nonnegative integers \((u,v)\) with \(1\le u+v\le n\), and asks whether a contiguous substring has exactly \(u\) zeroes and \(v\) ones. Answers must be exact. All retained text and tables count toward space. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. For each proposed \(a,\eta\), one finite construction/query pair and its constants must work for every \(n\) and every string; it receives no real parameter as input and may depend only on the chosen parameters. The infimum need not be attained. The cost of the original explicit input, indexing and output is included. The target is an exponent measured in powers of \(n\); no additive tolerance is applied to a big-O expression.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute distance from the defined exponent is at most \(1/100\). A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. Both sides must concern the unrestricted quantity in this card; an assumed hardness conjecture proves only a conditional statement. Repeating the defining infimum or giving only an upper bound is insufficient.
context:

The binary case differs from the larger-alphabet variants for which Amir and coauthors prove conditional preprocessing/query barriers.

The 2026 monotone-convolution result yields deterministic preprocessing exponent at most \(3/2\) for the binary application.

The index has linear word space and constant query time. The target is the best uniform deterministic preprocessing exponent. The numerical benchmark asks for a certified value to absolute accuracy one hundredth.

title: Polynomial-time construction of minimum-density DNA minimizers
importance_reason: This asks whether optimal seed selection can be constructed with cost polynomial in its explicit representation, connecting a widely used sequencing primitive to a sharp computational barrier.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm and a universal constant \(C\) that, for all integers \(k,w\ge2\), output a total order \(\rho\) on the \(4^k\) DNA k-mers minimizing expected minimizer density exactly, in \(O((4^k+w)^C)\) bit operations?
definitions: The fixed alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{A,C,G,T\}\). The input supplies \(k\) in binary and \(w\) in unary. The output lists every member of \(\Sigma^k\) once in order. For \(X\in\Sigma^{k+w}\), let \(p_0(X)\) be the smallest starting position in \(\{0,\ldots,w-1\}\) attaining the least k-mer under \(\rho\), and define \(p_1(X)\) in the same way over \(\{1,\ldots,w\}\). Define \(d(\rho)=4^{-(k+w)}|\{X:p_0(X)\ne p_1(X)\}|\). This is the expected sampling density on an independent uniform DNA sequence with leftmost tie-breaking. Optimality requires \(d(\rho)\le d(\pi)\) for every total order \(\pi\) on \(\Sigma^k\). Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine and includes all output bits and preprocessing. The same finite machine handles all \(k,w\), with no advice. The resource parameter is the explicit order-table size plus the unary window parameter; no claim of polynomial time in \(\log k+\log w\) is made.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.

Known exact exponential search does not meet that resource bound.

title: Linear-space LZ77 random access
importance_reason: Random access is a basic interface for compressed computation. The linear-space target would remove a persistent overhead for a central repetitiveness measure.
formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using \(O(z)\) words in total that returns \(S[i]\) for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case \(O(\log  N)\) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to \(a<b\) is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use \(1+\log  N\) at the smallest lengths.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the \(O(z)\) requirement.
context:
Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.
why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July LZ-End result. The stated parse convention, space parameter, and deterministic query guarantee are explicit.
progress: 2019 / 2021: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size. | 2025-05: Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access. | 2026-07: Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic \(O(z_{\mathrm{end}})\)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.
working_summary: An LZ77 parse represents repeated text through references to earlier occurrences, possibly allowing overlap. The reviewed question asks for random character access in logarithmic time using space linear in the number of phrases. The original uncompressed string is unavailable when queries arrive. A solution must navigate arbitrary chains of copied material while keeping every stored shortcut inside the compressed-space budget. The saved record distinguishes ordinary LZ77 from restricted parsing variants and notes that converting to a larger grammar does not automatically preserve the required linear space.

title: Faster elastic-degenerate string intersection
importance_reason: This is a fundamental comparison operation on succinct pangenome representations, with substantial room between general hardness and parameter-sensitive algorithms.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm deciding intersection of two elastic-degenerate strings in \(\widetilde O(N_1+N_2+n_2N_1^{\omega-1-\varepsilon}+n_1N_2^{\omega-1-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time, with probability of correctness at least \(2/3\) on every input?
definitions: An elastic-degenerate string \(E_i\) is an explicit list of \(n_i\ge1\) finite sets of distinct strings. Each set contains a nonempty string and may additionally contain the empty string. Its language consists of concatenations obtained by choosing one alternative from each set in order. Let \(N_i\) be the sum of the lengths of all alternatives, so \(N_i\ge n_i\). Delimiters are included in the encoding; the number of alternatives is at most \(2N_i\). Blocks containing only the empty string are omitted from this input convention. Symbols lie in \([0..(N_1+N_2)^2)\). The output says whether the two languages share any string; neither language is explicitly expanded. Set \(L=N_1+N_2\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Soft-O permits one fixed power of \(\log(L+2)\). Here \(\omega\) is the infimum of real exponents \(a\) such that square matrix multiplication over the rationals has uniform algebraic algorithms using \(O(t^{a+\eta})\) field operations for every fixed \(\eta>0\), with \(t\) the matrix dimension. The string algorithm need not be combinatorial. All constants and its finite program are independent of the input sizes.

A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.

A pangenome representation can store a sequence of alternative sequence fragments. Its represented language can be exponentially larger than the explicit alternatives.

The source gives an upper bound involving \(n_2N_1^{\omega-1}+n_1N_2^{\omega-1}\) and explicitly asks about a polynomial improvement in section 9.

The separate linear input term makes the target meaningful when the algebraic expression falls below the cost of reading the alternatives. It changes no requirement to compare entire represented languages.
