working_summary: Conjugacy asks whether two group elements differ by a transformation of the form \(w^{- 1}uw\). The reviewed question seeks one algorithm deciding this for every finitely presented group with a single defining relation. Equality of words is decidable in these groups, but searching possible conjugators only semidecides positive answers. An algorithm would settle a classical decision problem for a remarkably concise family of infinite algebraic structures. The saved review explains that decomposition methods preserving word-problem decidability do not automatically preserve decidable conjugacy.

title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
importance_reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given any two finite one-relator group presentations \(G=\langle x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k} | r=1\rangle\) and \(H=\langle y_{1},\ldots ,y_{\ell} | s=1\rangle\), decides whether G and H are isomorphic as abstract groups?
definitions: The input consists of integers \(k,\ell \ge 1\) and explicitly written finite words r and s in the respective generators and formal inverses. The groups are the free groups on these generators modulo the normal closures of r and s. An empty relator is permitted and presents a free group. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the resulting abstract groups; it need not carry a listed generator to a listed generator, preserve the spelling of a relator, or come from an automorphism of a free group on the given generators. The numbers of displayed generators may differ. The sought procedure is one deterministic Turing machine which halts and answers correctly on every valid pair of presentations. No polynomial-time, elementary-time or other quantitative runtime bound is imposed. There is no promise of torsion, hyperbolicity, nontrivial center, genericity or a supplied geometric decomposition.
answer_criterion: Give a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such pairs, or prove that the isomorphism language on these one-relator presentations is undecidable. A procedure that halts only for isomorphic pairs, or one correct only on a specified subclass or almost all random presentations, is insufficient. Undecidability for arbitrary finite presentations, systems of equations or other algebraic structures must be connected to this exact input class by a valid reduction to count as a negative solution.
context:
A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, \(\langle a,b | b=a^{2}\rangle\) and \(\langle x |\) empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{k}\) for the generators of G in H and \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.
why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.
progress: 1970s: Counterexamples to the Magnus conjecture show that free-group equivalence of relators cannot characterize all isomorphisms; torsion and center subclasses admit positive results. | 2003–2006: Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain obtain strong generic rigidity and fast isomorphism algorithms for random one-relator groups. | 2010–2011: Dahmani–Guirardel solve isomorphism for all hyperbolic groups, covering one-relator groups with torsion. | 30 January 2025: Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the unrestricted one-relator isomorphism problem as open. | 3 August 2026: Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability for the separate Diophantine problem in one-relator groups. | 18 August 2026: Kapovich’s preprint extends generic small-cancellation stability and isomorphism rigidity to fixed generator and relator counts.
working_summary: Two group presentations can describe the same abstract group despite using different generators and relations. The reviewed question asks to decide isomorphism between arbitrary finite one-relator presentations. Candidate mutually inverse homomorphisms can be enumerated and checked using the known word algorithm. The missing ingredient is an effective way to stop when no such isomorphism exists. A solution would distinguish complete algebraic types within this concise presentation class, extending beyond equality and conjugacy questions about elements of one already fixed group.

title: Bit complexity of integer multiplication
importance_reason: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\), the optimal worst-case running time for exactly multiplying two n-bit nonnegative binary integers by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine. The target is an attainable asymptotic upper bound with a matching lower bound for every correct machine in this model.
definitions: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate \(g(n)>0\) means some correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=O(g(n))\), while every correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=\Omega (g(n))\); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).
answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate \(g(n)\) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in \(O(g(n))\) worst-case time and an \(\Omega (g(n))\) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.
context:
For example, \(11_{2}\) multiplied by \(11_{2}\) is \(1001_{2}\): the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes \(O(n \log  n)\) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an \(s\times s\) binary matrix written row by row. Even a \(2\times 2\) matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs \(\Omega (s^{2} \log  s)\) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.
why: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted multitape lower bound open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching bound or faster general algorithm; the August 2026 OBDD result concerns a different model.
progress: 2021: An \(O(n \log  n)\) deterministic multitape upper bound is published. It does not include a matching lower bound. | 2025-03: A conjectured optimal matrix-transposition lower bound is shown to imply the corresponding multiplication lower bound. | 2026-08: New OBDD-width bounds concern a restricted branching-program model and do not close the multitape time gap.
working_summary: What is the optimal worst-case bit complexity of multiplying two n-bit integers? The model charges individual steps of a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine. An \(O(n \log  n)\) algorithm is known, but only a linear general lower bound is established. A 2025 theorem connects the conjectured matching lower bound to the unresolved cost of matrix transposition. Bounds for restricted branching programs do not determine the optimal cost in this model.

title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
importance_reason: A structural conjecture about the cost of all bilinear computations, extending well beyond one matrix-multiplication algorithm.
formal: For every \(n\ge 1\) and every tensor \(T\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{n}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{n}\) whose three flattenings all have rank n, is \(\lim _{k\to \infty} R(T^{\otimes}k)^{1/k}=n\)?
definitions: \(R(T)\) is the least r such that \(T=\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_{i}\otimes b_{i}\otimes c_{i}\) with \(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In \(T^{\otimes}k\) the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{k}}\). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to \(\inf _{k\ge 1} R(T^{\otimes}k)^{1/k}\). This is exact rank over \(\mathbb{C}\), not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

The cubic concise formulation is the target proposed in the personal list. It includes matrix-multiplication tensors, so a positive resolution would imply matrix multiplication exponent two; the reverse implication is not claimed. The 2024–2026 source studies structural properties of asymptotic rank without proving this equality.
why: A structural conjecture about the cost of all bilinear computations, extending well beyond one matrix-multiplication algorithm.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2024: The source establishes algebraic characterizations and upper semicomputability properties of asymptotic rank; the general conjecture is retained.

title: Unrestricted arithmetic lower bounds for the discrete Fourier transform
importance_reason: Tests whether the central FFT upper bound is inherently necessary in unrestricted arithmetic computation.
formal: Let \(S(n)\) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. Do constants \(c>0\) and N exist such that \(S(n)\ge c n \log _{2}n\) for every power of two \(n\ge N\), with no bound on the magnitudes of the constants used in the program?
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) set \(\omega _{n}=\exp (- 2\pi i/n)\), and define \(DFT_{n}(x)_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^{n- 1}\omega _{n}^{jk}x_{k}\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,n- 1\) and \(x\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every \(c>0\) and every threshold N there is a power of two \(n\ge N\) and a program of size less than \(c n \log _{2}n\). A family using \(o(n \log  n)\) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.
context:
For four inputs, form \(a=x_{0}+x_{2}, b=x_{1}+x_{3}, c=x_{0}- x_{2}\) and \(d=x_{1}- x_{3}\). The four Fourier outputs are \(a+b, c- id, a- b\) and \(c+id\). Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

Dividing all outputs by \(\sqrt{n}\) gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is \(n^{n/2}\), whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.
why: Tests whether the central FFT upper bound is inherently necessary in unrestricted arithmetic computation.
status_note: Full primary circuit and Fourier-model sources were checked, together with the 2026 publisher abstract and a search for subsequent DFT lower bounds through 11 September 2026. No resolution of the unbounded-coefficient straight-line target was found. The 2026 full PDF was unavailable; it is not claimed as independently read. This review does not audit the cited proofs.
progress: 1973 / 2004: The circuit reference recalls Morgenstern’s bounded-coefficient DFT lower bound and gives related bounded-coefficient bilinear lower bounds. Its model section distinguishes the unrestricted arithmetic and linear formulations. | 2013: Theorem 2.1 proves an n log n lower bound for normalized Fourier computation in a two-coordinate unitary model with n storage locations. | 2018 / 2020: The revised paraunitary paper and its journal version study speedup versus algebraic conditioning, retaining restrictions beyond this card’s model. | 2026: The SODA source proves division lower bounds for integer-point Toom-Cook interpolation in specified cost models, not the unrestricted DFT target.
working_summary: Must the discrete Fourier transform take order n log n exact arithmetic operations when constants are unrestricted? The target covers every sufficiently large power-of-two input length and all straight-line programs in the stated model. The FFT achieves this cost by sharing intermediate computations. Known matching lower bounds impose coefficient, gate, storage or conditioning restrictions. Normalization, bit precision and quantum state transformations require care because their computational models differ.

title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for exact permanent computation

formal: Is there epsilon>0 and an exact algorithm using O((2-epsilon)^n) arithmetic operations to compute the permanent of every n by n matrix over characteristic zero?
context:
TCS-0815 asks about the relation to SETH; TCS-4858 concerns adapting a particular technique. These must not be silently relabelled as the unrestricted arithmetic-operation question.

status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.
working_summary: Exact permanent computation evaluates the unsigned sum of permutation products of a square matrix. The saved question asks for an arithmetic algorithm with running time O((2−epsilon)^n) for some fixed positive epsilon over characteristic zero. The target is an exponential-base improvement, not a polynomial factor saved from a two-to-the-n procedure. It probes whether the familiar inclusion-exclusion scale reflects a genuine obstacle in this canonical counting polynomial. The source formulation counts arithmetic operations, so coefficient bit complexity and approximate evaluation require separate treatment before comparing algorithms to this target.

title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
importance_reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.
formal: For \(n \ge  2\), assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight \(x_{ij}\) to every unordered edge \(\{i,j\}\) of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{ij}\) and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates \(\min (a,b)\) or \(a+b\), unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute \(f_{n}\) exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is \(s(n)=Omega(n^{3})\)? Equivalently, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and n0 such that every such circuit has at least \(c n^{3}\) gates for every \(n\ge n0\)?
definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences \(x_{ij}\) and \(x_{ji}\) denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every \(c>0\) and every n0 there is an \(n\ge n0\) with a correct circuit using fewer than \(c n^{3}\) gates. An \(o(n^{3})\)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
context:
The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize \(d_{0}(1)=0\) and \(d_{0}(v)\)=infinity otherwise, and compute \(d_{k}(v)=\min\)(\(d_{k-1}(v), \min\) over u distinct from v of \(d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}\)). After n-1 layers, output \(d_{n-1}(n)\). Each layer uses \(O(n^{2})\) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives \(O(n^{3})\) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.
why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.
status_note: Open in the 2025 seminar and still listed in the author’s book supplements accessed on 10 September 2026. Current searches did not locate a resolution of this exact single-output, nonnegative-weight, min-plus-circuit question.
progress: 2015: Jukna gives the \(O(n^{3}) \min\)-plus upper bound and explicitly asks for a cubic lower bound for the single-pair connectivity polynomial; his framework distinguishes nonnegative tropical evaluation from formal polynomial production. | 2023 onward: The author’s book supplements discuss the known cubic all-pairs lower bound and the unresolved single-source and single-pair optimality questions. The all-pairs argument does not directly settle one output. | 2025: Koutris restates the question for complete undirected graphs over absorptive semirings, recording the \(O(n^{3})\) upper bound and the quadratic input-dependence lower bound, with the gap open already over the tropical semiring.
working_summary: A min-plus circuit computes by a fixed network of minimum and addition gates. The question asks whether even one shortest-path distance in a complete nonnegatively weighted graph requires cubic circuit size. Ordinary graph algorithms can branch on comparisons and therefore need not translate into equally small circuits. Repeated relaxation provides a cubic upper bound, while dependence on all edge inputs gives only a weaker basic lower bound. The project seeks to understand how much sharing fixed tropical computations can achieve across competing paths.

title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
importance_reason: A basic arithmetic operation supplies a concrete candidate for a central circuit-lower-bound barrier. The question is explicitly highlighted in Goldreich’s textbook and retained in Viola’s current manuscript; its nonuniform target is distinct from the catalogue’s machine-time question.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_{0}\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}, a\) Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
definitions: The circuit has input bits \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{n- 1},b_{0},\ldots ,b_{n- 1}\), representing \(a=\sum_{i}a_{i}2^{i}\) and \(b=\sum_{i}b_{i}2^{i}\), and output bits \(c_{0},\ldots ,c_{2n- 1}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j}c_{j}2\)ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let \(M(n)\) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is \(M(n)=O(n)\). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every \(n_{0}\) there is \(n\ge n_{0}\) with \(M(n)>Cn\). A lower bound \(c\cdot n\) with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.
context:
Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.
why: Determine whether multiplication has the same order of Boolean hardware complexity as addition, or provide an explicit superlinear lower bound in the unrestricted circuit model.
status_note: No resolution was identified in the primary-source review through 11 September 2026. The checked 2026 author manuscript explicitly retains this circuit-size question. Its revision year is not a claim that the problem was first posed in 2026.
progress: 2008: Goldreich explicitly asks whether multiplication has linear-size Boolean circuits. | 2026: Viola’s current manuscript retains the question and gives the linear-size equivalence with squaring.

title: Optimal multilinear-formula size of the permanent
importance_reason: The optimal multilinear formula size of the permanent concerns a canonical explicit algebraic lower bound with a qualitative quasipolynomial-to-exponential gap.
formal: Determine the growth of \(\log _{2} F(n)\) up to universal multiplicative constants as \(n\to \infty\), where \(F(n)\) is the minimum size of a multilinear arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb{C}\) computing \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\). Equivalently, find a positive function \(g(n)\) and constants \(a,A>0,n_{0}\) such that \(2^{a g(n)}\le F(n)\le 2^{A g(n)}\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\).
definitions: The permanent is \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}(X)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} x_{i,\pi (i)}\). An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted tree with variable or complex-constant leaves and binary addition or multiplication gates, evaluated as a commutative polynomial. Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. The formula must agree identically with \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{2}}\), not merely on Boolean inputs. Size counts all gates, including leaves. No restriction on the numerical complexity of complex constants is imposed. Let \(F(n)\) be the minimum such size; it is attained because sizes are positive integers and the defining sum of monomials is a valid finite multilinear formula. The independent variables are the \(n^{2}\) entries of the matrix; n denotes its row count. Internal computations are required to be multilinear as polynomials after cancellation, not just at the output. Sharing of subexpressions is forbidden by the tree model. The requested precision is constant factors in \(\log _{2} F(n)\), not constant factors in \(F(n)\).
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\) and prove the two bounds displayed in the statement for the specified formula model, with constants independent of n. Merely restating \(\log _{2} F(n)\), proving a bound for constant depth or prohibiting cancellation adds restrictions not present here. This is an asymptotic exponent target, not a pointwise 0.01 approximation. The original exponential lower-bound conjecture would give \(g(n)=n\), using the known exponential-size upper bound.
context:
Multilinear formulas give a restricted but important setting in which superpolynomial lower bounds are known for an explicit central polynomial. The exponential target asks how far that separation can be taken even after substantial algebraic structure is imposed.

Raz’s lower bound grows as \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\), which is superpolynomial but not exponential in n. The broader permanent circuit problem permits sharing subcomputations and intermediate nonmultilinear polynomials, so these are not interchangeable targets. The survey records the unresolved exponential strengthening.

The original conjecture asks for \(F(n)\ge 2^{cn}\). The retained card asks for its actual growth on the logarithmic scale, allowing an intermediate answer. Raz’s lower bound is \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\); the standard inclusion-exclusion formula gives an upper bound \(2^{O(n)}\) and is multilinear at every gate because its factors use different rows. No equivalence between the new determination task and the original conjecture is asserted.
why: Establish a qualitatively stronger explicit algebraic lower bound in one of the few models already admitting superpolynomial separations.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2017: The survey discusses \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) multilinear-formula lower bounds for determinant and permanent.
working_summary: The permanent is a canonical polynomial whose algebraic complexity captures a major explicit lower-bound challenge. A formula is a tree of additions and multiplications without shared intermediate results. Every intermediate polynomial must be multilinear, with complex constants and cancellation permitted. The question asks for the growth of the logarithm of the smallest formula size, up to constant factors. The known quasipolynomial lower bound and exponential upper bound leave a qualitative gap, with an exponential lower bound as the original conjectured endpoint.

title: Explicit rigidity at rank n over log log n

title: Approximate polynomial satisfiability in AM under GRH
importance_reason: The complexity of approaching a common polynomial zero is a basic question about algebraic closure and border computation; AM versus the known polynomial-space bound is a qualitative gap.
formal: Assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, is approximate polynomial satisfiability for rational-coefficient arithmetic circuits in AM? An instance consists of division-free circuits computing \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{m}\in \mathbb{Q} [x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\). It is a YES instance if, for every real \(\eta >0\), there is a point \(a\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\) with \(\max _{i} |f_{i}(a)|<\eta\); otherwise it is a NO instance. Equivalently, for every polynomial \(A\in \mathbb{Q} [y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m}]\), the identity \(A(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{m})=0\) must imply \(A(0,\ldots ,0)=0\). This equivalent decision predicate is AnnAtZero. Ask for one uniform public-coin protocol with verifier time, random-tape length and prover-message length polynomial in the full binary input length, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) on every instance.
definitions:
The integers n,m are positive and part of the instance. Each circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{j}\) or rational constants and binary +,−,× gates; no division by expressions is allowed. The encoding lists gates in topological order, their input indices, their types, and the output gates. A rational constant is given by signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. The bit length L counts this entire finite description, including constants and gate references. Variables can be relabeled so n is at most the description length; unused variables do not affect the predicate. Shared gates are allowed. Neither total degree nor the magnitudes of intermediate coefficients are promised polynomial in L. The target is a Turing bit-complexity bound, not unit-cost arithmetic with arbitrary complex constants.

An annihilator is a nonzero polynomial \(A(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\) such that substituting the \(f_{i}\) yields the zero polynomial. Equivalently one can quantify over all A, including zero as in the formal statement. AnnAtZero asks whether every such A has zero constant term, not whether some annihilator exists. In particular, algebraically independent \(f_{i}\) satisfy it vacuously. The same condition holds if the annihilator coefficients are allowed in the algebraic closure \(\bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}\). A further equivalent algebraic formulation is: there are finite Laurent polynomials \(\beta _{j}(t)\in \bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}[t,t^{- 1}]\) such that \(f_{i}(\beta _{1}(t),\ldots ,\beta _{n}(t))\in t\bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}[t]\) for every i. Negative powers in the \(\beta _{j}\) are permitted, but all nonpositive powers must disappear after evaluation of each \(f_{i}\). There is no input error tolerance or promised bound on the exponents, coefficient descriptions or sizes of these witnesses. The Laurent formulation is equivalent to the rational-function formulation in the source. Geometrically, the origin belongs to the Zariski closure of the polynomial image \(f(\mathbb{C} ^{n})\): the smallest set defined by polynomial equations containing that image. For complex polynomial maps this is also equivalent to membership in its Euclidean closure, giving the \(\eta\) formulation. The approximating points may escape every bounded region; the target does not require an exact common zero in \(\mathbb{C} ^{n}\).

AM means the following. There are a deterministic polynomial-time bit algorithm V and polynomials r,p such that Arthur samples a uniformly random string \(u\in \{0,1\}^{r(\mathrm{L})}\) and sends it to Merlin, who returns \(w\in \{0,1\}^{p(\mathrm{L})}\); then V(instance,u,w) accepts or rejects. Merlin knows the instance and u and has unlimited computation. All verifier randomness is in u; the verifier has no remaining private coins. For every YES instance, \(\Pr _{u}\)[\(\exists w:V\)(instance,u,w)=1]\(\ge 2/3\), and for every NO instance this probability is at most \(1/3\). Constants and polynomial exponents are universal across n,m,L. Shorter messages may be padded. GRH here is the usual number-field form: every nontrivial zero in \(0<Re(s)<1\) of the Dedekind zeta function \(\zeta _{K}(s)\) of every number field K has real part \(1/2\). It is an assumption, not an oracle supplied to the verifier. The task asks for the stated inclusion under that assumption; no certificate of the truth of GRH is demanded.
answer_criterion: Prove, under GRH, that one AM protocol satisfying the stated bounds decides every encoded instance, or refute the inclusion under the same assumption. A protocol only for exact common-root existence, algebraic dependence, bounded-degree special cases, or finite fields does not establish the target. A PSPACE algorithm or a test at one fixed positive numerical tolerance is insufficient. Failure of a proposed protocol is not a proof that APS is outside AM.
context:
For \(f_{1}=x\) and \(f_{2}=xy- 1\), the values at \((t,1/t)\) approach \((0,0)\) as t tends to zero, although no complex point makes both polynomials vanish. Thus exact Hilbert Nullstellensatz satisfiability and APS have different YES sets; the source’s conditional AM result for the former cannot simply be reused for the latter.

The source proves that APS is NP-hard and belongs to PSPACE, improving the earlier EXPSPACE upper bound. Its equivalence with AnnAtZero and with origin membership in the closure of an image explains the relevance to border complexity, where limits of small algebraic circuits matter.

The February 2026 preprint develops a strong approximative Nullstellensatz for containment of approximate-vanishing sets and proves a PSPACE upper bound for that containment problem. Its conclusion still identifies improved complexity bounds as an open direction. It does not establish AM membership for APS under GRH.

The source phrases the question over characteristic-zero fields and motivates it by the HN result for \(F=\mathbb{Q}\). This card fixes the usual rational-coefficient binary input version, with solutions over the algebraic closure or \(\mathbb{C}\). It makes no claim of equivalence to a model with arbitrary characteristic-zero fields supplied as computational inputs or with unencoded complex constants.
why: Would place a fundamental decision problem about limiting algebraic solutions inside a low level of interactive complexity rather than merely polynomial space. This would clarify the computational cost of passing from exact algebraic objects to their closures, a central operation in border complexity and geometric complexity theory.

title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
importance_reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem at the intersection of arithmetic algorithms, circuit reuse and cryptographic exponentiation. Its single-target complexity is repeatedly distinguished from the solved hardness of the generalized problem; it is not a numerical special case of Scholz–Brauer.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given an integer \(n\ge 1\) in binary, outputs its exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell\)\((n)\) in time polynomial in the binary input length?
definitions: An addition chain for n is a strictly increasing sequence of integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=n\) such that, for every \(i\ge 1\), there are \(j,k<i\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}; j=k\) is allowed. Its length is r, the number of additions, so \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). The input is the ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, of length \(b=\lfloor \log _{2}n\rfloor +1\). The output is \(\ell\)\((n)\) in binary. One fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine must halt within \(p(b)\) steps on every input, for one fixed polynomial p. All bit operations and output writing count. Subtraction, arbitrary constants other than the initial 1, and multiplication of previously formed exponents are not allowed chain operations. Chain entries can be reused arbitrarily. The cost of finding \(\ell\)\((n)\) is distinct from the number \(\ell\)\((n)\) of steps in the chain itself.
answer_criterion: Give such an exact algorithm with one polynomial bound, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An approximation to \(\ell\)\((n), a\) fast heuristic, polynomial time in n rather than log n, or exact results for a restricted family of exponents do not resolve the question. NP-hardness of a multiple-target variant does not establish hardness for this single-target problem. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption.
context:
Exponentiation can reuse powers: multiplying aʲ and \(a^{k}\) produces \(a^{j+k}\). Thus a chain specifies a multiplication-only program for an arbitrary formal power \(a^{n}\). Erickson’s notes explain why repeated squaring uses \(O(\log  n)\) multiplications and then ask whether the absolute minimum count can be computed efficiently.

For example, 1,2,3,5,10,15 gives five multiplications for \(a^{15}\). A convenient repeated-squaring implementation can use six. This small difference illustrates the exact optimization target: the asymptotic order of the chain length is already understood, while selecting its optimal integer value can require much more search.

Each chain step can at most double its largest entry, giving \(\ell\)\((n)\ge \lceil \log _{2}n\rceil\). Reading the binary digits of n gives a chain with at most \(2\lfloor \log _{2}n\rfloor\) steps. Consequently a shortest chain has \(O(b)\) entries of at most b bits. Exhaustive enumeration is finite and yields an exact algorithm, but not a polynomial bound in b.

The decision problem “\(\ell\)\((n)\le k\)?” is in NP: a short chain, together with its predecessor indices, is a polynomial-size certificate. Computing the exact length is equivalent to deciding these thresholds in polynomial time, by searching between the elementary bounds. This observation does not establish NP-completeness.

Koziel and coauthors explicitly distinguish the single-target problem from the generalized task of forming several specified values, for which NP-completeness is known. Their work develops efficient chains for cryptographic arithmetic. The 2025 primary article by Kempes and coauthors likewise describes the exact complexity of the single-target problem as unknown.

The Scholz–Brauer conjecture already appears as TCS-7170. It bounds \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\) in terms of \(\ell\)\((n)\); even its resolution would not supply a polynomial-time method for finding \(\ell\)\((n)\) on arbitrary binary input. The present algorithmic question has a different conclusion and computational significance.

title: Deterministic divisibility testing by a constant-degree polynomial
importance_reason: A basic derandomization question linking sparse divisibility and low-degree factorization. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every fixed integer \(\delta \ge 2\), is there a deterministic algorithm using \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s,d)\) arithmetic operations over Q that, given an explicitly s-sparse polynomial \(f\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) of total degree at most d and a nonzero polynomial \(g\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) of total degree at most \(\delta\), decides whether g divides f?
definitions: A sparse representation of f lists its nonzero rational coefficients and corresponding nonnegative integer exponent vectors; s is the number of listed monomials and d bounds the sum of exponents in each monomial. The candidate divisor g is supplied by its coefficients and exponent vectors; because \(\delta\) is fixed, it has at most \(binomial(n+\delta ,\delta )\) monomials, so dense and sparse explicit encodings are polynomially related. Divisibility means that a polynomial \(h\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) exists with \(f=gh\). The quotient need not be sparse and need not be output. The polynomial running-time exponent may depend on the fixed \(\delta\), but not on the input n,s,d. The source counts exact arithmetic operations over Q at unit cost. In particular, the requested bound is polynomial in the numerical degree d, not merely in log d, and is not a bound on rational-coefficient bit complexity. There is no promise that g is irreducible. The cases \(f=0\) or nonzero constant g have immediate affirmative answers; the first unsettled divisor degree is two.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic divisibility decision algorithm with the stated polynomial arithmetic cost for every fixed \(\delta\), or establish an obstruction to that precise guarantee. Randomized testing, quasipolynomial time, or a bound requiring the dividend f to have constant individual degree does not answer the question.
context:

For example, \(x^{D}- 1\) is sparse and divisible by \(x- 1\), but its quotient has D terms. Sparsity of f therefore gives no promise that a quotient has few monomials relative to the sparse input length.

Deterministic polynomial-time testing is available for linear divisors; for arbitrary fixed-degree nonlinear divisors, the cited general sparse-dividend result is quasipolynomial. The target removes that quasipolynomial overhead.

The 2026 result gives polynomial time when every variable’s degree in the dividend is a fixed constant. Here only the divisor g has fixed total degree: the dividend can have arbitrarily large individual degrees up to d.

title: Algebraic branching programs versus formulas
importance_reason: A basic separation in the algebraic complexity hierarchy, comparing formulas with reusable path computations. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For a fixed field F, is \(VF_{F} a\) proper subclass of \(VBP_{F}\)? Equivalently, is there a family \((f_{n})\) of polynomials of polynomially bounded degree in polynomially many commuting variables that has polynomial-size algebraic branching programs over F but no polynomial-size algebraic formulas over F? The field is a parameter of the question, as in the source; a result must state the fields to which it applies.
definitions: A polynomial family has \(f_{n}\in F[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m(n)}]\), where \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_{n}\) are at most \(n^{a}+a\) for some fixed a. An algebraic formula is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are variables or constants in F and whose internal gates are binary addition or multiplication. Its output is a formal polynomial; equality means coefficientwise equality in \(F[x]\), also when F is finite. Its size is its number of nodes. An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated source and sink and affine-linear polynomial labels on edges. It computes the sum, over all source-to-sink paths, of the product of the labels on that path. Count vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients used to describe edge labels as its size; these choices differ only polynomially from the usual size conventions. Field constants have unit algebraic cost, with no bit-length bound. \(VF_{F}\) and \(VBP_{F}\) consist respectively of the polynomial families with formula size and branching-program size bounded by \(n^{b}+b\) for some constant b independent of n. These are nonuniform classes: a different finite computation may be chosen for each n, with no requirement to generate it algorithmically. The separation asks for one family in \(VBP_{F}\) for which, for every b, some n requires formula size greater than \(n^{b}+b\). There is no restriction to multilinear computation, bounded depth, homogeneous intermediate gates or noncommuting variables.
answer_criterion: For the stated field F, prove \(VF_{F} \subsetneq  VBP_{F}\) by exhibiting a family in \(VBP_{F}\) and proving that its formula sizes are not polynomially bounded, or prove \(VF_{F}=VBP_{F}\) by showing that every polynomial-size branching-program family has polynomial-size formulas. Any characteristic or field restriction must be stated as part of the scope of the answer. A lower bound only for bounded-depth or multilinear formulas does not resolve the unrestricted question.
context:
A formula is a tree: an intermediate result used in two places must be copied. A branching program can share subpaths, and its output combines the products along all paths.

Every polynomial-size algebraic formula has a polynomial-size branching program. The question is whether this containment hides a strict difference in expressive power.

The source discusses a branching-program family that already requires more than a particular small depth in polynomial-size formulas. That does not rule out polynomial-size formulas of unrestricted depth.

The January 2026 paper recalls a known separation between syntactically multilinear formulas and branching programs. An unrestricted formula computing a multilinear output need not itself be syntactically multilinear, so that theorem does not settle VF versus VBP.
why: Separates two fundamental models of algebraic computation and asks whether sharing path computations gives a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic trees.
status_note: Recovered the exact containment from the source and checked subsequent work through 12 September 2026, including the January 2026 multilinear paper. No unrestricted resolution was located. The May revision notice for ECCC TR26-043 reports a gap in that separate barrier claim, which is not used as an established result here.
progress: 2023: The source explicitly records \(VF \subseteq\) VBP as a containment whose strictness is unknown and distinguishes it from depth-restricted lower bounds. | 2026-01-01: The later paper studies the restricted multilinear hierarchy and recounts its known formula-versus-branching-program separation; it does not claim the general separation.
working_summary: Algebraic formulas compute polynomials using arithmetic trees. Algebraic branching programs compute sums of products along paths and can share subcomputations. Every polynomial-size formula can be represented by a polynomial-size branching program. The question asks whether some branching-program family requires superpolynomial formula size over the specified field. Known results for bounded-depth or syntactically multilinear formulas do not settle this unrestricted separation.

title: A uniform exponent saving for arbitrary generalized convolution
importance_reason: A general exact-computation primitive whose improvements can transfer across many dynamic programs, rather than a speedup for one chosen operation. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist an absolute \(\varepsilon >0\) such that, for every fixed finite domain D with \(d=|D|\ge 2\) and every fixed function \(f:D\times D\to D\), the entire f-convolution of two integer tables on \(D^{n}\) can be computed exactly in \(\widetilde{O}\)\((d^{(2- \varepsilon )n}\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(2+M))\) time? The same \(\varepsilon\) must work for all domains and operations; n is unbounded and M bounds the absolute input values. No associativity, commutativity or algebraic structure of f is assumed.
definitions: Identify D with \(\{0,\ldots ,d- 1\}\). For \(u,w\in D^{n}\) set \((u\oplus _{f} w)_{j}=f(u_{j},w_{j})\) for \(1\le j\le n\). Input tables \(g,h:D^{n}\to \{- M,\ldots ,M\}\), with \(n\ge 1\) and \(M\ge 1\), list every signed integer in binary. The output is the full table \(C:D^{n}\to Z\), where \(C(v)=\sum_{u,w\in D^{n}: u\oplus _{f} w=v}g(u)h(w)\); an empty sum is zero. All arithmetic is ordinary integer arithmetic. In the source’s fixed-operation convention, D and the finite \(d^{2}\)-entry table of f specify the convolution problem; the growing inputs are g,h. More explicitly, the requested bound means a deterministic algorithm, uniform in n and the input tables, taking at most \(C_{D,f} d^{(2- \varepsilon )n}(1+n \log  d+\log (2+M))^{a_{D,f}}\) bit operations, for constants \(C_{D,f},a_{D,f}\) depending only on D,f. Any finite preparation of that fixed table can be included in \(C_{D,f}; \varepsilon\) is chosen before D,f. This states the fixed-domain asymptotic question from the source, not a bound for reading an arbitrary operation table when \(n=1\). Standard random-access storage of the listed tables is permitted, with arithmetic charged for operand bit length; addressing costs are absorbed in the displayed polynomial factor. Each output has \(O(n \log  d+\log (2+M))\) bits. The target concerns every output entry, not a query for a single specified v.
answer_criterion: Establish the bound with one positive \(\varepsilon\) independent of D and f, for all fixed finite operations and all input tables, or refute that universally quantified existence claim in the stated deterministic exact-computation model. An exponent saving that tends to zero with d, a theorem restricted to selected operations, or a faster single-entry query algorithm does not suffice.
context:
Many exact algorithms combine two tables of partial solutions coordinate by coordinate. The function f specifies how one pair of coordinate states combines; the convolution sums the contributions of every compatible pair.

There are \(d^{n}\) entries in each input table and in the output, whereas there are \(d^{2n}\) pairs of input indices. The question asks for a fixed saving in this exponent for arbitrary coordinate-combination rules.

The journal theorem computes the full convolution in \(\widetilde{O}\)\((((3/4)d^{2})^{n} \operatorname{polylog} M)\) for even d; for odd d the base is \((3/4)d^{2}+(1/4)d\). This improves the conference constant \(5/6\).

For even d the known bound corresponds to \(\varepsilon _{d}=\log _{d}(4/3)\). It is positive for each fixed d but approaches zero as d grows. The open question requires a single positive \(\varepsilon\) valid for all d.

The paper also obtains \(\widetilde{O}\)\((d^{\omega n/2} \operatorname{polylog} M)\) for one requested output entry, where \(\omega\) is the matrix-multiplication exponent. The card requires all \(d^{n}\) entries within the total time bound.
why: Would give a broadly applicable improvement for table-merging computations without requiring an algebraic law on the state-combination operation, strengthening a common primitive in exact and parameterized algorithms.
status_note: Read the IPEC question and the improved Algorithmica version, including its retained Section 6 question. Checked the January 2023 arXiv revision and later exact-title/generalized-convolution searches through 12 September 2026; no result meeting the uniform exponent target was found.
progress: 2022: The conference paper beats brute force by a factor \((6/5)^{n}\) for even d and asks for an absolute saving in the d-exponent. | 2023-01-30: The revised preprint improves the constant to \(3/4\); the Algorithmica version retains the absolute-exponent-saving question.

The card asks to compute the entire output table with a fixed saving over the brute-force exponent. The saving must be independent of the size of the coordinate domain. title: Efficient equations for VP with unrestricted complex coefficients
importance_reason: Tests the reach of algebraic natural-proof certificates for general polynomial-size circuits, with coefficient freedom as the unresolved boundary. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do there exist nonzero polynomials \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) in \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+n^{c},n)\) coefficient variables, with degree and algebraic circuit size at most \(C_{c} N_{n}^{a_{c}}\), such that for every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\) there is \(n_{0}(c,b)\) for which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\)(\(coeff(f)\))=0 whenever \(n\ge n_{0}(c,b)\) and \(f\in \mathbb{C} [x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) has total degree at most \(n^{c}\) and an algebraic circuit of size at most \(n^{b}\)? Constants \(C_{c},a_{c}\) and the family \((\mathrm{P}_{n})\) may depend on c, but not on b. Coefficients of f may be arbitrary complex numbers. This expresses the source’s eventual vanishing on every polynomial-size family, without demanding a common finite threshold across all circuit-size exponents.
definitions: An algebraic circuit over \(\mathbb{C}\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and arbitrary complex constants, binary addition and multiplication gates, and one output. Subtraction is allowed via multiplication by −1; there are no division gates. Its size is its number of vertices. It computes an exact formal polynomial, and each constant is one field element regardless of its bit description. \(VP_{\mathbb{C}}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded total degree and polynomially bounded nonuniform algebraic circuit size. For \(d=n^{c}\), list all monomials \(x_{1}^{\alpha _{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha _{n}}\) with \(\alpha _{i}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i}\alpha _{i}\le d\) in a fixed lexicographic order of exponent vectors. There are \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+d,n)\) such monomials. \(coeff(f)\) is the full vector of their coefficients, including zeros. \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a polynomial over \(\mathbb{C}\) whose variables are these \(N_{n}\) coordinates. Nonzero means not the zero formal polynomial; over \(\mathbb{C}\) it is equivalent to being nonzero at some coefficient vector. Both degree and circuit size of \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) are bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(N_{n}\), not in n. The equations themselves are nonuniform: there is no additional requirement to construct their circuits in polynomial time from n. Vanishing must hold for all circuits under each fixed polynomial size bound eventually; the threshold can depend on that bound. Restricting c,b to positive integers covers arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents by increasing them. The statement imposes no bound on output coefficients of f or on constants used inside its circuit, and requests no explicit hard polynomial on which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is nonzero.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a nontrivial polynomial-degree, polynomial-circuit-size family for every c, or refute the universal existence statement for at least one c. Vanishing only on polynomials with bounded integer coefficients, or only on a fixed restricted circuit architecture, does not establish the claim. Nonexistence of equations for VNP alone does not refute existence for VP.
context:
The input to \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is the description of another polynomial by all its coefficients. An equation vanishes on easy polynomials and is nonzero somewhere else. Its efficiency is measured against this much larger coefficient-vector dimension.

The known positive result restricts the final polynomial’s coefficients, for example to \(\{- 1,0,1\}\). Its computing circuit may still use arbitrary complex constants internally. Removing that semantic restriction is the question here.

The source’s phrase “efficiently constructible equations” is formalized by membership in VP. The checked revision explicitly describes its upper-bound proofs as existential; the card therefore does not add a uniform circuit-generation algorithm.

Under sufficiently strong permanent hardness, the source rules out efficient equations for VNP over characteristic-zero fields. Since VP is a smaller class, an equation vanishing on VP need not vanish on VNP, so the theorem does not answer this card.

title: Uniform compressed word problem for graph groups
importance_reason: A uniform algebraic-computation question separating general compressed inputs from fixed-group and power-word algorithms. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there a single deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple graph \((A,I)\) and a straight-line program \(S\) over \(A^{\pm1}\), decides whether \(\operatorname{val}(S)=1\) in the graph group \(G(A,I)=\langle A\mid ab=ba\text{ for }(a,b)\in I\rangle\)? The time bound must be polynomial in the combined encoded size of the graph and the program, uniformly over all graphs. This is the polynomial-time branch of the source question; membership in NP is its separate, weaker intermediate target.
definitions:
A graph group, also called a right-angled Artin group, has one generator for every vertex in A. An edge specifies that its two generators commute. I is symmetric and has no loops. The displayed presentation imposes these commutation relations and the group axioms, with no additional relations such as a²=1. The alphabet A±1 contains each generator and a formal inverse. Products are identified under insertion or deletion of adjacent inverse pairs and interchange of adjacent commuting letters, including their inverses. The identity is the class of the empty word. For instance aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is the identity when a and b are joined by an edge; without that edge, it is nontrivial in the two-generator free group.

A straight-line program is an acyclic sequence of string assignments. In a convenient normal form, X_i is assigned an alphabet letter, the empty word, or a concatenation X_jX_k with j,k<i. A designated final variable produces val(S). Reusing a variable means reusing its whole generated string; it does not introduce a new unknown group element. General finite right-hand sides can be put in this form with polynomial overhead. The expanded string can have exponential length in the program size and is not given explicitly.

Vertices and variables have binary indices. The graph is given explicitly, for example by its vertex and edge lists, and every program instruction is listed explicitly. Let L be the total bit length of this representation. The requested bound is L^{O(1)} bit operations on a deterministic machine, with one exponent and one algorithm for the entire input family. It cannot hide an arbitrary dependence on |A| or the commutation graph in a supposedly fixed constant. Equivalent explicit encodings differing by polynomial factors give the same P-membership question. Ill-formed graphs or cyclic programs may be rejected in polynomial time.

For the weaker NP question, every identity instance would need a certificate of length polynomial in L verifiable deterministically in polynomial time; nonidentity instances must have no accepting certificate. The known coRP result instead gives a randomized polynomial-time identity test that always accepts identities and accepts any nonidentity with probability at most 1/3. This does not by itself put identity instances in NP. The target concerns an arbitrary compressed word, not merely a product u₁^{z₁}⋯u_t^{z_t} of explicitly written words with given binary integer exponents, and not the existence of unknown exponents.
answer_criterion: Prove uniform deterministic polynomial-time decidability for arbitrary input commutation graphs and SLPs, or prove that no such algorithm exists, stating any complexity assumption used by a conditional obstruction. An NP upper bound is progress on the weaker branch and must not be reported as a positive answer to P-membership. A bound polynomial only for each fixed group, or an algorithm restricted to power words, does not settle this card.

title: Collapse of rational recurrence systems to single recurrences
importance_reason: A structural expressive-power boundary for rational recurrence systems, tied to algebraic dynamics and equivalence questions for weighted sequence models. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every rationally recursive sequence \(u:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) admit a single finite-depth rational recurrence? Explicitly, for every such \(u\), must there exist an integer \(d\geq1\) and polynomials \(A,B\in\mathbb Q[y_{0},\ldots,y_{d-1}]\) such that, for all \(n\geq0\), \[B(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})\ne0,\qquad u_{n+d}=\frac{A(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})}{B(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})}?\]
question_excerpt: Unlike in the case of polynomial updates, we conjecture that for rational updates we do have such a collapse.
definitions:
Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A sequence \(u\) is rationally recursive if there are an integer \(k\geq1\), rational initial values \(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\), and rational functions
\[F_{i}=P_{i}/Q_{i}\in\mathbb Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\qquad(1\leq i\leq k)\]
that generate a state sequence \(\mathbf z_{n}\in\mathbb Q^{k}\) by
\[\mathbf z_{0}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}),\qquad
z_{n+1,i}=F_{i}(\mathbf z_{n}),\qquad u_{n}=z_{n,1}.\]
All components are updated simultaneously from the preceding state. Each \(P_{i},Q_{i}\) is a finite polynomial with rational coefficients, \(Q_{i}\) is not the zero polynomial, and \(Q_{i}(\mathbf z_{n})\ne0\) for every \(i,n\). The other coordinates are auxiliary sequences.

The proposed scalar recurrence uses only the last \(d\) values of \(u\), in their stated order. Its coefficients are rational constants. It has no separate access to the index \(n\), the hidden coordinates, an externally supplied clock, or a rule that changes with \(n\). The first \(d\) actual values of \(u\) are its initial data.

The quantifiers permit \(d,A,B\) to depend on the entire sequence, including the original rational initial values. They must then work at every step. There is no requirement for one scalar recurrence to work uniformly for all initial vectors of a given mutual-update system, and no prescribed bound on \(d\), degree or coefficient size.

Denominators must be nonzero at every state or scalar window where the chosen fraction is evaluated. Algebraic cancellation may be used when choosing a fraction representation, but a recurrence is not allowed to evaluate \(0/0\), assign it an arbitrary value, or switch formulas to handle exceptional windows. The scalar recurrence must hold from \(n=0\), after its initial \(d\) values, rather than only on an unspecified eventual tail.

The claim is semantic existence of a finite recurrence over \(\mathbb Q\). It does not require an algorithm for finding one, a time bound for conversion, or an algorithm that checks whether an arbitrary proposed rational-update system avoids division by zero. The input class already consists of systems whose entire orbit is defined.

A scalar recurrence can always be expressed as a finite mutual system by retaining its finitely many preceding values as state. Thus the displayed direction is precisely the missing direction in the source’s equality of the two sequence classes.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed recurrence exists for every well-defined rationally recursive sequence over \(\mathbb Q\), or give such a sequence and prove that no finite \(d\) and no rational function with nonvanishing denominators along its windows can generate it in this way. A recurrence only for generic initial conditions, an implicit polynomial relation, or a rule with exceptional undefined evaluations does not settle the conjecture.
context:
For linear updates, finite mutual systems can be represented by single finite-depth linear recurrences. For polynomial updates the corresponding statement fails: the source recalls polynomially recursive sequences that have no single polynomial recurrence. Allowing division gives a distinct conjecture about expressive power.

Theorem 6 establishes a scalar rational recurrence when the original initial values are independent formal variables and the evolving values are rational functions of those variables. This is a theorem over a function field. It does not cover every fixed rational specialization of the initial vector.

The source explicitly explains why its symbolic result does not prove Conjecture 1: a denominator in the resulting scalar recurrence may vanish after substituting particular rational initial values, even when the original mutual system remains well-defined. An identity obtained by clearing denominators also need not specify a valid next value at those windows.

The source relates an effective version of the collapse to checking whether polynomially recursive sequences are identically zero and whether two such sequences agree everywhere. Those consequences require a suitable constructive conversion; they should not be built into this purely existential conjecture.
why: Asks whether auxiliary state increases the expressive power of rational recurrences, or whether finite memory of the observed sequence always suffices. It is a basic structural question about discrete algebraic dynamics and the sequence models underlying weighted and polynomial automata.
status_note: Read the full conference Conjecture 1, rational-recursion definitions, Theorem 6 and its specialization discussion, and the corresponding author-version formulation. Checked arXiv revision history and searched through 12 September 2026 for subsequent work; no resolution of the rational-initial-value collapse was found. The symbolic theorem, implicit polynomial identities and efficient conversion are kept distinct from the stated existence claim.
progress: 2022-10-04: The author preprint states the collapse conjecture and proves a variant with symbolic initial conditions. | 2023: The STACS paper publishes the symbolic theorem while retaining the rational-initial-value conjecture and explaining the specialization obstruction.
working_summary: A rationally recursive sequence is one coordinate of a finite system whose next state is a rational function of its current state. The conjecture asks whether finitely many past values of that coordinate always suffice to generate its next value. All coefficients and initial values are rational, and every denominator must remain nonzero along the sequence. A scalar recurrence may depend on the particular initial vector, but must work at every step. The known theorem with symbolic initial values does not settle the numerical case because specialization can make its denominators vanish.
