title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
importance_reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.
focus_reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
context:
Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.
why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.
status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

working_summary: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals asks whether an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial has a zero consisting of exact rational numbers. The target requires one deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides this for every number of variables, degree and coefficient size. There is no efficiency requirement, and merely enumerating rational solutions does not decide instances with no solution. Undecidability over integers, universal definitions and results with extra height predicates have different logical or arithmetic scope. Recent advances over rings of integers preserve that distinction, and the checked sources do not settle the rational-solvability question.

title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
importance_reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.
focus_reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(C>0\) and a classical randomized algorithm A running in polynomial time such that, for every rank-n rational lattice basis B, A outputs a nonzero integer vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\le n^{C} \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L}(B))\) with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Q} ^{d\times n}, d\ge n\ge 1\), with linearly independent columns. Each rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\}\) is the lattice, and \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{2}:0\ne v\in \mathrm{L}\}\) is the length of a shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean norm \(\Vert v\Vert _{2}=(\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\). Rank n, rather than ambient dimension d or coefficient magnitude, controls the approximation factor. There must be one polynomial P such that every run halts in at most \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L})\) bit operations, where L is the input’s total bit length; output bits and random bits are counted. Randomness consists of independent fair bits. Require z to be a nonzero integer vector on every run, while the length guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\). Both P and C are independent of all input parameters. There are no distributional, uniqueness, conditioning, ideal-lattice or basis-quality promises. A deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The one-dimensional case is exactly solvable by a basis vector. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A lattice basis can disguise very short vectors as cancellations between long columns. For example, \(b_{1}=(N,1)\) and \(b_{2}=(N+1,1)\) both have length about N, while \(b_{2}- b_{1}=(1,0)\) has length one. Simply selecting the shortest input column therefore has no dimension-only approximation guarantee. Basis reduction changes the representation without changing the lattice, aiming to expose short integer combinations.

The LLL algorithm solves a major version of this task in polynomial bit time: with the standard reduction parameter, it finds a nonzero vector within \(2^{(n- 1)/2}\) of the shortest length. The factor is exponential in rank, even though the running time is polynomial. This was enough to transform computational number theory and enable applications such as factoring rational polynomials, but it leaves the much stronger approximation asked for here open.

Block reduction improves the quality by solving shorter-vector problems in projected sublattices of limited rank. The best general polynomial-time guarantees summarized by Bennett have approximation factor \(2^{O(n \log  \log  n/\log  n)}\). That is smaller than the basic LLL factor but still grows faster than every fixed power of n. Larger blocks improve approximation at the cost of more expensive local computations; a polynomial number of calls to an expensive subroutine does not imply polynomial total time.

Known hardness results approach, but do not reach, the polynomial-factor regime. Haviv and Regev show that approximation within \(2^{(\log  n)^{1- \delta}}\), for fixed \(\delta >0\), cannot be polynomial time unless NP has randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Stronger assumptions give further nearly polynomial factors. Every such factor must be read with its quantifiers: hardness for a smaller approximation factor concerns a more demanding task and does not eliminate the possibility of a much looser \(n^{c}\) approximation.

Decision and search also need care. GapSVP distinguishes \(\lambda _{1}\le r\) from \(\lambda _{1}>\gamma r\), with no requirement on intermediate inputs. Aharonov and Regev place the decision problem with \(\gamma =O(\sqrt{n})\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\), using short certificates on both sides. This is strong evidence about its structural complexity and a barrier to certain NP-hardness proofs. It is not a polynomial-time search algorithm that finds a short lattice vector.

The intermediate approximation regime is central to lattice cryptography. Worst-case to average-case reductions relate particular polynomial-factor lattice problems to problems such as SIS and LWE at specified parameters. These implications have a direction: an efficient worst-case algorithm would invalidate the corresponding hardness premise, but the existence of a security reduction alone would not prove that every deployed cryptosystem is broken. The exponent, problem variant and cryptographic parameters all matter.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 PotBKZ algorithm guarantees termination after a polynomial number of calls to its potential-reducing enumeration routine. This improves control of the reduction process, including a self-dual variant. It does not give a polynomial-time polynomial-factor approximation for arbitrary rank, because the cost and quality of the block enumeration must still be accounted for.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s August 2026 preprint improves the randomness properties of lattice hardness reductions. Under a stated exponential lower-bound assumption for nondeterministic circuits, they obtain deterministic NP-hardness reductions for every constant Euclidean approximation factor. Both qualifications matter: the derandomization is conditional, and the approximation factors are constants, rather than all polynomial factors. Their separate parameterized hardness results also use a different resource measure.

The question isolates the large gap between useful reduction algorithms and the approximation range used in fundamental hardness assumptions. Even an algorithm with a very large fixed exponent C would be a major qualitative advance; the target does not demand exact SVP or a small approximation constant.
why: A central algorithmic gap in lattice complexity: known polynomial-time methods give superpolynomial approximation factors, while key computational and cryptographic questions lie in the polynomial-factor regime.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No classical polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed polynomial approximation factor was found for unrestricted Euclidean search SVP. Recent termination guarantees count costly subroutine calls, and the August conditional hardness theorem concerns constant factors. The card explicitly allows bounded-error classical randomization.

The reviewed question asks for polynomial-time approximation within some fixed polynomial in the lattice rank. Long basis vectors can cancel to form much shorter vectors, so the input representation hides the relevant geometry. Reaching polynomial factors would close a major gap between general reduction algorithms and fundamental lattice-hardness regimes. The saved review separates subexponential approximation factors, decision certificates, and constant-factor hardness from the requested polynomial-factor search guarantee.

title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
importance_reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
context:
Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.
why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.
status_note: The undated source survey explicitly asks for randomized polynomial-time factoring, and Harvey–Hittmeir Section 1.1 in the 5 June 2026 revision confirms the absence of a known polynomial-time factoring algorithm even with probabilistic methods. Bounded later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The cited heuristic estimate and quantum result are not certified as solutions in this classical model, and new proof claims were not independently verified.

The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length. | 2026-06-05: Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.
working_summary: Integer factorization recovers the ordered primes and positive multiplicities whose product is a given positive integer. The question asks for one classical randomized algorithm taking polynomial time in the number of input bits on every random sequence. Its full factor list must be correct with probability at least two thirds separately on every positive input. Efficient primality testing and verification do not resolve the task of finding the factors. Known quantum algorithms, heuristic sieve estimates and improved deterministic subroutines each leave a different gap to this target.

title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
importance_reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.
formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every prime p, every generator g of the multiplicative group \(F_{p}\)*, and every \(h\in F_{p}\)*, returns the unique integer \(x\in \{0,\ldots ,p- 2\}\) satisfying \(g^{x}\equiv h\) (mod p), with probability at least \(2/3\) and worst-case running time polynomial in \(\log _{2}p\)?
definitions: The input consists of ordinary binary integers \((p,g,h)\), with p prime and \(1\le g,h\le p- 1\), promised that g has multiplicative order \(p- 1\). Set \(n=\lceil \log _{2}(p+1)\rceil\); the total input length is \(\Theta (n)\). A single probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(C(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations on every random tape, for fixed constants C,c independent of p,g,h. It may output failure on unsuccessful runs. Success probability is over its own independent fair random bits and must be at least \(2/3\) separately on every promised input. Its only input is \((p,g,h)\): no factorization of \(p- 1\), precomputed logarithm table, advice, special-form description of p, or oracle is supplied. Any preprocessing it performs counts in its runtime. The algorithm may exploit the ordinary integer encoding and all efficiently computable arithmetic modulo p; it is not restricted to generic group operations. The group is multiplication of nonzero residues, not an elliptic-curve group or the additive group. For \(p=2\) the only logarithm is \(x=0\).
answer_criterion: Give and prove a classical algorithm with the specified uniform polynomial worst-case time and per-instance success guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A generic-group lower bound, a fast algorithm for a restricted family of primes, a quantum algorithm, or a polynomial bound in p rather than log p does not settle the question.
context:
Computing \(g^{x}\) mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as \(p- 2\). The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute \(g^{x}\) mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form \(\exp (O((\ln  p)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  p)^{2/3}))\). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound \((p\cdot d)^{2\log _{2}d+O(1)}\) for discrete logarithms in \(F_{p^{d}}\). For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields \(d=1\) and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.
why: A fundamental inversion problem in computational number theory and a central candidate for separating efficient classical from quantum computation. Its resolution would clarify which arithmetic structure can overcome generic group barriers and would reshape finite-field cryptographic assumptions.
status_note: Open in the cited computational-number-theory literature; checked through 10 September 2026. No uniform classical polynomial-in-log-p solver or unrestricted exclusion was found. The card keeps heuristic sieve analyses, fixed-characteristic extension fields, reusable preprocessing, and quantum algorithms separate.
progress: 1990s: Number-field-sieve methods give heuristic subexponential algorithms for prime-field discrete logarithms; their arithmetic relations go beyond the generic group model. | 1994–1997: Shor gives quantum polynomial-time algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms. The classical requirement in this question is essential. | 1997: Shoup proves square-root lower bounds for generic group algorithms, parameterized by the largest prime factor of the group order. These are model-restricted lower bounds. | 2019–2022: Kleinjung and Wesolowski prove quasipolynomial expected time for fixed-characteristic finite fields. Their theorem does not give polynomial time in log p for the prime-field family. | 2024: Al Aswad, Thomé, and Pierrot develop the Discrete Logarithm Factory approach to sharing sieve computations, while continuing to describe NFS variants as the leading methods outside small characteristic.
working_summary: A discrete logarithm in a prime field asks which exponent of a supplied generator produces a target nonzero residue. The question seeks a classical randomized algorithm with running time polynomial in log p for every promised input. Exponentiation is efficient, but reversing it requires identifying one exponent among \(p- 1\) possibilities. A solution would remove a foundational computational asymmetry used in finite-field cryptography. The saved review distinguishes prime fields from fixed-characteristic extension fields and explains why generic-group lower bounds do not rule out algorithms exploiting the concrete arithmetic of residues.

title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
importance_reason: A foundational quantum-algorithm question with broad relevance to lattice complexity and computational cryptography. The model and accuracy combination is distinct from both existing classical approximation and quantum exact-search cards.
formal: Do there exist a constant \(C>0\) and a uniform quantum algorithm A with polynomial running time such that, for every rational matrix \(B\in Q^{d\times n}\) with \(d\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, A outputs a nonzero \(z\in Z^{n}\) satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\le n^{C} \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L}(B))\) with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The full matrix, dimensions and every rational entry are given classically; rationals use signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Let N be the total encoding length. \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}, \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{2}:0\ne v\in \mathrm{L}\}\), and \(\Vert v\Vert _{2}=(\sum_{i} v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\). Approximation depends on rank n rather than the ambient dimension d or N. Use a uniform quantum circuit computation with classical polynomial-time control, polynomially many qubits initially in computational basis states, gates \(H=2^{- 1/2}[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\) and CNOT, and computational-basis measurements with classical feed-forward. The classical input bits may be copied into input qubits. One polynomial \(p(N)\) bounds total classical bit operations, gate applications, measurements and output bits on every branch. Classical control and circuit generation are uniform in the input length and use no advice or oracle; a unit-cost quantum random-access oracle for the input is not supplied. The output is a binary-encoded integer coefficient vector, required to be nonzero on every branch; the norm guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\). The constants C and p are independent of all inputs. There is no uniqueness, average-case, ideal-lattice, modular or conditioning promise.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
A short lattice vector may be hidden by cancellation among much longer basis columns. The task is to find an integer combination with length bounded relative to the shortest possible nonzero combination. Allowing a factor \(n^{C}\) is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search, yet remains far stronger than the guarantees of basic polynomial-time lattice reduction.

The existing TCS-6667 asks the same approximate search question for a classical randomized algorithm. TCS-7169 instead asks about a quantum algorithm for exact SVP. This card distinguishes the missing intermediate combination: quantum computation with a polynomial approximation factor. A classical solution of the matching approximation target would qualify here, but a quantum solution would not automatically give a classical one.

Regev’s worst-case to average-case reduction connects specified GapSVP and SIVP tasks to Learning With Errors. Its consequence has a direction: a suitable efficient LWE solver yields quantum algorithms for the lattice tasks in the theorem. It does not establish an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE parameter family.

The distinction matters for interpretation of a breakthrough. An algorithm satisfying this card would substantially change our understanding of quantum lattice reduction. Its effect on a particular cryptographic assumption would still depend on the approximation exponent, the exact lattice problem and the reduction parameters. Merely naming LWE is insufficient to infer that every parameter choice has been broken.

Rank and bit length are separate variables. Increasing coefficients must not be mistaken for increasing the allowed approximation factor, and a polynomial algorithm must include the cost of reading and manipulating their binary representations. The specified gate model permits ordinary quantum computation while excluding an additional oracle resource hidden in a data-access convention.
why: Isolate the potential power of quantum computation in the central polynomial-factor regime of worst-case lattice approximation.
status_note: No general quantum polynomial-time algorithm with a fixed polynomial approximation factor was found through 11 September 2026. This status is about the specified worst-case search target, not a claim about all LWE formulations.
progress: 2005–2009: Regev establishes a quantum worst-case-to-average-case reduction involving GapSVP, SIVP and LWE at specified parameters. | 2023: Bennett’s survey documents the large unresolved polynomial-factor region in general SVP complexity. | 2024-01-08: The posted Regev version preserves the earlier theorem, with a proof correction, rather than announcing a new lattice algorithm.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
importance_reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.
formal: Do absolute constants \(C,d>0\) and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(2^{Cn}\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bit operations and \(\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bits of working space?
definitions: The input is \(B\in Q^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}\), and \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )=\min\)_{\(z\in Z^{n}\)\{0}}\(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\), with the ordinary Euclidean norm in \(R^{m}\). Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}=\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking \(2^{\Theta (n \log  n)}\) time leave the question open.
context:
The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is \(n^{O(n)}\). Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve \(2^{O(n)}\) time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: \(n^{cn}=2^{cn \log _{2}n}\). For any fixed C, the factor \(\log _{2}n\) eventually makes \(n^{cn}\) exceed \(2^{Cn}\). Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time \(2^{100n}\) would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For \(B=I, a\) shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to \(O(n)\). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage \(O((M+K)n)\) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a \(2^{O(n)}\) iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some \(2^{Cn}\)-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.
why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?
status_note: Open for exact Euclidean SVP with the simultaneous worst-case time and space bounds stated here, following primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 sheaf-based proposal discusses a memory-saving regime but does not establish the required uniform exact-success and runtime theorem. Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.
progress: 1983–1987: Kannan obtains exact lattice algorithms using \(n^{O(n)}\) time and polynomial space. | 2001: Ajtai–Kumar–Sivakumar obtain randomized single-exponential-time SVP with exponential space, as described in the inherited paper. | 2007: Hanrot–Stehlé sharpen the enumeration analysis to \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) for SVP, retaining polynomial space. | 2010–2013: Micciancio–Voulgaris establish deterministic Voronoi-cell algorithms; the March 2012 revision gives roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, followed by the SIAM journal publication. | 2015: Micciancio–Walter reduce enumeration preprocessing overhead while retaining the \(n^{O(n)}\) time scale. | 2026-01-06: Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel discuss a coarse-grained polynomial-memory sieving regime; a general exact-success and single-exponential-time guarantee for that regime is not established in the inspected analysis. | 2026: Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite connect hinted-ISIS algorithms to polynomial-memory single-exponential algorithms for broader lattice tasks, relying on rather than proving time-space hardness.
working_summary: Exact Euclidean SVP asks for a shortest nonzero vector in a lattice given by a rational basis. The question seeks single-exponential time in the rank together with polynomial working space. Known fast approaches retain exponentially much geometric information, while small-memory enumeration has a larger worst-case time scale. Combining both resources would clarify whether memory is essential to the strongest exact lattice algorithms. The saved review requires every stored bit and all recomputation to count, and does not treat heuristic memory reductions or unverified framework proposals as a proof of the universal guarantee.

title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
importance_reason: A classical barrier in effective number theory governing the deterministic search for basic finite-field witnesses.
formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.
context:
Tao states the conjecture with a constant depending on the chosen exponent and records the general unconditional Burgess bound \(n(p)=O_\eta(p^{1/(4\sqrt e)+\eta})\) for every \(\eta>0\), where \(e=\exp(1)\). That fixed positive base exponent does not imply the conjecture.

The introduction records Ankeny’s stronger \(O((\log p)^2)\) bound under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It also notes results for almost all primes. Both are separated from the unconditional all-primes target.

Tao’s Theorem 1.3 proves that the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture on primes in arithmetic progressions implies Vinogradov’s conjecture. This is a conditional implication, not an unconditional resolution.

Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides continue to display the Burgess exponent as the unconditional bound. The following slide discusses a better constant in a logarithmic-square estimate and explicitly assumes GRH. That improvement therefore does not settle the statement here.
why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.
status_note: Tao’s Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 and Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides 14–15 were checked on 2026-09-14. The latter retains the unconditional Burgess bound and explicitly labels its stronger recent bound as conditional on GRH. A bounded search including 2026 work found no matching unconditional all-primes resolution. This is source-open status with those limits.
progress: 1952: Ankeny’s conditional logarithmic-square upper bound, as recorded in Tao’s introduction, shows that GRH implies substantially more than the target. | 2015: Tao publishes the implication from Elliott–Halberstam to Vinogradov’s least-nonresidue conjecture. | 2025-06: Quesada-Herrera distinguishes the unconditional Burgess bound from a new GRH-conditional improvement in the logarithmic-square constant.
working_summary: A quadratic nonresidue is a nonzero residue that is not a square modulo the prime. Vinogradov’s conjecture says that the least positive one eventually lies below every fixed positive power of the prime. The threshold may depend on the exponent, but the bound must cover every sufficiently large odd prime. Conditional logarithmic-square estimates and almost-all-prime results do not establish this unconditional statement. A refutation would require one fixed positive exponent and arbitrarily large primes violating its bound.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
importance_reason: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.
formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every integer matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Z} ^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs \(z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}\) satisfying ||\(Bz||_{2}=\min _{y\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}}||\)By||\(_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) elementary steps on every execution? L is the total binary encoding length of m, d and all entries of B.
definitions: The lattice generated by B is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\}; d\) is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals \(\lambda _{1}^{2}\), rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from \(1^{\mathrm{L}}, a\) circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT maps |\(a,b\rangle\) to |\(a,a\oplus b\rangle\). Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.
context:
The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.
why: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.
status_note: No polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the exact-search target was found through 11 September 2026. The checked August exact-SVP preprints claim exponential improvements, and the disputed DCP proposal concerns approximate SVP. Classical NP-hardness does not resolve the quantum target. Recent proofs and the response’s linked Lean development were not independently audited.

title: Quantum-ETH hardness of cryptographic-factor GapSVP
importance_reason: Standard-assumption hardness at cryptographic approximation factors would strengthen the foundations of lattice-based cryptography.
formal:
Does the quantum Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that, for some fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is no bounded-error uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm for Euclidean
\[\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k(n)=n^{3/2+1/k}?\]
Equivalently, the target is the conditional assertion
\[\mathrm{QETH}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k}\notin\mathrm{PromiseBQP}.\]
The source asks for hardness at \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) under a standard complexity assumption, without selecting that assumption. This card explicitly selects quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT; it is an editorial variant of that research direction, not a claim that the source stated this particular implication.
definitions:
An instance consists of an integer \(n\ge1\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational threshold \(r\). The columns of \(B\) form a full-rank lattice basis. Its lattice and shortest-vector length are
\[\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad \lambda_1(B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,\]
where \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum exists and is positive for a nonsingular basis. No ideal-lattice, module-lattice, random-lattice or special-basis promise is imposed.

The promise problem has YES instances with \(\lambda_1(B)\le r\) and NO instances with \(\lambda_1(B)>\gamma_k(n)r\). Either condition is promised. For \(r<\lambda_1(B)\le\gamma_k(n)r\), either answer is allowed. This preserves the source’s strict inequality on the NO side. The task is deciding the promise, not outputting a short vector. The dimension in the approximation factor is \(n\), not the bit length of the matrix entries.

Use a binary encoding of \(n\), the matrix entries and \(r\), each rational represented by its signed reduced numerator and positive denominator, with self-delimiting lengths. Let \(L\) denote the total input bit length. A quantum polynomial-time solver is one finite uniform quantum algorithm, for the fixed chosen \(k\), which uses at most \(C(L+1)^a\) elementary operations for constants \(C,a\) on every branch, and returns the correct promise answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every YES and every NO instance. It must halt on all inputs within the time bound; malformed encodings, singular matrices and inputs outside the promise require no particular answer. This is the meaning of \(\mathrm{PromiseBQP}\) here. The program and polynomial may depend on \(k\), which is not an instance parameter.

For definiteness, uniform quantum computation uses a classical Turing controller, qubits initially in computational-basis states, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), and computational-basis measurements with the Born probabilities. On one qubit, \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\). The controlled-not gate maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Classical tape work, input reading, generation of gate instructions, gate applications and measurements are charged. The algorithm has no advice, external oracle, uncharged quantum state or postselection. Adaptive classical control and classical randomization obtained by measurement are allowed.

Quantum ETH in this card is a statement about classical Boolean satisfiability. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three signed Boolean variables. It is satisfiable if some assignment makes every clause true. Let \(N\) be its number of variables and \(s\) its binary encoding length. The assumption asserts that there exists \(\delta>0\) for which no uniform quantum algorithm decides satisfiability on every such formula, with error at most \(1/3\), in time \(C2^{\delta N}(s+1)^a\) for any fixed constants \(C,a\). Time is worst-case over inputs and measurement outcomes, in the same uniform quantum model. This uses the positive exponential-rate formulation of Definition 4.25 in the cited quantum complexity paper; it is not a hypothesis about the quantum satisfiability or local-Hamiltonian problem.

The exponent increment is fixed before instances or candidate solvers are considered. Writing it as \(1/k\) loses no existence case from an arbitrary constant \(\varepsilon>0\): choosing \(1/k\le\varepsilon\) only reduces the approximation factor, and a solver for the smaller factor also solves the larger-factor promise. The source’s alternative LWE target is not bundled into this card. No lattice-hardness or cryptographic-security assumption is available in addition to the stated quantum ETH premise.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed conditional assertion with these encodings, norm, approximation factor and uniform quantum model. A positive answer may assume quantum ETH as defined but must establish the claimed exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms, rather than assume hardness of GapSVP or LWE. It must obtain a fixed positive exponent increment and cover all promised rational-basis inputs. A lower bound only for classical algorithms, a constant-factor approximation problem, another norm, or exact SVP alone does not establish this target. Refuting the conditional assertion requires more than showing that one proposed reduction fails; likewise, refuting quantum ETH alone would make the implication vacuously true rather than false.
context:

The named assumption is left open by the author; selecting the quantum 3-SAT hypothesis makes this card’s proof obligation concrete.

title: Baillie–PSW pseudoprimes
importance_reason: Tests the mathematical reliability of a widely used primality-testing combination.
formal: Does there exist a composite integer n that passes the strong base-2 probable-prime test and the strong Lucas probable-prime test with Selfridge’s Method A, including the parameter-search rejection rule specified below?
definitions: A composite integer is an integer \(n>1\) with a divisor strictly between 1 and n. Even integers greater than 2 and perfect squares are rejected; thus a candidate here is odd and nonsquare. Write \(n- 1=2^{s} d\) with d odd. The strong base-2 test accepts if \(2^{d}\equiv 1\) (mod n), or \(2^{2^{r} d}\equiv - 1\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<s\). For the Lucas test, examine \(D=5,- 7,9,- 11,13,- 15,\ldots\) in that order, namely \(D_{k}=(- 1)^{k}(2k+5)\) for \(k\ge 0\). At each step reject if \(1<\gcd (|D|,n)<n\); otherwise stop at the first D with Jacobi symbol \((D/n)=- 1\). For odd \(n=\prod p_{j}^{e_{j}}\), the Jacobi symbol \((a/n)\) is \(\prod (a/p_{j})^{e}_{j}\), where \((a/p)\) is 0 if p divides a, +1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and −1 otherwise. This defines the symbol without requiring factorization as an implementation. Squares were excluded because their Jacobi symbols cannot be −1; for odd nonsquares the search terminates. Set \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). Define integer sequences \(U_{0}=0, U_{1}=1, V_{0}=2, V_{1}=\mathrm{P}\) and, for \(j\ge 0, U_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} U_{j+1}- Q U_{j}\) and \(V_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} V_{j+1}- Q V_{j}\). Write \(n+1=2^{t} u\) with u odd. The strong Lucas test accepts if \(U_{u}\equiv 0\) (mod n), or \(V_{2^{r} u}\equiv 0\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<t\). Passing means surviving the parameter search and satisfying both strong tests, with exact integer congruences. The number 2 is accepted separately but cannot answer this composite-existence question. No extra trial-division cutoff, random bases or additional congruence checks are part of the specified variant.
answer_criterion: Give a composite n together with a proof of compositeness and exact verification of the parameter search and both acceptance conditions, or prove that no composite integer passes this specified variant. A finite search bound, a heuristic count of expected counterexamples or a counterexample to only one component does not settle the question.
context:
A composite can imitate some arithmetic properties of primes. For example, \(2047=23\cdot 89\) passes the strong base-2 test because \(2^{1023}\equiv 1\) modulo 2047. It fails the strong Lucas test with \(D=5\). The question is whether a composite can evade both parts together, however large it is.

Selfridge’s Method A fixes \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). The main source also describes Method A*, which changes P and Q to 5 when \(D=5\), and proves equivalence of the strong Lucas outcomes for integers coprime to 10. Its proposed strengthened test adds further congruences. This card keeps the imported strong base-2 plus strong Lucas target and spells out Method A.

The 2021 paper reports that no base-2 Fermat pseudoprime below \(2^{64}\) also passes its Lucas test, giving correctness through that finite range and hence ruling out smaller counterexamples to the strong combination. It reports no known larger counterexample. Such a bound leaves the existence question over all integers unanswered.

A January 2026 preprint reports that all 200 selected composites in its experiment fail the strong Lucas test despite passing several Miller–Rabin bases. This does not establish correctness for arbitrary integers or a rigorous independence theorem for the two tests. With the specified parameters, the test’s outcome on a fixed n is deterministic; “probable prime” describes the strength of the conclusion, not random choices made here.

title: Scholz–Brauer conjecture
importance_reason: The Scholz–Brauer conjecture is a longstanding universal law proposed for optimal addition chains, linking a basic arithmetic complexity measure across all exponents.
formal: For every positive integer n, is \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell (n)\), where \(\ell\)\((m)\) is the minimum length of an addition chain for m?
definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=m\) such that, for each \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,r\}\), there exist \(j,k\in \{0,\ldots ,i- 1\}\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}\). The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define \(\ell\)\((m)\) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because \(1,2,\ldots ,m\) is an allowed chain, and \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation \(a_{i}=a_{i- 1}+a_{j}\) with \(j<i\). Write \(\ell\)*\((m)\) for its minimum length. Thus \(\ell\)\((m)\le \ell *(m)\); the conjecture uses the unrestricted \(\ell\) on both sides. The integer \(2^{n}- 1\) has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes \(n=1\).
answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)>n- 1+\ell (n)\). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.
context:
An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once \(x^{a}\) and \(x^{b}\) have been computed, one multiplication produces \(x^{a+b}\). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of \(x^{m}\) with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For \(n=5\), the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for \(2^{5}- 1=31\) is therefore \(5- 1+3=7\). The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are \(24+6\) and \(30+1\). Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is \(n- 1\), with only \(\ell\)\((n)\) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives \(\ell\)*\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell *(n)\). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing \(\ell\)*\((n)\) by the potentially smaller \(\ell\)\((n)\) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of \(n\le N\) satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for \(2^{n}- 1\) being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing \(\ell\)\((n)\). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.
why: The conjecture predicts a precise relationship between optimal multiplication plans for an exponent and for its associated all-ones binary integer. Its restricted-chain theorem shows that the unresolved issue concerns how the freedom to reuse older values affects the best possible length.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. Wallner’s April 2026 paper still presents the unrestricted inequality as open. Later May and August 2026 preprints located in the search make density-one or restricted-optimal-chain claims, rather than covering every positive integer. No general resolution was found. Published special-case statements and preprint claims were read at the recorded depth; proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 1939: Brauer proves the inequality for the minimum star-chain length ℓ*, as recorded in Wallner’s Section 7. | 2024-05-27: Tall, Theorems 2–4, proves the conjecture for a specified infinite family with seven binary ones and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and for its doubles. | 2026-04-25: Wallner states the unrestricted Scholz–Brauer inequality among open addition-chain problems and distinguishes the star-chain result. | 2026-05-03: Agama’s preprint claims asymptotic density one and explicitly leaves the uniform all-integers version unanswered; not independently proof-audited. | 2026-08-06: Agama’s later preprint abstract claims the inequality for integers with an optimal chain in its quasi-closed class; abstract-only review.
working_summary: An addition chain starts at one and builds its target by repeatedly adding two already available values. Its length counts additions and corresponds to the number of multiplications in the associated repeated-power computation. The conjecture asks whether the minimum length for \(2^{n}- 1\) is always at most \(n- 1\) plus the minimum length for n. The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources. Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.

definitions: An input consists of integers \(d\ge r\ge 1, a\) rational \(d\times r\) matrix B with linearly independent columns, and a positive rational threshold R. title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
importance_reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.
