formal: Determine \(F(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2},\lambda )=\sup _{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2})}[\lambda R_{1}+(1- \lambda )R_{2}]\) for every \(a,b\in \mathbb{R}\), finite \(\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2}\ge 0\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). Here C is the capacity region of \(Y_{1},t=X_{1},t+aX_{2},t+Z_{1},t\) and \(Y_{2},t=bX_{1},t+X_{2},t+Z_{2},t\) with independent messages, average power constraints, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing average decoding error, as defined below.
definitions: For a block of n uses, messages \(M_{i}\) are independent and uniform on \(\{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\). Transmitter i applies a deterministic encoder \(f_{i,n}:\{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\to \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) depending only on its own message. Its codebook satisfies \((nK_{i,n})^{- 1}\sum _{m=1}^{K_{i,n}}\sum _{t=1}^{n} f_{i,n}(m)_{t}^{2}\le \mathrm{P}_{i}\). All \(Z_{i,t}\) are mutually independent \(N(0,1)\) random variables independent of the messages. Receiver i applies a measurable decoder \(g_{i,n}:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\) to its own received vector. The probability that either decoded message is wrong is averaged over both messages and all noise. A nonnegative pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with this error tending to zero and \(\liminf _{n\to \infty} n^{- 1} \log _{2} K_{i,n}\ge R_{i}\) for \(i=1,2\). C is the closure of achievable pairs, measured in bits per real channel use. Gains, powers and both codebooks are known to all terminals. Arbitrary encoding across time and predetermined time sharing with power allocation are permitted; transmitters have no messages in common, output feedback, or communication between them. C is compact, convex and downward closed, so the nonnegative supporting function F uniquely determines it.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real a,b, all finite real \(\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2}\ge 0\), and all real \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- F(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2},\lambda )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
context:
Two independent conversations share the same medium: each receiver sees its desired signal, a scaled version of the other sender’s signal, and Gaussian noise. With only one sender, Shannon’s formula gives the rate ½ \(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P})\). With two senders, improving one link can make the other harder to decode. The mathematical object is therefore a two-dimensional region of feasible rate pairs. Knowing its largest total rate does not identify all tradeoffs between the users.

Han–Kobayashi coding splits each message into a part decoded by both receivers and a private part decoded only by its intended receiver. It includes treating interference as noise and decoding interference as special strategies. Time sharing can also allocate different powers to different phases while meeting the average constraints. Shang and Chen’s monograph organizes these inner bounds and the exact results in particular regimes, including the distinction between full regions and sum-rate capacity.

Strong interference is a solved benchmark. When |\(a|\ge 1\) and |\(b|\ge 1\), the capacity region consists of \(R_{1}\le\)½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{1}), R_{2}\le\)½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{2})\), and \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le \min\){½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{1}+a^{2}\mathrm{P}_{2})\),½\(\log _{2}(1+b^{2}\mathrm{P}_{1}+\mathrm{P}_{2})\)}. Both receivers can decode both messages. With \(a=b=0\), the region is the rectangle given by the two individual bounds. These exact cases anchor the question but do not characterize arbitrary interference strengths.

Etkin, Tse and Wang show that a simple Han–Kobayashi strategy and new converse bounds locate the general region within a universal additive gap. Their celebrated one-bit theorem also gives high-signal-to-noise insights. A fixed gap can be extremely useful for system design while leaving the exact boundary unknown: it does not shrink merely because longer codes are allowed.

Recent work separates several different Gaussian-optimality questions. Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 result identifies a substantial parameter range in the one-sided, or Z, channel where the optimized Gaussian-signaling region needs no multiplexing. This optimizes a particular achievable region; it does not prove that no other signaling distribution or coding strategy can do better.

Their January 2026 manuscript then shows that Gaussian distributions can be suboptimal within a single-phase Han–Kobayashi region when power control is disallowed. Its Conjecture 1 still asks whether Gaussian signaling with power control achieves full Z-channel capacity. Remark 2 reports difficulty verifying parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim. The counterexamples concern the restricted single-phase statement and do not disprove optimality after the allowed power allocation and time sharing.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 work combines auxiliary-receiver and genie-aided converse techniques. Its Gaussian specialization captures known corner and sum-rate behavior, including associated changes in boundary slope. The theorem supplies an outer region rather than a general equality with an achievable region, so it advances the converse side without itself resolving the full target.

Khandani’s preprint, revised on 7 September 2026, makes a stronger claim: Gaussian Han–Kobayashi coding attains capacity throughout weak interference, with at most two time-sharing phases. This would settle a major part of the problem if established. The current revision has not been independently validated in this review. The earlier Nair–Zhao criticism predates it and cannot automatically be applied to every revised argument. This card therefore marks the present status as uncertain and records the claim explicitly.

The original short proposal cited a withdrawn paper by Huleihel and Merhav. Its claimed improvement using codewords with Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018. Nair and Ng subsequently establish that temporally correlated Gaussian inputs do not enlarge the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region once the comparison includes the appropriate scalar time sharing. The withdrawn result is retained only as a status correction, not as evidence of progress.
why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.
status_note: Status checked on 10 September 2026. Khandani arXiv:2501.14941v12 (7 September) claims capacity throughout weak interference. Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and disproves a restricted Gaussian-optimality statement without power control; that is not an adjudication of v12. This review has not established the correctness of the latest claim or a complete arbitrary-parameter characterization. Established partial results are separated from the claim. The original proposal’s arXiv:1508.05726 reference was withdrawn in 2018. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

working_summary: Two independent transmitters communicate through a real Gaussian channel in which each signal interferes with the other receiver. The power constraints average over uniform messages and channel uses, and neither feedback nor cooperation is supplied. The target is the weighted capacity as a function of both gains, both power limits and a weight between zero and one. Lean acceptance requires absolute error at most 0.01 bits per real channel use for every parameter choice. The saved uncertainty around recent weak-interference capacity claims remains separate from this editorial restoration.

title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
importance_reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.
focus_reason: The fundamental asymptotic binary coding tradeoff; its well-defined rate curve is restored as a distinct coding-theory focus alongside multiuser communication.
formal: Determine \(R_{2}(\delta )=\limsup _{n}\to \infty  (1/n)\log _{2} A_{2}(n,\lceil \delta n\rceil )\) for every fixed real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), where \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\); it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance \(d_{H}(x,y)\) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require \(d_{H}(x,y)\ge d\) for every pair of distinct codewords \(x,y\in C; a\) singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate \((\log _{2}|C|)/n\), measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance \(d/n\). The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. \(\delta\) is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is \(h_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\), with \(0 \log _{2}0=0\). The endpoint regimes are known: \(R_{2}(0)=1\) and \(R_{2}(\delta )=0\) for \(1/2\le \delta \le 1\).
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{2}(\delta )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve. For a lower bound \(\ell\)\((\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) arbitrarily large n admit codes of rate at least \(\ell\)\((\delta )- \varepsilon\) with distance at least \(\lceil \delta n\rceil\); for an upper bound \(u(\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) all sufficiently large n admit no such code of rate greater than \(u(\delta )+\varepsilon\). The proposed g must lie within \(1/100\) of the true rate throughout the domain, and polynomial-time construction or decoding is not required.
context:
A binary code represents messages by selected bit strings. Keeping codewords far apart lets a receiver distinguish them after errors, while selecting many codewords increases the amount of information carried by each transmitted block. The rate–distance function asks for the best possible compromise, allowing every conceivable code. It is therefore an information-theoretic limit that must be understood before asking how efficiently an optimal code can be built or decoded.

For a small example, the repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, so it corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The full set of eight three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, so it cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. Generally, disjoint Hamming balls of radius t around codewords are necessary and sufficient for unique correction of every pattern of at most t errors; this requires minimum distance at least \(2t+1\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees \(R_{2}(\delta )\ge 1- h_{2}(\delta )\). A maximal distance-d code covers the cube by balls of radius \(d- 1\), because otherwise another codeword could be inserted. Comparing the cube’s size with the volume of these balls gives the lower bound. In contrast, disjoint balls of radius roughly \(d/2\) give the elementary Hamming upper bound \(1- h_{2}(\delta /2)\). The different radii create a genuine asymptotic gap.

McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch’s 1977 linear-programming bounds greatly sharpen the converse. The first gives \(R_{2}(\delta )\le h_{2}(1/2- \sqrt{\delta (1- \delta )})\); the second also uses constant-weight restrictions and is never weaker. The argument constrains a code’s distribution of pairwise distances through positivity relations, extracting information that a volume count loses. These were the long-standing general benchmarks, but they are no longer the strongest reported bounds after August 2026.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s August 2026 preprint uses classical-input, quantum-output channels to prove stronger bounds for classical binary codes, including nonlinear codes. Mixed-qubit channels strictly improve the first MRRW bound, and a masked version strictly improves the second throughout \(0<\delta <1/2\). Quantum states enter the converse proof as an analytical tool; the codes whose sizes are bounded still consist of ordinary bit strings. The result narrows the gap without matching the Gilbert–Varshamov lower curve.

Barg’s September 2026 note explains the relationship between this channel argument and a concurrent Delsarte-certificate proof. For the improvement of the first bound, he shows that the two variational expressions coincide. The geometric change is to associate a moving subspace, rather than a single vector, with each codeword, allowing a stronger packing argument. This provides a further derivation and interpretation of the new bound; it does not establish the exact rate function.

Lower-bound improvements require equally careful interpretation. Jiang and Vardy improve the finite-length Gilbert bound by a factor proportional to n in the fixed-distance regime they cover. Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a concise probabilistic proof of a square-root-n improvement for linear codes and extends the method to quantum codes; the classical square-root factor had predecessors. After taking \(\log _{2}\) and dividing by n, any polynomial multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log  n/n)\). Such refinements do not increase the leading rate exponent.

Changing the error model also changes the answer. Capacity for independent random bit flips and capacity for list decoding are not the same quantity as the largest rate at a prescribed minimum distance. This card asks about worst-case pairwise separation with unrestricted binary codes. It also does not transfer improvements for sufficiently large alphabets directly to binary codes: changing alphabet and concatenating codes changes their rate and distance parameters.
why: The basic unresolved packing limit for reliable binary information. An exact answer would identify how much redundancy is intrinsically necessary for a prescribed worst-case separation, independently of algorithmic or algebraic restrictions on the code.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The August and September primary sources report genuine asymptotic upper-bound improvements beyond MRRW, but retain a gap above the binary GV lower curve. The exact function remains undetermined; polynomial multiplicative size improvements and results for other alphabets or coding models do not settle it. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
progress: 1952–1957: The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound yields the rate lower curve \(1- h_{2}(\delta )\). | 1977: MRRW establishes the two classical linear-programming upper bounds. | 2004: Jiang–Vardy improve code size by a polynomial factor without changing the leading asymptotic rate. | 2026-01-26: Yuan–Zhu give another proof of an improved linear-code GV factor and extend the method to quantum codes; the exponent remains unchanged. | 2026-08-10: Alrabiah–Guruswami report strict improvements to both MRRW upper bounds for arbitrary binary codes. | 2026-09-01: Barg relates the new channel and Delsarte approaches and identifies their coinciding first-bound optimization.
working_summary: A binary code is any subset of binary strings of one length with a prescribed minimum pairwise Hamming distance. The function \(R_{2}(\delta )\) is the limsup of the best achievable rate at relative distance \(\delta\). Determine this tradeoff for every real \(\delta\) between zero and one half, allowing nonlinear codes and arbitrary block lengths. The benchmark accepts a Lean-certified curve with absolute rate error at most 0.01 bits per transmitted bit. The original limsup convention and the distinction between existence and efficient coding are retained.

title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
importance_reason: A central multiuser capacity problem with a precisely defined rate region, decades of partial characterizations and recent challenges to the longstanding candidate inner bound.
formal: Determine the weighted capacity \(F(\mathrm{W},\lambda )=\sup \{\lambda R_{1}+(1- \lambda )R_{2}:(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(\mathrm{W})\}\) for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless broadcast channel W(y,z|x) with rational transition probabilities and every rational \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). \(C(\mathrm{W})\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, vanishing average decoding error, and no feedback. Determine this function with the certified numerical accuracy specified below.
definitions: The nonempty finite alphabets X,Y,Z and the full table of nonnegative rational numbers W(y,z|x), summing to one for each x, are explicitly given. Over n uses, the conditional law is \(\prod _{t=1}^{n} \mathrm{W}(y_{t},z_{t}|x_{t})\). Independent messages \(M_{1}\) and \(M_{2}\) are uniform on sets of sizes \(K_{1}\) and \(K_{2}\). One deterministic encoder, knowing both messages, sends \(x^{n}=f(M_{1},M_{2})\); receiver 1 observes only \(Y^{n}\) and estimates \(M_{1}\), while receiver 2 observes only \(Z^{n}\) and estimates \(M_{2}\). The average error is Pr[the first estimate is wrong or the second estimate is wrong], averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A rate pair is achievable if there are codes with block lengths tending to infinity, error tending to zero, and \(\liminf  (\log _{2}K_{i})/n\ge R_{i}\) for \(i=1,2\). \(C(\mathrm{W})\) is the closure of achievable nonnegative pairs. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, secrecy constraint, input-cost constraint or restriction on code complexity. Arbitrary dependence among a codeword’s symbols and time sharing are allowed. \(C(\mathrm{W})\) is compact, convex and downward closed; its support values for all rational \(\lambda\) determine it. Rational channel laws make the evaluation task a finite-input question.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on every rational finite-alphabet channel table W and rational \(\lambda \in [0,1]\) specified below, and prove in Lean that |\(g- F(\mathrm{W},\lambda )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve. If supplied as an evaluation algorithm, it must terminate on every such input and return a certified value with this error, without a running-time bound. An impossibility theorem for a stronger arbitrary-accuracy evaluation task does not substitute for this fixed-accuracy answer.
context:
A broadcast channel has one transmitter that knows both messages and two receivers with different observations. This differs from an interference channel, whose transmitters know separate messages. The difficulty is to use one sequence of transmitted symbols for two purposes simultaneously: some structure can help both receivers, while other structure must carry information tailored to only one. A capacity region records all achievable tradeoffs, not just the best sum of rates.

The two point-to-point capacities alone do not determine this tradeoff. If a noiseless binary symbol X is delivered identically to both receivers, each receiver separately has capacity one, but independent private messages must satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le 1\). If X instead consists of two bits and each receiver gets its own bit, the region is the square \(0\le R_{1},R_{2}\le 1\). Both examples have the same individual capacities and different joint possibilities.

Marton’s coding method introduces auxiliary random variables describing private and shared layers and uses correlated codebooks to coordinate their information. Its inner region is achievable, so it gives a lower bound on capacity. For important structured channel classes it is exact, but neither efficient evaluation of that inner region nor optimality on those classes determines the general answer.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite auxiliary-cardinality bounds for Marton’s region, turning the previously unrestricted optimization into a computable finite-dimensional problem. They also show that Marton’s inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region differ for some channels. A gap between an achievable region and an outer bound alone does not reveal which bound is loose; it is not evidence that an intermediate numerical value is capacity.

There is already an exact multiletter perspective: applying Marton’s construction to successively larger product channels and regularizing recovers the operational capacity region. Geng, Gohari, Nair and Yu develop this approach and establish new special cases. The obstacle in the present formulation is a certified finite answer: an asymptotic union without an effective convergence guarantee does not tell us how many channel uses must be examined for a requested accuracy.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s August 2026 preprint claims strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton region. It first finds a ternary-input example with a fixed-input-distribution advantage for two-letter coding, supported by interval-arithmetic bounds. A separate constraint-removal construction then produces a finite unconstrained channel with \(M(\mathrm{W}\otimes \mathrm{W})>2M(\mathrm{W})\), where M is Marton’s maximum private-message sum-rate. The unconstrained example has an enlarged alphabet; the result should not be stated as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample.

That claimed inequality means a two-use code can beat the one-letter inner bound after normalizing rates per use. It does not compute capacity: further block lengths may improve the region again, and a matching converse is still needed. The paper explicitly retains the general capacity question as open. Its numerical certificates and auxiliary construction have not been independently rerun as part of this card.

On the converse side, Gohari, Liu and Nair’s ISIT 2026 work introduces two auxiliary receivers to strengthen outer bounds. These are hypothetical observers used in the proof, not additional terminals allowed in the communication model. Their reported bounds improve the sum-rate upper bound for examples such as the binary skew-symmetric broadcast channel, while still leaving an inner/outer gap.

Finding globally optimal numerical values is also separate from deriving the correct region. Dou and coauthors develop Blahut–Arimoto-style methods for evaluating inner and outer bounds, with convergence statements tied to the optimization’s structure. Such methods help explore examples, but convergence to a local optimum or to an optimum of an unproved bound is not a capacity theorem.
why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general capacity question remains open in the checked primary literature, including the August 2026 paper. That paper’s narrower Marton-suboptimality claim is identified as a preprint result; accepting it would not solve the full characterization or certified-evaluation task. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
progress: 1979: Marton develops the general achievable region based on correlated auxiliary codebooks. | 2009–2012: Gohari–Anantharam prove finite cardinality bounds and computability of Marton’s inner region, while exhibiting gaps from a known outer region. | 2014: Geng and coauthors study product channels, regularization and new classes where Marton is optimal. | 2024-02-20: Dou and coauthors publish numerical algorithms for inner and outer bounds; these evaluate bounds rather than settle their tightness. | 2026: Gohari–Liu–Nair obtain stronger outer bounds using two auxiliary receivers, with strict improvements on example channels. | 2026-08-20: Huang–Liu–Liu post a claimed counterexample to one-letter Marton optimality, first with an input-distribution constraint and then on an enlarged unconstrained channel. The full capacity region remains unknown.
working_summary: A broadcast channel sends one transmitter's input to two receivers with different noisy observations. The target is the weighted supporting function of the private-message capacity region for every rational channel table and weight. One codeword must simultaneously carry information useful to each receiver, creating tradeoffs not determined by their individual capacities. A full characterization would resolve a fundamental multi-user communication problem beyond particular channel families. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.

title: Li–Li conjecture
importance_reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.
formal: For every finite undirected network with positive rational edge capacities and independent unicast sessions, is the zero-error causal network-coding rate region, under the entropy-capacity convention below, equal to its fractional multicommodity-routing region?
definitions: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph, with capacities \(c_{e}>0\), and let \((s_{i},t_{i}), i=1,\ldots ,k\), be ordered pairs of distinct vertices. Different pairs may share endpoints. Source \(s_{i}\) initially knows its own message \(M_{i}\), uniformly distributed over a finite alphabet; the messages are mutually independent. A finite deterministic code specifies in advance a finite sequence of directed edge uses. Each transmitted symbol is a function of messages initially at its sender and symbols previously received there. Every \(t_{i}\) must recover \(M_{i}\) for every message tuple. Local computation and storage are unrestricted; nonlinear functions are permitted. Let \(X_{u\to v}\) be the whole tuple sent from u to v on edge \(\{u,v\}\), and measure Shannon entropy H in bits. For a scale \(b>0\), the code supports \(r\in R_{\ge 0}^{k}\) when \(H(M_{i})\ge b r_{i}\) for all i and \(H(X_{u\to v})+H(X_{v\to u})\le b c_{uv}\) for every edge. Define \(C(G)\) as the closure in \(R^{k}\) of all such supported rate vectors, over all finite alphabets, codes and scales. This explicitly fixes the entropy formulation used in the cited network-coding literature, with exact decoding and capacity shared between directions; it is not a definition using two independent full-capacity arcs. Define \(R(G)\) by nonnegative real path flows \(f_{i,\mathrm{P}}\), for simple \(s_{i}\)-to-\(t_{i}\) paths P, satisfying \(\sum_{\mathrm{P}} f_{i,\mathrm{P}}\ge r_{i}\) and \(\sum_{i,\mathrm{P}:e\in \mathrm{P}} f_{i,\mathrm{P}}\le c_{e}\). The target is \(C(G)=R(G)\) for every G and session list. No multicast destinations, correlated sources, initial side information about other messages, or computation of functions in place of message recovery is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove \(C(G)\subseteq R(G)\) for every specified network and session list; the reverse inclusion follows by routing and closure. Alternatively, exhibit a finite undirected instance with a coding-supported rate vector outside the closed routing polytope, together with a valid causal code and a proof of fractional-routing infeasibility. The latter can use a linear-programming dual certificate. Beating integral edge-disjoint paths, a particular routing algorithm, or a cut bound that is already larger than the routing optimum is insufficient. A multicast or directed-network advantage does not refute this unicast conjecture. A theorem about vanishing-error codes must be related explicitly to this zero-error entropy formulation.
context:
Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits x and y, it may send \(x\oplus y; a\) receiver that already knows y can recover x. Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match the best coding rate for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide a necessary upper bound: information needed across a partition must cross its boundary. For multiple commodities, satisfying every cut constraint need not make the demands fractionally routable. Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval study the small \(K_{3,2}\) example with four same-side sessions. Its sparsity bound is one, while its maximum concurrent routing rate is \(3/4\); their entropy inequalities show that coding also cannot exceed \(3/4\). The gap between cuts and flows therefore does not by itself give a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that a counterexample would have consequences well beyond one small network. Any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family with a gap growing as a positive power of log |V|. A general logarithmic upper bound comes from multicommodity-flow and cut relationships. Thus even a modest strict separation would open the door to much larger asymptotic gains.

The conjecture is also connected to computation rather than communication alone. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that it implies an \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) lower bound for constant-degree Boolean circuits multiplying two n-bit integers. Their reduction turns a sufficiently small circuit into a forbidden network-coding advantage. This is a conditional circuit lower bound, not an already proved consequence of ordinary cut arguments.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.
why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.
status_note: The August 2026 primary papers explicitly leave the general conjecture unresolved. This card fixes causal zero-error coding with entropy capacities and closure of rates, as in the cited formal model. Restricted topology results, multicast gains and alternative error conventions are distinguished. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.
progress: 2004: Li and Li formulate the undirected no-coding-advantage conjecture, as recorded in the subsequent primary literature. | 2005: Jain and coauthors prove that the four-session \(K_{3,2}\) example has coding rate equal to routing rate \(3/4\). | 2017: Braverman–Garg–Schvartzman show that any constant strict advantage amplifies to a polylogarithmically growing gap. | 2019: Afshani and coauthors derive conditional multiplication-circuit lower bounds from the conjecture. | 2025-06: Vamsi–Thakor analyze specified asymmetric demands in layered networks. | 2025-10-21: Braverman–He give superconstant undirected multicast gaps; the unicast conjecture is explicitly left open. | 2026-08-06: Liu–Que–Li–Li report metric-based proofs for further network classes, including at most five terminal locations. | 2026-08-06: A separate session-interaction framework reduces the conjecture to a property of all irreducible cores; it does not establish that property universally. Its manuscript corrects a quantifier in the conference definition to require one common witnessing solution.
working_summary: In an undirected communication network, routing sends independent messages along paths and may split each message among several routes. Network coding additionally allows intermediate nodes to combine information from different messages. The Li-Li conjecture says that coding does not enlarge the achievable rate region for independent unicast sessions beyond fractional multicommodity routing. The saved formulation uses zero-error causal coding and one shared capacity budget for both directions of each edge. A proof or counterexample would determine whether coding provides a fundamental throughput advantage in undirected networks after routing has already been optimized globally.

title: Capacity of the binary deletion channel
importance_reason: The canonical capacity problem for synchronization errors, connecting coding, information theory, sequence reconstruction and the structure of optimal input processes.
formal: Determine the capacity function \(C(\delta )\) of the binary independent deletion channel for every fixed \(\delta \in [0,1]\), in bits per input bit.
definitions: For input \(x=x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), retain each bit independently with probability \(1- \delta\) and output the retained subsequence in its original order. The receiver sees the subsequence and its length, but neither terminal sees the deletion locations; there are no erasure markers, substitutions, insertions, feedback or side channels. Both terminals know n and \(\delta\). A block code consists of deterministic maps \(Enc_{n}:[M_{n}]\to \{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(Dec_{n}:\bigcup _{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^{k}\to [M_{n}]\). Its average error is Pr[\(Dec_{n}(Y)\ne M\)], where M is uniform on \([M_{n}]\) and Y is the channel output on \(Enc_{n}(M)\). A rate R is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with \(\liminf _{n\to \infty}(\log _{2} M_{n})/n\ge R\) and average error tending to zero. Define \(C(\delta )\) as the supremum of achievable nonnegative rates. Encoding and decoding have no computational or storage restrictions. The parameter \(\delta\) is fixed as n grows. Equivalently, Dobrushin’s coding theorem gives \(C(\delta )=\lim _{n\to \infty} C_{n}(\delta )\), where \(C_{n}(\delta )=(1/n) \max\)_{\(\mathrm{P}_{X}\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\)} I(X;Y), with base-two mutual information. These \(C_{n}\) are normalized per input bit; the random output length is not the normalization. The endpoints are \(C(0)=1\) and \(C(1)=0\).
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(\delta \in [0,1]\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- C(\delta )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
context:
A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity \(1- \delta\). Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so \(C(\delta )\le 1- \delta\) is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The basic coding theorem is known. Optimizing mutual information over distributions on n-bit inputs and letting n grow gives the operational capacity. Moreover, \(C_{n}(\delta )- \log _{2}(n+1)/n\le C(\delta )\le C_{n}(\delta )\). Thus the issue is not the absence of a definition or an approximation scheme in principle. The finite optimization has \(2^{n}\) possible inputs, and its rapidly growing size obstructs useful evaluation at large block lengths.

The input bits should not automatically be assumed independent. Correlations can make runs of equal symbols easier to identify after deletions. Run-based constructions choose a distribution on run lengths and analyze how deleted runs disappear and neighboring surviving runs merge. Rubinstein and Con optimize such distributions to prove \(C(\delta )>0.1221(1- \delta )\) for every \(0<\delta <1\). This establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the parameter range.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove \(C(\delta )=1+\delta  \log _{2} \delta - A_{1}\delta +A_{2}\delta ^{2}+O(\delta ^{3- \varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) as \(\delta\) tends to zero, with explicit constants \(A_{1}\approx 1.15416377\) and \(A_{2}\approx 1.67814594\). They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports \(C(\delta )\le 0.3578(1- \delta )\) for \(\delta \ge 0.64\). These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

The half-deletion point illustrates the remaining gap. Rubinstein and Con report an achievable rate above 0.104075, while the 2026 upper-bound table gives 0.1896. A universal lower bound proportional to \(1- \delta\) is useful for the whole curve, but it can be weaker than a pointwise run-length optimization. These different types of statements should therefore not be collapsed into one purported best numerical bound for every parameter.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the capacity curve with the certified accuracy required here.
why: The simplest channel with hidden synchronization errors still lacks an exact nontrivial capacity formula. Resolving it would establish how much information is fundamentally lost through missing alignment.

title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
importance_reason: Determine whether the basic random-coding benchmark is an intrinsic binary information limit.
formal: Do constants \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(\eta >0\) and binary codes \(C_{n}\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n}\) for arbitrarily large n exist with minimum Hamming distance at least \(\delta n\) and \(\log _{2}|C_{n}|/n\ge 1- H_{2}(\delta )+\eta\)?
definitions: A code is any nonempty subset of the binary strings of length n; linearity, explicit construction and efficient decoding are not required. Hamming distance is the number of unequal coordinates, and minimum distance is the minimum over distinct codewords. \(H_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\). The constants \(\delta\) and \(\eta\) must be chosen before n and remain fixed along an unbounded sequence of block lengths. Finite-length improvements vanishing in normalized rate do not meet the target.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The Gilbert–Varshamov bound describes a rate-distance tradeoff achievable by random binary codes. Whether an asymptotically better tradeoff exists is a fundamental question about the information lost to adversarial errors.

This is a nonconstructive existence question, independent of whether codes meeting the bound can be efficiently written down. A polynomial improvement in the number of codewords at fixed length need not yield a positive constant improvement in rate. The coding-course materials distinguish these two open challenges.

title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
importance_reason: A foundational decision problem at the intersection of information theory, computability and database theory; it asks whether exact universal entropy reasoning can be fully automated.
formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given \(n\ge 1\) and rational coefficients \((a_{S})\) for nonempty subsets \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}\), always halts and decides whether \(\sum_{\varnothing \ne S\subseteq [n]}a_{S} H(X_{S})\ge 0\) holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. \(X_{S}\) is the tuple \((X_{i})_{i\in S}\). Its Shannon entropy in bits is \(H(X_{S})=- \sum_{x} p_{S}(x)\log _{2} p_{S}(x)\), with \(0\log _{2}0=0\). Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict \(\ge 0\) and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. Runtime may be any computable function of the input length; polynomial time is not required. The number n varies with the input.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer supplies a total effective procedure for exact validity of every such rational inequality. A negative answer proves that this language of valid inequalities is undecidable. Finding a false input inequality or proving an individual new valid inequality answers an instance, not the meta-question. A procedure that may run forever on valid inputs, or requires a promised numerical gap, does not resolve exact decidability.
context:
For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with \(2^{n}- 1\) coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is \(H(X_{1})+H(X_{2})- H(X_{1},X_{2})\ge 0\). Conditional mutual information is \(H(X_{1},X_{3})+H(X_{2},X_{3})- H(X_{3})- H(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})\ge 0\). Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.
why: A basic computability question about the laws of Shannon information, with consequences for automated proofs, network and coding bounds, and database query reasoning.
status_note: Open for a single unconditional homogeneous rational linear inequality over all finite-valued distributions, based on primary sources and a later-result check through 11 September 2026. Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.
progress: 1998: Zhang–Yeung’s first non-Shannon inequality shows that the elementary Shannon proof system is incomplete, as recalled by the inherited source. | 2013: Kaced–Romashchenko distinguish conditional and unconditional inequalities and their behavior on entropic versus almost-entropic points. | 2020: Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu establish co-r.e. upper bounds for validity of unconditional and certain more general information constraints. | 2023: Li proves undecidability of conditional information inequalities, network coding and conditional-independence implication; the premise-free question remains separate. | 2024: Hannula classifies several restricted semantic and syntactic versions and explicitly states the general information-inequality decision problem as open. | 2025-09-28: Csirmaz’s revised exploration compares major inequality-generation methods and records open completeness questions. | 2026-03-03: E. P. Csirmaz–L. Csirmaz revise their five-variable work, giving two infinite inequality collections and an enumeration procedure within the proposed method.
working_summary: An information inequality is a linear combination of joint entropies asserted to be nonnegative for all distributions. The question asks whether an algorithm can always decide validity when the coefficients are rational and finite alphabet sizes are unrestricted. Standard Shannon inequalities certify many cases but do not describe every valid entropy inequality. A decision procedure would clarify the limits of automated reasoning about information, with implications for coding and database bounds. The saved review notes that invalidity can be semidecided and that undecidability results with conditional premises do not automatically settle this unconditional problem.

title: Capacity of the general two-user interference channel
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved network-information-theory model in which independent communications compete through interference.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with independent private messages and no feedback.
definitions: A channel has nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2,\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\) and arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for each input pair. Conditional on input sequences, an \(n\)-use output sequence has law \(\prod_{t=1}^n W(y_{1,t},y_{2,t}\mid x_{1,t},x_{2,t})\). Messages \(M_1,M_2\) are independent and uniform on \([K_{1,n}]\) and \([K_{2,n}]\), where \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and message counts are positive integers. Encoder \(i\) is a deterministic map \([K_{i,n}]\to\mathcal X_i^n\); its decoder is a deterministic map \(\mathcal Y_i^n\to[K_{i,n}]\). Error means at least one incorrectly decoded message, averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A pair \((R_1,R_2)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^2\) is achievable if there are codes with block lengths \(n_j\to\infty\), error tending to zero, and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both users. The capacity region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)\) is the closure of these achievable pairs. The channel and both codebooks are known to all terminals. There is no common message, feedback, terminal cooperation, input cost or computational bound. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The region is compact, convex and downward closed, so all its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. The function is measured in weighted bits per joint channel use. Channel laws and weights are mathematical real objects; no finite-precision input or algorithmic evaluation model is imposed.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on the entire stated domain and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) for every channel and weight. The proof must control both sides of the error; exact determination also qualifies. The guarantee concerns the support value in bits per joint use, with the coding model unchanged. Sample values, a plot or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit are insufficient. No prescribed formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is required.
context:
Two sender–receiver pairs share one channel while each sender knows only its own independent message. The full rate tradeoff records how the two communications constrain each other.

Han and Kobayashi provide a fundamental achievable region. The historical model reference states that the general capacity region is not known. The support-value formulation expresses the full tradeoff without requiring a particular single-letter form.

The 2010 notes are used for the model, not as current-status evidence; neither exact capacity nor the weaker numerical benchmark is certified as exhaustively searched.

The capacity region contains the asymptotically reliable pairs of rates under average block error. Its weighted upper support values describe the entire tradeoff in bits per joint channel use. title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
importance_reason: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
formal: Do there exist constants \(r\in\)(0,1], \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(A>0\) such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with \(k\le n\le k/r\), an encoding \(C:\{0,1\}^{k}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), and randomized local decoders \(Dec_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,k\}\), satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) differing from \(C(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) positions, and every requested index \(i, Dec_{i}\) with oracle access to z outputs \(x_{i}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) while making at most \(\lceil A \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bit queries on every execution.
definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is \(k/n\) and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants \(r, \delta\) and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple \((x,z,i)\); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.
context:
A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\) queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.
why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
status_note: The 2 April 2026 source explicitly identifies this binary problem as open. The January 2026 HDX result has different decoding guarantees. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated ordinary binary query model; this is a bounded literature check, not an independent proof audit.
progress: 2000 / 2017: As summarized in the April 2026 source, constant-rate local decoding has an \(\Omega (\log  n)\) query lower bound and a binary high-rate upper bound of \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\). | 2026-01-30: HDX constructions improve approximate local list decoding and give logarithmic-depth list decoding, in a distinct model. | 2026-04-02: The revised large-alphabet LDC paper explicitly retains the ordinary binary constant-rate \(O(\log  n)\)-query question as open.
working_summary: Can a binary code protect arbitrarily long messages at constant rate while recovering any requested bit with only logarithmically many bit queries? A fixed positive fraction of the stored bits may be corrupted adversarially. The local decoder must return the requested bit with probability at least two thirds for every admissible received word and index. Large-alphabet and list-decoding results satisfy different guarantees. The target asks for existence, without an extra requirement that the code be efficiently constructed.

title: Rate–distortion tradeoff for distributed lossy source coding
importance_reason: The basic unresolved limit of compressing correlated information without coordination between encoders.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{RD}}(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2,\lambda)=\inf_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal R(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet memoryless source pair, finite distortion tables, feasible distortion targets and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the rate region for separate encoders and a joint decoder.
definitions: The source alphabets \(\mathcal X_i\) and reproduction alphabets \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\), for \(i=1,2\), are nonempty finite sets. The pairs \((X_{1,t},X_{2,t})\) are independent identically distributed draws from an arbitrary real probability table \(P\) on \(\mathcal X_1\times\mathcal X_2\). Distortions are finite-valued functions \(d_i:\mathcal X_i\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Write \(P_i\) for the marginal source law and \(D_{i,\min}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_i}P_i(x)\min_{z\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_i}d_i(x,z)\). The domain requires finite real \(D_i\ge D_{i,\min}\). An \(n\)-block code consists of deterministic encoders \(f_{i,n}:\mathcal X_i^n\to[M_{i,n}]\), where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\) and \(M_{i,n}\ge1\), and a deterministic decoder from the pair of indices to \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_1^n\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_2^n\). Each encoder sees only its own source block. For the resulting reproductions define \(\Delta_{i,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[d_i(X_{i,t},\widehat X_{i,t})]\). A nonnegative pair is achievable if, along some \(n_j\to\infty\), codes satisfy \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2M_{i,n_j}\le R_i\) and \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}\Delta_{i,n_j}\le D_i\) for both sources. The region \(\mathcal R\) is the closure of achievable pairs. There is no interaction, extra side information, computational restriction or variable-length encoding; distortion is expected per-symbol distortion. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. Transmitting both source blocks and selecting minimum-distortion reproductions establishes feasibility on the stated domain; smaller distortion targets, which would give an empty region, are excluded. The region is convex and upward closed. Its nonnegative lower supporting values describe its lower rate boundary. The target is finite and nonnegative, in weighted bits per source pair. All tables are mathematical real objects, with no algorithmic representation requirement.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the whole source, distortion and weight domain above and a Lean proof of \(|g-F_{\mathrm{RD}}|\le1/100\) pointwise. This is an error bound on the weighted rate in bits per source pair; the distortion constraints remain exact. Prove both sides of the bound, or determine the function exactly. A finite sample of values or a restatement of the operational infimum or limit is insufficient. No specified formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed.
context:
Separate encoders describe correlated source blocks to one decoder. Correlation can reduce the total communication even though the encoders cannot inspect each other’s data. Allowing distortion changes the problem from lossless reconstruction.

The historical notes give inner and outer bounds and identify the general two-source lossy region as unresolved. This card measures its lower boundary by the minimum weighted rate and explicitly excludes infeasible distortion targets.

status_note: Open in the cited 2010 model notes. The definition and the numerical benchmark were rechecked on 13 September 2026. The available later-work review is bounded and did not identify a general solution; the historical notes do not establish current open status.

The function records the smallest weighted sum of the two description rates. Only feasible distortion targets are included, so every requested value is finite. The benchmark keeps the distortion constraints exact and requires a Lean-certified rate error of at most 0.01 on the whole domain.

title: Shannon capacity of \(C_{7}\)
importance_reason: The smallest odd-cycle zero-error capacity left unresolved after Lovasz's pentagon theorem.
formal: Determine the zero-error Shannon capacity \[\Theta(C_7)=\sup_{t\ge1}\alpha(C_7^{\boxtimes t})^{1/t}\] of the seven-cycle, in distinguishable symbols per channel use, with the graph power defined below.
definitions: \(C_{7}\) has vertex set \(\{0,\ldots ,6\}\), with distinct vertices adjacent when their difference modulo 7 is 1 or 6. For an integer \(t\ge 1\), the strong power has vertex set \(\{0,\ldots ,6\}^{t}\). Two distinct tuples are adjacent when, in every coordinate, their entries are equal or adjacent in \(C_{7}\). An independent set contains no adjacent distinct pair, and \(\alpha\) is its maximum cardinality. The capacity is measured in distinguishable symbols per channel use, rather than its logarithm in bits. It lies between 3 and 7; the supremum need not occur at a finite power. There is no computational restriction on independent sets or their construction.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a Lean proof that \(|a-\Theta(C_7)|\le1/100\). Certified lower and upper bounds \(\ell\le\Theta(C_7)\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). An exact value with proof also qualifies. A restatement of the defining supremum, a one-sided bound or an estimate without certified error does not suffice. This tolerance concerns the benchmark value, not an exact-capacity conjecture.
context:
The seven-cycle is the first odd cycle after the pentagon whose exact zero-error capacity remains unresolved in the cited literature. Independent sets in its strong powers represent collections of mutually distinguishable codewords.

The August 2026 preprint reports a lower bound of \(3.25883262\ldots\), while the Lovász upper bound is \(7\cos(\pi/7)/(1+\cos(\pi/7))\approx3.31766720\). Their gap is still larger than \(1/50\), so these bounds do not yet meet this card’s acceptance tolerance.
why: The smallest odd-cycle zero-error capacity left unresolved after Lovasz's pentagon theorem.
status_note: The 31 August 2026 preprint explicitly leaves the exact capacity unresolved. Its reported lower bound and the primary-source upper bound still leave a gap exceeding 0.02, so they do not settle this card’s 0.01 acceptance target. Checked on 13 September 2026; the new construction was not independently verified.
progress: 2019: Polak and Schrijver give \(\Theta(C_7)\ge367^{1/5}\) and state the Lovász upper bound \(7\cos(\pi/7)/(1+\cos(\pi/7))\). | 2026-08-31: Tandon’s preprint abstract reports a code in the 500th strong power giving \(\Theta(C_7)\ge3.25883262\ldots\). This is a reported preprint result; the construction and proof were not independently verified.
working_summary: The seven-cycle describes which pairs of seven channel symbols can be confused. Its Shannon capacity is the supremum of independence numbers of strong graph powers raised to the reciprocal power. The card asks for this real number in distinguishable symbols per use, rather than bits per use. No finite graph power is assumed to attain the supremum. The Lean benchmark accepts an explicit value with certified absolute error at most 0.01.

title: Capacity of the general two-way channel
importance_reason: Determines the fundamental value of interaction in simultaneous bidirectional communication.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{TW}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-way channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with both terminals allowed to adapt their transmissions to past received outputs.
definitions: The channel has nonempty finite input alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2\), output alphabets \(\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\), and a table of arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for every input pair. In an \(n\)-use code, terminal \(i\) holds a message \(M_i\) uniform on \([K_{i,n}]=\{1,\ldots,K_{i,n}\}\), with positive integer message counts and independent messages. At time \(t\), its input is \(X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})\), where \(f_{i,t}\) is deterministic and \(Y_i^{t-1}=(Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,t-1})\). Given the current inputs and full past history, the current output pair has distribution \(W\). Terminal 1 estimates \(M_2\) from \((M_1,Y_1^n)\), and terminal 2 estimates \(M_1\) from \((M_2,Y_2^n)\), by deterministic decoders. Error is the probability that either estimate is wrong, averaged over messages and channel draws. A nonnegative rate pair is achievable if codes along \(n_j\to\infty\) have error tending to zero and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both terminals. Thus \(R_1\) is the rate from terminal 1 to terminal 2, and \(R_2\) is the reverse rate. The region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)\) is the closure of achievable pairs. The law and all coding functions are public. There are no extra communication links, shared messages, input constraints or computational bounds. The received outputs provide the permitted feedback. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The capacity region is compact, convex and downward closed, so its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. Rates are in bits per simultaneous joint channel use, without an extra factor of two. The channel table and weight are mathematical real objects, not finite-precision algorithmic inputs.

title: Computability of graph Shannon capacity
importance_reason: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer \(k\ge 1, A\) on input \((G,k)\) halts and outputs integers a and \(b>0\) with |\(a/b- \Theta (G)|\le 2^{- k}\)? No bound on running time is imposed.
definitions: Encode G with vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 0\), by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For \(m\ge 1\), the strong power \(G^{\boxtimes m}\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}^{m}\). Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either \(x_{j}=y_{j}\) or \(\{x_{j},y_{j}\}\) is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; \(\alpha (H)\) is its maximum cardinality, with \(\alpha\) of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{m\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as \(m\to \infty\), and \(1\le \Theta (G)\le n\); set \(\Theta (G)=0\) when \(n=0\). The desired output approximates \(\Theta\) itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.
context:
Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity \(\sqrt{5}\). For nonempty graphs, \(\log _{2}\Theta (G)\) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of \(C_{7}\) is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.
