title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
importance_reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
focus_reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most \(C\cdot \varepsilon ^{- c}\) vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P}_{F})\) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) on the same vertex set, divided by \(n^{2}\); define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of \(\min \{n,s\}\) distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), every \(n\ge 1\) and every G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P}_{F})>\varepsilon\), this tester with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon ^{- c}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). It automatically accepts every graph in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\). The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The source survey asks for a characterization of finite forbidden-induced-subgraph families whose canonical sample complexity is polynomial in inverse accuracy. To make the requested output unambiguous, this card fixes an effective classification question: can that class of finite inputs be decided at all? This additional effectiveness requirement is an editorial specification, rather than wording attributed to the survey. It distinguishes the target from an equivalent reformulation involving another unresolved infinite condition.

There are two separate computational tasks. Given a fixed family F and a particular finite graph, exact membership in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) can be checked by searching for its finitely many forbidden patterns. The question here concerns a statement about every possible host graph and arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon\). Finite decidability of each individual membership test does not by itself provide a decision procedure for the existence of uniform polynomial sampling bounds.

The dense-model normalization matters. Being \(\varepsilon\)-far means that a positive \(\varepsilon\) fraction of all possible vertex pairs must be changed, up to the fixed normalization factor. It does not mean that an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the edges currently present must be removed. A sparse graph can therefore be close to a property even when many of its own edges would need modification. No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on \(\varepsilon\), but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding \(C_{4}\), its complement and \(C_{5}\), although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.

Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.

Induced \(C_{4}\)-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.

Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced \(C_{4}\)-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\).

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.

title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
importance_reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.
focus_reason: A universal polynomial tester-to-estimator implication would convert robust graph-property recognition into quantitative distance measurement across the dense model.
formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) nonempty for every \(n\ge 1\), does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in \(1/\varepsilon\), independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-\(\varepsilon\) distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
definitions: \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a nonempty subset of graphs on \([n]\), invariant under vertex permutations. For \(n\ge 2, \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})=\min _{H\in \mathrm{P}_{n}}|E(G)\triangle E(H)|/\operatorname{binom}(n,2)\); for \(n=1\) it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer \(t\ge 2\), with \(\varepsilon =1/t\), and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each \(G\in \mathrm{P}_{n}\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\) and rejects each G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})\ge \varepsilon\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\); no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants \(C,a\ge 1\) with at most \(Ct^{a}\) adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants \(C' ,b\ge 1\), using at most \(C' t^{b}\) queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with \(\Pr [|q- \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})|\le 1/t]\ge 2/3\) for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are \(\varepsilon\)-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on \(\varepsilon\). The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\varepsilon )\) can be replaced by \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.
why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
importance_reason: Tests the fundamental power of sublinear access to compare two sparse graphs without reading the entire input.
formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below. The target retains the sublinear-existence question in the saved card, which is one part of the source’s broader request to determine the full query complexity.
definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.
context:
Open Problem 2.4 explicitly separates testing against a known fixed graph from testing a pair of oracle inputs. This card chooses the latter, as in its saved formulation, and retains two-sided error.

Goldreich proves upper and lower query bounds of order \(n^{2/3}\), up to polylogarithmic factors and proximity dependence, when connected components have polylogarithmic size. The lower bound also applies to general inputs, but the upper bound retains its component-size restriction.

Goldreich and Tauber obtain a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) tester for almost all fixed regular target graphs, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Their model supplies the target graph in advance; it neither supplies both graphs only by oracle nor covers every possible target.

The relevant resource here is query complexity. A tester may perform extensive finite computation on its observations. Therefore a fast algorithm for explicit graph isomorphism does not, by itself, meet the oracle-query target, and a query bound does not by itself assert fast total runtime.
why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

title: Query complexity of directed acyclicity testing with bidirectional access
importance_reason: A sharp testing or correction bound for a specific distance, property, or sampling regime.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed degree bound \(d\ge 1\) and fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), the minimum worst-case number \(Q(n,d,\varepsilon )\) of incidence-list queries needed by an adaptive randomized two-sided-error tester to distinguish acyclic n-vertex digraphs from digraphs more than \(\varepsilon dn\) edge deletions away from acyclic, when every indegree and outdegree is at most d and both incoming and outgoing queries are allowed.
definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,d\}\); it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and \(\varepsilon\) are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k}, k\ge 2\), with arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\) and \(v_{k}\to v_{1}\); acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let \(\tau (G)\) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(\tau (G)>\varepsilon dn\). Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least \(2/3\) and reject each \(\varepsilon\)-far graph with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational \(\varepsilon\); there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested \(\Theta\) bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and \(\varepsilon\). One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound \(F(n,d,\varepsilon ), a\) uniform tester using \(O(F)\) queries, and a matching \(\Omega (F)\) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed \(d,\varepsilon\) in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.
context:
A long directed cycle can remain invisible in a small explored neighborhood. The tester sees only chosen incident edges, so even the ability to move both forward and backward does not directly reveal whether some distant portion closes a cycle.

A directed cycle on n vertices becomes acyclic after deleting one arc. Its normalized distance is \(1/(dn)\), so for fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) and large n it is outside the promised far case. Property testing asks for reliable rejection only when many arc deletions are unavoidable.

The source records an \(\Omega (n^{1/3})\) query lower bound for adaptive two-sided testing at suitable fixed parameters. Reading every outgoing list uses at most nd queries and determines the whole graph. The gap between such lower bounds and the linear bound motivates the sharp query question.

The 2023 model comparison distinguishes access to both directions from access only to outgoing arcs. A lower bound against the less informative oracle cannot automatically rule out an algorithm with incoming queries.

Yoshida’s preprint states stronger one-sided and two-sided lower bounds when queries only reveal outgoing neighbors and indegree is unrestricted. These hypotheses differ from the fixed bidirectional bounded-degree setting of the original question.

title: Efficient characterization of instance-optimal identity testing
importance_reason: A quantitative or model-specific learning frontier; resolving it would sharpen a useful guarantee but has more limited scope than a general learnability characterization.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(\Phi\) and a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite rational probability vector \(q\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1\),
\[C^{-1}n_*(q,\varepsilon)\le\Phi(q,\varepsilon)\le Cn_*(q,\varepsilon)?\]
The integer \(n_*(q,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest fixed number of independent samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon\), with each error probability at most \(1/3\), when the reference \(q\) is known and the unknown distribution \(p\) is otherwise arbitrary. Computation of the statistical test is unrestricted. Polynomial time is required of the evaluator of the characterization, in the binary input length of \((q,\varepsilon)\), and the multiplicative constant must hold at the same input \(\varepsilon\).

This is the finite, explicitly encoded version of the efficient-computability branch of the source's Open Question 1. The source also allows countably infinite domains and leaves “succinct” open to a closed-form interpretation; this card makes its computational interpretation and finite rational input scope explicit rather than treating those broader interpretations as equivalent.
definitions:
For an integer \(d\ge1\), write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and \(\Delta_d=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{d}:\sum_i p_i=1\}\). The input lists every entry of \(q\in\Delta_d\cap\mathbb Q^d\), including zeros, and the rational number \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\). Rationals are represented by binary nonnegative numerators and positive denominators in lowest terms, with delimiters; let \(B\) be the total bit length, including the length encoding of the list. No oracle or compressed description replaces this list. The alternative \(p\) ranges over all of \(\Delta_d\), including irrational probabilities and mass on coordinates where \(q_i=0\). Total variation is
\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d}|p_i-q_i|.\]

For a nonnegative integer \(s\), a possibly randomized statistical test is specified by a function \(\tau:[d]^s\to[0,1]\); \(\tau(x)\) is its conditional probability of rejecting the null on sample sequence \(x\). There is no time, space or representation constraint on this finite table of real probabilities. The product law \(p^{\otimes s}\) means that all \(s\) observations are independent and have law \(p\). A valid test satisfies
\[\mathbb E_{q^{\otimes s}}\tau\le1/3,\qquad
\forall p\in\Delta_d\text{ with }d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_{p^{\otimes s}}\tau\ge2/3.\]
The same test must work for every alternative at that fixed \((q,\varepsilon)\); it cannot be chosen after learning \(p\). The minimum such \(s\) defines \(n_*\). It is finite on every permitted input. The sample count is fixed in advance, not an expected stopping time, and the two errors are bounded separately. Cases with \(0<d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\le\varepsilon\) impose no condition.

The zero-sample case is included: \([d]^0\) is a singleton. The alternative is empty exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge1-\min_iq_i\), since the largest possible distance from \(q\) in this simplex is \(1-\min_iq_i\). In that case \(n_*=0\); otherwise \(n_*\ge1\). Thus the claimed multiplicative guarantee requires the evaluator to return exactly zero in empty-alternative cases, including \(d=1\). The strict inequality in the alternative is intentional.

The evaluator is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine. It outputs a nonnegative integer in binary and halts within \(K(B+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(K,a\), independent of \(d,q,\varepsilon\); input reading, bit arithmetic and output writing all count. It has no advice or oracles, and must halt within the same bound on malformed encodings, whose outputs are irrelevant. The quantifier order is existence of the evaluator and constants, followed by all valid inputs. There is no permission for polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) in place of polynomial dependence on its encoded length. The statistical tester whose existence defines \(n_*\) is a separate object and need not be produced by this evaluator.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence claim. A positive answer must specify the evaluator and prove its uniform polynomial running time and both bounds with one universal finite factor \(C\). A negative answer must refute the existence of every such evaluator and constant; failure of one proposed expression is insufficient. Neither defining \(\Phi\) by the minimum over all statistical tests without proving efficient evaluation, nor comparing upper and lower bounds at different multiples of \(\varepsilon\), satisfies this target. A conditional computational obstruction alone does not prove the unconditional negative claim. Countably infinite or implicitly described references are outside this explicitly selected variant.
context:

Binary rational inputs and polynomial bit complexity make that meaning a precise mathematical predicate. The broader closed-form and infinite-domain versions remain part of the source direction, and are not claimed equivalent to this variant.

Valiant and Valiant give reference-dependent bounds using the \(2/3\)-quasinorm of a vector after removal of its largest coordinate and a small-probability tail. Their theorem and following discussion explicitly permit constant-factor changes in the distance parameter as well as in the sample count. That is a different guarantee from a characterization at fixed \(\varepsilon\).

Canonne explains that the differing tail cutoffs can cause an arbitrarily large ratio between the resulting bounds, with harmonic probability profiles as an example. Section 2 discusses a second characterization using an interpolation functional, which has an analogous mismatch. Section 3 explains why bounds on the optimal separation radius up to constants do not automatically provide the requested fixed-distance sample characterization.

The source separately raises a proof-coverage issue for the earlier lower bound near point masses, and separates that repair as Open Question 3. It does not claim the lower-bound theorem false. title: A dimension-free directed \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) Poincaré inequality
importance_reason: A dimension-free analytic relationship between local violations and global distance from monotonicity, with significance for property testing. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Lipschitz function \(f:[0,1]^{n}\to \mathbb{R} , d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f) \le  C \int _{[0,1]^{n}} (\sum_{i=1}^{n} \max \{- \partial _{i}f(x),0\}^{2})^{1/2} dx\)? Here \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)\) is the \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) distance to the coordinatewise nondecreasing functions. The same C must work for every dimension and every finite Lipschitz constant.
definitions:
Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]^{n}\) has total mass one. A function \(g:[0,1]^{n}	o \mathbb{R}\) is coordinatewise nondecreasing if \(g(x)\le g(y)\) whenever \(x_{i}\le y_{i}\) for all i. Define \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)=\inf _{g} \int |f(x)- g(x)|dx\), over measurable integrable coordinatewise nondecreasing g; g need not have the same Lipschitz constant as f. A function f is Lipschitz if there is a finite L with |\(f(x)- f(y)|\le \mathrm{L}\Vert x- y\Vert _{2}\) for all x,y in the cube. Its gradient exists almost everywhere; its values on the exceptional null set may be set to zero without changing any integral. The negative gradient is \(
abla ^{-}f(x)=(\max \{- \partial _{1}f(x),0\},\ldots ,\max \{- \partial _{n}f(x),0\})\). The right-hand side is \(C\cdot E[\Vert 
abla ^{-}f(X)\Vert _{2}]\) for a uniform point X in the cube. It is not \(C\cdot (E[\Vert 
abla ^{-}f(X)\Vert _{2}^{2}])^{1/2}\). No boundary condition, mean-zero assumption or fixed bound on the range of f is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequality with one universal finite C, or refute the existence of such a C by showing that the ratio \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)/E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{2}\) is unbounded across the stated functions and dimensions (including a function with positive distance and zero denominator, if one existed). A bound whose constant grows with n, or a bound using the \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) norm of the gradient over the cube, is insufficient.
context:
A negative partial derivative witnesses a local decrease in one coordinate. The left-hand side measures the least average change to the entire function needed to remove all monotonicity violations.

The 2023 source proves a directed inequality using \(E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{1}\). Comparing \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) and \(\ell\)\(_{2}\) norms yields a bound with a factor \(\sqrt{n}\), whereas the conjecture asks to remove all dependence on dimension.

The later theorem bounds squared \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) distance to monotonicity by \(C\cdot E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{2}^{2}\). Even though \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) distance dominates \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) distance, the square root of this second moment can be much larger than \(E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{2}\). The author explicitly leaves the present conjecture open.

The 2025 thesis restates the inequality after obtaining a tester with sublinear dimension dependence from the \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) theorem. Thus the motivating algorithmic progress and the analytic conjecture have distinct statuses.
why: Would connect local directional decreases to global distance from monotonicity with a universal constant, extending a central isoperimetric principle to real-valued functions on continuous cubes.
status_note: The full 2023 conjecture, October 2024 preprint revision and July 2025 thesis were checked, including the explicit statement that the later norm inequality does not resolve this one. Searches through 12 September 2026 located no resolution of the full continuous-cube claim.
progress: 2023: The directed \((\mathrm{L}^{1},\ell _{1})\) inequality is proved; the dimension-free \((\mathrm{L}^{1},\ell _{2})\) version is Conjecture 1.8. | 2024: The directed \((\mathrm{L}^{2},\ell _{2})\) theorem yields improved testing bounds but explicitly does not settle this conjecture. | 2025-07-03: The thesis retains the same statement as Conjecture 4.43.
working_summary: The conjecture concerns every Lipschitz real-valued function on a continuous unit cube. It asks whether average distance to a monotone function is controlled by the average Euclidean magnitude of the negative gradient. The multiplicative constant must be independent of the dimension and the Lipschitz constant. A known inequality using the sum of coordinate decreases loses a square-root dimension factor. Later work proves a different inequality using squared quantities and explicitly leaves this conjecture open.

title: Optimal query cost of reducing testing adaptivity
importance_reason: A general resource tradeoff for adaptive Boolean property testing; a precise quantitative target is needed to distinguish a substantive advance from the existing simulations. Existing score retained.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors over all integers \(q,k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell<k\), \[F(q,k,\ell)=\sup\{q_\ell(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon):n\ge1,\ \varnothing\ne\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ 0<\varepsilon\le1,\ q_k(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\le q\},\] the worst query cost of reducing a Boolean property tester from \(k+1\) batches to \(\ell+1\) batches.
definitions: An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is available through queries to individual coordinates. Its distance to the known property \(\mathcal P\) is \(n^{-1}\min_{y\in\mathcal P}|\{i:x_i\ne y_i\}|\). A tester accepts every member with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects every input at distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\); other inputs have no correctness requirement. Under the source convention, \(j\) rounds of adaptivity mean \(j+1\) batches \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_j\). All coordinates in one batch are chosen before their answers are revealed. The coordinates and size of every later batch may depend on all earlier answers; empty batches are permitted. A randomized tester is a finite probability distribution over deterministic batch-query trees, each of which returns a bit on every input. Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers; this is the nonuniform query-complexity model, without a computational or randomness-generation cost. Each selected tree’s total queries are bounded on every input, and cost is their worst case over the support and inputs. Let \(q_j(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\) be the least such bound among all valid testers. Reading every coordinate shows \(q_j\le n\). The tester may depend arbitrarily on the fixed property, length and proximity parameter; no uniform synthesis from a property description is requested. Querying a coordinate already read gives no additional information and can be omitted. The same property, distance and error convention occur on both sides of \(F\). The source’s complete nonadaptive simulation shows \(F(q,k,\ell)\le2^q-1\), so the supremum is finite; since all values are integers, it is a maximum. The desired precision is a positive function \(g(q,k,\ell)\) and one absolute \(C\ge1\) with \(C^{-1}g\le F\le Cg\) for every admissible triple. The comparison constant must not depend on a parameter or on a hidden property.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function and a Lean proof of both universal constant-factor bounds on the full parameter domain. The upper bound must cover adaptive batch sizes, and the lower bound must be witnessed by permitted properties and proximity parameters. A bound only for deleting one round, fixed-size batches or a selected regime does not determine this tradeoff. Numerical 0.01 error is not the precision for this asymptotic-complexity target.

title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
importance_reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.
focus_reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.
formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most \(1/10\) and confidence at least \(9/10\), while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to \(\{0,1\}\). \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. \(LD(C)\) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{X}\) of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target \(h\in C\) and distribution D on X, with probability at least \(9/10\) over m independent draws \(x_{i}\) from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most \(1/10\). Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector \((h(x))_{h\in C}\) can be identified, giving at most \(2^{|}C|\) cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

The reviewed question asks whether sample complexity is polynomial in VC dimension and the iterated logarithm of Littlestone dimension. title: Optimal error for pure-DP continual counting
importance_reason: Continual counting is a basic privacy primitive; the target is the optimal price of pure privacy across the entire stream.
focus_reason: The saved target asks for optimal worst-time error when releasing every prefix sum under pure differential privacy. It complements sample-complexity bounds for private learning with a fundamental sequential data-release problem.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(T\to \infty , E(T)=\inf _{M} \max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{T}} E_{Y\sim M_{x}}[\max _{1\le t\le T}|Y_{t}- \sum_{i=1}^{t} x_{i}|]\), where the infimum is over all causal \((1/2,0)\)-differentially private mechanisms defined below.
definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.
answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.
context:
Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream \((1,0,1,1)\), the exact outputs are \((1,1,2,3)\). Changing its second bit gives \((1,1,1,1)\) and exact outputs \((1,2,3,4)\): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only \(1/T\). This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is \(O(\log ^{2}T)\). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for \(E(T)\) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.

title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
importance_reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete and widely used query family. It complements existing sample-complexity questions and has an explicit specialist open-problem formulation, while allowing non-synthetic outputs avoids a known source of misleading hardness claims.
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge 1, a\) function \(\alpha :N_{\ge 2}\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{d\to \infty}\alpha (d)=0, a\) uniform randomized mechanism M and a uniform deterministic evaluator E, such that for every \(d\ge 2\) and every database \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\) with \(n=d^{C}, M\) runs in time polynomial in n,d, satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite synopsis S for which, with probability at least \(2/3, E(S,q)\) approximates \(q(D)\) within \(\alpha (d)\) simultaneously for every marginal query q?
definitions: A marginal query is a pair \((J,a)\), where \(J\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,d\}\) and \(a\in \{0,1\}^{J}\), and \(q_{J,a}(D)=|\){\(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}:D_{ij}=a_{j}\) for all \(j\in J\)}|/n. The empty J query has value one. Queries of every order up to d are included. The database is an explicitly stored ordered n-by-d bit matrix; neighbouring databases have the same dimensions and differ in exactly one row. Differential privacy means that for every ordered pair of neighbours \(D,D'\) and every set O of output strings, \(\Pr [M(D)\in O]\le e\cdot \Pr [M(D' )\in O]+1/(100n^{2})\). M uses independent fair random bits and has one worst-case polynomial bound \(p(n+d)\) on bit operations, output length and random bits. Its output is a finite binary string S. E receives d,S,J,a, has a worst-case bound given by one polynomial in d+|S| and outputs a binary-encoded rational number. E has no access to D, private state of M or an additional oracle. Both algorithms are ordinary classical Turing machines, with no nonuniform advice. The accuracy event is simultaneous over all queries and its probability is over M’s randomness alone, separately for every D. S need not encode a synthetic database or a consistent probability distribution. \(C,\alpha ,p,M,E\) and the evaluator’s polynomial are fixed before d,D are chosen. No algorithm to compute \(\alpha\) and no prescribed rate of its convergence are required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
A marginal measures the fraction of records matching a pattern on selected coordinates. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.
why: Determine whether the information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional statistics can be achieved with polynomial computation and polynomially many records.

progress: 2013: Private marginal release on small databases is achieved with subexponential per-query computation and fixed additive error. | 2017: Open Problem 7.8 asks for polynomial-time estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error and \(n=\operatorname{poly}(d)\).

title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
importance_reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.
focus_reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.
formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem of distinguishing \(I\to A\) from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities \(a_{R}\). A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation \(R^{A}\subseteq A^{a_{R}}\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to A\) is a map on domains such that \((v_{1},\ldots ,v_{a})\in R^{I}\) implies \((h(v_{1}),\ldots ,h(v_{a}))\in R^{A}\) for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On \(I\to B\) but I↛A, either answer is allowed. \(A\to B\) makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in \(O(\mathrm{L}^{c})\), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas \(\varphi\) to structures \(I_{\varphi}\) such that satisfiable \(\varphi\) yield \(I_{\varphi}\to A\) and unsatisfiable \(\varphi\) yield \(I_{\varphi}\)↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Ordinary constraint satisfaction asks whether a collection of local requirements can all hold simultaneously. Promise CSPs keep two versions of each requirement: the input is guaranteed to admit a solution satisfying the stronger version, while the relaxed task uses the weaker one. For graph colouring, \(A=K_{k}\) and \(B=K_{c}\) with \(k\le c\) produces the decision task of distinguishing k-colourable graphs from graphs that are not c-colourable. Graphs in between impose no decision requirement.

When \(A=B\), the promise disappears. Bulatov and Zhuk independently proved in 2017 that every finite-template CSP is either in P or NP-complete. The present question asks whether a comparable exclusion of intermediate complexity survives arbitrary finite promises. It does not follow merely by applying the classical theorem to A and B separately: the relaxed task can be easier than either endpoint CSP.

A concrete tractable example promises that each listed triple of Boolean variables can have exactly one 1 and asks only for a not-all-equal assignment. Solve the equations \(x+y+z=1\) over the integers, then map positive values to 1 and nonpositive values to 0. No such triple can become all zero or all one. Barto proves that this tractability cannot be explained by sandwiching the pair through a tractable finite-domain CSP, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Finite templates can therefore need an infinite intermediate domain in this natural algorithmic framework.

The algebraic approach studies operations that combine several A-solutions coordinatewise into one B-solution. These polymorphisms capture useful structure for algorithms and reductions, but their input and output domains can differ, preventing the direct use of all the composition arguments available in ordinary CSP. The survey emphasizes that a full dichotomy was not yet backed by enough evidence to be asserted as a settled consensus conjecture; this card poses it as a precise open question.

Important subclasses are classified. Brakensiek and Guruswami obtain a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise CSPs allowing negations, with tractable cases going beyond a direct reuse of Schaefer’s classical Boolean CSP classification. That theorem does not classify all Boolean templates or all finite domains.

The 2026 work of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima expands the logical viewpoint by relating Promise MMSNP to finite-domain PCSPs. It also classifies a family defined by forbidden monochromatic cliques under the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. Both the restricted family and the additional assumption matter: this is not an unconditional classification of every finite template pair.
why: The main classification question for constraint satisfaction with promises, encompassing approximate colouring and many local relaxation tasks. A resolution would determine whether finite constraint languages force a sharp tractability boundary even when their exact and relaxed solutions differ.
status_note: Open classification question in the cited survey, with relevant partial results checked through 10 September 2026. The card asks for an unconditional decision dichotomy over all fixed finite template pairs; it does not assume decision/search equivalence or a complete algebraic classification.
progress: 2017: Bulatov proves the finite-domain CSP dichotomy, settling the special case \(A=B\). | 2017: Zhuk independently proves the finite-domain CSP dichotomy by a different algebraic algorithm. | 2018: Brakensiek and Guruswami establish a symmetric Boolean promise-CSP dichotomy with negations and develop the polymorphism framework. | 2019: Barto exhibits a polynomial-time finite-domain PCSP that cannot be sandwiched through a tractable finite-domain CSP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). | 2022: Krokhin and Opršal survey the open classification landscape and explicitly distinguish decision from search PCSPs. | 2026: Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima prove a Promise MMSNP correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification at LICS 2026. The full finite-pair dichotomy remains outside the theorem.
working_summary: A finite promise CSP distinguishes instances satisfying stronger local constraints from those failing even weaker constraints. The reviewed question asks whether every fixed finite template pair yields either a polynomial-time problem or an NP-hard one. Allowing different source and target domains changes how algebraic operations can combine solutions. A dichotomy would organize a broad class of approximation and relaxed-feasibility problems as the ordinary finite CSP theorem does. The saved review explains that the classical theorem does not automatically transfer, and even tractable finite promise templates may require infinite intermediate structures in natural algorithms.

title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
importance_reason: A central unifying conjecture about the boundary of polynomial-time constraint solving, with broad logical scope and active links to promise CSPs.
focus_reason: A central unifying conjecture about the boundary of polynomial-time constraint solving, with broad logical scope and active links to promise CSPs.
formal: For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous structure A over a finite relational signature, and every finite-signature first-order reduct B of A, is \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) either decidable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
definitions: A relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed finite arities. A is homogeneous if every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of A. It is finitely bounded if there is a finite set F of finite structures in its signature such that a finite structure embeds into A exactly when none of the structures in F embeds into it; embeddings preserve both relations and their complements. Countable allows finite or countably infinite domains. B has the same domain as A, with finitely many relations each definable by a first-order formula over A without parameters; it may forget original relations and introduce definable ones. For each fixed B, an input to \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) is an explicitly encoded finite structure I in B’s signature. Accept exactly when there is a map h from the domain of I to that of B preserving every relation tuple. Equivalently, a finite conjunction of atomic B-constraints must have a satisfying assignment. h need not be injective. A, B and their defining formulas are fixed, not part of the input; running times are measured in the finite instance’s bit length. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.
why: The main tractability-classification conjecture for well-behaved infinite-domain CSPs. It links algorithm design, universal algebra and model theory, and would extend the finite-domain dichotomy to substantially richer constraint languages.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The latest checked primary papers explicitly retain the general dichotomy as open. The July \(FO/\mathrm{L}\)-hard classification has both a different complexity boundary and an expansion hypothesis; the August interpretability result does not settle tractability.
progress: 2017: Bulatov and Zhuk independently prove the finite-domain CSP dichotomy; infinite domains require additional structural arguments. | 2020: Barto–Pinsker give a purely algebraic characterization of the relevant hardness obstruction for model-complete cores. The general tractability implication remains conjectural. | 2021–2026: Bodirsky’s monograph develops the framework; the checked author postprint is dated 31 January 2026. | 2026-05-06: The revised Three Fundamental Questions paper reduces the conjecture to templates without algebraicity and strengthens links with finite-domain promise CSPs. | 2026-07-14: Dorochko–Wrona’s v3 establishes an \(FO/\mathrm{L}\)-hard dichotomy for expansions of homogeneous model-complete cores, not the full \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy. | 2026-08-05: Feller–Pinsker’s v2 provides decidability and computable-core tools under additional structural hypotheses.
working_summary: Infinite-domain CSPs assign variables values from a fixed countable structure while satisfying finitely listed constraints. The conjecture asks for a P-versus-NP-complete dichotomy for reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. These restrictions provide symmetry and a finite description of forbidden patterns despite the unbounded value domain. A classification would show whether this structural description rules out intermediate complexity across many logical and combinatorial problems. The saved review identifies the missing general algorithmic step and separates special subclasses, lower logical dichotomies, and meta-problem decidability from a proof of the full conjecture.

title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
importance_reason: The paradigmatic approximate graph-colouring question, central to promise CSPs and to the gap between algorithmic relaxations and hardness with perfect completeness.
formal: Is there a fixed integer \(C\ge 3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph G promised to be 3-colourable, outputs a proper vertex colouring using at most C colours with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The input is an explicitly given graph \(G=([n],E), n\ge 1\), with no loops or parallel edges, encoded by its adjacency matrix. A proper k-colouring is a map \(c:[n]\to [k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\). The promise is existence of a proper 3-colouring; such a colouring is not supplied. There must be one C, one randomized Turing machine A, and fixed constants K,d such that A uses at most \(K(n+1)^{d}\) bit operations on every graph and every random tape. On each promised input, the probability, over independent unbiased internal random bits, of outputting a proper C-colouring is at least \(2/3\). Invalid outputs can be replaced by a failure symbol after checking all edges. No correctness requirement is imposed on non-3-colourable inputs, but the time bound still applies. The algorithm may colour such an input whenever it can; it need not recognize the promise. C is independent of n, degree, density and the input graph. No planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition promise is available. Randomization is explicitly permitted in this version of the inherited question; a deterministic algorithm would be a stronger positive result. The algorithm must colour every vertex and avoid every monochromatic edge on a successful run.
answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm for at least one fixed C, or prove that no such C and randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist. A growing colour bound, a partial colouring of most vertices, or a guarantee only on a restricted graph family is insufficient. NP-hardness of the 3-versus-C promise for every fixed C would establish the usual complexity-theoretic obstruction; excluding randomized algorithms from that obstruction additionally uses \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{RP}\). Hardness for \(C=5\) alone leaves all larger constants unresolved. Conditional hardness results must keep their assumptions explicit.
context:
The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove NP-hardness of finding a five-colouring of a three-colourable graph, as part of a broader algebraic framework. This is far stronger than hardness of finding the promised three-colouring, yet it excludes only particular small output domains under standard complexity assumptions. It does not rule out a successful algorithm using six, 100 or any other larger fixed number of colours.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.
