title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
importance_reason: A foundational search-versus-decision question spanning graph colouring, satisfiability and the algebraic classification of finite PCSPs.
formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures A and B with the same finite signature and \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise \(\mathrm{CSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept X whenever \(X\to A\) and reject X whenever X↛B. Search, on every X promised to satisfy \(X\to A\), must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\).
definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed positive integer arities. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and one relation \(R^{A}\subseteq A^{r}\) for each r-ary symbol R; B and the input X have relations with the same symbols and arities. A homomorphism \(h:X\to B\) is a map on domains such that \((x_{1},\ldots ,x_{r})\in R^{X}\) implies \((h(x_{1}),\ldots ,h(x_{r}))\in R^{B}\) for every symbol and tuple. Write \(X\to B\) when some such map exists. A and B are constants defining the computational problem, and are not part of each input. The input explicitly lists X’s vertices and relation tuples; its encoding length is N. Both algorithms are deterministic Turing machines with running time polynomial in N on all inputs; their constants and exponents may depend on A and B. The decision algorithm may answer either way when X↛A but \(X\to B\). The search algorithm receives no homomorphism to A, only the promise that one exists. It must output the image of every vertex and satisfy every B-relation on promised inputs; outside that promise it may output anything or a failure symbol, but must still halt within its polynomial bound. The quantifiers are \(\forall (A,B)\): (\(\exists\) polynomial-time decider D)⇒(\(\exists\) polynomial-time search algorithm S). No uniform procedure that discovers D or S from arbitrary templates, and no requirement to use D as a black-box oracle, is included.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or identify one fixed pair with a polynomial-time decision algorithm and prove that its promised search problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. An impossibility for one rounding scheme, an undecidable problem with the template as part of the input, or hardness on instances lacking \(X\to A\) does not refute the statement. A conditional separation is relevant progress but must retain its complexity assumption.
context:
A promise CSP separates the conditions known to be satisfiable from the conditions a solution must meet. The structure A describes the stronger requirements; B describes the weaker ones. The fixed homomorphism \(A\to B\) ensures that an A-solution can always be converted into a B-solution if it is known. The difficulty is that the input supplies only the existence promise, without the stronger solution itself.

Graph colouring is a concrete example. Take A to be the complete graph on three vertices and B the complete graph on six vertices. Search asks for an actual six-colouring of a graph known to be three-colourable. Decision merely separates three-colourable graphs from graphs that are not six-colourable. On graphs whose chromatic number is four, five or six, the decider may say anything. That unconstrained region is a central obstacle to turning its answers into a colouring.

Search immediately gives decision: run the search algorithm and check the proposed B-homomorphism. Every A-satisfiable input yields a valid output, while a graph or structure with no B-homomorphism can never pass verification. The all-input polynomial running-time requirement makes this argument valid even when the search promise fails. The unknown direction is whether a decider can always be made constructive.

For ordinary finite CSPs, where \(A=B\), polynomial-time decision and search are equivalent. With a genuine promise, a step-by-step fixing procedure has an extra difficulty. After committing a variable to a B-value, the residual instance may still have a B-solution but cease to have an A-solution. The original decision guarantee then no longer certifies which remaining choices are safe. Adding arbitrary pinning constraints can also change the fixed constraint language.

Some positive cases are immediate. If there is a fixed finite structure C with \(A\to C\to B\) and a polynomial-time solver for \(\mathrm{CSP}(C)\), solve in C and compose with the fixed map \(C\to B\). This includes the cases where \(\mathrm{CSP}(A)\) or \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) is tractable. But the general PCSP framework admits tractable examples that are not explained by an intermediate tractable finite CSP, assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), so this method does not cover the whole question.

There are also elementary constructive relaxations. Suppose Boolean variables occur in triples, with a promise of an assignment having exactly one 1 in every triple, and the goal is merely to make each triple nonconstant. Solve the integer linear system \(x+y+z=1\) for the listed triples, allowing arbitrary integers. The promise makes it feasible. Map positive integers to 1 and nonpositive integers to 0. No equation can have all three integers positive, or all three nonpositive, so this map satisfies every weaker triple. This illustrates a rounding rule whose correctness can be checked directly.

Larrauri’s FOCS 2025 work proves that finding a B-solution on every instance accepted by BLP, AIP or their combination can encode any chosen TFNP problem through a suitable fixed template. TFNP consists of polynomially verifiable search problems whose solutions are guaranteed to exist. The accepted instances need not satisfy \(X\to A\). Thus the rounding task can be harder than the promised search task. The May 2026 revision explicitly corrects earlier overbroad claims and keeps the general implication open.

The same work proves undecidability of several algorithmic meta-problems, where A and B are supplied as input and one asks whether a relaxation solves their PCSP. This concerns recognizing an entire family of templates. Our question permits a different fixed algorithm for each fixed template, so undecidability of that recognition task is logically compatible with a positive answer here.

Recent constructive progress also occurs under explicit algebraic hypotheses. The SODA 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives algorithms for Boolean PCSPs with majority polymorphisms when the stronger constraints are almost satisfiable, along with matching conditional tradeoffs in several settings. Such results identify useful rounding structure, but do not provide a transformation for an arbitrary tractable decision template.

The issue is fundamental because a feasibility guarantee is often only the beginning of an algorithmic application: one needs the assignment, colouring or schedule. A positive theorem would justify moving between classification of decision problems and construction of solutions throughout finite PCSPs. A negative theorem would reveal a precise local-constraint problem where efficient recognition of the promised gap conceals a harder search task.

title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
importance_reason: A widely recognized frontier example for promise constraint satisfaction, explicitly posed beyond the known five-colour hardness. Kept separately from the all-constant algorithm question because it asks for an individually significant fixed-template reduction.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction R from Boolean 3-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every 3-CNF formula F, satisfiability of F implies \(\chi (R(F))\le 3\) and unsatisfiability of F implies \(\chi (R(F))>6\)?
definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses containing at most three literals, each literal being a Boolean variable or its negation; the formula and variable indices have a standard explicit finite binary encoding. R is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that outputs a graph as a labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and a list of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edges. Its total running time and output length are bounded by one polynomial in the formula’s encoding length. A proper k-colouring assigns one of \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) to each vertex so that endpoints of every edge receive different colours. \(\chi (G)\) is the least such k, with \(\chi\) of the empty graph taken to be zero. The promise decision problem, also denoted \(PCSP(K_{3},K_{6})\), has yes-instances \(\chi \le 3\) and no-instances \(\chi >6\); graphs with \(\chi =4,5,6\) are outside the promise. \(K_{k}\) is the loopless complete graph on k vertices. No colouring or satisfiability witness is supplied as input. The reduction must satisfy the two implications unconditionally, without a Unique Games or Label Cover hardness hypothesis. Because 3-SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is precisely the usual deterministic many-one NP-hardness target for the promise problem.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
The input promise says that three colours suffice, but it does not reveal the three colour classes. Allowing a larger palette relaxes the output condition. The associated gap decision task distinguishes such promised yes-instances from graphs that cannot be coloured even with six colours. This isolates a small finite-template promise CSP with a particularly clear combinatorial meaning.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal establish hardness for colouring k-colourable graphs with \(2k- 1\) colours, including the 3-versus-5 case. The 3-versus-6 question remains explicitly posed in subsequent work. Increasing the permitted palette weakens the output requirement, so hardness at five colours does not imply hardness at six.

TCS-6637 asks whether some fixed constant C admits a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for every 3-colourable graph. A negative result for six colours alone does not exclude algorithms using seven, one hundred or another fixed palette. Conversely, an algorithm with a growing number of colours does not settle even the six-colour search problem. The new card is a precise frontier case, rather than a duplicate of the quantifier over arbitrary constants.

The decision and search tasks should also be kept distinct. A polynomial-time six-colouring algorithm on 3-colourable inputs would decide the gap by checking its output: on a graph requiring more than six colours, no valid output exists. This implication explains the algorithmic relevance of the decision hardness target without redefining NP-hardness as a blanket statement about every search reduction.

The six-colour case has value beyond its small numerical parameters. It tests how far promise relaxation can preserve intractability after the classical CSP dichotomy, and it provides a fixed finite object on which algebraic and combinatorial limitations can be stated. Its specialist home remains Constraint satisfaction under the catalogue’s graph-category expansion.

title: Exact exponential-time equivalence for nonnegative Boolean Max-CSP
importance_reason: A degree-based exact-time classification would organize all finite NP-hard Boolean Max-CSP languages with nonnegative weights under one invariant.
formal: Does the following extension of the source’s degree-based classification hold? For every fixed finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) that is neither 0-valid, 1-valid, nor 2-monotone, let \(d=\deg (\Gamma )\). For every fixed real \(\alpha >1\), if Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) has an exact deterministic algorithm running in \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\) time for every fixed constant \(c\ge 1\), must Max d-CNF-SAT with nonnegative integer weights of total weight at most \(n^{c}\) also have an exact deterministic \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for every fixed \(c\ge 1\)? The same base \(\alpha\) is required. Algorithms and polynomial factors may depend on \(\Gamma ,\alpha ,c\). This formulates the conclusion’s speedup question as extending Theorem 6.2 to all NP-hard nonnegative-weight languages; tractable languages are explicitly excluded.
definitions: A Boolean predicate f of arity r is a map \(\{0,1\}\)ʳ→\(\{0,1\}\). A language \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite set of such predicates, not part of an input instance. An instance \(\Phi\) has variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and weighted applications \((f,(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{r}),w)\), where \(f\in \Gamma\), each \(i_{j}\in [n]\) and w is a nonnegative integer. Indices may repeat. Arguments are variables themselves: constants and negated literals are available only if the corresponding predicate can already be expressed by a member of \(\Gamma\) with variable arguments. The value \(\Phi (x)\) is the sum of weights whose predicate applications evaluate to 1. Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) asks whether \(\max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{n}}\Phi (x)\ge t\) for an input integer t, under the promise that total weight is at most \(n^{c}\). Weights, indices and t use binary encoding; duplicate applications can be combined and zero-weight applications discarded. Trivial thresholds outside the possible objective range are handled during input reading. Polynomial-time normalization is included; equivalently the runtime has an additional input-reading term for a redundantly listed representation. The normalized input has polynomial length for fixed \(\Gamma ,c\). The algorithm must answer every promised instance correctly, and n denotes variables, not clauses, total weight or bit length. For each f there is a unique multilinear real polynomial \(\mathrm{P}_{f}\) agreeing with f on its Boolean cube. Its degree is the largest number of variables in a monomial with nonzero coefficient; \(\deg (\Gamma )=\max _{f\in \Gamma}\deg (\mathrm{P}_{f})\). This is neither maximum predicate arity nor polynomial degree over \(F_{2}\). Constants can be removed with a threshold adjustment. Disregarding constant predicates, a language is 0-valid if every predicate accepts its all-zero input, and 1-valid if every predicate accepts its all-one input. It is 2-monotone if each predicate has a DNF representation with at most two terms, one consisting only of positive variables and one only of negated variables. The excluded three cases are the source’s polynomial-time cases for nonnegative weights; the remaining cases are NP-hard and have \(d\ge 2\). Max d-CNF-SAT is the same threshold maximization problem for disjunctions of at most d literals, with both signs of variables allowed, and nonnegative integer clause weights. Equivalently one may use the source’s d-ary clause language and repeated variables. All complexity statements are worst-case exact running times in an ordinary discrete computation model, up to polynomial factors. The premise is quantified over every fixed polynomial weight bound c; a result for only one small weight range does not supply that premise.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every eligible fixed language \(\Gamma\) and every \(\alpha >1\), retaining the same exponential base and the all-c weight convention, or refute it by a language and a rigorously established failure of that implication. A theorem comparing only whether both problems are NP-hard, or comparing compression sizes or exponential rates after a constant-factor increase in variable count, does not establish the stated base-preserving classification.
context:
Theorem 6.2 places all degree-d signed-weight languages in the same exact exponential-base class as weighted Max d-CNF-SAT. The forward implication from Max d-CNF-SAT algorithms also covers its nonnegative-weight restrictions.

The same theorem covers nonnegative languages closed under predicate-output negation, \(f\mapsto 1- f\), or under substitution of literals for arguments. An arbitrary NP-hard language need not have either closure.

The source’s additive reductions introduce only \(O(1)\) variables, so \(\alpha ^{n+O(1)}\) preserves \(\alpha\). Its general conversion to nonnegative weights can instead introduce a linear number of variables. That suffices for transferring a polynomial compression exponent but can change an exponential base.

The March 2024 version repeats the nonnegative-weight speedup question after the exponential-time theorem. Its complete compression classification does not itself resolve the exact-time classification.

formal: Is there one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite crisp constraint language \(\Gamma\) over an explicitly given finite domain D and promised that \(\Gamma\) is a core, decides whether \(\Gamma\) admits an idempotent Siggers polymorphism? Equivalently on the core promise, decide whether \(\Gamma\) is solvable in the algebraic sense of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy. The polynomial must be uniform in the entire input, including |D|, the number of relations, their arities and their listed tuples; neither a polymorphism nor a tractability certificate is supplied.
definitions: A crisp language is a finite set \(\Gamma\) of relations \(R\subseteq D\)ʳ of possibly different finite arities on a finite nonempty explicitly listed domain D. Each relation is given by its arity and a list of its allowed tuples; unlisted tuples are forbidden. This is equivalent to a cost function with value 0 on allowed tuples and +∞ elsewhere. The input size N includes D, relation delimiters, arities and the binary encodings of all listed entries. There is no fixed bound on |D| or arity imposed outside the input. An m-ary operation \(g:D^{m}\to D\) preserves an r-ary relation R if, for every m tuples \(a^{1},\ldots ,a^{m}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple \((g(a^{1}_{1},\ldots ,a^{m}_{1}),\ldots ,g(a^{1}_{r},\ldots ,a^{m}_{r}))\) lies in R. A polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). The language is a core if every unary polymorphism \(u:D\to D\) is bijective; for a finite relational structure such a map is an automorphism. Core status is promised rather than something the requested algorithm must verify. An idempotent Siggers polymorphism is a four-ary operation \(s:D^{4}\to D\) that preserves every relation and satisfies \(s(x,x,x,x)=x\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(s(r,a,r,e)=s(a,r,e,a)\) for every \(r,a,e\in D\). On a core, existence of a Siggers operation without the idempotence identity is equivalent to existence of an idempotent one. An ordinary \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma )\) instance has variables and constraints requiring selected variable tuples to belong to relations of \(\Gamma\); it asks for a satisfying assignment from D. In the source’s terminology, solvable means satisfying the dichotomy’s polymorphism criterion. Such languages have polynomial-time CSP algorithms when \(\Gamma\) is fixed; failure of the criterion gives NP-hardness. The present target tests that algebraic criterion and does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in order to define its yes/no answers. The requested machine must halt in \(N^{O(1)}\) time on all inputs and be correct on every input satisfying the core promise. Its behavior on non-core inputs is unrestricted. The task only asks to decide existence, not to output the operation table, although a four-ary table has |\(D|^{4}\) entries and gives a polynomial-size, polynomially checkable existence certificate.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with one polynomial running-time bound in N that accepts exactly the promised core languages having such a polymorphism, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness statement requires the core promise to be respected. Testing whether the input is a core, classifying languages without that promise, or solving CSP instances for one fixed tractable template does not settle this meta-decision problem.
context:
Testing tractability for arbitrary crisp languages is NP-complete, and testing core status is itself difficult. The question assumes core status from the start; neither hardness result alone classifies the promised problem.

Theorem 16 gives a polynomial algorithm for the relevant binary symmetric fractional polymorphism of a core finite-valued language. Crisp relations use forbidden assignments with infinite cost, so that finite-valued theorem does not provide this Siggers test.

The source states that a uniform polynomial-time solver for all solvable core crisp languages would imply the desired test. The fixed-template dichotomy alone does not give a polynomial uniform in the varying input language.

Bodirsky and Weiß explicitly distinguish idempotent Siggers testing from the unrestricted NP-complete metaproblem and note the equivalence under the core promise. Their results on coset-generating and promise metaproblems do not give the general Siggers test.

title: Word equations with linear length constraints
importance_reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.
focus_reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.
formal: Is there a Turing machine that halts on every finite input consisting of a system of word equations \(U_{i}=V_{i}\) and a system of integer linear equalities and inequalities on the variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when a simultaneous solution exists in the free monoid \(\Sigma\)*? The alphabet, equations, variables, and arithmetic coefficients are part of the input, with the conventions below.
definitions: \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet of constant symbols and \(X=\{X_{1},\ldots ,X_{k}\}\) is a disjoint finite set of variables. Each \(U_{i},V_{i}\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma \cup X\); repeated occurrences of a variable must receive the same substitution. A solution assigns a finite word \(\sigma (X_{j})\in \Sigma\)* to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing every letter of \(\Sigma\). The empty word is allowed. Every substituted equality \(\sigma (U_{i})=\sigma (V_{i})\) must hold as a literal equality of words. The additional constraints are a finite conjunction of atoms \(\sum _{j} a_{j}|\sigma (X_{j})|\le b\) or \(\sum _{j} a_{j}|\sigma (X_{j})|=b\), where all coefficients and constants are signed binary integers. Length is the number of alphabet symbols. There is no product of two variable lengths, letter-frequency counter, regular-expression predicate, string-to-integer conversion, or universal quantifier. The requested decider need not run in polynomial, elementary, or any specified computable time bound, but must terminate on satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs alike. Nonempty-substitution requirements can be imposed using |\(\sigma (X_{j})|\ge 1\). In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation \(Xa=bX\) yields the harmless length identity |\(X|+1=1+|X|\). Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality \(a=b\). This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. This strengthens the PP-hardness stated in its first version. Its NEXP-completeness theorem is for arithmetic with divisibility, not for unrestricted word equations with lengths. Positive Boolean formulas can be expanded into finitely many conjunctions for purposes of decidability, but that expansion need not be polynomial. The result therefore records a substantial complexity barrier without establishing a general decider or undecidability.
why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The IJCAR 2026 primary source explicitly leaves general word-equation satisfiability with length constraints open. The two-variable quadratic theorem is a restricted case, and the July NEXP-hardness claim is a lower bound rather than a decidability result. This card fixes existential satisfiability with concatenation and integer linear length constraints only.
progress: 1977 onward: Makanin establishes decidability of plain word equations. Adding linear length constraints remains outside that theorem; the distinction is reviewed by Ciobanu. | 2024: Ciobanu’s survey explicitly separates the open length-constraint problem from undecidable letter-count and Parikh-image extensions. | 2025-11-05: Day and Konefal’s RP 2025 paper appears online, giving decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on solution lengths. The proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. | 2026-07-19: Version 3 of Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez claims NEXP-hardness for the nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation. Only its arithmetic-with-divisibility problem is asserted NEXP-complete. | 2026-07-24: Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 paper gives partial termination criteria for extended Nielsen transformations and explicitly retains general decidability as open.

Here the substitutions must also satisfy linear arithmetic constraints on their lengths, with all equations and coefficients supplied as input. The project asks for an algorithm that always decides whether these two kinds of constraints have a common solution. Length arithmetic alone forgets letter alignment, while separate string-solving procedures need not respect additional arithmetic restrictions. This is a basic decidability question for exact string constraints, before imposing practical running-time requirements.

title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
importance_reason: The basic unresolved decidability boundary in modal unification, already in the minimal normal modal logic.
focus_reason: The basic unresolved decidability boundary in modal unification, already in the minimal normal modal logic.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.
context:
A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇\(\psi\) is false for every replacement \(\psi\). Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.
why: Determines whether automated reasoning can decide the existence of a validity-making substitution in the basic normal modal logic, despite the decidability of checking each individual instance and the poorly behaved structure of its unifiers.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No decision procedure or undecidability theorem for this exact basic-K problem was located. Beklemishev’s 2025 introduction explicitly states it as open. Nullary unification type, undecidability with extra modalities and 2025 decidability for K5 extensions do not settle it.

The problem asks whether it is decidable that a finite formula has a substitution instance valid at every world of every such model. Substitutions act simultaneously on all input variables, may introduce new variables, and leave no designated parameters fixed. Frames may be finite or infinite, and no reflexivity or transitivity condition is imposed. The requested algorithm must halt on every input; its time and the size of a possible substitution have no prescribed bounds.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time equivalence testing for d-DNNFs
importance_reason: A basic unresolved operation in knowledge compilation, with consequences for checking and comparing compiled knowledge.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given two d-DNNF circuits \(C,D\), returns yes exactly when
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_C(a)=f_D(a),\]
where \(X\) is the union of the variables appearing in the two inputs?

The algorithm must work for all promised pairs, without any requirement that their internal decompositions or variable trees agree. It must give the exact yes/no answer in worst-case time polynomial in their total binary encoding length. The two circuits are supplied explicitly; no truth table, equivalence certificate, common compiled representation or source formula is supplied.
definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.

Equivalence concerns the same assignment in the two circuits; it does not allow renaming variables separately to obtain isomorphism. The inputs may have different numbers of gates and may mention different subsets of \(X\). Logical nonequivalence means that at least one assignment makes their outputs differ. Equal numbers of satisfying assignments do not by themselves establish equivalence. The only required output is the decision bit; construction of a distinguishing assignment is not an additional task.

For comparison with the known randomized result, a one-sided randomized equivalence test can always accept equivalent circuits while rejecting each nonequivalent pair with probability at least \(2/3\), in polynomial time using independent random bits. The target here removes randomness entirely. A probabilistic test, even with arbitrarily small failure probability, does not meet its guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the deterministic polynomial-time existence claim in the stated promise model. A positive answer must give one uniform algorithm, prove exact equivalence decisions on all promised pairs, and establish a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm; it need not produce a single pair that defeats every algorithm. A randomized algorithm, a procedure requiring a common variable tree, or a hardness result for arbitrary DNNFs without determinism does not by itself settle this problem. Neither does hardness of verifying a proposed conjunction of two circuits, which is a different input-output relation.
context:

This card retains the broader general d-DNNF question, independently stated in the knowledge-compilation map; it does not attribute that broader formulation solely to the structured-circuit paper.

Darwiche and Huang give a one-sided randomized polynomial-time equivalence test for general d-DNNFs. Their analysis includes a polynomial bound on the bit length of arithmetic values; the algorithmic claim is stronger than merely bounding the number of unit-cost arithmetic operations.

The knowledge-compilation map distinguishes exact model counting, equivalence and entailment. Efficient counting does not automatically decide whether two represented sets of assignments coincide, and a common variable order or compatible structured decomposition is an additional restriction.

The 2026 paper establishes efficiently checkable restricted restructuring steps while leaving the one-shot comparison across arbitrary trees open. Its hardness discussion for checking a conjunction relation concerns three representations and does not establish hardness of the two-circuit equivalence problem.

title: Greedy CDCL without restarts versus resolution
importance_reason: A concrete bridge between SAT solving and proof complexity: it isolates the computational role of restarts while allowing helpful search choices. The significance comes from the unresolved comparison with general resolution and explicit specialist discussion, not from an unspecified explanation of solver performance.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation which, given a CNF formula F and a resolution refutation \(\pi\) of F, outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same F, without restarts, in the asserting-learning model defined below? Both the transformation time and the output length are polynomial in the binary length of \((F,\pi )\).
definitions:
Literals are \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}\); clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives \((C\setminus \{x\})\cup (D\setminus \{\neg x\})\) from clauses C containing x and D containing \(\neg x\). A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially \(D=F\) and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with \(\pi\); mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
Clause learning stores consequences of encountered conflicts and reuses them during a SAT search. General resolution permits arbitrary reuse of earlier clauses, without requiring that they arise along a current partial assignment. This question asks whether the constraints of a greedy search, even with freely chosen decisions and learning, impose a superpolynomial cost when restarting is unavailable.

The operational model matters. Exhaustive unit propagation and immediate conflict processing constrain which trails are reachable. A restart discards the current trail while retaining learned information, whereas a backjump must be justified by the newly learned asserting clause. The statement specifies those actions separately rather than treating every return to decision level zero as a prohibited restart.

Vinyals gives an execution-trace proof system with explicit propagation reasons, conflict-analysis derivations, deletion rules and cost measures. The present card selects its no-restart policy and allows arbitrary trivial asserting analyses. This avoids making the question depend on a particular solver implementation, while retaining actual greedy search restrictions.

The supplied resolution proof is part of the translator’s input. An affirmative answer therefore would not give a polynomial-time SAT solver or a practical heuristic that discovers short proofs unaided. A theorem guaranteeing only polynomial-size traces, without a polynomial-time translation, would establish the corresponding size-simulation statement rather than the full p-simulation asked here.

Vinyals’ 2022 exposition distinguishes known simulations using non-greedy propagation or preprocessing from the unresolved greedy no-restart comparison. Buss and Thapen’s later work identifies candidate formulas for separating related resolution systems but does not prove that separation. These results motivate the target without establishing a resolution of the operational model on this card.
why: Determine whether eliminating restarts changes the proof-generating power of greedy clause-learning search by more than a polynomial factor.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No p-simulation or separation for the specified greedy operational model was found. Known non-greedy or preprocessing simulations do not meet its restrictions. The cited pool-resolution discussion does not by itself identify pool resolution with this particular trace system.
progress: 2017: The Vinyals thesis specifies a greedy operational CDCL proof system with explicit conflict analysis, deletion and restart policies. | 2022: The specialist exposition distinguishes the no-restart question from known non-greedy and preprocessing simulations. | 2026: Buss–Thapen discuss candidates for separating pool resolution from resolution without establishing such a separation. This is related evidence, not an equivalence claim for every CDCL model.

title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
importance_reason: A minimal and longstanding unresolved termination problem in rewriting theory.
formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
definitions: ['The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \\(\\varepsilon\\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.', 'One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \\(\\ell\\) and replaces it with \\(r\\), preserving the prefix \\(x\\) and suffix \\(y\\). If \\(\\ell=\\varepsilon\\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \\(\\ell=r\\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \\(\\ell\\).', 'Global termination means that for every \\(w_0\\in\\Sigma^{*}\\) there is no function \\(w:\\mathbb{N}\\to\\Sigma^{*}\\) with first value \\(w_0\\) and \\(w_i\\to w_{i+1}\\) for all \\(i\\geq0\\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.', 'Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.
context:
Geser’s paper gives decidability for grid rules: there is a letter \(b\) occurring on the left whose count on the right is no larger. It explicitly distinguishes this substantial subclass from the unresolved arbitrary one-rule problem.

RTA Problem 21 distinguishes the string case from the more general question for a single linear term-rewriting rule. This card asks only about replacements of contiguous substrings.

Kfoury’s August 2026 note restates global one-rule termination as Open Problem 8. It is a source-status update, rather than a new proof of either answer.
why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.
status_note: The 2002 primary paper and the August 2026 authored note present arbitrary one-rule termination as unresolved. A bounded check on 13 September 2026 found no later resolution. The note and historical proofs have not been independently verified; source-open status is not an exhaustive certification.
progress: 2002: Geser proves decidability for grid rules, while retaining the general one-rule question. | 2026-08-19: Open Problem 8 of the new note again asks for decidability of arbitrary one-rule global termination.
working_summary: A one-rule string system repeatedly replaces one fixed substring by another. The question is whether an algorithm can decide if every reduction sequence from every finite starting word eventually stops. Replacement positions are unrestricted, and the rule and alphabet are part of the input. Known decision procedures cover special rule families, while an August 2026 note still lists the arbitrary one-rule question as open. The answer must prove decidability or undecidability in Lean for global termination, rather than only termination from one supplied word.

title: Singly exponential shortest solutions of word equations
importance_reason: Would bound the hidden size of solutions and support efficient compressed certificates for a central string-constraint problem.
formal:
Do positive integers \(c,k\) exist such that every satisfiable word equation \(u=v\), over every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of constant letters and a disjoint finite set \(\mathcal X\) of variables, has a solution \(h\) satisfying
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|\le 2^{c(n+1)^k},\qquad n=|u|+|v|?\]
Here \(\mathcal X\) consists exactly of the variables occurring in the equation, each occurrence contributes one to \(n\), and the maximum over no variables is zero. A solution replaces each variable consistently by a finite word over \(\Sigma\), possibly empty, fixes the constant letters and makes the two expanded words identical.

The same constants \(c,k\) must work independently of the equation, the alphabet and the number of variables. This is the polynomial-exponent meaning of singly exponential. A linear exponent is welcome but is not required.
definitions:
For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) consists of all finite sequences of its letters, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Multiplication is concatenation, and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity. The length \(|w|\) is the number of letters in the sequence \(w\), with \(|\varepsilon|=0\). Distinct constant letters are distinct symbols, not variables or numbers. The alphabet may have any finite cardinality; if it is empty, its only word is \(\varepsilon\).

An equation is a pair of explicitly written words \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Each variable and each constant occurrence counts as one symbol in the equation size \(n\). No compressed input, binary-encoded repeat operator, regular-language membership condition, length constraint, inequality, involution or cancellation operation is supplied. Exponent notation in an example of an equation is only shorthand for its fully expanded string, and its expanded length is charged. Variables may occur arbitrarily many times and may appear on either or both sides.

A solution is a monoid morphism \(h:(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\to\Sigma^*\) that fixes every \(a\in\Sigma\) and satisfies \(h(u)=h(v)\). Equivalently, choose one word \(h(x)\in\Sigma^*\) for each variable, substitute the same word at every occurrence, and concatenate in the original order. Empty substitutions are allowed, and no letter outside \(\Sigma\) may occur in a substitution. This is solving an equation in a free monoid, not in a free group or a semigroup with mandatory nonempty substitutions.

For a satisfiable equation, define
\[m(u,v)=\min_{h:\,h(u)=h(v)}\ \max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|.\]
The minimum exists because the feasible lengths form a nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers. The claim is \(m(u,v)\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\) for all satisfiable equations. It asks for at least one bounded solution to each equation, not for a bound on every solution. An equation can have infinitely many solutions with unbounded lengths and still satisfy the proposed shortest-solution bound.

The source also measures a solution by the length of the common expanded word \(h(u)=h(v)\). For each solution with \(M=\max_x|h(x)|\), every occurring variable image is a factor of that common word, and
\[M\le |h(u)|\le n\max(1,M).\]
These inequalities also cover the no-variable case using \(M=0\). Thus existence of a singly exponential bound on the shortest common-word length and the displayed variable-image bound are equivalent after changing the universal polynomial in the exponent. The card does not assert equality of these two minimum-length quantities.

The negative answer is the quantified assertion that for every pair of positive integers \(c,k\), some satisfiable equation has no solution meeting \(\max_x|h(x)|\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\). It is not enough to exhibit an exponential-length solution when a shorter one exists, or to beat one chosen polynomial exponent. No efficient construction of a solution or of a counterexample family is part of this nonconstructive length question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the universal singly exponential bound. A proof must provide fixed positive integers \(c,k\) and prove the bound for all satisfiable equations under the free-monoid and explicit-symbol conventions. A refutation must prove that every such polynomial-exponent bound fails. Bounds for a fixed number of variables, bounded occurrence counts, a restricted equation family or only compressed solution sizes do not settle the general claim. Proving membership of satisfiability in NP by an unrelated argument does not by itself establish this specific length bound.
context:
Conjecture B concerns the length of a shortest solution. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 establish that this conjecture would imply the separate NP-membership conjecture for satisfiability. The implication depends on the proved compression property; an exponentially long explicit witness alone is not a polynomial-size certificate.

The source fixes letters and permits variable substitutions in the free monoid, hence allows erasing substitutions. The card retains its explicit occurrence-based equation size and uses a universal polynomial exponent to resolve the phrase singly exponential.

Jeż gives an independent proof of a doubly exponential general bound on the shortest common-word length. A bound of that scale does not establish the single-exponential claim, and bounds on repeated periodic blocks are not automatically bounds on the full solution length.

The 2026 paper gives stronger parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. It still describes membership in NP as open for unrestricted word equations. The fixed-variable, constant-free structural result does not cover the arbitrary equations in this card.
why: Very short equations can describe solutions whose expanded words are enormous. A universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound would constrain this hidden growth and, by the source’s compression theorem, imply NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. This links a basic combinatorial question about strings to the unresolved complexity of exact string constraints.

A bounded subsequent search, including July 2026 work on periodicity for constrained quadratic equations, found no matching universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound or refutation. The latter periodicity question has different quantifiers and restrictions. No exhaustive current-openness claim is made.

The conjecture says that every satisfiable equation of size n has some solution whose variable images have length at most two to a fixed polynomial in n. The bound must hold uniformly over all finite alphabets and arbitrarily many variable occurrences, with empty substitutions allowed. Known compression results make this length conjecture sufficient for NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. Doubly exponential bounds and newer results for restricted equation families do not meet the universal single-exponential target.

title: Polynomial-time complementation of d-DNNFs
importance_reason: Efficient closure transformations for structured circuits would improve a reusable representation tool in knowledge compilation.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given any d-DNNF circuit \(C\), outputs a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over the same variables such that
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The runtime is measured in the explicit binary input encoding and includes writing the entire output. The output may use different decompositions and share subcircuits arbitrarily, subject to the same d-DNNF conditions. It may omit irrelevant input variables, but may not introduce new variables, quantifiers or negation gates above leaves.

One uniform algorithm and one polynomial bound must work for all input sizes and all promised circuits. This is a construction question, distinct from the nonconstructive polynomial-size closure question.
definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such a uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm. A positive answer must prove the output d-DNNF properties, equality to the complement on every assignment and the full bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms meeting this promise specification, not merely one construction or one output structure. A polynomial-size existence theorem without an efficient construction does not prove the claim. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication unless the needed assumption is also proved.
context:
The source question explicitly separates efficient complementation from existence of a small complement. Every Boolean complement has some d-DNNF representation; the issue is a polynomial bound, and for the computational version a uniform algorithm achieving one.

The knowledge-compilation map treats negation as a transformation with an output representation, separately from queries such as counting satisfying assignments or comparing functions. Its d-DNNF negation entry is unresolved.

Vinall-Smeeth proves a superpolynomial complement-size lower bound when the output must remain structured, even without output determinism. The source leaves unstructured d-DNNF complementation open: removing the global variable-tree restriction changes the target of the lower bound.

The 2026 probabilistic-word paper connects complement gates in tractable circuit representations to the unresolved succinctness question for d-DNNFs. This is evidence of an additional counting-language connection, not a general complement construction or lower bound.
why: Complementation is a basic operation needed to reuse a compiled Boolean representation for exceptions, exclusions and opposite events. General d-DNNFs support useful counting and reasoning tasks, but it is unknown whether this logical transformation can always preserve their computational advantages with polynomial overhead. Resolving the construction question would clarify which operations can be performed directly on this succinct representation.

title: Polynomial-time recognition of abelian cores
importance_reason: A structural meta-algorithm question about recognizing a source of tractability for finite-algebra equation systems, with a quasipolynomial algorithm but no known polynomial bound. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite algebra \(\mathbf A\) by full tables of its basic operations and promised that \(\mathbf A\) has an idempotent Taylor term, decides whether the core of \(\mathbf A\) is abelian? This selects the decision part of Theorem 3, whose quasipolynomial running time is the subject of the source’s open question.
question_excerpt: We do not know whether the quasi-polynomial time algorithms in Theorem 3 can be improved to polynomial time.
definitions:
A finite algebra \(\mathbf A=(A;f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\) has a nonempty explicitly listed finite universe and a finite signature. Each basic operation \(f_{j}:A^{r_{j}}\to A\) is supplied by its complete table, with its arity. Nullary operations, when present, specify distinguished constants. The universe size, number of operations and arities may vary with the input. Let \(L\) be the total binary length of this description. A large-arity operation is not given by a succinct circuit or program.

A term is an expression made from variables and the given operation symbols; interpreting it on \(\mathbf A\) gives a term operation. Constants not in the given signature are not automatically available as term symbols.

The Taylor promise means that there are an arity \(r\geq2\) and a term operation \(t:A^{r}\to A\) such that \(t(a,\ldots,a)=a\) for every \(a\in A\), and for every coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there are two tuples \(\mathbf u_{i},\mathbf v_{i}\in\{x,y\}^{r}\) with \((\mathbf u_{i})_{i}=x\), \((\mathbf v_{i})_{i}=y\), satisfying
\[t(\mathbf u_{i}(a,b))=t(\mathbf v_{i}(a,b))\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in A.\]
The choices of \(r,t\) and identities may depend on the algebra. This is what the source means by membership in a Taylor variety. A witnessing term or operation table is not supplied, and recognizing whether the promise holds is not part of the task.

An endomorphism of \(\mathbf A\) is a map \(h:A\to A\) preserving every basic operation:
\[h(f_{j}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{j}}))=f_{j}(h(a_{1}),\ldots,h(a_{r_{j}})).\]
It must also fix the interpretation of every nullary symbol. Its image is a subalgebra. A core is an endomorphic image minimal under inclusion among such images, equipped with the restricted operations. For finite algebras these cores are unique up to isomorphism; equivalently, every endomorphism of the core is an automorphism.

Abelianness here is the universal-algebraic term-condition property. A concrete definition uses the algebra of \(2\times2\) matrices over a finite algebra \(\mathbf B\), with each basic operation applied entrywise. Let \(M_{\mathbf B}\) be the smallest subset of \(B^{2\times2}\) closed under these operations and containing all matrices
\[\begin{pmatrix}a&a\\ b&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\qquad(a,b,c,d\in B).\]
Then \(\mathbf B\) is abelian if every matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{pmatrix}\in M_{\mathbf B}\) satisfies \(x=y\Rightarrow z=w\). This is the source’s condition \([1_{\mathbf B},1_{\mathbf B}]=0_{\mathbf B}\). It is not a requirement that each basic operation be commutative.

One uniform deterministic algorithm must run in \(O(L^{k})\) bit operations for a fixed constant \(k\), with a fixed multiplicative constant, on all inputs. It must answer correctly for every well-formed algebra satisfying the Taylor promise. On other inputs the answer is unrestricted, but the polynomial time bound still applies. The requested output is only YES or NO; no particular representative of the core has to be chosen.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with a uniform polynomial bound in the full table encoding length that recognizes abelian cores on every promised input, or prove that none exists. A conditional lower bound must identify its assumption. The source also asks for faster construction of the core and its Mal’cev operation in positive cases; those are additional output tasks and are not silently asserted equivalent to the selected decision question.
context:
Theorem 3 decides abelianness of the core for every finite algebra in a Taylor variety. In positive cases it also computes the core and the table of its Mal’cev term operation. The open continuation asks whether the quasipolynomial algorithms can be made polynomial. The present card isolates recognition as one precise component.

Under the stronger congruence-modular assumption, Theorem 2 identifies abelian cores as the tractable side of the dichotomy for systems of term equations over a fixed algebra; the other side is NP-complete. This explains the recognition problem’s motivation. Theorem 3 itself has the broader Taylor promise, so that stronger assumption must not be substituted into its input specification.

The source notes that testing for a Taylor term on an arbitrary finite operation-table algebra is EXPTIME-complete. Here its existence is promised. Conversely, the not-necessarily-idempotent Taylor polymorphism used elsewhere in the paper’s general CSP dichotomy is a different notion from the idempotent Taylor term in this promise.

Aichinger’s June 2024 lecture on equations over finite algebras restates Mayr’s quasipolynomial recognition bound when discussing the congruence-modular case. It distinguishes the problem of classifying a supplied algebra from solving equations over a fixed one.
why: Measures the cost of recognizing algebraic structure that can make entire families of equation systems tractable. The question asks whether a useful structural classification can be found with polynomial preprocessing, rather than only being available as a theorem about each fixed algebra.
status_note: Read the complete original question, Theorems 1–3, core and Taylor definitions, the matrix definition of abelianness, and Section 5’s quasipolynomial bound. Read the June 2024 overview’s meta-problem discussion. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial-time improvement for the stated promise problem. The decision branch is explicitly selected; no equivalence with the additional constructive outputs or with unrestricted equation solving is assumed.
progress: 2023: Theorem 3 establishes quasipolynomial abelian-core recognition for finite algebras with a Taylor term, with additional construction guarantees on positive instances. | 2024-06: A subsequent overview restates the quasipolynomial classification algorithm in the congruence-modular setting.
working_summary: The input is an entire finite algebra specified by tables of its basic operations. It is promised to possess an idempotent Taylor term, although no witness is supplied. The task is to decide whether its smallest endomorphic image is abelian in the universal-algebraic sense. A quasipolynomial-time recognition algorithm is known. This is a classification problem for algebras, distinct from solving a particular list of term equations.

title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: The central proposed tractability boundary for first-order model checking on hereditary graph classes, connecting database queries, model theory, sparsity and dense graph structure.
focus_reason: The central proposed tractability boundary for first-order model checking on hereditary graph classes, connecting database queries, model theory, sparsity and dense graph structure.
formal: For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class C of finite simple graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{C}, a\) computable function \(f_{C}:N\to N\) and a constant \(d_{C}\) such that \(A_{C}\) decides whether G satisfies a first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in time \(f_{C}(|\varphi |)(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{C}}\) for every \(G\in C\)? The precise effectiveness condition is given below; the graph is supplied without a structural decomposition.
definitions: The class C is fixed, is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs, and is not part of each input. First-order sentences use equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual vertices. They do not quantify over sets, and no vertex order or arithmetic is supplied. The input is the explicitly represented graph G and the sentence \(\varphi\); the parameter \(k=|\varphi |\) is its encoded length. The algorithm must halt on every input, and its correctness and stated time bound are required when \(G\in C\); it need not recognize membership in C. To define monadic dependence, let \(\theta (x,y)\) be any fixed first-order formula using adjacency and finitely many additional unary predicates. A graph in \(T_{\theta}(G)\) is obtained by interpreting these predicates as arbitrary vertex subsets, putting an edge between distinct u,v whenever \(\theta (u,v)\) or \(\theta (v,u)\) holds, and taking any induced subgraph. C is monadically dependent when no single \(\theta\) gives all finite graphs among the outputs \(T_{\theta}(G), G\in C\). For an explicit effective version, define \(\mathrm{P}_{s}\) as the bipartite powerset graph with vertices \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{s}\) and \(b_{S}\) for every \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,s\}\), and edges \(a_{i} b_{S}\) exactly when \(i\in S\). Require a computable function \(b:N\to N_{\ge 1}\) such that, for every formula \(\theta\) and every \(G\in C, \mathrm{P}_{b(|\theta |)}\) is absent from \(T_{\theta}(G)\). Formula length includes its predicate symbols under a fixed effective encoding. This is the computable dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24. The programs computing b and the eventual algorithm may depend on C; they are not extra per-instance certificates. The exponent \(d_{C}\) is independent of k. The query-evaluation problem here is for the plain graph signature; unary colours occur in the structural definition. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
