context:
First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try \(n^{k}\) choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form \(f(k)n^{d}\): the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{AW}[*]\), this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive \(\eta\), the number of distinct sets \(N(v)\cap A\) is \(O(|A|^{1+\eta})\) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and \(\eta\). It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width \(n^{o(1)}\) in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

A positive answer would unify several major algorithmic graph frameworks through one logical condition and explain when small declarative queries can avoid repeated high-dimensional enumeration. A counterexample satisfying the effective hypothesis would show that the absence of arbitrary logical graph encoding is insufficient for tractability. Either outcome would sharpen the connection between graph structure and query evaluation.
why: Determine whether excluding arbitrary first-order graph encoding exactly supplies the structure needed for tractable logical queries on hereditary graph classes.

title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.
focus_reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.
formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with \(O_{q}(N)\) preprocessing and \(O_{q}(1)\) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
definitions: A query is a finite formula \(q(\bar\{x\})=\exists \bar\{y\} \land _{i} R_{i}(\bar\{z\}_{i})\), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain \([n]; N=1+n\)+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in \(O(\log (N+2))\) bits. \(q(D)\) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of \(O_{q}(\log (N+2))\) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants \(C_{q},B_{q}\) whose preprocessing takes at most \(C_{q} N\) steps, whose word length is at most \(B_{q} \log _{2}(N+2)\), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most \(C_{q}\) after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

context:
A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer \((x,z)\), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example \(\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge \(\{x,z\}\) creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query \(R(x,y)\land R(y,z)\land R(x,t)\land R(t,z)\). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with \(t=y\). When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.
why: A missing general tractability boundary for relational query evaluation, connecting logical syntax, enumeration algorithms and fine-grained lower bounds.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.
progress: 2007: Bagan–Durand–Grandjean establish the free-connex framework and conditional enumeration dichotomies for the classical acyclic setting. | 2022–2023: Carmeli–Segoufin demonstrate additional tractable self-join queries, prove partial classifications and give mirror-query algorithms; preprint 2022, PODS 2023. | 2 May 2025: Rouvroy’s preliminary research report gives further sufficient and necessary conditions for acyclic self-join queries with binary or unary atoms, leaving examples unclassified. | 5 June 2026: Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang study semiring-dependent incremental maintenance and obtain a dichotomy in a self-join-free insert-only setting; this is a different model.
working_summary: A conjunctive query joins relations and projects the resulting assignments to its output variables. The question asks for a terminating classifier deciding which queries allow linear preprocessing followed by constant-delay enumeration of distinct answers. Self-joins are allowed, so repeated uses of one relation can create symmetries and dependencies absent from simpler classifications. A complete answer would identify the exact boundary for efficiently generating query results in this basic language. The reviewed formulation fixes the RAM and termination conventions, and the classifier itself need not run quickly or output the enumeration algorithm.

title: A logic capturing polynomial time
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.
formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.
context:
A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.
why: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly states that no logic is known to capture PTIME on arbitrary finite structures. The review through 11 September 2026 found no general existence or impossibility result. Candidate-specific, ordered and structured-output results are distinguished.
progress: 2008: Grohe surveys the general capturing question and positive results for particular classes of structures. | 2015: Grädel–Grohe make the effective compiler and decidable-syntax requirements explicit in their survey of choiceless computation. | 2022 / 2023: Witnessed symmetric choice yields capture on classes with definable isomorphism in the extended formalism. | 2026-08: Group-order logic research retains the general question and studies restricted generating-set operations.
working_summary: Is there an effective logic for all polynomial-time properties of finite unordered structures? Its sentences must describe properties unchanged by renaming domain elements. Each sentence must compile effectively to an evaluation algorithm with a polynomial time bound. Fixed-point logic captures polynomial time when an order is supplied, but that is a different input model. Current candidate and restricted-class results leave the general existence question open.

title: Asser’s problem
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.
formal: For every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over a finite relational vocabulary, does there exist a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over some finite relational vocabulary such that, for every positive integer \(n, \psi\) has a model with exactly n elements if and only if \(\varphi\) has no model with exactly n elements?
definitions: A vocabulary is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified positive integer arity; the list and the arities may vary with the sentence and are not bounded by a fixed global constant. Equality is allowed. Sentences use variables, relation atoms, equality, Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, with no free variables. A finite model has a nonempty domain A and interprets each k-ary relation as a subset of \(A^{k}\), with equality interpreted as equality on A. The spectrum \(Spec(\varphi )\) is {\(n\in N:n\ge 1\) and some finite model of \(\varphi\) has cardinality n}. The required equality is \(Spec(\psi )=N_{>0}\) minus \(Spec(\varphi )\). The vocabulary of \(\psi\) need not be the vocabulary of \(\varphi\). No bound on the length of \(\psi\) and no effective transformation \(\varphi \mapsto \psi\) are required. Restricting to relational vocabularies loses no ordinary first-order spectra: functions and constants can be represented by their graph relations with first-order axioms for totality and uniqueness. This is closure of the class of spectra, not a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If \(\varphi\) describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies \(\neg \varphi\), so even numbers also belong to \(Spec(\neg \varphi )\). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence \(\psi\), chosen after \(\varphi\) but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing \(\psi  a\) different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.
why: Determine a basic closure property of finite first-order expressibility after taking possible model sizes.
status_note: No general resolution was found in the source and later-work searches through 11 September 2026. The principal detailed reference is the \(2009/2012\) survey; this is not a claim that every later paper on spectra was checked.
progress: 1950s: Asser formulates whether complements of spectra are spectra, as documented in the historical survey. | 2009–2012: The comprehensive survey retains the general complement question among its unresolved problems.

title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational question connecting description logics, database queries and infinite-model reasoning, with sharply different outcomes for nearby restrictions.
formal: Does one total algorithm decide, for every finite SROIQ knowledge base K and every Boolean conjunctive query q, whether \(K\models q\) under the standard semantics over all finite or infinite models?
definitions: Fix classical SROIQ without datatypes, using the syntax of Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler (2006), Definitions 1–6. Concept names denote subsets of a nonempty domain; nominal concept names denote singletons; individual names denote elements, without a unique-name assumption. Role names denote binary relations, inverse roles reverse their arguments, and U denotes the universal relation. Concepts are built from names, ⊤, ⊥, Boolean operations, \(\exists r\).C and \(\forall r\).C, qualified number restrictions \(\ge k s\).C and \(\le k s\).C, and \(\exists s\).Self. The last three require a simple role s. They mean, respectively, at least or at most k distinct s-successors satisfying C, and an s-edge from an element to itself. The nonnegative integer k is encoded in binary. K consists of concept inclusions C⊑D, individual assertions \(C(a), r(a,b), \neg r(a,b), a\ne b\), and a legal role box. Role inclusions have form w⊑R, with R a non-universal role name and w a nonempty string of non-universal roles, interpreted by relational composition. Regularity requires a strict partial order ≺ on roles satisfying S≺R iff \(Inv(S)\)≺R, such that each inclusion has \(w=RR, w=Inv(R)\), or \(w=S_{1}\ldots S_{t}, RS_{1}\ldots S_{t}\), or \(S_{1}\ldots S_{t}R\) with every \(S_{i}\)≺R. Equivalent roles can first be identified. Transitivity and symmetry are represented by RR⊑R and \(Inv(R)\)⊑R. A role is non-simple if a composition of length at least two is included in it, or in one of its subroles, closing under inverse; all other roles are simple. Reflexivity assertions are allowed; irreflexivity, strict asymmetry and role-disjointness assertions require simple roles. U cannot occur in role-box assertions. These are the standard global regularity and simplicity restrictions, not unrestricted role-chain rules. The query is \(q=\exists x_{1}\ldots x_{t} \land _{j}\alpha _{j}\), where each atom is \(A(u)\) or \(r(u,v), A\) is a concept name, r is a role name, and terms are variables or individual names. Query roles may be non-simple. Query atoms have no negation, inequality or regular-path operators; variables may receive the same value. A model satisfies q when some assignment makes every atom true. \(K\models q\) means every model of K satisfies q, including infinite models; an inconsistent K entails every query. Both K and q are input, and the sought algorithm must halt on every legal pair, with no prescribed complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let K assert \(Person(a)\) and Person⊑\(\exists\)knows.Person. Every model then contains a person who knows a person, so K entails \(\exists x\exists y\)(\(Person(x)\land knows(x,y)\land Person(y)\)). No named witness for y is needed. The same individual may serve as both variables when the model permits it. More complicated queries reuse variables across several edges, requiring a single assignment that satisfies all joins simultaneously.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with \(\neg q\) is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

To see the difference directly, require every domain element to have exactly one r-successor and at most one r-predecessor, and require a named element a to have no predecessor. The role r can be simple. Such a knowledge base has an infinite model, the natural-number successor chain, but no finite model: on a finite set, an injective total successor function would be surjective. A fresh predicate A may be empty in the infinite model, so \(\exists x A(x)\) is not entailed over all models. Over finite models it is vacuously entailed, because there are none.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.
why: A basic decidability boundary for querying expressive ontologies: the logic has decidable consistency, but unrestricted conjunctive-query entailment still lacks a general resolution.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No general decision procedure or undecidability proof for Boolean CQ entailment over all SROIQ models was found in the checked sources. Simple-role queries, Horn fragments, finite-model undecidability and the 2026 complexity result for S concern distinct restricted problems.
progress: 2006: Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler define SROIQ and prove decidability of its standard consistency reasoning tasks. | 2010: Rudolph–Glimm establish query decidability with nominals, inverses and counting, including SROIQ queries restricted to simple roles. | 2011: Ortiz–Rudolph–Šimkus establish decidable path-query answering for Horn-SROIQ. | 2016: Rudolph proves finite-model conjunctive-query entailment undecidable in a SROIQ fragment; this uses finite semantics. | 2019: Steigmiller–Glimm present absorption-based checking, while explicitly retaining the full decidability question and a termination condition involving new nominals. | 8 May 2026: The revised full version of the AAAI 2026 paper proves 2ExpTime-completeness for S, including Boolean-query hardness with two transitive roles.
working_summary: An expressive ontology describes facts and rules that can require additional unnamed objects in every model. The reviewed question asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide all Boolean conjunctive queries against finite SROIQ knowledge bases. Such a query looks for a relational pattern, including joins that require several conditions to hold for the same objects. Consistency checking and known decidable fragments do not settle the unrestricted combination of query joins, counting, inverse roles, and role compositions. The chosen semantics includes infinite models, so the saved undecidability result for finite-model entailment addresses a different question.

title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.
formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries \(q_{1}\) and \(q_{2}\) with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and \(D(A_{j}[h])\) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function \(U^{r}\) to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
context:
Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let \(q(x)\) have body \(R(x)\), and let \(r(x)\) have body \(R(x),R(x)\). If \(R(a)\) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns \(m^{2}\). Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as \(m=2\). This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.
why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.
status_note: Open in the 2025 seminar, the June 2025 revised CQ-versus-UCQ paper, and the maintained problem list accessed 10 September 2026. No resolution was located in current searches. The problem includes bag input multiplicities and is not the separate bag-set variant.
progress: 1993: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper. | 2024 / preprint posted 2025: Marcinkowski and Orda prove undecidability for nearby generalizations, including comparison after a supplied linear transformation of a Boolean query’s count. This is not the unmodified containment predicate. | 2025-03-21: Konstantinidis and Mogavero prove decidability when the left query is join-on-free and the right query is a general CQ. This extends the earlier projection-free decidable case. | 2025-06-01: The revised Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja paper develops techniques connecting CQ and UCQ containment, while explicitly leaving ordinary CQ-versus-CQ bag-containment decidability open. | 2026-09-10 check: Amarilli’s maintained question list continues to list bag-containment decidability. Current searches did not locate a resolution of the plain two-CQ formulation.
working_summary: Under bag semantics, database tuples and query answers have multiplicities rather than just presence or absence. The question asks whether containment of two conjunctive queries is decidable when their output multiplicities must be ordered on every finite bag database. Each query sums products of input multiplicities over satisfying assignments, so ordinary set-containment reasoning does not directly capture the comparison. A decision procedure would settle a basic semantic question relevant to duplicate-preserving query transformations. The saved review distinguishes progress for unions or restricted joins from the plain unrestricted conjunctive-query problem retained here.

title: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: Computability of entropic query-size bounds tests whether the strongest information-theoretic join estimates are algorithmically accessible.
formal: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
context: Logical queries over finite structures. Expressive power and evaluation models determine algorithmic possibilities.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Entropy-based bounds use information inequalities to limit the number of answers a database query can produce. The source asks whether the relevant entropic query-size bounds are computable. The issue is not merely evaluating one join, but determining an extremal bound over all data distributions or instances satisfying the supplied constraints. An effective method would strengthen the use of information theory in predicting query output size. The inherited label does not preserve the constraint language, exact-versus-approximate target, or entropy region, so these must be recovered before the computability claim is formalized.

title: Linear-round convergence over stable semirings
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.
formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer \(p\ge 0\), every \(n\ge 1\), every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map \(F:S^{n} -> S^{n}\) with coefficients in S? Starting with \(x^{0}=(0,\ldots ,0)\), perform synchronous iteration \(x^{t+1}=F(x^{t})\). There must exist an integer \(t\le C(p+1)n\) with \(x^{t+1}=x^{t}\). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.
definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times \(a=0\). No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and \(a^{0}=1\). Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by \((p+1)n\) is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
context:
In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only \(O(n)\), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma \(p n^{2}\) (\(n^{2} \log\)(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for \(O((p+1)n)\), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. title: Cai–Fürer–Immerman definability in choiceless polynomial time
area: Database theory and finite model theory

importance_reason: A foundational benchmark for descriptive complexity and the expressive power of symmetry-preserving polynomial computation. Existing score retained.
formal: Is the parity query for Cai–Fürer–Immerman graphs over arbitrary connected unordered base graphs definable in Choiceless Polynomial Time with counting? In the source’s construction below, is there one CPT program \(P\) that, for every finite connected base graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every \(T\subseteq V\), accepts the unordered input graph \(G^{T}\) exactly when \(|T|\) is odd?
question_excerpt: However, there are some properties for which we do not know whether they can be expressed in CPT, and which might witness a separation from […]
definitions:
The base graph is finite, nonempty, simple and undirected. Write \(E(v)\) for the edges incident with \(v\). Use the vertex-parity construction of Section 3 of the primary source. For each base edge \(e\), introduce two distinct vertices \(e_{0},e_{1}\). For each base vertex \(v\), introduce a vertex \(v^{X}\) for every subset \(X\subseteq E(v)\) satisfying
\[|X|\equiv\mathbf1_{v\in T}\pmod2.\]
For each such \(v^{X}\) and each \(e\in E(v)\), join \(v^{X}\) to \(e_{1}\) if \(e\in X\), and to \(e_{0}\) otherwise. These are all the edges in this primary-source convention. Thus an even gadget uses even subsets, and an odd gadget uses odd subsets.

The constructed names describe the mathematical construction; they are not readable labels in the input. The program receives only an unordered graph isomorphic to \(G^{T}\), through its adjacency relation. It receives no order of base vertices, no designation of which edge-gadget vertex is 0 or 1, no set \(T\), and no list of the subsets \(X\). There is no auxiliary coloring, padding or supplied circuit. The source’s parity query distinguishes the two CFI types over each connected base graph. Inputs outside the promised CFI family need not be recognized.

The resource parameter is \(N=|V(G^{T})|\), the size of the explicit expanded input, not \(|V(G)|\). A high-degree base vertex can generate exponentially many gadget vertices. The program and its polynomial resource bound must work uniformly over all base graphs and all twists \(T\).

CPT here includes counting. Its data domain consists of the input vertices as indivisible atoms and hereditarily finite sets built from these atoms: finite sets whose members are atoms or further such finite sets, with finite nesting depth. The available constants include the empty set and the set of all atoms. Operations are unordered pairing \(\{x,y\}\), union, extracting the unique member of a singleton (returning the empty set otherwise), and cardinality. Cardinalities are encoded as von Neumann ordinals, where \(0=\varnothing\) and \(m+1=m\cup\{m\}\). Counting an atom returns the empty set.

Terms are built from variables, these constants and operations, and bounded set comprehensions
\[\{s(\bar x,y):y\in r(\bar x)\text{ and }\varphi(\bar x,y)\}.\]
Tests use equality, membership and input adjacency, combined by Boolean connectives. Comprehensions range over an already constructed finite set; there is no primitive that arbitrarily chooses a member of a non-singleton set or provides an order on the atoms.

A program is fixed finite syntax for a state-update term and two tests, for halting and acceptance. Beginning with empty state, it repeatedly applies the update and checks the tests. There is a fixed polynomial bound in \(N+1\) on the number of iterations and on the number of distinct objects in the transitive closures of the states. A transitive closure includes all recursively nested members, so a huge set cannot be hidden inside a small outer container. Exceeding a bound aborts and rejects. Equivalent standard encodings of the CPT formalism give the same definability question.

All permitted operations respect permutations of the input atoms that preserve adjacency. Numerical ordinals can be ordered, but this does not authorize an arbitrary order of graph vertices. The question permits unbounded finite nesting depth subject to the polynomial size bound; it is not limited to fixed-rank sets or tuples.

A negative result for a restricted family of CPT programs, or failure to construct a particular auxiliary order, does not establish nondefinability in full CPT.

title: \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) conjecture
importance_reason: Would provide a universally informative comparison for sorting with partial-order information; retained as a computationally motivated combinatorial exception.
focus_reason: Would provide a universally informative comparison for sorting with partial-order information; retained as a computationally motivated combinatorial exception.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every partial order \(\mathrm{P}=([n],\le _{\mathrm{P}})\) that is not a total order, do there exist incomparable elements \(x,y\in [n]\) such that \(e(\mathrm{P})/3\le e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y)\le 2e(\mathrm{P})/3\)?
definitions: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive binary relation on \([n]\). Distinct elements \(x,y\) are incomparable if neither \(x\le_P y\) nor \(y\le_P x\); a total order has no incomparable pair. A linear extension is a bijection \(L:[n]\to[n]\) such that \(L(a)<L(b)\) whenever \(a\le_P b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(P)=|E(P)|\), and \(e_P(x,y)=|\{L\in E(P):L(x)<L(y)\}|\). Probabilities use the uniform distribution on the entire set \(E(P)\), so \(\Pr[L(x)<L(y)]=e_P(x,y)/e(P)\). The endpoints \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are included. The pair may depend on the full finite order; there is no algorithmic or representation restriction. In the context, width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements, height the largest size of a totally ordered subset, and the cover graph joins \(x,y\) if one is strictly below the other with no element strictly between them. The balance constant is \(\beta(P)=\max_{x\ne y}\min\{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)\}/e(P)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite non-total partial order has an incomparable pair with \(e(P)/3\le e_P(x,y)\le2e(P)/3\), or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair violates that closed interval. All extension counts and probabilities must use the full set of linear extensions defined here.
context:
A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.
why: Asks for the sharp universal quality of a comparison when sorting with partial information. It connects uncertainty among compatible rankings to an extremal property of every finite partial order.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Aires–Kahn state the general conjecture separately from their large-width theorems; Gupta reports a finite census through fourteen elements. No unrestricted resolution was located in the bounded later-work check. Census computations and source proofs were not rerun independently.
progress: 1995: Brightwell–Felsner–Trotter establish the general balance bound \((5- \sqrt{5})/10\). | 2023 onward: Chan–Pak survey distinguishes the open universal conjecture from established structural cases. | 2025: Aires–Kahn prove stronger balance under width and other size hypotheses. | 2026-07: Gupta reports exhaustive verification of Gold Partition through fourteen elements, implying the target in that finite range.
working_summary: A partial order records known comparisons, and its linear extensions are all compatible complete rankings. The conjecture asks whether every finite non-total order has an incomparable pair that appears in either relative order in at least one third of all extensions. The extensions are weighted uniformly, and both endpoints of the interval are allowed. A three-element order with only one comparison shows that the constant one third cannot be improved universally. A resolution would identify the sharp balance guarantee for a comparison in sorting with partial information.

title: Extremal size of sunflower-free set families
importance_reason: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
formal: For each fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), determine, up to constant factors as \(k\to \infty , S_{r}(k)\): the largest number of distinct k-element sets in a family containing no r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal, where the finite ground set is unrestricted.
definitions: The r members in a sunflower must be distinct. Their common pairwise intersection is the core, and deleting it leaves pairwise disjoint petals. For each integer \(k\ge 1\), take the maximum cardinality over all sunflower-free families on arbitrary finite universes. The classical sunflower bound makes these cardinalities bounded by an integer depending only on k,r, so the maximum exists despite the unrestricted universe. No algorithm or encoding bound is imposed. The parameter r is fixed before k grows; asymptotic constants may depend on r.
answer_criterion: Give functions \(f_{r}(k)\) and, for every fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), constants \(0<c_{r}\le C_{r}<\infty\) with \(c_{r} f_{r}(k)\le S_{r}(k)\le C_{r} f_{r}(k)\) for every \(k\ge 1\), absorbing finitely many small k into the constants if needed. Prove both a universal upper bound and existence of matching sunflower-free families in Lean. An exponential upper bound by itself does not determine the growth within constant factors.
context:
The target is the extremal function itself. The sunflower conjecture states that \(S_{r}(k)\) has at most exponential growth in k for each fixed r, a weaker qualitative question than matching its full asymptotic order.

Sunflowers capture a simple repeated pattern inside a large family of small sets. Bounds on their forced occurrence are basic tools in circuit complexity, pseudorandomness and kernelization.

The breakthrough bound of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang replaces a much larger dependence by roughly \((\log  k)^{O(k)}\) for fixed r. The conjecture asks for a constant base to the k-th power. This is admitted as a computationally motivated exception to the exclusion of general combinatorics, not to fill a combinatorics category.
why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2020: The source proves substantially improved bounds while leaving \(C_{r}^{k}\) open.
working_summary: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets with one common pairwise intersection. For fixed r, the target is the maximum size of a family of k-element sets containing no r-member sunflower. Determine its growth as k increases within constant factors that may depend on r. The ground set is any finite universe and the question imposes no algorithmic restrictions. The sunflower conjecture predicts at most exponential growth, a weaker claim than determining the full extremal order.
